The one failure is `cap_at_or_above_batch_size_is_ignored`, which already fails on macOS (#2922). - `RELEASE=1 pytest tests/test_e2e.py tests/test_functions.py`: 131 passed. - `cargo fmt --check` is clean, and clippy reports nothing in touched code. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) --- ## Summary by cubic Rejects query shapes the parser previously accepted and ran, matching C's syntax. Parenthesized `SET`/`REMOVE` targets now have to open a property lookup: `SET (n.x) = 5`, `SET (n) = {..}`, and `SET (n):L` / `REMOVE (n):L` are syntax errors instead of writes. Relationship types are parsed by a helper shared between patterns and `shortestPath` that joins alternatives only with `|` (optionally `|:`), so `[:A:B]` is rejected rather than read as `[:A|B]`. Valid spellings — `SET (n).x = 5`, `REMOVE (n).x`, `[:A|B]`, `[:A|:B]` — behave unchanged. Written for commit f8ff5fe9355ca06ec3d3a37cdc23423bb349d14f. Summary will update on new commits. ## Summary by CodeRabbit * **Query Validation** * Relationship-type alternatives joined by `|` are accepted, including the legacy `|:` form. Bare-colon-separated types are rejected, including in `shortestPath` relationships. * Parenthesized `SET` and `REMOVE` targets must be followed by a property lookup. Parenthesized whole-entity assignments, label updates, and property expressions are rejected. * Valid forms such as `(n).x` and `:A|:B` continue to work.

issues.title: [Rust] Parser accepts SET (n.x) = 5, SET (n) = {..}, SET/REMOVE (n):L and [:A:B] (C: syntax error)
issues.body:
### Summary

The parser accepts two things that are syntax errors in C and in openCypher, and runs them:

1. A parenthesized `SET`/`REMOVE` target that is not followed by a property lookup: `SET (n.x) = 5` sets `n.x`, `SET (n) = {..}` replaces the property map, `SET (n):L` adds a label and `REMOVE (n):L` removes it.
2. Relationship types joined by a bare `:`, as in `[:A:B]`, which is read as `[:A|B]`. An edge has exactly one type, so this shape is not in the grammar. The same applies inside `shortestPath(...)`.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ b033aecc6)

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE (:N {x: 1})"
GRAPH.QUERY g "MATCH (n) SET (n.x) = 5 RETURN n.x"     -> 5
GRAPH.QUERY g "MATCH (n) SET (n) = {a: 1}"             -> Properties set: 1, Properties removed: 1
GRAPH.QUERY g "MATCH (n) SET (n):L"                    -> Labels added: 1
GRAPH.QUERY g "MATCH (n) REMOVE (n):L"                 -> Labels removed: 1
GRAPH.QUERY g "MATCH ()-[:A:B]->() RETURN 1"           -> runs (as [:A|B])
GRAPH.QUERY g "MATCH (a),(b) RETURN shortestPath((a)-[:A:B*]->(b))" -> runs
```

C (`bin/macos-arm64v8-release/falkordb.so`):

```
SET (n.x) = 5      -> Invalid input '=': expected '.'
SET (n) = {a:1}    -> Invalid input '=': expected '<', '-' or '.'
SET (n):L          -> Invalid input ':': expected '<', '-' or '.'
REMOVE (n):L       -> Invalid input ':': expected '<', '-' or '.'
[:A:B], [r:A:B]    -> Invalid input ':': expected '|', '*', '{', a parameter or ']'
shortestPath((a)-[:A:B*]->(b)) -> same
```

`SET (n).x = 6`, `REMOVE (n).x` and `[:A|B]` / `[:A|:B]` are valid and work in both engines.

### Mechanism

- `parse_set_items` / `parse_remove_items` (`graph/src/parser/cypher.rs:3249-3263`, `3332-3337`): after a parenthesized target, the code goes on to the `=` / `+=` / `:` branches just as it would for a bare variable. It never requires the `.prop` that is the only reason to parenthesize.
- `parse_relationship_pattern` (~2990) and `parse_shortest_path_expr` (~1775): the type loop accepts `|` or `:` as the separator (`if pipe || colon { continue }`), so `A:B` joins like `A|B`.

### Expected

A syntax error, as C gives. Nothing written.

### Suggested fix

After a parenthesized target's `)`, require `.`. Parse the type list in one shared helper that takes `|` (optionally followed by the legacy `:`) as the only separator.

### Found by

Lean bug ledger, W4-parse-4.

issues.title: fix: refuse a GRAPH.EFFECT CREATE_NODE record that repeats a node id
issues.body: Closes #3247 ## Problem `apply_record` for `CREATE_NODE` turned the record's `IdList` into a `RoaringTreemap` and created that set. A repeated id was merged before anything could see it, so a client-sent `GRAPH.EFFECT` whose record names ids `[0, 0]` (count 2) created one node and replied `OK`. The label and attribute writes after it walk the list, not the set. `CREATE_EDGE` has refused the same shape since #2846 (`create_relationships_bulk`). ## Fix Before creating, compare the set's size with the record's id count. On a mismatch, refuse with the same wording as the edge path: `bulk node create got N ids of which only M are distinct; an id names one node`. The buffer is rejected and nothing is applied. | Record | Rust before | Rust after | C | |---|---|---|---| | `CREATE_NODE` ids `[0, 0]` on an empty graph | `OK`, 1 node | `effect apply failed: bulk node create got 2 ids of which only 1 are distinct; an id names one node`, 0 nodes | n/a: C reads effects only up to v2 (`version mismatch expected version <= 2 got: 3`) | | `CREATE_EDGE` ids `[1, 1]` | refused | refused (unchanged) | n/a | ## Tests - New unit test `effects::v3::apply::tests::a_repeated_node_id_in_one_create_is_refused`. - Before (with the check disabled): `expected a refusal, got Ok(())`. - After: `ok`. - New flow test `test_effects_wire.py:testEffects_01_UnreadableBuffer.test09_a_repeated_id_in_one_create_record_is_refused`. It sends a node record with ids `[2, 3, 2]` and an edge record with ids `[1, 1]`. It checks that both are refused, that there is no resync, that the graph is unchanged, and that the ids are still free for the next write. - Before: `AssertionError: a node id repeated was accepted; it must be refused`. - After: passes. - Flow suites (release): `test_effects_wire` 15/15, `test_effects_shapes` 22/22, `test_effects_opcodes` 12/12, `test_effects_batch` 4/4, `test_effects_commands` 7/7. - `RELEASE=1 pytest tests/test_e2e.py tests/test_functions.py`: 131 passed. `cargo test -p graph --lib`: all pass except the known macOS `cap_at_or_above_batch_size_is_ignored` (#2922). `fmt` and `clippy` are clean on the touched file. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) --- ## Summary by cubic Closes #3247. Refuses a `GRAPH.EFFECT CREATE_NODE` record that repeats a node id instead of silently creating one node, matching the refusal `CREATE_EDGE` has had since #2846. - Rejects the buffer with `bulk node create got N ids of which only M are distinct; an id names one node` and applies nothing. - Adds a Rust unit test and a flow test covering the refusal, no resync, unchanged graph, and freed ids for the next write. Written for commit ad9d88b3b1ff3a550bbc1858dcd998dc8559a0a9. Summary will update on new commits.

issues.title: fix: validate the clauses that follow a procedure CALL
issues.body: Closes #3279 ## Problem The `Call` arm of `QueryIR::inner_validate` (`graph/src/parser/ast.rs`) checked the procedure's own arguments and then returned `Ok(())`. It never validated the clauses after the `CALL`, so none of the usual checks ran there. A trailing `MATCH` reached the planner as the plan root and panicked in `utilize_node_by_id` (`parent().unwrap()` on `None`), which took the server down. ## Fix End the `Call` arm with `iter.next().map_or(Ok(()), |first| first.inner_validate(iter))`, as every other clause arm does. Graph: `CREATE (:N)`. | query | Rust before | Rust after | C | |---|---|---|---| | `CALL db.labels() YIELD label MATCH (n)` | **server crash** | Query cannot conclude with MATCH | same | | `CALL db.labels() YIELD label WITH label MATCH (n)` | **server crash** | Query cannot conclude with MATCH | same | | `CALL db.labels() YIELD label OPTIONAL MATCH (n)` | runs | Query cannot conclude with MATCH | same | | `CALL db.labels() YIELD label UNWIND [1] AS x` | runs | Query cannot conclude with UNWIND | same | | `CALL db.labels() YIELD label CREATE (a)-[:R\|S]->(b)` | creates an edge | Exactly one relationship type … CREATE pattern. | same | | `CALL db.labels() YIELD label MERGE (a)-[:R\|S]->(b)` | runs | Exactly one relationship type … MERGE pattern. | same | | `CALL db.labels() YIELD label MATCH (n) RETURN label, labels(n)` | rows | rows | **C crashes (SIGSEGV)** | ## Tests New flow test `test_procedures.py::test13_clauses_after_call_are_validated`. Before the fix (`main` @ b033aecc6) the server dies: `redis.exceptions.ConnectionError: Connection closed by server. … process is not alive`. After the fix: `[PASS]`. Also run: the whole flow suite (124 files, without replication/persistency/defrag/bulk/cluster). Everything passes except `test_effects_ddl::test02_a_drop_during_validation_is_not_resurrected`, which fails on `main` too. Also: TCK (`TCK_DONE`: 2456 scenarios passed, 0 failed), `tests/test_e2e.py tests/test_functions.py` (131 passed), `cargo test -p graph --lib` (only the known macOS failure `cap_at_or_above_batch_size_is_ignored`, #2922), `cargo fmt --check`, and no clippy warnings in the touched code. Validation-only change. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) --- ## Summary by cubic Fixes validation of clauses that follow a procedure `CALL` so they receive the same checks as anywhere else in a query. Previously, `CALL db.labels() YIELD label MATCH (n)` reached the planner and crashed the server, and trailing `UNWIND` or `CREATE`/`MERGE` with two relationship types also slipped through. - The `Call` arm in `inner_validate` now continues validating subsequent clauses like every other clause arm. - Adds a flow test covering invalid trailing clauses after a `CALL` and confirms valid queries still run. Closes #3279 Written for commit 694c1f440129846910ff8e777ff714537995185a. Summary will update on new commits.

issues.title: [Rust] Property filter on a var-length relationship after WITH r is a type error; C pushes it into the traversal and returns rows — needs decision
issues.body:
### Summary

A property filter on a variable-length relationship works directly after `MATCH` on both engines, because the optimizer moves it into the traversal as a per-edge filter. After a pass-through `WITH r`, C still moves it there and returns rows. Rust evaluates `r.w` on the bound value, which is a `Path`, and fails with a type error. **This needs a decision**, because C's answer comes from an optimizer rewrite rather than from the expression's meaning: openCypher, and both engines' own `RETURN r.w`, treat `r.w` on a var-length `r` as a type error.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ b033aecc6)

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE (:A)-[:R {w:1}]->(:B)-[:R {w:2}]->(:C)"
```

| query | Rust | C |
|---|---|---|
| `MATCH ()-[r*1..2]->() WHERE r.w = 1 RETURN count(*)` | `1` | `1` |
| `MATCH ()-[r*1..2]->() WITH r WHERE r.w = 1 RETURN count(*)` | `Type mismatch: expected Map, Node, Edge, … but was Path` | `1` |
| `MATCH ()-[r*1..2]->() WITH r, 1 AS k WHERE r.w = 1 RETURN count(*)` | type error | `1` |
| `MATCH ()-[r*1..2]->() WITH r ORDER BY size(r) WHERE r.w = 1 RETURN count(*)` | type error | type error (`size` of a Path) |
| `MATCH ()-[r*1..2]->() WITH r RETURN r.w` | type error | type error |
| `MATCH ()-[r*1..2]->() WHERE all(e IN r WHERE e.w = 1) RETURN count(*)` | `Type mismatch: expected List but was Path` | `Type mismatch: expected List or Null but was Edge` |

C's `1` is the path whose every edge has `w = 1`, which is the per-edge filter semantics, and the same answer both engines give without the `WITH`.

### Mechanism

`absorb_edge_filters_into_vlt` (`graph/src/planner/optimizer/absorb_edge_filters_into_vlt.rs`) absorbs a conjunct that reads only the edge alias into `CondVarLenTraverse.edge_filter`, but only when the `Filter` sits directly above the traversal. A `WITH r` (a `Project`) in between stops the absorption, so the filter evaluates `r.w` on the `Path` value. C's filter placement sees through a projection that only passes `r` along.

### Options

1. **Match C.** Let the absorption look through `Project`s that pass the alias through unchanged (no ordering, aggregation, `DISTINCT`, `SKIP`/`LIMIT` that depends on rows). This adds an optimizer case, and the result of the query depends on an optimization firing, as it already does without the `WITH`.
2. **Keep the type error.** It is consistent with `RETURN r.w` on both engines and with openCypher. Document that per-edge property predicates on a var-length relationship must sit in the `MATCH … WHERE` directly or in the pattern (`[r*1..2 {w:1}]`).
3. **Make the openCypher form work instead.** `all(e IN r WHERE e.w = 1)` fails on both engines today, because a var-length `r` is a `Path` and not a list of relationships. Accepting a `Path` as a list of its relationships in list contexts would give users a correct way to write this, independent of filter placement.

Recommendation: option 2 for the `WITH` case, plus option 3, which is a real conformance gap on both engines. Option 1 extends a semantics that differs from what `r.w` means everywhere else.

issues.title: [Rust] Temporal map constructors treat null/string components as absent and truncate floats (date({year:2020, month:null}) -> 2020-01-01; C: error) — needs decision
issues.body:
### Summary

The map forms of `date`, `localtime`, `localdatetime` and `duration` do not validate their components. A component that is `null` or a string is treated as absent, a float is truncated, and an unknown key is ignored. C rejects every one of these. A key the user wrote with a bad value therefore quietly becomes a default: `date({year:2020, month:null})` returns `2020-01-01`. **This needs a design decision**, because the fast path cannot currently tell an absent key from a null one (see Mechanism).

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ b033aecc6)

| query | Rust | C |
|---|---|---|
| `RETURN date({year:2020, month:null})` | `2020-01-01` | `month must be an integer value` |
| `WITH {year:2020, month:null} AS m RETURN date(m)` | `2020-01-01` | `month must be an integer value` |
| `RETURN date({year:'2020'})` | `1970-01-01` | `year must be an integer value` |
| `RETURN date({year:2020, month:1.5})` | `2020-01-01` | `month must be an integer value` |
| `RETURN date({year:2020, month:2.0})` | `2020-02-01` | `month must be an integer value` |
| `RETURN localtime({hour:null})` | `00:00:00` | `hour must be an integer value` |
| `RETURN localtime({hour:1.5})` | `01:00:00` | `hour must be an integer value` |
| `RETURN localdatetime({year:2020, hour:null})` | `2020-01-01T00:00:00` | `hour must be an integer value` |
| `RETURN date({year:2020, foo:5})` | `2020-01-01` | `datetime components map contains an unknown key` |
| `RETURN duration({days:null})` | `PT0S` | `days must be a numerical value` |
| `RETURN duration({days:'1'})` | `PT0S` | `days must be a numerical value` |
| `RETURN duration({days:1.5})` | `P1D` | `P1DT12H` |

### Mechanism

- Map path: `get_int_field` (`graph/src/runtime/functions/temporal.rs:50`) returns `None`, meaning absent, for any non-numeric value and truncates floats. `duration_pure` (`:556`) skips non-numeric values with `continue` and truncates floats with `as i64`. Unknown keys are never checked.
- Positional fast path: `rewrite_struct_constructor` (`graph/src/planner/binder.rs:2499`) rewrites a map literal with constant keys into one argument per slot, and **missing slots receive `Constant(Null)`**. `slot_to_int` (`temporal.rs:138`) then cannot distinguish an absent key from `month: null` or `month: $p` with `$p = null`. The rewrite already declines maps with unknown keys, but those fall back to the map path, which ignores them.

### Expected

As C: date and time components must be integers (`<key> must be an integer value`), duration components must be numbers and fractional values carry over into the smaller units (`days:1.5` → `P1DT12H`), and an unknown key is an error.

### Options

1. **Presence mask on the fast path.** The binder appends one constant `Int` child holding a bitmask of the slots the map actually wrote. The struct functions validate exactly those slots and default only the others. This is cheap per row and keeps the fast path, but each struct function signature gets one more slot, and the stack array in `eval.rs` grows from 10 to 11.
2. **Drop the rewrite when a present value is not provably numeric** (`Constant(Int)`, or an expression typed Integer/Float), so that the validated map path handles those calls. This is simpler, but `date({year: n.y, month: n.m})` (property reads with unknown types) would lose the fast path.
3. **A distinct "absent" marker value for missing slots.** `Value` has no spare variant, so this means adding one, which is invasive.

Recommendation: option 1, and validate the map path in the same change: a shared `int_component(map, key) -> Result<Option<i64>, String>` with C's messages, an unknown-key check, and fractional carry for `duration`. Related: #2585 covers the sub-second keys (`millisecond`, `microsecond`, `nanosecond`) that are dropped today.

issues.title: fix: AND/OR/XOR type mismatches name the operand's type like C
issues.body: Closes #3292 ## Problem When an `AND`/`OR`/`XOR` operand was not a boolean at runtime, the error printed the value in Rust's `Debug` form (`Type mismatch: expected Bool but was Int(3)`) and not its type. C, and Rust's own `NOT`, name the type. ## Fix The four messages (the `And`/`Or`/`Xor` arms in `eval.rs` and the vectorized connective in `vector_expr.rs`) now use `Value::name()` and C's wording for projections. | query | Rust `main` | this PR | C | |---|---|---|---| | `UNWIND [3] AS x RETURN x AND true` | `Type mismatch: expected Bool but was Int(3)` | `Type mismatch: expected Boolean or Null but was Integer` | same as this PR | | `UNWIND [3] AS x RETURN x OR false` | `… Bool but was Int(3)` | `… Boolean or Null but was Integer` | same as this PR | | `UNWIND [3] AS x RETURN x XOR true` | `… Bool but was Int(3)` | `… Boolean or Null but was Integer` | same as this PR | | `UNWIND ['a'] AS x RETURN x AND true` | `… Bool but was String("a")` | `… Boolean or Null but was String` | same as this PR | In a `WHERE` filter, C says `expected Boolean but was Integer` without "or Null". The evaluator does not know whether it is running a filter or a projection, so it uses the projection wording that `NOT` already uses. Whether `AND`/`OR` should short-circuit at all is a separate question, tracked in #3293 (needs decision), and this PR does not change it. ## Tests - New e2e test `test_boolean_operator_type_mismatch_names_the_type` covering the four queries above. - Before: `AssertionError: assert 'Type mismatch: expected Boolean or Null but was Integer' in 'Type mismatch: expected Bool but was Int(3)'` - After: passes. `pytest tests/test_e2e.py tests/test_functions.py`: 132 passed. - `cargo test -p graph --lib`: all pass except the known `cap_at_or_above_batch_size_is_ignored` (#2922). `cargo fmt --check` passes, and clippy reports no warnings in the touched files. - Flow tests (RLTest, release): `test_filters` 9/9, `test_query_validation` 51/51. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) --- ## Summary by cubic Fixes the error messages in AND/OR/XOR runtime type checks so they name the offending operand's type instead of printing its Rust `Debug` form. Messages now read `Type mismatch: expected Boolean or Null but was Integer` instead of `Type mismatch: expected Bool but was Int(3)`, matching C's wording and what `NOT` already emits. - Applies to the four scalar/vectorized connective paths in `eval.rs` and `vector_expr.rs`. - Since the evaluator can't tell a filter from a projection, WHERE clauses also get the "or Null" wording, which differs from C's filter message. - Leaves the separate short-circuit question (#3293) unchanged. - Adds an e2e test covering the four operator/operand combinations. Written for commit 1ef929506e53efd26cebe36409199f1e0dd03e8f. Summary will update on new commits.

issues.title: [Rust] AND/OR short-circuit in projections where C evaluates every operand (false AND (1+2) -> false; C: type error) — needs decision
issues.body:
### Summary

Rust short-circuits `AND`/`OR` everywhere. C short-circuits only in `WHERE` filters. In a projection, C evaluates every operand, so a non-boolean operand or an error on the side that is not needed still fails the query. As a result, the same expression is a type error, or `Division by zero`, on C and a value on Rust. **This needs a decision.**

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ b033aecc6)

| query | Rust | C |
|---|---|---|
| `RETURN false AND (1+2)` | `false` | `Type mismatch: expected Boolean or Null but was Integer` |
| `UNWIND [3] AS x RETURN false AND x` | `false` | `Type mismatch: … but was Integer` |
| `UNWIND [3] AS x RETURN true OR x` | `true` | `Type mismatch: … but was Integer` |
| `UNWIND [0] AS x RETURN x <> 0 AND 10/x > 1` | `false` | `Division by zero` |
| `UNWIND [0] AS x WITH x WHERE x <> 0 AND 10/x > 1 RETURN 1` | no rows | no rows (C short-circuits in `WHERE`) |
| `UNWIND [3] AS x WITH x WHERE false AND x RETURN 1` | no rows | no rows |
| `RETURN false AND 1` (literal) | bind-time `Type mismatch: expected Boolean` | type error |

`(x AND false)` with a non-boolean `x` on the left fails on both engines.

### Mechanism

`graph/src/runtime/eval.rs:629-697` and `graph/src/runtime/vector_expr.rs:~440` stop at the first deciding operand. The binder's static check (`validate_boolean_operands`, `graph/src/planner/binder.rs:2279`) rejects only literal non-boolean operands, so `(1+2)` and variables get through. C's projection evaluator (`AR_EXP_Evaluate`) evaluates every argument of `AND`/`OR`/`XOR` and type-checks them before applying the operator. Its filter tree (`FilterTree`) short-circuits.

### Expected / options

1. **Match C exactly.** Evaluate every operand in projections and short-circuit only in filters. This costs a full evaluation in projections, and the evaluator has to know whether it is in a projection or a filter.
2. **Keep short-circuiting and type-check the operands that are evaluated (current behaviour).** This is what Neo4j and most engines do, it is cheaper, and errors that guards are meant to prevent cannot fire, as in `x <> 0 AND 10/x > 1`. The difference from C stays, but only for queries that C rejects.
3. **Short-circuit, but type-check every operand statically where its type is known at bind time.** For example, `(1+2)` is known to be an Integer. This catches the constant cases C catches, without evaluating anything extra.

Recommendation: option 2, plus option 3 for the constant-foldable cases. Short-circuiting is what lets the guard pattern `x <> 0 AND 10/x > 1` work in projections. Rust already behaves like C's filters everywhere, and the only queries that change between the options are ones that C rejects.

issues.title: [Rust] AND/OR/XOR type-mismatch errors print Rust Debug values (Int(3)) instead of the type
issues.body:
### Summary

When an `AND`/`OR`/`XOR` operand is not a boolean at runtime, the error message prints the value in Rust's `Debug` form (`Int(3)`, `String("a")`) and not its type. C, and Rust's own `NOT`, name the type.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ b033aecc6)

| query | Rust | C |
|---|---|---|
| `UNWIND [3] AS x RETURN x AND true` | `Type mismatch: expected Bool but was Int(3)` | `Type mismatch: expected Boolean or Null but was Integer` |
| `UNWIND [3] AS x RETURN x OR false` | `… expected Bool but was Int(3)` | `… expected Boolean or Null but was Integer` |
| `UNWIND [3] AS x RETURN x XOR true` | `… expected Bool but was Int(3)` | `… expected Boolean or Null but was Integer` |
| `UNWIND ['a'] AS x RETURN x AND true` | `… expected Bool but was String("a")` | `… expected Boolean or Null but was String` |
| `UNWIND range(1,5) AS x WITH x WHERE (x > 0) AND x RETURN x` | `… expected Bool but was Int(1)` | `… expected Boolean but was Integer` |

### Mechanism

`graph/src/runtime/eval.rs:642, 666, 687` (the `Or`/`Xor`/`And` arms) and `graph/src/runtime/vector_expr.rs:457` format the value with `{:?}`. The `Not` arm next to them already uses `v.name()`.

### Expected

`Type mismatch: expected Boolean or Null but was <type>`, as C gives for projections and as `NOT` already reports.

### Suggested fix

Use `name()` in those four messages.

issues.title: fix: reject a query that ends with WITH
issues.body: Closes #3271 ## Problem `QueryIR::inner_validate` (`graph/src/parser/ast.rs`) handled `With` in the same arm as `Return`, so it accepted `WITH` as the last clause of a query or of a `CALL { … }` body. `MATCH (n) WITH n` returned the projection as the result set, and `CREATE (a) WITH a` ran its write. ## Fix Give `With` its own arm, which returns `Query cannot conclude with WITH (must be a RETURN clause, an update clause, a procedure call or a non-returning subquery)` when no clause follows. This is the same shape the `Match` and `Unwind` arms already use, and the same message as C. | query | Rust before | Rust after | C | |---|---|---|---| | `MATCH (n) WITH n` | returns every node | cannot conclude with WITH | cannot conclude with WITH | | `UNWIND [1] AS x WITH x` | `[[1]]` | error | error | | `WITH 1 AS x` | `[[1]]` | error | error | | `CREATE (a) WITH a` | creates the node | error, nothing created | error | | `MATCH (n) CALL { WITH n MATCH (m) WITH m } RETURN 1` | runs | error | error | | `MATCH (n) CALL { WITH n } RETURN 1` | runs | error | error | | `WITH 1 AS x RETURN x`, `MATCH (n) CALL { WITH n CREATE (:X) } RETURN 1` | run | run | run | A trailing `WITH` after a procedure `CALL` is still accepted until #3279 is fixed, because nothing after a `CALL` is validated yet. ## Tests New flow test `test_query_validation.py::test52_query_cannot_conclude_with_with`. Before the fix (`main` @ b033aecc6): ``` ❌ (FAIL): False == True [MATCH (n) WITH n] ❌ (FAIL): False == True [UNWIND [1] AS x WITH x] ❌ (FAIL): False == True [WITH 1 AS x] ❌ (FAIL): False == True [CREATE (a) WITH a] ❌ (FAIL): False == True [MATCH (n) CALL { WITH n MATCH (m) WITH m } RETURN 1] ❌ (FAIL): False == True [MATCH (n) CALL { WITH n } RETURN 1] ❌ (FAIL): [[1]] == [[0]] ``` After: `[PASS]`. Also run: the whole flow suite (124 files, without replication/persistency/defrag/bulk/cluster). Everything passes except `test_effects_ddl::test02_a_drop_during_validation_is_not_resurrected`, which fails on `main` too. Also: TCK (`TCK_DONE`: 2456 scenarios passed, 0 failed), `tests/test_e2e.py tests/test_functions.py` (131 passed), `cargo test -p graph --lib` (only the known macOS failure `cap_at_or_above_batch_size_is_ignored`, #2922), `cargo fmt --check`, and no clippy warnings in the touched code. Validation-only change. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) --- ## Summary by cubic Fixes query validation so a query or `CALL { … }` body can no longer end with `WITH`, matching the behavior C already has. - Previously, `MATCH (n) WITH n` returned the projection as the result set and `CREATE (a) WITH a` ran its write; both now error with "Query cannot conclude with WITH". - Adds a flow test covering rejected and still-valid queries, including confirming a rejected `CREATE` did not execute. Written for commit f1a98a9d4d9c8418c1e2d5cf7f997a586fa95733. Summary will update on new commits.

issues.title: fix: an inline write no longer fails while a queued write is matching
issues.body: Closes #3093 ## Problem A queued write claimed `MvccGraph`'s write slot (a CAS) as soon as it started, while it was still a reader matching without the GIL. An inline writer that ran in that window (`MULTI/EXEC`, Lua, `GRAPH.EFFECT`, anything on the main thread) took the GIL and the write lock, found the slot taken, and failed with `another write is in progress, retry the query`. Its write was lost. It could not wait instead, because the queued writer cannot escalate until the inline writer releases the GIL. C commits the inline write. ## Fix This is option A from the issue: claim the slot at escalation. - `MvccGraph::fork` makes a private version without claiming the slot. `MvccGraph::claim(fork)` claims it and checks that the fork still extends the committed version (`Claim::Busy` / `Claim::Stale`). `write()` is unchanged (claim + fork) for writers that already hold the write lock. - `QuerySession::write_version` hands a reader session an unclaimed fork. A writer session claims immediately. `upgrade_to_write` claims the fork right after escalating, under the GIL and the write lock. So the slot is only ever held by a thread that holds the write lock, and an inline writer never finds it taken. - If an inline writer committed while the query was matching, the claim reports `Stale`. At that point nothing has been mutated in shared state, no index document has been published, and nothing has been replied, so the query is dropped and run again from the start: - `execute_query_write` (GRAPH.QUERY / GRAPH.PROFILE) loops on a fresh session. - `GRAPH.BULK` rebuilds its fork. - `GRAPH.RECORD` (debug) reports the error. - `abandon_write` and `finish_write` release the slot only if this session claimed it (`QuerySession::release_slot`). `MULTI; GRAPH.QUERY mr "CREATE (:M)"; EXEC` sent 0.3 s after a queued `UNWIND range(1,40000000) AS x WITH count(x) AS c CREATE (:N {c:c})` (release build): | | MULTI reply | final counts | |---|---|---| | Rust before (`main` @ b033aecc6) | `another write is in progress, retry the query` (2/2 runs) | `N=1, Seed=1`, **M missing** | | Rust after | `Labels added: 1, Nodes created: 1` (3/3 runs) | `M=1, N=1, Seed=1` | | C (`bin/macos-arm64v8-release`) | `Labels added: 1, Nodes created: 1` | `M=1, N=1, Seed=1` (C also crashed on 2 of 3 runs of this race, a separate C bug, as noted in the issue) | The queued write still commits exactly once (`N=1`). ## Tests - New flow test `test_multi_exec.py::test_write_while_queued_write_matches`. It runs MULTI while a queued write is matching and asserts that the inline write commits, that the queued write commits exactly once, and that the two really overlapped. - Before: `FAIL True == False [another write is in progress, retry the query]` and `[['N', 1], ['Seed', 1]] == [['M', 1], ['N', 1], ['Seed', 1]]`. - After: PASS. - `tests/test_concurrency.py::_multi_write` no longer swallows `another write is in progress`. A MULTI write under concurrent queued-write load must now succeed. - New unit test `mvcc_graph::tests::a_fork_is_claimed_late_and_refused_once_stale`. - Also run: - `cargo fmt --check` and `cargo clippy` (no new warnings in touched code). - `cargo test --release -p graph --lib` (497 passed). - Flow suites, all pass: `test_multi_exec`, `test_bulk_insertion`, `test_concurrent_query`, `test_constraint`, `test_multi_writer`, `test_pause_replication_race`, `test_effects_commit`, `test_replication`. - `pytest tests/test_e2e.py tests/test_functions.py tests/test_mvcc.py tests/test_concurrency.py` (145 passed). Not hot-path: a queued write makes the same single `new_version()` as before. Only the CAS moves, from the start of the query to escalation. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) --- ## Summary by cubic Fixes #3093, where an inline write (e.g., inside MULTI/EXEC) failed with "another write is in progress" and lost its changes when it ran while a queued write was still matching. A queued write now builds into an unclaimed fork and claims the MVCC write slot only when it escalates under the write lock, so an inline writer never finds the slot taken. If an inline writer commits during matching, the queued write discards its fork and re-runs from the start. **Behavior** - GRAPH.RECORD returns a retryable error on a stale fork instead of retrying. - The write slot is only held by threads that hold the write lock. Written for commit ad2925117a40fdb47325867c5e9238c0d4feb0e0. Summary will update on new commits.

issues.title: fix: reject a relationship variable repeated in a named-path CREATE or a MERGE
issues.body: Closes #3287 ## Problem A relationship variable repeated inside one `CREATE` or `MERGE` pattern was dropped instead of rejected whenever the pattern had a path variable, and in every `MERGE`. The query created one edge where it wrote two. `CREATE ... RETURN p, q` also returned a `q` whose edge did not connect its nodes. `parse_pattern` checked the result of `QueryGraph::add_relationship` in four places, with different rules. The named-path and `allShortestPaths` branches only errored for `MATCH`, and the plain-path branch only for `MATCH` and `CREATE`. ## Fix All four call sites now go through a new `Parser::add_pattern_relationship`. It turns a repeat into the clause's error for every clause, using C's wording for `MERGE`. | Query | Rust before | Rust after | C | |---|---|---|---| | `CREATE p=(a)-[r:R]->(b), q=(c)-[r:R]->(d) RETURN p, q` | 4 nodes, 1 rel; `q = [(2), [0], (3)]` | `The bound variable 'r' can't be redeclared in a CREATE clause` | ``Variable `r` already declared`` | | `MERGE (a)-[r:R]->(b)-[r:R]->(c)` | 3 nodes, 1 rel | `The bound variable 'r' can't be redeclared in a MERGE clause` | same | | `MERGE p=(a)-[r:R]->(b)-[r:R]->(c)` | `Variable a not found` | `The bound variable 'r' can't be redeclared in a MERGE clause` | same | | `CREATE ()-[r:R]->()-[r:R]->()` | redeclared error | unchanged | error | ## Tests - `parser::cypher::tests::repeated_relationship_variable_is_rejected` covers six shapes (CREATE/MERGE/MATCH, with and without a path variable). Against the `main` parser it fails on the first silent shape (`CREATE p=..., q=...`: `left: None`). With this PR it passes. - Flow: `test_create_clause::test02_edge_reuse` gets the two named-path CREATE shapes, and `test_graph_merge::test31b_relationship_alias_redeclared` is new. On the `main` module they fail (`test_create_clause.py:58`, `test_graph_merge.py:633`). With this PR they pass: test_create_clause 8/8, test_graph_merge 39/39, test_graph_create 10/10, test_query_validation 51/51, test_path_filter 19/19. - `cargo test -p graph --lib`: 496 passed. The one failure is `cap_at_or_above_batch_size_is_ignored`, which already fails on macOS (#2922). - `RELEASE=1 pytest tests/test_e2e.py tests/test_functions.py`: 131 passed. - `cargo fmt --check` is clean, and clippy reports nothing in touched code. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) --- ## Summary by cubic Rejects a relationship variable repeated inside one `CREATE` or `MERGE` pattern instead of silently dropping the repeat. Closes #3287. - Previously, named-path `CREATE` patterns and all `MERGE` patterns created one edge where the query wrote two; only plain-path `MATCH` and `CREATE` raised an error. - All four `parse_pattern` call sites now route through `add_pattern_relationship`, which errors for every clause with a clause-specific message, with `MERGE` matching C's wording. - Adds unit and flow tests covering plain and named path shapes for `CREATE`, `MERGE`, and `MATCH`. Written for commit 9e3c117ac09b2a5b65441d5a614f576e452fbc5f. Summary will update on new commits.

issues.title: fix: a deleted node keeps labels set or removed earlier in the same query
issues.body: Closes #3245 ## Problem The project rule for Rust is that a node deleted by a query keeps all its details for the rest of the query. `DeleteOp` snapshotted a committed node's labels with `g.get_node_label_ids(id)`, which reads the committed label matrix. The attributes beside them already came from the pending view. So labels the same query set or removed before the `DELETE` were lost, and `labels(n)` / `n:L` answered from the committed labels. Both snapshot sites had this: `delete_nodes_bulk` (`DELETE n`) and `delete_entity` (`DELETE `, e.g. `coalesce(n)` or a path). ## Fix A new `staged_label_ids` overlays the query's staged adds/removes (`Pending::staged_node_labels`, which `update_node_labels` now uses too) on the committed label ids, and both snapshot sites use it. The snapshot is still collected straight into the `HashSet` that `DeletedNode` holds, so there is no extra allocation per node. | Query | Rust before | Rust after | C | |---|---|---|---| | `MATCH (n:A) SET n:C DELETE n RETURN labels(n), n:C` | `[A], false` | `[A, C], true` | `[], false` | | `MATCH (n:A) REMOVE n:A DELETE n RETURN labels(n), n:A` | `[A], true` | `[], false` | `[], false` | | same two with `DELETE coalesce(n)` | `[A], false` / `[A], true` | `[A, C], true` / `[], false` | `[], false` | C returns no labels at all for a deleted node. The "after" column follows the Rust rule (a deleted entity keeps all its details), not C. ## Tests - New flow test `test_access_del_entity.py:testAccessDelNode.test10_deleted_node_keeps_labels_staged_in_the_same_query`. It covers both delete paths (`n` and `coalesce(n)`), a staged `SET` and a staged `REMOVE`, and checks that nothing staged on the deleted node reaches the graph. - Before the fix: 6 assertion failures, e.g. `['A'] == ['A', 'C']` and `[['B', 'A'], True, True] == [['B'], False, True]`, on both paths. - After: passes. - Flow suites (release): `test_access_del_entity` 19/19, `test_results` 18/18, `test_graph_deletion` 45/45, `test_index_delete` 14/14, `test_label_update` 6/6, `test_mix_labels` 9/9, `test_multi_label` 12/12, `test_effects_batch` 4/4. - `RELEASE=1 pytest tests/test_e2e.py tests/test_functions.py`: 131 passed. `cargo test -p graph --lib`: all pass except the known macOS `cap_at_or_above_batch_size_is_ignored` (#2922). `fmt` and `clippy` are clean on the touched files. - Cost, measured on `MATCH (n:A) DELETE n RETURN count(labels(n))` over 200k `:A:B` nodes, which takes the snapshot path (median of 7 runs; the machine was at load ~20-45, so the numbers are noisy): | build | run 1 | run 2 | best single run | |---|---|---|---| | `main` | 209 ms | 158 ms | 154 ms | | this PR | 173 ms | 163 ms | 157 ms | | C | 120 ms | | 116 ms | No measurable change from `main`. The gap to C is older than this PR, and C keeps no labels for a deleted node. Separate and older than this PR: `DeletedNode.labels` is a `std::collections::HashSet`, so the *order* of a deleted node's labels is random between runs (`['B', 'A']` vs `['A', 'B']` in the failure output above). That is why the test sorts them. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) --- ## Summary by cubic Fixes deleted nodes losing labels that were set or removed earlier in the same query. The snapshot now overlays the query's staged label changes on the committed labels, so `labels(n)` and `n:L` reflect the node's state at the `DELETE`. - Uses a new `staged_label_ids` helper that reuses the same staging logic as live nodes; applied to both the bulk `DELETE n` and per-entity `DELETE ` paths without extra allocation per node. - Adds a flow test covering both delete paths and staged `SET`/`REMOVE` cases, ensuring staged changes don't leak into the graph. Written for commit 156912daa326add51baeee8e8081feb69644eb86. Summary will update on new commits.

issues.title: [Rust] A relationship variable repeated in a named-path CREATE or any MERGE pattern is silently dropped (C: already declared)
issues.body:
### Summary

A relationship variable repeated inside one `CREATE` or `MERGE` pattern is silently dropped instead of rejected, in every shape that goes through the named-path branch of `parse_pattern`, and in every `MERGE`. The query succeeds, creates one relationship where it wrote two, and (for `CREATE ... RETURN p, q`) returns a second path whose edge does not connect its nodes. C rejects all of these.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ b033aecc6)

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE p=(a)-[r:R]->(b), q=(c)-[r:R]->(d) RETURN p, q"
1) "p", "q"
2) "[(0), [0], (1)]", "[(2), [0], (3)]"      -- q claims edge 0 runs 2->3
   Nodes created: 4, Relationships created: 1

GRAPH.QUERY g2 "MERGE (a)-[r:R]->(b)-[r:R]->(c)"
   Nodes created: 3, Relationships created: 1
```

C (`bin/macos-arm64v8-release/falkordb.so`):

```
CREATE p=(a)-[r:R]->(b), q=(c)-[r:R]->(d) RETURN p, q  -> Variable `r` already declared
MERGE (a)-[r:R]->(b)-[r:R]->(c)                        -> The bound variable 'r' can't be redeclared in a MERGE clause
MERGE p=(a)-[r:R]->(b)-[r:R]->(c)                      -> The bound variable 'r' can't be redeclared in a MERGE clause
```

Without a path variable, `CREATE ()-[r:R]->()-[r:R]->()` is already rejected on `main`.

### Mechanism

`QueryGraph::add_relationship` (`graph/src/parser/ast.rs:733`) returns `false` and keeps the first relationship when the alias is already there. `parse_pattern` (`graph/src/parser/cypher.rs`) checks that result in four places with different rules:

- named path (`p = ...`, ~1513) and the two `allShortestPaths` branches: error only for `MATCH`; `CREATE` and `MERGE` fall through and the repeat is dropped;
- plain path (~1534): error for `MATCH` and `CREATE`; `MERGE` falls through.

### Expected

The same error C gives, for every path shape and clause; nothing created.

### Suggested fix

Route all four call sites through one helper that turns a `false` from `add_relationship` into the clause's error (`Cannot use the same relationship variable ...` for MATCH, `The bound variable 'r' can't be redeclared in a CREATE/MERGE clause` otherwise).

### Found by

Lean bug ledger, W4-parse-2 and W4-parse-3 (same mechanism, filed together).

issues.title: fix: virtual keys of one graph can no longer share a name
issues.body: Closes #3284 ## Problem `uuid_v4` names the virtual keys that a large graph is split into during an RDB save. It mixed the clock and a per-process counter as `a = t ^ seq` and derived every printed field from `a`. Two calls whose clock and counter changed in the same bits got the same name (`4 ^ 2 == 5 ^ 3`). The second `vkey_map.insert` then replaced the first virtual key, and that slice of the graph was missing from the save. ## Fix The mixing now lives in `const fn uuid_fields(t, seq)`, and the clock and the counter go in separate fields. The first three fields come from `t`, and the last 48 bits come from `seq * K + C` with `K` odd, which is a bijection modulo 2^48. Two calls in one process therefore always get different names, whatever the clock does, and the clock still separates names across restarts. The name keeps its UUID shape and its `{graph}graph_` key format. | calls | Rust `main` | this PR | C | |---|---|---|---| | `t=4, seq=2` vs `t=5, seq=3` | same name | different names | random UUID (`UUID_New`), no collision | | same `t`, consecutive `seq` | different | different | different | ## Tests This crate's unit tests cannot run outside Redis, because its global allocator is Redis's (`cargo test -p falkordb-rs` aborts with "the Redis Allocator isn't available"). The regression check is therefore a compile-time `const` assertion next to the function, and it runs in every build: - Before the fix, with the old `t ^ seq` mixing extracted unchanged into `uuid_fields`: `error[E0080]: evaluation panicked: virtual key names collide for (t=4, seq=2) and (t=5, seq=3)` - After: the build succeeds. The collision was not reproduced live because it depends on timing. On macOS the clock has microsecond resolution, so consecutive calls cannot collide there. On Linux, two calls exactly 1 ns apart can. - Flow tests (RLTest, release): `test_encode_decode` 19/19 (multi-key saves), `test_rdb_load` 2/2, `test_graph_copy` 9/9, `test_replication_states` 1/1. - `pytest tests/test_e2e.py tests/test_functions.py`: 131 passed. `cargo fmt --check` passes, and clippy reports no warnings in `redis_type.rs`. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) --- ## Summary by cubic Fixes a collision in virtual key naming that could drop a slice of a graph from RDB saves. `uuid_v4` mixed the clock and the call counter with XOR, so two calls whose clock and counter shifted in the same bits produced identical names, and the second virtual key replaced the first. The clock and counter now occupy separate fields, and a compile-time assertion prevents the colliding pair. Written for commit 55d4ca549c968200037e367d664cce185e74850a. Summary will update on new commits.

issues.title: fix: CowBTree rejects DOC_BYTES widths it cannot read back
issues.body: Closes #3238 ## Problem `CowBTree`'s const assert accepted `DOC_BYTES ∈ 1..=8`, but the doc field is read back with `read_width`, which loads only 1/2/4/8 bytes and treats any other width as 8. `CowBTree::<256, 256, 3>` compiled and panicked on its second insert. Latent: the only production instantiation (numeric index) uses `DOC_BYTES = 8`. Different from the two CowBTree bugs in #2893 / #2897; found by the Lean model of #2278 (`LeafAosD.docBytes3_*`). ## Fix The smaller of the two options in the issue: a `const fn is_read_width(width) -> bool { matches!(width, 1 | 2 | 4 | 8) }` next to `read_width`, used by the three const asserts (`Default`, `new`, `from_sorted`), so the accepted set is defined by the reader. Supporting 3/5/6/7 would need a variable-length load in the hot read path for no current user. Compile-time only; no runtime code changes. | `CowBTree::<256, 256, 3>::new()` then two `insert`s | Result | |---|---| | Rust before | compiles; 2nd insert panics — debug: `assertion left == right failed` (`mod.rs:98`); release: `range end index 16 out of range for slice of length 11` (`mod.rs:99`) | | Rust after | compile error: `DOC_BYTES must be 1, 2, 4 or 8: it is the AoS doc field width, read back with read_width, which loads only those widths` | | C | n/a (no equivalent structure) | ## Tests - `doc_bytes_accepts_exactly_the_readable_widths`: `is_read_width` over `0..=16` accepts exactly `[1, 2, 4, 8]`, and `read_width` round-trips each accepted width. (On main the gate was inline `1..=8` and would have accepted 3/5/6/7; the old repro above panicked at runtime on main @ b033aecc6 and is a compile error after.) - `cargo test -p graph --lib cow_btree` 34 passed; `cargo test -p graph --lib` 496 passed, 1 failed (pre-existing `cap_at_or_above_batch_size_is_ignored`, #2922). fmt / clippy clean; release build OK. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) --- ## Summary by cubic Fixes `CowBTree` so `DOC_BYTES` values its reader cannot load are rejected at compile time instead of panicking at runtime. - The const assert previously accepted `DOC_BYTES ∈ 1..=8`, but `read_width` only loads 1, 2, 4, or 8 bytes, so `CowBTree::<256, 256, 3>` compiled and panicked on its second insert. - Gates `DOC_BYTES` with the new `is_read_width` const fn, so widths 3/5/6/7 now fail to compile with a clear message. **Tests** - Adds a test verifying `is_read_width` accepts exactly `[1, 2, 4, 8]` and that each accepted width round-trips through `read_width`. - `cargo test -p graph --lib cow_btree` passes 34 tests; the full `graph` lib suite has one pre-existing failure unrelated to this change (#2922). Written for commit 3624880ed9acad54d578b2ead3321f5cd8960b84. Summary will update on new commits.

issues.title: [Rust] Virtual-key names can collide (t ^ seq), dropping a graph slice from the RDB save
issues.body:
### Summary

`uuid_v4`, which names the virtual keys a large graph is split into during an RDB save, combines the clock and a per-process counter as `t ^ seq`. Two calls get the same name whenever the clock and the counter changed in the same bits. For example, `t = 4, seq = 2` and `t = 5, seq = 3` both give `a = 6`, and every field of the name derives from `a`. If two virtual keys of one graph collide, the second `vkey_map.insert` replaces the first, and that key's slice of the graph is missing from the save.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ b033aecc6)

This depends on timing, so it was not reproduced live. On macOS the clock has microsecond resolution, so `t` is always a multiple of 1000. The XOR of two consecutive calls' `t` values is then even, while the XOR of consecutive counter values is odd, so back-to-back calls cannot collide there. On Linux (nanosecond clock), two calls exactly 1 ns apart with an even `t` and an even `seq` collide, and so does any pair where `t1 ^ t2 == seq1 ^ seq2`.

The collision is confirmed on the function itself. With `uuid_v4`'s mixing extracted unchanged into a `const fn uuid_fields(t, seq)`, a compile-time check that `uuid_fields(4, 2) != uuid_fields(5, 3)` fails:

```
error[E0080]: evaluation panicked: virtual key names collide for (t=4, seq=2) and (t=5, seq=3)
```

C names virtual keys with a random UUID (`UUID_New`), so this cannot happen in C.

### Mechanism

`src/redis_type.rs:783-806`: `let a = (t as u64) ^ seq;`. The printed fields are `a >> 32`, `(a >> 16) & 0xFFFF`, `a & 0xFFF`, and two fields of `b = a * K + C`. Everything is a function of `a`, and `a` is not injective in `(t, seq)`.

### Expected

Every call in a process returns a distinct name.

### Suggested fix

Keep the clock and the counter in separate fields: take `a` from `t`, and take the last 48 bits from `seq * K + C` with `K` odd. That is a bijection modulo 2^48, so the names differ for any two distinct `seq` values regardless of the clock.

issues.title: fix: CowBTree remove_batch never leaves a one-child non-root branch
issues.body: Closes #3237 ## Problem `CowBTree::remove_batch` repairs under-full children one level at a time (`merge_underfull`). A branch that ends with a single child cannot repair it — it has no sibling — so it reports its own underflow to its parent. If the parent also ends with one child, the grandparent merges it with a neighbour via `Node::combine`, which concatenates the two child lists; the one-child branch lands in the merged node and nothing re-examines it. A later `remove` that drains its lone leaf leaves an empty non-root leaf, and the next `insert_batch` panics in `Node::min`. Any `BRANCH_MAX >= 4`. Since #2350 the numeric index calls `remove_batch` on commit, but at the production fan-out (256/256) the shape needs a height-3 tree, so this was reproduced as a unit test, not a live query. Different from the two CowBTree bugs in #2893 / #2897; found by the Lean model of #2278 (`BugsBatch.lean`). ## Fix `merge_underfull` (batch path only) now, after each combine, re-runs itself over the children of the node(s) the combine produced (`Node::merge_underfull_below`, a no-op unless one of them is under-full) and re-checks the produced node. The single-key `rebalance` path is unchanged. | `CowBTree::<2, 4>`: 96 keys, `remove_batch(33..64)`, `remove(32)`, `insert_batch([(0,1),(95,1)])` | Result | |---|---| | Rust before | `check_invariants`: "branch must have >= 2 children: 1"; then `insert_batch` panics: `range end index 8 out of range for slice of length 0` (`mod.rs:83`) | | Rust after | well-formed after every step, contents correct | | C | n/a (no equivalent structure) | `remove_batch` timing (`CowBTree<256,256>`, 4M entries, release, median of 31) is within machine noise: main vs fix, two interleaved rounds each — scattered 2/3: 150.8 / 73.2 ms vs 69.6 / 152.5 ms; middle half: 36.1 / 22.8 ms vs 19.0 / 51.9 ms; 1k range: 0.025 / 0.025 ms vs 0.014 / 0.014 ms. ## Tests - `remove_batch_never_leaves_a_single_child_branch` — the exact repro. - `remove_batch_keeps_the_tree_well_formed_for_any_window` — every contiguous drain window at `<2,4>`, `<2,5>`, `<2,8>`, `<4,4>`, then a `remove` + `insert_batch`, checking invariants and contents. Before the fix (main @ b033aecc6): both FAILED (`tests.rs:1347` "branch must have >= 2 children"). After: `cargo test -p graph --lib cow_btree` 35 passed; `cargo test -p graph --lib` 497 passed, 1 failed (pre-existing `cap_at_or_above_batch_size_is_ignored`, #2922). `pytest tests/test_e2e.py tests/test_functions.py` 131 passed; flow `test_index_updates`, `test_index_delete`, `test_edge_index_updates`, `test_index_scans` all pass. fmt / clippy clean. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) --- ## Summary by cubic Fixes `CowBTree::remove_batch` leaving a one-child non-root branch that corrupted the tree: a later `remove` emptied its lone leaf, and the next `insert_batch` panicked in `Node::min`. The batch path now re-runs under-full repair on the children of every node a merge produces and re-checks the result; the single-key `rebalance` path is unchanged. Adds the exact repro and a sweep across drain windows and fan-outs that checks invariants and contents after each step, and shows batch-removal timing on a 4M-entry tree stays within machine noise. Written for commit 56c39c3dbc6924f7a1eede9d31832233b9f6a989. Summary will update on new commits.

issues.title: [Rust] CREATE with a named path as the last clause fails: "Variable _anon_0 not found" (regression from #2829)
issues.body:
### Summary

When a named-path `CREATE` is the last clause and follows another clause, the query fails with `Variable _anon_0 not found` and creates nothing. C creates the pattern. This is a regression from #2829 (eab2722c4), which wraps `CREATE p=…` in a `PathBuilder`. It is the same mechanism as #2993 (MERGE), which now also applies to CREATE.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ b033aecc6)

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE (:A), (:A)"
```

| query | Rust | C |
|---|---|---|
| `MATCH (a:A) CREATE p=(a)-[:R]->(:B)` | `Variable _anon_0 not found` | Nodes created: 2, Relationships created: 2 |
| `UNWIND [1,2] AS x CREATE p=(:N {x:x})` | `Variable _anon_0 not found` | Nodes created: 2, Properties set: 2 |
| `MATCH (a:A) CALL { WITH a CREATE p=(a)-[:R]->(:B) } RETURN count(*)` | `Variable _anon_0 not found` | 2; Nodes created: 2, Relationships created: 2 |
| `MATCH (a:A) CREATE p=(a)-[:R]->(:B) RETURN count(*)` (not last) | works | works |
| `CREATE p=(:N)` (only clause) | works | works |

### Mechanism

Since #2829, `plan_clause` plans `CREATE p=…` as `PathBuilder(Create)` (`graph/src/planner/mod.rs:3147-3152`). `plan_query`'s first walk, which finds where the previous clause goes for the last clause, does not step over a `PathBuilder`, while the stitching loop does. So the preceding clause becomes a sibling of the `Create` (`PathBuilder(prev, Create)`) instead of its input, and the `Create` runs without its input rows. This is the planner gap #2993 describes for MERGE.

### Expected

The pattern is created once per input row, as in C, and as when the CREATE is not the last clause.

### Suggested fix

Open PR #3101 (for #2993) adds `IR::PathBuilder(_)` to the first walk in `plan_query` and steps over a PathBuilder in the FOREACH body stitching. That covers CREATE too. Add the CREATE cases above to its tests.

issues.title: fix: OPTIONAL MATCH with a filter inside CALL {} no longer fails with "Variable n not found"
issues.body: Closes #2728 ## Problem `MATCH (x:A:B) CALL { OPTIONAL MATCH (n:A:B {id:3}) RETURN n.id AS nid } RETURN x.id, nid` fails with `Variable n not found`. C returns `[1,3],[2,3],[3,3]`. The query in #2728 (`Variable n1 not found`) fails for the same reason. `push_filters_down` (`graph/src/planner/optimizer/push_filters_down.rs:214-242`) handles a filter in the right branch of an `Apply` by walking up to the nearest `Apply` and adding its left branch's variables to the set the filter may be pushed under. The walk stepped over `Optional`, so the filter on `n` in the CALL body's `Optional` reached the outer `Apply` and inherited the outer query's variables (`x`). Variable sets here are ids only, and ids are per scope, so the body's `n` and the outer `x` share an id. The filter was then pushed below `n`'s scan onto its `Argument`, where `n` is unbound: ``` Optional Project Argument Node By Label Scan | (n:A:B) Filter <- n.id = 3, below the scan of n Argument ``` ## Fix The walk stops at the nearest `Apply` or `Optional`, since both feed their left branch's rows to the right branch through `Argument`. When that left branch is a `Project`/`Aggregate`, such as a CALL body's import, it inherits only the variables that operator names (`branch_output_variables`). The filter now stays above the scan: ``` Optional Project Argument Filter Node By Label Scan | (n:A:B) Argument ``` Setup: `UNWIND range(1,3) AS i CREATE (:A:B {id: i})` | query | Rust before | Rust after | C | |---|---|---|---| | `MATCH (x:A:B) CALL { OPTIONAL MATCH (n:A:B {id:3}) RETURN n.id AS nid } RETURN x.id, nid` | `Variable n not found` | `[1,3],[2,3],[3,3]` | `[1,3],[2,3],[3,3]` | | `MATCH (x:A:B) CALL { WITH x OPTIONAL MATCH (n:A:B) WHERE n.id = x.id + 1 RETURN n.id AS nid } RETURN x.id, nid` | `[1,2],[2,3],[3,null]` | same | same | | query from #2728 (empty graph) | `Variable n1 not found` | no rows, 1 node created | no rows, 1 node created | ## Tests New `tests/test_e2e.py::test_call_optional_match_filter_not_pushed_with_outer_variable_ids` covers both queries in the table and the query from #2728. - before (origin/main b033aecc6 build): `ResponseError: Variable n not found`, FAILED - after: passed Other checks (release build, private ports): - `pytest tests/test_e2e.py tests/test_functions.py`: 131 passed. The one failure, `test_load_csv`, fails the same way on main because the local import folder `/var/lib/FalkorDB/import/` is missing. - TCK (`TCK_DONE=tck_done.txt`): passed - Flow: `test_call_subquery` 56/56, `test_optional_match` 27/27, `test_filters` 9/9, `test_foreach` 19/19, `test_inline_pattern_attributes` 21/21, `test_multi_pattern` 7/7, `test_path_filter` 19/19, `test_relation_patterns` 13/13, `test_reversed_patterns` 1/1, `test_union` 10/10, `test_with_clause` 14/14, `test_graph_merge` 38/38 - `cargo test -p graph --lib`: 495 passed. The 1 failure is the known macOS-only `cap_at_or_above_batch_size_is_ignored` (#2922). - `cargo fmt --check` passes, and `cargo clippy -p graph --all-targets` reports no warnings in `push_filters_down.rs`. This change is optimizer-only and does not touch the runtime. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) --- ## Summary by cubic Fixes `OPTIONAL MATCH` with a filter inside a `CALL {}` body so the query no longer fails with "Variable n not found". **Bug Fixes** - `push_filters_down` now stops its ancestor walk at the nearest `Apply` or `Optional`, since both feed left-branch rows to the right through `Argument`. - When that left branch is a `Project`/`Aggregate` (a `CALL {}` import), only the variables it names are inherited, so body variables no longer collide with outer variables that share the same id. - The filter now stays above the body's scan instead of being pushed onto its `Argument` where the variable is unbound. - Added an e2e test covering the failing queries from #2728 and the regression cases; the change is optimizer-only and does not touch the runtime. Written for commit 39cac5dddcbdea1ce25db6d75f2a91f2c771f97b. Summary will update on new commits.

issues.title: fix: dbms.functions unions and the fulltext.drop error are spelled like C
issues.body: Part of #3272 (items 1 and 2; items 3–6 need a decision and are left open there). ## Problem - `type_to_dbms_string` (`graph/src/runtime/functions/procedures.rs`) joined `Type::Union` members in the order each signature declares them; `cargo clippy -p graph --all-targets` adds no warnings in touched code; `cargo test -p graph --lib` 495 pass (only the known macOS `cap_at_or_above_batch_size_is_ignored`, #2922). 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) --- ## Summary by cubic Fixes two mismatches with C's behavior: `dbms.functions()` now spells union types in C's fixed type order (e.g. "Null or Point" instead of "Point or Null"), and `db.idx.fulltext.drop` no longer prints empty parentheses in the "no such index" error when no attribute is named.
