issues.title: fix: refuse an unknown vector similarityFunction at any dimension; GRAPH.MEMORY errors match C
issues.body: Closes #3256 ## Problem - `similarityFunction` was only checked in `Index::register_fields`, inside `if dimension > 0`. So `CREATE VECTOR INDEX … OPTIONS {dimension:0, similarityFunction:'bogus'}` created an index with `similarityFunction: bogus`, and with a non-zero dimension the refusal had a different message than C's. - `GRAPH.MEMORY` sent its own error strings: `ERR SAMPLES must be …` (C sends no `ERR ` prefix), and different texts for a wrong `USAGE`/`SAMPLES` keyword. ## Fix - `map_to_index_options` (`graph/src/runtime/runtime.rs`) refuses an unknown name at parse time with C's `Invalid vector index configuration` prefix. `ip` is still accepted (Rust supports it; C does not). - `graph_memory` (`src/commands/memory.rs`) sends C's three error lines, from `Graph_Memory` in `cmd_memory.c`. | Command | `main` | This PR | C | |---|---|---|---| | `CREATE VECTOR INDEX … {dimension:0, similarityFunction:'bogus'}` | `Indices created: 1` | `Invalid vector index configuration: unknown similarityFunction 'bogus', …` | `Invalid vector index configuration` | | `CREATE VECTOR INDEX … {dimension:3, similarityFunction:'bogus'}` | `Unknown similarity function 'bogus', …` | `Invalid vector index configuration: unknown similarityFunction 'bogus', …` | `Invalid vector index configuration` | | `CREATE VECTOR INDEX … {dimension:0, similarityFunction:'euclidean'}` | created | created | created | | `GRAPH.MEMORY USAGE g SAMPLES -1` (raw) | `-ERR SAMPLES must be a non-negative integer` | `-SAMPLES must be a non-negative integer` | same as this PR | | `GRAPH.MEMORY USAGE g FOO 3` | `-ERR expected SAMPLES keyword` | `-ERR unknown subcommand 'FOO'. expecting GRAPH.MEMORY USAGE SAMPLES ` | same as this PR | | `GRAPH.MEMORY FOO g` | `-ERR unknown subcommand. Try …` | `-ERR unknown subcommand 'FOO'. expecting GRAPH.MEMORY USAGE ` | same as this PR | Not changed: fulltext `OPTIONS {weight:1, foo:1}` is still refused, as #3091 decided (C accepts it only through a loop bug). ## Tests - `test_index_create.py::test19_index_options_validation`: two bogus-function cases (dimension 2 and 0) must be refused, and `{dimension:0, similarityFunction:'cosine'}` must be accepted. - `test_memory_usage.py::test_invalid_call`: checks the three raw RESP error lines (redis-py strips a leading `ERR `, so the test reads the socket). - Before the fix both fail (`'-ERR SAMPLES must be …' == '-SAMPLES must be …'`, `False == True` for the dimension-0 statement). After: pass. The memory test and the new vector cases also pass on the C module. - Flow (RLTest, release): `test_memory_usage` 16/16, `test_index_create` 18/18, `test_index_delete` 14/14, `test_undo_log` 22/22, `test_index_scans` 38/38. - `pytest tests/test_e2e.py tests/test_functions.py`: 131 passed. `cargo test -p graph --lib`: 495 passed, 1 failed (`cap_at_or_above_batch_size_is_ignored`, pre-existing on macOS, #2922). `cargo fmt --check` and clippy clean on the touched code. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) --- ## Summary by cubic Aligned vector index and `GRAPH.MEMORY` error handling with the C module so malformed commands are refused consistently at any dimension. Previously, an unknown `similarityFunction` was only rejected when the dimension was non-zero, so `{dimension:0, similarityFunction:'bogus'}` silently created an index. Now `map_to_index_options` refuses unknown names at parse time with C's `Invalid vector index configuration` prefix, while still accepting `ip` as a Rust extension. `GRAPH.MEMORY` now sends C's error lines byte for byte: the SAMPLES error no longer carries the `ERR ` prefix, and wrong-keyword errors report the offending subcommand instead of a generic message. Written for commit 2a1198f533d4dfb54c270f88b86759646a21e462. Summary will update on new commits. ## Summary by CodeRabbit * **Bug Fixes** * Vector index creation now accepts `euclidean`, `cosine`, and `ip` similarity function names regardless of capitalization, and rejects unsupported names. * Memory command errors for unknown subcommands and unexpected keywords now use consistent, compatible formatting. Invalid sample-count errors no longer include the `ERR ` prefix. * Vector indexes with zero dimensions can now be created using the `cosine` similarity function.

issues.title: [Rust] Unknown vector similarityFunction accepted at dimension 0; GRAPH.MEMORY error texts differ from C
issues.body:
### Summary

Two leftovers after #3094 where Rust still answers differently from C:

1. `CREATE VECTOR INDEX … OPTIONS {dimension:0, similarityFunction:'bogus'}` creates the index (and `db.indexes()` reports `similarityFunction: bogus`). C refuses it. With a non-zero dimension Rust refuses, but with a different message than C's.
2. `GRAPH.MEMORY` error replies differ from C: the `SAMPLES` error carries an `ERR ` prefix C does not send, and the wrong-keyword errors have different text.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ b033aecc6)

| Command | Rust | C |
|---|---|---|
| `CREATE VECTOR INDEX FOR (n:V) ON (n.v) OPTIONS {dimension:0, similarityFunction:'bogus'}` | `Indices created: 1` | `Invalid vector index configuration` |
| `CREATE VECTOR INDEX FOR (n:V) ON (n.v) OPTIONS {dimension:3, similarityFunction:'bogus'}` | `Unknown similarity function 'bogus', expected 'euclidean', 'ip', or 'cosine'` | `Invalid vector index configuration` |
| `GRAPH.MEMORY USAGE g SAMPLES -1` (raw reply) | `-ERR SAMPLES must be a non-negative integer` | `-SAMPLES must be a non-negative integer` |
| `GRAPH.MEMORY USAGE g FOO 3` | `-ERR expected SAMPLES keyword` | `-ERR unknown subcommand 'FOO'. expecting GRAPH.MEMORY USAGE <key> SAMPLES <x>` |
| `GRAPH.MEMORY FOO g` | `-ERR unknown subcommand. Try GRAPH.MEMORY USAGE <key> [SAMPLES <count>]` | `-ERR unknown subcommand 'FOO'. expecting GRAPH.MEMORY USAGE <key>` |

Checked and already matching C, so out of scope: `{dimension:0, similarityFunction:'euclidean'}` is accepted by both. Fulltext `OPTIONS {weight:1.0, foo:true}` is created by C and refused by Rust; #3091 kept that difference on purpose (C re-checks the same known key on every loop iteration, so it lets an unknown key through) and `test_index_create.py::test19_index_options_validation` asserts it.

### Mechanism

- `map_to_index_options` (`graph/src/runtime/runtime.rs:1993`) lower-cases `similarityFunction` but does not check it. The only check is in `Index::register_fields` (`graph/src/index/mod.rs:1270-1286`), inside `if … vopts.dimension > 0`, so at dimension 0 any name is stored.
- `graph_memory` (`src/commands/memory.rs:196-219`) has its own error strings, and `RedisError::Str` sends them as-is, `ERR ` included.

### Expected

Refuse an unknown similarity function at parse time, whatever the dimension, with C's `Invalid vector index configuration` prefix (keeping `ip`, which Rust supports and C does not). Send C's `GRAPH.MEMORY` error lines.

### Suggested fix

Validate the name in `map_to_index_options`. Copy C's three texts from `Graph_Memory` (`src/commands/cmd_memory.c` on `master`).

issues.title: [Rust] UDF node.getNeighbors() with no argument throws "Error converting from js 'undefined'"
issues.body:
### Summary

`node.getNeighbors()` called with no argument throws instead of returning the outgoing neighbours. The config argument is documented as optional, and C accepts the call.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ b033aecc6)

```
GRAPH.UDF LOAD n "falkor.register('ids', function(n){ return n.getNeighbors().map(x => x.id); });"
GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE (a {id:0})-[:R]->(a), (a)-[:R]->(:B {id:1})"
GRAPH.QUERY g "MATCH (a {id:0}) RETURN n.ids(a)"
```

| | result |
|---|---|
| Rust | `UDF Exception: Error converting from js 'undefined' into type 'object'` |
| C | `[0, 1]` |

`n.getNeighbors({})` works on both.

### Mechanism

The shared JS method is `function(config) { return h(this.__falkor_node_id, config); }` (`graph/src/udf/js_classes.rs:195`). It always passes two arguments, so an omitted config reaches the native `js_get_neighbors_entry` (`js_classes.rs:350-353`) as an explicit `undefined`. Its parameter is `Opt<Object>`, which handles a *missing* argument but fails to convert a present `undefined` to `Object`.

### Expected

`[0, 1]`: no config means the defaults.

### Suggested fix

Take the config as `Opt<Option<Object>>` (rquickjs maps `undefined` / `null` to `None`), in `js_get_neighbors_entry` and, for `graph.traverse([n], undefined)`, `js_traverse_entry`.

issues.title: fix: reject an ORDER BY aggregate whose constants differ from the projection's (max(x % 4.0) vs max(x % 3))
issues.body: Closes #3236 ## Problem `replace_agg_subtrees` binds an ORDER BY aggregate to a projected aggregate when `raw_exprs_structurally_equal` says the two trees match. Its node comparison `expr_ir_eq` compared constant values only for same-type pairs. Every other pair fell back to comparing the `ExprIR` variant, so `Constant(Int(3))` equalled `Constant(Float(4.0))`, `Constant(String("3"))` and `Constant(Null)`. The same fallback ignored the payloads of `Quantifier`, `ListComprehension`, `Reduce`, `Case`, `ShortestPath` and `CompiledRegex`. `RETURN … max(n.v % 3) AS m ORDER BY max(n.v % 4.0)` therefore sorted by `m` instead of failing as it does in C. Open PR #3011 reuses `raw_exprs_structurally_equal` for non-aggregate ORDER BY expressions, where the same bug would bind `ORDER BY n.v % 4.0` to a projected `n.v % 3`. This fix covers that path too. ## Fix `expr_ir_eq` compares constants with `Value`'s `==` (Cypher equality). This is what C's `AR_EXP_Equals` does with `SIValue_Compare`: `3` still matches `3.0`, as in C. It also compares the payload of every variant that has one. Graph-pattern variants (`Pattern`, `PatternComprehension`, `NestedPlan`) keep the variant-only comparison: their anonymous elements get a fresh name per occurrence, so comparing the patterns would reject identical copies that C accepts. Setup: `UNWIND range(1,6) AS i CREATE (:N {g: i % 2, v: i})`, query `MATCH (n:N) RETURN n.g AS g, max(n.v % 3) AS m ORDER BY ` | `` | Rust before | Rust after | C | |---|---|---|---| | `max(n.v % 4.0)` | rows, sorted by `m` | `failed to map aggregation expression` | `failed to map aggregation expression within ORDER BY clause, please use alias` | | `max(n.v % '3')` | rows, sorted by `m` | error | error | | `max(coalesce(n.x, null))` vs projected `max(coalesce(n.x, 7))` | rows | error | error | | `max(n.v % 3.0)` | rows `[0,2],[1,2]` | same | same | | `max(n.v % 3)` | rows `[0,2],[1,2]` | same | same | ## Tests New `tests/test_e2e.py::test_order_by_aggregate_matches_projection_only_on_equal_constants`: - before (origin/main b033aecc6 build): `AssertionError: Expected an error`, FAILED - after: passed Every case was also checked against the C module on a live server. Other checks (release build, private ports): - `pytest tests/test_e2e.py tests/test_functions.py`: 131 passed. The one failure, `test_load_csv`, fails the same way on main because the local import folder `/var/lib/FalkorDB/import/` is missing. - Flow: `test_order_by` 9/9, `test_aggregation` 15/15, `test_with_clause` 14/14, `test_comprehension_functions` 25/25, `test_reduce` 14/14, `test_shortest_path` 7/7 - `cargo test -p graph --lib`: 495 passed. The 1 failure is the known macOS-only `cap_at_or_above_batch_size_is_ignored` (#2922). - `cargo fmt --check` passes, and `cargo clippy -p graph --all-targets` reports no warnings in `binder.rs`. This change is planner-only and runs at bind time, so the runtime is not affected. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) --- ## Summary by cubic Fixes the binding of ORDER BY aggregate expressions to projected aggregates so mismatched constants and payloads no longer pass as equal. Previously, `expr_ir_eq` compared only the `ExprIR` variant when types or payloads differed, so `max(n.v % 4.0)` matched a projected `max(n.v % 3)` and the query sorted by the wrong expression instead of failing. Constants are now compared by value equality—`3` still matches `3.0`, as in C—and the payloads of `Quantifier`, `ListComprehension`, `Reduce`, `Case`, `ShortestPath`, and `CompiledRegex` are compared too. - Added `tests/test_e2e.py::test_order_by_aggregate_matches_projection_only_on_equal_constants` covering mismatched and matching constants. Written for commit 9bcf4727d7a9ad3516c29f9c64576add14d039c8. Summary will update on new commits. ## Summary by CodeRabbit * **Bug Fixes** * Fixed aggregate sorting so `ORDER BY` correctly matches aggregates in the selected output when their constant values are equal, including equivalent integer and decimal values. * Sorting still reports an error when the aggregate expressions do not match.

issues.title: fix: graph.traverse reports the start node when it has a self-loop
issues.body: Closes #3240 ## Problem `js_traverse_impl` (`graph/src/udf/js_classes.rs`) seeded its BFS `visited` set with the start node, so when the start node is its own neighbour (a self-loop) it was never emitted. ## Fix Do not pre-mark the start node. It is reported once, when an edge reaches it. At the default depth 1 that only changes self-loops; with `maxDepth > 1` a start node on a cycle is reported once at the depth it is reached. `CREATE (a {id:0})-[:R]->(a), (a)-[:R]->(:B {id:1})`, `graph.traverse([a], {direction: d})[0]` ids: | direction | Rust before | Rust after | C | |---|---|---|---| | outgoing | `[1]` | `[0, 1]` | `[0, 1]` | | incoming | `[]` | `[0]` | `[0]` | | both | `[1]` | `[0, 1]` | `[0, 1]` | Independent of #3084 (self-loop *edge* reported twice in `collect_edges`); the two touch different lines of the same file. ## Tests - New flow test `tests/flow/test_udf.py::test_udf_javascript.test_traverse_self_loop_reports_start_node`. - Before (module built from `main`): FAIL (`[1] == [0, 1]`, `[] == [0]`, `[1] == [0, 1]`). - After: `tests/flow/test_udf.py` 47/47 pass. - `cargo fmt --check`, `cargo clippy -p graph --all-targets` clean; `cargo test -p graph --lib` 495 pass (only the known macOS `cap_at_or_above_batch_size_is_ignored`, #2922); `tests/test_e2e.py tests/test_functions.py` 131 pass. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) --- ## Summary by cubic Fixes `graph.traverse` so the start node is reported when it has a self-loop. The BFS pre-marked the start node as visited, so a self-loop edge to it was never emitted. It is now reported once, when an edge reaches it, matching C's behavior. At the default depth 1 only self-loops are affected; with `maxDepth > 1` a start node on a cycle is reported once at the depth it is reached. - Bug Fixes - Removes the pre-marking of the start node in the traversal's visited set. - Adds a flow test covering outgoing, incoming, and both directions with a self-loop. Written for commit 9e1e2747767a2a57d72f7c7c3687d10292d3ad63. Summary will update on new commits. ## Summary by CodeRabbit * **Bug Fixes** * Graph traversal now includes the starting node in results when a self-loop or a return edge reaches it, across supported traversal directions.

issues.title: fix: reload an index on an attribute named `range:x` under that name
issues.body: Closes #3239 ## Problem Since #2459 the RDB encoder writes each index field's bare attribute name, as C does. The decoder (`decode_index_field`, `src/serializers/mod.rs`) still stripped a `range:` / `vector:` prefix from the name it read, a leftover from before that change. An attribute literally called `range:x` (or `vector:v`) therefore came back after `DEBUG RELOAD` / restart as an index on `x`, and the index stopped serving `n.`range:x``. All released Rust versions (6.0.0+) already write bare names, so no released RDB carries a prefix. ## Fix Use the name as read. The prefixed RediSearch field name is still built by `create_index_sync` when the index is rebuilt. | After `CREATE INDEX FOR (n:L) ON (n.`range:x`)` + `DEBUG RELOAD` | `main` | This PR | C | |---|---|---|---| | `db.indexes()` properties | `[x]` | `[range:x]` | `[range:x]` | | `MATCH (n:L) WHERE n.`range:x` = 1` plan | Label Scan + Filter | Index Scan | Index Scan | ## Tests - New flow test `test_encode_decode.test_19_index_on_attribute_named_like_a_field_prefix` (range index on `range:x`, vector index on `vector:v`, reload, check names and that the index still serves the query). - Before: `['v', 'x'] == ['range:x', 'vector:v']` FAIL, and `'Aggregate / Filter / Node By Label Scan' should contain 'Index Scan'` FAIL. - After: pass. - Flow (RLTest, release): `test_encode_decode` 20/20, `test_rdb_load` 2/2, `test_index_create` 18/18, `test_vecsim` 12/12, `test_constraint` 26/26, `test_graph_copy` 9/9, `test_persistency` 11/11. - `pytest tests/test_e2e.py tests/test_functions.py`: 131 passed. `cargo fmt --check` clean; `clippy --all-targets` has no warnings in touched code. ## Release note RDBs written by pre-6.0 development builds of the Rust engine (before #2459) stored index fields under their RediSearch names (`range:age`). They now load with the index on an attribute of that literal name, which is left unused; re-create those range/vector indexes. Every 6.0.x release, and C, write the bare attribute name and are unaffected. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) --- ## Summary by cubic Fixes RDB reload so an index on an attribute literally named `range:x` or `vector:v` comes back under that name. The decoder in `src/serializers/mod.rs` still stripped `range:`/`vector:` prefixes that the encoder stopped writing in #2459, so such an attribute came back as an index on `x` and stopped serving queries. **Bug Fixes** - Read the index field name verbatim; the prefixed RediSearch field name is still built when the index is rebuilt. - Adds a flow test covering range and vector indexes on prefixed attribute names after `DEBUG RELOAD`, checking the name and that the index still serves the query. Written for commit a9f12a0d95a3e070ab36e54771f6802335db30f8. Summary will update on new commits. ## Summary by CodeRabbit * **Bug Fixes** * Indexes on attributes beginning with `range:` or `vector:` now retain their full names when listed and after an RDB reload. * Queries using a reloaded range index on an attribute beginning with `range:` now work correctly.

issues.title: [Rust] Graphs loaded from RDB ignore CACHE_SIZE (always 25)
issues.body:
### Summary

A graph loaded from an RDB gets a query-plan cache of 25 entries whatever `CACHE_SIZE` the module was loaded with. Graphs created at run-time honour it. So after a restart (or `DEBUG RELOAD`, or a replica's full sync) the cache size silently reverts to the default; with `CACHE_SIZE 0` caching comes back on.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ b033aecc6)

```
redis-server --enable-debug-command yes --loadmodule libfalkordb.dylib CACHE_SIZE 1
redis-cli GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE (:L)"
redis-cli DEBUG RELOAD
redis-cli GRAPH.QUERY g "RETURN 1" | grep Cached
redis-cli GRAPH.QUERY g "RETURN 2" | grep Cached
redis-cli GRAPH.QUERY g "RETURN 1" | grep Cached
```

Rust: `Cached execution: 0`, `0`, `1` (the cache holds two plans, so a 1-entry cache is not in effect).

C (`bin/macos-arm64v8-release/falkordb.so`, same arguments): `0`, `0`, `0`.

### Mechanism

`src/redis_type.rs:66` hard-codes `DEFAULT_CACHE_SIZE = 25` ("no Redis context available") and passes it to `rdb_load_graph` in `graph_rdb_load` (`:97`), to the multi-key placeholder (`:141`) and in `graphmeta_rdb_load` (`:856`). Every other construction site (`GRAPH.QUERY`, `GRAPH.RESTORE`, `GRAPH.COPY`, `GRAPH.BULK`, ...) reads `CONFIGURATION_CACHE_SIZE`.

### Expected

RDB-loaded graphs use the configured `CACHE_SIZE`, as C does.

### Suggested fix

The load callbacks run on the main thread, so the configured value can be read there: take a `Context` from the IO handle (`RedisModule_GetContextFromIO`) and lock `CONFIGURATION_CACHE_SIZE` with it, replacing the constant.

issues.title: fix: shrinking a tensor drops the multi-edge ids of pairs it cuts off
issues.body: Closes #3246 ## Problem `Tensor::resize` to smaller dimensions resized `m`, `dp`, `dm` and `mt`, but not `me`. `me` is keyed by `compound_key(src, dst)` and is `ME_DIM` rows whatever the node count, so a resize never reaches it. A multi-edge pair outside the new bounds lost its `MULTI_EDGE` sentinel but kept its ids: `iter_edges` still returned them and `edge_count` still counted them. Latent: the only caller that can shrink (`rebuild_derived_matrices` after an RDB load) resizes to `node_cap`, which covers every node id, so Cypher cannot reach it today. ## Fix In the shrink branch, collect the `me` entries whose `compound_key_inverse` falls outside `nrows x ncols` and remove them. One pass over `me`, on a shrink only; the grow path is unchanged. `Tensor::new(8, 8)` with multi pairs (0,1) and (5,6) and single pair (1,2), then `resize(4, 4)`: | | Rust before | Rust after | C | |---|---|---|---| | `iter_edges()` | `(0,1,10) (0,1,11) (1,2,12) (5,6,20) (5,6,21) (5,6,22)` | `(0,1,10) (0,1,11) (1,2,12)` | n/a (no shrink path) | | `edge_count()` | 5 | 3 | n/a | | `multi_pairs()` | 2 | 1 | n/a | ## Tests - New unit test `graph::graphblas::tensor::tests::shrinking_drops_the_multi_edge_ids_of_pairs_it_cuts_off`. - Before the fix: `FAILED … a pair outside the shrunk tensor kept its multi-edge ids` (left had `(5,6,20) (5,6,21) (5,6,22)`). - After: `ok`. - `cargo test -p graph --lib tensor`: 18 passed. `cargo test -p graph --lib`: all pass except the known macOS failure `cap_at_or_above_batch_size_is_ignored` (#2922); `list_literals_parse_in_linear_time` failed once under load and passes on rerun. - `cargo fmt --check` clean; no clippy warnings in `tensor.rs`. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) --- ## Summary by cubic Fixes `Tensor::resize` so shrinking drops the multi-edge ids of pairs that fall outside the new bounds. `me` is keyed by pair rather than sized by node count, so the shrink resizes never reached it: a cut-off multi pair kept its ids and stayed visible to `iter_edges` and `edge_count` with no forward entry leading to it. **Notes** - Removes the orphaned entries in one pass over `me`, only on the shrink path. - The bug is currently latent: the only shrink caller resizes to `node_cap`, which covers every node id. Written for commit defb47224b05c9b7c2bf2415109c73233ed8b8d1. Summary will update on new commits. ## Summary by CodeRabbit * **Bug Fixes** * Resizing a graph to smaller dimensions now removes multi-edge IDs for pairs that fall outside the new bounds, keeping edge counts consistent.

issues.title: fix: a range index beside a fulltext index on the same attribute answers queries
issues.body: Closes #3248 ## Problem An attribute keeps one RediSearch field per index type, in creation order. Every query-node builder in `graph/src/index/mod.rs` (numeric/string range, numeric/string equality, point, array-contains) took the attribute's first field, whatever its type. After `CREATE FULLTEXT INDEX FOR (n:L) ON (n.s)` then `CREATE INDEX FOR (n:L) ON (n.s)`, the numeric/tag/geo nodes targeted the fulltext field, so every range-index lookup on `n.s` returned no rows (nodes and relationships alike). ## Fix A `range_field(key)` helper returns the attribute's `IndexType::Range` field; the six sites use it instead of `.first()`. | Query (fulltext index created before the range index) | `main` | This PR | C | |---|---|---|---| | `MATCH (n:L) WHERE n.s = 'foo' RETURN n.s` | `[]` | `foo` | `foo` | | `MATCH (n:L) WHERE n.s > 'c' RETURN n.s` | `[]` | `dog`, `foo` | `dog`, `foo` | | `MATCH (n:L {s:'bar'}) RETURN n.s` | `[]` | `bar` | `bar` | | `MATCH (n:L) WHERE n.s IN ['foo','dog'] RETURN n.s` | `[]` | `dog`, `foo` | `dog`, `foo` | | `MATCH (n:L) WHERE n.v >= 2 RETURN n.s` | `[]` | `bar`, `dog` | `bar`, `dog` | ## Tests - New flow tests `test_index_scans.py::test_42_range_index_beside_fulltext_index` (nodes) and `test_edge_index_scans.py::test29_range_index_beside_fulltext_index` (relationships): string and numeric equality, range, inline map and `IN`, plus a fulltext query on the same attribute. - Before the fix: both fail, every lookup `[] == [...]`. - After: 2/2 pass. They also pass on the C module. - Flow suites (RLTest, release): `test_index_scans` 39/39, `test_edge_index_scans` 31/31, `test_index_create` 18/18, `test_index_updates` 11/11, `test_edge_index_updates` 6/6, `test_index_delete` 14/14, `test_fulltext_query` 5/5. - `pytest tests/test_e2e.py tests/test_functions.py`: 131 passed. `cargo test -p graph --lib`: 495 passed, 1 failed (`cap_at_or_above_batch_size_is_ignored`, pre-existing on macOS, #2922). `cargo fmt --check` and clippy clean on the touched code. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) --- ## Summary by cubic Fixes range-index lookups (numeric/string equality, range, geo, tag, array-contains) returning empty results when an attribute also has a fulltext index. Query-node builders were targeting the attribute's first field regardless of its index type, so a fulltext index created first made every range lookup miss. Adds a `range_field(key)` helper that selects the `IndexType::Range` field and uses it in all six query-node builders in `graph/src/index/mod.rs`. Closes #3248. **Tests** - New flow tests for nodes and relationships cover string/numeric equality, range, inline map, and `IN` queries on an attribute with both index types. - Verified that fulltext queries on the same attribute still return rows. Written for commit 847b4a8930f622e59e8074993e73862edc36b34f. Summary will update on new commits. ## Summary by CodeRabbit * **Bug Fixes** * Queries now select the appropriate range index when an attribute also has a full-text or vector index, improving results for equality, range, pattern, `IN`, geo-point, and array-contains queries. * Queries return no results when an attribute has no suitable range index. * **Tests** * Added coverage for queries using range and full-text indexes on the same attributes.

issues.title: [Rust] Range index on an attribute that also has a fulltext index returns no rows
issues.body:
### Summary

A range index on an attribute that already has a fulltext index never answers correctly. Every range-index lookup on that attribute (equality, range, inline property map, `IN`) returns no rows, on nodes and on relationships. C returns the matching rows.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ b033aecc6)

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE (:L {s:'foo'}), (:L {s:'bar'}), (:L {s:'dog'})"
GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE FULLTEXT INDEX FOR (n:L) ON (n.s)"
GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE INDEX FOR (n:L) ON (n.s)"
```

| Query | Rust | C |
|---|---|---|
| `MATCH (n:L) WHERE n.s = 'foo' RETURN n.s` | `[]` | `foo` |
| `MATCH (n:L) WHERE n.s > 'c' RETURN n.s` | `[]` | `dog`, `foo` |
| `MATCH (n:L {s:'bar'}) RETURN n.s` | `[]` | `bar` |
| `MATCH (n:L) WHERE n.s IN ['foo','dog'] RETURN n.s` | `[]` | `dog`, `foo` |

Both engines plan `Node By Index Scan`. Numeric attributes (`n.v = 2`, `n.v >= 2`) and relationship indexes (`Edge By Index Scan`) fail the same way. Creating the range index first, then the fulltext one, works.

### Mechanism

An attribute keeps one `Field` per index type in `Index::fields: HashMap<Arc<String>, Vec<Arc<Field>>>`, in creation order. Every query-node builder in `graph/src/index/mod.rs` takes the attribute's first field whatever its type: `build_numeric_range_node` (:1397), `build_string_range_node` (:1426), and `build_query_node` for numeric equality (:1484), string equality (:1496), point (:1554) and array-contains (:1615), all via `self.fields.get(key).and_then(|f| f.first())`. With the fulltext index created first, the numeric/tag/geo node targets the fulltext field's name, which holds no numeric/tag/geo data, so RediSearch returns nothing.

### Expected

The range lookup reads the range field and returns the rows, as in C.

### Suggested fix

Select the attribute's field whose type is `IndexType::Range` (one helper, used at all six sites) instead of the first one.

issues.title: [Rust] GRAPH.EFFECT CREATE_NODE with a repeated id is silently de-duplicated instead of refused
issues.body:
### Summary

A client-sent `GRAPH.EFFECT` whose `CREATE_NODE` record names the same node id twice (e.g. ids `[0, 0]`, count 2) is applied as one node and replies `OK`. The same mistake in a `CREATE_EDGE` record has been refused since #2846. A record that says it creates two nodes and creates one is a malformed buffer and should be refused like the edge case.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ b033aecc6)

v3 payloads (`u8 3 · u8 0` header, then the record), built as in `tests/flow/test_effects_wire.py`:

```
# empty graph; CREATE_NODE count 2, no labels/attrs, IdList [0, 0]
GRAPH.EFFECT dupn "\x03\x00" + CREATE_NODE(0, 0)
GRAPH.QUERY dupn "MATCH (n) RETURN count(n)"

# graph (:A)-[:R]->(:A); CREATE_EDGE count 2, type 0, ids [1, 1], src [0, 0], dst [1, 1]
GRAPH.EFFECT dupe "\x03\x00" + CREATE_EDGE([1, 1], 0, [0, 0], [1, 1])
```

| Record | Rust | 
|---|---|
| `CREATE_NODE` ids `[0, 0]` | `OK`, 1 node created |
| `CREATE_EDGE` ids `[1, 1]` | `effect apply failed: bulk relationship create got 2 ids of which only 1 are distinct; an id names one edge` |

No C comparison: the C module only reads effects up to v2 (`GRAPH.EFFECT version mismatch expected version <= 2 got: 3`).

### Mechanism

`apply_record` for `CreateNode` (`graph/src/effects/v3/apply.rs:207-218`) turns the `IdList` into a `RoaringTreemap` (`ids.to_roaring()`) and passes that set to `Graph::create_nodes`, so a repeated id is merged before anything can see it. `Graph::create_relationships_bulk` (`graph/src/graph/graph.rs:2601-2609`) compares the set size with the list length and refuses on a mismatch; nothing does that for nodes.

### Expected

The buffer is refused with an error naming the duplicate, the graph is unchanged, as for `CREATE_EDGE`.

### Suggested fix

In `CreateNode`, compare `nodes.len()` with the number of ids in the record and return the same kind of error as the edge path.

issues.title: [Rust] Tensor::resize shrinking keeps the multi-edge ids of pairs it cuts off (latent)
issues.body:
### Summary

Latent, not reachable from Cypher today. `Tensor::resize` to smaller dimensions drops the forward entries of pairs outside the new bounds but leaves their multi-edge ids in `me`. Those ids then show up as edges with no forward entry: `iter_edges` returns them and `edge_count` counts them.

### Reproduction (`main` @ b033aecc6)

Unit test, added in the linked PR:

```rust
let mut t = Tensor::new(8, 8);
// (0, 1) and (5, 6) are multi pairs, (1, 2) a single one.
t.set_all_from_slices(&[0, 0, 1, 5, 5, 5], &[1, 1, 2, 6, 6, 6], &[10, 11, 12, 20, 21, 22]);
t.flush();
t.resize(4, 4);
```

| | `main` | Expected |
|---|---|---|
| `iter_edges()` | `(0,1,10) (0,1,11) (1,2,12) (5,6,20) (5,6,21) (5,6,22)` | `(0,1,10) (0,1,11) (1,2,12)` |
| `edge_count()` | 5 | 3 |
| `multi_pairs()` | 2 | 1 |

No C comparison: C has no equivalent shrink path on its tensors.

### Mechanism

The shrink branch of `Tensor::resize` (`graph/src/graph/graphblas/tensor.rs:814-828`) resizes `m`, `dp`, `dm` and `mt`, but not `me`. `me` is keyed by `compound_key(src, dst)` and is `ME_DIM` rows wide whatever the node count, so a shrink never touches it.

Why it is latent: the only caller that can shrink is `Graph::rebuild_derived_matrices` after an RDB load (`graph.rs:978` → `resize_node_matrices`), and it resizes to `node_cap`, which covers every node id in the graph, so no pair is ever cut off.

### Expected

After a shrink, `me` holds no ids of pairs outside the new dimensions, so `iter_edges`, `edge_count` and `multi_pairs` agree with the forward matrix.

### Suggested fix

In the shrink branch, remove the `me` entries whose `compound_key_inverse` falls outside `nrows x ncols`. It costs one pass over `me`, only on a shrink.

issues.title: [Rust] A deleted node loses labels set or removed earlier in the same query
issues.body:
### Summary

A node deleted by a query is meant to keep all of its details for the rest of that query (the project rule for Rust: a deleted entity keeps everything). Labels the same query added or removed before the `DELETE` are lost: the snapshot is taken from the committed label matrix, not from the query's own view of the node.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ b033aecc6)

```
GRAPH.QUERY h "CREATE (:A {v: 1})"
GRAPH.QUERY h "MATCH (n:A) SET n:C DELETE n RETURN labels(n), n:C"

GRAPH.QUERY h2 "CREATE (:A {v: 1})"
GRAPH.QUERY h2 "MATCH (n:A) REMOVE n:A DELETE n RETURN labels(n), n:A"
```

| Query | Rust | Expected (Rust rule) | C |
|---|---|---|---|
| `SET n:C DELETE n RETURN labels(n), n:C` | `[A], false` | `[A, C], true` | `[], false` |
| `REMOVE n:A DELETE n RETURN labels(n), n:A` | `[A], true` | `[], false` | `[], false` |

C returns no labels at all for a deleted node. The expected values here follow the agreed Rust behaviour (a deleted entity keeps all its details), so they are the labels the node had in this query just before the `DELETE`, not C's.

### Mechanism

`DeleteOp` snapshots a committed node's labels with `g.get_node_label_ids(id)` — the committed label matrix — in both places:

- `delete_nodes_bulk`, `graph/src/runtime/ops/delete.rs:284`
- `delete_entity`, `graph/src/runtime/ops/delete.rs:464`

The attributes next to them are taken from the pending view (`update_node_attrs` / `get_node_attrs`), but the labels skip `Pending::update_node_labels`. `Runtime::get_node_labels` and `node_has_label_id` then answer from that snapshot.

### Expected

`labels(n)` and `n:L` on a deleted node give the labels as of the `DELETE`, including labels set or removed earlier in the same query.

### Suggested fix

Take the snapshot the same way `Runtime::get_node_labels` builds the live view: committed label ids with `pending.update_node_labels(id, ..)` applied, in both places.

issues.title: [Rust] A deleted edge keeps its type after a type is registered by a constraint, so a reused id reports the old type
issues.body:
### Summary

When a relationship type is registered by anything other than an edge write — `GRAPH.CONSTRAINT CREATE ... RELATIONSHIP <new type>`, or `ADD_SCHEMA` on a replica — `relationship_type_matrix` is not widened to the new type count. From then on, deleting an edge does not remove it from that matrix (in a release build; a debug build trips a `debug_assert`). The deleted edge keeps its old type, so when the next edge reuses the id it has two types, and `type(r)` reports the stale one.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ b033aecc6)

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE (:N)-[:A]->(:N)"
GRAPH.CONSTRAINT CREATE g MANDATORY RELATIONSHIP B PROPERTIES 1 x
GRAPH.QUERY g "MATCH ()-[r]->() DELETE r"
GRAPH.QUERY g "MATCH (a), (b) WHERE id(a) = 0 AND id(b) = 1 CREATE (a)-[r:C]->(b)"
GRAPH.QUERY g "MATCH ()-[r]->() RETURN id(r), type(r)"
GRAPH.QUERY g "MATCH ()-[r:A]->() RETURN count(r)"
```

| | Rust | C |
|---|---|---|
| `id(r), type(r)` | `0, A` | `0, C` |
| `count` of `:A` edges | `0` | `0` |

Rust's edge 0 sits in the `C` tensor but has both `A` and `C` in `relationship_type_matrix`; `type(r)` takes the first.

### Mechanism

- `Graph::get_type_id_mut` (`graph/src/graph/graph.rs:1250-1266`) pushes the type and its tensor but does not call `resize()`. `get_relationship_matrix_mut` (`graph.rs:1364-1380`) and `get_label_id_mut` (`graph.rs:1188`) both do, for this reason.
- `delete_relationships` (`graph.rs:2916-2921`) and `delete_implicit_edges` (`graph.rs:3023-3055`) build the removal mask as `relationship_cap x relationship_types.len()`. With the matrix still one column narrower, `remove_mask` → `tombstone_masked` gets `GrB_DIMENSION_MISMATCH`, which is only checked by `debug_assert_eq!` (`graphblas/matrix.rs:990`). In release the removal is skipped.
- Callers of `get_type_id_mut`: `src/commands/constraint.rs:74` (primary) and `graph/src/effects/v3/apply.rs:546` (`ADD_SCHEMA` on a replica), so replicas get the same bug. Bulk insert also calls it, but it resizes before writing.
- The matrix is only widened again once a write goes through `resize()` with `relationship_types.len() > ncols`, i.e. the first edge of a new type, which in the repro comes after the delete.

### Expected

`type(r)` is `C`, and a deleted edge leaves no row in `relationship_type_matrix`, on the primary and on a replica.

### Suggested fix

Call `self.resize()` in `get_type_id_mut` after registering the type, the same as `get_label_id_mut`. This fixes both paths.

issues.title: [Rust] Decision: UNIQUE constraint key for true vs 1 — C treats them as one value (RediSearch numeric), Cypher equality keeps them distinct
issues.body:
### Decision needed: should a UNIQUE constraint treat `true` and `1` (and `false` and `0`) as the same key?

C enforces UNIQUE through the RediSearch numeric field, and it indexes a Boolean as the number `1.0` / `0.0`. So under a UNIQUE constraint on C, `true`, `1` and `1.0` are one key, and `false` and `0` are another. openCypher says `true = 1` is `false`, and both engines agree on that. Rust's constraint key distinguishes all three today. The planned fix for #2774 will merge `1` and `1.0`, and it has to decide whether to merge Booleans too. **This issue is for that decision: copy C, or follow Cypher equality.** No PR is attached.

Results: Rust = release build of `main` @ b033aecc6. C = local `master` build of the C module (`bin/macos-arm64v8-release/falkordb.so`).

Setup (both engines): `GRAPH.QUERY u "CREATE INDEX FOR (n:P) ON (n.k)"`, then `GRAPH.CONSTRAINT CREATE u UNIQUE NODE P PROPERTIES 1 k` (status `OPERATIONAL` on both). Then the queries below run in order:

| # | Query | Rust | C | Cypher equality |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `CREATE (:P {k: true})` | created | created | — |
| 2 | `CREATE (:P {k: 1})` | created | `unique constraint violation on node of type P` | `true = 1` is `false` → distinct, accept |
| 3 | `CREATE (:P {k: 1.0})` | created (#2774) | violation | `1.0 = 1` is `true` → duplicate of #2, but distinct from `true` |
| 4 | `CREATE (:P {k: false})` | created | created | — |
| 5 | `CREATE (:P {k: 0})` | created | violation | `false = 0` is `false` → accept |
| 6 | `MATCH (n:P) RETURN n.k, typeOf(n.k) ORDER BY id(n)` | `true`/Boolean, `1`/Integer, `1`/Float, `false`/Boolean, `0`/Integer | `true`/Boolean, `false`/Boolean | — |
| 7 | `RETURN true = 1` | `false` | `false` | `false` |

Constraint creation over existing data behaves the same way (fresh graph):

| Steps | Rust | C |
|---|---|---|
| `CREATE (:P {k: 1}), (:P {k: true})`, then index + `GRAPH.CONSTRAINT CREATE … UNIQUE … k` | `OPERATIONAL` | `FAILED` |

### The same conflation leaks into equality lookups through the index (both engines)

Both engines store a Boolean in the numeric index as `1.0` / `0.0`. An index-backed `WHERE n.k = 1` therefore also matches `true`, and this disagrees with the same predicate evaluated without the index:

| Query on the Rust graph above (`true, 1, 1.0, false, 0`) | Rust |
|---|---|
| `MATCH (n:P) WHERE n.k = 1 RETURN count(n)` (plan: `Node By Index Scan`) | `3` (includes `true`) |
| `MATCH (n:P) WITH n, n.k AS k WHERE k = 1 RETURN count(n)` (no index) | `2` |
| `MATCH (n:P) WHERE n.k = true RETURN count(n)` (index) | `3` (includes `1` and `1.0`) |
| `MATCH (n:P) WITH n, n.k AS k WHERE k = true RETURN count(n)` (no index) | `1` |

On C, with only `true` and `false` stored, `WHERE n.k = 1` returns `1` through the index and `0` without it. This is the old RedisGraph report #363, and it is still open. However the constraint question is decided, this part is a wrong-result bug on both engines.

### Mechanism

- C: `Index_BuildUniqueConstraintQuery` (`src/constraint/unique_constraint.c:112`) queries the RediSearch index. `src/index/index.c:309` sends `T_BOOL` down the same `SI_GET_NUMERIC` path as `T_INT64`/`T_DOUBLE`, so `true` is the number `1.0`.
- Rust: `Graph::build_composite_key` (`graph/src/graph/graph.rs:4542`) encodes each value with `format!("{v:?}")`, so `Bool(true)`, `Int(1)` and `Float(1.0)` are three different keys. The numeric index encodes `Value::Bool(b)` as `f64::from(b)` (`graph/src/index/mod.rs:812`), which is the same conflation C has, but only for index lookups.

### What openCypher says

- Equality across types is `false` (`true = 1` is `false`), and Boolean and Integer are different types. The Cypher 25 / GQL property uniqueness constraints are defined in terms of that equality, so Neo4j is believed to accept `true` and `1` as distinct values under a uniqueness constraint (not checked here).
- The openCypher TCK has no constraint scenarios (constraints are not part of openCypher), so the TCK does not decide this.

### Options

1. **Follow Cypher equality.** The key is `a = b` ⇔ `key(a) = key(b)`: numerics are normalised (`1` ≡ `1.0`, which fixes #2774), and Booleans get their own type tag. Rust accepts rows 2 and 5 where C rejects them. A graph that loads on C (where they were rejected) still loads on Rust. The reverse direction (Rust data moved to C) can fail the constraint on C. To make index lookups agree with the non-index path, the numeric index also has to stop sending Booleans to the numeric field (#363). Medium change: a key encoding in `graph.rs` plus a separate Boolean field or tag in the index.
2. **Copy C.** Booleans map to `1`/`0` in the constraint key. This gives byte-for-byte parity, including `FAILED` on constraint creation over `{k:1},{k:true}`. The cost: the constraint rejects values that Cypher itself says are different, and this is hard-coded in the engine with no way out for users. Small change (encode `Bool` as the numeric `1.0`/`0.0` in the #2774 key).
3. **Follow Cypher for the constraint, and leave the index conflation for #363.** Same constraint behaviour as option 1, but the lookup fix ships separately. The constraint check and an index-backed `MATCH` can then disagree in the meantime: the constraint accepts `{k:1}` next to `{k:true}`, and `MATCH (n:P {k:1})` returns both.

### Recommendation

Option 1. The constraint should reject exactly the values the language calls equal. That means merging `1` and `1.0` (#2774) and keeping `true` and `1` apart, and it gives one equality relation that the constraint, the index and `=` all share. C's behaviour comes from the RediSearch numeric encoding, not from a design choice, and it is already reported as a bug (#363). Document the difference in the C→Rust migration notes ("Rust no longer rejects `true` next to `1` under UNIQUE"). Land the constraint-key change and the index Boolean fix together, so that the constraint and `MATCH` never disagree.

### Related

#2774 (Rust: `1` vs `1.0` treated as distinct; its fix must pick a side here), #363 (index conflates `1` and `true`), #3105 / #3028 (decision format).

issues.title: [Rust] Decision: integer division is exact in Rust but goes through double in C (9007199254740993 / 1, 4611686018427387903 / 4611686018427387904 = 1 on C)
issues.body:
### Decision needed: should `Integer / Integer` be exact (Rust) or go through `double` (C)?

C computes `Integer / Integer` by converting both operands to `double`, dividing, and truncating the result back to `int64`. Rust divides the two `i64` values directly. For operands up to 2^53 the answers agree. Above that they differ: C loses the low bits of the dividend, and can even round the quotient up to the next integer. Nothing crashes. This issue is for the decision: **keep exact division in Rust and document the C difference, or copy C.** No PR is attached.

Results: Rust = release build of `main` @ b033aecc6. C = local `master` build of the C module (`bin/macos-arm64v8-release/falkordb.so`, arm64).

| # | Query | Rust | C | Exact truncated quotient |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `RETURN 9007199254740993 / 1` | `9007199254740993` | `9007199254740992` | `9007199254740993` |
| 2 | `RETURN 9007199254740993 / 3` | `3002399751580331` | `3002399751580330` | `3002399751580331` |
| 3 | `RETURN 123456789012345678 / 10` | `12345678901234567` | `12345678901234568` (rounded **up**) | `12345678901234567` |
| 4 | `RETURN 1000000000000000001 / 7` | `142857142857142857` | `142857142857142864` | `142857142857142857` |
| 5 | `RETURN 9223372036854775807 / 2` | `4611686018427387903` | `4611686018427387904` | `4611686018427387903` |
| 6 | `RETURN -9223372036854775807 / 1` | `-9223372036854775807` | `-9223372036854775808` | `-9223372036854775807` |
| 7 | `RETURN 4611686018427387903 / 4611686018427387904` | `0` | `1` | `0` |
| 8 | `RETURN (9007199254740993 / 3) * 3 + 9007199254740993 % 3` | `9007199254740993` | `9007199254740990` | `9007199254740993` (`a = (a/b)*b + a%b`) |
| 9 | `RETURN -9223372036854775808 / -1` | `-9223372036854775808` (wraps) | `9223372036854775807` on arm64 (saturating cast); `-9223372036854775808` on x86-64 per #3205 | not representable |

Small operands and negative rounding agree on both engines. Both truncate toward zero: `-7 / 2 = -3`, `7 / -2 = -3`, `-7 % 2 = -1`, and `-9007199254740993 / 2 = -4503599627370496`.

### Mechanism

- C: `SIValue_Divide` (`src/value.c:749`) returns `SI_LongVal(SI_GET_NUMERIC(a) / SI_GET_NUMERIC(b))`. `SI_GET_NUMERIC` (`src/value.h:74`) is `(v).type == T_DOUBLE ? (v).doubleval : (v).longval`, and the ternary has type `double`, so both `int64` operands are promoted to `double` before the divide. `%` (`SIValue_Modulo`) uses `longval` directly and stays exact, which is why row 8 breaks the division identity on C. The final `double`→`int64` cast is undefined behaviour when the quotient is out of range, which is why row 9 depends on the CPU.
- Rust: `impl Div for Value` (`graph/src/runtime/value.rs:1130`) is `Int(a.wrapping_div(b))`. The vectorised path (`runtime/vector_expr.rs:901`) does the same.

### What openCypher says

- openCypher's INTEGER is a 64-bit signed integer, and `/` on two integers is integer division truncated toward zero. Neo4j is believed to use exact `long` division (not checked here). Nothing in the spec allows the result to depend on a floating-point round trip.
- The TCK covers integer division only with small operands (`Mathematical8`: `12 / 4 * 3 - 2 * 4`), where both engines pass. No TCK scenario tells the two apart.

### Options

1. **Keep exact division in Rust (current behaviour).** Matches openCypher, and keeps `a = (a/b)*b + a%b`. The cost is a result difference from C for any dividend or divisor above 2^53 (row 7 shows it is not only the low digits). It affects anyone dividing large ids, hashes or nanosecond timestamps, and should go in the C→Rust migration notes. No code change.
2. **Copy C (convert to `f64`, divide, truncate).** Bit-for-bit parity with C on arm64, but the answers are wrong by the spec, and `/` and `%` stop agreeing. The out-of-range cast also has to pick a platform, because C itself gives different answers on arm64 and x86-64 (row 9). Small change, and a deliberate regression.
3. **Keep exact division, and make `i64::MIN / -1` an error** (overflow, see #3205) instead of wrapping. This is option 1 plus the one case where neither engine is right today. Use `checked_div` in `value.rs` and `vector_expr.rs`. Small change.

### Recommendation

Option 3. Exact division is what the spec specifies. C's answers come from an implementation shortcut, not a design choice, and they are not even consistent across CPUs. Document the >2^53 difference as an intentional divergence. Fold the `i64::MIN / -1` overflow error into #3205 so that Rust raises an error where both engines silently return a wrong value today.

### Related

#3205 (`INT64_MIN / -1` wraps), #3105 (same decision format, for operator precedence).

issues.title: [Rust] NOT over a pattern predicate keeps rows where the inner predicate is null
issues.body:
### Summary

When `NOT` wraps a predicate that mixes a scalar test with a pattern, rows where the inner predicate is `null` pass the filter. `NOT null` is `null`, so these rows should be dropped. C drops them.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ b033aecc6)

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE (:N {v: 0}), (:N), (:N {v: 5}), (:N)-[:R]->(:M)"
GRAPH.QUERY g "MATCH (a:N) WHERE NOT (a.v > 1 OR (a)-->()) RETURN count(a)"
GRAPH.QUERY g "MATCH (a:N) WHERE NOT (a.v > 1 AND (a)-->()) RETURN count(a)"
```

| query | Rust | C |
|---|---|---|
| `NOT (a.v > 1 OR (a)-->())` | 2 | 1 |
| `NOT (a.v > 1 AND (a)-->())` | 4 | 3 |

In the `OR` case, the node with no `v` and no edge gives `NOT (null OR false)` = `null`, yet Rust counts it. The same happens in the `AND` case for the node with no `v` that has an edge: `NOT (null AND true)` = `null`.

### Mechanism

`Planner::expr_to_plan` (`graph/src/planner/mod.rs:1542-1549`) plans `NOT(complex)` as `AntiSemiApply(input, plan(inner))`. The inner plan passes a row only when the inner expression is `true`, so `AntiSemiApply` passes every row where it is not `true`, which includes `null`. That is two-valued negation, not Cypher's three-valued one.

### Expected

Rows where the negated predicate is `null` are filtered out (Rust 1 and 3 above, as in C).

### Suggested fix

Push the `NOT` down with De Morgan before planning: `NOT (A OR B)` becomes `NOT A AND NOT B`, `NOT (A AND B)` becomes `NOT A OR NOT B`, and `NOT NOT A` becomes `A`. These identities hold in three-valued logic. The leaves are then either `NOT pattern`, where `AntiSemiApply` is correct because a pattern is never `null`, or `NOT scalar`, which becomes an ordinary `Filter` that handles `null` correctly.

### Found by

Lean 4 model of the planner (`proofs/`, ledger entry W4-plan-1).

issues.title: [Rust] graph.traverse([a]) leaves a out when a has a self-loop
issues.body:
### Summary

`graph.traverse([a])` leaves `a` out of its own result when `a` has a self-loop. C returns it.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ b033aecc6)

```
GRAPH.UDF LOAD t "falkor.register('ids', function(n){ return graph.traverse([n])[0].map(x => x.id); });"
GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE (a {id:0})-[:R]->(a), (a)-[:R]->(:B {id:1})"
GRAPH.QUERY g "MATCH (a {id:0}) RETURN t.ids(a)"
```

| | `t.ids(a)` |
|---|---|
| Rust | `[1]` |
| C | `[0, 1]` |

`node.getNeighbors()` already returns `[0, 1]` on Rust; only `graph.traverse` drops it.

### Mechanism

`js_traverse_impl` (`graph/src/udf/js_classes.rs:743-744`) seeds the BFS `visited` set with the start node, so the self-loop's target (the start node) fails `visited.insert(neighbor_id)` and is never emitted.

### Expected

`[0, 1]`, as C and `getNeighbors()`.

### Suggested fix

Do not pre-mark the start node as visited: it is emitted (once) when an edge reaches it. With the default depth of 1 this only affects self-loops. With `maxDepth > 1` a start node on a cycle is reported once, at the depth it is reached, which is what reachability means everywhere else.

Related, not the same: #3083 / PR #3084 (a self-loop *edge* reported twice).

issues.title: [Rust] Index on an attribute named `range:x` / `vector:x` reloads from RDB as an index on `x`
issues.body:
### Summary

A range or vector index on an attribute whose name starts with `range:` or `vector:` comes back after an RDB round-trip as an index on the attribute without that prefix. `CREATE INDEX FOR (n:L) ON (n.`range:x`)` reloads as an index on `x`, so the index silently stops covering the attribute it was built for. C keeps `[range:x]`.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ b033aecc6)

```
redis-cli GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE (:L {x:1})"
redis-cli GRAPH.QUERY g 'CREATE INDEX FOR (n:L) ON (n.`range:x`)'
redis-cli DEBUG RELOAD
redis-cli GRAPH.QUERY g "CALL db.indexes() YIELD label, properties RETURN label, properties"
```

Rust:
```
L
[x]
```

C (`bin/macos-arm64v8-release/falkordb.so`):
```
L
[range:x]
```

### Mechanism

`decode_index_field` (`src/serializers/mod.rs:641-646`) strips a `range:` / `vector:` prefix from the field name it reads. Since #2459 the encoder (`src/serializers/mod.rs:363-382`) writes the bare attribute name, as C does, so on load the name never carries a RediSearch prefix. The strip only alters user attribute names that happen to start with those strings. It dates from the migration (#2279), before #2459 changed the encoder; every released Rust version (6.0.0+) contains #2459.

### Expected

The attribute name is read back verbatim, as C does.

### Suggested fix

Drop the prefix strip in `decode_index_field` and use the name as read.

issues.title: [Rust] CowBTree: DOC_BYTES 3/5/6/7 pass the const assert but the second insert panics (latent)
issues.body:
### Summary

`CowBTree<LEAF_MAX, BRANCH_MAX, DOC_BYTES>` (`graph/src/index/falkordb/data_structures/cow_btree/mod.rs`) accepts `DOC_BYTES ∈ 1..=8` in its const assert, but the doc field is read back with `read_width`, which handles only widths `1 / 2 / 4 / 8`. With `DOC_BYTES ∈ {3, 5, 6, 7}` the tree compiles and the **second insert panics**.

Latent: the only production instantiation (`index/falkordb/numeric.rs`) uses a supported width, so no query is affected; the repro is a Rust unit test. No C comparison applies. Found in the Lean model (`LeafAosD.docBytes3_*` on `proofs/lean4-verification`). Different from the two CowBTree bugs in #2893 / #2897.

### Reproduction (`main` @ b033aecc6, `cargo test -p graph --lib`)

```rust
let mut t = CowBTree::<256, 256, 3>::new();   // compiles: assert is DOC_BYTES >= 1 && DOC_BYTES <= 8
assert!(t.insert(1, 1));
assert!(t.insert(2, 2));                      // panics
```
```
debug:   panicked at cow_btree/mod.rs:98:13: assertion `left == right` failed   (debug_assert_eq!(width, 8))
release: panicked at cow_btree/mod.rs:99:33: range end index 16 out of range for slice of length 11
```

### Mechanism

`AosLeaf::doc` (`leaf/aos.rs:35`) calls `read_width(.., DOC_BYTES)`; `read_width` (`mod.rs:88-102`) matches `1 | 2 | 4` and treats every other width as 8. The const asserts in `Default::default` / `new` / `from_sorted` (`mod.rs:140, 162, 180`) only check `1 <= DOC_BYTES <= 8`.

### Expected

Either every `DOC_BYTES` the const assert accepts works, or the unsupported widths fail to compile.

### Suggested fix

Smaller change: tighten the const assert to `DOC_BYTES ∈ {1, 2, 4, 8}` (the widths `read_width` was designed for — "widths are powers of two so every read is a single fixed-size load"). Supporting 3/5/6/7 would need a variable-length read in a hot path for no current user.

issues.title: [Rust] CowBTree: remove_batch leaves a one-child non-root branch; a later insert_batch panics in Node::min
issues.body:
### Summary

`CowBTree::remove_batch` (`graph/src/index/falkordb/data_structures/cow_btree/`) can leave a **non-root branch with a single child** at any `BRANCH_MAX >= 4`. The tree's contents stay right, but the shape is broken: one later single-key `remove` that drains that branch's lone leaf leaves an **empty non-root leaf**, and the next `insert_batch` panics in `Node::min`.

Reachability: since #2350 the native numeric index calls `CowBTree::remove_batch` on every commit that removes entries (`FalkorIndex::merge`, `index/falkordb/falkordb_index.rs:335` → `numeric.rs:121`). At the production fan-out (`LEAF_MAX = BRANCH_MAX = 256`) the shape needs a tree of height >= 3 (more than 65,536 leaves, i.e. millions of entries in one `(label, attribute)` column) and a single commit that drains all but one leaf of a level-1 subtree, so it was **not reproduced through a live query**; the repro below is a Rust unit test at small fan-out. No C comparison applies (C has no equivalent structure). Found while proving #2278's CowBTree in Lean (`proofs/cow_btree/FalkorCowBTree/BugsBatch.lean` on `proofs/lean4-verification`). Different from the two CowBTree bugs in #2893 / #2897.

### Reproduction (`main` @ b033aecc6, `cargo test -p graph --lib`; debug and `--release` behave the same)

```rust
let pairs: Vec<(u64, u64)> = (0..96u64).map(|d| (d, 0)).collect();
let mut t = CowBTree::<2, 4>::from_sorted(&pairs);              // root -> 3 subtrees of 32
t.remove_batch(&(33..64u64).map(|d| (d, 0)).collect::<Vec<_>>());
check_invariants(&t, false);   // panics: "branch must have >= 2 children (a 1-child root should collapse): 1"
assert!(t.remove(32, 0));      // leaves an empty non-root leaf
t.insert_batch(&[(0, 1), (95, 1)]);
```
```
panicked at cow_btree/mod.rs:83:25:
range end index 8 out of range for slice of length 0
```
(without the `check_invariants` line; same message in a release test build).

### Mechanism

- `Node::remove_batch` (`node.rs:483-541`) repairs under-full children one level at a time with `merge_underfull` (`node.rs:148-160`). A branch `X` that ends with one child is under-full (`1 < BRANCH_MAX / 2`), but its own `merge_underfull` cannot run (`children.len() > 1`, `node.rs:153`); only its parent can repair it.
- If the parent `P` also ends with `X` as its only child, `P` is returned with one child too, and its parent merges `P` with a sibling via `Node::combine` (`node.rs:396-401`), which **concatenates** the two child lists. `X` lands in the merged node still with one child, and nothing re-examines the merged node's children.
- A later `remove` that drains `X`'s lone leaf: `Branch::rebalance` on `X` is a no-op (`node.rs:212`), so the empty leaf stays; `insert_batch` → `pack_branches` → `Node::min` reads `leaf.key(0)` on it (`node.rs:232`, `mod.rs:83`).

### Expected

After `remove_batch`, every non-root branch has `>= BRANCH_MAX / 2` children and every non-root leaf `>= LEAF_MAX / 2` entries (the same invariant `remove` keeps; `check_invariants` passes), and later `remove` / `insert_batch` never panic.

### Suggested fix

In the batch path, after `merge_underfull` combines a pair, re-run `merge_underfull` over the children of the node(s) the combine produced (they may now contain the under-full lone child of a one-child branch), recursively, and re-check the produced node itself. The single-key `rebalance` path is unaffected (it can never produce a one-child non-root branch at `BRANCH_MAX >= 4`).

issues.title: [Rust] ORDER BY aggregate is matched to a projection whose constants differ in type (max(x % 4.0) taken for max(x % 3))
issues.body:
### Summary

An aggregate in `ORDER BY` is matched to a projected aggregate whose constants differ in type. `max(n.v % 4.0)` is taken to be the projected `max(n.v % 3)`, so the query sorts by the wrong expression instead of being rejected. C rejects the query.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ b033aecc6)

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "UNWIND range(1,6) AS i CREATE (:N {g: i % 2, v: i})"
GRAPH.QUERY g "MATCH (n:N) RETURN n.g AS g, max(n.v % 3) AS m ORDER BY max(n.v % 4.0)"
```

Rust: returns rows `[0, 2], [1, 2]`, ordered by `m`.

C:

```
failed to map aggregation expression within ORDER BY clause, please use alias
```

With `% 4` (an Int, so Int is compared with Int) Rust already rejects it (`failed to map aggregation expression`). Only a difference across constant types slips through.

### Mechanism

`replace_agg_subtrees` (`graph/src/planner/binder.rs:2608`) replaces an ORDER BY aggregate with a projection alias when `raw_exprs_structurally_equal` says the trees match. Its node comparison `expr_ir_eq` (`graph/src/planner/binder.rs:2665-2680`) compares values only for same-type constant pairs (Int/Int, Float/Float, String/String, Bool/Bool). Every other pair falls back to `std::mem::discriminant(a) == std::mem::discriminant(b)`. Every constant is `ExprIR::Constant`, so `Constant(Int(3))` equals `Constant(Float(4.0))`, `Constant(Null)` equals `Constant(Int(7))`, and so on. The same fallback ignores the payload of `Quantifier`, `ListComprehension`, `Reduce`, `Case`, `ShortestPath`, `Pattern`/`PatternComprehension` and `CompiledRegex`.

Open PR #3011 reuses `raw_exprs_structurally_equal` for non-aggregate ORDER BY expressions too, so there `ORDER BY n.v % 4.0` would be bound to a projected `n.v % 3`.

### Expected

Constants match only when they are equal values. C's `AR_EXP_Equals` compares them with `SIValue_Compare`, so `3` matches `3.0`, while `4.0` does not match `3`, `'3'` does not match `3`, and `null` does not match `7`. In those cases the query fails as it does in C. (`max(n.v % '3')` against a projected `max(n.v % 3)` shows the same bug: Rust sorts by `m`, C rejects the query.)

### Suggested fix

Make `expr_ir_eq` compare `Constant` values with `Value`'s `==` (Cypher equality, the same as C's comparison). Also compare the payload of every variant that has one (`Quantifier`, `ListComprehension`, `Reduce`, `Case`, `ShortestPath`, `CompiledRegex`).

issues.title: fix: a refused GRAPH.EFFECT buffer no longer keeps its index DDL
issues.body: Closes #3023 ## Problem When `GRAPH.EFFECT` refuses a buffer, `MvccGraph::rollback` drops the private version. Index DDL survived that rollback. The `Indexer` map is shared by every MVCC version, so a `CREATE_INDEX` or `DROP_INDEX` that ran before the refusing record stayed applied, while everything else in the buffer was rolled back. ## Fix This implements option 1 from the issue. `apply_effects` still verifies each `CREATE_INDEX` / `DROP_INDEX` record in place: schema and attribute ids, label, index type. It then queues the statement instead of running it. The queue runs in record order after all records have applied and `Graph::validate` has passed, before `commit_index`. If a data record refuses the buffer, no DDL has run yet. Deferring the DDL created a problem with population. `docs` only collects documents for indexes that already exist, so an entity the buffer writes now has to reach a newly created index through population. Population reads the **committed** graph, and that graph lacks the buffer's writes until `MvccGraph::commit` publishes the version. To handle this, `populate_index` takes an optional `published_at` version, and the first batch reschedules until the committed graph reaches it. This uses the same 1 ms reschedule as the existing "graph not yet committed" path. The apply path uses the new `Graph::create_index_populated_at` / `drop_index_populated_at`, which pass `Some(g.version)`. `create_index` / `drop_index` pass `None`, so the primary's `CREATE INDEX` / `DROP INDEX` behave as before. Without the gate, a 50k-node buffer had 0 of its nodes in the index. The same race already exists on `main` when an entity comes before its `CREATE_INDEX` in a buffer, and the new test hits it. | Case (client-sent `GRAPH.EFFECT`) | `main` | This PR | C | |---|---|---|---| | `[CREATE_INDEX A(zz), CREATE_NODE 0]`, node 0 live → refused | `db.indexes()` lists `A [zz]` | `db.indexes()` empty | n/a: C cannot read v3 (logs `GRAPH.EFFECT version mismatch expected version <= 2 got: 3` and exits) | | `[DROP_INDEX A(zz), CREATE_NODE 0]` on an indexed graph → refused | index gone | index still there, still answers `n.zz = 1` | n/a | | `[CREATE_NODE ×50000 :F, CREATE FULLTEXT INDEX F(body)]` → accepted | 0 of 50000 indexed | 50000 indexed | n/a | | same, index record first | 50000 | 50000 | n/a | One case remains, also noted in a comment in `apply_effects`. If a deferred DDL statement is refused itself (index already exists, drop of a missing index), the DDL statements before it in the same buffer stay applied. A refusal by any data record is now fully undone. Covering that last case needs option 2 (undo log) or option 3 (per-version `Indexer`). ## Tests New class `testEffects_07_RefusedBufferIndexDDL` in `tests/flow/test_effects_ddl.py`. The payloads are captured from the replica's MONITOR feed for a statement run on a source graph with the same schema numbering, then spliced with a `CREATE_NODE 0` that the target refuses as already live. - `test01_a_refused_create_index_is_not_kept` - `main`: FAIL, `db.indexes()` = `[['A', ['zz'], …]] == []` - this PR: PASS - `test02_a_refused_drop_index_is_not_kept` - `main`: FAIL, `[] == [['A', ['zz'], …]]` - this PR: PASS - `test03_an_accepted_buffer_indexes_what_it_created` (both record orders, 50k nodes) - `main`: FAIL, `[[0]] == [[50000]]` (node first) - this PR with the deferral but **without** the population gate: FAIL in both orders - this PR: PASS Other runs (release build, RLTest): - `test_effects_{batch,commands,commit,ddl,opcodes,shapes,topology,values,wire}`: 4/7/4/21/12/22/3/9/14, all pass - `test_index_{create,delete,scans,updates}`: 18/14/38/11, all pass - `test_replication` 2/2, `test_replication_states` 1/1, `test_aof` 1/1 - `pytest tests/test_e2e.py tests/test_functions.py`: 131 passed - `cargo test -p graph --lib`: 495 passed. The 1 failure is the known `cap_at_or_above_batch_size_is_ignored` on macOS (#2922). - `cargo fmt --check` is clean, and `clippy -p graph --all-targets` adds no warnings in touched code. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) --- ## Summary by cubic Fixes #3023: a refused `GRAPH.EFFECT` buffer no longer keeps its index DDL. Index DDL is now verified in place but queued and run only after all records apply and `Graph::validate` passes, in record order. - Background index population now waits for the buffer's version to be committed, so entities the buffer wrote reach indexes the same buffer created. Without this gate, a 50k-node buffer indexed 0 of its nodes. - Deferred index DDL and index commits run through the shared `commit_index_docs` path after validation. - The primary's `CREATE INDEX` / `DROP INDEX` path is unchanged. - Adds tests for refused `CREATE_INDEX` / `DROP_INDEX` and for accepted buffers indexing what they created in both record orders. **Remaining gap**: a DDL statement that is itself refused still leaves the DDL statements before it applied. Covering that needs an undo log or a per-version index map. Written for commit 4642405ba7b664f1ba1a8fc31f87f5847c86236c. Summary will update on new commits. ## Summary by CodeRabbit * **Bug Fixes** * Index creation and removal are now applied only when the corresponding batch of changes is accepted, preventing refused batches from leaving index changes behind. * Accepted batches apply index changes consistently whether index creation is recorded before or after node creation. * Background index population waits until the relevant graph version is available, improving consistency of indexed results.

issues.title: fix: slow log no longer panics on a multi-byte character at byte 2048
issues.body: Closes #3233 ## Problem The slow log sliced the query and parameter text at byte 2048 (`entry_hash` and `truncate` in `src/slow_log.rs`). Slicing a `&str` inside a multi-byte character panics, so a query (or `CYPHER` parameter string) longer than 2048 bytes that ran past the 10 ms threshold, with a character straddling byte 2048, killed the server: ``` FalkorDB panic: panicked at src/slow_log.rs:49:10: end byte index 2048 is not a char boundary; it is inside 'é' (bytes 2047..2049 of string) ``` ## Fix A `prefix` helper returns the longest prefix of at most 2048 bytes that ends on a char boundary (`str::floor_char_boundary`, already used in the lexer). `entry_hash` hashes that prefix and `truncate` stores it plus `...`. Nothing else in `src/` slices text by a byte limit unsafely: `telemetry.rs` cuts by `char_indices`, `divergence_guard.rs::clip` walks to a boundary, and the `graph_core.rs` slices are at NUL / params offsets. Query: 2050 bytes, `é` at bytes 2047..2049, `UNWIND range(1, 2000000) …` so it is logged. | | `main` | This PR | C | |---|---|---|---| | query answers | no, server panics and exits | yes | yes | | `GRAPH.SLOWLOG` query text | — | 2047 bytes + `...` (2050 bytes, valid UTF-8) | 2048 bytes + `...` (2051 bytes, ends `\xc3...`: half of `é`, invalid UTF-8) | | same with the character in a `CYPHER p='…'` prefix | panics at `slow_log.rs:32` | params 2047 bytes + `...` | 2048 bytes + `...`, invalid UTF-8 | The stored text differs from C only where C stores a broken character; we drop the whole character (up to 3 bytes fewer) and keep the reply valid UTF-8. Matching C byte for byte would mean storing and returning non-UTF-8 bytes. Unchanged: C also appends `...` to text that is exactly 2048 bytes long, which Rust did not do before and still does not. ## Tests - New flow test `test_slowlog.py::test07_truncate_on_char_boundary`: for `é`, `€` and `😀` straddling byte 2048, in the query text and in the parameters, it checks the server answers and `GRAPH.SLOWLOG` holds both entries, cut before the character. - Before the fix (release build of `main`): fails, `Connection closed by server`, the server process is gone. - After: passes; `test_slowlog.py` 7/7. - No Rust unit test: the `falkordb-rs` crate's test binary aborts at start (`the Redis Allocator isn't available`), since the module's global allocator is Redis's, so `src/` has no runnable unit tests. - `cargo fmt --check` clean, no clippy warnings in `slow_log.rs`, `cargo test -p graph --lib` 495 passed (only the known #2922 failure), `pytest tests/test_e2e.py tests/test_functions.py` 131 passed. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) --- ## Summary by cubic Fixes a server panic when the slow log truncated a query or `CYPHER` parameter string longer than 2048 bytes whose multi-byte character straddled byte 2048; slicing the `&str` at that byte panicked and took down the server. Truncation and the dedup hash now cut at the nearest character boundary at or below 2048 bytes via `str::floor_char_boundary`, so the whole character is dropped and stored text stays valid UTF-8. This differs from C only where C stores a broken character; otherwise behavior matches, including not appending `...` to text that is exactly 2048 bytes. Adds a flow test covering `é`, `€`, and `😀` straddling byte 2048 in both the query text and the parameters. Closes #3233. Written for commit be7a3ae20320f44c8025faad721a2cb1c84920da. Summary will update on new commits. ## Summary by CodeRabbit * **Bug Fixes** * Slow-log entries now truncate long query text and CYPHER parameter values at valid character boundaries, preventing multibyte characters from being split or corrupted. * Truncated values end with an ellipsis. Long queries containing multibyte characters are also handled safely when generating query hashes.

issues.title: [Rust] Slow log panics and kills the server when a multi-byte character straddles byte 2048 of a slow query
issues.body:
### Summary

The slow log cuts the query text (and the parameter text) at byte 2048 without regard to UTF-8 character boundaries. A query longer than 2048 bytes that runs past the 10 ms slow-log threshold, with a multi-byte character straddling byte 2048, panics the worker and takes the server down. C answers normally and logs the query.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ b033aecc6)

Query: `UNWIND range(1, 2000000) AS x WITH x WHERE x < 0 RETURN count(x) AS c, '<a × 1975>é'` — 2050 bytes, `é` occupies bytes 2047..2049.

```python
prefix = "UNWIND range(1, 2000000) AS x WITH x WHERE x < 0 RETURN count(x) AS c, '"
q = prefix + "a" * (2047 - len(prefix.encode())) + "é" + "'"
r.execute_command("GRAPH.QUERY", "g", q)
r.execute_command("GRAPH.SLOWLOG", "g")
```

Rust: the connection drops and redis-server exits:

```
<module> FalkorDB panic: panicked at src/slow_log.rs:49:10:
end byte index 2048 is not a char boundary; it is inside 'é' (bytes 2047..2049 of string)
```

C (`master` module): the query returns, and `GRAPH.SLOWLOG g` holds one entry whose query is the first 2048 bytes followed by `...` (2051 bytes, ending `aaaa\xc3...` — the `é` cut in half, so the stored text is not valid UTF-8).

The same happens with a long parameter string (`CYPHER p='...é...'`), through `truncate` on the params text.

### Mechanism

`src/slow_log.rs`:
- `entry_hash` (:48-49) hashes `query[..min(len, 2048)]`; this is the first slice that panics.
- `truncate` (:30-32) stores `s[..2048]` + `"..."` for both the query and the params.

Both are byte slices of a `&str`, which panic when the index falls inside a character.

Other byte-limit slices in `src/` were checked: `telemetry.rs` truncates by `char_indices`, `divergence_guard.rs::clip` walks to a char boundary, and the `graph_core.rs` slices are at NUL / params offsets that are always boundaries. Only the slow log is affected.

### Expected

The query answers and the slow log records it, as in C.

### Suggested fix

Cut at the nearest char boundary at or below 2048 bytes (`str::floor_char_boundary`, already used in `graph/src/parser/lexer.rs`) in both `entry_hash` and `truncate`. The stored text then differs from C only when C would store a broken character: Rust keeps whole characters (up to 3 bytes fewer), C stores invalid UTF-8. Reproducing C's bytes exactly would mean storing and replying with non-UTF-8 bytes; keeping the stored text valid UTF-8 seems the better choice.

### Found by

Lean bug ledger, W4-redis-1.

Release notes

There is now a single config for enabling 64-bit time_t: libc_unstable_time64. This can be set unconditionally; it opts in to 64-bit time_t on the following platforms that use 32-bit by default:

  • 32-bit Linux-GNU
