issues.title: Schema-mutating commands bypass the single-writer election → schema/matrix corruption (crash or duplicate-label-id RDB)
issues.body:
GRAPH.CONSTRAINT (async worker thread) and GRAPH.EFFECT (main thread) acquire the graph write lock directly, outside the write_in_progress/pending_write_queue election that serializes GRAPH.QUERY writes. Because the GraphContext.writelocked reentrancy flag isn't thread-aware, a concurrent worker-thread query write and one of these commands can each skip the other's lock and mutate the shared schema/attribute arrays + label/relation matrices at the same time.

Result: a torn realloc → SIGSEGV, or a silently-corrupt graph where the schema block carries a duplicate label/relationship-type id (or schema-count ≠ matrix-count) that gets serialized into the RDB and then crashes any server that loads it — the customer-reported symptom.

issues.title: ci(images): rebuild the OS-package stages on every image build
issues.body:
Closes #3152

## Problem

The runtime image build restores a registry buildcache (`_build-flavour.yml`). Docker keys a cached `RUN` on its command text and parent layer, not on what the Debian archive holds. So when the `server` stage hits the cache, `apt-get upgrade` never runs and the image ships packages as old as the cache entry. A security update Debian publishes between two rebuilds of the `debian:trixie-slim` base is silently skipped.

This is what an external scan of `6.0.0` is asking for: it ships OpenSSL `3.5.7-1~deb13u2`, and Debian's `deb13u3` fixes the five reported CVEs.

## Change

On the build step in `_build-flavour.yml`:

```yaml
pull: true
no-cache-filters: |
  server
  full
```

- The `server` and `full` stages, the ones that install OS packages, are never served from the cache.
- The compile stages (`builder`, `redis-builder`) stay cached. `redis-server` and `falkordb.so` link `libssl`/`libcrypto`/`libz` dynamically (checked with `ldd`), so the versions that ship come from `server`.
- `full` is `FROM server` and already reruns with it; it is named so that does not depend on it.
- `Dockerfile.asan` has no `full` stage; a filter naming a stage that doesn't exist is ignored, not an error.

## Verification

Checked on the real `build/runtime/Dockerfile` with a fresh `docker-container` builder on `moby/buildkit:buildx-stable-1`, the image `setup-buildx-action` uses. The `builder` stage was swapped for the released `falkordb.so` via `--build-context` so nothing had to be compiled; `redis-builder`, `server` and `full` were built for real.

1. Seeded a local cache (`--cache-to type=local,mode=max`).
2. Cleared the builder's own state, then rebuilt from that cache two ways:

| Step | Current config | With this change |
|---|---|---|
| `[server 2/12]` apt install + `apt-get upgrade` | CACHED | ran (15.3 s) |
| `[full 1/5]` apt install | CACHED | ran (2.8 s) |
| `[redis-builder 6/6]` redis compile | CACHED | CACHED |

The image built with the change has `openssl`, `libssl3t64` and `openssl-provider-legacy` at `3.5.7-1~deb13u3`. A filter naming a missing stage exits 0 on the same builder.

CI can't show the difference on this PR. The buildcache was last written on 2026-09-17, before the current Debian base, so today every runtime build already reruns these steps (0 cached steps in merge-queue run 36303922883).

## Build time

None today, for the reason above. When the cache does hit, this adds the cost of the two stages: in run 36303922883, the `server` apt step took 12.7–15.7 s, the `full` apt step 2.6 s, and every other step in those stages under 1 s. They also run in parallel with the engine compile.

## Not in this PR

- Already-published images are untouched; releases retag the merge-queue image rather than building. `6.0` needs a patch release (6.0.1) to pick up the fix, plus a backport of this change.
- The buildcache stopped being written when #2718 moved image builds into the merge queue, because `cache-to` is gated on `refs/heads/main`. Whether to revive it is a separate, performance-only decision.


<!-- This is an auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->

## Summary by CodeRabbit

* **Chores**
  * Server and full builds now use current base images and do not reuse cached build results. Other stages remain eligible for the configured build cache.

<!-- end of auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->

issues.title: 6.0.0: server panics (`src/reply.rs:655:58`, `Option::unwrap()` on `None`) when a null precedes an aggregate in RETURN
issues.body:
## Summary

On `falkordb/falkordb:6.0.0`, a query whose `RETURN` has a null value in a column before an aggregate (`count`, `collect`) panics the module and brings down the whole server. The null can be a literal or a missing property. The smallest reproduction needs no data:

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "RETURN null AS x, count(1) AS n"
```

The same queries return the expected rows on `v4.20.4`.

## Environment

- Image: `falkordb/falkordb:6.0.0` (`sha256:92fbda814970a648b1fd80835bff221766bccd0f0ce958bc58a62976fea06620`, also `latest` as of 2026-09-29)
- Redis 8.10.2 (as reported by the image)
- Docker Desktop on macOS, Apple Silicon (linux/arm64). Seen on two machines.
- Default configuration (`docker run -p 6379:6379 falkordb/falkordb:6.0.0`)

## Steps to reproduce

```bash
docker run -d --name f6 -p 6379:6379 falkordb/falkordb:6.0.0
redis-cli GRAPH.QUERY g "RETURN null AS x, count(1) AS n"
# Error: Server closed the connection
docker logs f6 | grep -A3 panic
```

With data, a missing property as the null:

```bash
redis-cli GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE (:B {id:'b'})"
redis-cli GRAPH.QUERY g "MATCH (b:B) RETURN b.id AS k, b.missing AS x, count(b) AS n"
# Error: Server closed the connection
```

## Expected

One row each, as on `v4.20.4`:

| query | v4.20.4 result |
|---|---|
| `RETURN null AS x, count(1) AS n` | `x = null, n = 1` |
| `MATCH (b:B) RETURN b.id AS k, b.missing AS x, count(b) AS n` | `k = 'b', x = null, n = 1` |

## Actual

The server process exits:

```
# <module> FalkorDB panic: panicked at src/reply.rs:655:58:
called `Option::unwrap()` on a `None` value
Backtrace:
   0: <std::backtrace::Backtrace>::create
   1: falkordb::module_init::graph_init::{closure#0}
   2: std::panicking::panic_with_hook
   3: std::panicking::panic_handler::{closure#0}
   4: std::sys::backtrace::__rust_end_short_backtrace::<std::panicking::panic_handler::{closure#0}, !>
   5: __rustc::rust_begin_unwind
   6: core::panicking::panic_fmt
   7: core::panicking::panic
   8: core::option::unwrap_failed
   9: falkordb::reply::reply_compact
  10: falkordb::graph_core::execute_query
  11: <falkordb::graph_core::query_mut::{closure#0} as core::ops::function::FnOnce<()>>::call_once::{shim:vtable#0}
  12: <graph::threadpool::ThreadPool>::new::{closure#0}
  ...
```

With `restart: unless-stopped` the container comes back, and the next identical query crashes it again. One of our machines logged dozens of restarts in two hours.

## What triggers it

Each case was run three times on a fresh server, with the same result every time:

| query (on `CREATE (:A {id:'a'})-[:R]->(:B {id:'b'})`) | 6.0.0 |
|---|---|
| `RETURN null AS x, count(1) AS n` | **crash** |
| `RETURN null AS x, collect(1) AS n` | **crash** |
| `MATCH (b:B) RETURN b.id AS k, b.missing AS x, count(b) AS n` | **crash** |
| `RETURN count(1) AS n, null AS x` (null after the aggregate) | ok |
| `WITH null AS x RETURN x, count(1) AS n` (null projected first) | ok |
| `RETURN 1 AS x, count(1) AS n` (not null) | ok |
| `RETURN null AS x` (no aggregate) | ok |
| `MATCH (b:B) RETURN b.missing AS x, count(b) AS n` | ok |
| `MATCH (a:A)-[:R]->(b:B) RETURN b.id AS k, b.missing AS x, collect(a.id) AS n` | ok |

- The crash also happens with `GRAPH.RO_QUERY`, and without `--compact` (the verbose reply).
- It's not every null grouping key: the last two rows survive. So we can't say exactly which condition matters. What all the crashing cases share is a null grouping key before an aggregate.

## Where we hit it

A read query in our application, against a graph where the frame had no `maxDurationMin` property:

```cypher
MATCH (f)-[t:TRIGGERS_FRAME]->(fr:Frame) WHERE f.id IN $factors AND t.status = 'active'
OPTIONAL MATCH (fr)-[:ALLOWS_POSITION]->(p:Category)
RETURN fr.id AS frame, fr.name AS name, collect(DISTINCT f.id) AS triggeredBy, collect(DISTINCT t.strength) AS strengths,
       collect(DISTINCT p.id) AS positions, fr.maxDurationMin AS maxDurationMin, t.sourceIds AS sourceIds
```

It's sent from falkordb-py (`graph.query`, `--compact`), and it works on 4.x. As a workaround we have pinned `falkordb/falkordb:v4.20.4`.

## Related: 4.x can't start on data written by 6.0.0

After running 6.0.0, going back to `v4.20.4` on the same data volume fails at startup:

```
# Can't handle RDB format version 15
# Error reading the RDB base file appendonly.aof.1.base.rdb, AOF loading aborted
```

That may be expected for a major version, but it means users who got 6.0.0 through `latest` can't simply pin back without discarding their data. A note in the 6.0.0 release notes would help.

issues.title: Path finding issues - A* suboptimal paths, SPpaths pathCost, Yen cost prop
issues.body:
three post-merge review findings on the Yen/A*/all-shortest work:

    A* returned suboptimal paths when only some nodes have lat/lon: the haversine heuristic is admissible but inconsistent across coordinate / coordinate-less nodes, and AStarCtx_Run never reopened finalized nodes. Now a strictly shorter g to an already-finalized node reopens and re-expands it, restoring optimality; all-coords graphs stay consistent so no reopening occurs.

    algo.SPpaths pathCost regressed to 0 without costProp for the accelerated pathCount:0 / pathCount>1 paths (the DFS reported hop count). _sum_path_cost now sums a default of 1 per edge, so pathCost is the hop count without costProp -- matching the DFS -- across all pathCount values.

    The Yen fast path selected k paths by (weight, length), ignoring costProp, diverging from the DFS among equal-weight ties. Thread cost_prop (may be ATTRIBUTE_ID_NONE) into Yen_KShortestPaths / AStar_KShortestPaths and select by (weight, cost, length) -- matching path_cmp so selection and reported order agree. Without costProp, cost == hop count == length, so weight-only queries are unaffected.

issues.title: Exit with code 65 when a data load fails
issues.body:
Closes #3145

Stacked on #3141.

Redis ends a failed RDB/AOF load with a hard-coded exit status: 1, or **0** when the `redis-check-rdb` pass it runs after a failed load from a file finds the file structurally sound (e.g. FalkorDB rejects a graph whose checksum is valid). A failed load can look like a clean shutdown to whatever restarts the server, and the module API cannot change the code.

With this change, a process that exits while a load is unfinished exits with `EX_DATAERR` (65):
- `RedisModuleEvent_Loading`: a flag is set when an RDB, AOF or replication load starts and cleared when it ends. A start while a load is still open is `redis-check-rdb` re-reading the file on its way to `exit()`, so its own end/failed events are ignored.
- `RedisModuleEvent_CronLoop`: after a `FAILED` event, the next cron tick means Redis survived the failure (a diskless sync that lost its connection), so the flag is cleared.
- `atexit()`: if the flag is set in the main process, log, `fflush(NULL)` and `_exit(65)`.

Crashes (panic, segfault) skip `atexit` and keep their signal status.

**Behavior change:** the replica AOF-divergence bail-out exits while the AOF load is unfinished, so it now reports 65 instead of 1; `testAOFDivergence` is updated.

### Tests
`tests/flow/test_load_failure_exit_code.py` saves a graph, stops the server, damages `dump.rdb`, boots a fresh server on it and checks the exit status and the module's log line:

| Case | Without this PR | With it |
|---|---|---|
| Graph FalkorDB rejects, checksum valid | 0 | 65 |
| Truncated graph value | 1 | 65 |
| Bad checksum | 1 | 65 |
| Clean shutdown after a good load | 0 | 0 |

### Verification (local; a PR based on another PR's branch gets no CI)
Built with `ghcr.io/falkordb/falkordb-build:debian`, tested on Redis 8.10.2, linux arm64.
- New test: 4/4 pass; 3 fail against #3141 without this change.
- Flow suite: 1442/1470 pass. The 28 failures (test_concurrent_query, test_timeout, test_query_mem_limit, test_slowlog, test_pending_queries_limit, test_index_create, test_graph_copy, test_cache) fail identically with #3141's own CI-built module in the same environment (test server connection refused).
- Scenario runs: rejected full-sync payloads loaded from disk (checksum valid and broken) and a failed AOF load exit 65; a diskless sync that lost its connection followed by a clean stop exits 0.

issues.title: Exit with a distinct code when a data load fails
issues.body:
When Redis fails to load an RDB or AOF it exits with a hard-coded status: `exit(1)`, or `exit(0)` when the `redis-check-rdb` pass it runs in-process after a failed load from a file finds the file structurally sound (for example when FalkorDB rejects a graph whose checksum is valid). Whatever restarts the server (Kubernetes, systemd, an entrypoint script) therefore can't tell a failed load from a clean shutdown or any other startup error, and can't react to it, e.g. by moving a bad local `dump.rdb` aside so a replica resyncs instead of crash-looping on it.

The module API has no way to set the exit code. FalkorDB can still do it: track whether a load is in progress with the `Loading` and `CronLoop` server events, and replace the exit status with a dedicated code (`EX_DATAERR`, 65) from an `atexit()` handler when the process exits mid-load.

Builds on #3141.

issues.title: graph: add cdylib crate-type so the crate also emits a shared object
issues.body:
Closes discussion in #3129 (step 1 of the request; not a full closure).

## What

Adds a `[lib]` section to `graph/Cargo.toml` with `crate-type = ["rlib", "cdylib"]`. No source changes.

## Why

As documented in #3129, the Rust workspace currently only builds as an `rlib` linked into the C-side `falkordb.so`, so there is no way to produce a shared object from the Rust tree alone. The evidence in #3129 shows that `cargo rustc -p graph --release --crate-type cdylib` already compiles cleanly on this tree and emits `target/release/libgraph.so`. Declaring it in `[lib]` promotes that artifact to a plain `cargo build -p graph` output instead of an ad-hoc `rustc` invocation, which:

- lets downstream consumers link against the engine directly for embedding/experimentation,
- gives maintainers an always-built signal that the cdylib target stays healthy (rather than rotting silently off-tree).

## What this intentionally does not do

This does **not** make the crate a loadable Redis module: no `RedisModule_OnLoad` entrypoint / command registration / lifecycle binding is implemented on the Rust side (loading the resulting `libgraph.so` with `--loadmodule` still fails, as #3129 notes). A Rust-side module binding layer is a separate, larger piece of work - this PR is the minimal, zero-risk enablement step so that follow-up work (upstream or downstream) has a supported shared-library artifact to build on.

Refs #3129

issues.title: Bug: `--requirepass` (and other CLI args) silently ignored on `falkordb/falkordb-server` image
issues.body:
### Summary

Passing Redis CLI arguments to the `falkordb/falkordb-server` container — e.g. the standard Redis-image convention `docker run falkordb/falkordb-server --requirepass <password>` — silently has no effect. The server starts with no authentication configured, with no error or warning printed anywhere.

### Affected version

`v4.20.7` (also reproduced on current `master`).

### Root cause

The image's `ENTRYPOINT` is `build/docker/run.sh`. That script execs `redis-server` itself and only splices in the `${REDIS_ARGS}` and `${FALKORDB_ARGS}` **environment variables** — it never forwards its own positional arguments (`"$@"`) into the command it runs:

```sh
# build/docker/run.sh
else
    exec redis-server ${REDIS_ARGS} --protected-mode no \
        --dir "${FALKORDB_DATA_PATH}" \
        --loadmodule "${FALKORDB_BIN_PATH}/falkordb.so" ${FALKORDB_ARGS}
fi
```

Any arguments appended after the image name on `docker run` (e.g. `--requirepass foo`) become positional args (`$1`, `$2`, …) to `run.sh` via `ENTRYPOINT`, but the script never references `$1`/`$2`/`"$@"` anywhere, so they are silently dropped before `redis-server` is invoked.

This appears to date back to #1027 (switching the image from `CMD`-only to `ENTRYPOINT` + `CMD`) — the script was never updated to forward its arguments after that change.

### Steps to reproduce

```sh
docker run -p 6379:6379 falkordb/falkordb-server:v4.20.7 --requirepass mysecret
# in another shell:
redis-cli -p 6379 PING
# expected: (error) NOAUTH Authentication required.
# actual:   PONG   (no password required at all)
```

### Expected behavior

`--requirepass mysecret` (or any other redis-server CLI flag passed after the image name) should be honored, matching the behavior of the upstream `redis` image and standard Docker `ENTRYPOINT`/`CMD` conventions.

### Actual behavior

The flag is accepted by Docker but never reaches the `redis-server` process. No error, warning, or log line indicates it was dropped.

### Workaround

Set it via the `REDIS_ARGS` environment variable instead, since that value *is* spliced into the exec line:

```sh
docker run -p 6379:6379 -e REDIS_ARGS="--requirepass mysecret" falkordb/falkordb-server:v4.20.7
```

### Suggested fix

Forward the container's arguments to `redis-server` in `build/docker/run.sh`, e.g. append `"$@"` to both `exec redis-server ...` invocations (TLS and non-TLS branches).

issues.title: Handle short reads gracefully during RDB decode
issues.body:
Closes #3140

Also fixes the C side of #2506 (the Rust side is #2510).

## Problem

A truncated RDB payload (a diskless replication stream that drops mid-transfer, a truncated `RESTORE`/`MIGRATE` payload, a cut-off `dump.rdb`) crashed the server: FalkorDB never declared `REDISMODULE_OPTIONS_HANDLE_IO_ERRORS`, so Redis panicked on the first short read.

Malformed but checksum-valid payloads either crashed the server (`RedisModule_Assert`, and libc `assert`, which release builds keep on) or, where the check was a debug-only `ASSERT`, loaded silently in release builds.

## Changes

**Short reads**
- `module.c`: declare `REDISMODULE_OPTIONS_HANDLE_IO_ERRORS`.
- `SerializerIO`: a sticky error flag. Once a read fails, every later read returns zero or an empty buffer without touching the stream, and the decoders stop at their next checkpoint.
- v19 and v20 decoders: checkpoints in every loop. On failure the decoder returns NULL and frees the partial graph unless an earlier virtual key already registered it (`RdbLoadGraph`, `Decode_Previous`).
- Both graph key types (`graphdata` and the `graphmeta` virtual keys) hand NULL back to Redis instead of registering it.

**Malformed payloads** (v19, v20, and the buffered reader they share)
- `SerializerIO_SetError(io, reason)` fails the decode through the same flag. Converted to failures:
  - buffer framing and value type tags (these crashed release builds);
  - count and consistency checks that were debug-only `ASSERT`s;
  - GraphBLAS load results;
  - duplicate or out-of-order schemas and duplicate constraints;
  - out-of-range entity, label and constraint ids;
  - index language, field type and vector metric.
- One warning per rejected key, naming the key and the reason:
  `Failed loading graph key '<key>': <reason>`
  Short reads add no line of ours; Redis reports those itself.

**UDFs**
- Libraries in the RDB load with replace. Loading an RDB into a process that already holds a library (a replica's next full sync, `DEBUG RELOAD`) now leaves the RDB's version in place. Before, debug builds asserted and release builds kept the stale copy.
- A library that fails to load fails the load.

**RESTORE over a live graph of the same name** (fixes the C side of #2506)
- The decoder found the graph to extend by the name stored in the payload. That lookup is meant for graphs split across keys, but it matched any registered graph, live ones included.
- `RESTORE` decodes before deleting the value it replaces. So `RESTORE … REPLACE` of a graph's own dump, or a `RESTORE` under another key while the source is live, decoded into the live graph: its contents doubled, and with an index the server crashed in `Index_SetLanguage`.
- Now only a graph part-way through a multi-key load is extended. Otherwise the payload decodes into a new graph, and Redis frees the replaced one as usual.

**Merge with master (v20)**
- master moved the v19 decoder to `decoders/prev/v19` and added `decoders/current/v20`. The hardening is applied to both.
- `Decode_Previous` no longer frees the v19 serializer before checking it for an error.
- `CCHIndex_RdbLoad` returns NULL on a short read.

## Behavior changes

- `RESTORE … REPLACE` of a graph's own dump now restores exactly the dump. Before, it doubled the graph, and crashed when the graph had an index.

- Release builds now refuse payloads that broke a debug-only check and used to load silently:
  - `RESTORE` fails with `Bad data format`;
  - at startup, Redis exits;
  - on a replica's full sync, the replica exits.
- Replicas configured with `repl-diskless-load on-empty-db` now actually load from the socket. Before, Redis skipped diskless loading because a module didn't declare IO-error handling.
  - A dropped connection makes the replica retry.
  - Rejected data makes the replica exit, which is Redis's policy for corrupt data.

## Scope

- Covered: the v19 and v20 decoders, and the buffered reader they share.
- v14–v18: their decoders are unchanged, including the graph lookup by name. They pick up the short-read latch from the shared reader.
- v10–v13: read Redis's IO directly; unchanged.
- Out of scope:
  - `GRAPH.RESTORE` / `GRAPH.COPY`;
  - allocations sized from header counts;
  - GraphBLAS matrix contents.

## Tests

- `test_rdb_load.py`:
  - a short read inside every chunk of a multi-chunk graph;
  - a short read inside a `graphmeta` key;
  - a malformed type tag, buffer length and payload type;
  - `DEBUG RELOAD` replacing a UDF library;
  - `RESTORE … REPLACE` of a graph's own dump, with and without an index (the #2506 reproducer);
  - `RESTORE` under another key while the source graph is live.

  Each new test fails on the code before its fix; the multi-chunk short-read test on debug builds, where the assert it trips lives.
- Run locally (linux arm64, release and debug builds):
  - truncation inside every chunk of a 25 MB graph: all rejected cleanly, memory flat;
  - diskless replication with the stream cut at 17 points: all recover;
  - 400 seeded single-byte corruptions of a valid DUMP:

    | | Crashes before | Crashes after |
    |---|---|---|
    | Release | 134 (+5 hangs) | 3 |
    | Debug | 141 (+1 hang) | 4 (+1 hang) |

    The remaining crashes are GraphBLAS matrix contents and oversized header counts, both out of scope.

issues.body:
Resolve: #3138
A build-time error raised while constructing a clause left plan construction in a poisoned state: the clause / segment loops never checked ErrorCtx_EncounteredError(), so subsequent clauses (a segment boundary WITH, an OPTIONAL MATCH, ORDER BY, UNWIND, a CALL {} subquery, ...) were still built on top of a partially-constructed / NULL-rooted plan. The malformed plan then crashed the server when the segments were tied together (_tie_segments) or when the plan was freed (OpBase_Free -> HashTableRelease, the reported signature).

This is the general form of the MERGE-only fix in #239/#3116: the reported query is a read query whose erroring clause precedes an OPTIONAL MATCH.

Fixes:
- stop building once a clause raises an error (ExecutionPlan_Populate- ExecutionPlan) and once a segment raises an error (_process_segments)
- in ExecutionPlan_FromTLS_AST, tear down the partial segments and return NULL instead of tying / adding an implicit result to a broken plan
- guard buildCallSubqueryPlan against a NULL / errored embedded plan before dereferencing it (mirrors the buildMergeOp guard), matching the new NULL-on-error contract of ExecutionPlan_FromTLS_AST

Regression tests added to test_optional_match.py (test28, the reported read-query shape) and test_call_subquery.py (test_54). Both trigger the error during plan construction via a non-boolean WHERE predicate (which passes AST validation), and were verified to crash the server without the fix.

issues.title: FalkorDB 4.16.7 can persist a staged UPDATE_EDGE after deletion
issues.body:
### Summary

In a disposable test using FalkorDB 4.16.7, I reproduced a conditional ordering where an edge update is staged, a main-thread execution path deletes the edge before the updater commits, and the already-staged UPDATE_EDGE is persisted after the deletion.

This reports the reproduced behavior; it does not establish that this mechanism caused any particular production incident.

### Observed behavior

I paused an updater after it staged an edge-property update and before commit, then compared two cleanup paths:

- **Normal writer path:** a normal GRAPH.QUERY cleanup remained queued behind the updater. The update effect persisted before the deletion effect.
- **Main-thread bypass path:** a MULTI/EXEC cleanup deleted the edge while the updater was paused. The cleanup persisted first. When the updater resumed, the graph mutation was skipped because the edge had been deleted, but its previously staged UPDATE_EDGE effect was still persisted afterward.

The second schedule produced this synthetic AOF order:

```text
create GRAPH.EFFECT
cleanup GRAPH.QUERY
stale UPDATE_EDGE in GRAPH.EFFECT
```

The synthetic edge ID was 0. The test used disposable generated data and did not use production AOF/RDB inputs.

### Reproduction notes

The test used a controlled pause at `QueryCtx_LockForCommit` after update evaluation/effect staging:

1. Start an updater that stages an edge-property update.
2. Pause it before commit.
3. Submit deletion through the normal writer path (control), then repeat with the MULTI/EXEC main-thread path.
4. Resume the updater and inspect persisted command order.

Environment: FalkorDB 4.16.7, image `falkordb/falkordb:v4.16.7`; Redis 8.2.3.

The attached ZIP contains the synthetic AOF result fixtures for both cases and per-file SHA-256 checksums. They are captured outputs, not a standalone driver for reproducing the scheduling race. The two cases use separately generated base RDB files with logically equivalent initial state; the bases are not byte-identical.

### Expected behavior

When commit detects that the target edge was deleted after the update was staged, the stale update should not be persisted. Alternatively, the effect should be reconciled or rejected before it can create a replay sequence that references a deleted edge.

### Actual behavior

In the bypass-path schedule, commit skipped the graph mutation for the deleted edge, but the previously staged UPDATE_EDGE remained in the persisted effect and followed the deletion.

### Scope and limitations

This demonstrates a conditional defect class in the tested FalkorDB 4.16.7 path. It does not establish which dispatch context produced any historical sequence. The result shows capability for this schedule, not historical attribution.

A replay-side check that rejects updates to missing edges can detect the inconsistency, but it does not prevent the stale effect from being generated.

### Relevant source revisions

These are public upstream source revisions, not hashes of production or cluster artifacts:

- FalkorDB 4.16.7 tag: `606756cda1687ba80c1a69f8598c6df61f6e4cb3`
- FalkorDB 4.20.7 tag: `2811bc690c37558b345c0f8491c05424729e6953`
- Effects-only replication change, PR #2570: `ed5b31553987c44ed516829631a9379b4589bc74`

Relevant code:

- [4.16.7 update evaluation and commit flow](https://github.com/FalkorDB/FalkorDB/blob/606756cda1687ba80c1a69f8598c6df61f6e4cb3/src/execution_plan/ops/op_update.c#L83-L130)
- [4.16.7 deleted-entity check during commit](https://github.com/FalkorDB/FalkorDB/blob/606756cda1687ba80c1a69f8598c6df61f6e4cb3/src/execution_plan/ops/shared/update_functions.c#L41-L80)
- [4.16.7 effect staging](https://github.com/FalkorDB/FalkorDB/blob/606756cda1687ba80c1a69f8598c6df61f6e4cb3/src/effects/effects.c#L632-L742)
- [4.20.7 missing-edge validation during effect application](https://github.com/FalkorDB/FalkorDB/blob/2811bc690c37558b345c0f8491c05424729e6953/src/effects/update_edge_effect.c#L126-L154)
- [PR #2570](https://github.com/FalkorDB/FalkorDB/pull/2570)

Related reports that may help distinguish adjacent failure modes: [#2235](https://github.com/FalkorDB/FalkorDB/issues/2235), [#2201](https://github.com/FalkorDB/FalkorDB/issues/2201), [#2246](https://github.com/FalkorDB/FalkorDB/issues/2246), and [PR #2581](https://github.com/FalkorDB/FalkorDB/pull/2581). I have not confirmed that these describe the same producer-side behavior.

### Question for maintainers

Could you advise whether this ordering is expected to be possible in 4.16.7 when an update has staged effects and deletion runs through a path that bypasses normal graph-writer serialization? If so, should commit discard or regenerate the staged effect after detecting the deleted entity?

[falkordb-stale-update-edge-fixtures.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/32708497/falkordb-stale-update-edge-fixtures.zip)

issues.title: [Rust] a_collapsed_list_matches_what_the_formula_predicted builds Run's cost model and never asserts on it, so the collapse rule is not checked against the bytes it wrote
issues.body:
﻿### Summary

`a_collapsed_list_matches_what_the_formula_predicted` (`graph/src/effects/v3/id_list.rs:2191`) builds a `Run` cost model and then never asserts anything about it. The test's own comment claims "whatever the rule chose, the bytes it actually wrote are what the arithmetic said they would be", but the arithmetic is never compared to the bytes, so the test cannot fail for the reason it is named.

### The dead code

```rust
let mut cost = Run::default();
cost.add_range(0, 1);
for i in 1..10_000_u64 {
    cost.add_range(i * 2, 1);
}
let mut r = Reader::new(&buf);
assert_eq!(decoded(&mut r, 10_000), ids);
```

`cost` is built at 2206-2210 and never read. It only reaches `add_range(&mut self)`, so neither the compiler nor clippy sees it as unused. The single remaining assertion is a round trip, which passes regardless of what `Run::prefers_bitmap` decides.

### Why this matters more than tidiness

The collapse decision is **normative for cross-engine byte agreement** - `id_list.rs:2121-2124`: "The decision rule only has to be the same on both engines to keep the bytes identical." The rule is `5 + bitmap_bytes() < range_bytes` (documented at `:51`), so if the arithmetic in `Run::bitmap_bytes()` and roaring's actual `serialized_size()` ever disagree, the two engines can pick *different* segmentations for the same id set and produce different buffers, with nothing detecting it.

There are two tests covering that pair, and this was the end-to-end half:

- `predicted_matches_roaring` (`:2125`) compares `Run::bitmap_bytes()` against `RoaringTreemap::serialized_size()` for 12 hand-picked range shapes. It only feeds `add_range` and builds a separate bitmap; it never inspects the bitmap a real `collapse` produced.
- `construction_order_changes_the_bytes` (`:2228`) pins that the by-range construction is the one `RunCost` models.

So the model is validated against the crate in isolation, and the by-range construction is validated as normative - but the two are never checked against each other through the real `IdList::collapse` output, which is exactly what this test was supposed to do and no longer does.

This is the failure mode the repo has explicitly legislated against, 14 lines above, in the sibling test at `:1959-1967`:

> Any other variant means this sweep is passing for a reason unrelated to truncation, and the check it is named for could have stopped working without the test noticing.

### Suggested change

Read the bitmap back out of the segment the encoder actually chose and compare:

```rust
let written = list
    .segments
    .iter()
    .find_map(|s| match s {
        Segment::Ascending { bitmap, .. } => Some(bitmap.serialized_size()),
        _ => None,
    })
    .expect("this shape should have collapsed");
assert_eq!(
    cost.bitmap_bytes(),
    written,
    "the rule chose a bitmap the arithmetic does not account for"
);
```

`list.segments` is a private field in the same module and `Run::bitmap_bytes` is private to it, so this needs no new imports.

### I could not verify that this passes, which is the point

`predictated_matches_roaring`'s cases top out at 7 runs in one container. This case is 10,000 single-id ranges - 10,000 runs over a 20,000-wide span, still one container. Working through `bucket_body` (`:267`): 10,000 ids sparse is 20,000 bytes against a 8,192-byte bitset, and a run store for 10,000 length-1 runs is far larger still, so the model picks the bitset - and `roaring`'s `optimize()` starts from a run store and converts on a strict win, so the crate should land in the same place. But that is an argument, not a run, and this case is precisely the one the existing 12 do not cover.

So this is deliberately filed as an issue rather than a PR: whoever picks it up can run `cargo test -p graph` in one command and find out. If the assertion holds, it is a one-hunk test-only change with no production risk. **If it fails, that is the more valuable outcome** - it would mean `Run::bitmap_bytes()` is wrong for high-run-count shapes, which is a wire-format bug affecting both engines, and the test should be landed as a fix to `Run` rather than as a test edit.

fix(runtime): allow startNode() and endNode() to accept null (#2723)
issues.body:
Closes #2723.

## Problem
In the Rust query engine, passing `null` to `startNode()` or `endNode()` (such as when evaluating expressions over unmatched `OPTIONAL MATCH` patterns or literal scalar calls) failed with a runtime type mismatch error:
```
Type mismatch: expected Edge but was Null
```

Per the FalkorDB documentation and openCypher specification, `startNode(null)` and `endNode(null)` must return `null` (three-valued logic / null propagation). The C engine (`v4.20.4`) already returns `null` correctly.

## Root Cause
In `graph/src/runtime/functions/entity.rs`, `startnode` and `endnode` were registered with:
```rust
args: [Type::Relationship]
```
omitting `Type::Null`. Sibling entity functions (`labels`, `id`, `properties`, `type`, etc.) already accept `Type::union([..., Type::Null])`. Although `startnode` and `endnode` already had their return type registered as `Type::union([Type::Node, Type::Null])`, they also lacked the `Some(Value::Null) => Ok(Value::Null)` match arm.

## Fix
1. In `graph/src/runtime/functions/entity.rs`, updated `args` for `startnode` and `endnode` to:
   ```rust
   args: [Type::union([Type::Relationship, Type::Null])]
   ```
2. Added `Some(Value::Null) => Ok(Value::Null)` pattern matching arms to both function implementations.

## Behavior
```cypher
OPTIONAL MATCH (n)-[r:NONEXISTENT]->() WHERE false RETURN startNode(r), endNode(r);
RETURN startNode(null) AS s, endNode(null) AS e;
```
- **Before**: `Type mismatch: expected Edge but was Null`
- **After**: `[[null, null]]` (matches C engine v4.20.4)

## Tests & Verification
- Added regression tests to `test16_edge_endpoints` in `tests/flow/test_function_calls.py` covering both `OPTIONAL MATCH` null relationships and literal null evaluation.
- Audited all sibling entity functions across `graph/src/runtime/functions/*.rs` to confirm complete NULL-handling parity.
- Verified formatting with `cargo fmt --all -- --check` (clean, exit code 0).

issues.body:
### Summary

FalkorDB's query engine is now largely implemented in Rust (`graph/` crate), but the Rust workspace is currently only buildable as an `rlib` linked into the C-side `falkordb.so`. There is no `cdylib` target and no `RedisModule_OnLoad` entrypoint implemented on the Rust side, which makes it impossible to build or load a Redis module from the Rust code alone. We would like an upstream-supported way to produce a loadable shared library from the Rust crate (or a documented/endorsed integration path for embedding and extending FalkorDB from Rust).

### Use case

We are integrating FalkorDB as the graph engine in an in-house knowledge-graph platform (the Rust engine is the main reason we chose FalkorDB over alternatives). We want to:

- build the Rust engine as a standalone loadable module / shared library for controlled deployment environments, and
- incrementally add custom Redis module commands (in Rust) that reuse the `graph` crate's query execution and indexing, without maintaining a fork of the C module glue.

Today both are blocked because the crate is not exposed as a loadable library and exports no module entrypoint.

### What we observed (pinned at v4.20.6, commit `574dfe84a`)

All evidence below is from an unmodified checkout of `FalkorDB/FalkorDB@574dfe84a` ("bump version to 4.20.6 (#2844)"), built inside the project's own build image (Debian-based, clang 21, Rust via rustup, GraphBLAS 10.5.0).

1. **`graph/Cargo.toml` has no `[lib]` section and no `crate-type` declaration** — cargo therefore emits only the default `rlib`. A normal `cargo build --release -p graph` produces:
   - `target/release/libgraph.rlib` (~626 MB, `626,134,924` bytes)
   - **no `libgraph.so` / any shared object** for the graph crate.
   The only `crate-type` entries anywhere in the tree belong to the bundled RediSearch dependencies (staticlib/rlib); the workspace root lists only `graph`, `fuzz`, and `runtime-fuzz-target`.

2. **The Rust tree contains no module entrypoint.** A full-tree search of `graph/src` finds no `RedisModule_OnLoad` and no `RedisModule_CreateCommand` implementation (only FFI type references pointing at the RediSearch API). The only `RedisModule_OnLoad` in the whole repository is the C-side one (`src/module.c`).

3. **Forcing `cdylib` compiles, but the result is not a Redis module.** Running

   ```bash
   cargo rustc -p graph --release --crate-type cdylib
   ```

   succeeds (`Finished release profile [optimized] target(s) in 7m 14s`, cold build) and produces `target/release/libgraph.so` (634,240 bytes; `ELF 64-bit LSB shared object, x86-64, ... not stripped`). However:

   - `nm -D libgraph.so | grep 'T RedisModule_OnLoad'` → **0 matches**; in fact the shared object exports **no defined text symbols at all** (`nm -D` exported `T` count = 0) and references no undefined `RedisModule_*` symbols either;
   - loading it with the redis-server shipped in the same build image fails decisively:

     ```text
     $ redis-server --port 6399 --save "" --appendonly no --loadmodule ./libgraph.so
     # Module /data/target/release/libgraph.so does not export RedisModule_OnLoad() symbol. Module not loaded.
     # Can't load module from /data/target/release/libgraph.so: server aborting
     ```

     (the server process exits immediately — `SERVER_DIED_ON_LOAD`.)

   In other words, adding `crate-type = ["cdylib"]` is necessary but not sufficient: the module binding layer itself (entrypoint + command registration + lifecycle) is absent.

### What we'd like (any subset would unblock us)

1. **Expose a `cdylib` target** for the graph crate (e.g. `crate-type = ["rlib", "cdylib"]` in `graph/Cargo.toml`), kept wired in CI so it doesn't bit-rot.
2. **Provide the module entrypoint and registration layer** — either in the `graph` crate or in a thin companion crate (e.g. `falkordb-module`) that:
   - implements `RedisModule_OnLoad`,
   - registers commands via `RedisModule_CreateCommand`,
   - wires the type methods / RDB save-load / AOF rewrite callbacks and thread-safe-context (write escalation) handling,
   - reuses the existing `graph` crate instead of duplicating engine logic.
3. Or, if a separately loadable Rust artifact is explicitly **not** the intended architecture: document the supported extension pattern for adding Rust commands/capabilities (fork-and-edit-C-glue? a future SDK?), so downstream teams don't have to reverse-engineer the C/Rust boundary.

### Questions for maintainers

- Is a Rust-loadable module (cdylib + `OnLoad`) on the roadmap, or is the C shared object intended to remain the only supported module boundary indefinitely?
- If it is on the roadmap, is there a preferred shape (cdylib in `graph` itself vs. a separate wrapper crate) and any rough timeline?
- Would a PR adding `[lib] crate-type = ["rlib", "cdylib"]` plus a minimal `OnLoad` skeleton be welcome as a starting point?

### Environment

- FalkorDB: v4.20.6, commit `574dfe84ae96f8560d842bc9ed05304d73691a90`
- Build image: project-provided build container (Debian trixie, clang 21.1.8, Rust stable via rustup as pinned in the repo, GraphBLAS v10.5.0)
- Host kernel: Linux 7.0 (Ubuntu 26.04), x86_64
- License noted: `graph/Cargo.toml` declares SSPL-1.0 (mentioned in case it affects how downstream users can consume a cdylib artifact).

Thanks for all the work on the Rust engine — happy to provide build logs, symbol dumps, or a PoC patch if useful.

issues.title: String range index: < and <= return every row for strings of two or more characters (v4.20.7)
issues.body:
### Summary

On FalkorDB **v4.20.7** (C engine), when a string property has a range index, `prop < x` and `prop <= x` return **every row**: the upper bound is ignored. `>`, `>=` and `=` are correct. The same query without the index is correct. It happens whenever the compared strings are two or more characters long; single-character strings are correct.

This is related to, but not covered by, #2963 item 3. That item needs a space in the value and says C "is wrong differently". Here plain strings like `'a2'`, `'12'` and ISO-8601 dates fail too.

### Environment

- FalkorDB v4.20.7 module (`GRAPH` module ver 42007) on Redis 8.10.2, macOS 27 arm64
- Also observed on the `falkordb/falkordb:v4.20.7` image

### Minimal reproduction

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE (:L {v:'a1'}), (:L {v:'a2'}), (:L {v:'a3'})"
GRAPH.QUERY g "MATCH (n:L) WHERE n.v < 'a2' RETURN count(n)"    -- 1 (correct)
GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE INDEX FOR (n:L) ON (n.v)"
GRAPH.QUERY g "MATCH (n:L) WHERE n.v < 'a2' RETURN count(n)"    -- 3 (expected 1)
GRAPH.QUERY g "MATCH (n:L) WHERE n.v <= 'a2' RETURN count(n)"   -- 3 (expected 2)
GRAPH.QUERY g "MATCH (n:L) WHERE n.v > 'a2' RETURN count(n)"    -- 1 (correct)
```

`GRAPH.EXPLAIN` shows `Node By Index Scan | (n:L)` for the `<` query.

Measured `< middle value` over three indexed values (expected 1 each time):

| values | result |
|---|---|
| `a`, `b`, `c` | 1 |
| `1`, `2`, `3` | 1 |
| `a1`, `a2`, `a3` | **3** |
| `11`, `12`, `13` | **3** |
| `aa1`, `aa2`, `aa3` | **3** |
| `a-1`, `a:1`, `a+1`, `a.1`, `a 1` families | **3** |
| `2026-09-25`, `2026-09-26`, `2026-09-27` | **3** |

Edge indexes behave the same way. The attached script creates two edges with ISO-8601 timestamps and counts `r.v <= '2026-09-25T23:00:00+00:00'`:

```
unindexed=1 indexed=2 toString=1 (correct: 1)
FAULT: the index scan ignores the upper bound
```

### Probe script

```bash
#!/bin/bash
# FalkorDB range-index probe: string property, `<=` through a range index.
# Two edges dated 25 and 26 Sep; "v <= 25 Sep 23:00" must count 1.
# Needs redis-cli and a FalkorDB server (PORT defaults to 6379; set REDISCLI_AUTH if it has a password).
# Uses and then deletes a throwaway graph named range_index_probe.
set -euo pipefail
C() { redis-cli -p "${PORT:-6379}" "$@"; }
G=range_index_probe; T="'2026-09-25T23:00:00+00:00'"
q() { C GRAPH.RO_QUERY $G "$1" | sed -n 2p; }
C GRAPH.DELETE $G >/dev/null 2>&1 || true
C GRAPH.QUERY $G "CREATE ()-[:R {v:'2026-09-25T00:00:00+00:00'}]->(), ()-[:R {v:'2026-09-26T00:00:00+00:00'}]->()" >/dev/null
plain=$(q "MATCH ()-[r:R]->() WHERE r.v <= $T RETURN count(r)")
C GRAPH.QUERY $G "CREATE INDEX FOR ()-[r:R]-() ON (r.v)" >/dev/null
indexed=$(q "MATCH ()-[r:R]->() WHERE r.v <= $T RETURN count(r)")
wrapped=$(q "MATCH ()-[r:R]->() WHERE toString(r.v) <= $T RETURN count(r)")
C GRAPH.DELETE $G >/dev/null
echo "unindexed=$plain indexed=$indexed toString=$wrapped (correct: 1)"
[ "$indexed" = 1 ] && echo "OK" || echo "FAULT: the index scan ignores the upper bound"
```

### Expected

The index does not change the result: `<` and `<=` return the rows the full scan returns.

### Impact

Graphiti range-indexes `RELATES_TO.valid_at` and `invalid_at` (ISO-8601 strings) and filters them with `<` and `<=`. On 4.20.7, "valid as of date X" queries therefore return every edge, including facts that only became valid later.

### Workaround

Wrap the property in `toString()`. The comparison stays exact and the planner does not use the index:

```cypher
MATCH (n:L) WHERE toString(n.v) < 'a2' RETURN count(n)   -- 1
```

For Graphiti, patch its date-filter builder at import time:

```python
from graphiti_core.search import search_filters
from graphiti_core.search.search_filters import ComparisonOperator

_NULL_OPS = (ComparisonOperator.is_null, ComparisonOperator.is_not_null)

def _date_filter_query_constructor(value_name, param_name, operator):
    if operator in _NULL_OPS:
        return f"({value_name} {operator.value})"
    return f"(toString({value_name}) {operator.value} {param_name})"

search_filters.date_filter_query_constructor = _date_filter_query_constructor
```

issues.title: fix(functions): name received types in the engine's vocabulary in entity.rs
issues.body:
Closes #3126

﻿Four type-mismatch messages in `entity.rs` that are not written in the engine's own type vocabulary. Both are one-liners; this is a message-correctness fix, not a behaviour change.

## 1. `indegree`/`outdegree` use Rust's `Debug` spelling

`parse_degree_args` (`graph/src/runtime/functions/entity.rs:304`) hand-rolls its type check because `indegree`/`outdegree` are registered `var_arg: Type::Any` → `FnArguments::VarLength`, and both `GraphFn::validate` and `validate_args_type` are deliberate no-ops for var-len. So that check is the **only** one these functions get, and its message is the user-facing one. All three sites formatted the received type with `{:?}`.

`Type` derives `Debug` **and** has a hand-written `Display` impl at `mod.rs:610-654` whose entire purpose is the user-facing vocabulary (`Self::Int => "Integer"`, `Self::Bool => "Boolean"`, `Self::Relationship => "Edge"`). The framework's own message uses `{}` (`mod.rs:836-842`), and C uses `SIType_ToString`, which returns `"Integer"`.

| query | before | after / C |
|---|---|---|
| `RETURN indegree(1)` | `...but was Int` | `...but was Integer` |
| `RETURN outdegree(n, [1])` | `...but was Int` | `...but was Integer` |
| `RETURN outdegree(n, 'R', 1)` | `...but was Int` | `...but was Integer` |
| `RETURN outdegree(n, 'R', ['X'])` | `...but was List(List(Any))` | `...but was List` |

The last one is the worst: it leaks the internal `Type::List(Type::Any)` structure into a string a user reads. Three `{:?}` → `{}`.

## 2. `hasLabels` drops the received type on its catch-all

`has_labels` checks list element types by hand, and three arms name what arrived — `but was Integer`, `but was Float`, `but was Boolean`. The catch-all covers the other **12** `Value` variants and said nothing:

```
MATCH (n) WHERE hasLabels(n, ['person', null])   ->  Type mismatch: expected String
MATCH (n) WHERE hasLabels(n, ['person', {a:1}])  ->  Type mismatch: expected String
```

It was the only type-mismatch message in the file without a `but was X` clause. Now uses `Value::name()`, the same helper the rest of the codebase uses for this, and whose spellings match the three arms above it.

## Testing

**`cargo test -p graph`** — new `mod tests` in `entity.rs` (the file had none). `parse_degree_args` is a module-private pure function and every one of the three sites returns before a `Runtime` is touched, so no harness is needed:
- the four mismatch spellings above,
- `the_arity_message_is_untouched` — the "Received 3 arguments ... expected at most 2" path is a different branch and must not change,
- `the_accepted_shapes_are_untouched` — `degree(node)` and `degree(node, ['R'])` still parse.

**Flow suite** — new `test19a_hasLabels_type_mismatch_names_the_received_type` in `tests/flow/test_function_calls.py` (listed in `flow_tests_done.txt`), covering all six reachable element types. Written as `error = None` + `assertTrue(error is not None, ...)` rather than the try/except shape used by the neighbouring test, so it cannot pass vacuously if the query stops raising.

**No existing assertion moves.** `test_function_calls.py:2415`/`:2432` assert only the substrings `"Type mismatch"` / `"Received"`, and the existing `hasLabels` assertion at `:627` goes through the untouched `Value::Int` arm — and `Value::name()` returns `"Integer"` for it anyway. `Steps.py` in the TCK asserts only `"Type mismatch" in str(e)`.

## Relation to #340

#340 asks for *more* in these messages (function name, argument index). This is orthogonal — it makes the existing message well-formed rather than adding fields. Either can land first.

`cargo fmt` clean against `fn_params_layout = "Vertical"`.


<!-- This is an auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->
## Summary by CodeRabbit

* **Bug Fixes**
  * Type mismatch errors for label checks and degree-related functions now identify the type of the received value, including invalid labels, nodes, list elements, and variadic arguments.
* **Tests**
  * Added coverage for invalid label types and degree argument errors. Confirmed that accepted argument shapes, duplicate filtering, and arity handling remain unchanged.

issues.title: [Rust] entity.rs type-mismatch messages use Rust's Debug type names (Int, List(List(Any))) and hasLabels omits the received type
issues.body:
﻿### Summary

Four type-mismatch messages in `entity.rs` are not written in the engine's own type vocabulary, and one omits the received type altogether.

### The two problems

**1. `indegree` / `outdegree` name types with Rust's `Debug` spelling.** `parse_degree_args` (`graph/src/runtime/functions/entity.rs:304`) hand-rolls its type check because `indegree`/`outdegree` are registered `var_arg: Type::Any`, which produces `FnArguments::VarLength` - and `GraphFn::validate` / `validate_args_type` are both deliberate no-ops for var-len. So these are the *only* type check those functions get, and their messages are the user-facing ones. All three sites format with `{:?}`:

```rust
return Err(format!(
    "Type mismatch: expected Node but was {:?}",
    other.get_type()
));
```

`Type` derives `Debug` **and** hand-writes a `Display` impl (`graph/src/runtime/functions/mod.rs:610-654`) whose whole purpose is the user-facing vocabulary - `Self::Int => write!(f, "Integer")`, `Self::Bool => "Boolean"`, `Self::Relationship => "Edge"`. The framework's own type-mismatch message uses Display (`mod.rs:836-842`), and C uses `SIType_ToString`, which returns `"Integer"`.

| query | today | engine standard / C |
|---|---|---|
| `MATCH (n) RETURN indegree(1)` | `...but was Int` | `...but was Integer` |
| `MATCH (n) RETURN outdegree(n, [1])` | `...but was Int` | `...but was Integer` |
| `MATCH (n) RETURN outdegree(n, 'R', 1)` | `...but was Int` | `...but was Integer` |
| `MATCH (n) RETURN outdegree(n, 'R', ['X'])` | `...but was List(List(Any))` | `...but was List` |

The last row is the worst: it leaks the internal `Type::List(Type::Any)` structure into a user-facing string.

**2. `hasLabels` drops the received type on its catch-all arm.** `has_labels` (`:86`) checks list element types by hand and three arms name what arrived:

```rust
Value::Int(_)   => return Err("Type mismatch: expected String but was Integer".to_string()),
Value::Float(_) => return Err("Type mismatch: expected String but was Float".to_string()),
Value::Bool(_)  => return Err("Type mismatch: expected String but was Boolean".to_string()),
_ => return Err("Type mismatch: expected String".to_string()),
```

The catch-all handles 12 of the 15 `Value` variants and says nothing about what it got:

```
MATCH (n) WHERE hasLabels(n, ['person', null])   ->  Type mismatch: expected String
MATCH (n) WHERE hasLabels(n, ['person', {a:1}])  ->  Type mismatch: expected String
MATCH (n) WHERE hasLabels(n, ['person', [1]])    ->  Type mismatch: expected String
```

This is the only type-mismatch message in the file that lacks the `but was X` clause, so it is inconsistent with the three arms directly above it and with the framework.

### Expected

Every type-mismatch message names the received type using the engine's vocabulary: `Integer`, not `Int`; `List`, not `List(List(Any))`; and `hasLabels` should report what it received on every arm.

### Relationship to #340

#340 asks for *more* in these messages (the function name and the argument index). This is orthogonal: it makes the existing messages well-formed. The two compose and either can land first.

### Test impact

None expected. `tests/flow/test_function_calls.py:2415` and `:2432` assert only the substrings `"Type mismatch"` / `"Received"`, and the `hasLabels` assertion at `:627` goes through the `Value::Int` arm and keeps its exact wording.

issues.title: fix(temporal): reject non-digits in compact date and time strings
issues.body:
Closes #3124

﻿A second fix from the same area as #3118, and the same shape of defect: a parser that drops input it should have rejected.

`parse_date_string` (`graph/src/runtime/functions/temporal.rs:148`) built its digit buffer with `filter(char::is_ascii_digit)` - which *discards* non-digits rather than rejecting them - and then dispatched on the length of what survived. So:

```
RETURN toString(date('2o15o7o21'))          -- Rust: '2015-07-21'
RETURN toString(date('hello20230506world')) -- Rust: '2023-05-06'
RETURN toString(localtime('xx123456yy'))    -- Rust: '12:34:56'
```

Malformed input producing a valid-looking value with no error. `date('2o15o7o21')` quietly equalling `date('2015-07-21')` is the sharp form - a caller reading from a dirty source gets a plausible date out of a malformed string with no way to notice.

## The change

One guard in each of the two compact branches:

```rust
if !s.chars().all(char::is_ascii_digit) {
    return Err(format!("Invalid date string: {s}"));
}
```

Nothing that is currently valid changes - every documented compact form (`2015`, `201507`, `2015202`, `20150721`, and times `21` / `2140` / `214032`) is already pure ASCII digits, and `parse_time_string` strips a fractional part at `:274` before the check runs, so `214032.142` is unaffected. The filter was never load-bearing.

The defect is confined to the compact branches. The hyphenated date form and the colon time form use `split` + `parse` and already error correctly, and the `W` week-date form returns before either of these. Both are now covered by explicit tests so that stays true.

## Testing

New `mod compact_parser_rejects_junk_tests` in `temporal.rs` (run by `cargo test -p graph`, part of the required `ci-gate`):
- `compact_date_rejects_embedded_letters` / `compact_date_rejects_other_punctuation` - the four repro strings.
- `compact_date_keeps_every_documented_form` - all four compact date forms still produce the same dates, so the guard cannot over-reject.
- `the_hyphenated_and_week_forms_are_untouched` - pins the paths the change does not touch.
- `colon_less_time_rejects_embedded_letters` / `colon_less_time_keeps_every_documented_form` - same pair for times, including the fractional form.
- `the_colon_time_form_is_untouched`.

Breakage risk: `tests/flow/test_temporal.py` (in `flow_tests_done.txt`) only feeds clean inputs to the string parsers, and the TCK temporal features use clean ISO strings only. `date`/`localtime`/`localdatetime`/`duration` are deliberately **not** in `tests/test_functions.py`'s fuzzer parametrisation, so the random-string generator never reaches these parsers.

`cargo fmt` clean against `fn_params_layout = "Vertical"`.


<!-- This is an auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->
## Summary by CodeRabbit

* **Bug Fixes**
  * Compact dates and colonless times now reject inputs containing letters or punctuation instead of silently ignoring those characters.
  * Hyphenated dates, ISO week dates, and colon-separated times continue to parse as before.
<!-- end of auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->

issues.title: [Rust] date()/localtime() drop every non-digit from a compact string: date('2o15o7o21') silently returns 2015-07-21
issues.body:
﻿### Summary

`date()` and `localtime()` accept arbitrary junk embedded in a compact (separator-less) string. Every non-digit character is silently dropped before the string is interpreted, so a malformed input returns a valid-looking value with no error.

### Reproduction

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "RETURN toString(date('2o15o7o21'))"
-- Rust: '2015-07-21'
-- C:    error
```

The `o`s vanish and the result is indistinguishable from the correct answer. Same for:

| query | Rust | expected |
|---|---|---|
| `RETURN toString(date('2o15o7o21'))` | `2015-07-21` | error |
| `RETURN toString(date('hello20230506world'))` | `2023-05-06` | error |
| `RETURN toString(date('+2015'))` | `2015-01-01` | error |
| `RETURN toString(date('2015 07 21'))` | `2015-07-21` | error |
| `RETURN toString(localtime('xx123456yy'))` | `12:34:56` | error |

`date('2o15o7o21')` quietly equalling `date('2015-07-21')` is the sharp form: a caller reading from a dirty data source gets a plausible date out of a malformed string with no way to notice.

### Mechanism

`parse_date_string` (`graph/src/runtime/functions/temporal.rs:148`) builds its digit buffer by filtering, which discards rather than rejects:

```rust
let digits_only: String = s.chars().filter(char::is_ascii_digit).collect();
```

and then dispatches on the length of what survived:

```rust
} else {
    // Compact formats: YYYY, YYYYMM, YYYYDDD, YYYYMMDD
    match digits_only.len() {
```

`parse_time_string:296-297` has the identical pair for the colon-less time form.

The hyphenated date branch (`:160`) and the colon time branch (`:277`) are **not** affected - they use `split` plus `parse`, which already errors. The `W` week-date form returns at `:150`. So the defect is confined to the two compact branches.

The filter is not load-bearing: every documented compact form (`2015`, `201507`, `2015202`, `20150721`, and times `21` / `2140` / `214032`) is already pure ASCII digits, and `parse_time_string` strips a fractional part at `:274` before the filter runs.

### Expected

Reject any character that is not an ASCII digit, in both compact branches. Nothing that is currently valid changes.

### Scope notes

- Not the same as #2930 (a *panic* on a multi-byte week string) or #2936 (`dayOfWeek` base), both in the week-date path.
- Not #2937's conversion items; those are about `toString`/`toInteger` output shape, not about what the date parser accepts.
- `date('2015-W30-2')`, `date('2015-07-21')`, `localtime('21:40:32')` and the zero-argument `date()` / `localtime()` / `localdatetime()` forms are all unaffected.

issues.title: test(cluster): wait for announced hostnames before building the client
issues.body:
Closes #2941

Harness-only change: no test file is touched, and no assertion changes. It is the only kind of fix here that does not need a new assertion, because the thing being fixed is the wait that happens *before* the tests run.

## The race

`_bootstrap_cluster` (`tests/flow/common.py:382`) forms the cluster in three phases and its readiness gate is:

```python
if (fields.get("cluster_state", "").strip() == "ok"
        and int(fields.get("cluster_known_nodes", "0")) == n):
```

That only proves the **gossip topology** arrived. A peer learned through gossip counts as known before its `--cluster-announce-hostname` has been merged, and under `--cluster-preferred-endpoint-type hostname` (both set at `common.py:367-368`) an unmerged node is reported as `?`.

`Env()` then builds the client at `common.py:709`, which auto-detects cluster mode and returns a cluster-aware client. `RedisCluster` snapshots its slot map from `CLUSTER SLOTS` **at construction**, so `?:6379` is recorded then. In cluster mode `udf_load` opens a direct connection to every primary, so `test_udf_delete_propagation` (first alphabetically, so its `udf_load` is the first all-primaries command after bootstrap) is where it surfaces.

## The fix

A fourth phase, reusing the existing `attempts`/`interval` budget so there is no new tunable:

```python
for c, (h, p) in zip(clients, shard_addrs):
    for _ in range(attempts):
        try:
            if not _slots_have_unresolved_endpoint(
                    c.execute_command("CLUSTER", "SLOTS")):
                break
        except Exception:
            pass
        time.sleep(interval)
    else:
        raise RuntimeError(...)
```

`_slots_have_unresolved_endpoint` walks `entry[2:]` (the master plus any replicas, so it stays correct if cluster+replicas is ever wired up) and looks for `?` in the address. The bootstrap clients at `common.py:398-402` are built without `decode_responses`, so the address arrives as `bytes`; the helper accepts `str` too, so the check cannot silently degrade into a no-op if that ever changes.

Every shard announces a hostname, so `?` is never a steady state here. If it persists past the budget, failing with "announced hostnames have not propagated" is a better outcome than handing the test a client that cannot connect.

## Why this is safe

- **No assertion is touched.** Nothing becomes vacuous; the change only moves *when* `Env()` considers the cluster ready.
- **No-op for non-cluster paths.** `_bootstrap_cluster` is only reached from `_spawn_falkordb_cluster`, so every non-cluster `Env()` is unaffected.
- **Benefits the whole bucket.** `test_udf_cluster.py` is routed to the spawn bucket by `test_matrix_split.py:39-42` (`env='oss-cluster'`), and per the issue this race can hit any spawn-mode `oss-cluster` test - so every such test gets the wait, not just this file.
- **Cost when things are healthy:** one extra `CLUSTER SLOTS` round trip per shard, typically one 0.2 s poll. The full 20 s only elapses on a genuine failure, which then raises a precise message.

## Caveat worth stating

I could not verify the exact `?` rendering against Redis source in this repo (no `redis.conf` is vendored and code search only reaches the default branch), so that detail rests on the issue's own reproduction plus the flags, which I did read verbatim at `common.py:362-369`. The two flags are what make the reported endpoint type relevant, so if a maintainer wants to confirm the `CLUSTER SLOTS` shape against a live node before merging, that is the one thing worth checking - the helper is deliberately tolerant of both `bytes` and `str` addresses so a wrong guess degrades into a timeout with a clear message rather than a false pass.

issues.title: fix(algo): a costProp an edge does not have contributes 1, not 0
issues.body:
Closes #3121

Split out of #343, which asks for two things at once. This is the half that is a C-parity bug. The other half - replacing a *negative or zero* weight or cost with 1 - is not a parity bug (C does not clamp either, and `Dijkstra.h:21-31` states non-negative weights as a deliberately unguarded precondition), so it is a Rust-vs-C policy choice for a maintainer and is left alone here.

## The bug

`edge_numeric_attr` (`graph/src/runtime/functions/algo_procedures.rs:2104`) takes one `default` and uses it for two cases C keeps apart:

```rust
prop.map_or(default, |p| {
    match g.get_relationship_attribute(edge_id, p) {
        Some(Value::Float(f)) => f,
        Some(Value::Int(i)) => i as f64,
        _ => default,
    }
})
```

C's `_sum_path_cost` (`src/procedures/proc_sp_paths.c:472` on `master`) separates them:

```c
if(cost_prop == ATTRIBUTE_ID_NONE) {
    return 0;
}
...
    SIValue c = GraphEntity_GetNumericPropertyOrDefault ((GraphEntity *) Path_GetEdge(p, i),
            cost_prop, SI_LongVal(1));
```

| case | C | Rust (`default = 0.0`) |
|---|---|---|
| `costProp` not configured | `0` | `0` - already right |
| `costProp` configured, edge lacks it | `1` | `0` - **wrong** |
| `costProp` configured, edge has a value | that value | that value - already right |

So `pathCost` came out one too low per property-less edge. It is not only a reported number: `enumerate_paths` gates `maxCost` against the running `next_cost` (`:2528`), so a path C admits can be pruned by Rust and vice versa - the divergence changes results.

## The change

One accessor, mirroring C's split, and three call sites switched to it (`:2308` the Dijkstra result, `:2397` the backtracked chain, `:2518` `enumerate_paths`):

```rust
fn edge_cost_attr(
    g: &Graph,
    edge_id: RelationshipId,
    prop: Option<&Arc<String>>,
) -> f64 {
    prop.map_or(0.0, |p| match g.get_relationship_attribute(edge_id, p) {
        Some(Value::Float(f)) => f,
        Some(Value::Int(i)) => i as f64,
        _ => 1.0,
    })
}
```

The value handling is deliberately identical to `edge_numeric_attr` - a negative or zero cost is still reported as-is. That is not an oversight: C does not clamp, so clamping here would be an unrequested divergence in the other direction.

The three weight call sites already pass `default = 1.0`, which is exactly C's behaviour for both the unconfigured and the missing case, so they are untouched. `edge_numeric_attr` keeps its four remaining weight uses.

## Testing

New `test12a_costprop_missing_on_an_edge_contributes_one` in `tests/flow/test_path_algorithms.py` (`testAllShortestPaths`, in `flow_tests_done.txt` line 84, services bucket), on a two-hop path whose second edge deliberately has no `cost`:

| query | before | after | C |
|---|---|---|---|
| `weightProp: 'weight', costProp: 'cost'` | `pathCost` 2 | **3** | 3 |
| no `costProp` | `pathCost` 0 | 0 | 0 |
| `costProp: 'cost', maxCost: 2` | one row | **no rows** | no rows |

`pathCost` is `2 + 1` after the fix: the first edge has `cost: 2`, the second has no `cost` at all and `costProp` is configured, so it contributes the default 1. Before the fix the second edge contributed 0 and the total came out one low.

The three cases pin all three branches: the configured-and-missing default, the unconfigured default that must not move, and the `maxCost` gate - which is the assertion that shows this was not only a cosmetic reporting difference. Before the fix that third query returned a row, because the running cost was `2 + 0` and `2 > 2` is false.

Every existing fixture in that file gives each relationship a positive `cost`, so the default never fires there and no asserted number moves. `pathCost` is asserted in that one file repo-wide; the only two places that pass a `costProp` naming a missing property assert either an empty result or a `pathWeight` only.

## Checks

`cargo fmt` clean (verified against the repo's `fn_params_layout = "Vertical"`), and the new function plus all three call sites were type-checked standalone before pushing.

## Summary by CodeRabbit

* **Bug Fixes**
  * Path calculations now assign a cost of 1 when a configured edge-cost property is missing or nonnumeric. When no cost property is configured, edges continue to contribute 0.
  * Numeric edge costs, including negative and zero values, are used as provided when calculating path totals.
  * Maximum-cost limits exclude paths whose configured total cost exceeds the limit across supported path-finding operations.
<!-- end of auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->

issues.title: [Rust] algo.SPpaths/SSpaths: a costProp an edge does not have contributes 0, not 1 (C parity; pathCost under-reported and maxCost prunes differently)
issues.body:
﻿### Summary

`algo.SPpaths` / `algo.SSpaths` under-report `pathCost` when `costProp` names a property that a relationship on the path does not have. C contributes `1` for such an edge; Rust contributes `0`.

Split out of #343, which asks for two things at once. This is the half that is a C-parity bug and can be fixed without a policy decision. The other half of #343 - replacing a *negative or zero* weight or cost with 1 - is not a parity bug: C does not clamp either (`Dijkstra.h:21-31` states non-negative weights as an unguarded precondition), so that half is a Rust-vs-C policy choice for a maintainer and is deliberately not addressed here.

### Reproduction

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE (:L {id:'A'})-[:E {weight:1, cost:2}]->(:L {id:'B'})-[:E2 {weight:1}]->(:L {id:'C'})"
GRAPH.QUERY g "MATCH (s:L {id:'A'}), (t:L {id:'C'})
              CALL algo.SPpaths({sourceNode: s, targetNode: t,
                                 weightProp: 'weight', costProp: 'cost'})
              YIELD pathWeight, pathCost RETURN pathWeight, pathCost"
```

`costProp: 'cost'` is configured, and `:E2` does not have a `cost` property.

| engine | pathWeight | pathCost |
|---|---|---|
| Rust `main` | 2 | **1** |
| C `master` | 2 | **2** |

The two edges of the path contribute `2 + 0` on Rust and `2 + 1` on C.

It is not only the reported number. `maxCost` is checked against the running `next_cost` in `enumerate_paths` (`graph/src/runtime/functions/algo_procedures.rs:2528`), so a path that C admits under a given `maxCost` can be pruned by Rust and vice versa - the divergence changes results, not just output.

### Mechanism

`edge_numeric_attr` (`graph/src/runtime/functions/algo_procedures.rs:2104`) takes a single `default` and uses it for two different C cases:

```rust
prop.map_or(default, |p| {
    match g.get_relationship_attribute(edge_id, p) {
        Some(Value::Float(f)) => f,
        Some(Value::Int(i)) => i as f64,
        _ => default,
    }
})
```

C keeps the two apart. In `_sum_path_cost` (`src/procedures/proc_sp_paths.c:472`) on `master`:

```c
if(cost_prop == ATTRIBUTE_ID_NONE) {
    return 0;
}
...
    SIValue c = GraphEntity_GetNumericPropertyOrDefault ((GraphEntity *) Path_GetEdge(p, i),
            cost_prop, SI_LongVal(1));
```

So:

| case | C | Rust (`default = 0.0`) |
|---|---|---|
| `costProp` not configured | `0` | `0` - correct |
| `costProp` configured, edge lacks it | `1` | `0` - **wrong** |
| `costProp` configured, edge has a value | that value | that value - correct |

The weight call sites are already right: C uses `1` for both the unconfigured and the missing case, which is exactly what `default = 1.0` gives.

### Expected

A configured `costProp` falls back to `1` per edge that does not carry a positive numeric value; an unconfigured one still contributes nothing. Same rule for all three cost call sites (`:2308` Dijkstra result, `:2397` the backtracked chain, `:2518` `enumerate_paths`).

### Note on scope

`pathCost` is asserted in exactly one test file repo-wide, `tests/flow/test_path_algorithms.py`, and its fixtures give every relationship a positive `cost`, so the default never fires there and no asserted number moves. The two places that do pass a `costProp` naming a missing property assert an empty result or a `pathWeight` only.

issues.title: fix(algo): dedupe relTypes in algo.SPpaths/SSpaths config
issues.body:
Closes #2940

Splitting this out because it is not actually a flake: `relTypes: ['E', 'E']` returns duplicated paths on **every** run of current `main`. `test17_sp_duplicate_edges` is flaky only in that it usually fails to notice.

## The bug

`get_node_relationships_by_type` (`graph/src/graph/graph.rs:2085`) builds the candidate set as **one matrix per listed type**:

```rust
let matrices: Vec<&Tensor> = if types.is_empty() {
    self.relationship_matrices.iter().collect()
} else {
    types.iter().filter_map(|t| self.get_relationship_matrix(t)).collect()
};
```

`parse_common_path_config` pushed every entry of the `relTypes` list verbatim, so `['E', 'E']` produced `[E_tensor, E_tensor]`. From there:

1. `node_successors` and the `enumerate_paths` inner loop (`algo_procedures.rs:2158`, `:2254`, `:2353`) each iterate that vector, so every edge is yielded twice.
2. The DFS re-explores each subtree once per copy, so a path is found `2^hops` times.
3. `record_found_path` has no identity check, and the k-minimal result set fills with copies of one path.

`pathCount: 1` is unaffected - that arm keeps a single best path - which is why only the `pathCount >= 2` rows of the issue's table are wrong.

## The fix

Dedupe at the parse boundary, order-preserving:

```rust
Value::String(s) => {
    if !types.contains(s) {
        types.push(s.clone());
    }
}
```

`relTypes` is a set everywhere else it is read - existence validation at `:1336` and `:2704`, `get_src_dest_relationships` at `:2162` - so a repeat was never meaningful, only harmful. This narrows the accepted input space, and only for inputs that are wrong today. `extract_rel_types` (the separate `relationshipTypes` key used by the centrality/Louvain-family procedures) is deliberately not touched.

`graph.rs:2085` is also deliberately not touched. It has other callers - `all_shortest_paths.rs` and `cond_var_len_traverse.rs`, whose `rp.types` come from Cypher `*` patterns and already dedup through a visited set. Widening the fix there needs its own coverage.

## The test was not catching it

```python
self.env.assertEqual(len(dup.result_set), expected_len)
for row in dup.result_set:
    self.env.assertContains(row, single.result_set)
```

With the bug, `dup` is `[X, X, X]`, which has the right *length* and each of whose rows is a member of `single` - so the assertion passed whenever the random graph happened to offer 3+ qualifying paths, which is the common case. Replaced with a comparison of which paths came back:

```python
def node_ids(result):
    return sorted(tuple(n.id for n in row[0].nodes())
                  for row in result.result_set)

self.env.assertEqual(node_ids(dup), node_ids(single))
```

This is strictly stronger - it pins identity and multiplicity, where the old loop only checked membership - and it is strictly deterministic: the two queries are now literally the same query, so the two sets must match for any graph. Node ids rather than `Path` objects so the assertion rests on neither `Path.__eq__` nor on how RLTest compares two `Path`s, and sorted so it does not depend on the order the search emits.

Both hunks land together on purpose. The test change alone would turn the flake into a deterministic red.

## Testing

- `tests/flow/test_path_algorithms.py` is in `flow_tests_done.txt` (line 84, services bucket) and is where the original flake was observed (`a-sanitizer-flow-svc`, `release-flow-svc`).
- `test17` is the only test that passes a repeated `relTypes`; no other test in `tests/flow/`, `tests/test_functions.py` or `tests/tck/` does, so no other expected count moves.
- The other two `relTypes` tests (`relTypes: [1]`, `relTypes: ['a', 1]`) assert the "must be array of strings" error, which this change does not touch.
- The new snippet was type-checked standalone before pushing, and the file is `cargo fmt` clean.

  * Path algorithm tests verify that queries with duplicate relationship types return the same path node sequences as equivalent queries with single relationship types, regardless of result order.

issues.title: test(functions): bound the nesting depth of random LIST arguments
issues.body:
Closes #2938

`random_value` recursed into `Type.LIST` with no depth limit and wrapped each level in `str()`. `str()` on a list calls `repr()` per element, so every level re-quotes and re-escapes the entire subtree underneath it - the Cypher literal roughly doubles per level of nesting. The recursion does terminate (each level draws 0-9 elements, each of which is a LIST with probability 1/6), but the tail is long enough that ~6% of `pytest` runs produced a multi-gigabyte argument and the process was OOM-killed with exit 137.

## The change

One constant and one parameter:

```python
MAX_LIST_DEPTH = 2

def random_value(type, depth=0):
    ...
    elif type == Type.LIST:
        pool = all_types if depth < MAX_LIST_DEPTH else [t for t in all_types if t != Type.LIST]
        return str([random_value(choice(pool), depth + 1) for _ in range(choice(range(0, 10)))])
```

Past the depth cap the elements are drawn from the non-LIST types, so the literal is bounded at tens of KB for **any** seed rather than for an average one. Concretely: the innermost list holds at most 9 scalars of at most 100 characters; its `repr()` is ~1 KB; the level above holds 9 of those, whose escaped `repr()` is ~17 KB; that string is the return value and is not escaped again. So the worst case is bounded by a constant, not by luck.

`random_value` has exactly two callers - its own recursion and `validate_function:87` - so the new defaulted parameter touches nothing else.

## Why this does not weaken the test

Every assertion in `tests/test_functions.py` is about **arity**:

```
assert "Received {len(args)} arguments to function '{func}', expected at most {most}" in str(e)
```

`len(args)` is the number of arguments, which this change does not affect. The bound is on the *value* of an argument, not on how many there are, and no expected count moves.

The coverage that is lost is negligible and, per the issue, was not real to begin with: because `str()` re-quoted each level, a nested list was already always a list of *strings* - never a nested list, never an int, bool or null inside a list. The probability of ever reaching depth 26 (the point where the old growth actually bites) is ~2.6e-4 per draw.

## Deliberately not in this PR

The issue also suggests building list literals as Cypher text instead of via `str()`, and seeding the RNG. Both are left out on purpose:

- **Cypher-text literals** would change *what* is generated, not just how large it is - `str(['1', 'abc'])` is a Cypher list of two strings, where a hand-built literal would be a real list of mixed values. That is arguably a second bug, but it changes what the engine is asked to handle and could turn a CI-stability fix into a red PR. Worth its own change, once someone has looked at the new failures.
- **Seeding** would call `random.seed()`, and `test_functions.py` runs in the same pytest process as `test_e2e.py`, `test_mvcc.py` and `test_concurrency.py`. Seeding the global RNG would change the inputs those suites draw. With the OOM gone, replayability is much less urgent than it was.

## CI coverage

`tests/test_functions.py` is not in `flow_tests_done.txt` (that file lists `tests/flow/*` only), but it is run directly by the `ci-pipeline` job:

```
RELEASE=1 pytest tests/test_e2e.py tests/test_functions.py tests/test_mvcc.py tests/test_concurrency.py -vv
```

and again by `test-image` in the merge queue - which is where the exit-137 kills were landing (7 of the 15 affected PRs were merge-queue runs).

  * Slow-log scenarios now use updated workloads and query patterns, including concurrent execution through a connection pool and revised reset and replacement cases. The displacement scenario also uses a revised workload, and the entry-limit scenario description has been updated.
