issues.title: fix(temporal): reject an ISO 8601 duration whose last number has no unit
issues.body:
Closes #3117

`parse_duration_string` (`graph/src/runtime/functions/temporal.rs`) accumulates digits into `num_buf` and only converts them when a unit character (`Y`/`M`/`W`/`D`/`H`/`S`) closes them. Neither loop inspects `num_buf` afterwards, so a number with no unit after it is dropped instead of rejected.

| query | before | after | C |
|---|---|---|---|
| `RETURN duration('P5')` | `PT0S` | error | `null` |
| `RETURN duration('P-')` | `PT0S` | error | `null` |
| `RETURN duration('P1Y5')` | `P1Y` | error | `null` |
| `RETURN duration('P1M2')` | `P1M` | error | `null` |
| `RETURN duration('PT4H5')` | `PT4H` | error | `null` |

The silent part matters more than the acceptance: `duration('P1Y5')` used to *mean* `P1Y`, so a caller that builds an ISO string by concatenation got a different duration than it asked for with no signal at all.

## The change

One check, after the time part, where the two loops have shared `num_buf`:

```rust
if !num_buf.is_empty() {
    return Err(format!("Invalid duration, missing unit after: {num_buf}"));
}
```

One check is enough rather than one per loop: the buffer is cleared at the start of the time part, so a non-empty buffer at that point can only ever mean "digits that no unit closed". Putting it after the `if let` also covers the date-only case, where the leftover is still sitting in the buffer from the date loop.

Valid input is untouched - `P5D`, `P2W`, `P1Y2M3DT4H5M6S` and the negative components (`P-1D`) all parse as before, because in each of those a unit character closes every number.

## How it was tested

**`cargo test -p graph`** - new `mod parse_duration_string_tests` at the end of `temporal.rs`:
- `a_trailing_number_with_no_unit_is_rejected` - the six spellings from the table above all return `Err`.
- `a_number_with_a_unit_still_parses` - `P5D`, `P2W` and `P1Y2M3DT4H5M6S` still produce the same component tuples, so the fix is not "reject more".

**Flow suite** (`tests/flow/test_temporal.py`, in `flow_tests_done.txt`) - new `test_duration_from_string_rejects_a_number_with_no_unit` in `testTemporalDuration` runs the same six strings through `duration($str)` and asserts each raises. The existing `test_duration_from_string` covers the accepted spellings end to end and is unchanged.

Both were written before the fix and fail against `main`.

## Scope

Deliberately left alone, because each is a separate question rather than a bug in this loop:

- `duration('PT1.5S')` truncates the fraction (durations have one-second resolution) while C rejects it - #2595.
- `duration('P1DT')` - a trailing `T` with an empty time part - still returns `P1D`.
- The other conversions in #2937 (`toString(1.0)`, `toInteger`/`toFloat` string parsing) are untouched; this PR is only the one item from that issue that both engines already agree should be an error.

The parser rejecting the string (rather than returning `null`, as C does) matches Neo4j, which raises. The openCypher TCK does not cover these inputs.

  * Duration strings with numbers missing units now return a missing-unit error instead of silently discarding those values. This applies to both date and time portions, including values before the `T` separator, so malformed durations are rejected consistently.
* **Tests**
  * Added coverage for rejecting durations with unitless numbers and confirming that durations with units continue to parse.

issues.title: [Rust] duration() drops a trailing number that has no unit: duration('P5') returns PT0S
issues.body:
﻿### Summary

`duration('P5')` and `duration('P-')` are accepted and return a zero-length duration (`PT0S`). A number with no unit after it is not a valid ISO 8601 duration, and the digits that follow the last unit are dropped without any error.

### Reproduction (release build, `main`)

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "RETURN duration('P5')"
-- Rust: PT0S
-- C:    null
-- Neo4j: error
```

The same happens for every spelling whose last component has no unit:

| query | Rust | C |
|---|---|---|
| `RETURN duration('P5')` | `PT0S` | `null` |
| `RETURN duration('P-')` | `PT0S` | `null` |
| `RETURN duration('P1Y5')` | `P1Y` | `null` |
| `RETURN duration('P1M2')` | `P1M` | `null` |
| `RETURN duration('PT4H5')` | `PT4H` | `null` |

Note the second half of the table: the trailing component is not merely a syntax error, it is **discarded**, so `duration('P1Y5')` silently means `P1Y`. A caller that builds the string by concatenation gets a different duration than it asked for, with no signal.

### Mechanism

`parse_duration_string` (`graph/src/runtime/functions/temporal.rs:347`) accumulates digits into `num_buf` and only converts them when a unit character (`Y`/`M`/`W`/`D`/`H`/`S`) closes them:

```rust
for ch in date_part.chars() {
    if ch.is_ascii_digit() || ch == '-' {
        num_buf.push(ch);
    } else {
        let n: i64 = num_buf.parse()...;
        num_buf.clear();
        match ch { 'Y' => years = n, ... }
    }
}
```

Neither loop inspects `num_buf` after it finishes, so whatever is left over is dropped.

### Expected

Reject the string, the way C and Neo4j both do. Checking `num_buf` for emptiness once, after the time part, is enough: the two loops share the buffer, and a non-empty buffer at that point can only mean "a number with no unit".

### Notes

`duration('P1DT')` (a trailing `T` with an empty time part) and `duration('PT1.5S')` (fractional seconds, truncated because durations have one-second resolution) are left alone - they are separate questions, tracked in #2595 for the latter.

issues.title: fix: charge 1 per relationship in algo.SPpaths/SSpaths without costProp (#3109)
issues.body:
Closes #3109

## Problem

Without `costProp`, algo.SPpaths/SSpaths charged 0 per relationship, so `maxCost` limited nothing and `pathCost` was always 0 (e.g. path [0,1,3] with cost 0 where C returns [0,3] with cost 1).

Details, repro and C comparison: #3109.

## Fix

Without costProp (or when an edge lacks it) the bound pre-pass and the
DFS enumeration charged 0 per relationship, so maxCost limited nothing
and pathCost was always 0. C charges 1 per relationship. The Dijkstra
fast path keeps reporting 0, as C does.


## Tests

New `tests/flow/test_path_algorithms.py::test23` fails on origin/main, passes with this change, and also passes against the C module.

Also run on a merged build of the four traversal fixes: `cargo test -p graph --lib` 422 passed; `pytest tests/test_e2e.py tests/test_functions.py` 125 passed; flow suites bidirectional_traversals, all_shortest_paths, path_algorithms, traversal_construction, path, variable_length, shortest_path, path_projections all pass (RLTest on a private port). `cargo fmt` clean; no new clippy warnings in touched code.

issues.title: fix: return allShortestPaths directed cycles in walk order (#3108)
issues.body:
Closes #3108

## Problem

`allShortestPaths` whose source and destination are the same node returned a directed cycle with its relationships last-to-first, i.e. walked against the arrows (nodes [0,2,1,0] / rels [3,2,1] instead of [0,1,2,0] / [1,2,3]). C is also wrong here (differently); this PR returns the correct walk.

issues.title: fix: dedup chained anonymous undirected hops per input record (#3106)
issues.body:
Closes #3106

## Problem

Chained anonymous undirected hops (`(a)-[]-()-[]-(b)`) dedup rows on a key that ignores other columns, uses an intermediate node at 3+ hops, and resets per batch: `UNWIND [1,2] AS x MATCH (a)-[]-()-[]-(b)` returned 5 rows (C 10), 3 hops returned 7 pairs (C 12), and on K(2,3000) pair counts came out as 3 and 4 (C 1).

Details, repro and C comparison: #3106.

## Fix

The (source, destination) dedup that reproduces C's matrix-product
semantics for chained anonymous undirected hops keyed on the source
node, so it merged rows differing in other columns (and equal input
records), used an intermediate node as the source at 3+ hops, and was
cleared per child batch, so a start node spanning batches emitted its
destinations more than once.

Key it on a lineage id instead: the chain's first traverse numbers its
input records, each dedup traverse forwards the lineage of its input
rows, and the emitter reports the parent row of every emitted row. The
rows of one record arrive contiguously, so the seen-set is only cleared
at a record change once it has grown.

issues.title: [Rust] algo.SPpaths/SSpaths charge 0 per relationship without costProp, so maxCost limits nothing (C charges 1)
issues.body:
### Summary

`algo.SPpaths` / `algo.SSpaths` charge a cost of **0** per relationship when no `costProp` is given, so `maxCost` without `costProp` limits nothing and `pathCost` is always 0. C charges 1 per relationship (`GraphEntity_GetNumericPropertyOrDefault(..., SI_LongVal(1))`), so `maxCost` bounds the number of hops.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 2363723ac)

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE (s:N {id:0})-[:R {w:1}]->(a:N {id:1})-[:R {w:2}]->(b:N {id:2})-[:R {w:3}]->(s), (b)-[:R {w:4}]->(c:N {id:3}), (s)-[:R {w:10}]->(c), (a)-[:R {w:1}]->(c), (c)-[:R {w:1}]->(c)"
GRAPH.QUERY g "MATCH (a {id:0}), (b {id:3}) CALL algo.SPpaths({sourceNode: a, targetNode: b, relTypes: ['R'], weightProp: 'w', maxCost: 1, pathCount: 0}) YIELD path, pathWeight, pathCost RETURN [n in nodes(path) | n.id], pathWeight, pathCost"
-- Rust: [0, 1, 3] | 2 | 0      C: [0, 3] | 10 | 1
```

| config (no `costProp`) | Rust | C |
| --- | --- | --- |
| SPpaths `maxCost: 1, pathCount: 0` | `[0,1,3]`, cost 0 | `[0,3]`, cost 1 |
| SPpaths `pathCount: 0` | cost 0 | cost 2 |
| SPpaths `maxCost: 2, pathCount: 1` | cost 0 | cost 2 |
| SSpaths `maxCost: 1` / `pathCount: 1` | cost 0 | cost 1 |
| SPpaths `pathCount: 1` (Dijkstra fast path) | cost 0 | cost 0 |

### Mechanism

`graph/src/runtime/functions/algo_procedures.rs:2397` (`bfs_find_bound`) and `:2518` (the DFS enumeration shared by SPpaths/SSpaths) call `edge_numeric_attr(g, edge_id, config.cost_prop.as_ref(), 0.0)`: the `0.0` default applies both when `costProp` is not configured and when an edge lacks the property. C defaults both to 1.

### Expected

C: 1 per relationship without `costProp` (or when the edge lacks it). C's Dijkstra fast path (`pathCount: 1`, no `maxCost`, no `maxLen`) reports `pathCost` 0 when no `costProp` is given (`_sum_path_cost`); Rust already matches that at `:2308`.

### Suggested fix

Default the cost to `1.0` at `:2397` and `:2518`, leaving the reporting-only Dijkstra sum at `:2308` as is.

### Found by

Differential testing against C while building the Lean model of the traversal operators (`proofs/ops_traverse`, bug 6 in the header); Rust repro `graph/tests/lean_ops_traverse.rs::bug_sppaths_default_cost_is_zero`.

issues.title: [Rust] allShortestPaths returns a directed cycle in reverse (relationships last-to-first)
issues.body:
### Summary

`allShortestPaths` whose source and destination are the same node (a cycle) returns the path in backtrack order for a directed pattern. Relationships come out last-to-first, so the path is not a walk in the pattern's direction: for `(a)-[*]->(a)` Rust walks the cycle against the arrows, and for `(a)<-[*]-(a)` along them.

C is also wrong here, in a different way: for both patterns it returns nodes `[0,2,1,0]` with relationships `[1,2,3]`, which is inconsistent for `->`.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 2363723ac)

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE (s:N {id:0})-[:R {w:1}]->(a:N {id:1})-[:R {w:2}]->(b:N {id:2})-[:R {w:3}]->(s)"
GRAPH.QUERY g "MATCH (a {id:0}), (b {id:0}) WITH a, b MATCH p=allShortestPaths((a)-[*]->(b)) RETURN [n in nodes(p) | n.id], [r in relationships(p) | r.w]"
-- Rust: [0, 2, 1, 0] | [3, 2, 1]    C: [0, 2, 1, 0] | [1, 2, 3]    correct: [0, 1, 2, 0] | [1, 2, 3]
GRAPH.QUERY g "MATCH (a {id:0}), (b {id:0}) WITH a, b MATCH p=allShortestPaths((a)<-[*]-(b)) RETURN [n in nodes(p) | n.id], [r in relationships(p) | r.w]"
-- Rust: [0, 1, 2, 0] | [1, 2, 3]    C: [0, 2, 1, 0] | [1, 2, 3]    correct: [0, 2, 1, 0] | [3, 2, 1]
```

Undirected cycles are palindromes today and are unaffected.

### Mechanism

`AllShortestPathsOp::expand_row` (`graph/src/runtime/ops/all_shortest_paths.rs:284-288`) backtracks from `dst` to `src`, so edges are collected last-to-first, and reverses them into `src→dst` order only when `src != dst` ("Cycles keep the DFS predecessor-chain order"). `PathBuilder` then walks the edge list from `a`, which for a cycle gives the reversed walk.

The flow test `test_all_shortest_paths.py::test06_all_shortest_cycle` encodes the wrong order for `->` and asserts that `->` and `<-` give the same node lists, which cannot both be walks.

### Expected

openCypher: a path matched by `(a)-[*]->(a)` is a walk along the relationships, so `nodes(p)` = `[0,1,2,0]` and `relationships(p)` = `[1,2,3]`; for `<-` the mirror image. This deliberately deviates from C, which is also wrong.

### Suggested fix

Reverse the backtracked edge list for cycles too (drop the `if !is_cycle` guard), and fix `test06` to the correct walks.

### Found by

Lean 4 model of allShortestPaths (`proofs/ops_traverse`, `ASP.directed_cycle_backtrack_order`, `ASP.directed_cycle_not_a_walk`); Rust repro `graph/tests/lean_ops_traverse.rs::bug_all_shortest_paths_directed_cycle_reversed`.

issues.title: [Rust] Anonymous undirected hop returns each node pair twice when edges exist in both directions (CondTraverse and ExpandInto)
issues.body:
### Summary

An anonymous undirected single hop `(a)-[]-(b)` collapses parallel edges to one row per `(a, b)` pair (C semantics), but it does so separately for each stored direction. When edges exist in both directions between the same two nodes, every pair is returned twice. `ExpandInto` (both endpoints already bound) has the same bug.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 2363723ac)

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE (a:A {id:1})-[:R]->(b:B {id:2}), (b)-[:R]->(a), (a)-[:R]->(b)"
GRAPH.QUERY g "MATCH (a)-[]-(b) RETURN a.id, b.id"
-- Rust: 1|2, 1|2, 2|1, 2|1     C: 1|2, 2|1
GRAPH.QUERY g "MATCH (a:A), (b:B) WITH a, b MATCH (a)-[]-(b) RETURN a.id, b.id"
-- Rust: 1|2, 1|2               C: 1|2
```

### Mechanism

* `CondTraverseOp::expand_row` (`graph/src/runtime/ops/cond_traverse.rs:876-942`) runs the forward and the reverse scan, and `process_pairs` (`:1063-1081`) keeps one representative edge per *matrix* pair in each. `a→b` and `b→a` are different matrix pairs that map to the same pattern pair.
* `ExpandIntoOp::expand_row` (`graph/src/runtime/ops/expand_into.rs:182-221`) probes `(src,dst)` and `(dst,src)` and keeps a representative from each.

### Expected

C: one row per pattern pair (the traversal matrix is `A + Aᵀ` over the boolean semiring), so 2 rows and 1 row above.

### Suggested fix

In collapse mode (anonymous edge, no edge filter), drop reverse-scan results whose pattern pair the forward scan already produced; in `ExpandInto`, stop after the first direction that yields an edge.

### Found by

Lean 4 model (`proofs/ops_traverse`, `CondTraverse.bidir_collapse_duplicates_pair`, `expandInto_bidir_collapse_two_rows`); Rust repro `graph/tests/lean_ops_traverse.rs::bug_undirected_anonymous_collapse_duplicates_pairs`.

issues.title: [Rust] Chained anonymous undirected hops drop or duplicate rows: bidirectional dedup keys on the wrong tuple
issues.body:
### Summary

Two or more chained anonymous undirected hops (`(a)-[]-()-[]-(b)`) go through a cross-row `(source, destination)` dedup in `CondTraverse`. It is meant to reproduce C's matrix-multiply semantics: one row per *input record* and destination. The key it uses is wrong in three ways, so rows are silently dropped or duplicated:

1. It keys on the source **node**, not the input record, so rows that differ only in another column (`UNWIND [1,2] AS x ...`) are collapsed, and so are two equal input records.
2. At 3+ hops the source is the child traverse's `from` alias, which is an **intermediate** node, so rows from different start nodes collide.
3. The seen-set is **cleared per child batch**. When one start node's first hop spans more than one batch (> 1024 rows), its destinations are emitted once per batch.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 2363723ac)

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE (a:N {id:1})-[:R]->(b:N {id:2})-[:R]->(c:N {id:3})"
GRAPH.QUERY g "UNWIND [1,2] AS x MATCH (a)-[]-()-[]-(b) RETURN x, a.id, b.id"
-- Rust: 5 rows (all x=1).   C: 10 rows (5 per x)
GRAPH.QUERY g "UNWIND [1,1] AS x MATCH (a)-[]-()-[]-(b) RETURN x, a.id, b.id"
-- Rust: 5 rows.             C: 10 rows (one set per input record)
```

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE (a:N {id:1})-[:R]->(b:N {id:2})-[:R]->(c:N {id:3})-[:R]->(d:N {id:4}), (b)-[:R]->(e:N {id:5})"
GRAPH.QUERY g "MATCH (a)-[]-()-[]-()-[]-(b) RETURN a.id, b.id"
-- Rust: 7 rows (4|1, 4|3, 4|5, 5|2, 5|4 missing).   C: 12 rows
```

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE (u:U {id:1}), (v:U {id:2}) WITH u, v UNWIND range(1,3000) AS i CREATE (u)-[:R]->(:L {id:i})<-[:R]-(v)"
GRAPH.QUERY g "MATCH (a:U)-[]-()-[]-(b:U) RETURN a.id, b.id, count(*)"
-- Rust: 1|1|3, 1|2|3, 2|1|4, 2|2|4.   C: every count is 1
```

### Mechanism

`graph/src/runtime/ops/cond_traverse.rs`:
* `CondTraverseOp::new` (`:273-299`) picks `child_ct.relationship_pattern.from.alias` as the dedup source. For the third hop that is the first intermediate node, not the scan source.
* `expand_row` (`:947-968`) keys the seen-set on `(source node id, to node id)`. Every other column of the row is ignored, and two input records with equal values are merged.
* `next` (`:1267`) clears the seen-set on every child batch.

### Expected

C: consecutive anonymous hops are one algebraic expression, evaluated as `F · (A+Aᵀ) · (A+Aᵀ)`, where `F` has one row per input record. The result is one row per (input record, destination), independent of batch size.

### Suggested fix

Key the dedup on the identity of the record that entered the chain: a per-row lineage id that the chain's first traverse stamps and each dedup traverse forwards. The rows of one record are contiguous in the chain's output, so the seen-set can be reset when the record changes instead of per batch.

### Found by

Lean 4 model of the bidirectional dedup (`proofs/ops_traverse`, `BidirDedup.drops_outer_rows`, `BidirDedup.three_hops_collide`, `BidirDedup.batch_split_changes_result`); Rust repro `graph/tests/lean_ops_traverse.rs::bug_bidir_dedup_*`.

issues.title: [Rust] Decision: operator precedence where Rust follows openCypher and C does not (2^3^2, chained comparisons, STARTS WITH / IS NULL after +, SKIP (1))
issues.body:
### Decision needed: operator precedence where Rust follows openCypher and C does not

The Rust engine treats C as the reference, but in the cases below the Rust parser follows the openCypher grammar (`graph/src/Cypher.g4`) and C does not. Nothing here crashes. Each is a user-visible result difference between the engines, so each needs a decision: **keep the grammar behaviour (and document the C difference), or copy C.** This issue is for that decision; no PR is attached.

Results: Rust = release build of `main` @ 55204c94b. C = local `master` build of the C module (`bin/macos-arm64v8-release/falkordb.so`).

| # | Query | Rust | C | openCypher grammar |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `RETURN 2^3^2` | `64` | `512` | `PowerOfExpression = Unary ( '^' Unary )*`, left-associative → `(2^3)^2 = 64` |
| 2a | `RETURN 1 = 1 = 1` | `true` | `false` | Comparisons chain: `a op1 b op2 c` = `a op1 b AND b op2 c` → `true` |
| 2b | `RETURN 1 < 2 < 3 < 0` | `false` | **`true`** | chained → `false` |
| 2c | `CREATE (:N {x:0})` then `MATCH (n:N) WHERE n.x = 0 = true RETURN count(n)` | `0` | `1` | chained: `n.x = 0 AND 0 = true` → `0` rows |
| 3a | `RETURN 'a' + 'b' STARTS WITH 'ab'` | `true` | `'afalse'` | `StringListNullPredicate` sits *below* `+`: `('a' + 'b') STARTS WITH 'ab'` → `true` |
| 3b | `RETURN 1 + 2 IS NULL` | `false` | `1` | `(1 + 2) IS NULL` → `false` |
| 3c | `RETURN - 1 IS NULL` | `false` | `Type mismatch: expected Integer, Float, or Null but was Boolean` | `(-1) IS NULL` → `false` |
| 3d | `RETURN 5.0 / 0 IS NULL` | `false` | same type mismatch | `(5.0 / 0) IS NULL` → `false` |
| 4 | `UNWIND [1,2,3] AS x RETURN x SKIP (1)` | `SKIP specified value of invalid type, must be a positive integer` | `[[2], [3]]` | `SKIP Expression` → accepted, `[[2], [3]]` |

### Notes per item

1. **`^` associativity.** Most languages make `^` right-associative, and C does. The openCypher grammar is explicitly left-associative. Neo4j is believed to follow it (64), but that was not checked here.
2. **Chained comparisons.** The openCypher spec says `x < y <= z` means `x < y AND y <= z`. That was reported against RedisGraph as #382 (closed as completed), yet the C build still evaluates `(1 = 1) = 1`. Rust desugars chains to `AND` (`cypher.rs` level 4). 2b is the worst case: C answers `true` for a false chain.
3. **String/null predicates vs `+`.** In the grammar, `STARTS WITH` / `ENDS WITH` / `CONTAINS` / `IN` / `IS [NOT] NULL` bind looser than `+ - * /` and tighter than comparison. C binds them tighter than `+`. #2181 reported the `IS NULL` half against C (closed as completed), but this C build still gives the type error in 3c and 3d.
4. **`SKIP (1)`.** This is a Rust limitation, not a precedence question. Rust accepts only a literal or a parameter at the root of `SKIP`/`LIMIT`. C accepts a parenthesised literal. It overlaps with #2574 (dynamic `SKIP`/`LIMIT` expressions rejected on both engines). If the decision is "follow the grammar", this one means *relaxing* Rust, and could be folded into #2574.

### Recommendation

Keep the grammar behaviour for 1 to 3 in Rust. The Rust results are what openCypher specifies. The C results were already acknowledged as bugs in #382 and #2181. Copying C would reintroduce known-wrong answers (2b especially). Document the differences in the C-to-Rust migration notes. For 4, accept at least a constant parenthesised expression (fold it at plan time), tracked with #2574.

### Found by

Lean 4 model of the expression parser (`proofs/parser_grammar`). Theorems `binary_pairs_agree` and `chained_comparison` prove the Rust parser matches the grammar on all 400 operator pairs. The C side was checked live.

issues.title: fix: stop exponential backtracking on nested [(...)] lists in the parser
issues.body:
Closes #3103

## Problem

`parse_list_literal_or_comprehension` tried every `[` that is followed by `(` or a name as a pattern comprehension first (named, then unnamed). The attempt parsed the node pattern, including its property map. When no relationship followed, it restored the position and parsed the same text again as a list literal. A map value holding another `[(…)]` did the same inside both passes, so the work doubled with each level. `RETURN [(x {k: [(x {k: …})]})]` with 22 levels (251 bytes) took **20.5 s** on a live server before failing with `'x' not defined`.

## Fix

Both changes are in `parse_list_literal_or_comprehension`. Neither changes what is parsed, only what is attempted:

1. **Try only where it can succeed.** `list_has_top_level_pipe` counts brackets (it does not parse) from the `[` to its closing `]`. It reports whether a `|` comes first at nesting level 0, before any top-level `,`. A pattern comprehension always has such a `|` and no top-level `,`. A list literal can never have the `|`, so skipping the attempt when the scan says no gives the same result. The scan is also skipped unless the `[` is followed by `(` or a name, the only tokens either attempt can start with.
2. **Never repeat a failed attempt.** A failed attempt is recorded under a `PatternComprehensionAttempt` key (position, `allow_pattern_predicate`, forbidden-comprehension context, nesting depth). Those are all the inputs besides the query text that decide whether it succeeds, so a later visit to the same key skips it. This covers adversarial inputs that do contain a top-level `|` (e.g. `[(x {k: …}) - 1 | 1]`). Without this memo they were still exponential (20 levels: 5.8 s).

## Benchmarks

Its quadratic cost comes from tree wrapping, and this PR does not change it.

issues.title: [Rust] Exponential backtracking on nested [(x {k: [...]})] lists: a 251-byte query spends 20 s in the parser
issues.body:
### Summary

The parser backtracks exponentially on nested `[(...)]` lists. A 251-byte query keeps a worker busy for 20 s in the parser alone, and every extra level of nesting doubles that. No graph data or valid query is needed: the time is spent before the query is rejected (or planned), so this is a cheap DoS. C is exponential on the same shape too (8 levels > 500 s), so this is not a regression; it is a hole in both engines.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 55204c94b)

```python
e = "1"
for _ in range(22):
    e = "[(x {k: " + e + "})]"
q = "RETURN " + e            # 251 bytes
```

```
$ time redis-cli GRAPH.QUERY g "$q"
'x' not defined
real 20.50
```

Parse time alone, in process (best of 5):

| levels | bytes | parse time |
|---|---|---|
| 8 | 96 | 2.7 ms |
| 12 | 140 | 25 ms |
| 16 | 184 | 393 ms |
| 20 | 228 | 6.4 s |

The same happens with `[p = (x {k: …})]`, `[(x {k: …}) - 1]`, and in `WHERE (x {k: [ … ]})`.

### Mechanism

`parse_list_literal_or_comprehension` (`graph/src/parser/cypher.rs:2784-2803`) tries each `[` as a named, then an unnamed, pattern comprehension first. The attempt parses the node pattern `(x {k: …})` in full, including its property map. Only then does it find that no relationship follows, restore the position, and parse the same text again as a list literal. The map value holds the next `[(…)]`, which does the same thing inside both passes, so level *n* is parsed 2ⁿ times.

### Expected

Parse time proportional to what an equally nested list literal costs (`[{k: [{k: …}]}]`: 0.2 ms at 20 levels).

### Suggested fix

- Try the pattern comprehension only where it can succeed. A pattern comprehension has a `|` before the closing `]`, outside any nested bracket and before any top-level `,`. A list literal never has that `|`. A bracket-counting token scan can check this without parsing.
- Never repeat an attempt that already failed at the same position in the same context (`allow_pattern_predicate`, the forbidden-comprehension context, nesting depth). That covers adversarial inputs that do contain the `|`.

### Found by

Review of the parser while building the Lean model (`proofs/parser_grammar`). Rust repro: `graph/tests/lean_parser_grammar.rs::bug_pattern_comprehension_backtracking_is_exponential`.

issues.title: fix: plan a self-loop hop after the hop that binds its node
issues.body:
Closes #2999

## Problem
`MATCH (a)-[:R]->(b)-[:S*]->(c)-[:L]->(c) RETURN a.v, b.v, c.v` returns `[null,2,3]` on Rust and `[1,2,3]` on C. Var-length hops are sorted after fixed ones, so the self-loop `(c)-[:L]->(c)` was planned while `c` was still unbound. The chaining loop then built `ExpandInto(scan c, res)`, and the runtime only builds ExpandInto's first child, so every earlier hop was dropped.

## Fix
In `plan_match`, after the hop sort:
- move a fixed-length self-loop that sits past the first hop and whose node nothing has bound yet to just after the first later hop that binds that node. It then plans as `ExpandInto(res)` on a bound node, which is exactly C's plan (`Expand Into (c)->(c)` over the var-length traverse);
- in the fallback branch (no longer reached from connected components), put the scan on top of `res` instead of beside it, so no hop can be dropped.

## Tests
New `tests/test_e2e.py::test_self_loop_hop_after_other_hops_keeps_them`. It covers the var-length and `*1..1` forms, inline attrs on the loop node, the pattern written in reverse, and two self-loops on the same node.

issues.title: fix: correlate a MATCH … WHERE with the next MATCH's cartesian product
issues.body:
Closes #2992

## Problem
`MATCH (a) WHERE a.v = 0 MATCH (a)-[:R]->(b), (c:C) RETURN a.v, b.v, c.v` returns `[1,0,7]` on Rust and `[]` on C. The second MATCH is a CartesianProduct whose component `(a)-[:R]->(b)` was planned with `a` already bound. `plan_query` still prepended the first clause's `Filter(Scan a)` as one more independent branch, because `needs_apply_wrapping` treats every MATCH-shaped plan as "just another branch". In `plan_query`, also Apply-wrap the CartesianProduct / ValueHashJoin (the existing `Apply` + `Argument` path used for WITH/UNWIND) when a branch of it mentions a variable the stitched plan binds (`reads_plan_variables`: operator variables via `GetVariables`, plus expression reads via `ir_references_variable`, now `pub(crate)`; matched on (id, scope)). issues.title: fix: keep an earlier MATCH … WHERE stitched under a traversal
issues.body:
Closes #2972

## Problem
`MATCH (a) WHERE a.v = 99 MATCH (a)-[r:R]->(b) RETURN count(r)` returns 2 on Rust and 0 on C. With `DETACH DELETE b`, Rust deletes a node the WHERE excluded. `plan_query` stitches the first clause, `Filter(AllNodeScan a)`, under the second clause's leaf `CondTraverse`. `select_scan_node` took any Filter/scan chain there for "a scan the planner added", pruned it and rebuilt a bare scan. That dropped the WHERE, anything planned below the scan (an earlier `UNWIND`: 2 rows vs C's 4), and variables that do not belong to the chain (`MATCH (x:C) WHERE … MATCH (a)-->(b)` returned `x = null`).

## Fix
The planner never gives a `CondTraverse` a child: the bottom hop is always a leaf, and adding the scan is this pass's job. So a child that is already there is outer context, whatever its shape. In `select_scan_node`:
- remove `is_planner_scan_subtree` and its three prune paths, and keep any existing child (a transparent `Argument` is still replaced by a scan, as before);

issues.title: fix: index population no longer overwrites documents from concurrent writes
issues.body:
Closes #3095

## Problem

Background index population (`populate_index_batch`) builds documents from the **committed** graph. A writer publishes its index documents during the query, before its MVCC commit swaps in the new graph. A batch that ran between the two overwrote the writer's newer document with the pre-write value, or re-added a deleted entity. Nothing corrected that afterwards, so index scans kept returning wrong counts (`repro/poprace.py`: 4/4 rounds inconsistent; C: 0/3).

## Fix

While a generation is populating, the index records the ids whose documents a writer set or removed (`PendingSlots::written`, filled from `Graph::commit_index_kind` / `commit_edge_index_locked`). Population batches skip those ids, because the writer's document comes from newer state.
- Both sides already run under the indexer lock, so there is no new race.
- The set is only filled while `current_pending > 0`, and it is cleared when the generation's population completes or the generation is bumped. There is no steady-state memory cost.
- The same handling applies to edges, keyed by edge id.

## Tests

New flow test `test_index_updates.test12_concurrent_writes_during_index_population`: 200k nodes, and a writer thread running SET, DELETE and CREATE while `CREATE INDEX (n.v)` populates, for 3 rounds. After each round it checks that every value's index-scan count equals the label-scan count.
- Before (`main` @ 55204c94b): `FAIL 26793 == 27993 [v = 1]` (and more).
- After: PASS (3 runs).

`repro/poprace.py`, 200k nodes: before, 4/4 bad rounds; after, 0/6.

Also run on a private port, `--parallelism 1`: `test_index_updates` (12/12, twice), `test_index_create` (17/17), `test_index_delete` (14/14), `test_edge_index_updates` (6/6), `test_constraint` (26/26), `test_vecsim` (9/9), `test_undo_log` (22/22), `test_fulltext_query` (5/5). `cargo fmt --check` passes and `cargo clippy --all-targets` adds no warnings in the touched files.

## Benchmark

This touches the write path (one mutex per label per index commit) and population (one lookup per batch). Release build, A/B alternating on the same machine (load average ~2.4):

| | base p50 / p99 | fix p50 / p99 |
|---|---|---|
| `MATCH (n:L) SET n.w = i` on 100k nodes, indexed `w` (25 runs) | 117.7 / 125.6 ms | 118.9 / 126.6 ms |
| population of 1M nodes, range index (5 runs) | 779 ms | 779 ms |

Both are within noise.

issues.title: fix: write matrix container headers without heap addresses
issues.body:
Closes #3096

## Problem

`Matrix::encode` (`matrix.rs`) wrote the whole 608-byte `GxB_Container` struct after `GxB_unload_Matrix_into_Container`. Its `p`, `h`, `b`, `i`, `x` fields are the heap addresses of the unloaded component vectors, so every RDB file, `DUMP` payload and `GRAPH.COPY`/`GRAPH.RESTORE` payload carried live addresses of the server process. No reader uses them.

## Fix

Encode copies the header and zeroes every pointer field (`p h b i x`, `vector_future`, `Y`, `matrix_future`, `void_future`) before writing it. The layout and size are unchanged. The Rust decoder and C's `decode_matrix.c` both null these fields before loading, so old and new payloads load in both directions.

## Tests

- New unit test `matrix::tests::encode_writes_no_heap_addresses`: the encoded header's pointer ranges must be all zero. On main it fails (`vector / matrix pointers written into the payload: [80, a2, 19, 07, 01, 00, 00, 00, ...]`); passes here.
- Live, `GRAPH.COPY` payload of a 2-node multi-edge graph, first container's p,h,b,i,x words: main `0x10277e000 0x1091fe000 0x1091fdf00 0x1091fde00 0x109c88700`; this branch `0x0` ×5. The payload still restores (2 edges).

issues.title: [Rust] Serialized matrix headers (RDB, DUMP, GRAPH.COPY payloads) contain live heap addresses
issues.body:
### Summary

Every serialized matrix header contains live heap addresses of the writing process. `Matrix::encode` writes the whole 608-byte `GxB_Container` struct, including its `p`, `h`, `b`, `i`, `x` `GrB_Vector` pointers, into RDB files, `DUMP` payloads and the `GRAPH.RESTORE` payloads `GRAPH.COPY` replicates. Whoever can read one of these learns part of the server's heap layout. No reader uses the values: the decoder nulls them and rebuilds every component from the data that follows.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 55204c94b)

`GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE (a:A)-[:R]->(b:B), (a)-[:R]->(b)"`, then `GRAPH.COPY g g2`, take the `GRAPH.RESTORE` payload from the AOF, and read the pointer words of each 608-byte container record (offsets 192..232):

```
15 container structs in payload; first p,h,b,i,x words:
  ['0x10277e000', '0x1091fe000', '0x1091fdf00', '0x1091fde00', '0x109c88700'], ...
```

### Mechanism

`graph/src/graph/graphblas/matrix.rs:527-530` (`Encode<19> for Matrix<T>`): `w.write_buffer(slice::from_raw_parts(container, CONTAINER_STRUCT_SIZE))` after `GxB_unload_Matrix_into_Container`, so the struct's pointer fields hold the addresses of the unloaded component vectors. The C encoder does the same (`src/serializers/encoder/v19/encode_matrix.c`, `SerializerIO_WriteBuffer(rdb, container, sizeof(struct GxB_Container_struct))`).

### Expected

Serialized payloads carry no process addresses. Both decoders (Rust `Matrix::decode`, C `decode_matrix.c`) already null the component pointers before loading, so writing them as zero keeps every reader and the on-disk format compatible.

### Suggested fix

Copy the header and zero its pointer fields (`p h b i x`, `vector_future`, `Y`, `matrix_future`, `void_future`) before writing it. The C encoder could get the same change.

### Found by

Review of the Lean model of the GraphBLAS wrappers (`proofs/graphblas_wrappers`, "Suspicions / notes"), confirmed on a live payload.

issues.title: [Rust] Writes racing index population leave stale or resurrected index entries
issues.body:
### Summary

When writes run on a label while one of its indexes is being populated, the index can end up permanently inconsistent with the data: stale values stay indexed, and deleted entities can be resurrected in it. Index scans then return wrong counts until the entity is written again. C stays consistent.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 55204c94b)

`proofs/search_concurrency/repro/poprace.py`: 200k `(:L {k, v:0})` nodes, a writer loop running `MATCH (n:L) WHERE n.k % 50 = $m SET n.v = n.v + 1`, and `CREATE INDEX FOR (n:L) ON (n.v)` while it runs. After quiescence it compares the index count per value with a label scan:

```
round 0: mismatches=[(0, 132000, 132400), (1, 64000, 63600)]      # (v, scan count, index count)
round 1: mismatches=[(0, 72000, 72200), (1, 88000, 87800)]
...
BAD ROUNDS 4 (of 4)       C: BAD ROUNDS 0 (of 3)
```

### Mechanism

- `populate_index_batch` (`graph/src/graph/graph.rs:~469`) builds documents from the **committed** graph (`indexer.get_graph()`).
- A writer publishes its index documents during the query (`Graph::commit_index*`, under the indexer lock), **before** its MVCC commit swaps in the new graph.
- A batch that runs between those two steps reads the pre-write value from the committed graph and overwrites the writer's newer document. The same happens for a deleted entity, which the batch re-adds. Nothing corrects it afterwards.

This is a different root cause from #3069 (the missing generation bump), though it hits the same population code.

### Expected

Same as C: once population finishes, the index matches the data, whatever writes ran during it.

### Suggested fix

While a generation is populating, record the ids whose documents a writer set or removed (under the indexer lock the batches already take). Batches skip those ids, because the writer's document comes from newer state. Clear the set when the generation's population completes or the generation is bumped.

### Found by

Lean 4 model `proofs/search_concurrency` (`Tickets`, population protocol). Repro: `proofs/search_concurrency/repro/poprace.py`.

issues.title: fix: validate index OPTIONS like C (vector dimension/similarityFunction required, case-insensitive metric, unknown fulltext keys rejected)
issues.body:
Closes #3091

## Problem

`map_to_index_options` treated required vector options as optional and ignored unknown fulltext keys. The results:
- A vector index with no `OPTIONS` failed with an internal message (`field type 0x0010 and the options block disagree about the vector half`).
- `OPTIONS {}` and an index missing `dimension` or `similarityFunction` were accepted. With dimension 0, no vector can ever be indexed.
- `'Euclidean'` and `'COSINE'` were rejected.
- `CREATE FULLTEXT INDEX … OPTIONS {foo:1}` silently ignored `foo`.

C rejects or accepts each of these the other way.

## Fix

Match C (`src/index/index_vector_create.c` `_parseOptions`, `src/index/index_fulltext_create.c` `_validateOptions`):
- A vector index requires `dimension` and `similarityFunction`. A missing `OPTIONS` block is rejected too. Errors start with C's `Invalid vector index configuration`.
- `similarityFunction` is matched case-insensitively and stored lowercase, so `db.indexes()`, RDB and effects all carry the canonical form.
- A fulltext index rejects option keys other than `weight`, `nostem`, `phonetic`, `language`, `stopwords`.

Kept different from C on purpose:
- An unknown fulltext `language` is still rejected. C accepts it and then segfaults (#2448), and #2449 tracks the Rust side.
- `'ip'` stays supported. It is a Rust superset.
- `{weight:1, foo:1}` is rejected. C accepts it only because of a loop bug in `_validateOptions`, which re-checks the same known key on every iteration.

## Tests

New flow test `test_index_create.test19_index_options_validation` covers every row above plus the accepted forms and the lowercase storage.
- Before (`main` @ 55204c94b): 6 assertion failures (internal error message, accepted invalid options, `unknown option` missing).
- After: PASS.

Also run on a private port, `--parallelism 1`: `test_index_create` (18/18), `test_effects_ddl` (18/18), `test_fulltext_query` (5/5), `test_persistency` (11/11), `test_rdb_c_layout` (4/4), `test_query_validation` (50/50), `test_replication` (2/2), `test_index_delete` (14/14), `test_undo_log` (22/22), `test_vecsim` (9/9). `cargo fmt --check` passes and `cargo clippy --all-targets` adds no warnings in the touched files.

issues.title: [Rust] Write inside MULTI/EXEC fails with 'another write is in progress' while a queued write is still matching
issues.body:
### Summary

An inline write (inside `MULTI/EXEC`, and likewise Lua or any other path that must run on the main thread) fails with `another write is in progress, retry the query` whenever a queued write on the same graph is still in its read/match phase. The inline write is lost, even though nothing is actually writing yet. C executes it.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 55204c94b)

A queued write with a slow match phase on one connection; 0.3 s later, `MULTI; GRAPH.QUERY mr "CREATE (:M)"; EXEC` on another (`proofs/search_concurrency/repro/multi_race.py`, with the UNWIND raised to 40M so the match phase lasts about 0.5 s):

```
Rust: multi = ['another write is in progress, retry the query']   count: N=1, Seed=1   (M missing)   2/2 runs
C:    multi = ['Labels added: 1', 'Nodes created: 1', ...]        count: M=1, N=1, Seed=1
```

(C sometimes crashes on this repro. That is a separate C bug.)

### Mechanism

`execute_query_write` (`src/graph_core.rs:748`) claims the MVCC write slot (`MvccGraph::write`, a CAS) at the **start** of the queued write, while the query is still a reader: no GIL, graph read lock only. It escalates to GIL + write lock lazily at its first mutation. The inline writer runs on the main thread holding the GIL (`QuerySession::begin_writer`) and takes the write lock once the queued query drops its read lock to escalate. Its own `graph.write()` CAS then fails because the slot belongs to the queued writer. That writer cannot make progress until the inline writer releases the GIL, so waiting is impossible and the only option today is the error.

### Design options

The fix changes the MVCC write-slot protocol, so here are the options for review before implementing.

**A. Claim the slot at escalation (optimistic, recommended).** The queued writer builds its private COW version without claiming the slot. When it escalates (GIL + write lock held), it claims the slot and checks that the committed version is still the base of its private version. If another writer (necessarily an inline one) committed in between, it discards the private version and re-runs the query from the start. That is safe because escalation happens before the first mutation: nothing is mutated, nothing is replied, and no index documents have been published. Invariant: the slot is only ever held by a thread holding the graph write lock, so an inline writer never finds it taken.
- Pros: a small, local change (`MvccGraph::write` splits into "new private version" plus "claim(base)"; `QuerySession::upgrade_to_write` claims; `process_write_queued_query` retries on conflict). It removes the error entirely and matches `Mvcc.multi_write_ok_in_c`.
- Cons: two COW versions can exist from the same base at once. They are independent by construction (matrices `dup`, attribute store `new_version`), but that needs verifying. A queued write redoes its match phase after an inline commit; inline writes are rare, so starvation is not a practical concern.

**B. Pre-emption.** Keep claiming at start, but let an inline writer (GIL + write lock held, so any other holder must be a not-yet-escalated queued writer) steal the slot and bump an epoch. The queued writer checks the epoch at escalation and restarts if it changed.
- Pros: no change for the common path.
- Cons: two owners of one slot. Rollback/abandon paths must not release a slot they no longer own, which is easy to get wrong.

**C. Keep the error, but make it clearer or have the client retry.** Not a fix: the write inside `MULTI` is still lost, and C commits it.

Recommendation: **A**.

### Found by

Lean 4 model `proofs/search_concurrency` (`Mvcc.multi_write_refused` / `Mvcc.multi_write_ok_in_c`). Repro: `proofs/search_concurrency/repro/multi_race.py`.

issues.title: fix: stop optimizer variable sets from seeing through an aggregating WITH
issues.body:
Closes #3082

## Problem

`CREATE (:B {v:0}),(:B {v:5}) WITH count(*) AS s MATCH (b:B),(c:B) WHERE c.v=b.v RETURN count(*)` returns 0 where C returns 2. It was reported as a hash join over pending-created nodes, but the CREATE has nothing to do with it: `MATCH (x:B),(y:B) WITH count(*) AS s MATCH (b:B),(c:B) WHERE c.v=b.v RETURN count(*)` also returns 0. The query never gets a Value Hash Join. Filter push-down puts `c.v = b.v` under the `c` scan alone, and `b` is unbound there.

Variable ids are per-scope env indices, so `x`/`y` share ids with `b`/`c`. `collect_subtree_variables` walked the whole subtree and kept descending through `Aggregate`, so it reported `x` and `y`, which do not survive the aggregation, and it left out the aggregate output `s`. Push-down's Apply "Case 2" added that set to the right-hand branches that are fed through `Argument`, and matched the conjunct to the `c` branch by bare id.

## Fix

`collect_subtree_variables` now stops at `Project`/`Aggregate` and reports only their named outputs, which are the variables that actually reach the subtree's parent. `push_filters_down`, `replace_cartesian_with_hash_join` and `select_scan_node` all share this helper, so they all get the fix. The per-node match in `GetVariables` moves into `push_node_variables` so both walks use it. `GetVariables` behaves exactly as before, and most of the `runtime.rs` diff is re-indentation (`git diff -w` shows 27 lines).

This is an optimizer change and only affects plan time. It adds no runtime cost.

Possible conflict: #3034 also touches the hash-join area (`value_hash_join.rs`, `tests/flow/test_hashjoin.py`). This PR edits neither file, and the regression test lives in `test_filters.py`, so the two should merge cleanly.

## Tests

- New flow test `test_filters.py::test10_filter_after_aggregating_with_is_not_pushed_into_one_branch`. On origin/main it **fails** (`[[0]] == [[2]]` ×4, `[[0]] == [[3]]`, and the plan has no Value Hash Join). With the fix it **passes**.
- Full `flow_tests_done.txt` with the fixed module: 1595/1595 passed.
- `pytest tests/test_e2e.py tests/test_functions.py`: 125 passed. TCK (`TCK_DONE=tck_done.txt`): passed.
- `cargo test -p graph`: 421 passed, 1 failed. The failure is `batched_result_emitter::tests::cap_at_or_above_batch_size_is_ignored` (1025 vs 1024). It is in code this PR does not touch and it fails on origin/main too.
- `cargo fmt --check` passes. `clippy --all-targets` reports no warnings in the touched files.
- Checked against C: 12 queries of the form "something that binds several variables, then an aggregating `WITH`, then a multi-part MATCH". Every aggregate-after-multi-variable case now matches C. Two mismatches remain, `WITH x, count(*) ...` (512 vs C 64) and `WITH x.v AS s, y AS t ...`. They happen on main as well, come from #3012 (hash join inside a batched Apply), and this PR leaves them alone.

### Benchmark (200k × 200k integer-key hash join, release, 25 runs alternating base/fix/C, machine load ~12–17)

| query | base p50 / max | fix p50 / max | C p50 / max |
|---|---|---|---|
| `MATCH (a:L),(b:R) WHERE a.k=b.k RETURN count(*)` | 46.0 / 62.4 ms | 45.0 / 75.0 ms | 128.4 / 180.5 ms |
| same after `MATCH (x:L {k:1}),(y:R {k:1}) WITH count(*) AS s` | 17.8 ms (**wrong: 0 rows**) | 53.9 / 69.6 ms (200000) | 157.5 / 193.7 ms (200000) |

An earlier run of the first query gave base 49.6 / 56.9 and fix 49.1 / 55.3 ms, so the hash join itself is unchanged within noise. The second query was only fast on base because it skipped the join and returned the wrong answer.

issues.title: [Rust] Index OPTIONS validation diverges from C (missing vector dimension/similarityFunction accepted, 'Euclidean' rejected, unknown fulltext keys ignored)
issues.body:
### Summary

Index `OPTIONS` validation differs from C in several ways. All come from one cause: `map_to_index_options` treats required vector options as optional and does not check fulltext option keys.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 55204c94b)

| Query | Rust | C |
|---|---|---|
| `CREATE VECTOR INDEX FOR (n:A) ON (n.v)` (no OPTIONS) | `field type 0x0010 and the options block disagree about the vector half` | `Invalid vector index configuration` |
| `... OPTIONS {}` | accepted (dimension 0) | `Invalid vector index configuration` |
| `... OPTIONS {similarityFunction:'euclidean'}` (no dimension) | accepted (dimension 0: no vector can ever be indexed) | `Invalid vector index configuration` |
| `... OPTIONS {dimension:2}` (no similarityFunction) | accepted | `Invalid vector index configuration` |
| `... OPTIONS {dimension:2, similarityFunction:'Euclidean'}` / `'COSINE'` | `Unknown similarity function 'Euclidean'` | accepted (`strcasecmp`) |
| `CREATE FULLTEXT INDEX ... OPTIONS {foo:1}` | accepted, `foo` silently ignored | `invlaid index configuration` |

### Mechanism

`graph/src/runtime/runtime.rs` `map_to_index_options`:
- `dimension` defaults to `0` and `similarityFunction` to `None` when absent. C (`src/index/index_vector_create.c` `_parseOptions`) requires both.
- `similarityFunction` is compared case-sensitively later on (`graph/src/index/mod.rs:1265`). C uses `strcasecmp`.
- The fulltext branch reads only the keys it knows and ignores the rest. C's `_validateOptions` rejects unknown keys.
- `index_ddl::create_index` passes `None` options for a vector index straight through.

### Expected / suggested fix

Match C: require `dimension` and `similarityFunction` for vector indexes (error prefix `Invalid vector index configuration`), match the similarity function case-insensitively and store it lowercase, and reject unknown fulltext option keys.

Two deliberate differences from C:
- **Unknown fulltext `language`**: Rust keeps rejecting it. C accepts it and then segfaults (#2448), and #2449 tracks making the Rust rejection consistent. Here C is the odd one out.
- **`similarityFunction:'ip'`**: Rust supports inner product and C does not. Rust keeps it (superset).
- C's validation loop also accepts an unknown key when a known key is present (`{weight:1, foo:1}`), because it re-checks the same known key on every iteration. That is a C bug, so Rust rejects it.

### Found by

Lean 4 model `proofs/search_concurrency` (`Search` `#guard` option divergences, `parseDimension_*`, `metricOf_ok_iff`). Repro: `proofs/search_concurrency/repro/repro_search.py` case 3.

issues.title: fix: free a shared GrB_Matrix exactly once when clones drop concurrently
issues.body:
Closes #3089

## Problem

`Matrix::drop` and `Iter::drop` (`matrix.rs`) freed the shared `GrB_Matrix` only if `Arc::get_mut` succeeded, and the `Arc` field was decremented afterwards. The check and the decrement are two steps: two owners dropping at the same time could both see a count of 2, both skip the free, then both decrement to 0, and the matrix leaked. (No interleaving double-frees.)

## Fix

The handle now lives in a `Handle(GrB_Matrix)` newtype whose `Drop` calls `GrB_Matrix_free`, and `Matrix` / `Iter` hold `Arc<Handle>`. The `Arc`'s own atomic count decides who drops the last reference, so the free runs exactly once. The two `get_mut` drop blocks are gone. `Handle` derefs to `GrB_Matrix`, so the FFI call sites only change from `*x.m` to `**x.m` (the same code: `Handle` is a newtype). As a side effect, `Iter` now frees its `GxB_Iterator` before the matrix it is attached to (before, it freed the matrix first when it was the last owner).

## Tests

New integration test `graph/tests/matrix_concurrent_drop.rs` (its own binary, since it installs a counting allocator into GraphBLAS): 100,000 pairs of a matrix and a clone (a third of them an `Iter`), each pair dropped simultaneously on two threads; asserts no GraphBLAS block is left.

- main: `9918` / `3678` / `5895 GraphBLAS blocks never freed` (3 runs, all fail)
- this branch: 0 left, 3/3 runs pass

The counting-allocator repro from the Lean work (`bug_matrix_concurrent_drop_leaks`, not in this PR) leaked 65 matrices on main and 0 now. `ok_matrix_sequential_drop_frees` still passes.

Traversal (every row scan creates and drops an `Iter`), 100k nodes / 100k edges, 30 runs per query after 3 warm-up runs, release, alternated A/B three times (load average ~7–10):

| query | main p50 / p99 (ms) | this PR p50 / p99 (ms) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 2-hop count | 9.48 / 11.07, 11.94 / 12.70, 12.35 / 12.89 | 10.60 / 10.97, 11.69 / 12.41, 11.61 / 12.29 |
| expand-into | 3.60 / 3.77, 4.52 / 4.90, 4.26 / 4.59 | 4.09 / 4.17, 4.29 / 4.55, 4.13 / 4.26 |

issues.title: [Rust] Concurrent drop of two Matrix clones (or a clone and an Iter) leaks the GrB_Matrix
issues.body:
### Summary

Two clones of a `Matrix` (or a clone and an `Iter` over it) dropped at the same time on different threads can both skip freeing the shared `GrB_Matrix`, which then leaks. MVCC snapshots and read queries on the thread pool clone matrices constantly, so this can happen in normal operation. No interleaving double-frees; it is a leak only.

### Reproduction (`main` @ 55204c94b)

100,000 `Matrix::<bool>::new(4, 4)` clone pairs (a third of them an `Iter` + the matrix), each pair dropped simultaneously on two threads, with a counting allocator installed into GraphBLAS:

```
assertion `left == right` failed: 9918 GraphBLAS blocks never freed
assertion `left == right` failed: 3678 GraphBLAS blocks never freed
assertion `left == right` failed: 5895 GraphBLAS blocks never freed      (3 runs)
```

(`graph/tests/lean_graphblas_wrappers.rs::bug_matrix_concurrent_drop_leaks`: 19–65 of 200,000 pairs leaked per run.)

### Mechanism

`graph/src/graph/graphblas/matrix.rs:388` (`Matrix::drop`) and `:1588` (`Iter::drop`):

```rust
if let Some(m) = Arc::get_mut(&mut self.m) { GrB_Matrix_free(m); }
// ... then the Arc field is dropped (decrement)
```

`Arc::get_mut` and the later decrement are two separate steps. With two owners: both check `get_mut` while the count is 2 (both `None`), then both decrement to 0; nobody frees the handle.

### Expected

Exactly one free when the last owner goes, whatever the thread interleaving.

### Suggested fix

Put the `GrB_Matrix_free` in the `Drop` of an owned handle type stored *inside* the `Arc` (`Arc<Handle>`), so the `Arc`'s own atomic count decides who frees.

### Found by

Lean 4 model of the ownership protocol (`proofs/graphblas_wrappers`, `Own.lean`: `race_leaks` witness, `never_double_free`, `sequential_frees_once`); Rust repro named above.

issues.title: fix: clamp k in vector KNN queries instead of allocating k entries
issues.body:
Closes #3085

## Problem

`Graph::vector_query_nodes` / `vector_query_edges` created their output with `Vec::with_capacity(k)`, using the `k` the user passed to `db.idx.vector.queryNodes` / `queryRelationships`. `k = 10^15` aborted the allocation and killed the server. The unclamped `k` also went to `RediSearch_CreateVecSimNode`, and for `k = i64::MAX` the KNN query returned no rows. C returns every entity in both cases.

## Fix

- Size the output by the number of candidates the KNN iterator actually returned.
- Clamp `k` to the graph's node count (or relationship count for edges) before building the KNN query. That count is an O(1) upper bound on the index size, so the result is unchanged for any `k` that was already valid.

## Tests

New flow test `test_vecsim.test11_huge_k_is_clamped` runs `k = 10^15` and `k = i64::MAX` on the node and edge vector indexes. It asserts that all 1001 nodes come back, that the edge index returns results, and that the server still answers PING.

- Before (`main` @ 55204c94b): the server crashes (`process is not alive`).
- After: `test_vecsim` 10/10 pass.

Manual check: `k` = 1, 10, 10^15 and i64::MAX all return 1 row on a one-entity index, for nodes and for edges. C also returns 1. `cargo fmt --check` passes and `cargo clippy --all-targets` adds no warnings in the touched files. `cargo test -p graph --lib` gives 421 passed and 1 failed; the failure is the known macOS failure #2922, unrelated to this change.

issues.title: fix: a wrong-dimension vector no longer drops the entity from every index on its label
issues.body:
Closes #3075

`Document::set` added every `VecF32` value to a vector field without checking the index's dimension. RediSearch rejects the whole document when the vector has the wrong dimension. All of a label's fields share one spec and one document, so the entity dropped out of the label's range and fulltext indexes too, and `MATCH (n:L) WHERE n.name = 'a'` via the index returned nothing. issues.title: fix: populate a field added to an index while the index is still populating
issues.body:
Closes #3069

## Problem

`Indexer::create_index` bumped the index generation only when it added a vector field. A range or fulltext field added while the label's index was still populating therefore got a population ticket in the **same** generation as the running job. `populate_index_batch` bails when it sees more than one pending ticket, and the new job, whose snapshot has all fields, usually saw that first and bailed. The old job, whose snapshot lacked the new field, then finished and released its ticket. The index went OPERATIONAL with the new field empty, and index scans on it returned 0 rows.

## Fix

Bump the generation whenever a field is added to an existing entry, not only for vector rebuilds. The stale job fails `is_ticket_current` at its next batch and releases its stale ticket. The job spawned for the new generation then populates from the start with the full field set. The bump comes after every fallible step: the pending counters are shared with the published entry, so a bump on an entry that is never published would desynchronize them. `create_index` already holds the indexer lock, so the bump is serialized with population batches. This is the fix modelled by `Tickets.fixed_trace_complete` in `proofs/search_concurrency`.

## Tests

New flow test `test_index_create.test18_field_added_during_population_is_populated`: 5 rounds of 30k nodes, `CREATE INDEX (n.a)` then `(n.b)` back-to-back. Once OPERATIONAL, it asserts that both index scans return 30000.

- Before (`main` @ 55204c94b): `FAIL 0 == 30000 [index on L.b]`
- After: PASS

Manual repro (10 rounds each, back-to-back creates): before, 7/10 rounds wrong at 30k nodes and 8/10 at 100k (`b` → 0). After, 0/10 and 0/10. C: 0/5. `repro/twoidx.py` at 300k nodes with delays 0.05/0.1/0.2 s gives full counts after the fix.

Also run on a private port, `--parallelism 1`: `test_index_create` (18/18), `test_index_delete` (14/14), `test_index_updates` (11/11), `test_edge_index_updates` (6/6), `test_index_scans` (35/35), `test_edge_index_scans` (29/29), `test_fulltext_query` (5/5), `test_constraint` (26/26). `test_constraint` passed 5 consecutive runs; two earlier runs taken while the machine was heavily loaded each reported one failure, which did not reproduce. `cargo fmt --check` passes and `cargo clippy --all-targets` adds no warnings in the touched files.

The separate problem of writes racing population and leaving stale entries (`repro/poprace.py`) has a different root cause and is not fixed here.

issues.title: [Rust] Huge k in db.idx.vector.queryNodes crashes the server (Vec::with_capacity(k))
issues.body:
### Summary

A very large `k` in `db.idx.vector.queryNodes` / `queryRelationships` crashes the server. A `k` near `i64::MAX` returns no rows. C returns all matching rows in both cases.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 55204c94b)

```
GRAPH.QUERY hk "CREATE VECTOR INDEX FOR (n:L) ON (n.v) OPTIONS {dimension:2, similarityFunction:'euclidean'}"
GRAPH.QUERY hk "CREATE (:L {v:vecf32([1,2])})"
GRAPH.QUERY hk "CALL db.idx.vector.queryNodes('L','v',1000000000000000,vecf32([1,2])) YIELD node RETURN count(node)"
Rust: Error: Server closed the connection        C: 1
```

After fixing the allocation, `k = 9223372036854775807` returns `0` rows (C: `1`).

### Mechanism

- `Graph::vector_query_nodes` / `vector_query_edges` (`graph/src/graph/graph.rs:3744,3799`) call `Vec::with_capacity(k)` with the user's `k`. That aborts on allocation failure, which kills the server.
- The unclamped `k` also goes to `RediSearch_CreateVecSimNode`. For `k` near `i64::MAX` the KNN iterator yields nothing.

### Expected

Same as C: the call returns every indexed entity when `k` is at least the index size.

### Suggested fix

Size the output by the number of results rather than by `k`, and clamp `k` to the entity count, which is an upper bound on the index size, before building the KNN query.

### Found by

Lean 4 model `proofs/search_concurrency` (`Search.huge_k_kills_server`, fix: `Search.capped_capacity_ok`).

issues.title: fix: report a self-loop once in UDF getNeighbors / traverse edges
issues.body:
Closes #3083

## Problem

`collect_edges` (`graph/src/udf/js_classes.rs`), used by `node.getNeighbors()` and `graph.traverse()`, filtered `Graph::get_node_relationships` by `src == node` / `dst == node`. That iterator yields a self-loop once as outgoing and once as incoming, so with `returnType: 'edges'` a self-loop came back twice (`outgoing` `[2, 0, 4, 2]`, `incoming` `[3, 2, 2]`; C: `[2, 0, 4]`, `[2, 3]`).

## Fix

`collect_edges` remembers the self-loop edge ids it has emitted and skips the second copy. No allocation unless the node has a self-loop.

Matches C for 'outgoing' / 'incoming'. For 'both' Rust returns every incident edge once (`[3, 2, 0, 4]`); C returns only the outgoing edges there, which looks like a C bug, so that is not copied.

## Tests

- New flow test `tests/flow/test_udf.py::test_get_neighbors_self_loop_once`: getNeighbors and traverse edge ids for outgoing / incoming / both on a node with a self-loop.
  - Before (module built from `main`): FAIL (`[0, 2, 2, 4] == [0, 2, 4]`, `[2, 2, 3] == [2, 3]`, `[0, 2, 2, 3, 4] == [0, 2, 3, 4]`).
  - After: `tests/flow/test_udf` 45/45 pass (RLTest on a private port).

issues.title: [Rust] Filter after an aggregating WITH is pushed into one Cartesian branch (variable-id collision): 0 rows where C returns 2
issues.body:
### Summary

A MATCH that follows an aggregating `WITH` can lose all its rows. When the WHERE is an equality between two of its pattern parts, filter push-down puts the whole predicate into one branch of the Cartesian Product, where the other variable is unbound. Every row is then filtered out. This happens whenever an earlier clause bound enough variables for their ids to collide with the new ones. No write is needed: the CREATE in the original report only supplies the two colliding variables. It is not a pending-visibility problem.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 55204c94b)

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE (:B {v:0}),(:B {v:5}) WITH count(*) AS s MATCH (b:B),(c:B) WHERE c.v=b.v RETURN count(*)"
-- Rust: 0        C: 2

GRAPH.RO_QUERY g "MATCH (x:B),(y:B) WITH count(*) AS s MATCH (b:B),(c:B) WHERE c.v=b.v RETURN count(*)"
-- Rust: 0        C: 2
```

The plan shows the predicate pushed under the `c` scan instead of becoming a Value Hash Join:

```
Aggregate
    Apply
        Aggregate
            Commit
                Create | (_anon_0:B), (_anon_1:B),
        Cartesian Product
            Node By Label Scan | (b:B)
                Argument
            Filter                      <- c.v = b.v, but b is not bound here
                Node By Label Scan | (c:B)
                    Argument
```

With a single pre-WITH variable (`MATCH (x) WITH count(*) ...`) or a non-aggregating `WITH 1 AS s`, the same query is planned as a Value Hash Join and returns the right count. The following also return 0 on main: `... WHERE c.v=b.v AND s > 0`, `WITH collect(x) AS s ... WHERE c.v >= b.v`, and `MATCH (b:B) MATCH (c:B) WHERE c.v=b.v` after the same WITH.

### Mechanism

A `Variable::id` is an index into its own scope's env, so ids start again at every `WITH`, and `x`/`y` (scope 0) share ids with `b`/`c` (scope 1). The optimizer's variable sets are keyed on `id` alone:

- `collect_subtree_variables` (`graph/src/planner/optimizer/mod.rs:102`) walks the entire subtree through `GetVariables`. Its `Aggregate` arm (`graph/src/runtime/runtime.rs:319`) adds the group keys and then keeps descending, so it reports `x` and `y` even though they do not survive the `Aggregate`. It also leaves out the aggregate's own output, `s`.
- `push_filters_down` "Case 2" (`push_filters_down.rs:238`) uses that set for the Apply's left branch and adds it to every Argument-fed branch on the right. The `c` branch then seems to provide `{c, x, y}`, which as bare ids is `{c, b}`, so `c.v = b.v` gets routed there. The Filter no longer sits above the Cartesian Product, so `replace_cartesian_with_hash_join` has nothing to rewrite.

`select_scan_node` (`select_scan_node.rs:897`, the `initial_bound` hop set) and `replace_cartesian_with_hash_join` (`:117`) read the same helper, so they are exposed to the same collision.

### Expected

Same as C: 2 rows (and a Value Hash Join plan).

### Suggested fix

Make `collect_subtree_variables` stop at env-resetting operators (`Project`, `Aggregate`) and report only their named outputs, the variables that actually reach the subtree's parent. `push_filters_down` already does this one level deep through `branch_output_variables`. The fix goes in the shared helper, so all three optimizer passes get it.

### Found by

Reported by the binder-analysis agent (Wave 2, `proofs/binder`) while probing a Value Hash Join over nodes created earlier in the same query. Minimised here to the variable-id collision.

issues.title: fix: range index scans include ±inf for an open bound and emit undirected edges both ways
issues.body:
Part of #2963 (fixes items 1 and 5; items 2-4 need design and are left there). Closes #2100.

## Problem

Two range-index scans that gave different rows than the full scan, on both engines:

1. **An open bound excluded ±inf.** `build_numeric_range_node` replaced an absent bound with `RSRANGE_INF`/`RSRANGE_NEG_INF` but passed the operator's include flag, which is `false` for the absent side. So `n.v > 0` became `(0, +inf)` and missed a stored `+inf`, and `n.v >= 1.0/0.0` became `[inf, inf)`, which is empty.
2. **An undirected pattern was scanned one way.** `EdgeByIndexScan` emitted each edge once, `src → dst`. `CondTraverse` emits an undirected match in both orientations (a self-loop once). #2100's table, which C shares:

| Query (index on `:E(uuid)`) | no index | `main` + index | this PR |
|---|---|---|---|
| `MATCH ()-[r:E {uuid:'d1'}]-() RETURN count(r)` | 4 | 2 | 4 |
| `MATCH ()-[r:E]-() WHERE r.uuid='d1' RETURN count(r)` | 4 | 2 | 4 |
| `MATCH (a:P {id:'a'})-[r:E {uuid:'d1'}]-(b:P {id:'b'}) RETURN count(r)` | 2 | 1 | 2 |

## Fix

1. An absent bound is inclusive (`include_min || min.is_none()`, and the same for max).
2. For `rp.bidirectional`, the op expands each index hit `(src, dst, e)` into `(src, dst, e)` and `(dst, src, e)`, and only the first when `src == dst`. This happens before the existing bound-endpoint and self-loop-alias filter, so pinned endpoints pick the right orientation. The directed path is unchanged.

C has both bugs; this PR follows the full scan and openCypher (`inf > 0` is true, and an undirected match binds both orientations).

## Tests

- New flow test `test_index_scans.py::test_41_open_bound_includes_infinity` checks `> 0`, `< 0`, `>= inf` and `<= -inf` with and without the index. On `main` all 4 fail (for example `[['one']] == [['inf'], ['one']]`); with this PR they pass.
- New flow test `test_edge_index_scans.py::test_undirected_pattern_emits_both_orientations` runs 5 undirected queries (counts, endpoints, both pinned orders) with and without the index, with a self-loop in the data. On `main` all 5 fail (`[[3]] == [[5]]`, `[[0]] == [[0], [1]]`, …); with this PR they pass.
- Flow tests with RLTest on a private port: `test_index_scans` 36/36, `test_edge_index_scans` 30/30, `test_edge_index_updates` 6/6.
- `cargo fmt --check` passes, and clippy reports nothing in the touched files.
- Bench: 100k `(:L)-[:R]->(:M)`, indexes on `R.v` and `L.v`. Release build, 150 runs per query, base and fix alternated, load average about 15. No change on the directed path:

| query | base p50 / p99 | this PR p50 / p99 |
|---|---|---|
| `()-[r:R]->() WHERE r.v < 20000` count | 3803 / 12813 µs | 3720 / 11372 µs |
| `()-[r:R]->() WHERE r.v = 777` | 1327 / 6160 µs | 1233 / 4667 µs |
| `(n:L) WHERE n.v > 90000` count | 2404 / 11753 µs | 2340 / 12119 µs |

Found by the Lean model in `proofs/index_layer` (`bug_open_bound_excludes_inf`) and the differential run `proofs/index_layer/diff.py` (undirected edge scan).

issues.title: fix: stop Matrix::decode leaking its container's component vectors
issues.body:
Closes #3078

## Problem

`Matrix::decode` (`matrix.rs`) created a `GxB_Container` — which allocates an empty `GrB_Vector` for each of p, h, b, i, x — then `copy_nonoverlapping`'d the payload's whole 608-byte header over it and nulled the pointers. The five fresh vectors were never freed: five leaked blocks per matrix on every RDB load, `GRAPH.RESTORE` and full sync. When a component failed to decode, the `?` returned with the container and the components decoded so far owned by nobody (eight blocks). `GxB_load_Matrix_from_Container`'s result was only a `debug_assert`, and GraphBLAS loads an unknown `format` value without checking it.

## Fix

- The payload contributes only the scalar description (nrows, ncols, nrows/ncols_nonempty, nvals, format, orientation, iso, jumbled), read with `read_unaligned`. Its pointer fields (addresses in the writer's process) and the fresh container's allocator bookkeeping are no longer copied.
- Each decoded component replaces the empty one after freeing it.
- An `OwnedContainer` guard frees the container, and every component it holds, on every path, errors included.
- An unknown `format`, or a container `GxB_load_Matrix_from_Container` rejects, returns `Err` (the matrix is freed). `GxB_Container_new` / `GrB_Matrix_new` failures return `Err` too instead of asserting.

The on-disk format is unchanged: a payload written by main or by C loads the same way.

## Tests

- New flow test `test_persistency.py::test_reload_does_not_leak` (20 `DEBUG RELOAD`s of a small graph, `used_memory` growth per reload < 1 KB): **main fails** (+29,952 B per reload), this branch passes (−768 B).
- New unit test `matrix::tests::decode_round_trips_and_refuses_bad_payloads`: round trip, truncated payload → `Err`, unknown format → `Err`, too few rows → `Err` from GraphBLAS. On main it fails (`unknown sparsity format accepted`).
- Counting-allocator repros from the Lean work (not in this PR): `Matrix::decode` leaked 5.00 blocks per call (8.00 on the error path) on main, 0 now.

Memory and load time, `DEBUG RELOAD` loop on a 200k-node / 900k-edge graph (9 relationship types, 100k multi-edge pairs) plus 40 small graphs, release, alternated A/B/A/B (machine shared, load average ~10–16):

| build | reloads | p50 | p99 | used_memory growth | RSS growth |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| main | 40 | 457.1 ms | 524.6 ms | +810,424 B/reload | +820.8 KB/reload |
| this PR | 40 | 485.4 ms | 596.9 ms | +191 B/reload | +331.2 KB/reload |
| main | 40 | 624.7 ms | 645.2 ms | +810,440 B/reload | +831.6 KB/reload |
| this PR | 40 | 616.4 ms | 1151.4 ms | +208 B/reload | +146.4 KB/reload |

Over 80 reloads: main 62.7 MB → 127.5 MB used_memory (RSS +66 MB); this PR 61.08 → 61.10 MB (RSS +2.9 MB). Load time is the same within the noise.

Also run: `cargo fmt --all -- --check`, `CXX=clang++ cargo clippy --all-targets` (clean), `cargo test --release -p graph --lib` (423 passed), flow `test_graph_copy` 9/9, `test_persistency` 12/12, `test_rdb_load` 2/2, `test_rdb_c_layout` 4/4, `test_replication` 2/2. An RDB saved by the C module (100 triple multi-edge pairs plus single edges) loads with the same query results as C.

issues.title: [Rust] Matrix::decode leaks the container's five component vectors on every RDB load / RESTORE
issues.body:
### Summary

Every matrix loaded from an RDB / `GRAPH.RESTORE` / full sync leaks the five empty component vectors its `GxB_Container` was created with. On a 200k-node / 900k-edge graph plus 40 small graphs, `used_memory` grows by ~810 KB on every `DEBUG RELOAD`, without bound (80 reloads: 62.7 MB → 127.5 MB used_memory, RSS +66 MB).

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 55204c94b)

```
# graph: 200k :A nodes, 9 relationship types (100k multi-edge pairs), plus 40 small graphs
# 2 warm-up DEBUG RELOADs, then 80 more:
reloads=80  RSS 282128KB -> 348400KB (+828.4 KB/reload)  used_memory 62692264 -> 127526856 (+810432 B/reload)
```

A small graph (`UNWIND range(1,100) AS i CREATE (a:A:B {v:i})-[:R]->(b:C {v:i}), (a)-[:R]->(b), (a)-[:S]->(b), (b)-[:T]->(a)`) grows ~30 KB per reload.

Rust test with a counting allocator: `graph/tests/lean_graphblas_wrappers.rs::bug_matrix_decode_leaks_container_components` — 5.00 leaked blocks per `Matrix::decode`; `bug_matrix_decode_leaks_on_error_path` — 8.00 per call when decode fails part-way.

### Mechanism

`graph/src/graph/graphblas/matrix.rs:443-465` (`Matrix::decode`): `GxB_Container_new` allocates the container *and* an empty `GrB_Vector` for each of p, h, b, i, x. The code then `copy_nonoverlapping`s the payload's 608 header bytes over the whole struct, which overwrites those five pointers (with addresses from the writer's process), and nulls them. The fresh vectors are never freed.

On the error paths, the `?` after each `Vector::<bool>::decode` returns with the container and the components decoded so far owned by nobody (8 blocks). Also, `GxB_load_Matrix_from_Container`'s result is only a `debug_assert` (a container GraphBLAS rejects panics in debug and yields an empty matrix in release), and GraphBLAS loads an unknown `format` value without checking it.

### Expected

Loading a graph repeatedly keeps memory flat (C does not leak here), and a rejected container is a load error.

### Suggested fix

Copy only the scalar fields (dimensions, nvals, format, orientation, iso, jumbled) from the payload into the fresh container, replace each component by freeing the empty one first, and own the container in a guard that frees it on every path; return `Err` when the format is unknown or the load fails.

### Found by

Lean 4 model of the GraphBLAS wrappers (`proofs/graphblas_wrappers`, ownership model `Own`); Rust repros named above.

issues.title: fix: don't index temporals in the range index's numeric field
issues.body:
Closes #2959

## Problem

`Document::set` added temporals (Date, DateTime, LocalTime, Duration) to a range index as their raw number, in the same numeric field Int and Float queries use. So numeric predicates matched them:

| Query (index on `:L(v)`) | no index / C | `main` + index | this PR |
|---|---|---|---|
| `WHERE n.v > 0` | `int` | `date`, `dur`, `int`, `ldt` | `int` |
| `WHERE n.v < 0` (date before 1970) | — | `old` | — |
| `WHERE n.v = 86400` (`duration('P1D')`) | — | `dur` | — |

## Fix

Temporals are no longer added to the index. No index query is ever built for a temporal value: the scan ops' `can_utilize_index` refuses them and falls back to a label scan. So storing them only produced false positives, and no temporal query loses index acceleration. Serving temporal predicates from the index would need its own sub-field, as C uses per-type fields; that is a separate feature. Constraints don't read the range index (`validate_unique_constraint` scans the label), so they are unaffected.

## Tests

- New flow test `test_index_scans.py::test_40_temporals_not_in_numeric_range` stores Int, Date (after and before 1970), Duration and LocalDateTime values and compares `> 0`, `< 0` and `= 86400` with and without the index. On `main` all 3 fail. With this PR they pass.
- Flow tests with RLTest on a private port: `test_index_scans` 36/36, `test_index_updates` 11/11.
- `cargo fmt --check` passes, and clippy reports nothing in `index/mod.rs`. Index writes for temporals get cheaper (nothing is added); nothing else changes.

Found by the Lean model in `proofs/index_layer` (`bug_temporal_in_numeric_range`) and `proofs/optimizer_scan` (`IndexCex` C2).

issues.title: [Rust] A vector of the wrong dimension removes the entity from all indexes on its label
issues.body:
### Summary

When an entity's vector has a different dimension from the label's vector index, the entity drops out of **every** index on that label, including unrelated range and fulltext indexes. Index scans then miss it. C skips only the vector field and keeps the entity in the other indexes.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 55204c94b)

```
GRAPH.QUERY vd "CREATE INDEX FOR (n:L) ON (n.name)"
GRAPH.QUERY vd "CREATE VECTOR INDEX FOR (n:L) ON (n.v) OPTIONS {dimension:2, similarityFunction:'euclidean'}"
GRAPH.QUERY vd "CREATE (:L {name:'a', v:vecf32([1,2,3])})"
GRAPH.QUERY vd "MATCH (n:L) WHERE n.name='a' RETURN n.name"
Rust: (empty)       C: a
```

The same happens when the entity is indexed by background population, and when a later `SET` writes a wrong-dimension vector.

### Mechanism

`Document::set` (`graph/src/index/mod.rs:720-731`) adds every `VecF32` value to the vector field without checking the index's dimension. RediSearch rejects the whole document (all fields of the label share one spec and one document), so the entity is removed from every index on the label. C checks the dimension first and skips the vector field (`src/index/index.c:470-476`, "vector dimension mis-match, can't index this vector").

### Expected

Same as C: a vector of the wrong dimension is not added to the vector index, and the entity stays in the other indexes.

### Suggested fix

In `Document::set`, skip the vector field when `vec.len() != vector_options.dimension`.

### Found by

Lean 4 model `proofs/search_concurrency` (`Search.vector_dim_mismatch_drops_range_entry`, fix: `Search.fixed_doc_always_accepted`).

issues.title: fix: UDF results keep -0.0, constructor-keyed maps and non-finite vecf32
issues.body:
Closes #3073

## Problem

`js_to_value` (`graph/src/udf/type_convert.rs`) altered values C passes through an identity UDF unchanged:
- `-0.0` became `Int 0` (every integral number below 2^53 is an Int, and `-0.0 == floor(-0.0)`), so `1/rt.id(-0.0)` was `Division by zero` instead of `-inf`.
- Date / RegExp were detected by the object's `constructor.name`, so a Cypher map `{constructor: {name: 'Date'}}` failed with `Date getTime error`, and `{constructor: {name: 'RegExp'}}` came back as the string `'[object Object]'`.
- VecF32 elements had to be finite, so `rt.id(vecf32([1e39]))` failed although `vecf32()` accepts inf.

## Fix

- Keep `-0.0` a Float.
- Detect Date / RegExp with QuickJS's internal class checks (`JS_IsDate` / `JS_IsRegExp`) instead of the `constructor` property.
- Drop the finiteness check on VecF32 elements.

Matches C. (C loses a `date` through a UDF — `rt.id(date(...)) = date(...)` is false in C; Rust keeps returning true, covered by the test.)

## Tests

- New flow test `tests/flow/test_udf.py::test_roundtrip_fidelity`: `rt.id(-0.0)` is `-0.0` and `1/` it (and of a JS `-0`) is `-inf`; maps with `constructor: {name: 'Date'|'RegExp'}` round-trip equal; `vecf32([1e39, 1.5])` round-trips equal; real `localdatetime` / `date` values still round-trip.
  - Before (module built from `main`): ERROR (`Division by zero`).
  - After: `tests/flow/test_udf` 45/45 pass (RLTest on a private port). Live check: a UDF returning `/ab+c/i` and `new Date(0)` still gives `/ab+c/i` and `1970-01-01T00:00:00`.
- `cargo fmt --all -- --check`, `CXX=clang++ cargo clippy --all-targets`: clean for touched code.

issues.title: fix: an exclusive string range with equal bounds selects nothing
issues.body:
Closes #2961

## Problem

`n.v > 'a' AND n.v < 'a'` is merged into `Range { min: 'a', max: 'a', include_min: false, include_max: false }`. `build_string_range_node` turned any range with equal bounds into an exact-token match, ignoring the include flags, so the index returned `'a'`.
