issues.title: [Rust] Grouped count(DISTINCT) shares state between groups whose key rows collide in a 64-bit hash
issues.body:
### Summary

Grouped `count(DISTINCT ..)` / `collect(DISTINCT ..)` / `sum(DISTINCT ..)` keep each group's seen-set in a side table keyed by a 64-bit FxHash of the group's key row. Two different groups whose key rows hash the same share one seen-set, so a value seen in one group is skipped in the other. FxHash is unseeded and fast to invert, so a client can pick such keys on purpose.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 2363723ac)

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "UNWIND [[[0,0],1],[[1,-1452335207727870361],1]] AS p
               WITH p[0] AS k, p[1] AS v RETURN k, count(*) AS n, count(DISTINCT v) AS c"
Rust: [0, 0]|1|1 ; [1, -1452335207727870361]|1|0
C:    [0, 0]|1|1 ; [1, -1452335207727870361]|1|1
```

The grouping is correct (`count(*)` is 1 in each group) but the second group's `count(DISTINCT v)` is 0.

### Mechanism

- The groups themselves are collision-free: `GroupMap` is keyed by `GroupKey`, which resolves collisions with `Value::eq` (`graph/src/runtime/ops/aggregate.rs:59`, `:83`).
- The DISTINCT state is not. It lives in `Runtime::value_dedupers`, keyed by `(Distinct node, group_id)`, where `group_id = entry.0.hash_u64()`, an FxHash of the group's key row. That is `aggregate.rs:715` on the vectorized path and `:959` on the per-row path, which feeds `eval.rs:835`. Colliding groups therefore land on the same `ValuesDeduper`.

### How this differs from #2780 (closed, not planned)

#2780 is about the DISTINCT *values* (and `DistinctOp` rows) being remembered by their 64-bit hash with no equality check. Fixing that means storing every distinct value, which costs memory, and it was declined for that reason. This issue is a different site. Here it is two *groups* whose state gets merged, and the exact group key is already stored in `GroupMap`. Only the lookup into the side table throws it away and uses its hash. Fixing it costs nothing: give each group an id when it is inserted into `GroupMap`, and key the dedupers by that id. That also saves hashing the whole key row once per input row.

### Expected (C behaviour)

Each group has its own DISTINCT state: `c = 1` for both groups.

### Suggested fix

Store a sequential group id next to each `GroupMap` entry (the map length at insertion). Use it as `group_id`/`agg_group_key` on both the vectorized and the per-row paths, and drop `HashU64`.

### Found by

Lean 4 model of the aggregate operators (`proofs/ops_aggregate`), theorem `hashed_dedup_merges_groups`; Rust repro `graph/tests/lean_ops_aggregate.rs` (`bug_grouped_count_distinct_shares_state_on_group_hash_collision`).

issues.title: fix: reset only the sub-plan's DISTINCT state between CALL {} rows (#2779)
issues.body:
Closes #2779

## Problem

Per-row `ApplyOp` (the mode a `CALL {}` body with an aggregate, `LIMIT`, `ORDER BY`, ... runs in) called `runtime.value_dedupers.borrow_mut().clear()` after every invocation. The map is runtime-wide: every `DISTINCT` aggregate in the plan keys its seen-set there by `(Distinct node, group)`. So the clear also wiped the state of an enclosing aggregate that was still accumulating. That aggregate consumes Apply's output one 1024-row batch at a time, so each value was counted once per batch:

```
UNWIND range(1, 3000) AS i CALL { WITH i RETURN i % 2 AS v LIMIT 1 }
RETURN count(DISTINCT v), collect(DISTINCT v)
Rust main: 6, [1, 0, 1, 0, 1, 0]      C: 2, [1, 0]
```

## Fix

`ApplyOp::new` collects the `ExprIR::Distinct` nodes of the aggregates inside its own sub-plan, only when it runs per row. After each invocation it `retain`s every other entry instead of clearing the map. The sub-plan's own `DISTINCT` still starts fresh for every row, and nothing is done when the sub-plan has no `DISTINCT`.

## Tests

- New flow test `test_call_subquery:testCallSubqueryFlow.test_55_outer_distinct_aggregate_survives_call` covers keyless and grouped outer aggregates, plus an inner `count(DISTINCT)` that must still reset per row. Expected values checked against the C module.
  - Before (`main` @ 2363723ac): FAIL, `[[6, [1, 0, 1, 0, 1, 0]]] == [[2, [1, 0]]]` and `[[0, 15], [1, 15]] == [[0, 5], [1, 5]]`.
  - After: the whole `tests/flow/test_call_subquery` suite passes (55/55).
- Bench (release, alternating A/B runs, very loaded shared machine at load avg ~100). No difference beyond noise:

| query | main p50 / p99 | this PR p50 / p99 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `UNWIND range(1,20000) AS i CALL { WITH i UNWIND [i, i] AS x RETURN count(DISTINCT x) AS c } RETURN sum(c)` (60 runs, order A/B) | 168.9 / 307.0 ms | 151.7 / 434.6 ms |
| same (60 runs, order B/A) | 103.5 / 272.1 ms | 96.6 / 332.4 ms |
| `UNWIND range(1,20000) AS i CALL { WITH i RETURN i % 7 AS v LIMIT 1 } RETURN count(DISTINCT v)` (30 runs) | 65.5 / 160.8 ms | 65.8 / 129.3 ms |

issues.title: [Rust] SET/REMOVE on a relationship deleted earlier in the query is applied and counted
issues.body:
### Summary

A `SET`/`REMOVE` on a relationship that the same query has already deleted is applied and counted. For nodes the same write is skipped (C behaviour). Two holes:

- `REMOVE r.v` after `DELETE r`: `ops/remove.rs` has no deletion check for relationships at all (nodes have one).
- `SET r.v = …` on an edge that `DETACH DELETE a` cascades: the cascade is recorded only in the runtime's snapshot map (`Runtime::deleted_relationships`), not in `pending.deleted_relationships` (that happens at commit), so the check in `ops/set.rs:260` lets it through.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 2363723ac, fresh graph each)

| setup ; query | Rust | C |
|---|---|---|
| `CREATE ()-[:R {v:1}]->()` ; `MATCH ()-[r]->() DELETE r REMOVE r.v RETURN r.v` | `[[1]]`, `Properties removed: 1, Relationships deleted: 1` | `[[1]]`, `Relationships deleted: 1` |
| `CREATE (a)-[:R {v:1}]->()` ; `MATCH (a)-[r]->() DETACH DELETE a SET r.v = 2 RETURN r.v` | `[[1]]`, `Properties set: 1, Properties removed: 1, Nodes deleted: 1, Relationships deleted: 1` | `[[1]]`, `Nodes deleted: 1, Relationships deleted: 1` |
| `CREATE ()-[:R {v:1}]->()` ; `MATCH ()-[r]->() DELETE r SET r.v = 2 RETURN r.v` | same as C | `[[1]]`, `Relationships deleted: 1` |

The staged write is also carried into commit and the effects buffer for an edge that commit then deletes.

### Mechanism

`ops/remove.rs:145` (`Value::Relationship` arm) calls `set_pending_relationship_attr` unconditionally. `ops/set.rs:260` checks `g.is_relationship_deleted`, `pending.is_relationship_created` and `pending.is_relationship_deleted`, but an edge cascaded by a pending node delete is in none of them until commit; it is only in `Runtime::deleted_relationships`.

### Expected (C)

Writes to a deleted relationship are skipped and not counted, like writes to a deleted node.

### Suggested fix

One `Runtime` predicate "is this relationship deleted in this query" (committed-deleted and not pending-created, pending-deleted, or snapshotted as deleted), used by both SET and REMOVE; include the relationship snapshot map in SET's `skip_delete_checks` pre-check.

### Found by

Lean model `proofs/pending_commit` (counterexample 3 in `PendingCommit.lean`); Rust repro `graph/tests/lean_pending_commit.rs::bug_writes_to_deleted_relationship_are_counted`.

issues.title: [Rust] Entities created and deleted in the same segment vanish from write statistics
issues.body:
### Summary

An entity created and deleted inside the same commit segment vanishes from the write statistics: neither its create, nor its delete, nor its properties are counted. C counts all three. A pending edge deleted *directly* is counted, so Rust is inconsistent with itself too.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 2363723ac, fresh graph)

| query | Rust | C |
|---|---|---|
| `CREATE (a:L {v:1, w:2}) DELETE a` | `Labels added: 1` | `Labels added: 1, Nodes created: 1, Properties set: 2, Nodes deleted: 1` |
| `CREATE (a)-[:R]->(b) DELETE a` | `Nodes created: 1` | `Nodes created: 2, Relationships created: 1, Nodes deleted: 1, Relationships deleted: 1` |
| `CREATE (a)-[:R {x:1}]->(b {y:2}) DELETE a` | `Nodes created: 1, Properties set: 1` | `Nodes created: 2, Properties set: 2, Relationships created: 1, Nodes deleted: 1, Relationships deleted: 1` |
| after `CREATE (:A)`: `MATCH (a:A) CREATE (a)-[:R {x:1}]->(b) DELETE a` | `Nodes created: 1, Nodes deleted: 1` | `Nodes created: 1, Properties set: 1, Relationships created: 1, Nodes deleted: 1, Relationships deleted: 1` |
| `CREATE ()-[r:R {x:1}]->() DELETE r` (direct) | same as C | `Nodes created: 2, Properties set: 1, Relationships created: 1, Relationships deleted: 1` |

### Mechanism

Deleting a pending-created node takes the shortcut in `Pending::delete_pending_node` (`graph/src/runtime/pending.rs:710`): it unwinds the node (and, via `remove_pending_relationships_for_node`, its pending edges) out of `created_nodes`, `created_rels_by_type` and the staged attribute maps, and records the ids only in `cancelled_nodes` / `cancelled_relationships`. The counters in `Pending::commit` (`pending.rs:1141`, `:1147`, `:1226`, and the property counts from `import_*_attrs`) only look at what is left, so the cancelled entities are never counted. A pending edge deleted directly stays in `created_rels_by_type` and `deleted_relationships`, so it is counted.

### Expected (C)

Count a cancelled entity as created and deleted, and count the properties it was created with.

### Suggested fix

Count at the cancellation: `nodes_created`/`nodes_deleted` += 1 per cancelled node, `relationships_created`/`relationships_deleted` += 1 per cancelled edge, `properties_set` += the non-null staged attributes they carried. (Labels are not affected: `Labels added` is counted from the schema, #2655.)

### Found by

Lean model `proofs/pending_commit` (`Stats.c_eq_rust_plus_cancelled`: C's counters = Rust's + |cancelled| on every well-formed segment; `Stats.cancel_example`); Rust repro `graph/tests/lean_pending_commit.rs::bug_cancelled_*`.

(The separate net-vs-per-clause property counting question is #3028.)

issues.title: [Rust] Id seek on a graph that never held a node returns a phantom node 0; SET on it leaks into the next CREATE
issues.body:
### Summary

On a graph that has never held a node, an id seek returns a phantom node 0. Writes to it survive: `SET` on the phantom lands on the next node `CREATE` makes, and `DELETE` errors. C returns no rows.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 2363723ac, fresh graph each block)

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "MATCH (n) WHERE id(n) = 0 RETURN id(n)"
-- Rust: [[0]]      C: []
GRAPH.QUERY g "MATCH (n) WHERE id(n) >= 0 RETURN count(n)"
-- Rust: [[1]]      C: [[0]]
```

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "MATCH (n) WHERE id(n) = 0 SET n.x = 1, n:Z RETURN id(n)"
-- Rust: [[0]], Labels added: 1, Properties set: 1      C: [] and no stats
GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE (m:Q) RETURN id(m)"
GRAPH.QUERY g "MATCH (n) RETURN labels(n), properties(n)"
-- Rust: [[Z, Q], {x: 1}]      C: [[Q], {}]
```

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "MATCH (n) WHERE id(n) = 0 DELETE n"
-- Rust: error "0 was never allocated here"      C: no-op
```

### Mechanism

`Runtime::evaluate_id_filter` (`graph/src/runtime/runtime.rs:1316`) takes the upper bound from `Graph::max_node_id` (`graph/src/graph/graph.rs:1495`), which returns a `0` *sentinel* when `node_count == 0`. That is indistinguishable from "the highest id is 0", so the inclusive range is `{0}`. `NodeByIdSeekOp` (`node_by_id_seek.rs:67`) only subtracts the recycle bin, which is empty on a graph that never held a node, so id 0 survives. (Once any node has been deleted, the bin contains 0 and hides the bug.) `NodeByLabelAndIdScan` uses the same range but intersects it with the label matrix, so it is not affected.

### Expected (C)

No rows, no writes, no error.

### Suggested fix

Bound the range by `Graph::node_id_bound()` (exclusive; `node_count + deleted_nodes.len()`, which is exactly what `IdSpace` already uses and has no sentinel), and return no range when it is 0.

### Found by

Lean model `proofs/optimizer_scan` (`IdSeek.gEmpty` examples: `seek gEmpty [(.int 0, .eq)] 0 = true` vs `reference … = false`); Rust repro `graph/tests/lean_optimizer_scan.rs::bug_id_seek_phantom_node_*`.

issues.title: fix: drop a deleted entity's snapshot when its id is reissued (#2876)
issues.body:
Closes #2876
Closes #2759

## Problem

`Runtime::deleted_nodes` / `deleted_relationships` snapshot entities a query deletes, so later clauses can still read them. They are keyed by id, and every accessor (`runtime.rs:1460-1860`) reads them before the graph. Ids are recycled across commit boundaries inside a query, so a node or edge created after `DELETE … WITH` can be handed a snapshotted id. It then reads as the dead entity: wrong properties, labels, type and endpoints, `WHERE` filters it out, and `MERGE` misses it and **creates a duplicate** that stays in the graph. This also happens when nothing keeps the deleted entity reachable (`WITH count(*)`). The table is in the #2876 comment.

## Fix

When `CREATE` reserves ids (`ops/create.rs`, the only allocation path queries use, and the one MERGE and FOREACH go through), drop the snapshot of each reissued node or relationship id. From then on the id names the live entity.

Why not the "defer reuse to query end" proposal in #2876: it changes user-visible ids in delete-then-create queries, and `test_graph_deletion.py::test22_delete_reserve_id` asserts C's in-query reuse (`MATCH (a:A) DELETE a WITH * CREATE (b:A) RETURN id(b)` → 0..10). It also widens the matrices for that query shape. Evicting on reissue keeps the ids the same and gives C's answers. A variable still bound to the deleted node now reads the node that holds the id, which is what C returns (`CREATE (n {v:1}) DELETE n WITH n AS k CREATE (m {v:2}) RETURN id(k), k.v, id(m), m.v` → C `0,2,0,2`; this PR `0,2,0,2`; before `0,1,0,1`).

Lean: the model in `proofs/pending_commit` proves reads are sound as long as no snapshotted id is live (`Snapshot.sound_under_Good`). I checked that eviction keeps that invariant with the same model, in a scratch copy that is not part of this PR: `createEvict` = the current allocator plus dropping the reissued id's snapshot. `evict_preserves_Good` and `evict_reads_live_entity` build with no `sorry`.

Cost: nothing on the ordinary path. The eviction only runs when the query has snapshotted something, and then it is one hash removal per created id.

## Tests

New flow test `test_graph_deletion.py::test41_reused_id_is_not_shadowed_by_the_deleted_entity`. It covers MATCH, WHERE, labels, SET, the MERGE duplicate, a still-bound variable, the #2759 shape and relationships. Each expected value was checked against the C module.
- On `main`: fails with 9 failed assertions (e.g. `[[0, 1, ['A']]] == [[0, 2, []]]`, MERGE `2.0 == 1`, relationship `[[1, 'R', ['X'], ['Y']]]`).
- With the fix: passes.

Also run with the fix, all passing: flow `test_graph_deletion` (46/46), `test_create_clause`, `test_graph_merge`, `test_foreach`, `test_effects_commit`, `test_effects_shapes`, `test_effects_topology`, `test_replication` (one flaky failure under load, then 2/2 twice; it also passes on `main`), `test_replication_states`. `RELEASE=1 pytest tests/test_e2e.py tests/test_mvcc.py`: 94 passed. `cargo fmt --check` and clippy are clean.

issues.title: Range index vs full scan mismatches shared with C: open bounds miss ±inf, Bool = 1/0, TAG encoding order, empty string, undirected edge scan
issues.body:
### Summary

Range-index scans that give different rows than the same query without the index, on **both** engines (Rust `main` and C `master`). Each one is a place where the index layer's encoding or query building doesn't match Cypher semantics. Listed together because they share a component and C has them too; each is independent. Where an issue already exists it is linked.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 2363723ac; C = `bin/macos-arm64v8-release/falkordb.so`)

Each row: a fresh graph with `CREATE INDEX FOR (n:L) ON (n.v)` (edge row: `CREATE INDEX FOR ()-[r:R]-() ON (r.v)`), the setup, then the query.

| # | Setup | Query | no index | Rust + index | C + index |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `CREATE (:L {v:1.0/0.0, k:'inf'}), (:L {v:-1.0/0.0, k:'-inf'})` | `MATCH (n:L) WHERE n.v > 0 OR n.v < 0 RETURN n.k` | `-inf`, `inf` | **—** | **—** |
| 1 | `CREATE (:L {v:1.0/0.0, k:'inf'})` | `MATCH (n:L) WHERE n.v >= 1.0/0.0 RETURN n.k` | `inf` | **—** | **—** |
| 2 | `CREATE (:L {v:1, k:'int'}), (:L {v:true, k:'bool'})` | `MATCH (n:L) WHERE n.v = 1 RETURN n.k` | `int` | **`bool`, `int`** | **`bool`, `int`** |
| 2 | same | `MATCH (n:L) WHERE n.v = true RETURN n.k` | `bool` | **`bool`, `int`** | **`bool`, `int`** |
| 2 | `CREATE (:L {k:4, arr:[true,'X']}), (:L {k:5, arr:[1,'x']})` (index on `arr`) | `MATCH (n:L) WHERE 1 IN n.arr AND n.k > 0 RETURN n.k` | 5 | **4, 5** | **4, 5** |
| 3 | `CREATE (:L {v:'John Smith', k:'js'}), (:L {v:'Johnny', k:'jy'})` | `MATCH (n:L) WHERE n.v < 'JohnA' RETURN n.k` | `js` | **—** | **`js`, `jy`** |
| 3 | `CREATE (:L {v:'a b', k:'ab'})` | `MATCH (n:L) WHERE n.v > 'a!' RETURN n.k` | — | **`ab`** | — |
| 4 | `CREATE (:L {v:'', k:'empty'})` | `MATCH (n:L) WHERE n.v = '' RETURN n.k` | `empty` | **—** | **—** |
| 5 | `CREATE ({k:1})-[:R {v:2, k:'e'}]->({k:2})` | `MATCH ()-[r:R]-() WHERE r.v >= 1 RETURN r.k` | `e`, `e` | **`e`** | **`e`** |

### Mechanism

1. **An open bound excludes ±inf.** `build_numeric_range_node` (`graph/src/index/mod.rs:1364-1400`) turns an absent bound into `RSRANGE_INF` / `RSRANGE_NEG_INF` but passes the operator's include flag, which is `false` for the absent side (`build_op_query`, `utilize_index.rs:324`). So `n.v > 0` is `(0, +inf)` and misses a stored `+inf`; `n.v >= inf` is `[inf, inf)`, empty.
2. **Bool is indexed as 1/0** in the numeric field and the numeric array field (`Document::set`, `mod.rs:748`, `:800`; `value_to_numeric`, `mod.rs:1349`), so `= 1` and `= true` match each other. Array-contains keeps its post-filter only when it is the whole predicate (`utilize_index.rs:816-823`), so inside an `AND` the false positive reaches the result. Existing issue: #363.
3. **The TAG key encoding is not order-preserving.** `tag_encode_lower` (`mod.rs:565`) escapes bytes `<= 0x20`, `\` and `_` as `_XX`, and string range queries (`build_string_range_node`, `mod.rs:1432`) compare the encoded keys. `' '` (0x20) becomes `_20`, which sorts after `A` (0x41), so `'John Smith' < 'JohnA'` is false in the index. Wrong in both directions. C does not encode and is wrong differently.
4. **The empty string is not indexed** (TAG fields skip empty values without `INDEXEMPTY`), so `n.v = ''` and `n.v < 'a'` miss it. Existing issue: #647.
5. **An undirected pattern is scanned in one orientation.** `EdgeByIndexScan` (`runtime/ops/edge_by_index_scan.rs`) emits each edge once, `src → dst`; `CondTraverse` emits an undirected match in both orientations. Existing issue: #2100 (which also shows endpoint-pinned undirected matches losing edges).

(Also found, outside the model: geo radius queries near the poles, `|lat| > 85.05`, return nothing from the RediSearch geohash — full scan 21 rows, index 0 — on both engines.)

### Expected

The index must not change the result: each query returns the "no index" column.

### Suggested fix

1. Set the include flag for an absent bound (cheap, fixed in the linked PR).
2. Index Bool under its own sub-field (or not at all) and treat Bool values as not servable from the numeric field. (The array-contains-inside-`AND` symptom goes away with the per-conjunct post-filter in the PR for the "unservable value" issue.)
3. An order-preserving escape (e.g. map byte `b <= 0x21` to `0x21, 0x21 + b` and shift the escape byte itself), or keep the filter for string ranges.
4. A sentinel key for the empty string (it must sort first, so it combines with 3).
5. Emit each edge in both orientations (a self-loop once) from `EdgeByIndexScan` for an undirected pattern (cheap, fixed in the linked PR; closes #2100).

### Found by

Lean 4 model of the index layer, `proofs/index_layer`: `bug_open_bound_excludes_inf`, `bug_bool_eq_int`, `bug_string_range_order` / `tagEnc_not_monotone`, `bug_empty_string_not_indexed`; the undirected edge and geo cases by the differential run `proofs/index_layer/diff.py`. Array-contains inside `AND`: `proofs/optimizer_scan` (`IndexCex` C10).

issues.title: [Rust] IN with a computed indexed side is pushed as n.a IN [..]; 2 IN [n.a, n.b] becomes array-contains on n.a
issues.body:
### Summary

An `IN` predicate whose indexed side is an expression that merely *contains* the indexed property is pushed into the range index as if it were the bare property. `abs(n.a) IN [1]` becomes `n.a IN [1]`, and `2 IN [n.a, n.b]` becomes an array-contains lookup on `n.a`. Both return different rows than the same query without the index. C returns the right rows.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 2363723ac)

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE INDEX FOR (n:L) ON (n.a)"
GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE (:L {k:1, a:1}), (:L {k:2, a:-1}), (:L {k:3, a:2, b:7})"
```

| Query | no index | Rust + index | C + index |
|---|---|---|---|
| `MATCH (n:L) WHERE abs(n.a) IN [1] RETURN n.k` | 1, 2 | **1** | 1, 2 |
| `MATCH (n:L) WHERE toString(n.a) IN ['1'] RETURN n.k` | 1 | **—** | 1 |
| `MATCH (n:L) WHERE n.a + 1 IN [2] RETURN n.k` | 1 | **—** | error |
| `MATCH (n:L) WHERE 2 IN [n.a, n.b] RETURN n.k` | 3 | **—** | 3 |
| `MATCH (n:L) WHERE -1 IN [n.a] RETURN n.k` | 2 | **—** | error |

### Mechanism

`try_in_filter_scan` (`graph/src/planner/optimizer/utilize_index.rs:612-665`) only checks that one side *contains* a property of the scanned alias (`subtree_has_property_of`), then takes the first property it finds in that subtree (`extract_attribute_from_subtree`) and builds `InList { key: a, .. }` or `ArrayContains { key: a, .. }` from it. The filter is then dropped (or, for array-contains, kept but the index has already returned the wrong candidates). The comparison path (`try_single_filter_scan`) already requires the side to be `ExprIR::Property`.

### Expected

Same rows as without the index (C).

### Suggested fix

Push an `IN` only when the indexed side *is* `Property(scanned alias)`.

### Found by

Lean 4 model of the scan-selection passes, `proofs/optimizer_scan` (`IndexCex` C7, C7', C8). Live repro `proofs/optimizer_scan/repro.py`.

issues.title: [Rust] n.v > 'a' AND n.v < 'a' returns 'a' through a range index (equal-bounds shortcut ignores exclusivity)
issues.body:
### Summary

`n.v > 'a' AND n.v < 'a'` (or `>= 'a' AND < 'a'`) returns the node with `v = 'a'` when `v` has a range index. The range is empty; without the index, and on C, the query returns nothing.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 2363723ac)

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE INDEX FOR (n:L) ON (n.v)"
GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE (:L {v:'a', k:'a'})"
GRAPH.QUERY g "MATCH (n:L) WHERE n.v > 'a' AND n.v < 'a' RETURN n.k"
-- Rust + index: 'a'      no index: (empty)     C + index: (empty)
GRAPH.QUERY g "MATCH (n:L) WHERE n.v >= 'a' AND n.v < 'a' RETURN n.k"
-- Rust + index: 'a'      no index: (empty)     C + index: (empty)
```

### Mechanism

The two conjuncts are merged into one `Range { min: 'a', max: 'a', include_min: false, include_max: false }`. `build_string_range_node` (`graph/src/index/mod.rs:1403-1449`, shortcut at `:1418`) turns any string range with equal bounds into an exact-token match, ignoring both include flags.

### Expected

Empty result, like C and the full scan.

### Suggested fix

Take the exact-token shortcut only when both bounds are inclusive; otherwise return an empty node.

### Found by

Lean 4 model of the index layer, `proofs/index_layer` (`bug_exclusive_equal_bounds`; `strRange_exact` needs equal bounds to be inclusive), also `proofs/optimizer_scan` (`IndexCex` C11). Live repro `proofs/index_layer/repro.py`.

issues.title: [Rust] Multi-label (n:A:B): conditions on B's indexed property are pushed into A's index (AND returns nothing, OR loses rows)
issues.body:
### Summary

For a multi-label pattern `(n:A:B)` where `A` has a range index on `x` and `B` one on `y`, the Rust engine merges the condition on `B`'s property into a query on `A`'s index, which has no such field. `AND` returns nothing and `OR` loses rows. C returns the right rows.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 2363723ac)

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE INDEX FOR (n:A) ON (n.x)"
GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE INDEX FOR (n:B) ON (n.y)"
GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE (:A:B {x:1, y:2, k:'ab'}), (:A:B {x:1, y:3, k:'ab2'})"
```

| Query | no index | Rust + index | C + index |
|---|---|---|---|
| `MATCH (n:A:B) WHERE n.x = 1 AND n.y = 2 RETURN n.k` | `ab` | **—** | `ab` |
| `MATCH (n:B:A) WHERE n.y = 2 AND n.x = 1 RETURN n.k` | `ab` | **—** | `ab` |
| `MATCH (n:A:B) WHERE n.y = 2 OR n.x = 1 RETURN n.k` | `ab`, `ab2` | **`ab`** | `ab`, `ab2` |
| `MATCH (n:A:B {x:1, y:2}) RETURN n.k` | `ab` | **—** | `ab` |

### Mechanism

`try_single_filter_scan` picks, per conjunct, the first label that indexes the property. `try_filter_pushdown` (`graph/src/planner/optimizer/utilize_index.rs:770-826`) then merges every pushable conjunct (AND) or branch (OR) into one `IndexQuery` and keeps only the *first* label. At runtime `build_query_node` (`graph/src/index/mod.rs:1547`, `:1564`) can't find `y` in `A`'s index and returns a null node: a null `AND` child nulls the whole intersection (no rows), a null `OR` child is skipped (its rows are lost).

### Expected

Same rows as without the index (C).

### Suggested fix

In `try_filter_pushdown`, merge only conjuncts served by the same label as the first one and leave the rest in the post-filter; for `OR`, give up on the index when branches need different labels.

### Found by

Lean 4 model of the index layer, `proofs/index_layer` (`bug_multilabel_and`, `bug_multilabel_or`), also `proofs/optimizer_scan` (`IndexCex` C5, C6). Live repro `proofs/index_layer/repro.py`.

issues.title: [Rust] Range index stores temporals as plain numbers, so n.v > 0 returns dates
issues.body:
### Summary

A range index stores Date / DateTime / LocalTime / Duration values as their raw number in the same numeric field as Int and Float. A numeric range query then matches them: `n.v > 0` returns dates. Without the index, and on C, it does not.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 2363723ac)

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE INDEX FOR (n:L) ON (n.v)"
GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE (:L {v:5, k:'int'}), (:L {v:date('2020-01-01'), k:'date'})"
GRAPH.QUERY g "MATCH (n:L) WHERE n.v > 0 RETURN n.k"
-- Rust + index: 'date', 'int'     no index: 'int'     C + index: 'int'
```

`n.v < 0` with a date before 1970, and `n.v = <seconds of the date>` behave the same way.

### Mechanism

`Document::set` (`graph/src/index/mod.rs:785-792`) adds temporals with `RediSearch_DocumentAddFieldNumber` to the property's numeric field, the one Int/Float queries use. No query ever looks temporals up in the index: the scan op's `can_utilize_index` rejects every temporal value and falls back to a label scan. So indexing them buys nothing and only produces false positives for numeric queries.

### Expected

`n.v > 0` returns only numbers, like C (C indexes each type under its own field name).

### Suggested fix

Don't add temporals to the numeric field. (Indexing them under a separate sub-field, as C does, is a later feature: the Rust planner can't serve temporal predicates from the index today anyway.)

### Found by

Lean 4 model of the index layer, `proofs/index_layer` (`bug_temporal_in_numeric_range`), also `proofs/optimizer_scan` (`IndexCex` C2). Live repro `proofs/index_layer/repro.py`.

issues.title: [Rust] Range index returns every node of the label, or drops rows, when the value is one it can't look up (date(), point(), computed ints >= 2^52, IN [date(), ..])
issues.body:
### Summary

When a range index serves a predicate whose value the index can't look up exactly, the Rust engine returns wrong rows. The scan either falls back to *every* node of the label with the filter already removed, or looks the value up and silently finds nothing. All of these give the right answer without the index, and on C with the index.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 2363723ac)

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE INDEX FOR (n:L) ON (n.v)"
GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE (:L {v:5, k:'int'}), (:L {v:date('2020-01-01'), k:'date'})"
```

| Query | no index | Rust + index | C + index |
|---|---|---|---|
| `MATCH (n:L) WHERE n.v = date('2020-01-01') RETURN n.k` | `date` | **`date`, `int`** | `date` |
| `MATCH (n:L {v: date('2020-01-01')}) RETURN n.k` | `date` | **`date`, `int`** | `date` |
| `MATCH (n:L) WHERE n.v > date('2019-01-01') RETURN n.k` | `date` | **`date`, `int`** | `date` |
| `MATCH (n:L) WHERE n.v IN [date('2020-01-01'), 5] RETURN n.k` | `date`, `int` | **`int`** | `date`, `int` |
| `MATCH (n:L) WHERE n.v = 4503599627370495 + 4503599627370495 + 3 RETURN n.k` | — | **`date`, `int`** (every node) | — |
| `MATCH (n:L) WHERE n.v > 4503599627370495 * 2 RETURN n.k` | — | **every node** | — |

and with `CREATE (:L {v: point({latitude:1.0, longitude:2.0}), k:'p'})`:

| `MATCH (n:L) WHERE n.v = point({latitude:1.0, longitude:2.0}) RETURN n.k` | `p` | **—** | `p` |
|---|---|---|---|

### Mechanism

The optimizer drops the `Filter` when it believes the index answers the predicate exactly, and the index-scan op falls back to a plain label scan when the evaluated value is one it can't serve (`can_utilize_index`). The two checks disagree:

1. **Filter dropped for values the runtime then refuses.** `is_non_indexable_subexpr` (`graph/src/planner/optimizer/utilize_index.rs:910-928`) is a deny-list: it flags variables, parameters, lists, maps, function calls and lossy *literal* ints. A constant-folded `Constant(Date)` / `Constant(Point)` and arithmetic (`Add`, `Mul`, …) pass. So `n.v = date(..)` and `n.v = 2^52-1 + 2^52-1 + 3` lose their filter, `can_utilize_index` (`runtime/ops/node_by_index_scan.rs:249-287`) rejects the Date / lossy Int, and the op returns every node of the label unfiltered.
2. **IN list silently drops items.** `evaluate_index_query`'s `InList` arm (`node_by_index_scan.rs:216-232`, same in `edge_by_index_scan.rs`) keeps only Int/Float/String/Bool items, so `IN [date(..), 5]` becomes `= 5`: the filter is kept, but the index never returns the date node for it to keep.
3. **Point equality is "servable" but has no index lookup.** `is_indexable` accepts `Value::Point`, but `build_query_node` (`graph/src/index/mod.rs:1451-1662`) has no `Equal`-on-Point arm, returns a null node, and `Index::query` turns that into an empty iterator.

### Expected

Same rows as without the index (C behaves this way; it keeps unresolved filters).

### Suggested fix

- Make `is_non_indexable_subexpr` an allow-list: only the predicate structure (`AND`/`OR`/comparisons/`IN`), the scanned property and scalar literals the index stores exactly (Null, Bool, Float, String, non-lossy Int) let the filter go; everything else keeps it.
- Decide keep-the-filter per *pushed* conjunct, not over the whole filter.
- One shared `can_be_served` for the node and edge scan ops that rejects Point equality and temporals, and an IN-list expansion that keeps every non-null item so an unservable one forces the fallback.

### Found by

Lean 4 model of the index layer, `proofs/index_layer` (`bug_folded_temporal_constant`, `bug_point_equality`, `bug_in_list_drops_item`), and of the scan-selection passes, `proofs/optimizer_scan` (`IndexCex` C4: computed constants ≥ 2^52). Live repro `proofs/index_layer/repro.py`, `proofs/optimizer_scan/repro.py`.

issues.title: [Rust] LIMIT/SKIP budget is a hard stop through traverses and counts one SKIP: two-hop, ExpandInto, stacked-SKIP and ORDER BY+MATCH queries drop rows
issues.body:
### Summary

A `LIMIT` (optionally with `SKIP`) above two traverses, above a traverse fed by a stacked `SKIP`, or above a `Sort` feeding a traverse silently drops rows: Rust returns `[]` where C returns the answer. The runtime pushes the `Limit`/`Skip` row budget down the plan as a *hard* stop for `CondTraverse`, `ExpandInto` and Sort's top-k, but computes it with a walk that crosses operators which can discard rows, and counts only the first `Skip`.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 2363723ac; C = `bin/macos-arm64v8-release/falkordb.so`)

| graph | query | Rust | C |
|---|---|---|---|
| `CREATE (a1:A {id:1})-[:R]->(:B {id:10}), (a2:A {id:2})-[:R]->(b2:B {id:20}), (b2)-[:R]->(a2)` | `MATCH (a:A)-[:R]->(b)-[:R]->(a) RETURN a.id LIMIT 1` | `[]` | `[2]` |
| `CREATE (:A {id:1})-[:R]->(:B {id:10}), (:A {id:2})-[:R]->(:B {id:20})-[:R]->(:C {id:30})` | `MATCH (a:A)-[:R]->(b)-[:R]->(c) RETURN c.id LIMIT 1` | `[]` | `[30]` |
| `UNWIND range(1,3) AS i CREATE (:A {id:i})-[:R]->(:B {id:10*i})-[:R]->(:C {id:100*i})` | `MATCH (a:A)-[:R]->(b)-[:R]->(c) RETURN c.id SKIP 1 LIMIT 1` | `[]` | `[200]` |
| same | `MATCH (a:A)-[:R]->(b) WITH b SKIP 0 RETURN b.id SKIP 1 LIMIT 1` | `[]` | `[20]` |
| `CREATE (:A {id:1}), (:A {id:2})-[:R]->(:B {id:20})` | `MATCH (a:A) WITH a ORDER BY a.id MATCH (a)-[:R]->(b) RETURN b.id LIMIT 1` | `[]` | `[]` (openCypher: `[20]`) |

At scale: 500k chains `(:N)-[:R]->(:N)-[:R]->(:N)` (1M edges), `MATCH (a)-[:R]->(b)-[:R]->(c) RETURN b, c SKIP 100 LIMIT 10` returns 0 rows on Rust, 10 on C.

### Mechanism

- `Runtime::effective_limit` (`graph/src/runtime/runtime.rs:594-597`) treats `CondTraverse`/`ExpandInto` as transparent, but those map one row to *zero* or more rows. `CondTraverseOp` (`ops/cond_traverse.rs:1179`) and `ExpandIntoOp` (`ops/expand_into.rs:271`) use the resulting `record_cap` as a hard stop, so the lower traverse stops after `LIMIT` rows even when the upper one discards them.
- `Runtime::effective_skip` (`runtime.rs:618-626`) returns the *first* `Skip` it meets, so stacked `Skip`s under one `Limit` under-budget the cap (this is also #2659, the Sort variant).
- `SortOp`'s top-k (`ops/sort.rs:491`) takes the same two walks, so a `CondTraverse` between the `Sort` and the `Limit` shrinks the heap below what is needed (row 3 of the table; C has the same bug).

### Expected

C's answers for rows 1-4. For row 5 C is also wrong; openCypher requires `[20]` (the `LIMIT` applies after the second `MATCH`).

### Suggested fix

Give hard-cap consumers the budget that is sound as a stop: from the operator up to the `Limit`, `Project` passes it, every `Skip` adds, anything else (including `CondTraverse`/`ExpandInto`) is a barrier. Keep the current through-traverse walk only as a batch-sizing hint for `BatchedResultEmitter`'s pack ceiling (where it cannot change results), so early termination on `MATCH (a)-[:R]->(b) RETURN b LIMIT k` is kept.

### Found by

Lean model `proofs/runtime_core` (`RuntimeCore/Budget.lean`): `Budget.need_sound` proves the reference budget sound; `hard_cap_unsound_expandInto`, `hard_cap_unsound_condTraverse`, `hard_cap_unsound_through_traverse` and `hard_cap_unsound_stacked_skip` are concrete counterexamples for the current walk.

issues.title: [Rust] coalesce() with zero arguments is accepted (C: expected at least 1)
issues.body:
### Summary

`coalesce()` with no arguments is accepted and returns `null`. C rejects it at compile time.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 2363723ac)

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "RETURN coalesce()"
-- Rust: null
-- C:    Received 0 arguments to function 'coalesce', expected at least 1
```

### Mechanism

`coalesce` is registered as `var_arg` (`graph/src/runtime/functions/math.rs:314`). `GraphFn::validate` (`graph/src/runtime/functions/mod.rs:787`) does no arity check for `FnArguments::VarLength`. The other built-in variadics, `indegree`/`outdegree`, check `args.is_empty()` themselves at runtime (`entity.rs:310`).

### Expected

Every built-in variadic function needs at least one argument (true of `coalesce`, `indegree` and `outdegree` in C). Reject zero arguments in `validate` for non-UDF `VarLength` functions, using C's message. UDFs stay unconstrained.

### Found by

Lean 4 model (`proofs/value_math`, theorem `coalesce_zero_args_accepted`, TypeCheck.lean); Rust repro `graph/tests/lean_value_math.rs::bug_coalesce_accepts_zero_arguments`.

issues.title: [Rust] toInteger('-9223372036854775809') returns i64::MIN instead of null (f64 fallback rounds to -2^63)
issues.body:
### Summary

`toInteger()` of an integer string just below `i64::MIN` returns `i64::MIN` instead of `null`. `toIntegerList` inherits the bug. C returns `null`, and the positive side is already `null` in both engines.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 2363723ac)

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "RETURN toInteger('-9223372036854775809'), toInteger('-9223372036854776832'), toIntegerList(['-9223372036854775809'])"
-- Rust: -9223372036854775808, -9223372036854775808, [-9223372036854775808]
-- C:    null, null, [NULL]

GRAPH.QUERY g "RETURN toInteger('9223372036854775808')"
-- Rust and C: null
```

### Mechanism

`value_to_integer` (`graph/src/runtime/functions/conversion.rs:53-64`): `s.parse::<i64>()` fails with overflow, so the code falls back to `s.parse::<f64>()`. Every value in `[-2^63-1024, -2^63-1]` rounds to exactly `-2^63`, and the guard `floored < i64::MIN as f64` is strict, so the rounded value passes as `i64::MIN`.

### Expected

Match C: a plain integer string (optional sign, digits only) that doesn't fit in i64 is `null`. Only strings with a fraction or exponent go through the float path (where C also gives `toInteger('-9223372036854775807.5') = -9223372036854775808`).

### Found by

Lean 4 model of `conversion.rs` (`proofs/value_math`); Rust repro `graph/tests/lean_value_math.rs::bug_to_integer_negative_overflow_clamps_to_min`.

issues.title: fix: list comprehension over null is null, over a scalar a type error
issues.body:
Closes #2928

## Problem

A list comprehension sent its source through `eval_iter_expr`, whose fallback applies UNWIND semantics: null gives no rows and a scalar gives one row. So `[x IN null | x]` returned `[]` and `[x IN 5 | x]` returned `[5]`. C and openCypher give `null` and `Type mismatch: expected List or Null but was Integer`. `reduce()` and the quantifiers already behave that way.

## Fix

In `ExprIR::ListComprehension` (`graph/src/runtime/eval.rs`), list literals and `range(..)` still go through `eval_iter_expr`, since they always produce a list. This keeps the streaming path that avoids building the list. Every other source is evaluated with `eval_node` and handled like `Reduce`: a `List` is iterated, `Null` gives `null`, and anything else is the C type-mismatch error. Matches C.

## Tests

- New `tests/test_e2e.py::test_list_comprehension_non_list_source` (null literal, null variable, null with WHERE, integer and string scalars, plus empty list / empty range still `[]`).
  - on `main`: FAILED, `RETURN [x IN null | x]` gave `[[[]]]`, expected `[[None]]`
  - with the fix: passes
- `RELEASE=1 pytest tests/test_e2e.py tests/test_functions.py`: 126 passed
- `RELEASE=1 TEST=tests/flow/test_comprehension_functions ./flow.sh`: 25/25, `tests/flow/test_list`: 15/15
- `cargo fmt --check`, `CXX=clang++ cargo clippy --all-targets`: clean

## Benchmark (eval hot path)

Release build, 30 runs per query per build, main and fix servers alternated A/B/B/A, two rounds. The machine was shared (load average around 36).

| query | main p50 / p99 | fix p50 / p99 |
|---|---|---|
| `UNWIND range(1,2000) AS i WITH i, [1..8] AS l RETURN count([x IN l WHERE x > 2 \| x + i])` | 3.86 / 6.17 ms, 3.65 / 3.93 ms | 3.88 / 9.48 ms, 3.63 / 4.06 ms |
| `UNWIND range(1,2000) AS i RETURN count([x IN range(1,8) WHERE x > 2 \| x + i])` | 2.88 / 4.86 ms, 2.70 / 4.20 ms | 2.82 / 3.31 ms, 2.76 / 2.94 ms |

p50 is the same within noise. The single 9.48 ms p99 did not repeat in the second round (4.06 ms), so it looks like load.

issues.title: fix: toLower/toUpper accept strings containing U+FFFD
issues.body:
Closes #2927

## Problem

`toLower` / `toUpper` returned `Invalid UTF8 string` for any string that contains U+FFFD, e.g. `RETURN toLower('A�')` (`graph/src/runtime/functions/string.rs:148,170`). Removed the check from both functions, along with the module doc line that described it.

That is a C `replace` bug and not something case mapping should copy. Those assertions now expect the mapped string, plus a direct `toLower('A�b')` / `toUpper('a�B')` case. Direct `toLower`/`toUpper` on U+FFFD now matches C.

issues.title: fix: clamp list.remove's span end instead of overflowing on a huge count
issues.body:
Closes #2926

## Problem

`list.remove(list, idx, count)` computed the span end as `normalized + count` (`graph/src/runtime/functions/list.rs:168`). `RETURN list.remove([1,2,3], 1, 9223372036854775807)` panics in debug builds (*attempt to add with overflow*); release wraps and gets `[1]` only because `as usize` + `.min(len)` happens to rescue it. issues.title: fix: keep a list literal of aggregates intact (#2945)
issues.body:
Closes #2945

## Problem

`ExprEval::eval_compound` evaluates a list literal on an explicit stack. When an element is a finished aggregate, the `FuncInvocation` arm finalized it with `return`, which left the whole stack machine. The pending list frame and the other elements were dropped. `UNWIND [1,2] AS x RETURN [min(x), max(x)]` returned `2` (C: `[1, 2]`), and `size([count(x)])` failed with a type mismatch (C: `1`).

## Fix

Push the finalized value onto the result stack and `continue`, like every other arm (`graph/src/runtime/eval.rs`).

## Tests

- New flow test `test_aggregation:testAggregations.test_list_literal_of_aggregates` covers keyless, `size(...)` and grouped forms.
  - Before, on `main` @ 2363723ac: FAIL, `[[2, 2]] == [[[1, 2], [2, 5]]]`.
  - After: PASS. The whole `tests/flow/test_aggregation` suite passes (16/16).
- `cargo fmt --all -- --check`: no diffs in the changed files.
- Bench (release, 30 alternating runs each, loaded shared machine at load avg ~39). The change is on the aggregate-finalize path of `eval_compound`, and it is neutral:

issues.title: fix: temporal constructors never panic on out-of-range components
issues.body:
Closes #2930

## Problem

`date({year:2020, week:10000000000})`, `localdatetime({year:2020, week:-9223372036854775807})`, `date({year:2020, quarter:2, dayOfQuarter:i64::MAX})` and `date('2020W1é')` panic inside `date_from_components` / `parse_week_date` (chrono's `NaiveDate + TimeDelta` and `TimeDelta::days` overflow, and a byte slice that splits a multi-byte character). The panic takes the server down. C returns an error for each.

## Fix

In `graph/src/runtime/functions/temporal.rs`:
- `check_range` validates `week` 1-53, `quarter` 1-4 and `dayOfQuarter` 1-92, with C's message `Invalid value for X (valid values a - b)`. This also rejects `date({year:2021, quarter:1, dayOfQuarter:200})`, which used to return 2021-07-19 (C errors too).
- `year`/`month`/`day` go through `try_from` instead of `as i32`/`as u32`, so `year: 4294969316` is no longer silently read as 2020.
- The week offset is a single bounded day count, added with `checked_add_signed`, so there is no panic at chrono's MIN/MAX year either.
- `parse_week_date` uses `split_at_checked(2)`.

This covers the map, positional-slot (`date_struct_pure`/`localdatetime_struct_pure`) and string forms. The `dayOfWeek` range is left alone here and handled in #2936.

## Tests

- Rust unit tests `runtime::functions::temporal::tests` (new): before the fix, 2 of 3 fail (`assertion failed: date_pure(...week...).is_err()` and `byte index 2 is not a char boundary`). After it, all 3 pass.
- Flow test `test_temporal:testTemporalDate.test_date_out_of_range_components` (new): before the fix the server crashed ("process is not alive"). After it the test passes, and the whole `tests/flow/test_temporal` file passes (23/23).
- `cargo fmt --all -- --check` passes, and `CXX=clang++ cargo clippy --all-targets` shows no warnings in the touched file.

Not a hot path: these are constructor argument checks.

issues.title: Port algo.CCH and algo.CCH.query from the C engine to Rust
issues.body:
## Gap
The Customizable Contraction Hierarchies procedures, `algo.CCH` and `algo.CCH.query`, exist only on the C engine's `master` branch. They aren't in the Rust engine (`main`, 6.0) or in any C release; `CALL dbms.procedures()` on v4.20.7 and on the 6.0 RC lists neither. Since 6.0 replaces the C engine, CCH reaches users only if it is ported.

## What C has
- **#2680** (merged to `master` 2026-09-01, for #2692) adds CCH for fast shortest-path queries:
  - `algo.CCH` builds the hierarchy: a weight matrix over the configured relationship types, an elimination order, chordal triangulation, and shortcut edges. Its configuration takes exactly 5 keys, including `relTypes` and `weightProp`.
  - `algo.CCH.query` answers path queries against it.
  - Code: `src/algorithms/cch.{c,h}`, `src/procedures/proc_cch.c`, `src/procedures/proc_cch_query.c`.
- **#2721** (merged 2026-09-04) continues it; follow-up work is tracked in #2731, which is still open.

## Port
- `algo.CCH` and `algo.CCH.query` with the same configuration keys, outputs and error messages as C.
- Their flow tests: `tests/flow/test_cch.py` (8 `algo.CCH` and 10 `algo.CCH.query` calls), plus the CCH cases in `test_procedures.py`.
- Decide where the built hierarchy lives and how it is invalidated when the graph changes, since the Rust engine's storage and MVCC model differ from C's.

issues.title: Port algo.AStar (and #2630's algo.SPpaths routing) from the C engine to Rust
issues.body:
## Gap
`algo.AStar` exists only on the C engine's `master` branch. It isn't in the Rust engine (`main`, 6.0) or in any C release: `CALL dbms.procedures()` on v4.20.7 and on the 6.0 RC lists the same 24 procedures, with no A\*. Since 6.0 replaces the C engine, A\* reaches users only if it is ported.

## What C has
- **#2630** (merged to `master` 2026-08-26) adds `algo.AStar`: an A\* search that uses great-circle (haversine) distance over user-supplied `latitudeProperty` / `longitudeProperty` as its heuristic. It supports relationship-type and direction filters and parallel edges, and has a k-shortest variant built on Yen's algorithm and driven by the same A\* engine. Code: `src/algorithms/AStar.{c,h}`, `src/algorithms/yen.{c,h}`, `src/procedures/proc_astar_paths.c`.
- **#2720** (merged 2026-09-04) adds a goal-directed spur to Yen, for #2730, which is still open.
- **Also in #2630:** `algo.SPpaths` no longer enumerates paths with a DFS in the unconstrained case (`src != dst`, no `maxCost`, no `maxLen`):
  - `pathCount: 1` uses Dijkstra;
  - `pathCount: 0` uses bidirectional Dijkstra plus shortest-path DAG enumeration;
  - `pathCount > 1` uses Yen's k-shortest loopless paths.

  The Rust `algo.SPpaths` takes its own approach (#2276), so compare the two when porting rather than assuming parity.

## Port
- `algo.AStar` with the same signature, outputs and error messages as C.
- Its flow tests: `tests/flow/test_astar.py` (24 `algo.AStar` calls), plus the A\* cases in `test_path_algorithms.py` and `test_procedures.py` from #2630.
- Whether Rust's `algo.SPpaths` should adopt #2630's algorithm routing, measured against C.

Open C follow-ups: #2656 (A\* optimality, `pathCost` hop count) and #2732 (k-shortest-paths landmark mode). Port those as well if they merge.

issues.title: [Rust] A write that only registers schema or only cancels entities replicates nothing: next payload refused (full resync), AOF load exits, or silent dictionary divergence
issues.body:
### Summary

A write that only registers a name, or whose every entity is created and deleted in the same query, puts **nothing** on the replication stream or in the AOF. It still changes the primary: the label/attribute dictionary grows and the id space moves (the cancelled ids sit in the recycle bin). The replica never hears about it, so:

* the **next** payload's `ADD_SCHEMA` is refused ("assigns label 'B' id 2, but this replica would assign 0") and the replica is forced into a **full resync**;
* during **AOF load** the same refusal **shuts the server down** ("A full resync cannot repair already-loaded state, shutting down");
* for a cancelled edge attribute (`CREATE (a)-[:T1 {p4:1}]->(b) DELETE a, b`) the replica **silently** ends up with a shorter attribute dictionary than its primary, with no error.

Examples: `CREATE (a:A {p:1}) DELETE a`, `OPTIONAL MATCH (n:Nope) SET n:L6`, `MERGE (a:M1 {p5:1}) DELETE a`, `CREATE (a)-[:T1 {p4:1}]->(b) DELETE a, b`.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 2363723ac, primary + replica)

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE (a:A {p:1}) DELETE a"
GRAPH.QUERY g "OPTIONAL MATCH (n:Nope) SET n:L6"
GRAPH.QUERY g "MERGE (a:M1 {p5:1}) DELETE a"
GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE (a)-[:T1 {p4:1}]->(b) DELETE a, b"
GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE (:B {q:2})"
GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE (:K4)-[:T2]->()"
```

Replica: `cmdstat_graph.EFFECT failed_calls` goes 0 → 1, the logs gain 3 "diverged" lines (`... Scheduling a forced full resync`), and the primary's `sync_full` goes 1 → 2.

AOF (`appendonly yes`, then `CREATE (a:A {p:1}) DELETE a`, `OPTIONAL MATCH (n:Nope) SET n:L6`, `CREATE (:B {q:2})`, `DEBUG LOADAOF`):

```
Diverged applying GRAPH.EFFECT on graph 'aof_replay' while loading from disk: effects buffer assigns label 'B' id 2, but this replica would assign 0. The two engines have diverged; the buffer was not applied.. A full resync cannot repair already-loaded state, shutting down.
```

In-process (master `MvccGraph` → payload → replica `apply_effects`), the silent variant:

```
schema dictionaries diverged with no error
  left:  labels=["K4"] types=["T2"] attrs=["p4"]
  right: labels=["K4"] types=["T2"] attrs=[]
```

A random differential (200 seeds × 30 writes) diverges on 134/200 seeds once fully-cancelled writes are mixed in, and on 0/200 without them.

### Mechanism

* `graph/src/runtime/ops/commit.rs:108` only calls `EffectsBuffer::build` when `Pending::effects_count() > 0`.
* `Pending::effects_count` (`graph/src/runtime/pending.rs:1688`) counts created/deleted/updated entities and labels. It does not count `cancelled_nodes`/`cancelled_relationships`, or names registered since the `SchemaBaseline`.
* So `emit_schema_additions` and `digest_cancelled` (`graph/src/effects/v3/emit.rs:61, 397`), which exist to ship exactly these, never run for such a commit. `modified` is false as well, so `commit_and_replicate` sends nothing.

### Expected

The replica and an AOF replay agree with the primary, and nothing is refused. C (Redis 8.6.2) replicates these writes without a resync and reloads the AOF cleanly. C's `OPTIONAL MATCH (n:Nope) SET n:L6` aborts separately (`blocked.c:346`), which is a C-side issue.

### Suggested fix

Gate on what the emitter actually wrote, not on an estimate of it. Always run `buf.build` when effects are being built; an empty buffer is already dropped by `take_effects_buffer`. The other option, adding `cancelled_*` and the schema delta to `effects_count`, would duplicate the emitter's own knowledge of what a commit implies.

### Found by

Lean: `gate_drops_cancelled`, `gate_drops_schema_only`, `next_payload_refused`, `cancelled_edge_attr_dropped`, and `commitShips_eq_iff` (the gate is sound iff the schema+cancelled residue is empty). All are in `proofs/effects_emit_apply`.

issues.title: [Rust] A list literal of aggregates collapses to one aggregate: [min(x), max(x)] returns 2
issues.body:
### Summary

A list literal whose elements include an aggregate collapses to the value of that one aggregate. `[min(x), max(x)]` returns `2`, not `[1, 2]`, and `size([count(x)])` fails with a type error.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 2363723ac)

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "UNWIND [1,2] AS x RETURN [min(x), max(x)] AS a, [count(x), 5] AS b"
Rust: 2, 2
C:    [1, 2], [2, 5]

GRAPH.QUERY g "UNWIND [1,2] AS x RETURN size([count(x)])"
Rust: Type mismatch: expected List, String, or Null but was Integer
C:    1
```

### Mechanism

`ExprEval::eval_compound` (`graph/src/runtime/eval.rs:525`) evaluates `ExprIR::List` on an explicit stack: it pushes a re-enter frame for the list, then one frame per element. When an element is a finished aggregate, the `FuncInvocation` arm (`eval.rs:864-880`) reads the accumulator and finalizes it with `return match finalize { .. }`. That `return` leaves the whole stack machine, so the list frame and the other elements are thrown away and the aggregate's value becomes the value of the whole expression. `[count(x)+0]`, maps and function arguments go through `eval_node` recursion and are not affected.

### Expected (C behaviour)

`[1, 2]`, `[2, 5]` and `1`.

### Suggested fix

Push the finalized value onto the result stack and `continue`, like every other arm.

### Found by

Lean 4 model of the aggregate operators (`proofs/ops_aggregate`), theorem `stackEval_return_drops_frame`; Rust repro `graph/tests/lean_ops_aggregate.rs` (`bug_list_literal_of_aggregates_collapses`).

issues.title: test(slowlog): populate the slowlog serially
issues.body:
Fixes #1896

## Summary

`populate_slowlog` fires its queries concurrently. A slowlog entry records the query's own wall-clock latency, measured inside the worker from planning to reply (`execute_query` in `src/graph_core.rs`; queue wait is excluded). Queries executing side by side on the thread pool therefore also record the contention between them. On the coverage build that inflates every retained entry by an order of magnitude or more. `test01` and `test06` then run their displacing queries **alone** and assert that they out-rank those inflated entries, so the result depends on the runner rather than on query size.

#2765 gave test01's displacer the same shape as the populate queries, but kept a 3x row margin, which is well inside that inflation. Both tests kept failing. In the last 7 days (PRs and merge queue for `main`/`6.0`):

| lane | test_slowlog jobs failed |
|---|---|
| `coverage-flow` | 24 / 133 |
| `coverage-flow-svc` | 2 / 13 |
| `release-flow(-svc)`, `a-sanitizer-flow-svc` | 0 / 421 |

Every one of the 26 failures was one of two:
- `test01_slowlog` at `:107`: `assertNotEqual(A, B)`, meaning the displacer was never admitted.
- `test06_force_replace` at `:324`/`:325`: q0 or q1 was never admitted.

## Change (tests only)

- `populate_slowlog` now runs its queries one at a time. The asyncio pool and its imports are gone.
  - Nothing in the file asserts on concurrent behaviour.
  - The Rust slowlog is a single mutex-guarded list per graph, so there is no per-thread state that the concurrency was exercising.
- Every query ranked against a populate entry is built by one helper, `slow_query(rows, divisor)`, so their ordering depends only on row count. That now includes test06's `q0`/`q1`, which used a nested `UNWIND`.
- `DISPLACER_ROWS = POPULATE_ROWS * 10`: displacers are sized from the populate size so the two can't drift apart again. #2628 raised the populate size 10x without touching the displacers.
- test02 populates with 20 queries instead of 36, in both calls. It only asserts that the log is non-empty or empty, and 20 already fills the 10-entry log. The 36 dates back to the C engine (#575). Once the populate became serial, those extra queries more than doubled the coverage-lane time on CI (see Cost).
- Displacing queries stay on one line and under Redis's 128-byte slowlog argument limit, so test01's Redis-slowlog assertion still matches the full command.
- test03's comment no longer claims it shares test01's pattern.

The approach comes from #2766, which was closed without being merged, applied here on top of #2765.

## Validation

The engine was built the same way `build-engine-coverage` builds it: `RUSTFLAGS="-C instrument-coverage ..." cargo build` inside `ghcr.io/falkordb/falkordb-build`. Tests ran through `TEST=tests/flow/test_slowlog ./flow.sh`, as `coverage-flow` runs them, pinned with `--cpuset-cpus` (`THREAD_COUNT` follows the CPU count):

| engine | CPUs | `main` | this PR |
|---|---|---|---|
| coverage | 4 (= `ubuntu-latest`) | **8/8 fail** (`:107`, plus `:324`/`:325` without fail-fast) | 8/8 pass |
| coverage | 10 | **3/3 fail** | 3/3 pass |
| coverage | 2 | 3/3 pass | 3/3 pass |
| release `main` (`edge-rs`), services mode | 4 | 3/3 pass | 3/3 pass |
| release `6.0` (`rc-mg-d51b549e`), services mode | 4 | 3/3 pass | 3/3 pass |

These runs used the first commit. The test02 trim does not touch anything ranked against a populate entry. After it, I re-ran the 4-CPU coverage row (3/3 pass) and the `edge-rs` services row (2/2 pass).

Slowlog latencies measured on the coverage build with 4 CPUs:

| | latency |
|---|---|
| 10 entries left by the **concurrent** populate (current) | 1.44–2.55 s |
| 10 entries left by the **serial** populate (this PR) | 128–190 ms |
| `main`'s displacers, run alone: test01 7.5M `%1` / test06 nested q0, q1 | ~570 ms / ~490 ms |
| this PR's displacers, run alone: 25M `%1` / `%2` / `%3` | ~1.91 / 1.59 / 1.45 s |

The new displacers beat the slowest serial entry by at least 7.6x. The larger size alone would not have fixed it: 25M `%3` (~1.45 s) sits at the concurrent floor. Running populate serially is what removes the dependence on the runner.

These local runs are arm64 (Docker on Apple Silicon), while CI is amd64. Inflation is larger locally than in the CI runs that pass, which is why `main` fails every time here instead of in ~18% of `coverage-flow` runs.

On this PR's CI, all four test_slowlog lanes pass: `coverage-flow`, `release-flow-svc` amd64 and arm64, and `a-sanitizer-flow-svc`.

## Cost

Duration of the test_slowlog `Run Flow test` step on CI:

| lane | `main`, passing runs | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| `coverage-flow` amd64 | 45 s | 50 s |
| `release-flow-svc` amd64 / arm64 | 7–10 s / 6 s | 15 s / 11 s |
| `a-sanitizer-flow-svc` amd64 | 36–37 s | 57 s |

On CI the concurrent populate was buying real throughput whenever contention stayed low. That is the same runner variance that decided whether the test passed. With test02 still at 36, the first commit's coverage step took 111 s, which is why the second commit trims it.

The test_slowlog jobs are still not the slowest in their lanes. Whole-job times:
- coverage: `test_effects_ddl` 215 s vs 165 s
- asan: `test_index_create` 216 s vs 163 s

Locally (arm64, coverage, 4 CPUs, full file) the run got faster: 45–49 s → ~20 s. There, contention made the concurrent populate slower than running it serially.

<details><summary>Reproduce</summary>

```sh
docker run --rm -v "$PWD":/work -w /work -v slowlog-cov:/t -e CARGO_TARGET_DIR=/t \
  ghcr.io/falkordb/falkordb-build:latest \
  bash -c 'RUSTFLAGS="-C instrument-coverage -C link-arg=-Wl,--allow-multiple-definition" cargo build'
docker run --rm --cpuset-cpus=0-3 -v "$PWD":/work -w /work -v slowlog-cov:/t \
  -e TARGET_DIR=/t/debug -e CODE_COVERAGE=1 ghcr.io/falkordb/falkordb-build:latest \
  bash -c '. /data/venv/bin/activate && TEST=tests/flow/test_slowlog FAIL_FAST=1 ./flow.sh'
```
</details>

## Backport

`tests/flow/test_slowlog.py` is identical on `6.0`, and the same flake hit the 6.0 merge queue (#2888, `:107`). This PR is labeled `6.0` so batch-backport picks it up; the patch applies cleanly.

* **Tests**
  * Updated slow-log checks to use sequential queries and consistent query sizing when validating entry ranking, capacity limits, and forced replacement.
  * Adjusted reset testing to populate the log with enough queries to fill its capacity both before and after reset.
  * Increased the size of displacing queries to provide a clearer margin when checking which entries remain in the slow log.
