issues.title: [Flaky] test_udf_cluster: spawn-mode cluster bootstrap doesn't wait for announced hostnames, so the client connects to "?:6379"
issues.body:
## Summary

`test_udf_cluster:testUDFCluster.test_udf_delete_propagation` sometimes errors on its first `udf_load` (test line 93):

```
  File "/__w/FalkorDB/FalkorDB/tests/flow/test_udf_cluster.py", line 93, in test_udf_delete_propagation
    res = self.db.udf_load(lib, script)
  File ".../falkordb/falkordb.py", line 288, in udf_load
    resp = client.execute_command(*args)
  ...
redis.exceptions.ConnectionError: Error -2 connecting to ?:6379. Name or service not known.
```

It's rare: 2 failures in ~290 `release-flow` runs this week, one of them in the merge queue. It's a race in the test harness rather than a product bug, and it can hit any spawn-mode `oss-cluster` test.

## Evidence (Sep 17–24; PRs to `main`/`6.0` plus the merge queue)

| PR | Lane | Job |
|---|---|---|
| #2846 | `release-flow` amd64 | https://github.com/FalkorDB/FalkorDB/actions/runs/35915227485/job/107367542497 |
| merge queue (#2533) | `release-flow` arm64 | https://github.com/FalkorDB/FalkorDB/actions/runs/35983587637/job/107582756419 |

| Lane | Failed / passed |
|---|---|
| `release-flow` amd64 | 1 / 145 |
| `release-flow` arm64 | 1 / 142 |
| `a-sanitizer-flow` | 0 / 134 |
| `coverage-flow` | 0 / 147 |

## Root cause

1. `_spawn_falkordb_cluster` (`tests/flow/common.py`) starts each shard with `--cluster-announce-hostname <alias> --cluster-preferred-endpoint-type hostname`. With that setting, a node whose hostname isn't known yet is reported as **`?`** in `CLUSTER SLOTS` and MOVED replies (documented in `redis.conf`: "If the preferred endpoint type is set to hostname, but no announced hostname is set, a '?' will be returned instead").
2. `_bootstrap_cluster` returns as soon as every shard reports `cluster_state:ok` and `cluster_known_nodes == n`. A peer that was learned through gossip counts as known before its hostname has arrived, so this check doesn't guarantee the hostnames have spread to every shard.
3. `Env()` builds the `FalkorDB` client right away. `RedisCluster` loads its slot map from `CLUSTER SLOTS` and can record a shard as `?:6379`.
4. In cluster mode, `udf_load` opens a direct connection to every primary in that map (`get_primaries()` → `get_redis_connection(node)`), so it fails on the `?` entry.

`test_udf_delete_propagation` is the first test in the class (RLTest runs methods alphabetically), so its `udf_load` is the first command that goes to every primary, immediately after the per-class bootstrap.

## Suggested fix

In `_bootstrap_cluster`, after the `cluster_state=ok` loop, also poll `CLUSTER SLOTS` (or `CLUSTER SHARDS`) on every shard until no endpoint is `?`, i.e. until every shard knows every peer's announced hostname.

issues.title: [Flaky] test17_sp_duplicate_edges: algo.SPpaths/SSpaths return duplicate paths when relTypes repeats a type
issues.body:
## Summary

When `relTypes` lists the same type more than once, `algo.SPpaths` and `algo.SSpaths` return the same path several times. This happens every time on current trunk. It also explains why `test_path_algorithms:testAllShortestPaths.test17_sp_duplicate_edges` is flaky: the test only notices the duplicates on some random graphs.

## Reproduction

Run against `falkordb/falkordb-server:edge-rs` (built 2026-09-24 from `main`):

```cypher
CREATE (a:L {v: 1}), (b:L {v: 2}), (c:L {v: 3}), (d:L {v: 4}),
       (a)-[:E {weight: 1}]->(b), (b)-[:E {weight: 1}]->(d),
       (a)-[:E {weight: 2}]->(c), (c)-[:E {weight: 2}]->(d)

MATCH (n:L {v: 1}), (m:L {v: 4})
CALL algo.SPpaths({sourceNode: n, targetNode: m, relTypes: ['E', 'E'],
                   weightProp: 'weight', maxLen: 3, pathCount: 3})
YIELD path RETURN [x IN nodes(path) | x.v]
```

| Call | `relTypes: ['E']` | `relTypes: ['E', 'E']` |
|---|---|---|
| SPpaths `pathCount: 3` (graph above, 2 paths) | `[1,2,4]`, `[1,3,4]` | `[1,2,4]` ×3 |
| SPpaths `pathCount: 3`, plus `(a)-[:E {weight: 5}]->(d)` (3 paths) | `[1,2,4]`, `[1,3,4]`, `[1,4]` | `[1,2,4]` ×3 |
| SPpaths `pathCount: 3`, only `(a)-[:E]->(d)` (1 path, 1 hop) | `[1,4]` | `[1,4]` ×2 |
| SPpaths `pathCount: 0` (all minimal) | `[1,2,4]` | `[1,2,4]` ×4 |
| SPpaths `pathCount: 1` | `[1,2,4]` | `[1,2,4]` (correct) |
| SSpaths from `a`, `maxLen: 2`, `pathCount: 10` | 4 paths | 10 rows: each path ×2 (1 hop) or ×4 (2 hops), cut off by `pathCount` |

## Root cause

`relTypes` is never deduplicated:
- `parse_common_path_config` (`graph/src/runtime/functions/algo_procedures.rs`) copies the list as given.
- `Graph::get_node_relationships_by_type` (`graph/src/graph/graph.rs`) collects one matrix per listed type, so it scans `E` twice.

As a result, `node_successors` yields every edge once per repeat. `enumerate_paths` then explores each subtree once per copy, so every path is found 2^hops times. `record_found_path` doesn't drop identical paths, so the copies take up the k result slots. `pathCount: 1` isn't affected because it keeps only a single path.

## Why test17 is flaky and not always red

Part (b) of test17 compares `relTypes: ["E", "E"]` against `["E"]` with `pathCount: 3`, but only checks two things:
- `len(dup) == min(len(sp_paths), 3)`
- each `dup` row appears in `single`

When the randomly chosen pair has **3 or more** qualifying paths (the usual case), the buggy result `[X, X, X]` still passes both checks. The test only fails when the pair has fewer than 3 paths. `populate_graph` builds the graph with unseeded `rand()`, which is why the failure comes and goes.

CI, Sep 17–24: 4 failures at `test_path_algorithms.py:865`, never in the merge queue. The output was `3 == 2` three times and `2 == 1` once, matching the 2-path and 1-hop rows in the table above. Neither the test nor `algo_procedures.rs` changed during that window.

| PR | Lane | Output | Job |
|---|---|---|---|
| #2469 | `a-sanitizer-flow-svc` amd64 | `3 == 2` | https://github.com/FalkorDB/FalkorDB/actions/runs/35196485924/job/105123436304 |
| #2854 | `release-flow-svc` amd64 | `3 == 2` | https://github.com/FalkorDB/FalkorDB/actions/runs/35477756321/job/105993214889 |
| #2855 | `a-sanitizer-flow-svc` amd64 | `3 == 2` | https://github.com/FalkorDB/FalkorDB/actions/runs/35477772040/job/105993699428 |
| #2861 | `release-flow-svc` arm64 | `2 == 1` | https://github.com/FalkorDB/FalkorDB/actions/runs/35477882321/job/105990795919 |

## Suggested fix

- Deduplicate `rel_types` in `parse_common_path_config`. Consider doing it in `get_node_relationships_by_type` too, since its other callers could pass duplicates as well.
- Make test17(b) independent of the random graph: assert that `dup.result_set == single.result_set` (or that `dup` has no repeated rows), and add a small fixed graph like the one above.

issues.title: [Flaky] test_effects_ddl test02: primary and replica disagree on node count after a constraint is dropped during validation
issues.body:
## Summary

`test_effects_ddl:testEffects_06_ConstraintSettlingRaces.test02_a_drop_during_validation_is_not_resurrected` intermittently fails its last probe:

```python
self.assert_agree("MATCH (n:Huge {a: 1, b: 1}) RETURN count(n)", [[2]])
```

The test's comment already records this as a known flake and describes it as "master short and replica right". The last week of CI shows it fails **in both directions**: sometimes the primary is missing a node, sometimes the replica is. That points to a real divergence between primary and replica (data or index), not a one-sided timing problem in the test. No issue tracks it yet.

## Evidence (Sep 17–24; PRs to `main`/`6.0` plus the merge queue)

6 failures, all in services-mode lanes. 5 of the 6 runs passed on re-run. No merge-queue failures so far.

| Lane | Failed / passed |
|---|---|
| `release-flow-svc` amd64 | 2 / 87 |
| `release-flow-svc` arm64 | 3 / 86 |
| `coverage-flow-svc` amd64 (lane renamed during the window) | 1 / 2 |
| `a-sanitizer-flow-svc` amd64 | 0 / 82 |
| `coverage-flow` amd64 (spawn mode) | 0 / 90 |

`assert_agree` first checks `m == expected` (`effects_common.py:223`), then `r == m` (`:224`).

| Symptom | Assertion output | Jobs |
|---|---|---|
| **Primary short** (primary 1, replica 2) | `:223 [[1]] == [[2]]` and `:224 [[2]] == [[1]]` | [#2869 arm64](https://github.com/FalkorDB/FalkorDB/actions/runs/35981611432/job/107576277325), [#2900 amd64](https://github.com/FalkorDB/FalkorDB/actions/runs/36016201932/job/107691668221), [#2920 arm64](https://github.com/FalkorDB/FalkorDB/actions/runs/36021408393/job/107709335266) |
| **Replica short** (primary 2, replica 1) | only `:224 [[1]] == [[2]]` | [#2921 arm64](https://github.com/FalkorDB/FalkorDB/actions/runs/36023406782/job/107724959969), [#2846 amd64](https://github.com/FalkorDB/FalkorDB/actions/runs/35915227485/job/107367551789) (this PR changes id allocation, so it may be the cause there), [#2704 coverage-flow-svc amd64](https://github.com/FalkorDB/FalkorDB/actions/runs/35187241197/job/105092834245) |

The #2704 failure is the `38ab02b9e` sighting that the test comment lists under "master short and replica right". At that commit the class was `testEffects_06b_ConstraintSettlingRaces` and the failing line was `effects_common.py:214`, which on that commit is `assertEqual(r, m)`. So in that run it was actually the **replica** that returned 1.

## What the probe does

1. `_build` creates 1M `:Huge {a: x, b: x, c: x}` nodes and range indexes on `a`, `b` and `c`.
2. The test starts a UNIQUE constraint, drops it while it's still being validated, and waits on the replication stream.
3. It runs `CREATE (:Huge {a: 1, b: 1, c: 1})` on the primary, waits for the replica offset, and expects both sides to count 2: the x=1 node from `_build` plus the new one.

One side sometimes counts 1.

One observation, not a diagnosis: `_build` calls `wait_for_indices_to_sync(self.master_graph)`, which waits for the indexes to become `OPERATIONAL` on the **primary only**.

## Suggested next steps

- When the probe fails, capture more state from both sides before asserting, to tell a missing node from a missing index entry:
  - a count that can't use the index
  - `CALL db.indexes()` and `CALL db.constraints()`
  - `GRAPH.EXPLAIN` of the probe
- Update the in-test comment: the failure isn't only "master short".

issues.title: [Flaky] tests/test_functions.py: random LIST generator builds multi-GB literals and pytest gets OOM-killed (exit 137)
issues.body:
## Summary

`tests/test_functions.py` sometimes kills the `test`, `test-image` and `coverage` jobs with **exit code 137** (bash prints `Killed`). The problem is in the test, not the server. `random_value(Type.LIST)` recurses with no depth limit and wraps each level in `str()`, so the argument literal roughly **doubles in size with every nesting level**. A few percent of runs build a literal of hundreds of MB to several GB, and the runner OOM-kills pytest.

## Evidence (Sep 17–24; PRs to `main`/`6.0` plus the merge queue)

26 failed jobs across 15 PRs, **7 of them in the merge queue**. That's about **6% of pytest jobs**:

| Job | Failed / passed |
|---|---|
| `test-image` | 11 / 116 |
| `coverage` | 10 / 137 |
| `test` | 5 / 141 |

- 25 of the 26 were SIGKILLs (exit 137).
- The other one failed in the same test (`string.join`) with `Error 104 while writing to socket. Connection reset by peer`. That's probably the same cause: a request larger than Redis's 512 MB `proto-max-bulk-len` gets its connection dropped.
- Parametrized case that was running when the job was killed: `replace` 8 times, `substring` 7, `range` 5, `test_extra_functions` (`string.matchRegEx` / `string.replaceRegEx`) 4, `left` 1. These are mostly the 3-argument functions, which draw the most LIST arguments.
- Every kill came after a 38–156 s stall (median ~56 s) inside that single case.

Example jobs:
- merge queue (#2867), `test-image`: https://github.com/FalkorDB/FalkorDB/actions/runs/35843090761/job/107124259284
- merge queue (#2533), `test-image`: https://github.com/FalkorDB/FalkorDB/actions/runs/35981283570/job/107575218119
- merge queue (#2469), `coverage`, connection reset: https://github.com/FalkorDB/FalkorDB/actions/runs/35283734891/job/105411370180
- PR #2916, `test-image`: https://github.com/FalkorDB/FalkorDB/actions/runs/36019756463/job/107703633297
- PR #2918, `test`: https://github.com/FalkorDB/FalkorDB/actions/runs/36021111618/job/107709131489
- PR #2461, `test`: https://github.com/FalkorDB/FalkorDB/actions/runs/35196486387/job/105121929381

## Root cause

```python
elif type == Type.LIST:
    return str([random_value(choice(all_types)) for _ in range(choice(range(0, 10)))])
```

1. **No depth cap.** A list has 0–9 elements, and each element is itself a LIST with probability 1/6. That's 0.75 nested lists per list on average, so generation always stops, but depth has a long tail. Per top-level LIST draw, P(depth ≥ 26) ≈ 2.6e-4 and P(depth ≥ 30) ≈ 8.2e-5.
2. **Size doubles per level.** The elements are already Python strings, so `str(list)` calls `repr()` on each one. Every level re-quotes the inner text and doubles its backslashes. A chain with one element per level measures ~2 MiB at depth 20, ~32 MiB at depth 24 and ~2 GiB at depth 30 (about 2^depth bytes).
3. **Many draws per run.** `validate_function` loops over `product(all_types, ...)`, so a k-argument function makes k·6^(k-1) LIST draws. That's 4 three-argument functions × 108, plus 6 two-argument × 12, plus 22 one-argument × 1: about 526 draws per run.
   - About 13% of runs produce at least one literal of 128 MiB or more.
   - About 7% produce one of 512 MiB or more.
   - About 4% produce one of 2 GiB or more.
   
   That matches the ~6% kill rate.
4. **Can't be reproduced.** The RNG isn't seeded and the inputs aren't logged, so a failing input can't be replayed.

Side effect: because of the double quoting, LIST arguments are always Cypher lists of *strings*, e.g. `['"abc"', '12', 'null']`. The LIST cases never actually pass ints, bools, nulls or nested lists.

## Suggested fix

- Build list literals as Cypher text, not Python reprs: `"[" + ", ".join(items) + "]"`.
- Cap nesting, e.g. no LIST elements below depth 2–3.
- Seed `random` from an environment variable (defaulting to a time-based seed) and print the seed, so a failure can be replayed.

issues.title: [Rust] Conversion divergences vs C: toString(1.0), toInteger/toFloat string parsing, duration('P5') (TCK position per case)
issues.body:
### Summary

Five string/number conversions give different answers on Rust and C. None of them crash. This issue records each one with the openCypher TCK position, so that the policy can be decided in one place. **No fix is proposed here where C and the TCK disagree or the TCK is silent.**

### Reproduction (release builds, Rust `main` @ 2363723ac vs C `bin/macos-arm64v8-release/falkordb.so`)

| Query | Rust | C | openCypher TCK (`tests/tck/features`) | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `toString(1.0)` | `'1'` | `'1.000000'` | not covered for integral floats; `TypeConversion4` [5] requires `toString(2.3) = '2.3'`, which C fails (`'2.300000'`) | Do **not** match C's `%f`. Rust's `'1'` is ambiguous with an Integer, and the code comment in `conversion.rs:124` says "ensure at least one decimal" but it doesn't. Neo4j prints `'1.0'`. Suggest `'1.0'` (shortest round-trip + `.0` when integral), pending a decision |
| `toString(0.1+0.2)` | `'0.30000000000000004'` | `'0.300000'` | not covered | same as above: shortest round-trip is the openCypher/Neo4j behaviour |
| `toString(0.0/0)` | `'NaN'` | `'nan'` | not covered | Neo4j `'NaN'`; keep |
| `toInteger('1e3')` | `1000` | `null` | not covered | Intentional in Rust: #2210 was closed as fixed by the Rust engine (Neo4j/Memgraph also return 1000). Keep |
| `toInteger(' 12')`, `toFloat(' 1')` | `null`, `null` | `12`, `1.0` | not covered | Tracked by #2282 (still open). C accepts only *leading* spaces (`'12 '` and `' 12 '` are null on both); Neo4j trims both sides. Needs a decision on #2282; not changed here |
| `toFloat('0x10')` | `null` | `16.0` | not covered | C accepts hex only because it uses `strtod`; `toInteger('0x10')` is null on both, and Neo4j returns null. Keep Rust |
| `duration('P5')`, `duration('P-')` | `PT0S` | `null` | not covered | Rust accepts a dangling number/sign with no unit and drops it. Both engines should reject it; C returns null, Neo4j raises an error. Candidate fix: error on leftover digits in `parse_duration_string` (`temporal.rs:356`) |
| `duration('PT1.5S')` | `PT1S` | `null` | `Temporal2` (fractional seconds are valid ISO) | Rust truncates the fraction because durations have one-second resolution; C rejects it. Related to #2595 |

### Mechanism

- `toString(Float)`: `format!("{f}")` (`graph/src/runtime/functions/conversion.rs:124`) vs C's `%f`.
- `toInteger`/`toFloat` on strings: Rust uses `str::parse` (no trimming, no hex); C uses `strtoll`/`strtod`, which skip leading whitespace and take hex floats.
- `duration(String)`: `parse_duration_string` (`graph/src/runtime/functions/temporal.rs:356`) never checks that `num_buf` is empty after the loop, so trailing digits are dropped.

### Found by

Lean 4 study of `functions_temporal` / `conversion.rs` (`proofs/functions_temporal`, header section "Divergences, conversions"); checked live on Rust vs C.

issues.title: [Rust] date({week, dayOfWeek}) is 0-based with 0 = Sunday; C/openCypher use 1..7 with 7 = Sunday
issues.body:
### Summary

The map form of `date()` / `localdatetime()` takes `dayOfWeek` as 0..6 with 0 = Sunday. openCypher, C and Rust's own string form (`'2021-W01-7'`) use ISO 1..7 with 1 = Monday, 7 = Sunday. So Sunday is spelled differently depending on the constructor, and `dayOfWeek: 7` is rejected.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 2363723ac)

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "RETURN toString(date({year:2021, week:1, dayOfWeek:7}))"
-- Rust: error "Invalid dayOfWeek: 7, expected 0..6"
-- C:    '2021-01-10'

GRAPH.QUERY g "RETURN toString(date({year:2021, week:1, dayOfWeek:0}))"
-- Rust: '2021-01-10'
-- C:    error "Invalid value for dayOfWeek (valid values 1 - 7)"

GRAPH.QUERY g "RETURN toString(date('2021-W01-7'))"
-- Rust and C: '2021-01-10'
```

### Mechanism

`date_from_components` (`graph/src/runtime/functions/temporal.rs:75`) accepts `0..=6` and maps 0 to Sunday (`:84`); `parse_week_date` (`:251`) uses 1..7.

### Expected

Accept 1..=7 (7 = Sunday) and reject 0 with C's message "Invalid value for dayOfWeek (valid values 1 - 7)". Days 1..6 are unchanged.

### Found by

Lean 4 model (`proofs/functions_temporal`, theorems `dayOfWeek_seven_rejected`, `dayOfWeek_zero_is_sunday`); Rust repro `graph/tests/lean_functions_temporal.rs::bug_date_map_day_of_week_is_zero_based`.

issues.title: [Rust] duration('P2635249153387078803W') silently wraps to P5D (unchecked week/day arithmetic in the ISO parser)
issues.body:
### Summary

The ISO duration string parser multiplies and adds the week/day counts with unchecked `i64` arithmetic. In release builds a huge week count silently wraps to a small, plausible duration; in debug builds it panics. The map form of the same value is already rejected with an overflow error.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 2363723ac)

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "RETURN toString(duration('P2635249153387078803W'))"
-- Rust: 'P5D'      (2635249153387078803 * 7 wraps to 5)
-- C:    'P-35277664Y10M-1.28849019e+10DT1S'   (garbage, but not P5D)

GRAPH.QUERY g "RETURN toString(duration({weeks:2635249153387078803}))"
-- Rust: error "Duration overflow: weeks=…"
```

### Mechanism

`parse_duration_string` (`graph/src/runtime/functions/temporal.rs:376`): `'W' => days += n * 7` and `'D' => days += n` use plain `*` / `+=` (wrap in release, panic in debug). `construct_duration_secs` then receives an already-wrapped value.

### Expected

Use `checked_mul` / `checked_add` and return the same "Duration overflow" error the map form returns. C has no usable answer here (its result is garbage), so matching the Rust map form is the consistent choice.

### Found by

Lean 4 model `wrapMul` (`proofs/functions_temporal`, theorem `week_string_wraps`); Rust repro `graph/tests/lean_functions_temporal.rs::bug_duration_week_string_wraps`.

issues.title: [Rust] toString(date) truncates the year to 4 digits and drops its sign (date({year:12345}) prints 2345-01-01)
issues.body:
### Summary

Dates are printed with the year taken modulo 10 000 and without its sign, so distinct dates print identically (and `date(toString(d)) <> d`). Datetimes outside chrono's range print `<invalid timestamp: …>`, and negative datetime years print as `-005`. This affects `toString()` and the reply formatter.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 2363723ac)

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "RETURN toString(date({year:12345})), toString(date('2020-01-01') + duration({years:10000})), toString(date({year:-5})), toString(date({year:5}))"
-- Rust: '2345-01-01', '2020-01-01', '0005-01-01', '0005-01-01'
-- C:    '12345-01-01', '12020-01-01', '1969-12-31', '1969-12-31'

GRAPH.QUERY g "RETURN toString(localdatetime('2020-01-01T10:20:30') + duration({years:300000})), toString(localdatetime({year:-5}))"
-- Rust: '<invalid timestamp: 9468663474030>', '-005-01-01T00:00:00'
-- C:    '302020-01-01T10:20:30', '1969-12-31T23:59:59'
```

(C is itself wrong for negative years: it prints 1969-12-31.)

### Mechanism

- `write_date_into` (`graph/src/runtime/value.rs:803`) writes exactly four year digits of `y.unsigned_abs()`: the sign is dropped and years ≥ 10 000 are truncated. Used by `Value::format_date` (`:274`) → `toString()` and `src/reply.rs`.
- `Value::format_datetime` (`:256`) goes through `chrono::Utc.timestamp_opt`, which only covers ±262 143 years, and `{:04}` on a negative `i32` gives `-005`.

### Expected

Match C for years ≥ 10 000 (`12345-01-01`, all digits, no `+`). For negative years C is broken, so use the ISO 8601 form `-0005-01-01` (sign + at least four digits) (openCypher accepts signed years, e.g. `-999999999-01-01` in TCK `Temporal10`). Format datetimes from `civil_from_days` like dates, so every stored timestamp prints.

### Found by

Lean 4 model `formatDateDigits` (`proofs/functions_temporal`, theorem `formatDate_not_injective`; `formatDate_injective_4digit` proves the four-digit range is fine); Rust repro `graph/tests/lean_functions_temporal.rs::bug_format_date_truncates_year`.

issues.title: [Rust] localtime ± duration is not reduced modulo a day, so localtime('01:00') + duration({days:1}) <> localtime('01:00')
issues.body:
### Summary

`localtime + duration` / `localtime - duration` is not reduced modulo a day, so the result carries the duration's days/months and compares unequal to the same wall-clock time. C (and openCypher, TCK `Temporal8` [2]) keep only the time of day.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 2363723ac)

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "RETURN localtime('01:00') + duration({days:1}) = localtime('01:00')"
-- Rust: false
-- C:    true

GRAPH.QUERY g "RETURN localtime('01:00') + duration({months:1}) = localtime('01:00')"
-- Rust: false
-- C:    true
```

`toString()` looks right (`01:00:00`) because the formatter only prints the clock part, which hides the bad value; `=`, `<`, `ORDER BY`, `DISTINCT` and index lookups see the full timestamp.

### Mechanism

`impl Add for Value` / `impl Sub for Value` (`graph/src/runtime/value.rs:1027`, `:1072`) route `Time ± Duration` through `add_duration_to_timestamp` / `sub_duration_from_timestamp`, which apply years/months/days and return a timestamp outside `[0, 86400)`.

### Expected

`Time ± Duration = (t ± dur).rem_euclid(86400)`. Every duration encoding is a whole number of days (years/months/days) plus a clock offset, so the time of day of `t ± dur` is exactly the openCypher result. (C's own `localtime('01:00') - duration({hours:2})` gives `23:59:59`, which is a C bug; the fix gives `23:00:00` like today.)

### Found by

Lean 4 model (`proofs/functions_temporal`, theorem `time_not_normalised`); Rust repro `graph/tests/lean_functions_temporal.rs::bug_time_plus_day_not_normalised`.

issues.title: [Rust] date - duration({months:n}) clamps to month end while date + duration({months:-n}) rolls over (C rolls over in both)
issues.body:
### Summary

Subtracting a month-based duration clamps the day to the end of the month, while adding the negated duration rolls the overflow into the next month. So `d - dur` and `d + (-dur)` disagree. C rolls over in both directions.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 2363723ac)

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "RETURN toString(date('2020-03-31') - duration({months:1})), toString(date('2020-03-31') + duration({months:-1}))"
-- Rust: '2020-02-29', '2020-03-02'
-- C:    '2020-03-02', '2020-03-02'

GRAPH.QUERY g "RETURN toString(localdatetime('2020-03-31T10:00:00') - duration({months:1}))"
-- Rust: '2020-02-29T10:00:00'
-- C:    '2020-03-02T10:00:00'
```

### Mechanism

`add_duration_to_timestamp` (`graph/src/runtime/value.rs:696`) moves the overflowing days into the next month (`:712-722`), the same as C's `timegm` normalisation, and `tests/flow/test_temporal.py::test_month_end_duration_arithmetic` pins `2024-01-31 + P1M = 2024-03-02`. `sub_duration_from_timestamp` (`:730`) instead does `d.min(max_day)` (`:746`).

### Expected

Match C (and Rust's own `+`): `sub` uses the same month-end rule as `add`, so `d - dur == d + (-dur)`. (Neo4j clamps in both directions; FalkorDB's documented `+` behaviour rolls over, and the fix makes `-` consistent with it.)

### Found by

Lean 4 model `addDur` / `subDur` (`proofs/functions_temporal/FalkorTemporal/Duration.lean`, theorem `sub_vs_add_neg`); Rust repro `graph/tests/lean_functions_temporal.rs::bug_date_minus_month_disagrees_with_plus_negative_month`.

issues.title: [Rust] distance() returns NaN for antipodal points (haversine term rounds above 1)
issues.body:
### Summary

`distance()` between (near-)antipodal points returns `NaN`. C returns ~20 037 km.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 2363723ac)

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "RETURN distance(point({latitude:-88.3, longitude:-180}), point({latitude:88.3, longitude:0}))"
-- Rust: nan
-- C:    20037518
```

On a 0.1° grid, 35 428 of 6 485 401 antipodal pairs give `NaN`.

### Mechanism

`Point::distance` (`graph/src/runtime/value.rs:121`) computes the haversine `a = sin²(Δφ/2) + cos φ1 cos φ2 sin²(Δλ/2)` and then `2 * atan2(√a, √(1 - a))` (`:137`). For antipodal points `a` is mathematically 1 but rounds to `1 + ε`, so `(1.0 - a).sqrt()` is `NaN`.

### Expected

Clamp `a` to `[0, 1]` before the square roots (the standard haversine guard). Matches C.

### Found by

Lean 4 model `Spatial.haversine` (`proofs/functions_temporal/FalkorTemporal/Spatial.lean`); Rust repro `graph/tests/lean_functions_temporal.rs::bug_distance_antipodal_nan`.

issues.title: [Rust] date()/localdatetime() panic and crash the server on out-of-range week/dayOfQuarter or a multi-byte week string
issues.body:
### Summary

Three `date()` / `localdatetime()` inputs panic inside the temporal constructors, and the panic hook takes the whole server down. They are plain constant queries, no graph needed. C returns an error for each.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 2363723ac)

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "RETURN date({year:2020, week:10000000000})"
-- Error: Server closed the connection
-- panicked at graph/src/runtime/functions/temporal.rs:83:29: `NaiveDate + TimeDelta` overflowed

GRAPH.QUERY g "RETURN localdatetime({year:2020, week:-9223372036854775807})"
-- Error: Server closed the connection
-- panicked at chrono-0.4.45/src/lib.rs:717:17: TimeDelta::days out of bounds

GRAPH.QUERY g "RETURN date({year:2020, quarter:2, dayOfQuarter:9223372036854775807})"
-- Error: Server closed the connection
-- panicked at chrono-0.4.45/src/lib.rs:717:17: TimeDelta::days out of bounds

GRAPH.QUERY g "RETURN date('2020W1é')"
-- Error: Server closed the connection
-- panicked at graph/src/runtime/functions/temporal.rs:248:29 (byte index 2 is not a char boundary)
```

C (`bin/macos-arm64v8-release/falkordb.so`):

```
date({year:2020, week:10000000000})                       -> Invalid value for week (valid values 1 - 53)
date({year:2020, quarter:2, dayOfQuarter:922...807})      -> Invalid value for dayOfQuarter (valid values 1 - 92)
date('2020W1é')                                           -> Failed to parse date
```

Related, no crash but wrong: `date({year:2021, quarter:1, dayOfQuarter:200})` returns `2021-07-19` (C: "Invalid value for dayOfQuarter (valid values 1 - 92)"), and `year`/`month`/`day` are cast with `as i32`/`as u32`, so e.g. `year: 4294969316` silently becomes 2020.

### Mechanism

`date_from_components` (`graph/src/runtime/functions/temporal.rs:62`, shared by `date`, `localdatetime`, and their positional-slot forms):
- week mode: `chrono::Duration::days((week - 1) * 7)` and `target_monday + …` (`:83`) with an unvalidated `week` — `TimeDelta::days` panics when out of range and `NaiveDate + TimeDelta` panics on overflow;
- quarter mode: `chrono::Duration::days(doq - 1)` (`:95`) panics before `checked_add_signed` gets a chance; `quarter` and `dayOfQuarter` are never range-checked.

`parse_week_date` (`:248`): `rest[..2]` / `rest[2..]` slice by byte index, which panics when byte 2 is inside a multi-byte character.

### Expected

Match C: range-check the map components before any chrono arithmetic (`week` 1-53, `quarter` 1-4, `dayOfQuarter` 1-92, with C's "Invalid value for X (valid values a - b)" message), use checked date arithmetic, and reject a non-ASCII week string with an error instead of slicing it.

### Suggested fix

`check_range` for week/quarter/dayOfQuarter, `i32::try_from`/`u32::try_from` for year/month/day, compute the week offset as one bounded day count and add it with `checked_add_signed`; `split_at_checked(2)` in `parse_week_date`.

### Found by

Lean 4 model of the temporal constructors (`proofs/functions_temporal`, theorems `week_panics`, `week_panics_delta`, `quarter_panics`, `week_slice_panics`; `weekPath_total` proves the bounded path is panic-free); Rust repros `graph/tests/lean_functions_temporal.rs::bug_date_week_huge_panics`, `bug_date_day_of_quarter_panics`, `bug_date_week_string_char_boundary_panics`.

issues.title: [Rust] string.replaceRegEx expands $-references in the replacement; C copies it literally ($5 silently becomes '')
issues.body:
### Summary

`string.replaceRegEx(text, pattern, replacement)` expands `$`-references in the replacement (regex-crate syntax: `$1`, `${1}`, `$name`, `$$`); C copies the replacement literally. Replacement text that merely *contains* a `$` is silently changed — a reference to a group that does not exist becomes the empty string, with no error.

Unlike the other items found in this pass this is not a plain bug: the expansion is a deliberate Rust extension, asserted by `tests/test_e2e.py::test_string_replace_regex` (marked `@pytest.mark.extra`, "extra for the new rust database"). So this issue asks for a decision rather than shipping a fix.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 2363723ac)

| query | Rust | C |
|---|---|---|
| `RETURN string.replaceRegEx('price: X', 'X', '$5')` | `'price: '` | `'price: $5'` |
| `RETURN string.replaceRegEx('abc', 'b', '$0x')` | `'ac'` (`$0x` = named group "0x", absent) | `'a$0xc'` |
| `RETURN string.replaceRegEx('abc', 'b', '[$0]')` | `'a[b]c'` | `'a[$0]c'` |
| `RETURN string.replaceRegEx('a-b', '(a)-(b)', '$2$1')` | `'ba'` | `'$2$1'` |
| `RETURN string.replaceRegEx('x', 'x', '$$')` | `'$'` | `'$$'` |

Both the generic path and the bind-time compiled path behave the same.

### Mechanism

`Regex::replace_all(text, &str)` treats a `&str` replacement as an expansion template: `graph/src/runtime/functions/string.rs:469` and `graph/src/runtime/eval.rs:1302` (`CompiledRegex` / `RegexFnKind::Replace`). The regex crate's template syntax takes the *longest* identifier after `$`, so `$0x` means group `0x`, and a missing group expands to `""`.

### Options

1. **Match C: literal replacement** — `replace_all(text, regex::NoExpand(repl))` at both call sites (2 lines). Removes the extension; `test_string_replace_regex`'s `$1`/`${1}`/`$first` cases would change to literal expectations. Users migrating from C see no change; users relying on the Rust-only `$1` lose it.
2. **Keep expansion, make it safe** — keep `$n`/`${name}`, but reject (error) a reference to a group the pattern does not have, instead of expanding it to `""`. Keeps the feature; `'$5'` against a group-less pattern becomes an error instead of silent data loss, but it is still a divergence from C for any replacement containing `$`.
3. **Keep as is, document** — document the template syntax (`$$` for a literal `$`) as a Rust extension and a known difference from C.

### Recommendation

Option 1. C is the reference, and `$` is common in replacement text (prices, shell/template snippets); silently turning `'$5'` into `''` is a data change nobody asked for. If group references are wanted, they are better exposed explicitly (e.g. a flag or a separate function) than by changing the meaning of existing replacement strings. Needs a maintainer call because it removes a tested extension.

### Found by

Lean 4 model (`proofs/functions_str_list`, theorem `replaceRegex_dollar`, model `expandRust`); Rust repro `graph/tests/lean_functions_str_list.rs::bug_replace_regex_dollar_expansion`.

issues.title: [Rust] List comprehension over null returns [] and over a scalar returns [x] (C: null / type error)
issues.body:
### Summary

A list comprehension whose source is not a list uses UNWIND semantics instead of list semantics: `[x IN null | x]` returns `[]` (C and openCypher: `null`), and `[x IN 5 | x]` returns `[5]` (C: `Type mismatch: expected List or Null but was Integer`). `reduce()` and the quantifiers (`all/any/none/single`) already return null / a type error for the same sources.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 2363723ac)

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "RETURN [x IN null | x]"                 -- Rust: []    C: null
GRAPH.QUERY g "RETURN [x IN null WHERE x > 1]"         -- Rust: []    C: null
GRAPH.QUERY g "RETURN [x IN 5 | x]"                    -- Rust: [5]   C: Type mismatch: expected List or Null but was Integer
GRAPH.QUERY g "RETURN reduce(a = 0, x IN null | a)"    -- Rust: null  (already right)
```

### Mechanism

`ExprIR::ListComprehension` (`graph/src/runtime/eval.rs:1018-1033`) iterates the source through `eval_iter_expr`, whose fallback arm (`eval.rs:1234-1243`) implements UNWIND: `Null` → no rows (`None`, so the comprehension returns an empty list), any scalar → one row (`RowIter::one`). Those are the right semantics for `UNWIND`, not for a comprehension.

### Expected

Match C / openCypher: a null source gives `null`; a non-list, non-null source is `Type mismatch: expected List or Null but was <T>`.

### Suggested fix

Keep `eval_iter_expr` for the shapes that always produce a list (list literal, lazy `range()`), which keeps the no-materialisation fast path; evaluate any other source with `eval_node` and dispatch `List` / `Null` / other like `Reduce` does.

### Found by

Lean 4 model of comprehensions (`proofs/functions_str_list`, theorems `comprehension_diverges` and `comprehension_agrees_on_lists`); Rust repro `graph/tests/lean_functions_str_list.rs::bug_list_comprehension_null_and_scalar_source`.

issues.title: [Rust] toLower/toUpper reject valid strings containing U+FFFD with "Invalid UTF8 string"
issues.body:
### Summary

`toLower` / `toUpper` fail with `Invalid UTF8 string` for any valid string that contains the code point U+FFFD (REPLACEMENT CHARACTER). C returns the mapped string.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 2363723ac)

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "RETURN toLower('A�'), toUpper('a�b')"
-- Rust: Invalid UTF8 string
-- C:    'a�', 'A�B'
```

### Mechanism

`graph/src/runtime/functions/string.rs:148` and `:170`:

```rust
// Match C behavior: detect replacement character which indicates invalid UTF-8
if s.contains('\u{FFFD}') {
    return Err(String::from("Invalid UTF8 string"));
}
```

The check tries to mirror C's `str_tolower`, which returns an error on an invalid UTF-8 byte sequence. But a Rust `String` is valid UTF-8 by construction, so there is no invalid input to detect here; U+FFFD is an ordinary code point and the check can only misfire.

The flow tests `test65_ToLower` / `test66_ToUpper` (`tests/flow/test_function_calls.py:1856,1871`) assert the error for `toLower(replace("�", "", "   "))`. On C that errors only because C's `replace(s, '', t)` inserts `t` between the *bytes* of the multi-byte character and so produces invalid UTF-8 (`-\xef-\xbf-\xbd-`); on Rust `replace` yields a valid `'   �   '`, so the test is exercising a C `replace` bug, not case mapping.

### Expected

`toLower('A�') = 'a�'`, `toUpper('a�b') = 'A�B'` (C, Neo4j).

### Suggested fix

Delete the U+FFFD check in both functions and update the two flow-test assertions.

### Found by

Lean 4 model of case mapping (`proofs/functions_str_list`, theorem `toLower_rejects_valid`); Rust repro `graph/tests/lean_functions_str_list.rs::bug_case_map_rejects_replacement_char`.

issues.title: [Rust] list.remove overflows on a huge count (debug panic; release right only by accident)
issues.body:
### Summary

`list.remove(list, idx, count)` computes the end of the removed span as `normalized + count` with an unchecked `i64` add. A huge `count` overflows: debug builds panic (*attempt to add with overflow*); release builds wrap to a negative number, cast it to `usize` (2^63) and are rescued by `.min(len)`, so the release answer is right only by accident. C returns `[1]`.

### Reproduction (`main` @ 2363723ac)

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "RETURN list.remove([1,2,3], 1, 9223372036854775807)"
```

- debug build: panic `attempt to add with overflow` at `graph/src/runtime/functions/list.rs:168`
- release build: `[1]` (wrapped add, then `as usize` = 2^63, `.min(3)`)
- C: `[1]`

### Mechanism

`graph/src/runtime/functions/list.rs:168`:

```rust
let end = ((normalized + count) as usize).min(vs.len());
```

`normalized ∈ [0, len)` and `count > 0` are checked just above, but nothing bounds `count`, so `normalized + count` can exceed `i64::MAX`.

### Expected

`[1]` in every build: the span is clamped to the end of the list (C behaviour).

### Suggested fix

`normalized.saturating_add(count)`; the result is clamped to `len` anyway.

### Found by

Lean 4 model of `list.remove` (`proofs/functions_str_list`, theorems `listRemove_end_overflows` and `listRemoveRelease_eq_spec` — the latter proves the wrapped release result equals the spec, which is why only debug fails); Rust repro `graph/tests/lean_functions_str_list.rs::bug_list_remove_count_overflow`.

issues.title: [Rust] ORDER BY <projected expr> LIMIT 10 over 1M nodes is 15-40% slower than C; aliased form is 2x faster (key re-evaluated per row, Project fast path lost)
issues.body:
### Summary

`MATCH (n:N) RETURN n.x ORDER BY n.x LIMIT 10` over 1M nodes is 15–40% slower than C for int and float keys. The same query written with an alias, `RETURN n.x AS k ORDER BY k LIMIT 10`, is about **2x faster than C**. The gap therefore does not come from sorting. It comes from ORDER BY not reusing the projected column: the key is re-evaluated row by row inside the top-k, and the projection is pushed off its fast path.

### Measurements (release LTO build, `main` @ 2363723ac, vs C `bin/macos-arm64v8-release/falkordb.so`, macOS arm64)

Dataset, identical on both engines:

```
UNWIND range(0, 999999) AS x CREATE (:N {i: (x * 7919) % 1000003, f: toFloat((x * 104729) % 1000033) / 1000033.0})
```

The client alternated Rust and C on every iteration. Before each query there were 3 warm-up runs. Times are wall-clock ms from `redis-py`.

Cleanest run (40 runs each, load average about 11):

| query | Rust p50 / p99 | C p50 / p99 | Rust / C (p50, p99) |
|---|---|---|---|
| `RETURN n.i ORDER BY n.i LIMIT 10` | 69.4 / 75.1 | 60.3 / 64.4 | 1.15, 1.17 |
| `RETURN n.f ORDER BY n.f LIMIT 10` | 85.8 / 120.1 | 70.2 / 90.3 | 1.22, 1.33 |
| `RETURN n.i ORDER BY n.i DESC LIMIT 10` | 86.2 / 121.8 | 72.1 / 97.5 | 1.20, 1.25 |

The host was shared with parallel builds, so the next run was taken at load average about 50 and its absolute p50/p99 are inflated. The min column is the best comparison (60 interleaved runs):

| query | Rust min / p50 | C min / p50 |
|---|---|---|
| `RETURN n.i ORDER BY n.i LIMIT 10` | 99.1 / 1010 | 69.1 / 611 |
| `RETURN n.f ORDER BY n.f LIMIT 10` | 79.3 / 136 | 67.5 / 99.7 |
| `RETURN n.i AS k ORDER BY k LIMIT 10` | **39.6** / 312 | 63.5 / 651 |
| `RETURN n.f AS k ORDER BY k LIMIT 10` | **32.9** / 49.1 | 63.5 / 91.0 |

Every run agrees: the unaliased form is 1.15–1.65x C, and the aliased form is 0.5–0.6x C.

### Profile (samply, `profiling` profile, 40× the int query, 3092 active samples)

Inclusive, under `SortOp::next`, 95.8% of the query:

| % | frame |
|---|---|
| 64.3 | `ProjectOp::next` |
| 20.0 | `ExprEval::eval_node::<BatchRow>` called from **`SortOp::next`** (`build_top_k`), the per-row re-evaluation of `n.i` |
| 12.7 | `BatchBuilder::push_row_with`, from `ProjectOp`'s row-by-row path |
| 7.7 | `Row::insert_by_id`, same path |
| 11.0 (self) | `drop_glue::<Value>`, the per-row `Row`/`SmallVec<Value>` and `SmallVec<OrderedKey>` teardown |
| 10.5 | `VectorEval::eval_values` → `materialize_node_property_values`, the one bulk fetch that is needed |

`GRAPH.PROFILE` for the int query: Scan 9 ms, Project 40 ms, Sort 23 ms. C: Scan 20 ms, Project 49 ms, Sort 21 ms.

### Mechanism

1. **The binder rewrites ORDER BY to projected aliases only for aggregations.** `graph/src/planner/binder.rs:1171-1181` calls `replace_agg_subtrees` (`binder.rs:2568`) only `if expr.is_aggregation()`. `ORDER BY n.i` next to `RETURN n.i` is therefore bound as the original expression over `n`, and `n` has to be carried through the projection (`copy_from_parent`).
2. **A carried variable disables Project's columnar fast path.** In `graph/src/runtime/ops/project.rs:81-91`, the fast path requires `copy_from_parent.is_empty()`. With `n` carried, every row goes through `Row::with_capacity` + `insert` + `BatchBuilder::push_row` (`project.rs:94-117`). That path accounts for the `push_row_with` / `insert_by_id` / `drop_glue` share above.
3. **Top-k evaluates each key per row with the scalar evaluator.** `graph/src/runtime/ops/sort.rs:412-419` (`build_top_k`) calls `ExprEval::eval` once per row per key. That repeats the attribute lookup Project already did in bulk, and allocates a `SmallVec<OrderedKey>` per row. The full-sort path already uses `eval_batch` (`sort.rs:301`), but the top-k path does not.

The aliased form avoids 1 and 2, and for 3 the key is a plain variable read. That is why it beats C by about 2x.

### Expected

p50 and p99 match or beat C for `ORDER BY <projected expr> LIMIT k`. That is the performance bar in CLAUDE.md, and the aliased form shows the engine can already do it.

### Suggested fix (general, shared paths)

* **Binder:** generalise the `replace_agg_subtrees` rewrite so it applies to any ORDER BY subtree that is structurally equal to a projected expression, not just aggregations. The `RETURN` / `WITH` alias then replaces it. Every `ORDER BY` that repeats a projection benefits, and the carried `n` usually drops out, which restores Project's fast path.
* **Sort:** in `build_top_k`, evaluate the keys per batch with `eval_batch`, as `build_full_sort` does, and compare against the heap's worst entry from the column. Only rows that enter the heap then get materialised.

### Found by

Perf sweep against the C module. Measured with interleaved Rust/C runs and profiled with samply.

issues.title: [Rust] Client GRAPH.EFFECT CREATE_EDGE with a non-live src/dst is applied: dangling edge, phantom endpoints, next node inherits it, survives RDB
issues.body:
### Summary

A client-sent `GRAPH.EFFECT` whose `CREATE_EDGE` record names a `src`/`dst` that is not a live node is **applied and answers `OK`**. The server did not crash in any of the cases I tried. What it does instead is keep a dangling relationship, and that corruption is persistent and spreads:

* `startNode`/`endNode` return a node that `MATCH (n)` does not have.
* The next node created **inherits the phantom edge**.
* `count(r)` disagrees with what `MATCH ()-[r]->()` returns.
* `DETACH DELETE` of the live endpoint leaks the edge forever.
* All of this **survives `SAVE` + restart and `DEBUG RELOAD`**.

`src/divergence_guard.rs:32-37` says a client `GRAPH.EFFECT` "is just a malformed command", i.e. a bad request to refuse. For every other malformed id the apply path does refuse (`AlreadyLive`, `IdsHaveAHole`, unknown type/label). Edge endpoints are the one input it takes on trust.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 2363723ac)

Payloads are built with the v3 encoder, the same way as `lean_id_space.rs::dump_buffers_for_e2e`. Each one is `AddRelType{0,"R"}`, then an optional `CreateNode`, then `CreateEdge{ids:[0], relation_id:0, src:[s], dst:[d]}`:

| payload | nodes created | edge |
|---|---|---|
| `near.bin` | `[0]` | `0 → 1` (node 1 never created) |
| `far.bin` | `[0]` | `0 → 1_000_000` |
| `none.bin` | — | `7 → 7` |

```rust
let mut b = new_buffer();
Record::AddRelType { id: 0, name: "R".to_owned() }.encode(&mut b)?;
Record::CreateNode { ids: IdList::from([0]), labels: vec![], attr_ids: vec![], rows: vec![] }.encode(&mut b)?;
Record::CreateEdge { ids: IdList::from([0]), relation_id: 0,
    src: IdList::from([0]), dst: IdList::from([1]), attr_ids: vec![], rows: vec![] }.encode(&mut b)?;
```

```
$ redis-cli -x GRAPH.EFFECT gnear < near.bin
OK
MATCH (n) RETURN id(n)                                        -> 0                  (one node)
MATCH ()-[r]->() RETURN id(r), id(startNode(r)), id(endNode(r)) -> 0, 0, 1        (endpoint 1 does not exist)
MATCH (a)-[r]->() RETURN endNode(r)                           -> (id 1, no labels, no properties)
CREATE (x:New {name:'fresh'}) RETURN id(x)                    -> 1
MATCH (x:New)<-[r]-(a) RETURN id(x), id(r), id(a)             -> 1, 0, 0           <- fresh node already has an incoming edge
MATCH (x:New) DELETE x                                        -> Nodes deleted: 1, Relationships deleted: 1
```

```
$ redis-cli -x GRAPH.EFFECT gfar < far.bin          -> OK
MATCH ()-[r]->() RETURN count(r)                     -> 1
MATCH ()-[r:R]->() RETURN count(r)                   -> 0
MATCH ()-[r]->() RETURN id(r), ...                   -> (no rows)
MATCH (a) DETACH DELETE a                            -> Nodes deleted: 1   (no relationship deleted)
MATCH ()-[r]->() RETURN count(r)                     -> 1                  (leaked)
CREATE (:X)-[:R]->(:X); MATCH ()-[r]->() RETURN count(r) -> 2 (only 1 enumerable)

$ redis-cli -x GRAPH.EFFECT gnone < none.bin        -> OK
MATCH (n) RETURN count(n)                            -> 0
MATCH ()-[r]->() RETURN count(r)                     -> 1
MATCH ()-[r]->() RETURN id(r), ...                   -> (no rows)
```

After `SAVE`, a restart (RDB load) and `DEBUG RELOAD`, the RDB loads cleanly and every graph comes back in the same state: `rnear` still returns `0, 0, 1`, and `rfar`/`rnone` still report `count(r) = 1` with no enumerable edge. `PING` answered throughout, with no panic in the log.

For comparison, C refuses the payload at the version check (`GRAPH.EFFECT version mismatch expected version <= 2 got: 3`) and exits the process, which is the unconditional guard that `divergence_guard.rs` deliberately does not copy. There is no C equivalent to compare the apply behaviour against.

### Mechanism

* `graph/src/effects/v3/apply.rs:272-288` (`Record::CreateEdge`) resolves the type, then calls `create_relationships_bulk` with the record's `src`/`dst` as given.
* `Graph::create_relationships_bulk` (`graph/src/graph/graph.rs:2301-2347`) checks the **edge** ids against the `IdSpace` (`record_created`). It never checks that each `src`/`dst` is below `node_cap`, or live (not in `deleted_nodes` and below the node id bound). It writes the pairs straight into the type tensor, `edge_endpoints` and the adjacency matrix. Endpoints past the matrix size (`far`) are dropped from the matrices, but `relationship_count` is still incremented. That explains why `count(r)` (counter) and enumeration (matrices) disagree.
* The RDB encoder serialises the tensor and endpoint index as they are, and the loader does not validate them, so the corruption persists.

### Severity

It needs a client allowed to run `GRAPH.EFFECT` (a write command), and a well-behaved master never emits such a record. I observed no crash, so I would not call it a DoS. It is silent, persistent graph corruption that one command can cause, and it leaks into ordinary later writes (the next `CREATE` adopts the edge). It also sits on the path a replica uses. If a primary bug ever emitted a bad endpoint, the replica would absorb it with no `divergence_guard` signal, where it should refuse the buffer.

### Expected

The buffer is refused like the other malformed-id cases, e.g. `ERR effect apply failed: relationship 0 names node 1, which is not live`, and nothing is applied (the MVCC rollback already covers a failed buffer).

### Suggested fix

In the `CreateEdge` arm of `apply.rs`, before `create_relationships_bulk`, reject any `src`/`dst` that is not a live node: below the node id bound and not in `deleted_nodes`. That also covers nodes created earlier in the same buffer. Return a new `ApplyError` variant, parallel to `AlreadyLive`. The check belongs in the effects apply layer, not the Cypher write path, which only ever passes live endpoints. Optionally add a `debug_assert!` in `create_relationships_bulk`.

### Found by

Review of the effects-v3 apply path during the `proofs/id_space` sweep (the same area as #2892, which covers huge *node* ids in `CreateNode`). Reproduced live with v3 payloads encoded by a throwaway test.

issues.title: [Rust] Inline property map referencing a variable from an earlier MATCH / pattern part: "'r' not defined" for relationships, silent 0 rows for nodes
issues.body:
### Summary

When an inline property map in a later `MATCH`, or in a later comma-separated pattern part, refers to a variable from an earlier part of the same pattern, Rust gets it wrong in one of two ways. C handles both.

* **Relationship variable** (`id(r)`): the query is rejected at bind time with `'r' not defined`.
* **Node variable** (`id(a)`): it binds, then **silently returns 0 rows**, because the filter runs inside a Cartesian Product branch where `a` is not bound.

Moving the same predicate to `WHERE`, or putting `WITH` between the clauses, gives the correct answer.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 2363723ac)

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE (:A)-[:R]->(:B {v:0})"      -- a: id 0, r: id 0, c: v = 0
```

| query | C (`bin/macos-arm64v8-release/falkordb.so`) | Rust |
|---|---|---|
| `MATCH (a)-[r]->(b) MATCH (c:B {v: id(r)*0}) RETURN count(*)` | 1 | **`'r' not defined`** |
| `MATCH (a)-[r]->(b) MATCH (c {v: id(r)}) RETURN count(*)` | 1 | **`'r' not defined`** |
| `MATCH (a)-[r]->(b), (c:B {v: id(r)}) RETURN count(*)` | 1 | **`'r' not defined`** |
| `MATCH ()-[r]->() MATCH (c:B)-[q {x: id(r)}]->() RETURN count(*)` | 0 | **`Variable r not found`** (runtime) |
| `MATCH (a:A) MATCH (c:B {v: id(a)}) RETURN count(*)` | 1 | **0** (silent wrong result) |
| `MATCH (a:A), (c:B {v: id(a)}) RETURN count(*)` | 1 | **0** |
| `MATCH (a)-[r]->(b) MATCH (c:B {v: id(a)*0}) RETURN count(*)` | 1 | **0** |
| `MATCH (a:A) MATCH (c:B) WHERE c.v = id(a) RETURN count(*)` | 1 | 1 ✅ |
| `MATCH (a)-[r]->(b) WITH r MATCH (c:B {v: id(r)*0}) RETURN count(*)` | 1 | 1 ✅ |

Rust plan for the wrong-result case. The `Filter` (`c.v = id(a)`) sits under the second Cartesian branch, where `a` is never bound:

```
Aggregate
    Cartesian Product
        Node By Label Scan | (a:A)
        Filter
            Node By Label Scan | (c:B)
```

C plans it as `Value Hash Join | property(c,v,0) = id(a)`.

### Mechanism

1. **The parser fuses consecutive `MATCH` clauses into one pattern.** In `parse_pattern`, `graph/src/parser/cypher.rs:1551-1556`, if the next token is the same clause keyword (`token == *clause`), it is consumed and parsing continues into the same `QueryGraph`. So `MATCH p1 MATCH p2` becomes the same thing as `MATCH p1, p2`.
2. **`bind_graph` binds all node attrs before any relationship alias is defined.** `graph/src/planner/binder.rs:1322-1324` defines each node and binds its `attrs`, and only after that loop are relationships defined (`binder.rs:1349`). When `c`'s `{v: id(r)}` is bound, `r` is not yet in scope, so `resolve` (`binder.rs:2211`) returns `'r' not defined`. A node variable such as `a` is already in scope at that point, so it binds.
3. **The planner attaches an unbound node's inline-attr filter directly over its own scan.** `plan_match`, `graph/src/planner/mod.rs:1838-1853` (`inline_attrs_to_filter` → `IR::Filter` over `NodeByLabelScan`), does this inside the component's sub-plan. Each connected component becomes a separate `CartesianProduct` child (`mod.rs:2270-2274`), so a filter that references another component's variable is evaluated where that variable is unbound: `id(null)` → null → no row passes. For relationship attrs, the same placement produces the runtime `Variable r not found` (`graph/src/runtime/eval.rs:292`).

### Relation to #2654

#2654 has the same root cause, **consecutive same-keyword clauses fused by `parse_pattern`** (`cypher.rs:1551-1556`), hit through `CREATE`. There, `CREATE (a) CREATE (b {x: id(a)})` fails because the fused CREATE's property expressions are validated before the first CREATE's aliases are defined.

This issue covers the `MATCH` side, which #2654 does not mention:

* It also affects the explicit comma form `MATCH p1, p2` in a single clause, so un-fusing the clauses alone would not fix it.
* Besides the `not defined` error, which only hits relationship aliases because of the node-then-relationship bind order, it has a **silent wrong-result** mode for node aliases. That comes from the planner's filter placement (step 3), and #2654 does not cover it.

A fix for #2654 that only stops fusing `CREATE` clauses would leave all of the above in place.

### Expected

Match C: an inline property map may reference any variable bound earlier in the same query, including other parts of the same pattern. The resulting predicate has to be placed where all its variables are bound: above the Cartesian Product (or as a hash-join key, as C does), not under the scan of one branch.

### Suggested fix

* **Binder:** define every node *and* relationship alias of the pattern before binding any inline `attrs`. `bind_graph` already defines node aliases before their attrs so self-references work, and relationships need the same treatment.
* **Planner:** in `plan_match`, collect the variables of each inline-attr filter (`collect_expr_variables`). If any of them belong to another component of the same pattern, push the filter to `bound_filters`, which is applied above the joined components, instead of wrapping the scan. The existing `ValueHashJoin` rewrite can then pick up the equality, as it does for the `WHERE` form.
* Consider not fusing consecutive `MATCH` clauses in `parse_pattern`. This is not required once the two points above hold.

### Found by

Divergence sweep against the C module, followed up with `GRAPH.EXPLAIN` on both engines.

issues.title: [Rust] cap_at_or_above_batch_size_is_ignored fails on macOS arm64: LLVM drops the `cap < BATCH_SIZE` guard in BatchedResultEmitter::with_binding
issues.body:
### Summary

`runtime::ops::batched_result_emitter::tests::cap_at_or_above_batch_size_is_ignored` fails on a clean `main` checkout on macOS arm64 (`left: 1025, right: 1024`). The Rust source is correct: LLVM miscompiles the guarded `match` in `BatchedResultEmitter::with_binding` and drops the `cap < BATCH_SIZE` guard, so the ceiling comes out as `cap` itself. Linux CI is green, so this only shows up in local runs on aarch64-apple-darwin.

The test has failed since it was added in 770449f99 (`perf: size a scan's first batch to the downstream LIMIT (#2757)`). The same test at 770449f99 fails the same way, and the test does not exist at its parent. No later commit touched the logic.

### Reproduction (`main` @ 2363723ac, clean worktree, rustc 1.98.1 / LLVM 22.1.8, aarch64-apple-darwin)

```
$ cargo test -p graph --lib batched_result_emitter
test runtime::ops::batched_result_emitter::tests::cap_at_or_above_batch_size_is_ignored ... FAILED
panicked at graph/src/runtime/ops/batched_result_emitter.rs:818:13:
assertion `left == right` failed          # cap = BATCH_SIZE + 1 = 1025
  left: 1025
 right: 1024
```

Results by opt level and toolchain for the same test:

| build | result |
|---|---|
| `opt-level=0` (`CARGO_PROFILE_DEV_OPT_LEVEL=0`) | pass |
| `opt-level=1` | fail, and it prints **`left: 1024, right: 1024`**, a miscompile tell |
| `opt-level=2` (the repo's `profile.dev`) / `3` | fail, `left: 1025` |
| `cargo +1.97.1` | fail |

Standalone repro, no FalkorDB code:

```rust
#[inline(never)]
fn f(cap: Option<usize>) -> usize {
    match cap { Some(cap) if cap < 1024 => cap.max(1), _ => 1024 }
}
fn main() { println!("{}", f(std::hint::black_box(Some(1025usize)))); }
```

| toolchain (LLVM) | `-C opt-level=2` prints |
|---|---|
| 1.85.0 (LLVM 19.1.7) | 1024 ✅ |
| 1.91.1 (LLVM 21.1.2) | **1025** ❌ |
| 1.97.1 / 1.98.1 stable (LLVM 22.1.8) | **1025** ❌ |
| nightly-2026-08-31 (LLVM 23.1.0) | **1025** ❌ |
| nightly 2026-09-07 (LLVM 23.1.1) | 1024 ✅ |

The IR emitted for `f` shows the guard turned into an unconditional `range` assumption on the `umax` operand, after which the compare is deleted:

```llvm
%_0.sroa.0.0.i = tail call range(i64 1, 1024) i64 @llvm.umax.i64(i64 range(i64 0, 1024) %1, i64 1)
%spec.select   = select i1 %2, i64 %_0.sroa.0.0.i, i64 1024
```

```asm
cmp  x1, #1
csinc x8, x1, xzr, hi     ; max(cap, 1)
tst  w0, #0x1             ; is Some?
mov  w9, #1024
csel x0, x8, x9, ne       ; no `cap < 1024` check left
```

### Mechanism

`graph/src/runtime/ops/batched_result_emitter.rs:557-560`:

```rust
let pack_ceiling = match record_cap {
    Some(cap) if cap < BATCH_SIZE => cap.max(1),
    _ => BATCH_SIZE,
};
```

This is an upstream LLVM bug, not a FalkorDB logic bug. It matters for us because the `pack_ceiling <= BATCH_SIZE` invariant depends on this guard. With the guard gone, a `Skip`+`Limit` budget of 1024 or more could size a batch past `BATCH_SIZE` in any binary built with an affected toolchain. On a live macOS release (LTO) build, `MATCH (n) WITH n LIMIT 3000`, `SKIP 10 LIMIT 3000`, `UNWIND range(1,5000) ... LIMIT 4000` and `RETURN n.v LIMIT 2000` all returned correct results, so I did not observe any user-visible wrong result.

### Expected

The test passes and `pack_ceiling` never exceeds `BATCH_SIZE`, whatever toolchain builds the module.

### Suggested fix

Write the clamp without the guarded arm. This form compiles correctly on the affected toolchain (standalone repro prints 1024 on 1.98.1 `-O2`):

```rust
let pack_ceiling = record_cap.map_or(BATCH_SIZE, |cap| cap.clamp(1, BATCH_SIZE));
```

Also add a `debug_assert!(self.pack_ceiling <= BATCH_SIZE)` where the ceiling is consumed, so a future miscompile or refactor fails loudly. Filing the standalone repro upstream (rust-lang/rust, `I-unsound` / `A-LLVM`) would be worthwhile if it is not already fixed there. Nightly 2026-09-07 no longer reproduces.

### Found by

Running `cargo test -p graph` on a clean `origin/main` worktree on macOS arm64 during the Lean-proof bug sweep. I bisected the test by building 770449f99 and its parent.

issues.title: fix(info): stop INFO reporting RediSearch's version as graph_version; Redis 8.10.2
issues.body:
Closes #2915

## 1. Stop `INFO` reporting RediSearch's version as `graph_version`

**Problem.** On the Rust engine, `INFO modules` showed RediSearch's info sections under the `graph_` prefix: `graph_version:8.6.1`, `graph_redis_version:0.0.0 - enterprise`, and RediSearch's settings such as `graph_query_timeout_ms:500`. The C engine shows none of these. Details are in #2915.

**Cause.** Redis keeps one INFO callback per module, and the last one registered wins.
- The `redis_module!` macro registers our callback (`macros.rs:438` at the pinned redismodule-rs) *before* it calls `graph_init`.
- `graph_init` then calls `RediSearch_Init` (`src/module_init.rs`), which registers RediSearch's callback on our module and replaces ours.
- C does the same two steps in the opposite order: `RediSearch_Init` at `module.c:191`, then `setupCrashHandlers` at `module.c:383`, which registers FalkorDB's own callback.

**Fix.**
- Register our callback again right after `RediSearch_Init`, matching C's order.
- It adds nothing to a normal `INFO`, the same as C's `InfoFunc` (`debug.c`).
- For a crash report it keeps redis-module's default trace info (`basic_info_command_handler`) and adds an `executing commands` section, with one `command` field per running query, as C does.
- The running-query registry is read with a new `telemetry::try_snapshot_running`, which skips any shard whose lock is held. The crashing thread may be the one holding it, and blocking there would hang the crash report.
- One difference from C: each line is `<graph> <query>`, where C writes `<command name> <query>`. The Rust registry doesn't store the command name, and the graph name is more useful in a crash report.

**`INFO modules`, before and after.**

Before: the 6.0.0 RC, `ghcr.io/falkordb/falkordb:rc-mg-d51b549e1…`, abridged.
```
# Modules
module:name=vectorset,ver=1,api=1,filters=0,usedby=[],using=[],options=[handle-io-errors|handle-repl-async-load]
module:name=graph,ver=60000,api=1,filters=0,usedby=[],using=[],options=[]

# graph_version
graph_version:8.6.1
graph_redis_version:0.0.0 - enterprise
graph_redis_enterprise_version:0.0.0-0

# graph_indexes
graph_number_of_indexes:0
...
# graph_runtime_configurations
graph_default_scorer:TFIDF
graph_query_timeout_ms:500
...
```

After: this PR's image, `ghcr.io/falkordb/falkordb:rc-pr-2921`. The output is identical on all four images (`falkordb` and `falkordb-server`, amd64 and arm64). Only the order of the two `module:` lines varies between them.
```
# Modules
module:name=vectorset,ver=1,api=1,filters=0,usedby=[],using=[],options=[handle-io-errors|handle-repl-async-load]
module:name=graph,ver=999999,api=1,filters=0,usedby=[],using=[],options=[]
```
This matches the C engine (`falkordb/falkordb-server:edge-c`), which also prints only the two `module:` lines. `ver=999999` is `main`'s development version (`Cargo.toml` `99.99.99`); the `6.0` backport reports `60000`.

## 2. Redis 8.10.1 → 8.10.2

`build/Dockerfile`, `build/runtime/Dockerfile`, `Dockerfile.asan` and `Dockerfile.coverage`. [8.10.2](https://github.com/redis/redis/releases/tag/8.10.2) is a security release:
- #15673: MULTI/EXEC could use keys whose ACL permissions were revoked before EXEC.
- #15722: the cluster bus port has no authentication without TLS, so the node now warns about it at startup.
- Crash fixes in bundled modules. Of those, only Vector Sets ships in our images.

`build/Dockerfile` is on `check-files`' list, so this PR also rebuilds the toolchain image, and CI runs on 8.10.2.

## Verification
Built and run in `ghcr.io/falkordb/falkordb-build:latest`. That image still has Redis 8.10.1, so these results are for the INFO fix; CI covers 8.10.2.
- New flow test `test_commands_registration.py::test_info_has_no_redisearch_sections`: asserts `graph` is still loaded, `INFO everything` has no `graph_*` fields, and `INFO graph` is empty.
  - With the fix: **pass**, as do the file's other two tests.
  - With the re-registration line removed: **fail**, showing exactly `{'graph_version': '8.6.1', 'graph_redis_version': '0.0.0 - enterprise', …}`. So the test catches the bug it is written for.
- `cargo fmt --check` passes. `cargo clippy --all-targets` shows no new warnings: its five warnings are all already on `main`, in files this PR doesn't change.
- **This PR's CI images** (`rc-pr-2921`, all four images):
  - Redis `8.10.2` (`sha=498ecd0d`, which matches the upstream tag).
  - `INFO everything` has 0 `graph_*` fields and `INFO graph` is empty.
  - Graph queries work, and RediSearch still works: a fulltext index query returns the node, and a vector KNN query returns the nearest node.
  - The full image's browser returns HTTP 200.
- **Not tested:** the crash-report path. Exercising it means crashing a server and reading its log.

Once this merges it goes to `6.0` through the merge queue, for 6.0.1.

issues.title: fix: start a decoded IdList's run after its last segment
issues.body:
Closes #2919

## Problem

`IdList::from_segments`, which `read_ids` uses to build a decoded list, set `run.start = segments.len() - 1`. That put the last decoded segment inside the builder's run, whatever shape it had. A later `push` that collapsed the run then folded that segment into the bitmap:

- A decoded descending tail `[10, 9, 8]`, followed by ascending gapped pushes, came back as `8, 9, 10, 20, 22, …`. The ids were reordered, so rows would pair with the wrong entities (the same class of bug as #2842).
- A decoded `Repeat` tail `[7, 7]` tripped the `assert!` in `maybe_collapse_run`: `a run under consideration holds only ranges, found Repeat { id: 7, count: 2 }`.

This is latent: no production path pushes onto a decoded list today. The doc comment said the only consequence was a missed collapse, which was wrong.

## Fix

`run.start = segments.len()`. The run now begins after every decoded segment, which is the state `maybe_collapse_run` leaves after a collapse (`restart(start + 1)`). The hot paths can still extend the last decoded segment in place, but no collapse can fold a decoded segment in. Encoding and decoding are unchanged, because the segments are still adopted and written verbatim. The doc comment now describes this behaviour and says why the old placement was wrong.

## Tests

New module `effects::v3::id_list::pushing_onto_a_decoded_list`. Each test decodes a list, pushes more ids, and asserts the ids in push order, both in memory and after another encode/decode:

- `a_descending_tail_is_not_reversed_by_a_later_collapse` and `a_repeat_tail_is_not_folded_into_a_later_collapse`: the two cases from the issue.
- `every_tail_shape_survives_being_extended`: every tail shape the wire can end on (lone id, ascending and descending range, repeat, ascending and descending bitmap) crossed with 7 push shapes.
- `random_sequences_split_anywhere_survive`: 2,000 seeded phase-built sequences (consecutive up and down, repeats, gapped walks both ways, jumps), each split at a random point.

**Before** (old `from_segments`): all four fail. Examples:
- `left: [8, 9, 10, 20, …]` for the descending case.
- The collapse assert for the `Repeat` case.
- `[7, 6, 5] + [1000, 1002, …]` → `[5, 6, 7, 1000, …]` in the shape sweep.

**After:** all pass. The Lean repros in `graph/tests/lean_id_list.rs` (not part of this PR) also go from 2 failing to 8/8 passing.

Commands run:
- `cargo fmt --all -- --check`: clean.
- `CXX=clang++ cargo clippy --all-targets`: no warnings in touched code.
- `cargo test --release -p graph`: 426 passed, 0 failed.

Performance: `from_segments` does the same constant work as before, and the encode/decode paths are unchanged, so I did not run a benchmark.

Found by the Lean 4 model of `IdList` (`proofs/id_list`: `decoded_then_pushed_reorders`, `decoded_then_pushed_asserts`).

issues.title: [Rust] IdList::from_segments: pushing onto a decoded list reorders ids or trips the collapse assert
issues.body:
### Summary

`IdList::from_segments`, the constructor `read_ids` uses for a decoded list, starts the builder's run *at the last decoded segment*. That segment can be anything the wire held, but a run may only contain ranges read in the run's direction. So calling `push` (which is `pub`) on a decoded list can do either of two things:

* **Silently reorder the ids.** The decoded tail `[10, 9, 8]` is followed by ascending gapped pushes until the run collapses. The collapse folds the descending range into an *ascending* bitmap, so the list reads `8, 9, 10, 20, 22, …`. An `IdList` is positional (row *k* belongs to the *k*-th id), so rows would pair with the wrong entities. This is the same class of bug as #2842.
* **Panic.** A decoded tail `[7, 7]` (a `Repeat`) followed by the same pushes trips the collapse's real `assert!` at `id_list.rs:1051`.

This is latent: no production path pushes onto a decoded list today (emit builds fresh lists, and apply only iterates). But the doc comment claims the only consequence is that "a later push would not collapse across the boundary", which is false.

### Reproduction (`main` @ 2363723ac, release)

```
cargo test --release -p graph --test lean_id_list push_after_decode -- --nocapture
```
```
push_after_decode_reorders_a_descending_tail:
  expected [10, 9, 8, 20, 22, 24]
  got      [8, 9, 10, 20, 22, 24]
push_after_decode_of_a_repeat_hits_the_collapse_assert:
  panicked at graph/src/effects/v3/id_list.rs:1051:13: a run under consideration holds only
  ranges, found Repeat { id: 7, count: 2 } — whichever `restart` admitted it is one index too low
```

### Mechanism

`from_segments` (`graph/src/effects/v3/id_list.rs:1176`) sets `run.start = segments.len() - 1` with a fresh tally and `desc = None`, whatever that last segment is. `maybe_collapse_run` then folds `segments[run.start..]` into one bitmap in `run.desc` order, and asserts that every segment in the run is a range. Everywhere else, the builder keeps a non-range segment out of the run: after a collapse it calls `restart(start + 1)`, and after a `Repeat` it calls `restart(len)`.

### Expected

A decoded list, extended by pushes, iterates to the decoded ids followed by the pushed ids, in order, and never panics. This holds for any list built by pushes alone (Lean `push_ok`).

C: not applicable (a Rust-internal builder invariant).

### Suggested fix

Set `run.start = segments.len()` in `from_segments`, so the run begins after every decoded segment. That is the state `maybe_collapse_run` leaves after a collapse. The last decoded segment can still be extended in place by the hot paths, but no collapse can fold it in. Fix the doc comment to match.

### Found by

Lean 4 model of `IdList` (`proofs/id_list`): `decoded_then_pushed_reorders` and `decoded_then_pushed_asserts` show that `from_segments` does not establish the push invariant `Inv`. Rust repro: `graph/tests/lean_id_list.rs::{push_after_decode_reorders_a_descending_tail, push_after_decode_of_a_repeat_hits_the_collapse_assert}`.

issues.title: fix: see edge/path reads outside the traverse's ancestors (CALL {}, OPTIONAL, CREATE, UNWIND, ...)
issues.body:
Closes #2896

## Problem

Four optimizer passes (`reduce_expand_into`, `reduce_bound_edge`, `reduce_var_len_path`, `fuse_anonymous_traverse`) decide "is this edge / path / intermediate variable read?" by walking only the traverse's **ancestors**. A variable read from a sibling branch of a binary operator never counted: the body of `CALL {}`, the right side of an `OPTIONAL MATCH` or pattern-predicate `Apply`, a pattern comprehension sub-plan, a `FOREACH` body. On top of that, `ir_references_variable` ended in `_ => false`, so `CREATE`/`MERGE` pattern properties, the `UNWIND` list (it checked the bound `var` instead), the `FOREACH` list, procedure args, `LOAD CSV`, `Aggregate.projections`, index/id-seek lookups and var-len edge filters were never inspected.

When the answer was wrongly "unread", parallel edges between one `(src, dst)` pair collapsed to one row, the edge stayed unbound, or the var-len path was not built. On a graph with 2 parallel `:R` edges:

- `MATCH (a:A)-[r:R]->(b) CALL { WITH r CREATE (:Q) }` created 1 node (C: 2)
- `... CALL { WITH r RETURN 1 AS one } RETURN count(*)` returned 1 (C: 2)
- `... CALL { WITH r DELETE r }` deleted 1 edge (expected 2; C also deletes 1)
- `... CREATE (:Q {w: id(r)})`, `MERGE (:Q {w: id(r)})`, `UNWIND [r] ...`, `OPTIONAL MATCH ... WHERE ... id(r)` all ran once
- `MATCH (a:A)-[p:R*1..2]->(b) UNWIND p AS x ...` / `CREATE (:Q {n: length(p)})` failed with `Variable p not found`; `CALL { WITH p RETURN length(p) AS s }` returned one `NULL` row

The full table is in the issue.

## Fix

- New `variable_read_outside(plan, idx, var_id, scope_id)` in `reduce_expand_into.rs`. It checks every operator outside the traverse's own subtree, meaning each ancestor plus all of that ancestor's other branches. A row produced at `idx` can only be read by those operators. Nodes that can't actually see the row, such as the other side of a `CartesianProduct`, can only mention the variable by binding it themselves, so over-counting them is conservative, never wrong.
- All four passes use this one helper instead of their own copies of the ancestor walk.
- `ir_references_variable` is now an exhaustive `match` over `IR`, with no `_ =>` arm. Every variant states which of its fields are reads. `CREATE`/`MERGE` count only their inline properties, not their own aliases, so a `MERGE`'s edge keeps today's (C-matching) one-row-per-pair behaviour.

This is plan-time only: plans are cached, and nothing changes in the runtime operators. The unread-edge optimizations still apply: `MATCH (a)-[r]->(b) RETURN count(*)` and `CALL { WITH a ... }` (r not imported) still collapse, as in C.

## Tests

- `tests/test_e2e.py`: `test_parallel_edges_read_outside_traverse_ancestors` (14 read shapes), `test_parallel_edges_written_outside_traverse_ancestors` (6 write shapes), `test_parallel_edges_deleted_inside_call_subquery`. **Before:** all 21 fail on origin/main (e.g. `assert [[1]] == [[2]]`). **After:** 21 passed.
- Unit tests: `reduce_expand_into::tests::{unread_edge_collapses, edge_read_outside_the_ancestors_is_emitted}`, `reduce_bound_edge::tests::edge_read_inside_a_call_subquery_is_bound`, `reduce_var_len_path::tests::path_read_outside_the_ancestors_is_kept`. **Before:** the 3 "read" tests fail against the origin/main pass code. **After:** all optimizer tests pass (15/15).
- Every query from the issue now gives C's result. The one exception is `CALL { WITH r DELETE r }`, where Rust now deletes both edges and C deletes only one.
- `cargo fmt --all -- --check`: clean. `CXX=clang++ cargo clippy --all-targets`: no warnings in touched files.
- `cargo test -p graph`: 425 passed, 1 failed. The failure is `batched_result_emitter::tests::cap_at_or_above_batch_size_is_ignored`, which is pre-existing: it fails identically with this change reverted.
- `RELEASE=1 pytest tests/test_e2e.py tests/test_functions.py`: 146 passed. The TCK (`TCK_DONE=tck_done.txt`) passed.
- Flow tests (`flow_tests_done.txt`, release): every non-cluster test passed (1483 + 84). The cluster-env classes (`test_udf_cluster`, `test_undo_log`) could not start locally because of the pinned port. They don't touch the planner.
