pulls.title: build(docker): run redis-server as the falkordb user
pulls.body: Closes #3180 Runs `redis-server` in the Docker image as the unprivileged `falkordb` user instead of root, following the official redis image's entrypoint. ### `build/runtime/run.sh` The container starts as root, as before. When it is root, has `CAP_SETUID` and `CAP_SETGID`, and `SKIP_DROP_PRIVS` is unset, `run.sh`: 1. hands the data directory to `falkordb` (`chown` of whatever it does not already own), but only when the directory holds nothing except `*.rdb`, `nodes*.conf` and `appendonlydir`, and prints a notice otherwise; 2. after `gen-certs.sh` (with `TLS=1`), hands `falkordb` the certificate and key files that script generates, and only those; 3. sets `umask 0077` when the umask is the default `0022`; 4. execs `redis-server` through `gosu falkordb`, so `redis-server` stays PID 1. `SKIP_FIX_PERMS=1` skips steps 1 and 2. Started with `--user`, without those capabilities, or with `SKIP_DROP_PRIVS=1`, it runs `redis-server` as the current user. The variable names and the data-directory check follow the official image; `nodes*.conf` is added for cluster nodes. The browser still starts first and drops to `nextjs` through its own entrypoint. ### `build/runtime/Dockerfile` - creates `falkordb` (uid/gid 999) in place of the `redis` account at the same ids; - installs `gosu` in the `server` stage (the `full` stage installed it for the browser; it now inherits it); - owns `/var/lib/falkordb/data` and `/var/lib/falkordb/tls` as `root:falkordb`, mode 0775, so `falkordb` writes through the group and root remains the owner. ### CI images and test harness - `Dockerfile.asan` and `Dockerfile.coverage` set `SKIP_DROP_PRIVS=1`; the coverage image's account is renamed to `falkordb` to match. - `tests/flow/common.py` sets mode 0777 on the `--logfile` directory and on `mountable_mkdtemp()` directories it creates for spawned containers, so `redis-server` can use them as `falkordb`. --- ## Summary by cubic Runs redis-server in the Docker image as the unprivileged `falkordb` user (uid/gid 999) instead of root, matching the official redis image's entrypoint. Closes #3180. The container still starts as root: run.sh hands the data directory and the TLS files gen-certs.sh generates to `falkordb`, then execs redis-server through gosu so it stays PID 1. It stays root when started with `--user`, without CAP_SETUID/CAP_SETGID, or with `SKIP_DROP_PRIVS=1`; `SKIP_FIX_PERMS=1` skips the ownership steps. The data directory is re-owned only when it holds nothing but `*.rdb`, `nodes*.conf` and `appendonlydir`; anything else prints a notice and is left alone. If any handover chown fails, redis-server also stays root. New files are created with `umask 0077`. The `redis` account at uid/gid 999 is now `falkordb`; `gosu` moves to the server stage, and the data and TLS directories are `root:falkordb` mode 0775. The ASAN and coverage images set `SKIP_DROP_PRIVS=1` and the coverage account is renamed to match. The flow-test harness makes its log and temp directories writable by `falkordb`. Written for commit fc239e8cde959463a5c40a81f9884927ed1a29ab. Summary will update on new commits. ## Summary by CodeRabbit * **Runtime** * Runtime containers now use a dedicated service account instead of the Redis account. * When supported, the server drops root privileges before starting and adjusts permissions for recognized data and TLS files. If the data directory contains unrecognized files or ownership cannot be changed, Redis continues running as root. * Permission changes can be skipped. Runtime variants without the required account or tools continue to run without privilege dropping. * Runtime data and TLS directories have updated ownership and access permissions. * **Bug Fixes** * CI-created temporary and log directories now have permissions that allow mounted workflows to access them.

pulls.title: ci: port master's Trivy image scan; drop util-linux from the runtime image
pulls.body:
Closes #3178

Ports master's Trivy image gate (`security-scan` in `build.yml`) to the Rust pipeline, which had no image scan, and removes `util-linux` from the runtime image, which clears 32 of the 36 unfixed HIGH Debian findings in `:edge`.

### What it does

New `security-scan` job in `_ci-pipeline.yml`, after `build-rc-image`, image vehicle only:

- scans `ghcr.io/falkordb/falkordb:rc-<ci_key>-{x64,arm64v8}` (`full` is `FROM server`, so it covers both repos);
- fails on HIGH/CRITICAL with a fixed version (`ignore-unfixed`), same rule as master;
- uploads the full JSON report as `trivy-report-<arch>` (30 days);
- lists blocking findings in the run summary. Master posts a PR comment instead, which needs `pull-requests: write` and has nowhere to go in the merge queue.

Pins match master: trivy-action `ed142fd…` (verified as upstream `v0.36.0`), Trivy `v0.69.2`. A failure fails `ci-pipeline`, which `ci-gate` already requires.

The queue scans `rc-mg-<sha>`, which is what `:edge` and releases retag, so the gate covers what ships. Fork PRs build no image and skip the job; their queue entry is scanned.

### Trivy gate: verified locally (Trivy v0.69.2, same flags)

| Image | Result |
|---|---|
| `falkordb/falkordb:edge` (built 2026-10-07), amd64 + arm64 | passes: 0 blocking (36 HIGH Debian, none fixable) |
| `falkordb/falkordb:v4.0.7` | fails: 1,433 blocking (run with `--exit-code 3` to rule out an error exit) |
| `ghcr.io/falkordb/falkordb:rc-pr-2908-{x64,arm64v8}`, no `--image-src` | both arches resolve from the registry; 10 blocking (image built 2026-09-24) |

The summary's `jq` filter selects the same 1,433 findings as the gate on `v4.0.7`. `actionlint` is clean on the changed file. This PR's own CI is the first real run of the job.

### Runtime image: drop util-linux, mount, bsdutils

`build/runtime/Dockerfile` (server stage) now force-purges `util-linux`, `mount`, `bsdutils` and their libraries (`libmount1`, `libblkid1`, `libuuid1`, `libsmartcols1`, `liblastlog2-2`), next to the existing ncurses/perl/login/passwd trim.

`:edge` has 36 HIGH Debian findings, all `affected` (Debian has no fixed package yet). They are 7 CVEs counted once per binary package, and 4 util-linux CVEs across those 8 packages make up 32 of them: privilege escalation through the setuid `mount`/`umount`/`su` and `nsenter`. Nothing in the image uses them. `run.sh`, `gen-certs.sh` and the browser's `docker-entrypoint.sh` call none of their commands, and `apt-cache rdepends --installed` finds no other installed package that depends on the eight.

This purge has no `|| true`. If a dependent ever appears, the build fails instead of silently keeping the packages, which the gate would not flag because it ignores unfixed findings.

Verified on arm64 by building the real Dockerfile's `full` target with only `builder` and `redis-builder` swapped for `:edge`'s binaries (`--build-context`):

| Check | `:edge` | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| Image build, incl. server-stage sanity RUN and `full` stage's `apt-get install` after the purge | — | passes |
| `GRAPH.QUERY` (create + aggregate) | ok | identical result |
| Browser on :3000 | 200 | 200 |
| `TLS=1` (`gen-certs.sh`, query over TLS) | — | ok |
| `apt-get install curl` in a derived image, `dpkg --audit` | — | ok, clean |
| setuid binaries in the image | `mount`, `umount`, `su` | none |
| Trivy Debian HIGH / MEDIUM / LOW | 36 / 58 / 53 | 4 / 50 / 45 |
| Trivy gate | pass | pass |

The 4 HIGH left are systemd-homed (`libsystemd0`, `libudev1`), `libacl1` and `libtinfo6`; neither `redis-server` nor `falkordb.so` links any of them. amd64 is exercised by this PR's own CI.

Behaviour change: `su`, `mount` and `nsenter` are gone from the image. Anything that `docker exec`s into a container and uses them breaks; `USER` in a derived Dockerfile is unaffected, and the `full` image keeps `gosu`.

### Known limits

- `redis-server` still runs as root in the image (`run.sh` never drops to the `redis` user). Out of scope here; it changes data-volume ownership.
- Trivy sees Debian packages and the browser's `node_modules`, not the crates in `libfalkordb.so` or the from-source `redis-server`.
- Browser CVEs can block engine PRs (3 of the 10 above were `next`, `sharp`, `source-map-js`). Same as master.

pulls.title: proofs: Lean 4 proofs of the Rust engine, and a skill for working with them
pulls.body: Closes #3171 ## Problem The Lean 4 models and proofs of the Rust engine lived outside version control. They found the bugs fixed by many recent PRs, but nobody else could build, extend or review them. They also drifted whenever main moved, unless someone re-targeted them by hand. ## What this adds - **`proofs/`**: 35 standalone Lake projects, one per engine area. Lean 4.35, core only, no Mathlib; each project pins its toolchain in `lean-toolchain`. - Each project's root `.lean` header is its report: a table mapping each Lean definition to the Rust `file:line` it models, then the theorems, the bugs found and the modelling gaps. - Review projects (`pr_review/`) model a PR's merged code while it is under review; once the PR merges, their theorems are folded into the owning projects and the review project is deleted (as done for #2845 and #2917). - `aeneas_pilot/` is the Aeneas/Charon extraction pilot: `narrow_int` is proven against extracted code. Its generated output (`.llbc`, `full/`) is git-ignored and regenerated by `extract.sh`. - **`proofs/lean_ci.sh`**: runs `lake build` for every project, then fails on any `sorry`, `admit`, `native_decide`, or an `axiom` without a `-- AXIOM-OK:` justification. Comments are stripped before the scan. - **`proofs/coverage.sh`**: reads every project's `COVERAGE.tsv` (one row per Rust function: PROVEN / CONDITIONAL / AXIOMATISED / MODELLED / NOT COVERED; CONDITIONAL means the proof rests on an undischarged hypothesis about other Rust code), checks the rows against the functions actually in `graph/src` and `src`, and prints coverage per file and in total. Test and bench code is counted separately. It reads the Rust from `$COVERAGE_RUST_ROOT`, or from this checkout if that is unset. - **`proofs/FINDINGS.md`**: the bug ledger. Each entry has the repro, the Rust vs C output, the Lean theorem and the issue or PR that fixed it, plus notes recording which commits fixed what. - **`.claude/skills/proofs/`** (`SKILL.md` + `REFERENCE.md`): how to build and check the proofs, re-target them after main moves, prove a new or changed function, confirm a bug a model finds, and review a PR against the proofs. It also lists the testing hazards hit along the way. ## Current state The proofs cite `origin/main` at cab3cf192. | | functions | |---|---:| | PROVEN | 2565 of the 2602 non-FFI, non-test functions in `graph/src` + `src` (98.6%) | | CONDITIONAL (proven given a stated hypothesis about other Rust code) | 36 | | AXIOMATISED (FFI: GraphBLAS, LAGraph, RediSearch, Redis module API, QuickJS, libc) | 1292 | | MODELLED / NOT COVERED / unlisted | 0 | The headline theorems depend only on `propext`, `Quot.sound` and `Classical.choice`. ## Limits - The models are hand-written from the Rust, not extracted from it, so they can drift as the code changes. The skill's re-target workflow is how they stay in sync. - f64 arithmetic is abstract (a float class with only the laws used), and concurrency is modelled as sequentially consistent. ## Not included - The Rust repro tests used while finding bugs (`graph/tests/lean_*.rs`). Many of them assert the correct behaviour and fail until the corresponding fix lands, so they would turn `cargo test` red. Every repro is recorded in `FINDINGS.md`. - A CI job running `proofs/lean_ci.sh`. That is a follow-up, and needs elan in the CI image. ## Tests - `bash proofs/lean_ci.sh` → 36 projects, 0 failing. - `bash proofs/coverage.sh` → 2565/2602 non-FFI, non-test functions PROVEN and 36 CONDITIONAL (1 trait declaration NOT COVERED), 0 unlisted, 0 unmatched. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) --- ## Summary by cubic Brings the Lean 4 proofs of the Rust engine into version control with tooling to build, check, and extend them, re-targeted to `origin/main` cab3cf192. The proofs previously lived outside the repo, so only their author could build or review them, and they drifted whenever main moved. - `proofs/` holds 37 standalone Lake projects (Lean v4.35.0, core only), one per engine area; each project header documents the Lean↔Rust `file:line` mapping. The `pr2845_review` and `pr2917_review` review projects are retired with their theorems folded into their owners (binder, optimizer_rewrites, columnar, ops_aggregate). Shared foundations live in `proofs/core` (`FalkorCore`: Value, float model F, i64, orderings) and are imported via Lake path dependencies instead of copies. The `aeneas_pilot` full Charon/Aeneas extraction is git-ignored and regenerated by `extract.sh`; only `narrow_int` is proven against extracted code. - 2565 of the 2602 non-FFI, non-test functions in `graph/src` and `src` are PROVEN; 36 are CONDITIONAL on a named hypothesis; 1 is NOT COVERED (a trait declaration); FFI boundaries are axiomatised (1291 functions). - `proofs/lean_ci.sh` builds all projects and fails on `sorry`, `admit`, `native_decide`, or an unjustified axiom; `proofs/coverage.sh` cross-checks `COVERAGE.tsv` rows against the actual Rust functions. A `grind` pilot kept the two replacements that are not slower than the original tactic proofs (−4 lines, statements and axioms unchanged); the rest were reverted. - `proofs/FINDINGS.md` is the bug ledger (repro, Rust vs C output, Lean theorem, fixing PR); `.claude/skills/proofs/` documents building, re-targeting after main moves, proving new functions, confirming bugs, and reviewing PRs. Re-targeting to cab3cf192 modelled #2897 (BRANCH_MAX ≥ 4), #3285 (readable DOC_BYTES widths) and #3336 (UDF conversion nesting cap, cyclic values included). Re-targeting to b080a44c1 added `proofs/native_index` for #2350/#3307 (order-preserving key encoding, index scan ≡ label scan + filter, batched apply ≡ sequential, snapshot isolation); 13 of its rows are CONDITIONAL on CowBTree's tree invariant, which `remove_batch` still breaks (PR #3283). The `pr2917_review` model caught `GroupKey::eq` and `Value::hash` disagreeing on `VecF32`/`Point` float components; with #2912/#2917 merged, those hypotheses are now proven on main. **Limits and follow-ups** - Models are hand-written, not extracted, except the Aeneas pilot proving `narrow_int` against Aeneas-extracted code; f64 arithmetic is abstract and concurrency is modelled as sequentially consistent. - The Rust repro tests are not committed because they assert correct behaviour and fail until the fix lands; a CI job for `lean_ci.sh` is a follow-up. Closes #3171. Written for commit c6bf376353b26504d3aa7ccf88a681f4e2b8a006. Summary will update on new commits.

pulls.title: build(native-deps): include <string> in VecSim's vec_utils.cpp for libc++ 23
pulls.body: Closes #3169. ## Why On macOS with Homebrew LLVM 23, RediSearch fails to build. VectorSimilarity's `vec_utils.cpp` uses `std::string` without including ``, and libc++ 23 no longer provides it through `` (details in #3169). VectorSimilarity master has the same code, so bumping the submodule doesn't help. ## What - **`native-deps/src/recipes/redisearch.rs`:** a new `include_string_in_vec_utils` step, next to `relax_vecsim_warnings`, adds `#include ` after `#include ` while the build runs. `SourceGuard` puts the file back afterwards, as it already does for the `-Werror` edit. - If the file already includes ``, the step does nothing, so it stops having any effect once upstream fixes the file. - If `#include ` is no longer there, the build fails, so an upstream rewrite gets looked at rather than built unfixed. - **Three unit tests:** - the include is added once and removed when the guard is dropped; - a file that already includes `` is left alone; - a missing anchor fails without writing the file. - **`recipes/mod.rs`:** the `SourceGuard` doc comment now lists this edit. The recipe hash covers `src/recipes/*.rs`, so this gives all three deps new cache keys. Every machine rebuilds GraphBLAS, LAGraph and RediSearch once. ## Testing - **Unit tests:** `cargo test --manifest-path native-deps/Cargo.toml` passes all 33. When the insert is replaced by writing the text back unchanged, `vec_utils_gains_string_include_until_the_build_ends` fails. - **Lint:** `cargo fmt --all -- --check` and `CXX=clang++ cargo clippy --all-targets` on `native-deps` are clean. - **macOS build with Homebrew clang 23.1.2** (`CC`/`CXX` set): - `cargo build` builds all three deps from unmodified submodules, and RediSearch is published under a regular key, not a `local-` one. - Afterwards, `git -C deps/RediSearch diff HEAD --submodule=diff` is empty. - The module loads in `redis-server`, and a vector KNN query and a fulltext query return the expected rows. - **Linux:** not run locally. CI already builds with clang-23 (#3163), and this edit only adds an include. --- ## Summary by cubic Fixes RediSearch failing to build on macOS with Homebrew LLVM 23: VectorSimilarity's `vec_utils.cpp` uses `std::string` without including ``, which libc++ 23 no longer pulls in through `` (closes #3169). - Adds `#include ` to `vec_utils.cpp` for the length of the build, alongside the existing `-Werror` edit; SourceGuard restores the file afterward. - The edit is a no-op once upstream includes `` itself, and fails the build if the `#include ` anchor moves. - The recipe hash change gives all three native deps new cache keys, so every machine rebuilds GraphBLAS, LAGraph, and RediSearch once. - Adds three unit tests covering the insert, the already-fixed file, and the missing anchor. Written for commit e5f5b46358e399d21136bf3e18abc79bc2096305. Summary will update on new commits. ## Summary by CodeRabbit * **Bug Fixes** * Improved RediSearch build reliability in Docker contexts where the source submodule’s Git metadata is unavailable. * Builds now handle a missing standard-library include automatically, while leaving sources unchanged when the include is already present. * Source changes made during the build are restored afterward, and builds report an error if the expected source structure is missing.

pulls.title: fix(restore): return an error for malformed GRAPH.RESTORE payloads
pulls.body: Closes #3168 ## What `GRAPH.RESTORE` crashes the server when the payload is empty or cut short. This PR makes it return an error instead. ## Why it happens `GRAPH.RESTORE` decodes with `BufferedReader::from_slice`, which sets `rdb` to null. When the reader runs out of bytes, `ensure_available` calls `load_chunk`, and that calls `raw::load_string_buffer(self.rdb)` with the null pointer. Redis dereferences it. The `TYPE_BLOB` branch in `read_buffer` already checks for a null handle, `load_chunk` didn't. Simplest way to hit it: ``` GRAPH.RESTORE x "" ``` While I was in there I also noticed the header, schema and payload directory decoders do `Vec::with_capacity(count as usize)` with counts read from the payload. A small payload with a huge count makes the process abort on the allocation. `GRAPH.BULK` already caps this kind of thing, so I did the same here. ## Changes - `load_chunk` returns an error if there is no IO handle - added `decode_capacity()` and used it for the pre-allocations in the header, schema and payload directory decoding - new flow test `tests/flow/test_graph_restore.py` (empty payload, truncated payload, wrong tag, huge counts), added to `flow_tests_done.txt` The RDB load path is not affected by the first change since it always has a real handle. ## Testing I don't have the full build set up locally (GraphBLAS / RediSearch), so I haven't run the flow tests myself and I'm relying on CI for that. Happy to fix anything it turns up. --- ## Summary by cubic `GRAPH.RESTORE` no longer crashes the server on empty, truncated, or malformed payloads; it returns an error instead. It also caps buffer pre-allocation sizes derived from payload counts to prevent process aborts from huge values. - `load_chunk` returns an error when there's no Redis IO handle instead of dereferencing null. - Count-based pre-allocations in header, schema, payload-directory, per-entity attributes, and `Value` arrays are capped at 1024 elements; vector dimensions are checked against buffer length. - Added flow tests for empty, truncated, wrong-tag, and oversized-count payloads, plus unit tests for the value and attribute decoders. Written for commit a1598bf77c98416f5f81f1b36db70f3c68b9ab2e. Summary will update on new commits. ## Summary by CodeRabbit * **Bug Fixes** * Invalid or incomplete graph restore payloads are rejected with an error, while the server remains responsive and does not create a restored graph. * Decoding limits initial memory allocation for payload-specified counts, helping avoid excessive allocations when processing malformed data.

pulls.title: ci: move the toolchain to LLVM 23
pulls.body: Fixes #3162. ## Why Rust 1.99 is built on LLVM 23 and writes raw coverage profiles in format v11. CI merges them with `llvm-profdata-22`, which only reads v10, so every coverage job fails with `raw profile version mismatch ... no profile can be merged` (details in #3162). ## What - **Toolchain image** (`build/Dockerfile`): `CLANG_MAJOR=22` → `23`. - **`build/libomp.sh`**: LLVM 23 removed OpenMP's standalone CMake build (`The legacy standalone build mode has been removed`), so the script now builds through `runtimes/` with `-DLLVM_ENABLE_RUNTIMES=openmp`. It sets `LLVM_ENABLE_PER_TARGET_RUNTIME_DIR=OFF` so `libomp.a` stays in `${PREFIX}/lib`, and the sparse checkout adds `llvm/cmake`, `llvm/utils` and `third-party`. `runtimes/` also works for earlier majors. - **Workflows**: `llvm-profdata-23` / `llvm-cov-23` in `_flow-artifact.yml`, `_flow-flavour.yml`, `rust-pr.yml` and `rust-push.yml`; `clang++-23` for clippy, fuzz, and the build/release artifact matrices. - **Runtime images**: `build/runtime/Dockerfile`, `Dockerfile.asan` (clang, objdump/objcopy, `libLLVM.so.23.1`, symbolizer path) and `Dockerfile.coverage`. - **`graph/build.rs`**: adds the `/usr/lib/llvm-23/lib` search path and `-23` tool names; 22/21/20 stay as fallbacks for local builds. - **Devcontainer and docs**: `.devcontainer/`, `README.md`. Because `build/Dockerfile` and `build/libomp.sh` change, this PR builds its own `falkordb-build:pr-` toolchain image and all jobs run in it. `:latest` gets the image on merge through the usual promotion. macOS needs no change: it uses unpinned Homebrew `llvm`. The GraphBLAS PreJIT kernels contain no compiler-version strings, so they don't need regenerating. ## Verified locally - `build/Dockerfile` builds (linux/arm64, Docker Desktop) with LLVM 23.1.2. libomp builds from `llvmorg-23.1.2` with the new script (the unchanged script fails with the standalone-mode error), and GraphBLAS, LAGraph and RediSearch build with clang-23. - The image has `/opt/libomp/lib/libomp.a`, `/usr/lib/llvm-23/lib/libLLVM.so.23.1`, `/usr/lib/llvm-23/bin/llvm-symbolizer` and `llvm-profdata-23` / `llvm-cov-23`. Its `rustc` is 1.99.0 on LLVM 23.1.1, the same major as the profile tools. - The full coverage flow inside the image (instrumented build, profile merge, lcov export) was still running when this PR was opened. CI runs the same flow on amd64. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) --- ## Summary by cubic Moves the toolchain to LLVM 23 so coverage jobs stop failing. Rust 1.99 is built on LLVM 23 and writes raw coverage profiles in format v11, which `llvm-profdata-22` can't merge, so every coverage job failed with "raw profile version mismatch." - Updates every LLVM 22 reference to 23: toolchain and runtime images, workflows, devcontainer, `graph/build.rs` search paths, and docs. - Reworks `build/libomp.sh` to build through `runtimes/` with `-DLLVM_ENABLE_RUNTIMES=openmp`, since LLVM 23 removed OpenMP's standalone CMake build; `libomp.a` still lands in `${PREFIX}/lib`. - This PR runs all jobs on its own `falkordb-build:pr-` toolchain image; `:latest` is rebuilt on merge. - macOS is unaffected (unpinned Homebrew LLVM), and GraphBLAS PreJIT kernels don't need regenerating. Written for commit 974a88bc2988113d2f2e315a1a03514b34a30038. Summary will update on new commits. ## Summary by CodeRabbit * **Chores** * Updated Linux build and development toolchains to LLVM/Clang 23, including compiler and OpenMP versions. * Updated coverage collection tools to LLVM 23 across build, test, and release workflows. * Updated the AddressSanitizer build to use LLVM 23 and its matching symbolizer. * **Documentation** * Updated Linux toolchain prerequisites and build instructions to reference Clang 23.

pulls.title: fix(rdb): save virtual keys as graphmeta so C keeps graphs in GRAPH.LIST
pulls.body: Fixes the `GRAPH.LIST` part of #3160. ## Problem When a graph is large enough to be saved across several RDB keys (more than `VKEY_MAX_ENTITY_COUNT` entities, 100k by default), Rust saved the extra "virtual" keys with the `graphdata` type. C uses `graphmeta` for these keys. When C 4.20.x loads such an RDB: 1. It loads each `graphdata` virtual key as a graph and adds the graph to its list of graphs. 2. When loading ends, it deletes the virtual keys. 3. Deleting a `graphdata` key runs `_GraphContextType_Free`, which calls `Globals_RemoveGraph(gc)`. That removes the shared graph from the list `GRAPH.LIST` reads. As a result, after a downgrade the graph is still queryable but missing from `GRAPH.LIST`. C also removes graphs from that list while iterating over it, so other graphs' virtual keys were skipped and stayed in the keyspace. ## Fix - Rust now saves virtual keys as `graphmeta`, the type C uses. The key holds only the dummy value `graphmeta_free` already expects. - `graphmeta_rdb_save` now writes the key's slice of the graph, using a `save_key_slice` helper shared with `graph_rdb_save`. - Rust already loads `graphmeta` keys through the C-RDB load path, so loading C RDBs or Rust's own RDBs is unchanged. RDBs from 6.0.x (with `graphdata` virtual keys) still load as before. - Removed the comments claiming C can't load `graphmeta`. ## Verification Rust-saved RDB loaded by C (local macOS C build, `VKEY_MAX_ENTITY_COUNT 10`, two graphs with deleted nodes and edges): | | `GRAPH.LIST` on C | leftover virtual keys | ids / counts | |---|---|---|---| | before | *(empty)* | 5 keys of graph `b` | preserved | | after | `a b` | none | preserved | The same before-result reproduces with the published images (`falkordb/falkordb:6.0.1` → `:v4.20.7`). Also checked: - C → fixed Rust → fixed Rust: `GRAPH.LIST`, node ids and counts preserved, no leftover keys. - Flow tests: `test_rdb_load` now asserts that virtual keys are typed `graphmeta`. It fails on the pre-fix module and passes with the fix. `test_encode_decode` (19 tests) and `test_graph_copy` (9 tests) pass. ## Not covered The issue also reports node ids changing after the downgrade. I couldn't reproduce that with deleted node/edge ids, range and vector indexes, a 150k-node graph, deleted-id lists split across 6 virtual keys, or C save/reload cycles after the downgrade. I've left it open on the issue. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) --- ## Summary by cubic Fixes graphs vanishing from `GRAPH.LIST` after a C FalkorDB downgrade loads an RDB saved by Rust. When a graph spans multiple RDB keys, Rust saved the virtual keys as `graphdata`. C loads each as a graph, then deletes them, and its free callback removes the shared graph from the list `GRAPH.LIST` reads, making the graph disappear from the list while staying queryable. Rust now types virtual keys `graphmeta`, matching C. `graphmeta_rdb_save` writes each key's slice via a `save_key_slice` helper also used by `graph_rdb_save`. Loading is unchanged: Rust already reads `graphmeta` keys, and RDBs from 6.0.x with `graphdata` virtual keys still load as before. Written for commit abd835bd0490793535ccbb578f59154d3aa0162d. Summary will update on new commits. ## Summary by CodeRabbit * **Bug Fixes** * RDB saves now preserve assigned slices for graph keys and virtual keys. When a slice cannot be applied, the graph is saved directly instead. * Virtual keys created during saves use the `graphmeta` Redis type, and restored virtual keys are checked to retain that type. * Virtual keys without an assigned slice are not written to the RDB file.

pulls.title: ci(images): rebuild the OS-package stages on every image build
pulls.body:
Closes #3152

## Problem

The runtime image build restores a registry buildcache (`_build-flavour.yml`). Docker keys a cached `RUN` on its command text and parent layer, not on what the Debian archive holds. So when the `server` stage hits the cache, `apt-get upgrade` never runs and the image ships packages as old as the cache entry. A security update Debian publishes between two rebuilds of the `debian:trixie-slim` base is silently skipped.

This is what an external scan of `6.0.0` is asking for: it ships OpenSSL `3.5.7-1~deb13u2`, and Debian's `deb13u3` fixes the five reported CVEs.

## Change

On the build step in `_build-flavour.yml`:

```yaml
pull: true
no-cache-filters: |
  server
  full
```

- The `server` and `full` stages, the ones that install OS packages, are never served from the cache.
- The compile stages (`builder`, `redis-builder`) stay cached. `redis-server` and `falkordb.so` link `libssl`/`libcrypto`/`libz` dynamically (checked with `ldd`), so the versions that ship come from `server`.
- `full` is `FROM server` and already reruns with it; it is named so that does not depend on it.
- `Dockerfile.asan` has no `full` stage; a filter naming a stage that doesn't exist is ignored, not an error.

## Verification

Checked on the real `build/runtime/Dockerfile` with a fresh `docker-container` builder on `moby/buildkit:buildx-stable-1`, the image `setup-buildx-action` uses. The `builder` stage was swapped for the released `falkordb.so` via `--build-context` so nothing had to be compiled; `redis-builder`, `server` and `full` were built for real.

1. Seeded a local cache (`--cache-to type=local,mode=max`).
2. Cleared the builder's own state, then rebuilt from that cache two ways:

| Step | Current config | With this change |
|---|---|---|
| `[server 2/12]` apt install + `apt-get upgrade` | CACHED | ran (15.3 s) |
| `[full 1/5]` apt install | CACHED | ran (2.8 s) |
| `[redis-builder 6/6]` redis compile | CACHED | CACHED |

The image built with the change has `openssl`, `libssl3t64` and `openssl-provider-legacy` at `3.5.7-1~deb13u3`. A filter naming a missing stage exits 0 on the same builder.

CI can't show the difference on this PR. The buildcache was last written on 2026-09-17, before the current Debian base, so today every runtime build already reruns these steps (0 cached steps in merge-queue run 36303922883).

## Build time

None today, for the reason above. When the cache does hit, this adds the cost of the two stages: in run 36303922883, the `server` apt step took 12.7–15.7 s, the `full` apt step 2.6 s, and every other step in those stages under 1 s. They also run in parallel with the engine compile.

## Not in this PR

- Already-published images are untouched; releases retag the merge-queue image rather than building. `6.0` needs a patch release (6.0.1) to pick up the fix, plus a backport of this change.
- The buildcache stopped being written when #2718 moved image builds into the merge queue, because `cache-to` is gated on `refs/heads/main`. Whether to revive it is a separate, performance-only decision.

## Summary by CodeRabbit

* **Chores**
  * Server and full builds now use current base images and do not reuse cached build results. Other stages remain eligible for the configured build cache.

pulls.title: Exit with code 65 when a data load fails
pulls.body:
Closes #3145

Stacked on #3141.

Redis ends a failed RDB/AOF load with a hard-coded exit status: 1, or **0** when the `redis-check-rdb` pass it runs after a failed load from a file finds the file structurally sound (e.g. FalkorDB rejects a graph whose checksum is valid). A failed load can look like a clean shutdown to whatever restarts the server, and the module API cannot change the code.

With this change, a process that exits while a load is unfinished exits with `EX_DATAERR` (65):
- `RedisModuleEvent_Loading`: a flag is set when an RDB, AOF or replication load starts and cleared when it ends. A start while a load is still open is `redis-check-rdb` re-reading the file on its way to `exit()`, so its own end/failed events are ignored.
- `RedisModuleEvent_CronLoop`: after a `FAILED` event, the next cron tick means Redis survived the failure (a diskless sync that lost its connection), so the flag is cleared.
- `atexit()`: if the flag is set in the main process, log, `fflush(NULL)` and `_exit(65)`.

Crashes (panic, segfault) skip `atexit` and keep their signal status.

**Behavior change:** the replica AOF-divergence bail-out exits while the AOF load is unfinished, so it now reports 65 instead of 1; `testAOFDivergence` is updated.

### Tests
`tests/flow/test_load_failure_exit_code.py` saves a graph, stops the server, damages `dump.rdb`, boots a fresh server on it and checks the exit status and the module's log line:

| Case | Without this PR | With it |
|---|---|---|
| Graph FalkorDB rejects, checksum valid | 0 | 65 |
| Truncated graph value | 1 | 65 |
| Bad checksum | 1 | 65 |
| Clean shutdown after a good load | 0 | 0 |

### Verification (local; a PR based on another PR's branch gets no CI)
Built with `ghcr.io/falkordb/falkordb-build:debian`, tested on Redis 8.10.2, linux arm64.
- New test: 4/4 pass; 3 fail against #3141 without this change.
- Flow suite: 1442/1470 pass. The 28 failures (test_concurrent_query, test_timeout, test_query_mem_limit, test_slowlog, test_pending_queries_limit, test_index_create, test_graph_copy, test_cache) fail identically with #3141's own CI-built module in the same environment (test server connection refused).
- Scenario runs: rejected full-sync payloads loaded from disk (checksum valid and broken) and a failed AOF load exit 65; a diskless sync that lost its connection followed by a clean stop exits 0.

pulls.title: graph: add cdylib crate-type so the crate also emits a shared object
pulls.body:
Closes discussion in #3129 (step 1 of the request; not a full closure).

## What

Adds a `[lib]` section to `graph/Cargo.toml` with `crate-type = ["rlib", "cdylib"]`. No source changes.

## Why

As documented in #3129, the Rust workspace currently only builds as an `rlib` linked into the C-side `falkordb.so`, so there is no way to produce a shared object from the Rust tree alone. The evidence in #3129 shows that `cargo rustc -p graph --release --crate-type cdylib` already compiles cleanly on this tree and emits `target/release/libgraph.so`. Declaring it in `[lib]` promotes that artifact to a plain `cargo build -p graph` output instead of an ad-hoc `rustc` invocation, which:

- lets downstream consumers link against the engine directly for embedding/experimentation,
- gives maintainers an always-built signal that the cdylib target stays healthy (rather than rotting silently off-tree).

## What this intentionally does not do

This does **not** make the crate a loadable Redis module: no `RedisModule_OnLoad` entrypoint / command registration / lifecycle binding is implemented on the Rust side (loading the resulting `libgraph.so` with `--loadmodule` still fails, as #3129 notes). A Rust-side module binding layer is a separate, larger piece of work - this PR is the minimal, zero-risk enablement step so that follow-up work (upstream or downstream) has a supported shared-library artifact to build on.

Refs #3129

## Summary by CodeRabbit

* **Chores**
  * The graph component now builds a shared-library-compatible artifact in addition to its standard Rust library. It is not a loadable Redis module.

pulls.title: Handle short reads gracefully during RDB decode
pulls.body:
Closes #3140

Also fixes the C side of #2506 (the Rust side is #2510).

## Problem

A truncated RDB payload (a diskless replication stream that drops mid-transfer, a truncated `RESTORE`/`MIGRATE` payload, a cut-off `dump.rdb`) crashed the server: FalkorDB never declared `REDISMODULE_OPTIONS_HANDLE_IO_ERRORS`, so Redis panicked on the first short read.

Malformed but checksum-valid payloads either crashed the server (`RedisModule_Assert`, and libc `assert`, which release builds keep on) or, where the check was a debug-only `ASSERT`, loaded silently in release builds.

## Changes

**Short reads**
- `module.c`: declare `REDISMODULE_OPTIONS_HANDLE_IO_ERRORS`.
- `SerializerIO`: a sticky error flag. Once a read fails, every later read returns zero or an empty buffer without touching the stream, and the decoders stop at their next checkpoint.
- v19 and v20 decoders: checkpoints in every loop. On failure the decoder returns NULL and frees the partial graph unless an earlier virtual key already registered it (`RdbLoadGraph`, `Decode_Previous`).
- Both graph key types (`graphdata` and the `graphmeta` virtual keys) hand NULL back to Redis instead of registering it.

**Malformed payloads** (v19, v20, and the buffered reader they share)
- `SerializerIO_SetError(io, reason)` fails the decode through the same flag. Converted to failures:
  - buffer framing and value type tags (these crashed release builds);
  - count and consistency checks that were debug-only `ASSERT`s;
  - GraphBLAS load results;
  - duplicate or out-of-order schemas and duplicate constraints;
  - out-of-range entity, label and constraint ids;
  - index language, field type and vector metric.
- One warning per rejected key, naming the key and the reason:
  `Failed loading graph key '<key>': <reason>`
  Short reads add no line of ours; Redis reports those itself.

**UDFs**
- Libraries in the RDB load with replace. Loading an RDB into a process that already holds a library (a replica's next full sync, `DEBUG RELOAD`) now leaves the RDB's version in place. Before, debug builds asserted and release builds kept the stale copy.
- A library that fails to load fails the load.

**RESTORE over a live graph of the same name** (fixes the C side of #2506)
- The decoder found the graph to extend by the name stored in the payload. That lookup is meant for graphs split across keys, but it matched any registered graph, live ones included.
- `RESTORE` decodes before deleting the value it replaces. So `RESTORE … REPLACE` of a graph's own dump, or a `RESTORE` under another key while the source is live, decoded into the live graph: its contents doubled, and with an index the server crashed in `Index_SetLanguage`.
- Now only a graph part-way through a multi-key load is extended. Otherwise the payload decodes into a new graph, and Redis frees the replaced one as usual.

**Merge with master (v20)**
- master moved the v19 decoder to `decoders/prev/v19` and added `decoders/current/v20`. The hardening is applied to both.
- `Decode_Previous` no longer frees the v19 serializer before checking it for an error.
- `CCHIndex_RdbLoad` returns NULL on a short read.

## Behavior changes

- `RESTORE … REPLACE` of a graph's own dump now restores exactly the dump. Before, it doubled the graph, and crashed when the graph had an index.

- Release builds now refuse payloads that broke a debug-only check and used to load silently:
  - `RESTORE` fails with `Bad data format`;
  - at startup, Redis exits;
  - on a replica's full sync, the replica exits.
- Replicas configured with `repl-diskless-load on-empty-db` now actually load from the socket. Before, Redis skipped diskless loading because a module didn't declare IO-error handling.
  - A dropped connection makes the replica retry.
  - Rejected data makes the replica exit, which is Redis's policy for corrupt data.

## Scope

- Covered: the v19 and v20 decoders, and the buffered reader they share.
- v14–v18: their decoders are unchanged, including the graph lookup by name. They pick up the short-read latch from the shared reader.
- v10–v13: read Redis's IO directly; unchanged.
- Out of scope:
  - `GRAPH.RESTORE` / `GRAPH.COPY`;
  - allocations sized from header counts;
  - GraphBLAS matrix contents.

## Tests

- `test_rdb_load.py`:
  - a short read inside every chunk of a multi-chunk graph;
  - a short read inside a `graphmeta` key;
  - a malformed type tag, buffer length and payload type;
  - `DEBUG RELOAD` replacing a UDF library;
  - `RESTORE … REPLACE` of a graph's own dump, with and without an index (the #2506 reproducer);
  - `RESTORE` under another key while the source graph is live.

  Each new test fails on the code before its fix; the multi-chunk short-read test on debug builds, where the assert it trips lives.
- Run locally (linux arm64, release and debug builds):
  - truncation inside every chunk of a 25 MB graph: all rejected cleanly, memory flat;
  - diskless replication with the stream cut at 17 points: all recover;
  - 400 seeded single-byte corruptions of a valid DUMP:

    | | Crashes before | Crashes after |
    |---|---|---|
    | Release | 134 (+5 hangs) | 3 |
    | Debug | 141 (+1 hang) | 4 (+1 hang) |

    The remaining crashes are GraphBLAS matrix contents and oversized header counts, both out of scope.

pulls.title: Fix crash when a clause errors mid plan-build (#250)
pulls.body:
Resolve: #3138
A build-time error raised while constructing a clause left plan construction in a poisoned state: the clause / segment loops never checked ErrorCtx_EncounteredError(), so subsequent clauses (a segment boundary WITH, an OPTIONAL MATCH, ORDER BY, UNWIND, a CALL {} subquery, ...) were still built on top of a partially-constructed / NULL-rooted plan. The malformed plan then crashed the server when the segments were tied together (_tie_segments) or when the plan was freed (OpBase_Free -> HashTableRelease, the reported signature).

This is the general form of the MERGE-only fix in #239/#3116: the reported query is a read query whose erroring clause precedes an OPTIONAL MATCH.

Fixes:
- stop building once a clause raises an error (ExecutionPlan_Populate- ExecutionPlan) and once a segment raises an error (_process_segments)
- in ExecutionPlan_FromTLS_AST, tear down the partial segments and return NULL instead of tying / adding an implicit result to a broken plan
- guard buildCallSubqueryPlan against a NULL / errored embedded plan before dereferencing it (mirrors the buildMergeOp guard), matching the new NULL-on-error contract of ExecutionPlan_FromTLS_AST

Regression tests added to test_optional_match.py (test28, the reported read-query shape) and test_call_subquery.py (test_54). Both trigger the error during plan construction via a non-boolean WHERE predicate (which passes AST validation), and were verified to crash the server without the fix.

pulls.title: fix(runtime): allow startNode() and endNode() to accept null (#2723)
pulls.body:
Closes #2723.

## Problem
In the Rust query engine, passing `null` to `startNode()` or `endNode()` (such as when evaluating expressions over unmatched `OPTIONAL MATCH` patterns or literal scalar calls) failed with a runtime type mismatch error:
```
Type mismatch: expected Edge but was Null
```

Per the FalkorDB documentation and openCypher specification, `startNode(null)` and `endNode(null)` must return `null` (three-valued logic / null propagation). The C engine (`v4.20.4`) already returns `null` correctly.

## Root Cause
In `graph/src/runtime/functions/entity.rs`, `startnode` and `endnode` were registered with:
```rust
args: [Type::Relationship]
```
omitting `Type::Null`. Sibling entity functions (`labels`, `id`, `properties`, `type`, etc.) already accept `Type::union([..., Type::Null])`. Although `startnode` and `endnode` already had their return type registered as `Type::union([Type::Node, Type::Null])`, they also lacked the `Some(Value::Null) => Ok(Value::Null)` match arm.

## Fix
1. In `graph/src/runtime/functions/entity.rs`, updated `args` for `startnode` and `endnode` to:
   ```rust
   args: [Type::union([Type::Relationship, Type::Null])]
   ```
2. Added `Some(Value::Null) => Ok(Value::Null)` pattern matching arms to both function implementations.

## Behavior
```cypher
OPTIONAL MATCH (n)-[r:NONEXISTENT]->() WHERE false RETURN startNode(r), endNode(r);
RETURN startNode(null) AS s, endNode(null) AS e;
```
- **Before**: `Type mismatch: expected Edge but was Null`
- **After**: `[[null, null]]` (matches C engine v4.20.4)

## Tests & Verification
- Added regression tests to `test16_edge_endpoints` in `tests/flow/test_function_calls.py` covering both `OPTIONAL MATCH` null relationships and literal null evaluation.
- Audited all sibling entity functions across `graph/src/runtime/functions/*.rs` to confirm complete NULL-handling parity.
- Verified formatting with `cargo fmt --all -- --check` (clean, exit code 0).


<!-- This is an auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->
## Summary by CodeRabbit

* **Bug Fixes**
  * `startNode` and `endNode` now return `null` when given a null relationship.

pulls.title: fix(functions): name received types in the engine's vocabulary in entity.rs
pulls.body:
Closes #3126

﻿Four type-mismatch messages in `entity.rs` that are not written in the engine's own type vocabulary. Both are one-liners; this is a message-correctness fix, not a behaviour change.

## 1. `indegree`/`outdegree` use Rust's `Debug` spelling

`parse_degree_args` (`graph/src/runtime/functions/entity.rs:304`) hand-rolls its type check because `indegree`/`outdegree` are registered `var_arg: Type::Any` → `FnArguments::VarLength`, and both `GraphFn::validate` and `validate_args_type` are deliberate no-ops for var-len. So that check is the **only** one these functions get, and its message is the user-facing one. All three sites formatted the received type with `{:?}`.

`Type` derives `Debug` **and** has a hand-written `Display` impl at `mod.rs:610-654` whose entire purpose is the user-facing vocabulary (`Self::Int => "Integer"`, `Self::Bool => "Boolean"`, `Self::Relationship => "Edge"`). The framework's own message uses `{}` (`mod.rs:836-842`), and C uses `SIType_ToString`, which returns `"Integer"`.

| query | before | after / C |
|---|---|---|
| `RETURN indegree(1)` | `...but was Int` | `...but was Integer` |
| `RETURN outdegree(n, [1])` | `...but was Int` | `...but was Integer` |
| `RETURN outdegree(n, 'R', 1)` | `...but was Int` | `...but was Integer` |
| `RETURN outdegree(n, 'R', ['X'])` | `...but was List(List(Any))` | `...but was List` |

The last one is the worst: it leaks the internal `Type::List(Type::Any)` structure into a string a user reads. Three `{:?}` → `{}`.

## 2. `hasLabels` drops the received type on its catch-all

`has_labels` checks list element types by hand, and three arms name what arrived — `but was Integer`, `but was Float`, `but was Boolean`. The catch-all covers the other **12** `Value` variants and said nothing:

```
MATCH (n) WHERE hasLabels(n, ['person', null])   ->  Type mismatch: expected String
MATCH (n) WHERE hasLabels(n, ['person', {a:1}])  ->  Type mismatch: expected String
```

It was the only type-mismatch message in the file without a `but was X` clause. Now uses `Value::name()`, the same helper the rest of the codebase uses for this, and whose spellings match the three arms above it.

## Testing

**`cargo test -p graph`** — new `mod tests` in `entity.rs` (the file had none). `parse_degree_args` is a module-private pure function and every one of the three sites returns before a `Runtime` is touched, so no harness is needed:
- the four mismatch spellings above,
- `the_arity_message_is_untouched` — the "Received 3 arguments ... expected at most 2" path is a different branch and must not change,
- `the_accepted_shapes_are_untouched` — `degree(node)` and `degree(node, ['R'])` still parse.

**Flow suite** — new `test19a_hasLabels_type_mismatch_names_the_received_type` in `tests/flow/test_function_calls.py` (listed in `flow_tests_done.txt`), covering all six reachable element types. Written as `error = None` + `assertTrue(error is not None, ...)` rather than the try/except shape used by the neighbouring test, so it cannot pass vacuously if the query stops raising.

**No existing assertion moves.** `test_function_calls.py:2415`/`:2432` assert only the substrings `"Type mismatch"` / `"Received"`, and the existing `hasLabels` assertion at `:627` goes through the untouched `Value::Int` arm — and `Value::name()` returns `"Integer"` for it anyway. `Steps.py` in the TCK asserts only `"Type mismatch" in str(e)`.

## Relation to #340

#340 asks for *more* in these messages (function name, argument index). This is orthogonal — it makes the existing message well-formed rather than adding fields. Either can land first.

`cargo fmt` clean against `fn_params_layout = "Vertical"`.


<!-- This is an auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->
## Summary by CodeRabbit

* **Bug Fixes**
  * Type mismatch errors for label checks and degree-related functions now identify the type of the received value, including invalid labels, nodes, list elements, and variadic arguments.
* **Tests**
  * Added coverage for invalid label types and degree argument errors. Confirmed that accepted argument shapes, duplicate filtering, and arity handling remain unchanged.

pulls.title: fix(temporal): reject non-digits in compact date and time strings
pulls.body:
Closes #3124

﻿A second fix from the same area as #3118, and the same shape of defect: a parser that drops input it should have rejected.

`parse_date_string` (`graph/src/runtime/functions/temporal.rs:148`) built its digit buffer with `filter(char::is_ascii_digit)` - which *discards* non-digits rather than rejecting them - and then dispatched on the length of what survived. So:

```
RETURN toString(date('2o15o7o21'))          -- Rust: '2015-07-21'
RETURN toString(date('hello20230506world')) -- Rust: '2023-05-06'
RETURN toString(localtime('xx123456yy'))    -- Rust: '12:34:56'
```

Malformed input producing a valid-looking value with no error. `date('2o15o7o21')` quietly equalling `date('2015-07-21')` is the sharp form - a caller reading from a dirty source gets a plausible date out of a malformed string with no way to notice.

## The change

One guard in each of the two compact branches:

```rust
if !s.chars().all(char::is_ascii_digit) {
    return Err(format!("Invalid date string: {s}"));
}
```

Nothing that is currently valid changes - every documented compact form (`2015`, `201507`, `2015202`, `20150721`, and times `21` / `2140` / `214032`) is already pure ASCII digits, and `parse_time_string` strips a fractional part at `:274` before the check runs, so `214032.142` is unaffected. The filter was never load-bearing.

The defect is confined to the compact branches. The hyphenated date form and the colon time form use `split` + `parse` and already error correctly, and the `W` week-date form returns before either of these. Both are now covered by explicit tests so that stays true.

## Testing

New `mod compact_parser_rejects_junk_tests` in `temporal.rs` (run by `cargo test -p graph`, part of the required `ci-gate`):
- `compact_date_rejects_embedded_letters` / `compact_date_rejects_other_punctuation` - the four repro strings.
- `compact_date_keeps_every_documented_form` - all four compact date forms still produce the same dates, so the guard cannot over-reject.
- `the_hyphenated_and_week_forms_are_untouched` - pins the paths the change does not touch.
- `colon_less_time_rejects_embedded_letters` / `colon_less_time_keeps_every_documented_form` - same pair for times, including the fractional form.
- `the_colon_time_form_is_untouched`.

Breakage risk: `tests/flow/test_temporal.py` (in `flow_tests_done.txt`) only feeds clean inputs to the string parsers, and the TCK temporal features use clean ISO strings only. `date`/`localtime`/`localdatetime`/`duration` are deliberately **not** in `tests/test_functions.py`'s fuzzer parametrisation, so the random-string generator never reaches these parsers.

`cargo fmt` clean against `fn_params_layout = "Vertical"`.

## Summary by CodeRabbit

* **Bug Fixes**
  * Compact dates and colonless times now reject inputs containing letters or punctuation instead of silently ignoring those characters.
  * Hyphenated dates, ISO week dates, and colon-separated times continue to parse as before.

pulls.title: test(cluster): wait for announced hostnames before building the client
pulls.body:
Closes #2941

Harness-only change: no test file is touched, and no assertion changes. It is the only kind of fix here that does not need a new assertion, because the thing being fixed is the wait that happens *before* the tests run.

## The race

`_bootstrap_cluster` (`tests/flow/common.py:382`) forms the cluster in three phases and its readiness gate is:

```python
if (fields.get("cluster_state", "").strip() == "ok"
        and int(fields.get("cluster_known_nodes", "0")) == n):
```

That only proves the **gossip topology** arrived. A peer learned through gossip counts as known before its `--cluster-announce-hostname` has been merged, and under `--cluster-preferred-endpoint-type hostname` (both set at `common.py:367-368`) an unmerged node is reported as `?`.

`Env()` then builds the client at `common.py:709`, which auto-detects cluster mode and returns a cluster-aware client. `RedisCluster` snapshots its slot map from `CLUSTER SLOTS` **at construction**, so `?:6379` is recorded then. In cluster mode `udf_load` opens a direct connection to every primary, so `test_udf_delete_propagation` (first alphabetically, so its `udf_load` is the first all-primaries command after bootstrap) is where it surfaces.

## The fix

A fourth phase, reusing the existing `attempts`/`interval` budget so there is no new tunable:

```python
for c, (h, p) in zip(clients, shard_addrs):
    for _ in range(attempts):
        try:
            if not _slots_have_unresolved_endpoint(
                    c.execute_command("CLUSTER", "SLOTS")):
                break
        except Exception:
            pass
        time.sleep(interval)
    else:
        raise RuntimeError(...)
```

`_slots_have_unresolved_endpoint` walks `entry[2:]` (the master plus any replicas, so it stays correct if cluster+replicas is ever wired up) and looks for `?` in the address. The bootstrap clients at `common.py:398-402` are built without `decode_responses`, so the address arrives as `bytes`; the helper accepts `str` too, so the check cannot silently degrade into a no-op if that ever changes.

Every shard announces a hostname, so `?` is never a steady state here. If it persists past the budget, failing with "announced hostnames have not propagated" is a better outcome than handing the test a client that cannot connect.

## Why this is safe

- **No assertion is touched.** Nothing becomes vacuous; the change only moves *when* `Env()` considers the cluster ready.
- **No-op for non-cluster paths.** `_bootstrap_cluster` is only reached from `_spawn_falkordb_cluster`, so every non-cluster `Env()` is unaffected.
- **Benefits the whole bucket.** `test_udf_cluster.py` is routed to the spawn bucket by `test_matrix_split.py:39-42` (`env='oss-cluster'`), and per the issue this race can hit any spawn-mode `oss-cluster` test - so every such test gets the wait, not just this file.
- **Cost when things are healthy:** one extra `CLUSTER SLOTS` round trip per shard, typically one 0.2 s poll. The full 20 s only elapses on a genuine failure, which then raises a precise message.

## Caveat worth stating

I could not verify the exact `?` rendering against Redis source in this repo (no `redis.conf` is vendored and code search only reaches the default branch), so that detail rests on the issue's own reproduction plus the flags, which I did read verbatim at `common.py:362-369`. The two flags are what make the reported endpoint type relevant, so if a maintainer wants to confirm the `CLUSTER SLOTS` shape against a live node before merging, that is the one thing worth checking - the helper is deliberately tolerant of both `bytes` and `str` addresses so a wrong guess degrades into a timeout with a clear message rather than a false pass.


<!-- This is an auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->
## Summary by CodeRabbit

* **Tests**
  * Cluster test setup confirms shard endpoints are resolved before proceeding. Temporary errors during readiness checks are retried, and setup reports an error if endpoints remain unresolved after the configured attempts.
  * Slow-log tests now exercise larger query workloads, concurrent population, reset behavior, and entry replacement. These changes affect test coverage and initialization only; no end-user-facing changes are included.
<!-- end of auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->

pulls.title: fix(algo): a costProp an edge does not have contributes 1, not 0
pulls.body:
Closes #3121

Split out of #343, which asks for two things at once. This is the half that is a C-parity bug. The other half - replacing a *negative or zero* weight or cost with 1 - is not a parity bug (C does not clamp either, and `Dijkstra.h:21-31` states non-negative weights as a deliberately unguarded precondition), so it is a Rust-vs-C policy choice for a maintainer and is left alone here.

## The bug

`edge_numeric_attr` (`graph/src/runtime/functions/algo_procedures.rs:2104`) takes one `default` and uses it for two cases C keeps apart:

```rust
prop.map_or(default, |p| {
    match g.get_relationship_attribute(edge_id, p) {
        Some(Value::Float(f)) => f,
        Some(Value::Int(i)) => i as f64,
        _ => default,
    }
})
```

C's `_sum_path_cost` (`src/procedures/proc_sp_paths.c:472` on `master`) separates them:

```c
if(cost_prop == ATTRIBUTE_ID_NONE) {
    return 0;
}
...
    SIValue c = GraphEntity_GetNumericPropertyOrDefault ((GraphEntity *) Path_GetEdge(p, i),
            cost_prop, SI_LongVal(1));
```

| case | C | Rust (`default = 0.0`) |
|---|---|---|
| `costProp` not configured | `0` | `0` - already right |
| `costProp` configured, edge lacks it | `1` | `0` - **wrong** |
| `costProp` configured, edge has a value | that value | that value - already right |

So `pathCost` came out one too low per property-less edge. It is not only a reported number: `enumerate_paths` gates `maxCost` against the running `next_cost` (`:2528`), so a path C admits can be pruned by Rust and vice versa - the divergence changes results.

## The change

One accessor, mirroring C's split, and three call sites switched to it (`:2308` the Dijkstra result, `:2397` the backtracked chain, `:2518` `enumerate_paths`):

```rust
fn edge_cost_attr(
    g: &Graph,
    edge_id: RelationshipId,
    prop: Option<&Arc<String>>,
) -> f64 {
    prop.map_or(0.0, |p| match g.get_relationship_attribute(edge_id, p) {
        Some(Value::Float(f)) => f,
        Some(Value::Int(i)) => i as f64,
        _ => 1.0,
    })
}
```

The value handling is deliberately identical to `edge_numeric_attr` - a negative or zero cost is still reported as-is. That is not an oversight: C does not clamp, so clamping here would be an unrequested divergence in the other direction.

The three weight call sites already pass `default = 1.0`, which is exactly C's behaviour for both the unconfigured and the missing case, so they are untouched. `edge_numeric_attr` keeps its four remaining weight uses.

## Testing

New `test12a_costprop_missing_on_an_edge_contributes_one` in `tests/flow/test_path_algorithms.py` (`testAllShortestPaths`, in `flow_tests_done.txt` line 84, services bucket), on a two-hop path whose second edge deliberately has no `cost`:

| query | before | after | C |
|---|---|---|---|
| `weightProp: 'weight', costProp: 'cost'` | `pathCost` 2 | **3** | 3 |
| no `costProp` | `pathCost` 0 | 0 | 0 |
| `costProp: 'cost', maxCost: 2` | one row | **no rows** | no rows |

`pathCost` is `2 + 1` after the fix: the first edge has `cost: 2`, the second has no `cost` at all and `costProp` is configured, so it contributes the default 1. Before the fix the second edge contributed 0 and the total came out one low.

The three cases pin all three branches: the configured-and-missing default, the unconfigured default that must not move, and the `maxCost` gate - which is the assertion that shows this was not only a cosmetic reporting difference. Before the fix that third query returned a row, because the running cost was `2 + 0` and `2 > 2` is false.

Every existing fixture in that file gives each relationship a positive `cost`, so the default never fires there and no asserted number moves. `pathCost` is asserted in that one file repo-wide; the only two places that pass a `costProp` naming a missing property assert either an empty result or a `pathWeight` only.

## Checks

`cargo fmt` clean (verified against the repo's `fn_params_layout = "Vertical"`), and the new function plus all three call sites were type-checked standalone before pushing.


<!-- This is an auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->
## Summary by CodeRabbit

* **Bug Fixes**
  * Path calculations now assign a cost of 1 when a configured edge-cost property is missing or nonnumeric. When no cost property is configured, edges continue to contribute 0.
  * Numeric edge costs, including negative and zero values, are used as provided when calculating path totals.
  * Maximum-cost limits exclude paths whose configured total cost exceeds the limit across supported path-finding operations.
<!-- end of auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->

pulls.title: fix(algo): dedupe relTypes in algo.SPpaths/SSpaths config
pulls.body:
Closes #2940

Splitting this out because it is not actually a flake: `relTypes: ['E', 'E']` returns duplicated paths on **every** run of current `main`. `test17_sp_duplicate_edges` is flaky only in that it usually fails to notice.

## The bug

`get_node_relationships_by_type` (`graph/src/graph/graph.rs:2085`) builds the candidate set as **one matrix per listed type**:

```rust
let matrices: Vec<&Tensor> = if types.is_empty() {
    self.relationship_matrices.iter().collect()
} else {
    types.iter().filter_map(|t| self.get_relationship_matrix(t)).collect()
};
```

`parse_common_path_config` pushed every entry of the `relTypes` list verbatim, so `['E', 'E']` produced `[E_tensor, E_tensor]`. From there:

1. `node_successors` and the `enumerate_paths` inner loop (`algo_procedures.rs:2158`, `:2254`, `:2353`) each iterate that vector, so every edge is yielded twice.
2. The DFS re-explores each subtree once per copy, so a path is found `2^hops` times.
3. `record_found_path` has no identity check, and the k-minimal result set fills with copies of one path.

`pathCount: 1` is unaffected - that arm keeps a single best path - which is why only the `pathCount >= 2` rows of the issue's table are wrong.

## The fix

Dedupe at the parse boundary, order-preserving:

```rust
Value::String(s) => {
    if !types.contains(s) {
        types.push(s.clone());
    }
}
```

`relTypes` is a set everywhere else it is read - existence validation at `:1336` and `:2704`, `get_src_dest_relationships` at `:2162` - so a repeat was never meaningful, only harmful. This narrows the accepted input space, and only for inputs that are wrong today. `extract_rel_types` (the separate `relationshipTypes` key used by the centrality/Louvain-family procedures) is deliberately not touched.

`graph.rs:2085` is also deliberately not touched. It has other callers - `all_shortest_paths.rs` and `cond_var_len_traverse.rs`, whose `rp.types` come from Cypher `*` patterns and already dedup through a visited set. Widening the fix there needs its own coverage.

## The test was not catching it

```python
self.env.assertEqual(len(dup.result_set), expected_len)
for row in dup.result_set:
    self.env.assertContains(row, single.result_set)
```

With the bug, `dup` is `[X, X, X]`, which has the right *length* and each of whose rows is a member of `single` - so the assertion passed whenever the random graph happened to offer 3+ qualifying paths, which is the common case. Replaced with a comparison of which paths came back:

```python
def node_ids(result):
    return sorted(tuple(n.id for n in row[0].nodes())
                  for row in result.result_set)

self.env.assertEqual(node_ids(dup), node_ids(single))
```

This is strictly stronger - it pins identity and multiplicity, where the old loop only checked membership - and it is strictly deterministic: the two queries are now literally the same query, so the two sets must match for any graph. Node ids rather than `Path` objects so the assertion rests on neither `Path.__eq__` nor on how RLTest compares two `Path`s, and sorted so it does not depend on the order the search emits.

Both hunks land together on purpose. The test change alone would turn the flake into a deterministic red.

## Testing

- `tests/flow/test_path_algorithms.py` is in `flow_tests_done.txt` (line 84, services bucket) and is where the original flake was observed (`a-sanitizer-flow-svc`, `release-flow-svc`).
- `test17` is the only test that passes a repeated `relTypes`; no other test in `tests/flow/`, `tests/test_functions.py` or `tests/tck/` does, so no other expected count moves.
- The other two `relTypes` tests (`relTypes: [1]`, `relTypes: ['a', 1]`) assert the "must be array of strings" error, which this change does not touch.
- The new snippet was type-checked standalone before pushing, and the file is `cargo fmt` clean.

pulls.title: test(functions): bound the nesting depth of random LIST arguments
pulls.body:
Closes #2938

`random_value` recursed into `Type.LIST` with no depth limit and wrapped each level in `str()`. `str()` on a list calls `repr()` per element, so every level re-quotes and re-escapes the entire subtree underneath it - the Cypher literal roughly doubles per level of nesting. The recursion does terminate (each level draws 0-9 elements, each of which is a LIST with probability 1/6), but the tail is long enough that ~6% of `pytest` runs produced a multi-gigabyte argument and the process was OOM-killed with exit 137.

## The change

One constant and one parameter:

```python
MAX_LIST_DEPTH = 2

def random_value(type, depth=0):
    ...
    elif type == Type.LIST:
        pool = all_types if depth < MAX_LIST_DEPTH else [t for t in all_types if t != Type.LIST]
        return str([random_value(choice(pool), depth + 1) for _ in range(choice(range(0, 10)))])
```

Past the depth cap the elements are drawn from the non-LIST types, so the literal is bounded at tens of KB for **any** seed rather than for an average one. Concretely: the innermost list holds at most 9 scalars of at most 100 characters; its `repr()` is ~1 KB; the level above holds 9 of those, whose escaped `repr()` is ~17 KB; that string is the return value and is not escaped again. So the worst case is bounded by a constant, not by luck.

`random_value` has exactly two callers - its own recursion and `validate_function:87` - so the new defaulted parameter touches nothing else.

## Why this does not weaken the test

Every assertion in `tests/test_functions.py` is about **arity**:

```
assert "Received {len(args)} arguments to function '{func}', expected at most {most}" in str(e)
```

`len(args)` is the number of arguments, which this change does not affect. The bound is on the *value* of an argument, not on how many there are, and no expected count moves.

The coverage that is lost is negligible and, per the issue, was not real to begin with: because `str()` re-quoted each level, a nested list was already always a list of *strings* - never a nested list, never an int, bool or null inside a list. The probability of ever reaching depth 26 (the point where the old growth actually bites) is ~2.6e-4 per draw.

## Deliberately not in this PR

The issue also suggests building list literals as Cypher text instead of via `str()`, and seeding the RNG. Both are left out on purpose:

- **Cypher-text literals** would change *what* is generated, not just how large it is - `str(['1', 'abc'])` is a Cypher list of two strings, where a hand-built literal would be a real list of mixed values. That is arguably a second bug, but it changes what the engine is asked to handle and could turn a CI-stability fix into a red PR. Worth its own change, once someone has looked at the new failures.
- **Seeding** would call `random.seed()`, and `test_functions.py` runs in the same pytest process as `test_e2e.py`, `test_mvcc.py` and `test_concurrency.py`. Seeding the global RNG would change the inputs those suites draw. With the OOM gone, replayability is much less urgent than it was.

## CI coverage

`tests/test_functions.py` is not in `flow_tests_done.txt` (that file lists `tests/flow/*` only), but it is run directly by the `ci-pipeline` job:

```
RELEASE=1 pytest tests/test_e2e.py tests/test_functions.py tests/test_mvcc.py tests/test_concurrency.py -vv
```

and again by `test-image` in the merge queue - which is where the exit-137 kills were landing (7 of the 15 affected PRs were merge-queue runs).

pulls.title: fix(temporal): reject an ISO 8601 duration whose last number has no unit
pulls.body:
Closes #3117

`parse_duration_string` (`graph/src/runtime/functions/temporal.rs`) accumulates digits into `num_buf` and only converts them when a unit character (`Y`/`M`/`W`/`D`/`H`/`S`) closes them. Neither loop inspects `num_buf` afterwards, so a number with no unit after it is dropped instead of rejected.

| query | before | after | C |
|---|---|---|---|
| `RETURN duration('P5')` | `PT0S` | error | `null` |
| `RETURN duration('P-')` | `PT0S` | error | `null` |
| `RETURN duration('P1Y5')` | `P1Y` | error | `null` |
| `RETURN duration('P1M2')` | `P1M` | error | `null` |
| `RETURN duration('PT4H5')` | `PT4H` | error | `null` |

The silent part matters more than the acceptance: `duration('P1Y5')` used to *mean* `P1Y`, so a caller that builds an ISO string by concatenation got a different duration than it asked for with no signal at all.

## The change

One check, after the time part, where the two loops have shared `num_buf`:

```rust
if !num_buf.is_empty() {
    return Err(format!("Invalid duration, missing unit after: {num_buf}"));
}
```

One check is enough rather than one per loop: the buffer is cleared at the start of the time part, so a non-empty buffer at that point can only ever mean "digits that no unit closed". Putting it after the `if let` also covers the date-only case, where the leftover is still sitting in the buffer from the date loop.

Valid input is untouched - `P5D`, `P2W`, `P1Y2M3DT4H5M6S` and the negative components (`P-1D`) all parse as before, because in each of those a unit character closes every number.

## How it was tested

**`cargo test -p graph`** - new `mod parse_duration_string_tests` at the end of `temporal.rs`:
- `a_trailing_number_with_no_unit_is_rejected` - the six spellings from the table above all return `Err`.
- `a_number_with_a_unit_still_parses` - `P5D`, `P2W` and `P1Y2M3DT4H5M6S` still produce the same component tuples, so the fix is not "reject more".

**Flow suite** (`tests/flow/test_temporal.py`, in `flow_tests_done.txt`) - new `test_duration_from_string_rejects_a_number_with_no_unit` in `testTemporalDuration` runs the same six strings through `duration($str)` and asserts each raises. The existing `test_duration_from_string` covers the accepted spellings end to end and is unchanged.

Both were written before the fix and fail against `main`.

## Scope

Deliberately left alone, because each is a separate question rather than a bug in this loop:

- `duration('PT1.5S')` truncates the fraction (durations have one-second resolution) while C rejects it - #2595.
- `duration('P1DT')` - a trailing `T` with an empty time part - still returns `P1D`.
- The other conversions in #2937 (`toString(1.0)`, `toInteger`/`toFloat` string parsing) are untouched; this PR is only the one item from that issue that both engines already agree should be an error.

The parser rejecting the string (rather than returning `null`, as C does) matches Neo4j, which raises. The openCypher TCK does not cover these inputs.

* **Tests**
  * Added coverage for rejecting durations with unitless numbers and confirming that durations with units continue to parse.

Closes #3109

## Problem

Without `costProp`, algo.SPpaths/SSpaths charged 0 per relationship, so `maxCost` limited nothing and `pathCost` was always 0 (e.g. path [0,1,3] with cost 0 where C returns [0,3] with cost 1).

pulls.title: fix: return allShortestPaths directed cycles in walk order (#3108)
pulls.body:
Closes #3108

## Problem

`allShortestPaths` whose source and destination are the same node returned a directed cycle with its relationships last-to-first, i.e. walked against the arrows (nodes [0,2,1,0] / rels [3,2,1] instead of [0,1,2,0] / [1,2,3]). C is also wrong here (differently); this PR returns the correct walk.

Details, repro and C comparison: #3108.

## Fix

The backtracked edge list was flipped into source-to-destination order
only when source != destination, so a directed cycle came out with its
relationships last-to-first and PathBuilder walked it against the
arrows. Flip cycles too. test06 asserted the old (and C's) reversed
node lists; it now checks the actual walks for -> and <-.


(a)<-[*]-(a) swaps from/to onto the same alias, so the parser could not
tell it from (a)-[*]->(a) and planned it Forward; with cycles now
returned in walk order it came out along the arrows. Record the arrow
direction before parsing the relationship.


## Tests

`tests/flow/test_all_shortest_paths.py::test06` asserted the old reversed order; it now checks the actual walks for `->` and `<-` and the relationship order. The new checks fail on origin/main and pass with this change.

Also run on a merged build of the four traversal fixes: `cargo test -p graph --lib` 422 passed; `pytest tests/test_e2e.py tests/test_functions.py` 125 passed; flow suites bidirectional_traversals, all_shortest_paths, path_algorithms, traversal_construction, path, variable_length, shortest_path, path_projections all pass (RLTest on a private port). `cargo fmt` clean; no new clippy warnings in touched code.

pulls.body:
Closes #3107

## Problem

`MATCH (a)-[]-(b)` returned every node pair twice when edges exist in both directions (4 rows vs C's 2); ExpandInto had the same bug (2 vs 1).

Details, repro and C comparison: #3107.

## Fix

Collapse mode keeps one representative edge per matrix pair, and the
forward and reverse scans each kept one, so a pair stored in both
directions (a->b and b->a) came out twice. Drop reverse results the
forward scan already produced in CondTraverse, and stop after the first
direction that yields an edge in ExpandInto. Matches C (A + A^T).

New `test_bidirectional_traversals.py::test14` fails on origin/main (4 / 2 rows) and passes with this change (2 / 1, same as C).

pulls.title: fix: dedup chained anonymous undirected hops per input record (#3106)
pulls.body:
Closes #3106

## Problem

Chained anonymous undirected hops (`(a)-[]-()-[]-(b)`) dedup rows on a key that ignores other columns, uses an intermediate node at 3+ hops, and resets per batch: `UNWIND [1,2] AS x MATCH (a)-[]-()-[]-(b)` returned 5 rows (C 10), 3 hops returned 7 pairs (C 12), and on K(2,3000) pair counts came out as 3 and 4 (C 1).

Details, repro and C comparison: #3106.

## Fix

The (source, destination) dedup that reproduces C's matrix-product
semantics for chained anonymous undirected hops keyed on the source
node, so it merged rows differing in other columns (and equal input
records), used an intermediate node as the source at 3+ hops, and was
cleared per child batch, so a start node spanning batches emitted its
destinations more than once.

Key it on a lineage id instead: the chain's first traverse numbers its
input records, each dedup traverse forwards the lineage of its input
rows, and the emitter reports the parent row of every emitted row. The
rows of one record arrive contiguously, so the seen-set is only cleared
at a record change once it has grown.


## Tests

New `tests/flow/test_bidirectional_traversals.py::test15` fails on origin/main and passes with this change; all three shapes above now match C.

pulls.title: fix: stop exponential backtracking on nested [(...)] lists in the parser
pulls.body:
Closes #3103

## Problem

`parse_list_literal_or_comprehension` tried every `[` that is followed by `(` or a name as a pattern comprehension first (named, then unnamed). The attempt parsed the node pattern, including its property map. When no relationship followed, it restored the position and parsed the same text again as a list literal. A map value holding another `[(…)]` did the same inside both passes, so the work doubled with each level. `RETURN [(x {k: [(x {k: …})]})]` with 22 levels (251 bytes) took **20.5 s** on a live server before failing with `'x' not defined`.

## Fix

Both changes are in `parse_list_literal_or_comprehension`. Neither changes what is parsed, only what is attempted:

1. **Try only where it can succeed.** `list_has_top_level_pipe` counts brackets (it does not parse) from the `[` to its closing `]`. It reports whether a `|` comes first at nesting level 0, before any top-level `,`. A pattern comprehension always has such a `|` and no top-level `,`. A list literal can never have the `|`, so skipping the attempt when the scan says no gives the same result. The scan is also skipped unless the `[` is followed by `(` or a name, the only tokens either attempt can start with.
2. **Never repeat a failed attempt.** A failed attempt is recorded under a `PatternComprehensionAttempt` key (position, `allow_pattern_predicate`, forbidden-comprehension context, nesting depth). Those are all the inputs besides the query text that decide whether it succeeds, so a later visit to the same key skips it. This covers adversarial inputs that do contain a top-level `|` (e.g. `[(x {k: …}) - 1 | 1]`). Without this memo they were still exponential (20 levels: 5.8 s).

## Benchmarks

The benchmark measures parse time only, in process, on a release build (best of 5). The machine was shared and loaded, and runs alternated between builds. `maplist` is the same nesting with no ambiguity (`[{k: [{k: …}]}]`); it is the parser's baseline. Its quadratic cost comes from tree wrapping, and this PR does not change it.

| shape | levels | `main` | this PR |
|---|---|---|---|
| `[(x {k: …})]` | 8 / 12 / 16 / 20 | 2.65 / 24.7 / 393 / **6366** ms | 0.16 / 0.27 / 0.44 / **0.65** ms |
| `[(x {k: …}) - 1]` | 8 / 12 / 16 / 20 | 2.12 / 34.6 / 557 / **9526** ms | 0.14 / 0.29 / 0.47 / **0.68** ms |
| `[p = (x {k: …})]` | 8 / 12 / 16 / 20 | 2.24 / 35.3 / 530 / **8657** ms | 0.12 / 0.24 / 0.39 / **0.58** ms |
| `WHERE (x {k: [ … ]})` | 8 / 12 / 16 / 20 | 1.19 / 19.2 / 308 / **5011** ms | 0.08 / 0.15 / 0.25 / **0.37** ms |
| `[(x {k: …}) - 1 \| 1]` (rejected) | 8 / 12 / 16 / 20 | 1.13 / 18.3 / 291 / **4724** ms | 0.13 / 0.25 / 0.42 / **0.63** ms |
