pulls.title: ci(asan): get llvm-symbolizer from the builder, not apt.llvm.org
pulls.body:
## Summary

The ASAN image installed LLVM from **apt.llvm.org** at build time, which fails
intermittently and ejects PRs from the merge queue. **3 of the last 18 `Rust PR`
runs** hit it; PR #2469 was kicked out three times, never for anything in its own
diff. Full diagnosis in #2872.

The whole step existed to obtain one file — `/usr/bin/llvm-symbolizer-22` — that
the toolchain image **already has**. This copies it across the stage boundary
instead, so the runtime stage talks to `deb.debian.org` only.

## Why the builder already has it

`llvm.sh` runs `apt-get install -y clang-22 …` *without* `--no-install-recommends`;
`clang-22` Recommends `llvm-22-dev`, which Depends on `llvm-22` — the package that
ships the symbolizer, and the `llvm-objcopy-22` the builder stage already uses:

```
$ docker run --rm ghcr.io/falkordb/falkordb-build:latest \
    sh -c 'dpkg -S /usr/bin/llvm-symbolizer-22'
llvm-22: /usr/bin/llvm-symbolizer-22
```

The runtime stage couldn't see it only because it's a separate stage
(`FROM debian:trixie-slim`).

## Changes

- Drop `wget`/`gnupg`/`lsb-release`, the `llvm.sh` fetch, the `apt.llvm.org` repo
  and `llvm-22` — **four round-trips to one third-party host, gone**.
- `COPY --from=builder` the symbolizer (101 KB) and the `libLLVM.so.22.1` it links
  (143 MB), preserving the `/usr/lib/llvm-22/{bin,lib}` layout. Its `RUNPATH` is
  `$ORIGIN/../lib`, so it is self-locating — no `LD_LIBRARY_PATH`, no `ldconfig`,
  no multiarch path to get wrong.
- Add the libLLVM runtime closure explicitly from Debian: `libcurl4` for the binary,
  `libedit2 libffi8 libxml2 libz3-4 libzstd1 zlib1g` for the library.
- `RUN llvm-symbolizer --version` as a build-time smoke test. `apt` used to resolve
  that closure for us; this makes a stale list fail the build loudly instead of
  silently degrading ASAN output to raw addresses at test time.
- Point `ASAN_SYMBOLIZER_PATH` at `/usr/lib/llvm-22/bin/llvm-symbolizer`.

## Testing

Built a probe image with the new `apt` list + `COPY` lines **verbatim** on the same
`debian:trixie-slim` base, then ran a real sanitizer trace through it — an
ASAN-instrumented binary compiled with `clang-22` in the toolchain image, executed
in the probe image:

```
==1==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow on address 0xfc1fbdde001d
WRITE of size 1 at 0xfc1fbdde001d thread T0
    #0 0xaaaab5620b14 in main /w/boom.c:4:11
…
allocated by thread T0 here:
    #1 0xaaaab5620ac4 in main /w/boom.c:3:23
```

Full `file:line:column` symbolization. The first probe attempt **failed** on a
missing `libedit.so.2` — that is how the dependency list above was derived, and why
the smoke test is in the Dockerfile.

The full ASAN image build is this PR's own `build-rc-asan-image` job; the stage's
other steps are unchanged.

## Memory / Performance Impact

Measured on the isolated stage (same base, only the `apt`/`COPY` portion, arm64
locally — CI builds amd64, so exact figures will differ):

| | image |
|---|---|
| before | **1.22 GB** |
| after | **301 MB** |

~920 MB smaller. The old `llvm.sh 22` pulled `clang-22`, `lldb-22`, `lld-22` and
`clangd-22` into a runtime image that never compiles anything — its default package
set, which the `apt-get purge` (wget/gnupg/lsb-release only) never removed — plus
~90 MB of unused `llvm-22` tools. Only the 143 MB `libLLVM` and the 101 KB binary
remain.

## Related Issues

Closes #2872

Not addressed here: `build/Dockerfile:74` has the same unpinned `apt.llvm.org`
pattern, but that image is prebuilt and cached in ghcr, so it is hit far less often.
Worth hardening separately.

pulls.title: Seek by id: accept compound value expressions opposite ID(n)
pulls.body:
Resolve: #2871

The seek-by-id optimizer recognized the ID(n) side of a filter by AST node type (AR_EXP_OP vs AR_EXP_OPERAND), so it only reduced a scan+filter to a NodeByIdSeek when the value compared against ID(n) was a bare operand (constant, parameter, or variable). A compound expression such as x + 1 is itself an AR_EXP_OP, so both sides were operations and the filter was not recognized, leaving a full scan + filter, e.g.:

  UNWIND range(0,10) AS x MATCH (a) WHERE ID(a) = x + 1 RETURN a

Recognize the ID(n) side by the scanned alias instead: the scanned node must be referenced on exactly one side, that side must be exactly ID(n), and the other side is taken as the value expression - which is then guaranteed to be independent of the scanned node and hence resolvable from the incoming record. The NodeByIdSeek op already evaluates its range expression per record, so no runtime changes are needed.

This enables the optimization for value expressions over upstream variables (ID(a) = x + 1), previously resolved nodes (WITH a MATCH (b) WHERE ID(b) = ID(a) + 1), reversed operands, inequalities and multi-bound ranges, and the label-scan variant, while still rejecting self-referential filters such as ID(a) = a.v.

Add flow-test coverage in test_node_by_id.py.

pulls.title: chore(deps): group Dependabot updates into one PR per ecosystem
pulls.body:
Thirteen single-dependency Dependabot PRs are open (8 on `main`, 5 on `master`), each burning a full CI matrix run and a separate review. Three of the six entries in `.github/dependabot.yml` still lacked `groups`; the `pip`, `uv` and `docker` entries were already aggregating.

## Changes

- **`github-actions` at `/`** → group `github-actions` (currently #2854, #2855, #2861)
- **`cargo` at `/`** → group `cargo-deps` (currently #2856–#2860)
- **`github-actions` at `/` with `target-branch: master`** → group `github-actions-master` (currently #2478, #2611, #2613, #2614, #2615)
- Refreshed the `master` entry's comment, which claimed it mirrored master's own config "verbatim" — it now carries a group that master's copy does not.

```yaml
- directory: /
  package-ecosystem: cargo
  schedule:
    interval: weekly
  groups:
    cargo-deps:
      patterns:
        - "*"
```

## Notes for review

- **Group names are unique across entries on purpose.** The two `github-actions` entries otherwise differ only by the branch segment of the generated group branch name.
- **One PR against `main` covers both engines.** Dependabot reads `dependabot.yml` from the default branch only; `master`'s copy is dead config, and C's bumps already flow through the `target-branch: master` entry that lives here (see #2255). Grouping `master`'s orphaned copy would need its own PR and only matters if the default branch is ever flipped back.
- **Majors are inside the groups** (`patterns: ["*"]`), consistent with the pre-existing entries, so one bad major blocks its group's PR. Splitting them out via a second group keyed on `update-types: ["version-update:semver-major"]` is a one-line follow-up if preferred.
- **The existing PRs are untouched.** Closing a Dependabot PR by hand tells it not to recreate that specific version, so the safer sequence is to let the first grouped run land before cleaning up whatever remains.

pulls.title: feat(effects): let v3 index records name several schema entities
pulls.body:
Closes #2866

## What changed

`CREATE_INDEX` and `DROP_INDEX` now name *n* schema entities instead of one. In the record head, straight after the `u32` schema tag:

```
was:  u32 label_id · string label
now:  u16 n · (u32 id, string name) × n      // n >= 1, sorted ascending by id
```

Everything from `u32 field_type` onward is byte-identical, and the position in the record is unchanged.

Id *and* name per entry, never a bare id, for the reason the attribute refs already work that way: the replica verifies the id against the name rather than trusting it. The count is guarded before allocating, as `IndexFields` already was.

Both records, symmetrically — a create that can name several entities and a drop that cannot would leave such an index undroppable over the wire.

**Attributes needed no change.** `fields` has been a list since the codec landed, per statement rather than per field; issue section 2 records what was verified and why it must stay that way.

## Unknown `field_type` bits are now refused

Previously ignored, which was not inert: the bits gate conditional sections of the options block, so a bit this build did not know meant the block was read one section short and the *next* record was parsed from inside this one. Where it did not — a drop carries no options — `index_type_of` called the unknown type a range index. Either way, a future C emitting CCH at a replica that predates it produced a misparse or a silently wrong index; it is now a clean refusal and a resync.

Known mask is `INDEX_FLD_KNOWN = 0x1F`, pinned by a test so widening it is a deliberate edit rather than a side effect. The writer is held to the same rule: this build will not emit a bit it could not read back.

## Ordering contract

Stated in both directions, because it is the one property a conformance fixture cannot arbitrate — a generated fixture is already in some order, so a corpus run passes whether the decoder enforces or tolerates.

> An encoder **MUST** sort ascending by id, so two engines agreeing on the set produce identical bytes. A decoder **MUST** accept any order, and keeps it as sent; re-encoding is what canonicalises.

Tolerant on purpose. Requiring ascending at decode is exactly what makes C's written-order attribute ids resync a Rust replica forever while C-to-C looks healthy. The attribute list has a reason this one lacks — its ids are positional against the value rows and `insert_attrs_rows` binary-searches the span — whereas every entry here carries its own id and name, so order is presentation.

## Version

`EFFECTS_VERSION` stays 3. v3 is in no tagged release, C master is still `EFFECTS_VERSION 2` with no v3 reader, and C's v3 branches are unmerged — so there is no deployed reader for this layout change to break, and a bump would document a compatibility story that does not exist. C's branches absorb the layout change before they merge; raising their version ceiling is not the gate.

## Apply

This build still applies only single-entity index records, because `Graph::create_index` takes one label. A record naming more is refused by name (`ApplyError::MultiSchemaIndexUnsupported`) rather than applied to its first entry, which would leave a replica indexing a subset of what the primary indexed with nothing to say so. The wire is ready for the new index type; the engine says plainly that it is not.

## Testing

176 `effects::v3` tests, up from 166. Every new guard was mutation-tested — removed on purpose, and the matching test confirmed to fail:

| guard removed | result |
|---|---|
| decode unknown-bit check | 2 tests fail |
| encode unknown-bit check | fails |
| encoder sort | fails |
| empty schema list check | fails |
| decoder tolerance (made strict) | fails |
| multi-schema apply refusal | fails (SIGSEGV — apply reaches `create_index` with no globals initialised, so it is caught but not by its assertion) |

**Flow tests.** All 92 effects flow tests pass on this branch — 18 in `test_effects_ddl.py` including the million-node constraint-race classes, and 74 across the other eight files.

One was added. Every index statement in the effects flow suite named a single attribute, so the record's attribute list — the part that was already a list before this branch — was only ever exercised at length one, and nothing end-to-end checked that both attributes cross. `test03_a_multi_attribute_statement_crosses_as_one_statement` covers create and drop. It is load-bearing rather than assumed: truncating the emitter's `fields` to its first entry fails it with `[['first']] == [['first', 'second']]` on the replica comparison while the primary stays correct — the quiet failure being guarded, since a replica with the narrower index still lists it and still answers queries, just not about the second property.

Two failures in the wider `cargo test -p graph` run, `build_bool_is_iso_and_grb_build_is_not` and `cap_at_or_above_batch_size_is_ignored`, reproduce with these five files reverted at HEAD and are not from this change.

## Dev AOFs will not replay

Effects buffers are built for the AOF as well as replication (`src/graph_core.rs:767`), and a failed apply under `LOADING` is `exit(1)` (`src/divergence_guard.rs:67-75`). A dev build with `appendonly yes` that created or dropped an index holds pre-list records and **will not restart**. Delete the AOF; it is disposable.

A test pins the property that matters there, over both opcodes: an old-layout record is refused, never misread, whatever the label id was — and refused without attempting the allocation, since `Reader::string` bounds-checks through `take` before copying. Measured across six label ids; the two opcodes do not even fail the same way, because a drop is five bytes shorter and its count guard fires where the create's does not.

## Follow-up, not in this PR

Five fixtures on `origin/effects-v3-corpus` (`rec_create_index`, `rec_create_index_text_partial`, `rec_create_index_vector`, `rec_create_index_vector_partial`, `rec_drop_index`) are invalidated by this change — all five verified refused, none misread. Their committed bytes were correct until now; the generator has not compiled against the engine since `77e9527f9` (9 Sep), so regenerating needs that ported first. Corpus maintenance is separately owned.

pulls.title: CCH path index: DDL syntax, incremental maintenance, full RDB seriali…
pulls.body:
Resolve: #3151
…zation

Convert Customizable Contraction Hierarchies from a pair of graph-mutating procedures into a first-class, graph-level index.

Index model
- CCHIndex keyed by the full (sorted+deduped relationship-type set, weight attribute); the hierarchy (ranks, shortcuts, up/down adjacency) is internal and never materialized as SHORTCUT edges / rank properties in the user graph.
- db.idx.cch.query performs rank-pruned bidirectional Dijkstra over the index.

DDL
- CREATE / DROP CCH INDEX FOR ()-[e:A|B]->() ON (e.w), sharing a single consolidated create-index grammar rule; index type is parsed as a plain string, multi-relationship-type patterns supported, multi-label nodes in CREATE INDEX rejected. db.idx.cch.create / .drop procedures removed.

Incremental maintenance
- Commit-coalesced dirty tracking (CLEAN < RECUSTOMIZE < REBUILD) with a scoped recustomize kernel (per-edge seed + scoped customize over lower common neighbours) for weight/edge changes, and a staleness valve; topology changes that add/remove hierarchy adjacency escalate to a full rebuild.

Effects & replication
- Dedicated create/drop CCH effects keyed by the full set; missing relationship types / weight attribute are created via GraphHub so they replicate before the CCH effect. Verified across GRAPH.EFFECT replication and a fresh replica FULLRESYNC.

Persistence (RDB v20, edited in place)
- The entire hierarchy is serialized into / restored from the RDB in a dedicated ENCODE_STATE_CCH_INDICES payload; no rebuild on load. Phase-1 triangulation scratch (xadj/adjncy/parent) is freed after build (~113 MB on se_vag). v19 decoder moved under decoders/prev; encoder/decoder bumped v19 -> v20.

Tests
- test_cch.py flow coverage: create/query/drop, key exactness (rel-type set + weight attr, order-agnostic, deduped), scoped recustomize vs SPpaths oracle, edge/node add/delete, memory report, single- and multi-index RDB reload, replica full-sync, AOF replay.

Validated at continental scale (se_vag, 3.14M nodes / 6.45M edges): build ~12s, point-to-point query p50 ~1.15ms, scoped updates sub-ms, RDB reload restores the index correct and live.

pulls.title: fix(stats): count Labels-added per assignment, not per new label type (#2655)
pulls.body:
## Summary

Fixes #2655 — the Rust engine's `Labels added` query statistic was computed as the delta in the schema's registered label count, i.e. the number of new label *types*, not the number of label *assignments* to nodes. The two happen to agree only when a query introduces each label type exactly once, so at any scale the value drifts far below the real count and, in the common `SET` on an already-known label, is dropped entirely (implicit `0`). The issue's four reproductions all fail on `edge-rs` today.

The C engine and Neo4j both count assignments; this PR aligns the Rust counter with that.

## Changes

- **`graph/src/runtime/runtime.rs`** — remove the schema-delta increment at the end of `Runtime::query` that produced the bug.
- **`graph/src/runtime/ops/create.rs`** — after `pending.set_nodes_labels(...)`, increment by `node_ids.len() * node.labels.len()`. Every node reserved in a CREATE is fresh, so each label in the pattern is a new assignment on each of them. `MergeOp` routes through the same `Runtime::create_batch`, so MERGE's create path is covered too.
- **`graph/src/runtime/ops/set.rs`** — in the `SetItem::Label` arm, count only labels the node does not already carry, consulting `Runtime::node_has_label_id` (which reads pending before the committed matrix). A repeated `SET n:L` in one query therefore counts once, and `SET n:L:L` (whose `OrderSet` dedups to a single label) counts once.

## Tests

New `tests/flow/test_labels_added_stat.py` pins:

- the four cases from #2655's report;
- a `SET` of an already-present label (must be `0`);
- the same `(node, label)` touched twice within one query (must be `1`).

## Test plan

- [ ] `cargo build`
- [ ] `cargo test -p graph`
- [ ] `RELEASE=1 pytest tests/flow/test_labels_added_stat.py -vv`
- [ ] Full flow-test suite

## Known follow-up

Several existing flow-test assertions on `labels_added` were calibrated against the previous (buggy) counter — for example `tests/flow/test_label_update.py::test_large_update_set` expects `1` for a `SET n:L` across ~5121 matched nodes, and `tests/flow/test_multi_label.py::test06_multi_label_merge` expects `1` for a `MERGE (:L2:L3)` where both labels are fresh on the new node. Those assertions will need to be updated to match the corrected semantics (per-assignment counts). I've kept them out of this PR to keep the diff focused and reviewable — happy to update them in this PR or a follow-up per maintainer preference, or to hand them a target list.

## Notes

- No changes to the wire format, the plan cache, or persistence — only the per-query stats counter.
- No new dependencies.
- The `Runtime::node_has_label_id` call in the SET path is O(#labels_on_node); this is bounded by pattern size in practice.

pulls.title: Fix duplicate nodes in concurrent read-only vector query pages
pulls.body:
## Problem

Two concurrent read-only `db.idx.vector.queryNodes` calls could make each other return **the same node several times in one result page**, silently displacing genuine neighbours (in the issue's six-querier measurement, a 160-row page came back with only 5 unique ids). Sequential queries and concurrent *non-vector* queries were unaffected, and the Rust engine does not reproduce it.

Full reproduction and measurements: #2848 (@ruze00 — thank you for an exemplary report).

## Root cause

`db.idx.vector.queryNodes` is served by RediSearch's vector-index path (HNSW in VectorSimilarity). Every search over an index shared **one** `VisitedNodesHandler` (the visited-set used to avoid revisiting nodes). With concurrent searches that shared state is corrupted in three ways — each can make a node be visited twice within a single search and returned twice in one page, at adjacent row positions (exactly the shape observed in the issue):

1. search entry points reassign the shared handler member, clobbering the handler an in-flight search is using;
2. `getFreshTag()` is a non-atomic `cur_tag++`, so two concurrent searches can receive the same tag;
3. a tag-wrap `reset()` (every 65536 scans) wipes the tags of in-flight scans.

## Fix

Every search now acquires a **dedicated visited-nodes handler from a mutex-guarded pool** for its whole lifetime and returns it when done:

- top-K, range search, and insertion-time layer searches acquire/release around the scan;
- batch iterators hold their handler across batches and return it on destruction;
- the tags array is passed to the scan helpers explicitly instead of through shared index state;
- `resizeIndex` resets handler storage when growing instead of refreshing tags in place;
- grow-on-demand pool, handlers reused across searches.

The change is in VectorSimilarity, delivered via submodule bumps:

- VectorSimilarity: [`fix-2848-concurrent-vector-query-dupes`](https://github.com/arnavgoel17/VectorSimilarity/tree/fix-2848-concurrent-vector-query-dupes) (based on the currently pinned `98d6a4d2`; mirrors the pool-based direction upstream `main` has since taken)
- RediSearch: FalkorDB/RediSearch#28 bumps `deps/VectorSimilarity` to it
- this PR bumps `deps/RediSearch` to that commit (`311f9012` → `b75e2b81`)

> ⚠️ **Merge order / CI note:** the pinned submodule commits must exist in the upstream repos for CI to resolve them. No current branch of `FalkorDB/VectorSimilarity` contains the pinned `98d6a4d2` anymore, so the VectorSimilarity-side commit needs to land there first (branch `fix-2848-concurrent-vector-query-dupes` is pushed to my fork and ready to be re-pointed wherever maintainers prefer). Until then, CI jobs that init submodules will fail with "reference is not a tree".

## Test

`test10_concurrent_knn_no_duplicates` (flow): while a second connection hammers the same vector index with KNN queries, 20 measured `k=160` KNN pages must each contain exactly `k` rows with **no duplicate ids** — the exact scenario from the issue, as a standing regression guard.

Fixes #2848

pulls.title: fix(effects/v3): end a run when a segment reads against it
pulls.body:
Closes #2842.

A run is collapsed into one bitmap and read back in a single direction, so every
segment inside it has to read that way too. Two paths put a segment into a run
going the other way, and both return early, before the `continues_run` check
that would have ended it:

* the lone-`Range` step-down rewrite claimed the run's direction only
  `if self.run.desc.is_none()`, so a run already committed to ascending kept a
  `RangeDescending`;
* the ordinary `Range` extension in the hot path grows a singleton into an
  ascending pair without consulting the run, which is the mirror — an ascending
  pair inside a descending run.

Every id survives the collapse and `len` stays right, so the decoder's
cardinality check passes and the buffer applies. An `IdList` is positional — row
*k* belongs to the *k*-th id as written — so two entities exchange values on the
replica with no error, no log and no resync. A state-only comparison calls it
green.

## Measured end to end

A primary/replica pair, same workload both ways, the replica taking three
`GRAPH.EFFECT` and no verbatim command either time:

```
before   master mispaired 0   replica mispaired 2   [[4, 5], [5, 4]]
after    master mispaired 0   replica mispaired 0
```

## The fix

One rule: a segment may take a direction only inside a run reading the same way,
and where it cannot, the run ends at that segment.

It is applied where a segment *acquires* a direction rather than where it is
charged. The charge point does observe the mirror case — but it cannot act
before the collapse, which is the actual argument for the earlier placement.

`restart` clears the direction, so the new run's direction is set at the same
moment; leaving it for the next push to decide reproduces the same bug one
segment further along.

## Cross-engine

C carried an independently written version of the same rule. A differential run
found the two designs diverged on a restarted run whose head is a two-id range —
order preserved on both sides, bytes different. C ported this structure. The two
builders now agree on 3,404 sequences with zero segmentation differences, and
this file reproduces those dumps exactly.

The 39-fixture conformance corpus is unaffected: all 36 id sequences in it encode
identically before and after.

## Tests

They assert the pairing, not the population. The id set, the count and `len` are
each blind to this by construction, and the pre-existing
`a_reversal_ends_a_run_rather_than_extending_it` passes on the unfixed builder
because it asserts the segment's *kind* — the property that matters is the
segment's direction relative to the run.

* `a_reversal_inside_a_run_does_not_reorder_the_ids` — a reversal at every
  position of a run long enough to collapse, both directions, through encode and
  decode.
* `a_restarted_run_head_is_folded_into_its_bitmap` — the one case order cannot
  see. Moving the restart one index later leaves every order-based test green,
  including the sweep below; only this one fails.
* `push_order_survives_the_wire_for_arbitrary_sequences` — a seeded sweep whose
  distribution is deliberately lopsided. 20,000 *uniform* random walks all passed
  against the unfixed builder, because a balanced walk reverses too often for any
  run to reach the collapse threshold.

All three were verified failing against a real `origin/main` checkout, with the
non-test code asserted byte-identical to main.

pulls.title: refactor(graph): make IdSpace the id allocation authority
pulls.body:
Closes #2839.

`IdSpace` judged id spaces while `Graph` owned the state it judged: two
counters and two recycle bins, moved by twelve raw writes across six
operations. This makes it the authority instead — it owns `live` and
`recycled`, and every id that changes state changes it through a method here.

### What moved

```rust
pub struct IdSpace {
    live: u64,                 // the entity count
    recycled: RoaringTreemap,  // the free set
    entry_bound: u64,          // where the open batch began
    taken: RoaringTreemap,     // what it has taken since
}
```

`Graph` keeps two of these and no counter or bitmap of its own;
`node_count()` and `recycled_node_ids()` read through. `reserve`, `cancel`,
`create` and `release` are methods on the space, taking no state but the ids.

That is the point rather than a side effect: the boundary is
`live + recycled.len()`, so every operation has to move both halves or
neither. A free-set write that nothing counted was #2797, and the
node-id-liveness bug before it.

### The invariant

```text
live + recycled.len() == entry_bound + taken.len()
```

True at every moment and **returned as an error**, not asserted — a corrupt
id space hands out ids that are already live, and a `debug_assert` says
nothing in the build where that matters. Failing is also the cheap outcome: a
write query holds a private MVCC version, so the damage is discarded rather
than published and replicated.

Making it total required a change of meaning. `taken` counts ids the batch
*took* — created, or reserved and then cancelled — because both move the
boundary. Counting only creates made the equation false for every cancelled
reservation, which is exactly what kept `verify` off the write path:
`CREATE (a)-[:R]->(b) DELETE b` reported
`Miscounted { graph_bound: 2, expected: 1 }` on a legitimate query.

With that fixed, the write path is now held to the same check a replica is
(#2839 step 4). It is the one change here that can fail a user's query.

### Batches cannot be left unopened

Forgetting to open a batch was **silent**. Measured by deleting the only
load-bearing call: the entire flow suite passed while
`CREATE (n) DELETE n WITH 1 AS x CREATE (m)` allocated id 1 instead of 0.
Against a C primary that is a divergence in id-reuse order, which costs a
full resync per delete-then-create cycle and which a state-only comparison
calls green.

- `Graph::in_batch(f)` for callers whose batch *is* a scope — a whole effects
  buffer, one `GRAPH.BULK` command. Opens before, verifies after.
- `Graph::roll_id_batches()` for the write path, whose batch is not: it ends
  and the next begins partway through one `next()` of a pull-based operator,
  across many `AtomicRefCell` borrows. Fused into `Pending::end_segment`, so
  forgetting it also forgets to discard the segment's mutations and the next
  commit dies with `node 0 is already live below the boundary 0`.

One residual, stated because it is not closed: a segment whose only content
is a cancellation still fails silently, since a batch that never rolled over
is indistinguishable from a longer one and `verify` passes on either.
Catching it needs an epoch the id space does not have.

### Naming

`Graph::deleted_nodes()` returned the recycle bin — ids free to hand out
again — while `Pending::deleted_nodes` held ids about to be deleted. Two
names, one spelling, opposite predicates, and the same collision in
`is_node_deleted` on both types. Now `recycled_node_ids` / `node_deletes` /
`is_node_pending_delete`. The collision demonstrated itself during the
rename: a mechanical pass rewrote `Pending::deleted_nodes()` into
`recycled_node_ids()` at `include_pending.rs:95`, which is the exact
inversion. The compiler caught it.

### Tests

Two new kinds, both checked against deliberate breaks rather than assumed to
cover anything:

- A **differential test** drives random sequences of every operation against
  a reference model built from plain `BTreeSet`s. It caught an unstated
  precondition — every reservation must be settled before a batch closes,
  because the boundary deliberately does not count reservations (they would
  grow the GraphBLAS matrix dimension `algo_procedures.rs` derives from it
  while leaving its liveness gate off). Now documented and pinned.
- `release`'s two-set contract, which fails if `requested` and `freed` are
  collapsed into one.

Breaks confirmed caught: `reserve` ignoring `taken` (by the model),
`release` skipping the counter (by the invariant), `cancel` not recording
(by the invariant), and the batch shape shifted by one (by `verify`, on the
write path).

### Deliberately not in this PR

Issue step 3 — returning the skipped set from `delete_relationships`. I made
the skip fatal and ran everything: flow 1507/1507, e2e 89/89, TCK 2456/0.
**It never fires.** Widening the signature would add surface for a path with
no traffic. The skip is untested rather than unreachable, and on the apply
path silently skipping an edge a replica does not have would hide divergence
rather than guard it — worth its own issue.

### Verification

Built against `GRAPHBLAS_LIB_DIR=$HOME/.local/lib`; the `/usr/local/lib`
fallback is a month older than the checked-in bindings and fails
`build_bool_is_iso_and_grb_build_is_not`, which is the canary for exactly
that.

| suite | result |
|---|---|
| `cargo test -p graph --release --lib` | 404 passed, 0 failed |
| `cargo test -p graph --lib` (debug) | 403 passed, 1 failed |
| flow | 1507 / 1507 |
| e2e + functions | 124 passed |
| mvcc + concurrency | 14 passed |
| TCK | 173 features, 2456 scenarios, 0 failed |

The debug failure is `cap_at_or_above_batch_size_is_ignored` — debug-only and
pre-existing from #2757. `fmt` clean; `clippy --all-targets` has the same
three pre-existing arg-count warnings and no new ones.

pulls.title: fix: give every CALL {} body its entry projection as a record boundary
pulls.body:
Fixes #2602
Fixes #2601

Both issues are the same defect, so they're fixed together.

## The bug

C's invariant is narrower than "record indices are per-plan-segment". In `build_call_subquery.c`, `_find_feeding_points` plants an `Argument` **only beneath a childless `Project`**, and `ProjectConsume` allocates a fresh record from its own plan's map, copies only the projected expressions in, and deletes its input. So in C the outer record enters a subquery body *only* through a projection that rebuilds it — **no body operator ever sees the outer record.** For a body that imports nothing there is no such tap, so C plants no `Argument` at all, and its row-at-a-time `ApplyConsume` (`nargs == 0`) resets and re-runs the body per outer record, which is where the cardinality comes from.

Rust already had the first of those two routes, and used it correctly — that is why every `CALL { WITH x ... }` variant was already right on `main`. But it emitted the entry projection only when something was actually imported. Without one, the `Argument` feeds the body's scans and traversals **directly**, so the outer row reaches them — and because a runtime row is a dense array indexed by `Variable.id` alone (`scope_id` never reaches the row) while the body's ids restart at 0 in its fresh scope, the outer row doesn't merely leak in, it occupies the very slots the body is about to write.

That single missing boundary produces both reported symptoms:

**#2602** — the body's predicate is tested against the imported value. `x` (scope 1, id 0) and `n` (body scope, id 0) are the same slot, so `push_filters_down` legitimately concludes the `Argument` provides the conjunct's variable and pushes the filter *under* the scan, leaving `n` unfiltered:

```
        Apply
            Project
                Node By Label Scan | (x:A:B)
            Project
                Node By Label Scan | (n:A:B)
                    Filter                  <-- tested against x
                        Argument
```

With a non-entity import the same read raises `Type mismatch: expected Map, Node, Edge, ... but was Integer`, and a `SET` in the body escapes its filter and writes to the whole label.

**#2601** — the incoming row already has that slot bound, so an unbound scan endpoint looks already bound and a full relationship scan degrades into an expand out of the imported node; the count tracks that node's out-degree.

## The fix

Rust cannot take C's second route — its `Apply` is batched, and the `Argument` is what carries cardinality and `origin_row` correlation into the sub-plan (`BatchOp::set_argument_batch` installs the input batch at that leaf; without it the batch is dropped). So it takes C's *other* route for every body: **emit the body's entry projection unconditionally, projecting nothing when nothing is imported.**

The plan gains a `Project` above the body's `Argument` — the same shape the explicit-import path already produced — and the filter now sits above the body's scan, as in C:

```
Project
    Apply
        Project
            Node By Label Scan | (x:A:B)
        Project
            Filter                          <-- above the scan, as in C
                Node By Label Scan | (n:A:B)
                    Project                 <-- the body's record boundary
                        Argument
```

No new concept is introduced: `ProjectOp` already builds a fresh batch holding only what it projects and drops its input, exactly as `ProjectConsume` does. An empty projection still carries row count and `origin_row`, which is all a body importing nothing needs from the outer stream.

Two supporting changes the empty projection needs:

- **`ProjectOp` fast path** — build the columnless batch directly (`Batch::rows_only`) instead of walking every row to push an empty `Row`.
- **`BatchedResultEmitter::start_batch`** gathered parent state only when the parent had *columns*, documenting the assumption that *"a parent carrying origins always has at least one column"* — true only because origins had been stamped exclusively by `clone_active_rows_seq_origin`, which clones the outer batch's columns. A columnless entry projection breaks that assumption, and dropping the origins detached every result from the input row it belonged to (the `3 x 3` cross product collapsed onto the first `x`). It now gathers when the parent carries columns **or** origins. Caught by the added tests, not by reading.

## Verification

Reproduced both issues on `main` first, then re-ran the same repros. Every row of both issues' tables, including the triage comments' extra variants, now matches C:

| #2602 | before | after / C |
|---|---|---|
| `MATCH (x:A:B) WITH x CALL { MATCH (n:A:B {id:1}) RETURN n.id AS id } RETURN x.id, id` | `(1,1) (1,2) (1,3)` | `(1,1) (2,1) (3,1)` ✅ |
| `WITH 1 AS keep CALL {…} RETURN count(id)` | `Type mismatch … was Integer` | `1` ✅ |
| `WITH 'q' AS keep CALL {…} RETURN count(id)` | `Type mismatch … was String` | `1` ✅ |
| `WHERE n.id = 1` instead of the inline map | `(1,1) (1,2) (1,3)` | `(1,1) (2,1) (3,1)` ✅ |
| no `WITH` (`MATCH (x:A:B) CALL {…}`) | `(1,1) (1,2) (1,3)` | `(1,1) (2,1) (3,1)` ✅ |
| `CALL { MATCH (n:A:B {id:1}) SET n.hit = true … }` | `Properties set: 3`, all 3 nodes | `Properties set: 1`, only `id:1` ✅ |

| #2601 | before | after / C |
|---|---|---|
| `CREATE (a:Seed)-[:R]->(b:Seed) WITH * CALL { MATCH p=(n3:l10)-[]-(n4:l5) … }` | `0` | `64` ✅ |
| `MATCH (a:Hub) WITH *` + full rel scan in body | `5` (Hub's out-degree) | `6` ✅ |
| `MATCH (a:Leaf) WITH *` / `(a:Iso) WITH *` | `1` / `0` | `6` / `6` ✅ |
| `WITH a, 1 AS k` / `WITH 1 AS k, a` / `WITH a, b` | `0` | `6` ✅ |
| rel probe inside the body after a rel `CREATE` | `1` of `33` | `33` ✅ |

All controls that were already correct stay correct: no-import `CALL {}`, no-filter body, node-only `CREATE`, `MERGE`, `DELETE`, `SET`, read-only leading clause, and the `-[*0..1]-` variable-length form.

Regression tests in `tests/flow/test_call_subquery.py` (`test_54`, `test_55`) cover both issues' full variant tables plus the correlation cases that caught the emitter bug. Both fail on unpatched `main` with exactly the reported symptoms.

Suites, all on this branch:

- `cargo test -p graph --release` — 400 passed, 0 failed
- flow (`./flow.sh`) — **1509 passed, 0 failed**
- `tests/test_e2e.py tests/test_functions.py tests/test_mvcc.py tests/test_concurrency.py` — 138 passed
- TCK — 173 features / 2456 scenarios / 10140 steps passed, 0 failed
- `cargo fmt --all --check` clean; `cargo clippy --all-targets` adds no new warning (the 7 remaining are all in untouched files)

Not benchmarked: the entry projection is reachable only from `CALL {}` body binding, and the emitter change only adds a gather where correlation would otherwise be lost, so no shared path gets slower.

## Note on the commits

The first commit took a different approach — reserving the outer row's slots in the body scope so the body's ids started above them. It fixed both repros and passed every suite, but it avoided the collision without establishing the boundary that causes it. The second commit replaces it with the boundary itself and deletes the reservation. Review the second.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

- **Bug Fixes**
  - Improved `CALL` subqueries with no imported variables so results stay associated with the correct input rows.
  - Fixed subquery scope isolation so body variables and filters don’t inadvertently use imported values.
  - Corrected unbound relationship scans and fixed-length pattern matching so they operate independently of imported values.
  - Fixed cross products, constant returns, and entity writes in subqueries to preserve input-row associations and affect only the entity selected within the subquery.

pulls.title: perf(graph): read narrow label rows by point probe instead of a row iterator
pulls.body:
## Summary

`Graph::get_node_label_ids` allocated a fresh GraphBLAS row iterator for **every node it read**. Attaching and freeing a `GxB_Iterator` costs ~1,700 instructions — a number already measured and documented in `matrix.rs` — and that cost is paid per node to read a row that, on the overwhelmingly common narrow-schema graph, contains a single entry. The iterator setup dominates the read it performs.

This is the label-projection path shared by `RETURN n` serialization, `labels(n)`, node delete, `expand_into` and effects emit.

The repo had already applied exactly this fix pattern twice elsewhere but never here: `node_has_label_id` uses a cheap `node_labels_matrix.get(row, col)` point read (documented with measured numbers), and `delete_relationships` reuses one re-seekable iterator. This PR extends the point-read pattern to label projection.

## Changes

- `graph/src/graph/graphblas/versioned_matrix.rs`
  - Add `VersionedMatrix::<bool>::probe_row_into`, which fills a caller-owned `SmallVec` by point-probing a row. It has a fast path that reads the committed base alone when both deltas are empty, and a general path through `self.get` that resolves `dp`/`dm` normally.
- `graph/src/graph/graph.rs`
  - Add `LABEL_PROBE_MAX = 6`, documented with the measured crossover sweep.
  - `get_node_label_ids` now branches on schema width: probe when `node_labels.len() <= LABEL_PROBE_MAX`, otherwise keep the existing iterator. Returns `Either` so neither arm boxes.

The threshold was **measured, not estimated**. An instruction-count estimate predicted a crossover near 32 labels; interleaved A/B measurement put it near 8:

| labels | Δ |
|---|---|
| 1 | **-8.0%** |
| 4 | **-6.7%** |
| 6 | **-7.2%** |
| 8 | break-even |
| 12 | +5.5% |
| 32 | +45% |

Hence 6, with wide schemas explicitly left on the iterator. The doc comment records this sweep so the next person does not have to rediscover it.

### Column-range safety

`get_label_id_mut` calls `self.resize()` immediately after `intern_label`, reconciling `node_labels_matrix` to nodes × labels. So every column `< node_labels.len()` is in bounds — the same guarantee `node_has_label_id` already relies on. Ordering is preserved because the probe walks columns ascending, matching the iterator's ascending `(row, col)` order.

## Testing

- `cargo fmt --all -- --check` — clean
- `CXX=clang++ cargo clippy --all-targets` — no new warnings (3 pre-existing "too many arguments" on untouched functions)
- `cargo test -p graph --release` — 392 passed. 1 failure, `build_bool_is_iso_and_grb_build_is_not`, **verified pre-existing** by stashing and re-running on base
- `pytest tests/test_e2e.py tests/test_functions.py` — 124 passed
- `pytest tests/test_mvcc.py tests/test_concurrency.py` — 14 passed
- TCK — 173 features, **2456 scenarios passed, 0 failed**
- `./flow.sh` — 1502/1503. The one failure (`test_replication_states::test_replication_permutations`) **verified pre-existing** by running it against a base-module build via `TARGET_DIR`
- Extended the existing randomized `delta_invariants_hold_across_mutation_sequences` harness so `probe_row_into` is asserted against the model on every row after **every** mutation step. That sequence drives `set`/`remove`/`set_all`/`remove_mask`, folds and version boundaries, so the probe is checked against `dp`-shadowed and `dm`-masked pairs that only the three-way merge normally resolves — the exact cases where a point read could plausibly diverge from `iter`.
- Differential label-semantics test (multi-label, `SET n:X`, `REMOVE n:X`, combined set+remove, node delete, `CREATE ... WITH ... MATCH` pending-state mixing): output **byte-identical** to base excluding timing lines.

## Memory / Performance Impact

**Memory:** strictly lower. Removes a per-node `GxB_Iterator` allocation/free pair on the label path; the replacement writes into a caller-owned `SmallVec<[u64; 4]>` that stays inline for up to 4 labels. No per-entity overhead is added, and no new allocation occurs in the narrow-schema case.

**Performance**, 10k-node single-label graph, 9 interleaved reps, medians:

| Query | base | this PR | Δ |
|---|---|---|---|
| `MATCH (n:Person) RETURN n` | 9.039ms | 8.223ms | **-9.0%** |
| `MATCH (n:Person) RETURN labels(n)` | 5.031ms | 4.495ms | **-10.7%** |
| `MATCH (n:Person) RETURN n.name` | 1.287ms | 1.159ms | noise — never calls the changed code |
| `MATCH (n:Person) RETURN count(n)` | — | — | 0.0% |

Measurements interleave base and PR rounds within a single time window and compare medians *and* minimums, because the host is shared and single-shot A/B was not reproducible. An earlier run showed `labels(n)` at -24.4%; the conservative 9-rep figure is quoted as the headline.

**Honest limitation:** the canonical `bench/` SETUP graph registers ~13 labels, which is above `LABEL_PROBE_MAX`, so the standard 317-query suite will show no change. The win targets narrow-schema graphs, which are the common case in practice; wide schemas are deliberately left on the iterator, and the sweep above shows why.

pulls.title: Fix Debian runtime builds masking package upgrade failures
pulls.body:
## Problem

In both Debian runtime Dockerfiles, the ungrouped `|| true` after the final optional `apt-get autoremove` applies to the preceding `&&` chain. An earlier `apt-get update`, installation or `dist-upgrade` failure can therefore be hidden, and the image build reports success after cleanup.

Group that fallback so it tolerates only the intended optional cleanup. This targets the supported `4.20` branch; it does not change the image's package selection or scanner policy.

## Validation

- Added a dependency-free regression which executes the actual Dockerfile RUN instructions under `/bin/sh` with inert command stubs. All 16 scenarios pass: required failures propagate, successful installation passes, and explicitly optional cleanup failures remain tolerated. The original Dockerfiles fail all eight required-failure scenarios.
- Run the regression in the existing pre-build CI job: `python3 tests/docker/test_runtime_package_failures.py`.
- Built the patched Debian server runtime locally on Linux amd64 with fresh base image/package metadata and no build cache, reusing the unchanged published v4.20.4 module. Redis/graph create, read, save, container replacement and subsequent writes passed. This validates the runtime image; it is not a fresh engine compilation or an arm64 test.

- Trivy 0.70.0 against the rebuilt server runtime (15 September 2026 database): zero fixable HIGH/CRITICAL findings. The unfiltered scan still reports 36 HIGH findings without an available fix; no clean-all-severities claim is made.

The failure-masking bug is reproduced directly; there is no claim that a historical upgrade failure caused the current published image's dependency findings. Published full images also need the separate browser dependency fixes and a rebuild (the Sharp update is already tracked in FalkorDB/falkordb-browser#2091).

pulls.title: fix: identify virtual keys the way the C engine does
pulls.body:
Fixes #2773. Replaces #2786, which fixed the same issue a different way — see **Why not #2786** below.

## Reproduction

A single synchronous `SAVE` destroyed any graph whose key began with `__placeholder` / `__vkey_placeholder`, with no error to the client. `SHUTDOWN` saves too, so a restart lost it as well.

```
GRAPH.QUERY "__placeholder_mydata" "UNWIND range(1,200) AS i CREATE (:Keep {v:i})"
EXISTS "__placeholder_mydata"     --> 1
SAVE                              --> OK
EXISTS "__placeholder_mydata"     --> 0    <-- destroyed
```

## Root cause

The pre-save sweep scanned the keyspace for `graphdata` keys and then had to decide, key by key, which results were real graphs and which were the module's own bookkeeping. It decided by the graph's **name**:

```rust
let name = g.borrow().name().to_string();
if name.starts_with("__placeholder") || name.starts_with("__vkey_placeholder") {
    stale_keys.push(key_name);   // deleted below
}
```

The only evidence was a prefix the client is free to choose.

## How the C engine avoids the question

C never asks whether a key is a real graph or its own bookkeeping — three things make the question unnecessary (`src/module_event_handlers.c` on `master`):

| | C |
|---|---|
| Enumerate graphs to save | `Globals_ScanGraphs` — the module's own registry, no keyspace SCAN |
| Delete virtual keys after **save** | exact names recorded by `GraphEncodeContext_AddMetaKey` |
| Delete virtual keys after **load** | exact names recorded by `GraphDecodeContext_AddMetaKey`, identified at decode time by *"the virtual key name is not equal the graph name"* |

C also keeps that last comparison honest: `GraphContext_Rename` re-points `gc->graph_name` at the new key.

## Fix

Port that structure.

* **`create_virtual_keys` enumerates `GRAPH_REGISTRY`** instead of scanning — Rust's existing analogue of `Globals_ScanGraphs`. Virtual keys are never registered, so no test is needed to exclude them. `scan_and_clean_graphdata_keys` and its prefix match are deleted (~140 lines).
* **`DECODE_STATE.meta_keys`** records each key of a multi-key graph whose name differs from the graph's, and `delete_stale_virtual_keys` deletes exactly those once the load ends — `GraphDecodeContext` plus `_ClearKeySpaceMetaKeys(ctx, /*decode=*/true)`. `delete_virtual_keys` already did the encode-side equivalent from `VKEY_STATE`.
* **`rdb_load_graph` returns a `LoadedKey`** saying which kind of key it decoded, so a virtual key is not registered as a graph.

A registry entry does not by itself prove a key of that name holds that graph — the registry is keyed by a lossy `String`, and a graph kept under a non-UTF-8 key (`test_binary_key_name_scan_skip`) is indexed under a name that addresses nothing. `key_holds_graph` re-opens the key and compares the stored value's allocation, so such a graph is left whole rather than scattered across virtual keys named after a key it does not occupy. This is the same graph the old scan skipped, for the same reason.

## Second bug this surfaced

The decode-time comparison needs the header's name to track the key, and it did not. A `RENAME` moves the graph but leaves `Graph::name()` alone, where C's `GraphContext_Rename` updates it. Every key of a renamed multi-key graph therefore looked like a virtual key of a graph nobody was loading, and **the graph was lost outright on the next restart** — pre-existing on `main`, and reproduced here before the fix:

```
--- SAVE, restart from RDB ---
keys: plain              <-- `renamed` gone, 200 nodes with it
renamed -> (empty)
```

The header now carries the Redis key the graph is written under. `Graph::name()` had two consumers; the buggy prefix check was the other one.

## Why not #2786

That PR kept the scan and kept asking the question — it swapped the evidence from a name prefix to an `AtomicBool` on `ThreadedGraph`. That flag has to be set at every construction site, cleared at every promotion site, made atomic because the sweep reads it through `data_ptr()` without the lock, and justified with a memory-ordering argument pairing a `Release` store against an `Acquire` load. C needs none of that, because it does not scan. Removing the scan removes the flag, the ordering argument, and the two construction sites that must not forget it.

## Regression tests

Both confirmed failing on `main` and passing here.

* `test_encode_decode.py::test_18_user_graph_named_like_internal_placeholder` — covers `__placeholder_mydata`, `__vkey_placeholder_mydata`, `__placeholder` and `__vkey_placeholder`, asserting each survives `SAVE`, a `DEBUG RELOAD` round-trip and a second `SAVE` with its contents intact, and that each save leaves the keyspace exactly as it found it (proving every virtual key it created was cleaned up). The suite runs with `VKEY_MAX_ENTITY_COUNT 10`, so its 200-node graphs span 19 virtual keys each.
* `test_encode_decode.py::test_encode_decode_rename::test_01_renamed_multi_key_graph_round_trips` — its own `Env`, and a genuine `SAVE` + process restart. Both `DEBUG RELOAD` and RLTest's `restartAndReload` (which rewrites the AOF and never touches an RDB) hide this one, and with another graph alongside it in the RDB the recovery is order-dependent, hence the separate env.

## Validation

* `cargo fmt --all -- --check` — clean
* `CXX=clang++ cargo clippy --all-targets` — no errors, no new warnings
* `cargo test -p graph` — 384 passed; 1 pre-existing failure (`batched_result_emitter::cap_at_or_above_batch_size_is_ignored`, confirmed failing on a stashed tree, from #2757)
* `./flow.sh` — 1498/1498
* `pytest tests/test_e2e.py tests/test_functions.py tests/test_mvcc.py tests/test_concurrency.py` — 138/138

TCK was not run: nothing on the query path changed.

* **Tests**
  * Added coverage for graph names matching internal key patterns.
  * Added validation that renamed graphs remain available after restart.

pulls.title: fix(graph): order-insensitive constraint matching and duplicate property validation
pulls.body:
Resolves #2792

### Overview
In FalkorDB's Rust graph engine, `Constraint::matches` previously compared property slices position-by-position using `.zip().all()`. Consequently:
1. `(a, b)` and `(b, a)` were treated as distinct constraints in Rust, whereas the C engine canonicalizes/sorts attributes, causing state divergence across replication (e.g. effects-v3 replication where master emits both orders).
2. Dropping a constraint using a different property order (e.g. `GRAPH.CONSTRAINT DROP g MANDATORY NODE P PROPERTIES 2 b a`) failed with `Constraint does not exist`.
3. Creating a constraint with duplicate properties (e.g. `PROPERTIES 2 a a`) was not rejected upfront, whereas C rejects it with `"Properties cannot contain duplicates"`.

Following maintainer recommendation (**Option A** in #2792):
- Updated `Constraint::matches` to compare property sets without regard to order (`p1.sort_unstable(); p2.sort_unstable(); p1 == p2`).
- Added duplicate property validation in `Graph::create_constraint`: checks for duplicates and returns `Err("Properties cannot contain duplicates".into())`, matching C engine behavior.
- Retained caller-defined property ordering in `self.properties` so user-facing inspection via `CALL db.constraints()` preserves the original property order declared at creation.

### Testing
- **Rust unit tests:**
  - `graph/src/graph/constraint.rs`: Verified `Constraint::matches` with identical order, reversed order, 3-element permutations, non-matching properties, different lengths, labels, entity types, and constraint types.
  - `graph/src/graph/graph.rs`: Verified duplicate property rejection (`"Properties cannot contain duplicates"`), order-insensitive duplicate constraint detection (`"Constraint already exists"`), and dropping using reversed property ordering.
- **Python flow tests:**
  - `tests/flow/test_constraint.py`: Added `testOrderInsensitiveConstraintMatching` testing end-to-end node and relationship constraint creation, duplicate property rejection, order-insensitive duplicate detection, and dropping with reversed order.

pulls.title: fix(query-engine): clear pending properties on SET replace branches
pulls.body:
Cypher replacement form (\SET x = {...}\ or \SET x = y\) is required to replace the target entity's full property map. Previously, only the node-target/map-source branch cleared pending properties staged earlier in the query, while the remaining branches only cleared committed properties from the graph. In addition, Pending lacked a clear_relationship_attributes counterpart.

This commit:
- Adds \clear_relationship_attributes\ on \Pending\ to remove pending attributes for both newly created and existing relationships.
- Calls \clear_node_attributes\ and \clear_relationship_attributes\ Resolves #2776
- 
- ### Summary of Changes
- 
- In Cypher, property replacement (`SET x = { ... }` or `SET x = y`) must replace the target entity's full property map, removing any existing properties.
- 
- While committed graph properties were already cleared, 5 of 6 replacement branches in `SetOp` (`graph/src/runtime/ops/set.rs`) were omitting the call to clear uncommitted `Pending` state. In addition, `Pending` (`graph/src/runtime/pending.rs`) lacked a `clear_relationship_attributes` method.
- 
- As a result, mutations or initial property definitions staged earlier in the same query (or in chained mutations without an intermediate commit) survived the replace operation, silently turning replacement (`=`) into merge (`+=`).
- 
- ### Details
- 1. **`graph/src/runtime/pending.rs`**:
-    - Implemented `clear_relationship_attributes(id: RelationshipId)` matching `clear_node_attributes(id: NodeId)`. Clears both `new_relationships_attrs` and `existing_relationships_attrs`.
- 2. **`graph/src/runtime/ops/set.rs`**:
-    - Added `clear_node_attributes(id)` to:
-      - Node target, Node source (`Value::Node(tid)`)
-      - Node target, Relationship source (`Value::Relationship(rel)`)
-    - Added `clear_relationship_attributes(target_rel)` to:
-      - Relationship target, Map source (`Value::Map(map)`)
-      - Relationship target, Node source (`Value::Node(sid)`)
-      - Relationship target, Relationship source (`Value::Relationship(source_rel)`)
- 3. **`tests/flow/test_entity_update.py`**:
-    - Added `test42_set_replace_clears_pending_properties` covering all 6 replacement paths and existing-entity mutations within uncommitted transactions.across all missing replace branches in \SetOp\.
- Adds regression flow test \	est42_set_replace_clears_pending_properties\ covering all 6 replacement paths and existing-entity mutations.

Fixes #2776.

- **Bug Fixes**
  - Corrected property replacement behavior for nodes and relationships.
  - Replacing an entity’s properties now consistently removes previously staged or existing properties, including updates made earlier in the same query.
  - Improved consistency when replacing properties from maps or other nodes and relationships.

pulls.title: fix: canonical constraint key encoding for numeric equivalence (#2774)
pulls.body:
## Summary
`Graph::build_composite_key` previously used `format!("{v:?}")` with literal `'|'` delimiters to build uniqueness keys for `UNIQUE` constraint validation and enforcement. Because Rust's `Debug` format for `Value` is type-tagged (`Int(1)` vs `Float(1.0)`), `UNIQUE` constraints failed to reject numeric duplicates that differed only by numeric representation, even though Cypher equality considers `1 == 1.0`. In addition, literal pipe delimiters were vulnerable to value collisions.

## Changes
- Implemented `Value::encode_constraint_key(&self, buf: &mut Vec<u8>)` with canonical binary key encoding:
-   - Whole floats within 64-bit integer range normalize to `TAG_INT` (including `-0.0` and `0.0` normalizing to `0i64`), ensuring `Value::Int(1)` and `Value::Float(1.0)` produce byte-for-byte identical keys.
-   - Distinct types (such as `String("1")` and `Int(1)`) are unambiguously tagged.
-   - Other types (`Point`, `VecF32`, `List`, `Map`, `Datetime`, `Date`, etc.) are canonically encoded.
- - Updated `Graph::build_composite_key` to frame each property segment with a length prefix, eliminating delimiter collisions.
- - Added unit tests in `composite_key_tests` verifying numeric equivalence (`1` and `1.0`, `0` and `0.0` / `-0.0`), distinct type non-collision, and delimiter safety.
- - Added regression flow test `test10_unique_constraint_numeric_type_equivalence` in `tests/flow/test_constraint.py`.
Fixes #2774

<!-- This is an auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->

## Summary by CodeRabbit

- **Bug Fixes**
  - Improved uniqueness constraint handling for values with different representations but equivalent numeric values, such as `1` and `1.0`.
  - Prevented uniqueness key collisions between different value types and complex values containing delimiter characters.
  - Ensured unordered map values are handled consistently when checking uniqueness constraints.

- **Tests**
  - Added coverage for numeric equivalence, value-type distinctions, embedded delimiters, and multi-property uniqueness keys.

pulls.title: fix(planner): materialize named paths created by CREATE (#1279)
pulls.body:
Fixes #1279.

## Problem Description
Executing `CREATE p=(n) RETURN p` or `CREATE p=(a)-[r:R]->(b) RETURN p` in FalkorDB failed with `'p0' not defined` or produced an unmaterialized path result containing `NULL`.

## Root Cause
In `graph/src/planner/mod.rs`, the `QueryIR::Create` planning branch was emitting `tree!(IR::Create(Box::new(filtered)))` directly without checking for declared paths. Unlike `QueryIR::Merge` (which wraps its plan in `tree!(IR::PathBuilder(paths.to_vec()), merge)`), `CREATE` was omitting `IR::PathBuilder`, leaving the bound `Type::Path` variable unmaterialized in the tuple stream prior to projection.

## Changes Made
1. **Planner (`graph/src/planner/mod.rs`):**
   - Extract declared named paths from `filtered.paths().to_vec()`.
   - Wrap `IR::Create` with `tree!(IR::PathBuilder(paths), create)` whenever paths are present, mirroring the MERGE clause pattern.
   - Using `filtered.paths()` rather than `pattern.paths()` ensures paths visited in earlier clauses are not erroneously overwritten or re-materialized.

2. **Regression Tests (`tests/flow/test_create_clause.py`):**
   - Added `test04_named_path_in_create` testing:
     - Single-node named paths: `CREATE p=(n:Person {name: 'Alice'}) RETURN p`
     - Relationship named paths: `CREATE p=(a:Person {name: 'Bob'})-[r:KNOWS {since: 2026}]->(b:Person {name: 'Charlie'}) RETURN p`
     - Path functions on created paths: `length(p)`, `nodes(p)`
   - Full docstrings meeting code quality and pre-merge review standards.

## Opire Bounty Claim
/claim #1279

- **Bug Fixes**
  - Fixed `CREATE` queries to preserve already-bound path variables and make newly created named paths available in results, including paths with nodes and relationships.
  - Named paths created in a `CREATE` clause can be used with functions such as `length()` and `nodes()`.

- **Tests**

pulls.title: fix(docker): restore redis-sentinel / redis-check-rdb / redis-check-aof entry points in the runtime image
pulls.body:
`build/runtime/Dockerfile` builds Redis itself and copies only `redis-server` and `redis-cli` out of the `redis-builder` stage. `make install` does create `redis-sentinel`, `redis-check-rdb` and `redis-check-aof` as symlinks to `redis-server` (the binary picks its mode from `argv[0]`), but they never reach the runtime image — so `:edge` images lack entry points every previous FalkorDB image shipped, breaking consumers that exec them (e.g. JFalkorDB's `SentinelIT`: `exec: "redis-sentinel": executable file not found in $PATH`).

Both changes are in the `server` stage, which `full` inherits, so they cover `falkordb/falkordb:edge` and `falkordb/falkordb-server:edge`.

### Changes

- **Recreate the three entry points** after the existing `COPY`s. Recreated rather than `COPY`'d because Docker dereferences symlinks — copying would triple the 4.8 MB binary. As relative symlinks they cost 12 bytes each.

  ```dockerfile
  RUN ln -s redis-server /usr/local/bin/redis-sentinel && \
      ln -s redis-server /usr/local/bin/redis-check-rdb && \
      ln -s redis-server /usr/local/bin/redis-check-aof
  ```

- **Extend the runtime sanity check** so a future COPY-only refactor cannot silently drop them again:

  ```dockerfile
      redis-server --version && \
      redis-cli --version && \
      redis-sentinel --version && \
      redis-check-rdb --version && \
      redis-check-aof --version
  ```

  `redis-check-rdb`/`-aof` otherwise treat their first argument as a filename; both explicitly special-case `-v`/`--version` and exit 0 (`src/redis-check-rdb.c:443`, `src/redis-check-aof.c:527` in 8.10.1), so the check is a valid presence assertion rather than an accidental file-open.

### Out of scope

`redis-benchmark` is a real ~6.5 MB binary, not a symlink; restoring it is a separate size trade-off, as noted in the issue.

- Fixes #2827

pulls.title: ci: bump cargo-fuzz to 0.13.2 so the fuzz job can install it
pulls.body:
Fixes #2821. Unblocks the red `fuzz` job on every open PR, including #2757 and #2570.

## What is failing

The `fuzz` job never reaches the fuzzing — that step is skipped. Installing the tool is what breaks:

```
error: attributes starting with `rustc` are reserved for use by the `rustc` compiler
28 | #[cfg_attr(rustc_attrs, rustc_layout_scalar_valid_range_start(0xf001))]
error: cannot find attribute `rustc_layout_scalar_valid_range_start` in this scope
error: could not compile `rustix` (lib) due to 4 previous errors
error: failed to compile `cargo-fuzz v0.13.1`
```

## Why

The workflow pairs an **unpinned nightly** with a **pinned old tool**:

```yaml
- run: rustup default nightly
- run: cargo install --root ... --version ${{ env.CARGO_FUZZ_VERSION }} cargo-fuzz   # 0.13.1
```

`cargo-fuzz 0.13.1` resolves **`rustix v0.36.5`**, which declares internal compiler attributes behind `cfg(rustc_attrs)`. Current nightly refuses them, so the dependency cannot build. This is unrelated to the fuzz targets or to any branch's code.

It stayed hidden while the `cargo-fuzz-bin-<version>` cache was warm — a cache hit skips the install entirely. Once that entry was evicted, the rebuild met today's nightly and failed.

Repo-wide, not branch-specific: failing on `perf/limit-aware-scan-batching` and `feat/effects-v3-tests` alike, and **no run in the last 60 has a green `fuzz` job**.

## The fix, verified

`cargo-fuzz 0.13.2` resolves **`rustix v1.1.4`**, which carries no such attributes. Tested against `rustc 1.100.0-nightly (cea272fa3 2026-09-07)`, close to CI's:

```
$ cargo +nightly install --version 0.13.2 cargo-fuzz
   Compiling rustix v1.1.4
   Installed package `cargo-fuzz v0.13.2` (executable `cargo-fuzz`)
```

Against the same toolchain, 0.13.1 fails exactly as CI does. The version is also the cache key, so this cannot reuse the stale entry.

## Left alone deliberately

`rustup default nightly` is unpinned, so this class of breakage recurs whenever nightly moves under a pinned tool — a dated nightly would make the job reproducible at the cost of having to advance it on purpose. That is a policy call rather than an unblock, so it is noted in #2821 and not changed here.

pulls.title: Bump pinned Redis from 8.6.3 to 8.10.1
pulls.body:
Every image that builds `redis-server`/`redis-cli` from source pinned the upstream tag at `8.6.3`. This moves the pin to `8.10.1`.

### Version pins

- `build/Dockerfile`, `build/runtime/Dockerfile`, `build/runtime/Dockerfile.coverage` — `ARG REDIS_VERSION=8.10.1`
- `build/runtime/Dockerfile.asan` — `ARG REDIS_ASAN_VER=8.10.1`

### Comments

- `build/runtime/Dockerfile` — 8.10 removed `BUILD_WITH_MODULES`; the bundled stack modules are now cloned on demand by `make modules-update`, so a plain tag clone is redis-only by default. The `export BUILD_WITH_MODULES=no` stays (a no-op on 8.10, still meaningful if the pin is ever moved back to an 8.6.x tag) with the comment corrected to say why.
- `build/runtime/Dockerfile.asan` — `redis:8.6.x` → `redis:8.10.x` in the trixie-slim rationale.
- `bench/Dockerfile` — dropped the hardcoded `8.6.3`; that redis comes from the published `:edge-c` image, not from this pin, so naming a version here just goes stale.

### Not touched

`Dockerfile.amazonlinux2023` and `Dockerfile.rhel9` build only `libfalkordb.so`; `.devcontainer/Dockerfile` installs the distro's unpinned `redis-server`. None carry a Redis version on this branch.

### Notes for review

8.10 reworked the top-level Makefile (`.DEFAULT_GOAL := build`, recipes delegating to `scripts/build.sh`), so this is not purely a number change in effect:

- `make all` → `build` → `scripts/build.sh` → `make -C src all`, printing `==> No cloned modules under modules/*/src, Redis-only build`.
- The `protected-mode` sed/grep guard and the jemalloc page-size sed still match 8.10.1's sources; the guard would fail the build loudly if they stopped matching.
- Command-line make variables still reach `src/` through `MAKEFLAGS` despite the shell-script hop, so the ASAN stage's `SANITIZER=address OPTIMIZATION=-O1` continues to produce an instrumented binary that clears the Dockerfile's `__asan_` symbol-count check.

This branch targets `main`; `master` needs its own PR — its Dockerfile set differs (`bench/` and `.devcontainer/` carry `REDIS_VERSION` there).

pulls.title: test(cow_btree): eliminate flaky snapshot test failure under thread contention (closes #2795)
pulls.body:
## Problem
In `snapshot_is_isolated_from_a_concurrent_writer`, the reader thread looped on `while !done_reader.load(Ordering::Relaxed)`. Under high thread contention (e.g. `--test-threads=16`), the main writer thread could complete all its mutations and set `done = true` before the OS scheduled the spawned reader thread for its first iteration. This resulted in `reads == 0` and triggered a false-positive assertion failure `assert!(reads > 0, "reader thread never completed a read")`.

## Solution
Changed the reader loop structure to execute at least one full read pass unconditionally (`loop { ... reads += 1; if done_reader.load(Ordering::Relaxed) { break; } }`) before exiting. This guarantees deterministic liveness and removes the thread-scheduling timing assumption while fully preserving the concurrent isolation test coverage.

Closes #2795
