pulls.title: fix(planner): enforce relationship uniqueness for anonymous edges
pulls.body:
## Summary

`MATCH (a)-[:R]-(b)-[:R]-(c)` on a graph holding a **single** `R` edge returned
rows (issue #2441). Cypher's relationship-uniqueness rule forbids binding the
same relationship twice inside one `MATCH`, so the correct answer is no rows.

The planner only listed **named** edges in `sibling_edges`, the list the runtime
uses for its uniqueness check, deliberately excluding anonymous `_anon*` edges
to match the C engine. Named patterns were therefore already correct
(`(a)-[r1:R]-(b)-[r2:R]-(c)` → 0 rows) while anonymous ones were not.

## Changes

- `graph/src/planner/mod.rs`: `sibling_edges` is now computed per relationship
  and includes anonymous edges. Siblings that cannot bind the same physical edge
  are left out — var-length/allShortestPaths patterns (they bind a path) and
  siblings whose relationship-type set cannot overlap. When nothing can collide
  the list stays empty, which keeps the runtime's batched/fused traversal fast
  paths eligible (e.g. `-[:R]->()-[:R2]->`).
- `graph/src/planner/optimizer/reduce_expand_into.rs`: `ir_references_variable`
  now inspects `UNWIND`/`FOREACH` source expressions and `CREATE`/`MERGE`
  patterns. Previously an edge alias was kept alive by accident because its own
  id always appeared in `sibling_edges`; once that list can legitimately be
  empty, queries such as `MATCH ()-[a]->() UNWIND a AS x RETURN id(x)` and
  `MATCH (p)-[e:knows]->() CREATE (:clone {t: TYPE(e)})` failed with
  "Variable not found". Both are covered by existing flow tests.
- `tests/flow/test_bidirectional_traversals.py`: new `test14_relationship_uniqueness`
  and `test15_relationship_uniqueness_disjoint_types`; `test13_multiple_bidirectional_edges`
  updated — it asserted the buggy result (`v1→v1`, `v2→v2`, `v3→v3` obtained by
  walking one edge back and forth).
- `tests/flow/imdb/imdb_queries.py`: "Which actors played along side Nicolas
  Cage?" no longer expects Nicolas Cage himself; matching him requires reusing
  his single `act` edge for both hops.

## Testing

- `cargo test -p graph --lib` — 158 passed.
- Flow suite (`RELEASE=1 ./flow.sh`) — 1392 tests, only two failures, both
  environment-related and unrelated: `test_replication.test_bulk_replication`
  (`No module named 'falkordb_bulk_loader'`) and
  `test_replication_states.test_replication_permutations`
  (`DUMP payload version or checksum are wrong`).
- TCK (`RELEASE=1 pytest tests/tck/test_tck.py -s`) — 2466 scenarios passed,
  0 failed, including `CountingSubgraphMatches` and `TriadicSelection`, which
  exercise relationship uniqueness.
- `cargo fmt --all -- --check` clean; `cargo clippy --all-targets` reports no new
  warnings.
- Manual checks on a single-edge graph: `(a)-[:R]-(b)-[:R]-(c)`, `(a)--(b)--(c)`,
  `(a)-[]-(b)-[]-(c)`, the named variants and `p = ...` all return 0 rows, while
  the single hop still returns both directions; a 3-node chain returns exactly
  `(v1,v2,v3)` and `(v3,v2,v1)`; a self-loop cannot fill a two-hop pattern.

## Memory / Performance Impact

No change to graph storage or allocation. Uniqueness is enforced by the existing
`edge_already_used` runtime check, so only planning metadata changed.

Patterns whose hops share a relationship type (or are untyped) now carry a
non-empty `sibling_edges` list and lose the batched-traverse / anonymous-fusion
fast paths for those hops — the cost of returning correct results. Patterns with
disjoint types keep the exact plan they had before, which the type-overlap filter
was added specifically to preserve.

Known remaining gap (pre-existing, also true for named edges, out of scope here):
uniqueness is enforced per connected pattern component, so
`MATCH (a)-[:R]->(b), (c)-[:R]->(d)` can still bind the same edge twice.

## Related Issues

Closes #2441

* **Bug Fixes**
  * Improved graph query results by enforcing relationship uniqueness across anonymous and named relationship patterns.
  * Prevented traversal queries from reusing the same relationship edge within a path.
  * Preserved correct behavior for variable-length paths, shortest-path queries, self-loops, and separate match scopes.
  * Fixed relationship-emitting queries involving `CREATE`, `MERGE`, `UNWIND`, and `FOR EACH` expressions.
* **Tests**
  * Expanded coverage for bidirectional traversals, named paths, overlapping relationship types, and collision-free traversals.

## Summary

Adds regression coverage for #2440: `UNIQUE` constraints were silently not enforced for property values larger than 4096 bytes on the C engine (and crashed the server on v4.20.1 / v4.20.3). The Rust engine on `main` enforces them correctly at any length — these tests lock that in so the behaviour can't regress.

Verification of the reported bug across published images (details in [the issue comment](https://github.com/FalkorDB/FalkorDB/issues/2440#issuecomment-5303669298)):

| Build | duplicate 4097-byte value under `UNIQUE` |
|---|---|
| `edge` (Rust, this branch's engine) | rejected — correct |
| `edge-c` / `v4.20.2` | silently accepted (2 nodes) |
| `v4.20.3` (= `latest`) | 💥 SIGSEGV in `EnforceUniqueEntity`, exit 139 |

## Changes

Extends `tests/flow/test_constraint.py::testConstraintNodes` (no new file):

- `test09_long_string_values` — for 4096 (the old boundary), 4097 and 65536-byte values: the constraint reaches `OPERATIONAL`, a duplicate `CREATE` is rejected, and a `SET` to a duplicate value is rejected. Asserts the node count afterwards so a silently-accepted duplicate fails the test.
- `test10_long_string_values_constraint_creation` — a constraint created over *pre-existing* 4097-byte duplicates must end up `FAILED` rather than silently becoming operational (the second half of the report: pre-existing duplicates were not detected either).

N/A — tests only, no engine changes.

pulls.title: fix(rdb): don't abort on RESTORE .. REPLACE of an indexed graph's own dump
pulls.body:
## Summary

Started as regression coverage for #2506 (`RESTORE <key> 0 <blob> REPLACE` of an indexed
graph's own `DUMP`, which SIGSEGVs the C engine in `Index_SetLanguage`). The new test then
found a **real bug on our side**: the same sequence aborts the Rust engine on any build with
debug assertions — the coverage and ASAN images — so this PR carries the fix too.

```
FalkorDB panic: panicked at src/graph_core.rs:97:5:
register_graph: name already registered; missing graph_free or placeholder swap
```

`RESTORE ... REPLACE` deserializes the payload *before* it deletes the value currently bound
to the key (deliberately — a corrupt payload must leave the existing key intact). So
`graph_rdb_load` registers the decoded graph while the graph it replaces is still registered
under the same name, which is exactly what `register_graph`'s invariant forbids.

## Changes

**Fix — `src/graph_core.rs`, `src/redis_type.rs`**

- New `register_decoded_graph`, used by the three `graph_rdb_load` registration sites, which
  displaces an existing registration without asserting.
- Displacing is safe there: Redis frees the replaced value moments later and `graph_free`
  unregisters by `data_ptr`, so it only ever removes entries pointing at the graph being
  freed — never the one the loader just installed. A query still holding the replaced graph
  sees `graph_is_registered` go false and aborts its write, which is the intended outcome for
  a key replaced underneath it.
- The strict invariant stays in force for every command path (`GRAPH.QUERY`, `GRAPH.COPY`,
  `GRAPH.RESTORE`, bulk insert, effects, constraints), which is where a duplicate registration
  really would mean a leaked Arc. The displaced-Arc background drop is factored into
  `drop_displaced_graph` and shared by both entry points.

**Test — `tests/flow/test_rdb_load.py`**

Extends the existing `testRdbLoad` class rather than adding a file — it is already the home of
the DUMP/RESTORE round-trip coverage:

- `test_restore_replace_indexed_graph` — a graph with a node range index and an edge range
  index, both warmed by an index-backed read before the dump, then replaced by its own blob
  three times in a row so each restore decodes into the graph left behind by the previous one.
  Asserts the server survives every replace, both indexes come back `OPERATIONAL`, the planner
  still resolves to `Node By Index Scan`, and node/edge data is intact.
- `test_restore_replace_fulltext_indexed_graph` — same shape for a fulltext index created with
  `language` and `stopwords`, the field the C crash faulted on. Asserts both survive the
  replace and the fulltext query still returns.

Both tests flush the keyspace on entry and exit so they stay independent of the existing
`test_rdb_load` key-count assertions regardless of execution order.

## Testing

Local debug build (debug assertions on, which is what surfaces the panic),
`redis-server --loadmodule target/debug/libfalkordb.so`, driven through flow.sh's
service mode:

- **Without** the `graph_core.rs` change — the server dies mid-run, reproducing the CI failure:

```
	test_rdb_load:testRdbLoad.test_rdb_load: [PASS]
	test_rdb_load:testRdbLoad.test_restore_replace_fulltext_indexed_graph: [ERROR]
	Unhandled exception: Connection closed by server.
# redis.log:
# FalkorDB panic: panicked at src/graph_core.rs:97:5:
# register_graph: name already registered; missing graph_free or placeholder swap
```

- **With** the fix — `Total Tests Run: 3, Total Tests Failed: 0, Total Tests Passed: 3`.

Neighbouring RDB/registry suites on the same build: `test_aof` 1/1, `test_graph_copy` 8/9,
`test_intern_string` 9/10 — the two failures are the local box having no `replica` service
container, unrelated to this change.

`cargo fmt --all -- --check` clean; `CXX=clang++ cargo clippy --all-targets` reports only
pre-existing `too_many_arguments` warnings.

For reference, the same test run against the published images: `falkordb/falkordb:edge`
(release Rust, no debug assertions) passes, while `falkordb/falkordb-server:edge-c` (C master)
dies with `Exited (139)` / `Index_SetLanguage+0x10` — i.e. the test does catch the reported
bug rather than passing vacuously.

## Memory / Performance Impact

None. The change swaps one `HashMap::insert` call site for another with the same work; the
displaced-Arc background drop is unchanged, just factored into a helper.

## Related Issues

Closes #2506


<!-- This is an auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->
## Summary by CodeRabbit

* **Bug Fixes**
  * Improved reliability when restoring indexed graphs with `RESTORE ... REPLACE`.
  * Preserved graph data and index metadata during restoration.
  * Ensured range and full-text indexes remain available and usable after restore.
  * Maintained server responsiveness throughout the restore process.
  * Safely replaced existing graph data without disrupting restored graph availability.
  * Improved handling of restored graphs when replacing previously loaded data.

pulls.title: test(optional-match): cover filter after WITH on empty optional match
pulls.body:
## Summary

Adds a regression test for #2508 . A `WHERE` clause following a `WITH` after an
`OPTIONAL MATCH` must be evaluated **above** the `Optional` operation. When the
filter is pushed below `Optional` it lands on the scan branch, which produces no
rows for an empty optional match, so the synthesized all-NULL row bypasses the
predicate entirely and is wrongly returned.

The Rust engine already behaves correctly; this test locks that behavior in.

## Changes

- `tests/flow/test_optional_match.py`: new
  `test28_filter_after_with_on_empty_optional_match` extending the existing
  `testOptionalFlow` suite.

It asserts:
- both queries from the report return zero rows
- the predicate shapes sharing the same root cause return zero rows:
  `WITH * WHERE n IS NOT NULL`, `WITH * WHERE n.id IS NOT NULL`,
  `WITH * WHERE n.id = 4`, `WITH n WHERE n IS NOT NULL`
- the shapes that never regressed still behave: `WITH n AS m WHERE m IS NOT NULL`
  and `WITH * WHERE false` return zero rows, `WITH * WHERE n IS NULL` keeps the
  NULL row, and `RETURN count(n)` over the filtered stream is `0`
- a `Filter` op is present in the plan
- a **positive** case: a node that does match is not discarded by the same filter

## Testing

Full `test_optional_match` suite against `falkordb/falkordb:edge` (Rust engine):

```
Total Tests Run: 27, Total Tests Failed: 0, Total Tests Passed: 27
  test_optional_match:testOptionalFlow.test28_filter_after_with_on_empty_optional_match: [PASS]
```

The test is a genuine regression guard — it **fails** on the C engine
(`falkordb/falkordb-server:edge-c`) on exactly the 5 affected assertions:

```
Total Tests Run: 1, Total Tests Failed: 1
  ❌ (FAIL): [[None]] == []   (x5)
```

Behavior matrix from verifying the issue:

| Image | graph ver | LEFT | RIGHT |
|---|---|---|---|
| `falkordb/falkordb:v4.20.1` | 42001 | ❌ 1 row `[null]` | ✅ 0 rows |
| `falkordb/falkordb:latest` | 42003 | ❌ 1 row `[null]` | ✅ 0 rows |
| `falkordb/falkordb-server:edge-c` | edge (C) | ❌ 1 row `[null]` | ✅ 0 rows |
| `falkordb/falkordb:edge` (Rust) | 8.6.1 | ✅ 0 rows | ✅ 0 rows |

## Memory / Performance Impact

N/A — test-only change.

## Related Issues

References #2508

pulls.title: fix(planner): keep path multiplicity when fusing anonymous traversals
pulls.body:
fix #2470

## Summary

`MATCH (a:A)-[:R]->()-[:R]->(c) RETURN count(*)` returns **1** where it must return **2** when two distinct 2-hop paths connect the same pair of endpoints. The `fuse_anonymous_traverse` optimizer pass collapses the two hops into one fused `Conditional Traverse`, and the runtime evaluates a fused chain as a **boolean** matrix product — which records whether a destination is *reachable*, never how many paths reach it. Cypher relationship-isomorphism requires one row per distinct relationship pair.

The pass reasoned "the intermediate is anonymous and unreferenced, therefore invisible, therefore safe to collapse". The flaw is that **invisible is not irrelevant**: the intermediate still multiplies rows, and that multiplicity *is* the result-set cardinality feeding `count(*)` and every aggregate.

### Reproduction

```cypher
CREATE (a:A), (b1:B), (b2:B), (c:C),
       (a)-[:R]->(b1), (a)-[:R]->(b2), (b1)-[:R]->(c), (b2)-[:R]->(c)
```

| Query | Before | After | Expected |
|---|---|---|---|
| `MATCH (a:A)-[:R]->()-[:R]->(c:C) RETURN count(*)`  | **1** | 2 | 2 |
| `MATCH (a:A)-[:R]->(m)-[:R]->(c:C) RETURN count(*)` | 2 | 2 | 2 |
| `MATCH p = (a:A)-[:R]->()-[:R]->(c:C) RETURN count(*)` | 2 | 2 | 2 |

Only the anonymous-intermediate spelling was wrong — the three forms are semantically identical and now agree.

## Changes

- `graph/src/planner/optimizer/fuse_anonymous_traverse.rs`
  - New helper `feeds_existence_only`, which walks the ancestor chain from a candidate `CondTraverse`, passing through `CondTraverse` and `Filter` nodes, and returns true only when it reaches a `SemiApply`/`AntiSemiApply` **via child index 1**, or an `OrApplyMultiplexer` via **any child index >= 1**.
  - `can_fuse` now requires `feeds_existence_only`.
  - Module docs gained a "Why fusion is restricted to existence tests" section with the diamond counter-example.
- `tests/flow/test_traversal_construction.py` — new regression test.
- Plan-level unit tests for the gate, in a new `tests` module in the same file.

### Why the `SemiApply` carve-out is sound

`semi_apply.rs:51` resolves the existence branch as `plan.node(idx).child(1)`; child 0 is the driving stream. `SemiApply`/`AntiSemiApply` run that branch solely to learn whether **at least one** row arrives and then discard the rows. `OrApplyMultiplexer` (which serves `WHERE (...) OR (...)`) has the same shape with one branch per disjunct: `OrApplyMultiplexerOp::new` collects `branch_indices` from `child(1..=num_branches)`, and `next()` uses each branch only to populate `overall_matched` before building a selection vector over the *input* batch. Collapsing N paths into 1 there cannot change the answer, so the optimization is preserved exactly where it was doing the most good — the perf-sensitive pattern-predicate path — and abandoned only where cardinality is observable.

**Plan shapes after the fix**

```
-- pattern predicate: STILL fuses
Semi Apply
    Node By Label Scan | (a:A)
    Conditional Traverse | (a)->(_anon_1) (+ 1 fused hop)

-- plain MATCH: no longer fuses
Conditional Traverse | (_anon_1)->(c)
    Conditional Traverse | (a)->(_anon_1)
        Node By Label Scan | (a:A)
```

## Testing

- New `test_anonymous_intermediate_keeps_path_multiplicity` asserts the three spellings agree, that a 3-hop anonymous chain is also correct, that `EXPLAIN` of the plain `MATCH` no longer contains `fused hop`, and that `WHERE (a)-[:R]->()-[:R]->()`, `WHERE NOT (...)` and an `OR` of two pattern predicates still fuse **and** still return the right counts. `tests/flow/test_traversal_construction.py` is listed in `flow_tests_done.txt`, so it runs in CI.
- **Negative test performed**: with the source change stashed and the tree rebuilt, the new test fails with `[[1]] == [[2]]` and on the `should not contain 'fused hop'` assertion — confirming this change is what fixes it, then restored.
- Five new plan-level unit tests in `fuse_anonymous_traverse.rs` assert the gate directly, without needing a live GraphBLAS context: a plain `MATCH` and a named intermediate must not fuse; a pattern predicate, a negated pattern predicate, and each branch of an `OR` of pattern predicates must still fuse.
- `cargo test -p graph --lib` — 158 passed, 0 failed.
- `cargo fmt --all -- --check` clean; `CXX=clang++ cargo clippy --all-targets` produces only two pre-existing warnings in `tensor.rs` and an unrelated `too many arguments`.
- Full flow suite: **1380 run, 1374 passed**. The 6 failures are environmental in this sandbox (`ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'falkordb_bulk_loader'`); `test_function_calls.py` passes 93/93 in isolation.

## Memory / Performance Impact

No memory impact. **There is a potential latency impact that reviewers should weigh.** Multi-hop patterns with anonymous intermediates outside a pattern predicate now execute as two stacked `Conditional Traverse` ops instead of one fused matrix product. I did **not** run the benchmark suite, so I cannot quantify it.

The alternative that would keep the optimization everywhere is a **counting semiring** — evaluate the fused chain over an integer semiring so `f[row, dest]` holds the path count, then emit that many rows. I did not attempt it because it has real edge cases around self-loops and parallel edges that need their own design. I chose correctness first; happy to follow up with the semiring approach if maintainers prefer to retain the fusion.

## Related Issues

Closes #2470

<!-- This is an auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->

## Summary by CodeRabbit

* **Bug Fixes**
  * Preserved duplicate path results when traversals include anonymous intermediate nodes.
  * Prevented traversal optimizations from changing observable row counts.
  * Maintained correct behavior for positive, negative, and OR-based pattern predicates.

* **Tests**
  * Added coverage for multi-hop traversals, named intermediates, named paths, and existence-based predicates.

<!-- end of auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->

pulls.title: perf(runtime): answer a label predicate from the label matrix (1.77x)
pulls.body:
## What

`n:Label` reaches the runtime as a `hasLabels` call, answered via `Runtime::get_node_labels`, which per row:

1. builds an `OrderSet<LabelId>` from the label matrix,
2. applies pending label changes into it,
3. builds a **second** `OrderSet<Arc<String>>` of label *names*,

and then the predicate compares strings. Two allocations and a name comparison per row, to read what is one bit of the label matrix.

## Measured

Benchmark graph (10k `:Person` plus the `:Doc`/`:Geo` corpus, 15k nodes), 100 executions each, instructions per query:

| query | before | after | | C engine |
|---|---:|---:|---|---:|
| `MATCH (n) WHERE n:Person RETURN count(n)` | 48,942,607 | **27,642,373** | 1.77x | 22,369,592 |
| `label predicate` (`… AND n.id < 5`) | 55,573,511 | **34,261,231** | 1.62x | 24,896,439 |

Per row that is 3.3k → 1.8k, against C's 1.5k; the ratio to C goes 2.19 → 1.24 and 2.23 → 1.38.

For contrast, the same scan filtering on a *property* — `MATCH (n) WHERE n.id < 5` — costs 1,987,320 here against 8,985,762 on C. Property access was never the problem; the label test was.

## How

`Runtime::node_has_label(id, name)` is the one place a label test is decided, and it decides it for every node the query can see, in the order `get_node_labels` uses: a node this query deleted answers from the labels captured at the delete, a label this query staged answers from `Pending::node_has_label` (a removal winning over an add, the precedence `update_node_labels` applies), and everything else is one bit of the committed label matrix. Nothing falls back, so a pending node gets the cheap path too, and `hasLabels` no longer carries a second copy that compares label *names* against a materialized `OrderSet`. `NodeByIndexScan`'s extra-label filter was a third copy of the same per-row test; it now runs through the same function.

Resolving the name is per-row too, so `Graph::get_label_id` no longer walks `node_labels`: a `node_labels_index` reverse map makes it O(1), mirroring what the attribute dictionary already does. On a 500-label schema that took `MATCH (n) WHERE n:Person RETURN count(n)` over 10k nodes from 2.87ms to 1.37ms — the one-label cost. On the benchmark graph's small schema it is a wash (35.04M → 35.08M instructions).

## Scope — half of the lead this came from

This is the per-row **predicate** half. The **aggregate** half is untouched and still open:

| | Rust | C | ratio |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| `collect DISTINCT` | 36.3M | 16.8M | 2.16 |
| `percentileCont` | 26.7M | 12.9M | 2.07 |
| `collect` | 21.4M | 12.1M | 1.77 |
| `count` / `sum` / `min` | 5.1–5.5M | 11.2–11.7M | **0.45–0.49** |
| `count(DISTINCT p.age)` | 7.0M | 16.4M | **0.43** |

The losers are exactly the aggregates that materialize values into a list, while the streaming ones already beat C by 2x. That points at the per-value append path, not at aggregation in general — a separate change.

## Tests

`test11_label_predicate_against_pending_labels` pins every case the fast path must decline (label SET or REMOVEd in the same query, node created in it, node deleted in it) plus multi-label AND, an unknown label, and `hasLabels()` itself. **It passes on the parent commit too** — that is deliberate: it constrains semantics, not the optimization.

TCK 2456 scenarios pass / 0 fail · `cargo test -p graph` 153 pass · fmt clean, no new clippy warnings · flow suite clean (three failures in the parallel full run — `bulk_insertion` ×2, `replication_states` — pass in isolation on both this build and the parent; local parallel-run flakiness).

Found while producing a full Rust-vs-C benchmark report; this was lead #4 of 5.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

  * Kept label predicates accurate when labels are added or removed, including within the same query.
  * Correctly handles unknown, unused, and invalid label values.
  * Improved label filtering for indexed node searches.
  * Improved label lookup performance.

* **Tests**

pulls.title: fix: C-parity for GRAPH.INFO — the telemetry write path (1.46x → 1.06x of C), CMD_INFO, bare calls, and the run-time config surface
pulls.body:
Two commits. The first makes the switch work; the second makes the switch unnecessary.

## The problem

The full 317-query benchmark showed a flat **+78k instructions on every query** versus C — the `RETURN 1` floor at 1.48x. Stage ablation (M3 Pro, 2000 executions via redis-benchmark) found it in one place:

| | instr/query |
|---|---:|
| full path | 232,289 |
| without slow_log + telemetry | 149,316 |
| → slow_log alone | ~300 |
| → **telemetry** | **~83,000** |
| …channel send + flusher wakeup + formatting + GIL | 49,154 |
| …argument RedisString creation | 5,656 |
| …the XADD itself | 25,534 |
| …replicating the XADD | 2,395 |

C, same host, same command: **159,343** with logging on, **148,324** with `CMD_INFO no` — so **11,019** for the same feature. Everything else was already at parity: `PING` 43,622 vs 43,077, `GRAPH.EXPLAIN` 137,390 vs 132,452.

## 1 · `CMD_INFO` gated nothing

It was registered, documented, reported by `GRAPH.CONFIG GET` — and read by nothing, so there was no way to opt out. Now it is honoured, mirroring C where `CMD_INFO no` also stops the stream. Mirrored into an atomic because the config lives behind a `RedisGILGuard` and the query path holds no GIL.

## 2 · The enabled path now works like C's

Four changes, all mirroring `cron/tasks/stream_finished_queries.c`:

- **`StreamAdd` on an opened key** instead of `RM_Call("XADD", …)` — no command lookup, dispatch or reply machinery, and no per-entry replication.
- **A reusable field-name template** (C's `_event`): the ten constant field names become `RedisModuleString`s once per flusher thread, not once per entry.
- **One key open and one `StreamTrimByLength` per graph per batch**, by grouping the batch by graph.
- **A batch window the flusher sleeps out.** A blocking wait returns the moment an entry is queued, so the thread woke once per query and only the *flush* was batched — and waking is most of the cost. Asleep, a sender's push is an atomic with nobody to wake, which is C's position: its cron runs on a timer and the query thread only appends to a buffer.

| `GRAPH.QUERY g "RETURN 1"` | instr | telemetry's share |
|---|---:|---:|
| before | 232,743 | ~83,000 |
| **after** | **166,677** | **14,073** |
| C (logging on) | 159,343 | 11,019 |

**1.28x of C's cost for the feature, down from 7.5x; 1.06x of C for the whole query, down from 1.46x.** `CREATE (:Tmp {x: 1})`: 331,455 → 270,539.

## Two consequences to weigh before merging

**The stream is no longer replicated — which is parity with C, not a departure from it.** A key-API write is not propagated, where `RM_Call(..., replicate)` was. C's cron writes through the same API, so it never replicated telemetry either:

- **#1399** (`e2fd7377a`, "replicate telemetry changes, truncate long strings") is titled as though it did, but its 20-file diff contains no `RedisModule_Replicate*` call. It shipped `test01_stream_replication` **commented out**, and only reindented the already-commented `RedisModuleEvent_ReplicationRoleChanged` subscription.
- **#1568** (`4cc0f280c`) later deleted the leftover dead `_ReplicationRoleChangedEventHandler`. `src/module_event_handlers.c:424` still carries the commented-out subscription today.
- `git grep RedisModule_Replicate` over `src/cron`, `src/queries_log`, `src/slow_log` and `graphcontext.c` on master returns nothing, and Redis does not make up the difference: `moduleCloseKey` calls `keyModified` (WATCH + keyspace notification) and `signalKeyAsReady` for blocked `XREAD`, but propagation needs a command context or an explicit `RM_Replicate*`, and the cron's detached context has neither.

So the replicated XADD was a Rust-only behaviour, costing 2,395 instructions a query for something the reference engine abandoned. Dropping it restores parity.

One related asymmetry left alone deliberately: `enqueue_entry` still skips on replicas. That guard existed *because* the master's XADDs replicated, so it was there to avoid duplicates — with replication gone, C's equivalent would have each instance log the queries it served. Flipping that is a separate behaviour change and not in this PR.

**Entries land a few milliseconds after the query.** They always landed asynchronously; the window is now explicit. Two tests had the old latency baked in:

- `test_replication_states` counts the keyspace exactly, and a late write recreated the stream key of a graph `FLUSHALL` had removed — on the master only, now that writes don't replicate. **Fixed in the engine, not the test**: entries for a graph that no longer exists are dropped, which is what C gets for free by iterating the graphs currently in the keyspace.
- `test_rdb_load` listed the keyspace right after a query and expected the stream to be there. That was always a race with a background thread; it now waits for the stream instead of assuming.

## Validation

TCK 2456 scenarios / 0 fail · `cargo test -p graph` 153 pass · `test_graph_info` 9/9 · `test_config` 16/16 · flow suite otherwise unchanged (9 failures, all in the index/limit/slowlog/timeout families, identical without this change) · fmt clean, no new clippy warnings.

Stream contents verified by hand: one stream per graph, all ten fields with correct values, and the approximate cap holds — 1,047 entries for 2,000 queries, against the cap test's `< 1200` bound.

## Absorbs #2525 (fa146cd20)

The two PRs collided on `CMD_INFO`: both noticed it gated nothing and gave the query path a lock-free way to read it. #2525's version wins outright and this branch's is deleted, so **#2525 is now contained here and can be closed**.

- `CONFIGURATION_CMD_INFO` becomes an `AtomicBool` in `config.rs` — one storage location shared by the config registration, `CONFIG SET graph.*` and `GRAPH.CONFIG SET`. `enqueue_entry` reads it directly.
- This branch's `LOG_QUERIES` mirror, `set_log_queries` and the `module_init` publish step are gone. The mirror only existed because `CONFIGURATION_CMD_INFO` lived behind a `RedisGILGuard` and `CMD_INFO` was registered `IMMUTABLE`. #2525 makes both untrue — and a mirror of a *runtime-settable* config would have gone stale on the first `GRAPH.CONFIG SET`, so keeping it would have been a bug.

Also arriving with #2525: bare `GRAPH.INFO` reports every section (fixes #2434), and `MAX_INFO_QUERIES` / `DELAY_INDEXING` become runtime-settable, with `MAX_INFO_QUERIES` finally honouring its load-time module argument.

Suite after the merge: test_graph_info 13/13, test_config 19/19, test_intern_string 11/11, test_rdb_load, test_replication_states, test_role_change_race, test_pause_replication_race all pass; `cargo test -p graph` 158.

## Review round (6bb95fdc6)

- The ten field-name `RedisModuleString`s are created **once**, at module init on the main thread, rather than per flusher thread — which also frees them on unload and stops `StreamTemplate::new` calling into the module API before it holds the GIL.
- `PreparedEntry`/`prepare_entry` deleted; `StreamTemplate::add` formats straight from the queued entry. Measured either way: median 28,450 vs 28,694 ops/s, p50/p95/p99 identical at 0.031/0.039/0.047ms, both inside a ~4% run-to-run spread.
- `StreamAdd` failures counted and reported once per graph per batch; a negative `StreamTrimByLength` return logged.
- A queued entry is kept only if its graph is the one registered under **the name the entry carries** (`graph_is_registered_as`). The handle alone missed plain `RENAME`: the graph is still alive under the new key, and the entry recreated the stream the rename had just deleted. New test `test02_stale_entry_not_written_under_a_renamed_key`.
- The replica-guard comment no longer claims the master's XADDs replicate to us.

Found while producing a full Rust-vs-C benchmark report.

Closes #2497
Fixes #2434 — via #2525, which this PR absorbed and which is now closed.

pulls.title: fix(bench): read jemalloc stats by column, not by whitespace
pulls.body:
## The bug

`jemalloc_totals` splits the `bins:`/`large:` rows of `MEMORY MALLOC-STATS` on whitespace. Those tables are fixed-width and right-aligned, and the `(#/sec)` rate fields are 8 characters wide — so a rate ≥ 10,000,000/sec fills its field exactly and leaves no space before the `nmalloc` next to it:

```text
nmalloc (#/sec)      ndalloc (#/sec)
    1379247  689623      1355704  677852     <- fine, 6-digit rates
21949879 10974939 21947904 10973952          <- fused, 8-digit rates
```

`line.split()` reads that `nmalloc` as one 16-digit number and shifts every later column left, so `ndalloc` picks up a fused value too. The cumulative total jumps ~7e16 bytes when a hot size class crosses 10M allocs/sec and drops back when it cools — and since `measure` reports **deltas** between two snapshots, that lands as per-query allocation in the petabytes, or negative when the fusion clears between snapshots.

## Not hypothetical

Three full 317-query runs on one host, each producing exactly 8 physically impossible rows, consistently:

| query | rep 1 | rep 2 | rep 3 | with this fix |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `MSF nodes yield` | 351,207,481,011,826 | 351,207,097,013,232 | 351,210,249,012,702 | **10,649,197** |
| `write 1m` | −39,655,479,199,115,760 | −39,656,013,599,155,096 | −39,656,194,399,073,920 | — |
| `write 100k` | 320,185,648,034,151 | 320,142,448,020,056 | 320,139,888,012,900 | — |
| `write 1k` | 3,182,176,503,580 | — | — | **485,442** |

`alloc_bytes` is the column the `benchmark-cov` CI comment uses **against the C engine** (callgrind can't measure that engine reliably), so this breaks the one vs-C reading CI has. It needs a full run to trigger — a handful of queries never gets a size class hot enough — which is why it survived.

## The fix

Slice each field by the character range of its own table's header. Overflow in a right-aligned field spills *left*, so a field read up to its own end column stays correct and only its left neighbour (a rate nothing here uses) is damaged. A field runs from the previous column's end rather than its own label's start, because values are routinely wider than their labels (`size` labels a 5-digit 49152).

`bench/tests/test_jemalloc_stats.py` guards it with real captured rows — the fused one included — and asserts both parses agree where the rates are narrow enough to be unambiguous. 95 bench tests pass.

Found while producing a full Rust-vs-C benchmark report; this was lead #5 of 5. The fix itself was already sitting in a local working tree, unlanded.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

<!-- This is an auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->

## Summary by CodeRabbit

* **Bug Fixes**
  * Improved jemalloc statistics parsing across standard and large allocation tables.
  * Correctly reads allocation and deallocation counts when columns are separated or combined.
  * Prevents malformed, unsupported, or incomplete rows from producing inaccurate statistics.
  * Ensures reported allocation counts remain consistent and reliable across supported table layouts.

<!-- end of auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->

Closes #2496

pulls.title: fix(planner): order a reversed traversal chain from its new anchor (78x), and run the most selective hop first
pulls.body:
Two commits, both in `select_scan_node`'s chain rewrite.

## 1 · The bottom hop had no bound endpoint (78x)

The pass reverses a `CondTraverse` chain when the better scan endpoint is at the top. It reversed the hop list, then walked that list backwards again while rebuilding — so the hop placed directly on the new scan was the one *furthest* from it, with neither endpoint bound by anything below. The runtime can only answer that by enumerating every edge of the relationship type, once per input row.

The plan stayed *correct* (brute force finds the same rows), so it never showed up as a test failure — only as cost.

10k-node benchmark graph, 300 executions per query, `bench`'s rusage backend:

| query | before | after | | C engine |
|---|---:|---:|---|---:|
| `reversed 2hop chain` | 34,365,659 | **439,796** | 78x | 418,834 |
| `reversed chain mid filter` | 35,906,332 | **499,645** | 72x | 413,612 |
| `reverse 3hop` | 40,420,641 | **508,481** | 79x | 450,593 |
| `reverse 1hop` | 370,879 | 378,692 | — | 380,558 |
| `forward 2hop` | 445,173 | 448,374 | — | 409,717 |

Those were the worst two Rust/C ratios in the whole 317-query set (134x and 142x on query work); they now land at ~1.05x of C. p99 for `reversed 2hop chain` was 1.791 ms against C's 0.087 ms. It also fixes their **allocation**: 775,626 B → 2,263 B and 813,275 B → 2,016 B, i.e. down to the per-query floor ([measurement](https://github.com/FalkorDB/FalkorDB/pull/2491#issuecomment-5277173606)).

Dropping the second reversal alone is not enough: once the pattern branches — `(a)-->(b)-->(c), (b)-->(d)` — the hop leaving the branch point still has to run in storage direction, so `transposed` is not a property of the chain. Doing only that made the branching query return **0 rows instead of 2**. Hops are therefore ordered greedily, each oriented to start from an endpoint that is already bound, and the pass leaves the plan alone if no such order exists.

## 2 · The order was pattern order, not a cheap order

Greedy-first-fit produces a *valid* arrangement, not a good one. Now, among the hops that can run next:

- a hop with **both** endpoints bound goes first — it closes a cycle, so it can only filter (and `reduce_expand_into` then turns it into an `ExpandInto`);
- otherwise the hop whose **newly bound endpoint scores best** under the same `score_endpoint` that picks the scan: bound → filtered → labelled, fewest label nodes breaking ties.

And ordering now runs for **every** chain, not just reversed ones — it used to be gated on `need_swap`, so a chain whose best endpoint was already at the bottom kept pattern order however bad it was, which is most chains. The computation is hoisted above the branch chain (it is pure) and the rebuild is skipped when the arrangement equals the one already in the plan, so untouched plans are not pruned and reconstructed for nothing.

200-node branch, one side reaching 50 nodes and the other a single labelled one, pattern mentioning the wide side first:

```
MATCH (a:A {v: 0})-[:E]->(b)-[:E]->(h:H), (b)-[:E]->(r:R) RETURN count(*)
```

| | order chosen | instr |
|---|---|---:|
| before | `(b)->(h:H)` then `(b)->(r:R)` | 1,712,085 |
| after | **`(b)->(r:R)` then `(b)->(h:H)`** | **662,156** |
| C | same order as *after* | 802,371 |

So it reaches the arrangement C's scored search reaches, then beats it — without importing that search. C sorts by score and backtracks (`_valid_expressions` is O(n·i) per position *and* allocates, so O(n³) typical and exponential worst case, plus O(n²) `strcmp` on alias names in `_resolve_winning_sequence`). Greedy is O(n²) on alias ids and needs no backtracking: "shares an endpoint with something bound" is exactly the eligibility rule, so a connected pattern always completes.

## Across the 317-query set: neutral

geomean 1.0013, median 0.9998, total instructions 0.982x. That set is micro-heavy with few branching patterns, so this is the expected shape. The three rows that look like regressions are not this pass's business — `multi-type traverse` (1.20x) is a single-hop chain, `unicode escapes` (1.10x) has no traversal at all, and re-measured in isolation on identical graph state both modules agree to 0.03% (38,259,814 vs 38,269,823). They move with the graph state that preceding write queries leave behind.

## Tests

- `test_reversed_chain_hop_order` — asserts the invariant directly (every traverse's source alias is bound by an operator below it) over six shapes, two branching. **Fails 8 times** on `main`.
- `test_selective_hop_runs_first` — asserts the narrow side is traversed before the wide one. **Fails** on commit 1.
- `test_reversed_chain_results_match` — pins the rows, because the broken order produced correct ones.
- `test_filter_as_early_as_possible` — asserted positions only reachable via the old plan; its named property (each filtered node filtered right after the operator that binds it) is unchanged and still asserted, one hop deeper.

TCK 2456 scenarios pass / 0 fail · `cargo test -p graph` 153 pass · `cargo fmt --check` clean, no new clippy warnings · flow suite has no plan-shape failures (12 failures, all in the concurrency/limit/slowlog families, identical without this change).

Found while producing a full Rust-vs-C benchmark report.

Closes #2495

## Summary by CodeRabbit

* **New Features**
  * Improved graph traversal planning to dynamically choose efficient relationship order and direction.
  * Applies filters as soon as the required data becomes available, improving query execution.

* **Bug Fixes**
  * Corrected reversed and branching traversal behavior.
  * Improved results for complex traversal patterns and intermediate filters.

pulls.title: test(all-shortest-paths): cover aggregating WITH * over unresolved endpoints
pulls.body:
## Summary

Regression test for #2127, a SIGSEGV: `allShortestPaths()` whose endpoints are declared **inline in its own pattern** correctly raises `Source and destination must already be resolved`, but when the clause was followed by an **aggregating `WITH *`**, raising that error with an aggregation still pending took the whole server down.

## Changes

**Extended `test01_invalid_shortest_paths`** — that test already enumerates the invalid `allShortestPaths` forms and asserts a clean error for each, so this is the same narrative rather than a new test. Added:

- `MATCH p = allShortestPaths((a:Paper)-[*..2]-(b:Paper)) WITH *, count(a) AS count_a RETURN p` → `Source and destination must already be resolved to call allShortestPaths`
- a trailing `RETURN 1` asserting the **server is still alive** — the property that actually regressed

## Testing

`RELEASE=1 VERBOSE=0 TEST=tests/flow/test_all_shortest_paths ./flow.sh` → **7/7 pass**.

I bisected the reported query on the era image to isolate what actually crashes, because the issue's own root-cause analysis (hashing `Path`/`Array` as `GROUP BY` keys) turns out not to be the trigger:

| query on `v4.18.10` | result |
|---|---|
| `MATCH p = allShortestPaths((a:Paper)-[*..2]-(b:Paper)) RETURN p` | clean error ✅ |
| the same **+ `WITH *, count(a)`** | `Server closed the connection` 💥 |
| `MATCH p = (a:Paper)-[*..2]-(b:Paper) WITH *, count(a) ...` | works ✅ |
| `MATCH (a:Paper) WITH *, [a.x, 1] AS arr, count(a) ...` | works ✅ |

So grouping by a `Path` or an `Array` was never the problem — the crash needs the **error path** and the **pending aggregation** together. The test asserts exactly that combination.

I also checked the case already covered by this test's first assertion (`MATCH (v1),(v4), p = allShortestPaths((v1)-[*]->(v4))`): it errors cleanly on `v4.18.10`, so it never covered this crash and the extension is not duplication.

## Memory / Performance Impact

N/A — tests only.

## Related Issues

Closes #2127

<!-- This is an auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->

## Summary by CodeRabbit

* **Bug Fixes**
  * Improved handling of unresolved `allShortestPaths` endpoints followed by `WITH *` aggregation.
  * Confirmed the server remains operational after the expected error occurs.

<!-- end of auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->

pulls.title: test(reduce): cover nested reduce with shadowed iterator names
pulls.body:
## Summary

Regression test for #1481, a memory-corruption crash: nesting `reduce()` inside a list comprehension while **shadowing** the accumulator and iterator names in the inner scopes took the server down with a SIGSEGV. Fixed by the Rust engine, untested until now.

## Changes

**Extended `test_nested_reduction`** — the file already had a nested-`reduce()` test, but it used *distinct* variable names in each scope, so the shadowing path was never exercised. The extension follows that test's narrative:

- the reporter's minimal PoC — `[x IN [1] | reduce(s=0, x IN [1] | s + [x IN [1] | x][0])][0]` → `1`
- three levels deep, shadowing **both** the accumulator `s` and the iterator `x` → `1`
- the original `WHERE`-clause form, which must be rejected with `Expected boolean predicate` (the projection yields an integer, not a boolean) rather than evaluated
- a trailing `RETURN 1` asserting the **server survived and the outer scope is uncorrupted** — the property that actually regressed

## Testing

`RELEASE=1 VERBOSE=0 TEST=tests/flow/test_reduce ./flow.sh` → **14/14 pass**.

Reproduced on the era image first:

| query | `v4.20.1` | `main` |
|---|---|---|
| `MATCH (n) WHERE [x IN [0] \| reduce(s=0, x IN [0] \| s + reduce(s=0, x IN [0] \| s + 1))][0] RETURN 1` | `Server closed the connection` 💥 | `Expected boolean predicate` |
| minimal PoC (`RETURN [x IN [1] \| ...][0]`) | `1` | `1` |

Worth noting the minimal PoC from the issue does **not** crash `v4.20.1` — only the deeper `WHERE`-clause form does, which is why that form is included rather than the minimal one alone.

`tests/flow/test_reduce.py` is already listed in `flow_tests_done.txt` (line 85), so this runs in CI.

## Memory / Performance Impact

N/A — tests only.

## Related Issues

Closes #1481

<!-- This is an auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->
## Summary by CodeRabbit

* **Bug Fixes**
  * Improved handling of nested reduction expressions when accumulator and iterator names overlap.
  * Prevented invalid reduction expressions from being accepted as filter conditions.
  * Confirmed subsequent queries continue to work correctly after invalid expressions are evaluated.
<!-- end of auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->

pulls.title: test(functions): cover crash-inducing arguments to range() and exists()
pulls.body:
## Summary

Regression tests for two `fixed-rust` crashes in which hostile arguments took the **whole server down** (SIGSEGV/SIGFPE, `ExitCode=139`) instead of producing a query error. Both are fixed by the Rust engine; neither had a test.

## Changes

**Extended `test79_Range`** (#385) — `range()` negated `i64::MIN` while computing its span, which is undefined at the 64-bit boundary:

- `range(0, -9223372036854775808, -1)` — the original report
- `range(0, -9223372036854775807, -1)` — the adjacent value, which used to OOM instead
- `range(-9223372036854775808, 0, 1)` — the same limit as the *start* bound

All must raise `Range too large`. Also pinned the neighbouring `step = 0` error so the two failure modes stay distinct.

**Added `test96_exists_unbound_variables`** (#2264) — `exists()` dereferenced unresolved entities when its traversal pattern referenced unbound variables and reused a relationship variable:

- `RETURN exists( (n0)-[r1]-(n1), (n1)-[r1]-(n0) )` → `'n0' not defined`
- `RETURN exists( (n0)-[r1]-(n1) )` and the bound-source variant → `traversal patterns are not allowed as arguments to exists()`
- a trailing `RETURN 1` asserts the **server is still responsive**, which is the property that actually regressed

## Testing

`RELEASE=1 VERBOSE=0 TEST=tests/flow/test_function_calls ./flow.sh` → **94/94 pass**.

Both crashes were reproduced on the era image before writing the tests:

| issue | query | `v4.20.1` | `main` |
|---|---|---|---|
| #385 | `range(0, -9223372036854775808, -1)` | `Server closed the connection` 💥 | `Range too large` |
| #2264 | `exists( (n0)-[r1]-(n1), (n1)-[r1]-(n0) )` | `Server closed the connection` 💥 | `'n0' not defined` |

In both cases the container died and the follow-up `PING` returned `Connection reset by peer`.

## Memory / Performance Impact

N/A — tests only.

## Related Issues

Closes #385
Closes #2264

<!-- This is an auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->

## Summary by CodeRabbit

* **Bug Fixes**
  * Improved validation for invalid `range()` inputs, including boundary values and zero steps.
  * Improved handling of invalid traversal patterns in `exists()`, returning clear validation errors without disrupting later queries.

<!-- end of auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->

pulls.title: ci: exempt Dependabot PRs from the "PR closes an issue" check
pulls.body:
The required `PR closes an issue` job fails on every Dependabot PR ([run 31624938048](https://github.com/FalkorDB/FalkorDB/actions/runs/31624938048/job/94208797670), PR #2474). The assert is unsatisfiable for Dependabot — the app cannot attach an issue through the Development sidebar, `Closes #N` keywords only register on the default branch (these PRs target `main`), and Dependabot-triggered runs get a read-only Dependabot-scoped token — so `closingIssuesReferences.totalCount` is always `0` and every dependency bump is permanently blocked.

### Changes to `.github/workflows/pr-linked-issue.yml`

- **Exempt Dependabot** — the step exits 0 with an explanatory job summary when `github.event.pull_request.user.login` is `dependabot[bot]` (or legacy `dependabot-preview[bot]`), before the GraphQL query runs.
- **Exemption lives inside the step, not a job-level `if:`** — the check is required in branch protection, so it must always report a conclusion rather than leave the PR waiting on a status that never arrives. This mirrors the workflow's existing "no `paths:` filter" rationale.
- **Header comment updated** — the block previously declared "There are no exemptions: bot PRs (dependabot, batch-backport) must also close an issue"; it now documents the single exemption and why. Every other author, bots included, is unchanged.

```bash
PR_AUTHOR: ${{ github.event.pull_request.user.login }}
...
if [ "${PR_AUTHOR:-}" = "dependabot[bot]" ] || [ "${PR_AUTHOR:-}" = "dependabot-preview[bot]" ]; then
  ...
  exit 0
fi
```

Literal string comparison rather than a `case` glob is deliberate: `[bot]` in a glob pattern is a character class and would match `dependabott` but not the actual login.

### Companion issue

The sandbox has no write-capable GitHub credential (`gh` unauthenticated, MCP GitHub tools read-only), so the issue could not be filed from here. Suggested text:

> **`PR closes an issue` check blocks all Dependabot PRs**
>
> The required `PR closes an issue` job fails on every Dependabot PR (e.g. #2474, run 31624938048). Dependabot cannot link a closing issue: no access to the Development sidebar, `Closes #N` only works on the default branch, and its runs get a read-only scoped token. The assert is unsatisfiable, so every dependency bump is permanently blocked. Dependabot-authored PRs should be exempt while the check still reports a passing conclusion.

pulls.title: fix(dependabot): stop widening the deliberate redis<8.1 test pin
pulls.body:
## Summary

Follow-up to #2464. The `pip` entry I added for `/tests` carried no `ignore` rule, on the incorrect assumption — stated in a comment in that PR — that Dependabot treats a `<` ceiling as a hard constraint. It does not: the pip ecosystem defaults to `versioning-strategy: auto`, which widens ranges.

Dependabot then opened #2476, raising `redis<8.1` to `redis<8.2`.

## Why that is a problem

**It re-admits the exact release the pin excludes.** `<8.2` permits redis-py 8.1.0, which adds `himport_registry` to `ConnectionPool.connection_kwargs`; falkordb-py 1.6.2 forwards it to the sync `Redis()` constructor, and every flow test that builds its own pool fails with a `TypeError`.

**It desyncs two pins that must move together.** The identical pin lives at `build/Dockerfile:141`, and the comment above it says "Keep in sync with build/Dockerfile". #2476 touches only `tests/requirements.txt`.

**CI gives false assurance.** `tests/requirements.txt` is installed by *no* workflow — the flow suites run inside `ghcr.io/falkordb/falkordb-build`, which bakes its own copy of the pin. So `flow-test-matrix` passes on #2476 without ever exercising the changed file. The breakage surfaces only on local and non-container runs, which is why this needs a config guard rather than a test.

## Changes

- Add `ignore: [dependency-name: "redis"]` to the `/tests` pip entry
- Replace the comment that made the wrong claim, recording why the ignore exists, that CI cannot catch the regression, and the condition for removing it

## Testing

- `.github/dependabot.yml` parses under `yaml.safe_load`; all six update entries verified intact with the `ignore` attached to the `pip` `/tests` entry only
- Confirmed `tests/requirements.txt` matches no reference in `.github/workflows/`
- Confirmed the duplicate pin at `build/Dockerfile:141`
- No change to the other five ecosystems; the `target-branch: master` github-actions entry is untouched

## Memory / Performance Impact

N/A — CI configuration only.

## Related Issues

Closes #2483

Once merged, #2476 should be closed unmerged; Dependabot will not reopen it.

## Summary by CodeRabbit

* **Chores**
  * Updated automated dependency update settings to keep Redis below version 8.1 for test environments.
  * Added documentation explaining the compatibility constraint, CI limitations, and criteria for revisiting the restriction.

pulls.body:
Bumps [github/codeql-action/init](https://github.com/github/codeql-action) from 4.37.0 to 4.37.6.
Release notes

Sourced from github/codeql-action/init's releases.

v4.37.6

  • Changed the default filepath for the new remote file address format that was introduced in CodeQL Action 4.37.0 / 3.37.0 to .github/codeql-config.yml to align it with the suggested path that is used elsewhere. #4070

v4.37.5

  • Fixed a bug where a network error while streaming the download of the CodeQL bundle could terminate the init Action instead of falling back to downloading the bundle before extracting it. #4061

v4.37.4

  • This version of the CodeQL Action adds support for the tools input for the codeql-action/init step to be specified using a github-codeql-tools repository property. This feature will gradually be rolled out following the release of this version. Once rolled out, this allows for the CodeQL CLI version that is used in GitHub-managed workflows, such as Default Setup, to be set to a custom value. For example, customers who run into issues with rate limits when a new CodeQL CLI version is released can set the value to toolcache to always use the CodeQL CLI version that is available in the runner toolcache. For Advanced Setup workflows, the value provided for tools in the workflow definition always takes precedence unless the value of the repository property starts with !. #4037
  • Update default CodeQL bundle version to 2.26.2. #4051

v4.37.3

No user facing changes.

v4.37.2

  • The new address format for the config-file input that was introduced in CodeQL Action 4.37.0 is now enabled by default. In addition to the format described there, the remote= prefix can now be used to explicitly indicate that the input refers to a remote file. All previous input formats continue to be accepted as well. #4023
  • The CodeQL Action can now make use of configured private registries in Default Setup to retrieve CodeQL configuration files from remote repositories that require authentication. This will allow customers to store their CodeQL configuration in a single repository that can then be referenced by Default Setup workflows in other repositories. We expect to roll this and other, related changes out to everyone in July. #4007

Changelog

Change Log for spellcheck-github-actions

0.66.0, 2026-08-11, maintenance release, update not required

  • Docker image updated to Python 3.14.7-slim-trixie via PR #391 from Dependabot.

0.65.0, 2026-08-08, security release, update recommended

  • Bumped lxml from 5.4.0 to 6.1.1 to address CVE-2026-41066 (XXE via iterparse()/ETCompatXMLParser defaulting resolve_entities=True) and libxslt vulnerabilities CVE-2025-7424 and CVE-2025-11731, via PR #388 from Dependabot.

  • Bumped pymdown-extensions from 10.21.3 to 11.0.1 to address CVE-2026-67422 (ReDoS in the caret, tilde, betterem, and magiclink inline processors) and CVE-2026-61632 (path traversal in the b64 extension).

  • Bumped soupsieve from 2.6 to 2.9.2 to address CVE-2026-49476 (memory exhaustion via large comma-separated selector lists) and CVE-2026-49477 (ReDoS via the selector parser).

0.64.0, 2026-07-31, maintenance release, update not required

  • Adopted pip-compile (pip-tools) for Python dependency management via PR #380. requirements.in is now the source of truth for direct dependencies (pyspelling, pymdown-extensions); requirements.txt is generated from it rather than hand-maintained, so transitive pins can no longer silently fall out of sync the way bracex did in issue #378.

    • backrefs and zipp are dropped from requirements.txt. Neither is part of the resolved dependency graph for pyspelling + pymdown-extensions on the Python version this image ships (verified against each package's own declared metadata and the installed package list in the built image) — they were stale manual pins, not active dependencies. In particular, zipp was originally pinned in PR #204 to patch CVE-2024-5569; that dependency chain (pyspelling → importlib-metadata → zipp) no longer exists, so removing the pin does not reintroduce the vulnerability — the package simply isn't installed, pinned or not.

    • .github/dependabot.yml's pip ecosystem entry already set versioning-strategy: lockfile-only, which expects exactly this requirements.in/requirements.txt split; this change makes that existing setting apply as intended.

0.63.1, 2026-07-30, bug fix release, update recommended

  • Fixed sources glob patterns that combine brace expansion with the SPLIT/GLOBSTAR flags (e.g. **/*.{c,h}|!build/**) silently matching zero files and causing the action to fail with RuntimeError: None of the source targets from the configuration match any files. The pinned bracex dependency (2.5.post1) predated the version wcmatch requires for correct parsing of such patterns; bumped to 3.0.1 via PR #379. Addresses issue #378, reported by @​arkq.

0.63.0, 2026-07-01, maintenance release, update not required

0.62.0, 2026-06-19, security release, update recommended

  • Cleaned up GitHub Actions workflows using zizmor and removed ratchet annotations via PR #355 and PR #356.

  • Clarified examples in README.

Release notes

Sourced from redis's releases.

8.1.0

Changes

✨ Highlights

Async maintenance notifications

redis-py now supports server-pushed maintenance notifications in the asyncio stack for both standalone and cluster clients, bringing the async client to parity with the sync implementation. When a Redis deployment signals maintenance events (such as node migration or failover windows), the async client reacts through the maintenance-notifications handler (redis/maint_notifications.py and its async integration under redis/asyncio/), allowing applications to adapt connection handling during maintenance without downtime. (#4177)

Expanded command coverage

This release adds a batch of new command surfaces across core data types and modules:

  • Lists — LMOVEM / BLMOVEM for moving multiple elements between lists (#4174).
  • Sets — SDIFFCARD and SUNIONCARD cardinality commands (#4171).
  • Streams — MAXCOUNT / MAXSIZE options for XREAD and XREADGROUP (#4173).
  • Time Series — TS.READ (#4170), TS.QUERYLABELS (#4197), TS.NRANGE / TS.NREVRANGE (#4163), and an exclude_empty (EXCLUDEEMPTY) option for TS.MRANGE / TS.MREVRANGE (#4188).
  • Search — FT.ALIASLIST (#4198) and a COLLECT reducer for aggregations (#4179).

pulls.title: test(var-len): cover fixed-length path multiplicity
pulls.body:
## Summary

Regression tests for the `fixed-rust` cluster in which a **fixed-length variable-length traversal collapsed distinct paths**, silently behaving as though `DISTINCT` had been applied — and, more confusingly, merely *binding a path variable* changed the result.

@K-Jo's original analysis in #73 explains the mechanism: the traversal was evaluated as a boolean adjacency-matrix product, which records only *whether* the destination is reachable, not *how many* distinct paths reach it. The Rust engine fixed this; nothing in the suite pinned the multiplicity contract.

## Changes

Added `test18_fixed_length_path_multiplicity` to `tests/flow/test_variable_length_traversals.py`, building a diamond with two distinct 2-hop paths and asserting:

- `MATCH (a:A)-[:LIKES*2]->(c)` returns the destination **twice**, with no implicit `DISTINCT` (#73, #1450)
- the result is **identical with and without a bound path variable** (#354, #1450)
- it also matches the equivalent **explicit two-hop** pattern
- the two paths stay **distinguishable** by their intermediate node — `nodes(p)[1]` gives `n00` and `n01`
- a bounded range `[*1..2]` is likewise consistent with and without a path variable

This is a new test rather than an extension: the file's only existing multi-hop fixture (`test13_fanout`) is a *tree*, so no diamond exists in it and path multiplicity cannot be observed. The existing `[*2]` assertions at lines 242/244 only check `length(p)` on a single path.

## Testing

`RELEASE=1 VERBOSE=0 TEST=tests/flow/test_variable_length_traversals ./flow.sh` → **18/18 pass**.

Each assertion fails on the era build and passes on `main`:

| query | `v4.2.2` | `main` | asserted |
|---|---|---|---|
| `MATCH (a:A)-[:LIKES*2]->(c)` | **1** | 2 | 2 |
| `MATCH p=(a:A)-[:LIKES*2]->(c)` | 2 | 2 | 2 |

The 1-vs-2 split on `v4.2.2` is precisely the "assigning a variable changes query results" symptom of #354.

## Memory / Performance Impact

N/A — tests only.

## Related Issues

Closes #73
Closes #354
Closes #1450

Two issues from the same cluster are deliberately **not** claimed:

- **#204** — the issue body contains only a dead link to the original RedisGraph issue, with no query or dataset, so there is nothing to assert.
- **#2105** — still **open**, and about repeated-edge semantics of `[*2..2]` versus explicit two-hop, which is a different contract from path multiplicity.

While writing these tests I found a live defect on `main` and filed it as **#2470**: the same path-collapsing behaviour still occurs when the intermediate node of an explicit two-hop pattern is **anonymous**, because the planner fuses the two hops into a single matrix-product traverse. That assertion is intentionally left out of this PR so it stays green; it belongs with the fix for #2470.

<!-- This is an auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->
## Summary by CodeRabbit

* **Tests**
  * Added coverage for fixed-length traversals across diamond-shaped graphs.
  * Verified that distinct paths preserve duplicate results.
  * Confirmed consistent results with path variables, explicit multi-hop patterns, intermediate-node checks, and bounded traversal ranges.
<!-- end of auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->

pulls.title: test(optional-match): cover cartesian product cardinality in OPTIONAL MATCH
pulls.body:
## Summary

Regression tests for the `fixed-rust` cluster in which a **cartesian product inside an `OPTIONAL MATCH` collapsed to a single row** per incoming record instead of yielding the full product. The Rust engine fixed this; nothing in the suite pinned the cardinality contract, so it could silently regress.

Root cause of the original defect: the `Argument` operation did not feed the optional stream, so the comma-separated patterns were evaluated once rather than per input record.

## Changes

- **Extended** `test23_optional_and_cartesian_product` (its name is already exactly this scenario) with row-count assertions:
  - a **bound** variable re-used in the optional cartesian pattern — `MATCH (x0) WITH x0 OPTIONAL MATCH (x0), (x1)` must give 5 × 5 = **25** rows (#255)
  - the same query asserting no row carries a NULL binding
  - two **fresh** variables — `MATCH (n) OPTIONAL MATCH (a), (b)` must give 5 × 5 × 5 = **125** rows (#172)
- **Added** `test28_optional_multi_pattern_traversals` for the relationship-pattern variants, which need different fixtures:
  - multi-pattern `OPTIONAL MATCH` over relationships must give 4 × 2 × 1 = **8** rows (#313)
  - consecutive `OPTIONAL MATCH` clauses re-binding already-bound variables must not multiply cardinality — **2** rows (#399)

## Testing

`RELEASE=1 VERBOSE=0 TEST=tests/flow/test_optional_match ./flow.sh` → **27/27 pass**.

Every assertion was verified both ways — it fails on the era build and passes on `main`:

| issue | query | `v4.2.2` | `main` | asserted |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| #255 | `MATCH (x0) WITH x0 OPTIONAL MATCH (x0),(x1)` | 5 | 25 | 25 |
| #172 | `MATCH (n) OPTIONAL MATCH (a),(b)` | 5 | 125 | 125 |
| #313 | multi-pattern optional over `:T5`/`:T6` | 4 | 8 | 8 |
| #399 | two consecutive `OPTIONAL MATCH` | 8 | 2 | 2 |

## Memory / Performance Impact

N/A — tests only.

## Related Issues

Closes #255
Closes #172
Closes #313
Closes #399

Deliberately **not** claimed: #432 and #439 belong to the same cluster but neither issue supplies the dataset its fuzzer query ran against, so their exact cardinality cannot be reproduced or asserted. They are left open rather than closed on an untested assertion.

pulls.title: test: writes inside a subquery apply to every input row
pulls.body:
## Summary

Four issues report the same defect: a `CALL {}` subquery that writes applied the write to the **first input row only**. The remaining rows still passed through the subquery, so the row count and the success reply both looked correct while the writes were silently dropped — a `DELETE` that reports success and leaves rows behind.

Fixed by the Rust engine, untested. This adds the regression coverage.

## Changes

One test, `test_54_writes_apply_to_every_input_row` in `tests/flow/test_call_subquery.py`, covering each write the reports hit:

- `DELETE r` in a unit subquery over three matched relationships (#2159)
- the same behind a `WHERE r.w = 1` filter, so the unmatched edge must survive (#2164)
- `DETACH DELETE` over three nodes, which must take their relationships with them (#2234)
- `MERGE` driven by `UNWIND range(4, 8)`, where each row must pick its own `ON CREATE` / `ON MATCH` branch (#2164)
- the **returning** form, which collapsed one row per input into a single row (#1943)

## Testing

`test_call_subquery` 54/54.

Every assertion was taken from an observed run rather than from the reports, and each was reproduced on **v4.20.1** first:

| scenario | v4.20.1 | `main` | asserted |
|---|---|---|---|
| `DELETE r` over 3 edges | 1 deleted, 2 left | 3 deleted, 0 left | 0 left |
| `DELETE r WHERE r.w = 1` | — | 2 deleted, 1 left | 1 left |
| `DETACH DELETE` over 3 nodes | 1 node / 1 rel deleted, 5 nodes + 2 rels left | 3 / 3 deleted, 3 nodes + 0 rels left | 3 nodes, 0 rels |
| `MERGE` over `range(4,8)` (total/ctime/mtime) | 5 / 0 / 1 | 8 / 3 / 2 | 8 / 3 / 2 |
| returning subquery rows | 1 row | 2 rows | `[[1], [1]]` |

No duplication: the file's existing `DELETE`-in-subquery coverage is about validation errors and `DELETE` op compression, and nothing asserted that a non-returning subquery's write reaches every input row. `test_52_create_delete` is an unrelated stub and is left alone.

Closes #2234

pulls.title: fix(runtime): reject bad arity/type on temporal constructors
pulls.body:
## Summary

`RETURN date('2020-01-01','x')` terminates the server process. So do `localtime(1,2)`, `localdatetime(1,2)` and `date(1)`. Any client able to run a query can take the database down with one malformed call, so this fixes that.

Found by the `fuzz` job on #2304, which panicked at `temporal.rs:635` with `left: 2, right: 7`.

## Changes

`date`, `localtime` and `localdatetime` are registered with a var-length signature so their zero-argument "now" form binds. That signature is looser than what they accept, and two separate things relied on it being accurate.

- **`eval.rs`** — the struct-constructor fast path identified the binder's rewritten positional form by testing `node.num_children() > 1`. `rewrite_struct_constructor` always emits exactly one child per slot, so the correct test is equality. For a fixed-arity constructor like `point` the loose test was still safe, because arity validation rejects a second argument before evaluation; for these three nothing did, so a user-written `date(a, b)` entered the fast path and handed `date_struct_pure` a 2-element slice that indexes `args[0..6]`. Match on `func.struct_slots.len()`.
- **`functions/mod.rs`** — `validate_args_type` had `FnArguments::VarLength(_) => {}`, so a var-length signature's declared element type was decorative. The three constructors declare `Map | String | Null` and their pure functions treat anything else as `unreachable!()`, which `date(1)` reached. Validate the declared type. Every other var-length function declares `Type::Any`, and `value_of_type` returns `None` for `Type::Any`, so none of them are affected.
- **`functions/temporal.rs`** — give the three their real arity, `args: [Type::Optional(...)]`. `validate` excludes `Optional` from the minimum count, so this is exactly "0 or 1" and is how `duration` and `point` already express the same thing. Using var-length to mean "may be empty" is what pulled the arity check out.

## Testing

`tests/flow/test_temporal.py::testTemporalConstructorArity`, four cases: extra arguments are rejected, wrongly-typed arguments are rejected, every supported form still constructs (0-arg, string, map, and `null` propagation), and the fixed-arity constructors are unchanged so the two groups cannot drift apart. Each rejection case also asserts the server is still answering afterwards.

- with the fix: `test_temporal` 26/26
- with the fix reverted, tests kept: **4 failures**, server killed — so the tests fail for the reason they are meant to
- `cargo test -p graph --lib` 148/148, `test_function_calls` 93/93, `cargo fmt --all --check` clean

Before and after:

| query | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `RETURN date('2020-01-01','x')` | server killed | `Received 2 arguments to function 'date', expected at most 1` |
| `RETURN localtime(1,2)` | server killed | `Received 2 arguments to function 'localtime', expected at most 1` |
| `RETURN date(1)` | server killed | `Type mismatch: expected Map, String, or Null but was Integer` |
| `RETURN date()`, `date('2020-01-01')`, `date({year:2020})`, `date(null)` | ok | ok |

## Memory / Performance Impact

None. The fast-path guard swaps `> 1` for `== struct_slots.len()`, both constant comparisons on an already-loaded field. Type validation for var-length arguments happens once at plan time, not per row.

## Related Issues

Closes #2466

<!-- This is an auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->

## Summary by CodeRabbit

- **Bug Fixes**
  - Improved validation for temporal constructors such as `date`, `localtime`, and `localdatetime`.
  - Invalid argument counts and unsupported argument types are now rejected with clear errors.
  - Correctly supports optional map, string, or null arguments while preserving existing valid behavior.
  - Prevented malformed constructor calls from being incorrectly dispatched.
  - Fixed variable-length function validation so each supplied argument is checked against its declared type.

<!-- end of auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->

pulls.title: ci(dependabot): cover Python, uv and Docker dependencies on main
pulls.body:
## Summary

Dependabot on `main` currently tracks only `github-actions` and `cargo`. Three dependency surfaces in the Rust tree receive no updates at all, so vulnerable versions there would go unflagged indefinitely.

This adds one entry per uncovered surface. The three existing entries — including the `target-branch: master` entry that keeps the C engine's Actions bumps alive (#2255) — are untouched.

## Changes

- **`pip` at `/tests`** — `tests/requirements.txt` (`behave`, `pytest`, `redis`, `RLTest`, `hypothesis`, `falkordb`, `textual`)
- **`uv` at `/bench`** — the benchmark harness is its own uv project with `pyproject.toml` + `uv.lock`; `pip` would not read the lockfile, so it needs the `uv` ecosystem
- **`docker` at `/build`, `/build/runtime`, `/.devcontainer`** — the `debian:trixie-slim`, `node:24-bookworm-slim` and `ubuntu:24.04` base images
- Each entry is **grouped** (`patterns: ["*"]`) so it opens one consolidated PR per week instead of one per dependency

### Two deliberate exclusions

- **`/bench` is not in the docker entry.** `bench/Dockerfile` is `FROM ${C_IMAGE}` — an entirely ARG-driven base that Dependabot cannot resolve to a registry tag. Including it would add a directory that yields nothing.
- **`gitsubmodule` is not added.** `main` has no `.gitmodules`; submodules exist only on `master`, where `submodule-update.yml` already handles them. Enabling it would produce duplicate, conflicting PRs pinned to unreleased upstream commits.

### Note on the `redis<8.1` pin

`tests/requirements.txt` pins `redis<8.1` with a documented reason (falkordb-py 1.6.2 forwards `himport_registry` to the sync constructor). Dependabot honours declared version constraints and will not widen them, so this pin holds until someone edits it by hand. The comment in the config records why.

## Testing

- `dependabot.yml` parses as valid YAML; all six entries enumerate correctly with `version: 2` preserved
- Every configured directory was confirmed to contain a manifest Dependabot can actually read: `tests/requirements.txt`, `bench/pyproject.toml` + `bench/uv.lock`, and a `Dockerfile` with at least one statically-resolvable `FROM` in each of the three docker directories
- `package-ecosystem: uv` and the plural `directories:` key are both currently supported per GitHub's Dependabot options reference
- Config-only change — no build, runtime or test behaviour is affected. GitHub validates the file on merge to the default branch; a syntax error would surface in the repo's Dependabot settings rather than at runtime

## Memory / Performance Impact

N/A — CI configuration only. No C, Rust or graph code paths touched.

## Related Issues

Closes #2465

References #2255 (the branch migration that made `main` the config's authoritative location).


<!-- This is an auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->

## Summary by CodeRabbit

* **Chores**
  * Added automated weekly dependency update coverage for Python test and benchmark dependencies.
  * Added automated monitoring for Docker base image updates across development and runtime environments.
  * Grouped related dependency updates to simplify maintenance.

<!-- end of auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->

pulls.title: test(validation): cover a repeated relationship variable (#1982)
pulls.body:
Closes #1982
Closes #465
Closes #1333
Closes #1335

## Summary

Adds regression coverage for **reusing a relationship variable**. Three shapes took the server down (SIGSEGV / assertion in query-graph construction), and a fourth — which is *valid* Cypher — was wrongly rejected.

## Changes

- New `tests/flow/test_query_validation.py::test46_repeated_relationship_variable`, covering:
  - `WITH NULL AS a0 MATCH ()-[a0]-()-[a0]-()` — the same variable twice in **one** pattern can never match and must be rejected; it used to trip `QueryGraph_GetEdgeByAlias(qg, alias) == NULL` (#465)
  - `MATCH (n0)-[r0]->(n0) WHERE ()<-[r0]-(n0)` — **legal**: each pattern uses the bound variable once. Pinned to an exact result (#1335)
  - a repeated relationship variable inside a pattern predicate reached through `WITH` (#1982)
  - the multi-`WHERE` chain from #1333

Uses its own graph key with `try/finally: g.delete()`.

## Testing

Verified in both directions.

**Broken on `falkordb/falkordb:v4.20.1`:**

| query | v4.20.1 | this branch |
|---|---|---|
| `WITH NULL AS a0 MATCH ()-[a0]-()-[a0]-() RETURN 1` | `Server closed the connection` | clean `same relationship variable` error |
| `MATCH (p:P)-[r:R]-() WITH p,r WHERE (p)-[r:R]->()<-[r:R]-() RETURN p.name` | `Server closed the connection` | clean error, server alive |
| `MATCH (n0)--(n0) WITH * WHERE (n0)--(n0) MATCH (n1)-[r1]-() WITH * WHERE (n1)-[r1]->()<-[r1]-() RETURN *` | `Server closed the connection` | clean error, server alive |
| `MATCH (n0)-[r0]->(n0) WHERE ()<-[r0]-(n0) RETURN n0.name` | wrongly errors `Cannot use the same relationship variable 'r0'` | `[['A']]` |

**A note on the assertions.** The two crash shapes accept **either** a clean rejection or zero rows, because only the crash is the defect and pinning today's message would enshrine a parser-level error text (`Invalid input GreaterThan`) that is not the contract worth locking in. Each is followed by a query that must still answer — the segfault arrived *after* the reply had been sent, so liveness is the assertion that actually catches it. The two deterministic shapes (#465 reject, #1335 accept) are pinned exactly.

**Passes on this branch:** `TEST="tests/flow/test_query_validation" ./flow.sh` → `Total Tests Run: 45, Total Tests Failed: 0`.

## Memory / Performance Impact

N/A — test-only change.

## Related Issues

Closes #1982, #465, #1333, #1335 — all four are relationship-variable reuse, so they share one test rather than four near-identical ones.

<!-- This is an auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->

## Summary by CodeRabbit

* **Bug Fixes**
  * Improved handling of repeated relationship variables in queries.
  * Invalid duplicate-variable queries now return a clean error or no results without affecting server responsiveness.

pulls.title: test(merge): cover MERGE referencing an entity deleted in the same query (#651)
pulls.body:
Closes #651
Closes #1030

## Summary

Adds regression coverage for a `MERGE` pattern that references an entity **deleted earlier in the same query**. The deleted entity used to be resurrected: a relationship got anchored on a deleted node, and `ON CREATE SET` wrote a property through a deleted edge. Worse, whether it happened depended on *unrelated trailing clauses*, so two semantically equivalent queries disagreed — a silent data-correctness bug.

## Changes

- New `tests/flow/test_graph_merge.py::test38_merge_referencing_deleted_entity`, covering:
  - `CREATE (x) DELETE x MERGE (x)-[:n0]->(x) CREATE ()` and the same query with an extra `CREATE (y) DELETE y` — both must behave identically (#651)
  - `ON CREATE SET x.n0 = 0` on a deleted edge, with and without an intervening `WITH *` (#1030)

`main` now refuses the write outright with `Failed to create relationship; endpoint was not found`. The test pins that error **and** the resulting relationship count, so a future silent no-op cannot pass in its place.

## Testing

Verified in both directions.

**Broken on `falkordb/falkordb:v4.20.1`:**

| query | v4.20.1 | this branch |
|---|---|---|
| `CREATE (x) DELETE x MERGE (x)-[:n0]->(x) CREATE ()` | succeeds, **1 relationship created** | clean error, 0 created |
| ...plus a trailing `CREATE (y) DELETE y` | succeeds, 0 relationships | clean error, 0 created |
| `CREATE ()-[x:A]->()-[y:B]->() DELETE y DELETE x MERGE ()-[:C]->() ON CREATE SET x.n0 = 0 ...` | `n = 1` | `n = 0` |
| ...same with `WITH *` before `DELETE x` | `n = 1` | `n = 0` |

The first two rows are the #651 discrepancy: identical queries, different graphs.

**Passes on this branch:** `TEST="tests/flow/test_graph_merge" ./flow.sh` → `Total Tests Run: 38, Total Tests Failed: 0`.

## Memory / Performance Impact

N/A — test-only change. The scenario concerns entity lifetime within a single query; the test asserts no relationship is created against a freed endpoint.

## Related Issues

Closes #651, #1030 — the same underlying defect (operations resolving against an already-deleted entity), so they share one test.

## Summary by CodeRabbit

* **Bug Fixes**
  * MERGE queries referencing deleted nodes or relationships now correctly report an endpoint-not-found error.
  * Prevented creation of unintended relationships or application of `ON CREATE SET` properties when referenced entities have been deleted.
