pulls.title: docs: the relationship tensor's design, mechanised invariants and measured cost
pulls.body:
Closes #2432.

Documentation, proofs and the measurement harnesses the paper reports on. **No change to shipped behaviour, CI or Cargo**: the Rust in the diff is `#[cfg(test)]` bench modules plus one test-only hook and two `pub(super)` constants those benches read, so nothing here is compiled into the module. (An earlier revision of this description said "zero changes to Rust" — that was true when the harnesses lived on a separate branch, and is no longer.)

## What lands

**`docs/papers/tensor.tex`** — a 40-page standalone treatment of the relationship tensor: the design space it sits in, the ten-state per-pair automaton, the invariant set, the algorithms with their proof strategies, the fold policy's cost model, and a measured evaluation.

**`proofs/tensor/`** — the Lean 4 mechanisation the paper reports on: ~7,200 lines, ~380 theorems (of which `Tensor/` is ~6,200 and ~320), `lake build` clean, `#print axioms` showing no `sorry`. It has already earned its keep by identifying two unreachable branches that were subsequently removed from the engine, one of which fabricated edge id 0 on a backward read.

## The design, in one paragraph

Three ways to store a multigraph's edge identities inside a GraphBLAS matrix: **(A)** a heap container per multi-edge cell, reached by a tagged pointer — what the C engine does; **(B)** keep the adjacency Boolean and hold every id in a second structure; **(C)** make the adjacency `UINT64`, store a lone id inline, and promote a pair into an overflow matrix only when it gains a second edge, marking the cell with a reserved sentinel. (C) is what this engine does. It buys the common case at the price of a state transition and the invariant discipline that transition requires.

## The evaluation, and what it changed

Measured with instruction counts rather than wall clock, |E| = 176,000 held fixed while multiplicity varies, at both the engine level and — via a C harness linking the shipped static archive with no stubs — at the data-structure boundary on both sides.

It did not simply confirm the analytic story:

- **The engine-level read estimates were overstated** — by 1.8x for (C) and 5.1x for (A) — against the boundary measurement. Reading (A)'s tagged-pointer cell costs exactly what an inline cell costs; the container tax is entirely in walking it. 64% of that read is delta layers probing *empty* matrices, not edge storage at all.
- **The scan advantage is not edge storage.** (C) wins the engine-level scan at 0.43x but *loses* iteration at the boundary (1.09x, 1.34x). The paper attributes the win to the engine and says (C)'s case on scans is that it does not lose.
- **The oscillation regime — the paper's own predicted weak spot — was worse than the design predicts**, and the measurement found a real defect: demotion was quadratic in the batch (#2429), now fixed (#2431). It is reported as defect, instrumented cause, fix, and residual: a constant again at 7,421 instructions against (A)'s 2,355.
- **Design (B)'s space is a labelled model** over measured components, not a measurement, because (B) exists nowhere. The paper says so, and says what the model assumes.
- **A methodological result:** the promotion transition is not isolable by differencing at engine level. Three of four controls yield negative costs, and (A)'s boundary control also fails, because appending an id to an existing `GrB_Vector` re-materialises the whole vector. Differencing works only where the control is genuinely cheaper.

## Honest limits, stated in the paper

Design (B) itself is unimplemented; fan-out beyond k=2 at the boundary is unmeasured for reads; all reads are warm and sequential; wall clock and cycles are not reported because some runs shared the machine; everything is macOS/arm64 with the C side pinned to GraphBLAS 10.3.1; and whether multiplicity distributions dominated by 1 describe real deployments is a question about deployments, not data structures.

The reproduction path is committed: harnesses at `bench/studies/edge_storage/` and `graph/src/graph/graphblas/tensor_cost_bench.rs` (on `measure/design-b-and-boundary`, not yet merged).

PDFs are gitignored, so the built paper is not in the diff; `docs/papers/README.md` says how to build it.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

---

## Update: merged `main`, and re-measured what #2579 moved

The branch was behind `main` and conflicting. Resolving it turned out to be more
than a merge, because two merged PRs changed exactly what this paper is about.

**#2579** (fixing #2578) replaced the compound key and narrowed `me`.
**#2565** made the cardinality identity checked.

### The merge was not mechanical

- `edge_versioned()` is gone. The benches take `edge_versioned_block_0()`, not
  `edge_versioned_all()`: every fixture pair is within `BLOCK_SHIFT` bits per
  axis, so block (0,0) is the only live block and the reading is the one the
  published numbers were taken under.
- `compound_key` returns `(block, row)`; the space fixture takes `.1`, and its
  standalone mirror now tracks `(ME_DIM, ME_NARROW_NCOLS)` instead of restating
  the pre-#2579 square geometry.
- Both `matrix.rs` hooks are **dropped**, not merged — `integer_bits_for_test`
  collided with one `main` landed independently, and neither it nor
  `force_materialize_for_test` had a caller. `matrix.rs` is untouched again.

### Two harness defects found

- `engine_space_and_transition.py` imported `rss` from `falkorbench.counters`,
  **which has never existed in any branch**. The harness this paper cites as its
  reproduction path could not run as committed. Implemented locally over `ps`.
- The Rust-side measurements must run `--test-threads=1`. In parallel a point
  read measures 8,156 instructions against 722 serially. Now documented.

### The proofs: `Bounded` is deleted, not weakened

`Bounded p` existed only to make the old key injective and in range — 40 sites
across 9 files, including three `InvCore` fields. The new key is total, so the
hypothesis has no successor and what remains is strictly stronger:

| before | after |
| --- | --- |
| `key_inj : Bounded p → Bounded q → key p = key q → p = q` | `key_inj : key p = key q → p = q` |
| `key_lt : Bounded p → key p < 2^64` | `row_lt : ∀ p, row p < 2^60` |
| `keyHi`/`keyLo` under `Bounded` | `inv_key : ∀ p, keyInverse (blockOf p) (row p) = p` |
| — | `row_le_grbIndexMax : ∀ p, row p ≤ GrBIndexMax` — the property whose absence **was** #2578 |
| `InvCore.bounded`, `WellFormed.bounded` | *removed* — a decoder no longer has to check node-id width |

The refactor also exposed a modelling bug it did not introduce: `iter_edges`'
forward half was modelled with the numeral `2^64 - 1`, which only typechecked
while `Bounded` was quietly supplying that node ids are u64-representable. It is
now `fwdIterAll` — every row, no filter — which is what `u64::MAX` means in the
Rust. `lake build` clean, 2024 jobs, no `sorry`, axioms unchanged.

### Measurements: before/after on one machine

Every published figure reproduces **exactly** at the pre-merge commit, which is
what licenses attributing the moves to #2579 rather than to the machine.

| | paper / before | after | |
|---|---|---|---|
| aux matrix, 1 id/row | 38.63 ✓ | 34.63 | −4.00 B/id |
| `me` B/id at k=2/4/8/16 | 24.32 / 16.66 / 12.83 / 10.91 ✓ | 20.32 / 12.66 / 8.83 / 6.91 | −4.00 each |
| adjacency UINT64 / BOOL | 12.01 / 4.01 ✓ | 12.01 / 4.01 | unchanged |
| engine-level marginal B/id | 9.09 ✓ (C engine: 8.04) | **5.24** | ordering **inverts** |

Exactly −4.00 everywhere with adjacency untouched is the signature of the
column-index array going 8 → 4 bytes, and nothing else.

**Two results, not just errata.** (C)'s marginal cost per identifier was 13%
*above* the C engine's and is now 35% *below* it — so the paper's claim that (A)
is marginally cheaper per identifier, and that the designs differ only in a fixed
per-pair charge, is false in both halves. And the composed (B)-vs-(C) ratio
**falls**, 3.55 → 3.22: narrowing helps (B) more than (C), because the auxiliary
matrix is the whole of what (B) is made of. An optimisation to this design
narrowed its own advantage, and the paper says that rather than reporting 3.22 as
an improvement.

**Reads did not move.** inline 726.9 → 721.9, sentinel 2,922.8 → 2,928.8,
promote 3,174.2 → 3,229.8 (+1.8%), third-edge control 1,417.3 → 1,478.7 (+4.3%).
Blocking costs the write path one comparison per identifier written and reads
nothing. The gap to the table's 566/2,502 is the GraphBLAS 10.5.0 drift the paper
already recorded — not this change.

### Where the paper was wrong about its own proposal

§limits had already designed this repair. Two predictions were wrong and now say
so: the block must be a **pair** (splitting only the source moves the ceiling
onto the destination), and the guard is **gone** rather than corrected, because
totality beats a correct assertion. Two were right: migration-free, and the
mechanised restatement being an improvement. A third — "a sparse map" — had the
right quantity and the wrong structure: every real graph is one block, so it is a
`SmallVec` sized for one, a compare rather than a hash.

### Honest limit on this update

`tab:evalwrite`'s space columns are **not** re-measured — different fixture and
harness (|E| = 176,000, the benchmark suite), not re-run. They are flagged in the
paper as upper bounds on (C) with the direction of the correction and its second
cause: the same PR replaced the edge-endpoint side table with a tiered structure,
which is outside the tensor but inside those megabytes.

Paper builds clean: 53 pages, no errors, no undefined references. `cargo fmt`
clean, clippy adds nothing, 176 Rust tests pass.

pulls.title: perf: make the multi-edge demote path linear in the batch (26x)
pulls.body:
Closes #2429.

Deleting an edge from a 2-edge pair — the *demote* transition that returns the surviving id to the inline cell — was ~95x C's cost and **quadratic in how many pairs one query demotes**.

### Cause

Instrumented per call site inside `Tensor::remove_all`, rather than guessed. At 1,000 demoted pairs the function was 13.18 ms of a 14.35 ms query:

| site | 125 | 250 | 500 | 1000 pairs |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `me.iter` right after `me.remove` | 269 µs | 1.76 ms | 3.50 ms | **9.88 ms** |
| `eff_get` right after the `dp` write | 14 µs | 995 µs | 1.54 ms | **2.90 ms** |
| the writes themselves | 28 µs | 104 µs | 167 µs | 0.32 ms |

Read-after-write on an MVCC delta layer *inside* the per-edge loop: each read has to materialise the tuples the previous iteration left pending. The originally suspected `dp`/`wait_fwd` path is only ~22% of it — the dominant term is `me`, where `me.remove` dirties the delta and the very next `me.iter` waits on it. The original evidence (quadratic in batch, flat in `|me|`) could not separate the two, since neither scans `me`'s base.

### Fix

The slow path is split into a read phase and a write phase — the same shape `set_all_from_slices` already uses on the insert side. The read phase touches no layer it also reads: it reads each multi pair's `me` row **once per pair** rather than twice per edge, replays that pair's transitions in a per-pair `PairPlan` (`Multi` → `Single{demoted}` → `Emptied`), and buffers the `me` removals. The write phase applies them, probing only committed bases, with all `dp` erases ordered ahead of all `dp` inserts so no probe can observe another write's pending tuples.

Layer writes, `multi_count`, `mt` and cancel-to-clean make byte-for-byte the same decisions as the old loop, so the documented delta invariants — and the Lean proofs over them — are untouched. Three regression tests cover the state machine the old loop got for free by re-reading its own writes; they were mutation-tested (breaking the demote-then-empty case makes `batch_can_demote_and_then_empty_the_same_pair` fail).

### Measured

Instructions via `proc_pid_rusage` on the server pid, macOS arm64, release. Same query with and without the transition, 1,000 pairs:

| engine | demote 2→1 | empty a 1-edge pair | the transition |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| C | 10,743 | 8,388 | **2,355** |
| Rust before | 230,028 | 8,795 | **221,233** |
| Rust after | 16,263 | 8,842 | **7,421** |

Scaling — only the number of demoted pairs varies (instr/pair):

| pairs | before | after | C |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 125 | 65,004 | 26,773 | 23,266 |
| 250 | 130,063 | 19,551 | 16,052 |
| 500 | 161,406 | 17,580 | 12,740 |
| 1000 | 228,855 | 16,299 | 10,878 |

Per-pair cost now *falls* with batch size, as C's does. Also: 500 demotes with `|me|` grown 17x is flat and now beats C at the largest (24,636 vs 47,929); a full promote+demote cycle 237,018 → 24,566 against C's 25,683; in-function time at 1,000 pairs 13.18 ms → 0.75 ms.

All numbers above were reproduced independently of the authoring session, on a separate build and driver.

### Not fixed

Rust is still **1.5x C** on the whole delete query at 1,000 pairs (16,299 vs 10,878) and the isolated transition is 7,421 vs 2,355 — same order, no longer quadratic, but not parity. The residual is no longer concentrated in `remove_all` (0.75 ms of a 2.57 ms query); most of it is elsewhere in the delete path, untouched here. Separate work.

Reading a multi pair's whole `me` row is O(k) once per pair where the old code read 2 entries per edge, so a pair with very many parallel edges does more list work than before — but strictly less than the O(pending) GraphBLAS wait it replaces. The removal search is a binary search, with a debug assert that the row really is ascending.

pulls.title: perf: skip the edge-id lookup when nothing reads the edge (1.99x)
pulls.body:
Closes #2427.

A chain-less `CondTraverse` binds its edge alias to a representative edge id for every row it emits, and finding one costs a tensor lookup per row — `Tensor::get` → `eff_get`, up to three GraphBLAS `extractElement` calls to read the effective value through the `dp`/`dm`/`m` delta layers. On a traversal that never reads the edge, all of it is waste.

### Why `emit_relationship` couldn't already decide this

`emit_relationship` answers row *multiplicity*: false means one row per `(src, dst)` pair instead of one per edge. An anonymous edge inside a named path gets `emit_relationship: false` — one row per pair is correct — and still has to be bound, because `PathBuilder` reads the alias to assemble the path. The runtime comment said exactly that, and resolved it by always doing the lookup.

So the two questions get two answers. `CondTraverse` gains `bind_relationship`, conservatively `true` at planning time and lowered by a new `reduce_bound_edge` pass that walks ancestors looking for a reference to the edge alias. This is the same shape as the existing `emit_path` / `reduce_var_len_path` pair, and reuses its `ir_references_variable`.

The pass runs **last** in the pipeline, after everything that rebuilds a `CondTraverse` or moves its ancestors (including `fuse_optional_traverse`). Every constructor sets `bind_relationship: true`, so a rebuilding pass can only ever be conservative and this pass has the final say.

Dropping the lookup also drops its `found_id` guard, which never fired: `f` is built from these same tensors, so every pair it yields has at least one edge in one of them.

### Measured

1,000 nodes, 88,000 `(src, dst)` pairs, release build, instructions per pair (median of 5, macOS `proc_pid_rusage`):

| query | before | after | |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| `MATCH (a:N)-[:R]->(x:N) RETURN count(x)` | 1,467 | 736 | **1.99x** |
| `MATCH (a:N)-[r:R]->(x:N) RETURN sum(r.k)` | 3,944 | 3,938 | unchanged |

Identical at multiplicity 2 (735/pair) — one row per pair either way, so the win does not depend on multi-edges.

Full `bench measure` suite, instructions:

| query | ratio |
|---|---:|
| traversal + count | 0.677x |
| expand-into inline rel attrs | 0.710x |
| multi-type traverse | 0.879x |
| **suite total** | **0.9771x** |
| suite total allocated bytes | 1.0000x |

The handful of rows above 1.0x are all sub-600k-instruction queries, inside the run-to-run band that same-binary repeat runs show on this host.

### Correctness

- **Differential against `main`**: 19 traversal queries — named paths, `relationships(p)` element values, multi-type `:R|S`, `OPTIONAL MATCH`, var-length, bidirectional, inline edge filters, `SKIP`/`LIMIT`, `DISTINCT`, `WITH` barriers — plus the `EXPLAIN` output. All byte-identical.
- **8 new planner unit tests**, including the regression that matters: an anonymous edge inside a named path must stay bound.
- `cargo test -p graph` 134 passed; e2e + functions + mvcc + concurrency 136 passed; TCK green; clippy clean.

  * Improved traversal efficiency by skipping unnecessary relationship lookups and output columns when relationship aliases are not used.
  * Preserved relationship data for filters, projections, deletes, path construction, and optional traversals.
* **Bug Fixes**
  * Improved consistency when optimizing and combining conditional traversals.

pulls.title: fix(bulk): replicate GRAPH.BULK from the background writer
pulls.body:
Closes #2347

## What was wrong

`GRAPH.BULK` never reached replicas — silently, with a healthy replication link and no error anywhere. It also corrupted the AOF, which the issue did not cover.

The background-writer path replicated with `RM_ReplicateVerbatim` on a **thread-safe context**. That API propagates `ctx->client->argv`, and the client behind a thread-safe context is a *fake pooled* one carrying no argv. Redis says so inline (`module.c`):

> Even when the context is associated with a blocked client, we can't access it safely from another thread, so we use a fake client here

`alsoPropagate()` with `argc == 0` is **not** a no-op — it emits a zero-element RESP array. Every bulk batch propagated a literal `*0`:

```
*2..$6..SELECT..$1..0..*0..*26..$4..XADD..
                        ^^^^ the propagated zero-arg command
```

Replicas skip that frame, hence the silent divergence. The AOF is less forgiving — `*0` makes it unparseable, so an AOF-enabled server **refused to restart at all** after a bulk load:

```
# Bad file format reading the append only file appendonlydir/appendonly.aof.1.incr.aof at offset 23
```

Both `GRAPH.BULK` paths were affected: the `BEGIN` batch and the append batch.

## The fix

**1. Rebuild the command instead of replicating verbatim.** This is what C does when it replicates off the main thread — `QueryCtx_Replicate` calls `RM_Replicate` (`query_ctx.c`) — and what `graph_core::replicate_effects` already does from this same position. `RM_Replicate` builds its own argv, so the fake client stops mattering.

The arg slice borrows the tokens already copied for the worker, so the payload is not copied a second time. The key is carried as raw bytes because `to_string()` is lossy and would rewrite a non-UTF-8 graph name into replacement characters and address a different key on the replica.

**2. Widen the inline guard to C's dispatcher predicate.** This is *required* to make (1) safe, not optional hardening. Once the command actually reached the AOF, replaying it took the blocking path and tripped a hard assertion — AOF replay drives a fake client with no `CLIENT_MASTER`, so `REPLICATED` is not set for it:

```
# ==> aof.c:1692 '(fakeClient->flags & CLIENT_BLOCKED) == 0' is not true
# crashed by signal: 11
```

The guard now mirrors `cmd_dispatcher.c`: `MULTI | REPLICATED | LUA | DENY_BLOCKING | LOADING`. `REPLICATED` additionally makes a replica apply the batch *before* the handler returns, rather than letting Redis advance the replication offset while the write is still queued — the same reasoning already documented in `graph_core.rs`.

## Verification

Anchored to `main` at `27edbd566`, measured before and after on the same build:

| | pristine `main` | with this PR |
|---|---|---|
| Replica node counts (BEGIN / append) | `0 / 0` | `100 / 50` |
| Control write (plain `CREATE`) | `1` | `1` |
| `GRAPH.BULK` in AOF | `0` | `1` |
| Stray `*0` frames in AOF | present (offset 23) | none |
| Restart from AOF only | refuses to start | `PONG`, 100 nodes |

The new `test_bulk_replication` fails against the unfixed module (`0 == 100`, `0 == 50`) and passes with the fix.

Suites on the rebased base: `test_replication` 2/2, `test_bulk_insertion` 13/13, `test_effects` 22/22, `test_replication_states` 1/1, `test_graph_copy` 9/9, `test_persistency` 11/11, MVCC + concurrency 14 passed, `cargo test -p graph` 114+2 passed. `cargo fmt --check` clean, `clippy --all-targets` exit 0 (two pre-existing `too_many_arguments` warnings, both in functions this PR does not touch).

## Note on the regression test

An earlier version of this test **passed against the unfixed module** and was worthless. RLTest's replica is still handshaking when the class starts (`master_link_status:down`, `master_repl_offset:0`), so it attached *after* the load and received the graph in a full RDB transfer — masking the bug completely.

The test now gates on `WAIT 1 0` before the first batch so the replica is attached, and asserts `sync_full` is unchanged afterwards, proving the rows arrived through the replication stream rather than an RDB snapshot. Without that second assertion a late-attaching replica would satisfy the counts with the fix reverted.

## Follow-up, not in this PR

`graph_core.rs` guards the query write path on `MULTI || REPLICATED` but not `LUA || DENY_BLOCKING || LOADING`, so the same `aof.c:1692` assertion crash is reachable on `main` today for `GRAPH.QUERY`. It is **not** limited to index/constraint DDL and so is not resolved by #2419: `should_use_effects` also falls back to verbatim `GRAPH.QUERY` whenever a write's average per-effect time is below `EFFECTS_THRESHOLD` (default 300µs). Confirmed with two plain `CREATE` statements, no index or constraint anywhere. Same `c parity` gap — C's `cmd_dispatcher.c` has all five flags. Filing separately; the sibling guards in `memory.rs`, `record.rs` and `explain.rs` want the same audit.

pulls.title: perf: keep edge-property aggregates on the vectorized path (2.3x)
pulls.body:
Closes #2415.

## What

`sum(r.prop)` over a relationship classifies as `AggInputKind::Property`, whose bulk materialiser is node-only — `extract_node_ids` returns `Some` only for `Column::NodeIds`, and there is no relationship counterpart. Classification does not consult the variable's type, so edge aggregates took that path, failed on every batch, and fell through to `consume_batch_per_row`, which calls `to_owned_row()` and allocates a `Vec` of every column per row.

`sum(r.prop * 2)` classifies as `Computed`, stays on the vectorized path, and reads through a borrowed `BatchRow`. That is the whole difference, and it is why wrapping a property in an expression was *cheaper* than reading it plainly.

This reads the column per row when it is not a node column, keeping the batch vectorized. One property lookup per row — what the expression path already paid.

## Measured

`main` (`27edbd56`) vs this branch. 176,000 edges over 1,000 nodes, instructions from `proc_pid_rusage` on the server pid, so the driver is not in the numbers.

| query | before | after | |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| `MATCH ()-[r:R]->() RETURN sum(r.k)` | 2,864 | **1,252** | **2.29x** |
| `MATCH ()-[r:R]->() RETURN sum(r.k * 2)` | 1,601 | 1,600 | unchanged |

`sum(r.k)` is now cheaper than `sum(r.k * 2)`, which is the ordering that should always have held.

Against the C implementation on a whole-graph scan, across a multiplicity sweep at fixed `|E|` (instructions/edge; this branch was measured on top of `fold-policy` for the sweep, since that is where the sweep harness lives):

| mu | before | after | C | after vs C |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| 1.0 | 3,191 | 1,578 | 3,222 | **2.04x better** |
| 1.1 | 3,379 | 1,766 | 3,056 | **1.73x better** |
| 2.0 | 4,138 | 2,525 | 2,315 | 1.09x worse |
| 4.0 | 3,274 | 1,662 | 1,779 | **1.07x better** |
| 16.0 | 2,610 | 997 | 1,376 | **1.38x better** |

The residual loss at mu=2 is a **different** bug, not this one: multi-edge traversal pays per edge where C pays per pair, visible even with no edge alias bound. Tracked separately; deliberately not addressed here.

## Correctness

Checked on **distinct per-edge values** (`k = x.id * 7`) rather than a uniform fixture — a wrong lookup against a uniform fixture cannot be seen:

- `sum`, `collect`, `max`, `count` over `r.k` return the same values as the expression path
- a missing property still aggregates as null
- `sum(n.id)` over nodes is unchanged (node aggregates still take the bulk materialiser)

## Tests

- `cargo test -p graph` — 114 passed
- e2e + functions — 122 passed (on the fold-policy base, where the sweep harness lives)
- `cargo fmt --check`, `cargo clippy --all-targets` — clean

## Follow-up

A bulk relationship materialiser would beat this again. It adds a second materialiser to review, so it is left out; this change is the one that stops the regression.


<!-- This is an auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->
## Summary by CodeRabbit

* **Bug Fixes**
  * Relationship properties are now supported during vectorized aggregation when bulk extraction is unavailable.
  * Missing or unsupported relationship and node attributes now return `Null` instead of aborting processing.
  * Aggregation continues using efficient batch processing in more scenarios, including queries involving multiple relationships.
  * Relationship property values are now resolved consistently across persisted data and in-progress changes.

pulls.body:
Bumps [github/codeql-action/analyze](https://github.com/github/codeql-action) from 4.37.0 to 4.37.4.
Release notes

Sourced from github/codeql-action/analyze's releases.

v4.37.4

  • This version of the CodeQL Action adds support for the tools input for the codeql-action/init step to be specified using a github-codeql-tools repository property. This feature will gradually be rolled out following the release of this version. Once rolled out, this allows for the CodeQL CLI version that is used in GitHub-managed workflows, such as Default Setup, to be set to a custom value. For example, customers who run into issues with rate limits when a new CodeQL CLI version is released can set the value to toolcache to always use the CodeQL CLI version that is available in the runner toolcache. For Advanced Setup workflows, the value provided for tools in the workflow definition always takes precedence unless the value of the repository property starts with !. #4037
  • Update default CodeQL bundle version to 2.26.2. #4051

v4.37.3

No user facing changes.

v4.37.2

  • The new address format for the config-file input that was introduced in CodeQL Action 4.37.0 is now enabled by default. In addition to the format described there, the remote= prefix can now be used to explicitly indicate that the input refers to a remote file. All previous input formats continue to be accepted as well. #4023
  • The CodeQL Action can now make use of configured private registries in Default Setup to retrieve CodeQL configuration files from remote repositories that require authentication. This will allow customers to store their CodeQL configuration in a single repository that can then be referenced by Default Setup workflows in other repositories. We expect to roll this and other, related changes out to everyone in July. #4007

v4.37.1

  • Upcoming breaking change: Add a deprecation warning for customers using CodeQL version 2.20.6 and earlier. These versions of CodeQL were discontinued on 1 July 2026 alongside GitHub Enterprise Server 3.16, and will be unsupported by the next minor release of the CodeQL Action. #3956
  • Update default CodeQL bundle version to 2.26.1. #4019

  • Update default CodeQL bundle version to 2.26.2. #4051

pulls.title: fix(udf): bound JS evaluation, fail RDB load loudly, mark the command a write
pulls.body:
## What

The three C-side defects in #2401, confirmed against a local `master` build.

**Nothing capped CPU.** `JS_SetMemoryLimit` caps memory, but the only interrupt handler lived in `AR_UDF` and was installed only when `TIMEOUT_DEFAULT` was non-zero, which is not the default. Validation, registration and the per-thread context populate had none at any setting.

**`AUXLoadUDF_latest` validated with `ASSERT`**, which compiles out in release, so a library that failed to load was skipped and the server came up reporting success with it missing. `lib_len--` / `script_len--` were unconditional, underflowing `size_t` to `SIZE_MAX` on a zero-length buffer.

**`graph.UDF` was not a write**, so a read-only replica accepts it and ends up holding libraries the primary does not have.

## Fix

`UDF_ArmJSDeadline` / `UDF_DisarmJSDeadline` in `udf/utils.c`, armed around every JS evaluation: validation, registration, `UDF_RepoPopulateJSContext`, and `AR_UDF` when no timeout is configured. Budget is the query timeout, capped by `UDF_JS_TIMEOUT_CAP_MS` so a "no limit" setting still cannot hold a thread. The populate path is the one worth noting: it evaluates library code on the worker thread that first calls in, separately from the validation done at registration.

`AUXLoadUDF_latest` logs and fails the load, which meant returning `bool` up through `AUXLoad` to `_GraphContextType_AuxLoad`. Zero-length buffers are rejected before the decrement, and a count wider than the `unsigned int` the encoder writes is rejected outright.

`graph.UDF` registered `write deny-oom deny-script`.

Bounding the loop made two adjacent failures visible, both fixed here:

- a library that fails to evaluate into a worker's context now reports why, per library, instead of `Unknown function`. `TIMEOUT_DEFAULT` joins the JS heap and stack limits in bumping the repo version, so raising it retries a load the old value interrupted.
- a failed `LOAD REPLACE` whose rollback also fails now says the library is gone, rather than asserting and leaving it silently removed.

Refs #2401

## Proof

Local `master` build, before and after, same input.

```
$ redis-cli COMMAND INFO graph.UDF
graph.UDF ... module noscript                    # before
graph.UDF ... write denyoom module noscript      # after

$ redis-cli GRAPH.UDF LOAD spin "falkor.register('spin', function() { while(true) {} });"
$ redis-cli GRAPH.QUERY g "RETURN spin.spin()"    # TIMEOUT_DEFAULT unset
<no response, killed after 5 minutes; thread pinned>          # before
UDF Exception: interrupted            (30s, the cap)          # after
```

A library that cannot rebuild reports why, without poisoning its neighbours:

```
bigA.ga()   -> Failed to load UDF library 'bigA': InternalError: out of memory
bigB.gb()   -> Failed to load UDF library 'bigB': InternalError: out of memory
ok.add(2,3) -> 5
ok.nosuch() -> Unknown function 'ok.nosuch'
```

and clears once the timeout that caused it is raised:

```
budget 5s   -> ok
budget 0.5s -> Failed to load UDF library 'slow': InternalError: interrupted
budget 5s   -> ok
```

A failed replace whose rollback also fails now says so, and `GRAPH.UDF LIST` confirms the library really is gone:

```
Failed to register UDF library: 'big'. Restoring the previous version also failed:
... InternalError: out of memory. Library 'big' is no longer loaded
```

The decoder change demonstrated itself: an RDB holding the runaway library was interrupted at the cap on load, logged the reason, and failed the load, where the old `ASSERT` would have skipped it silently. A normal RDB round trip still works: register, `2+3` = 5, `SAVE`, restart, `4+5` = 9.

## Tests

None added. The C suite has no UDF timeout coverage to extend, and the natural test hangs on unfixed code rather than failing. Happy to add one and to say where.

## Worth a decision

A library that fails to load now **fails the RDB load**, so a poisoned dump refuses to start the server. That is the first option the issue lists and beats the old silent skip, but log-and-continue is the softer alternative if you would rather the server start with the library absent.

A policy cap on the library count is left to #2376, which is where the issue puts it.

The Rust engine on `main` is covered separately by #2402.

pulls.title: fix(udf): bound the JS evaluation that rebuilds a worker's context
pulls.body:
## What

Problem 3 in #2401 is present on `main` in a different place than the issue describes, and is worse than filed: a registered UDF can hang every worker thread until no graph query is served at all.

A library's top-level code is evaluated **twice** — by `validate_script` at registration, and again by `rebuild_context` on each worker thread that first calls into it. Only the first was bounded.

## Why it happened

The two evaluations install different globals. `__falkor_registered_names` exists only while validating, `__falkor_current_lib` only at runtime, so a script can read `globalThis` to tell them apart and loop only in the second:

```js
if (typeof globalThis.__falkor_registered_names === 'undefined') {
    while (true) {}
}
falkor.register('spin', function() { return 1; });
```

That passes registration and spins in `rebuild_context`, which had no interrupt handler.

## Fix

`graph/src/udf/js_context.rs`: install the same interrupt handler `validate_script` uses, and clear it after the rebuild so a load-time deadline cannot fire during a later call. The call path already installs its own per invocation.

Two smaller items from the same issue, also on this branch:

- `graph.UDF` gains `deny-oom` in `src/lib.rs`, matching the other mutating commands. It already had `write`.
- `src/redis_type.rs` no longer sizes its allocation from the entry count just read off the RDB.

Closes #2401

## Proof

Registering the script above, then calling it. Before, on the merge base:

```
$ redis-cli GRAPH.UDF LOAD probe "$(cat probe.js)"
OK                                    # validation takes the safe branch

$ redis-cli GRAPH.QUERY g "RETURN probe.probe()"
                                      # never returns
$ ps -o %cpu <server>
99.0                                  # one worker pinned, permanently
```

Threads accumulate. Four calls, then twelve, against the default pool of ten:

```
%cpu after 4 calls    395.1
%cpu after 12 calls   946.0
$ redis-cli -t 5 GRAPH.QUERY g "RETURN 1"
                                      # no response: pool exhausted
$ redis-cli PING
PONG                                  # server still up, queries all dead
```

After:

```
$ redis-cli GRAPH.QUERY g "RETURN probe.probe()"
Failed to load UDF library 'probe': InternalError: interrupted
$ ps -o %cpu <server>
0.3                                   # worker released
$ redis-cli GRAPH.QUERY g "RETURN 1"
1
```

The bound follows the configured timeout, capped at the validation budget:

```
$ redis-cli GRAPH.CONFIG SET TIMEOUT_DEFAULT 1000
$ time redis-cli GRAPH.QUERY g "RETURN probe.probe()"
Failed to load UDF library 'probe': InternalError: interrupted
elapsed: 1s
```

And `deny-oom` is live:

```
$ redis-cli COMMAND INFO graph.UDF
graph.UDF ... write denyoom module noscript
```

## Tests

`test_runaway_top_level_code_is_interrupted` in `tests/flow/test_udf.py` registers the discriminating script, calls it, and asserts an `interrupted` error plus a healthy server afterwards. It uses its own 30s-socket-timeout connection so unfixed code fails the test in seconds rather than stalling on the suite's 600s default — on the merge base it reports `rebuild ran unbounded: the call neither returned nor errored`.

`test_udf` 45/45, `test_udf_cluster` 3/3, full flow suite 1409/1409, TCK, pytest 142, `cargo test -p graph`, fmt and clippy all clean.

## Still open on master

Problems 1 and 2 as filed are C-side and untouched here. On `master` the fail-open `ASSERT (res == true)`, the unconditional `lib_len--` / `script_len--`, and the missing `write` flag all still stand. Rust never had the ASSERT or the underflow — `deserialize` validates every library and fails the load — so those parts do not port. A C-side PR follows; until it lands the issue is only half addressed, so reopen or fork it if the closing link here is unwanted.


<!-- This is an auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->
## Summary by CodeRabbit

- **Bug Fixes**
  - UDF library loading now interrupts scripts that exceed the configured validation timeout, preventing runaway evaluations from blocking the server.
  - Timeout handling is cleared after library loading so it does not affect later UDF calls.
  - Improved protection against excessive memory allocation when loading UDF libraries.
  - The `GRAPH.UDF` command now correctly respects out-of-memory safeguards.
- **Tests**
  - Added coverage confirming the server remains responsive after interrupted UDF evaluation.

pulls.title: fix(lexer): accept subnormal float literals
pulls.body:
## What

`RETURN 2.2e-308` failed with `Float overflow '2.2e-308'`. Subnormals are finite and representable, and nothing about them overflows. Neo4j and Memgraph accept them

## Why it happened

`str2number_token` in `graph/src/parser/lexer.rs` excluded them by hand, alongside the infinities:

```rust
Ok(f) if f.is_finite() && !f.is_subnormal() => Ok(Token::Float(f)),
Ok(_) => Err(format!("Float overflow '{str}'")),
```

The engine already produces these magnitudes on its own, so the parser and the evaluator disagreed about the same value depending on how it was written

## Fix

Drop the `!f.is_subnormal()` clause. Genuine overflow is still caught by `is_finite`

Closes #2182

## Proof

```
$ redis-cli GRAPH.QUERY g "RETURN 2.2e-308"
Float overflow '2.2e-308'      # before
2.2e-308                       # after

$ redis-cli GRAPH.QUERY g "RETURN 1.0e-307 / 10 = 1.0e-308"
Float overflow '1.0e-308'      # before, the division alone returned 1e-308
true                           # after, parser and evaluator agree
```

Still rejected: `1e400`, `1.8e308`. Still accepted and unchanged: `1.7976931348623157e308`, `0.0`, `1e-400` (underflows to zero). Values survive a round trip: `CREATE (n {v: 2.2e-308}) RETURN n.v` gives `2.2e-308`

## Tests

Two unit tests in the lexer's own module. `subnormal_float_literals_are_accepted` covers four literals down to the smallest positive subnormal and asserts each lexes to a subnormal; it fails on the base with `2.2e-308 should lex, got Float overflow '2.2e-308'`. `float_literals_beyond_the_representable_range_still_overflow` pins the overflow path so this cannot be loosened into accepting infinities; it passes either way, which is the point

Full flow suite, TCK, `cargo test -p graph` (116), pytest 142, fmt and clippy all clean. The flow suite's usual failures are unchanged and come from a redis-py version mismatch in my local venv

## Enabling the e2e subnormals turned up a second bug

Flipping the nine `allow_subnormal=False` guards to `True`, as requested, made `test_avg_mixed` fail on `[1, 5e-324]`. That one is not the lexer:

```
UNWIND [1, 5e-324] AS x RETURN count(DISTINCT x)   ->  1, expected 2
```

Value hashing gives `Int` and `Float` the same tag so `1` and `1.0`, which compare equal, hash alike. A non-integral float then hashes its raw bits under that shared tag, and the bits of a small subnormal are a small integer: `5e-324` has bit pattern 1, so it hashed exactly like `Int(1)`. `Distinct` dedups on the hash alone with no equality fallback, so a row was silently dropped

It predates this branch and needs no subnormal literal to reach:

```
UNWIND [1, 1e-323 / 2] AS x RETURN count(DISTINCT x)   ->  1, expected 2
```

A non-integral float cannot equal any integer, so it no longer shares the integer's tag. Integral floats keep it, so `1` and `1.0` still collapse to one row. Regression test in `tests/flow/test_distinct.py` covers all three cases and fails on the base

Happy to split this into its own PR if you'd rather keep the lexer change alone, though the e2e change you asked for cannot go green without it

<!-- This is an auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->
## Summary by CodeRabbit

* **Bug Fixes**
  * Finite subnormal floating-point literals are now parsed successfully.
  * Values beyond the representable range continue to be rejected.
  * The largest representable normal floating-point value is supported.
  * Distinct-value handling now keeps subnormal floats separate from integers while still deduplicating numerically equal values.

* **Tests**
  * Added coverage for subnormal, overflow, and maximum normal float literals.
  * Expanded numeric operation and distinct-value tests to include subnormal floats.

pulls.title: fix(eval): stop a simple CASE matching null against null
pulls.body:
## What

A simple `CASE` treated `null` as matching `null`, so `CASE null WHEN null THEN 'match' ELSE 'no match' END` answered `'match'`. Neo4j and Memgraph select no branch here

## Why it happened

The value form compared with `==`. `PartialEq for Value` keeps only the ordering half of `compare_value` and drops the flag saying a null took part, and two nulls order equal. `=` reads that flag and answers `null`, so the same pair compared two different ways depending on how the query was written

## Fix

`eval_case` in `graph/src/runtime/eval.rs` now compares on the same terms as `=`: equal ordering *and* no null involved. Covers nulls nested in a list or map too, since `=` is null for those as well

Closes #2208

## Proof

```
$ redis-cli GRAPH.QUERY g "RETURN CASE null WHEN null THEN 'match' ELSE 'no match' END"
match                       # before
no match                    # after

$ redis-cli GRAPH.QUERY g "RETURN [1,null] = [1,null], CASE [1,null] WHEN [1,null] THEN 'm' ELSE 'no' END"
(nil)  m                    # before, `=` and CASE disagree
(nil)  no                   # after
```

Unchanged: `CASE 1 WHEN 1` matches, `CASE 1.0 WHEN 1` matches, `CASE 1 WHEN null` and `CASE null WHEN 1` do not, and the searched form `CASE WHEN null` is untouched

## Tests

New `test09_null_simple_case` in `test_null_handling.py` checks ten subject/WHEN pairs, pinning the exact answer `=` gives each one and asserting the branch is taken exactly when that answer is true. Fails on the base (`'m' == 'no'`, `[['one'], ['isnull'], ['other']] == [['one'], ['other'], ['other']]`), passes here

Full flow suite, TCK, `cargo test -p graph`, fmt and clippy all clean. The suite's usual failures are unchanged; they come from a redis-py version mismatch in my local venv, plus one or two parallelism flakes that move between runs

## One thing to confirm

This diverges from the C engine, which answers `match` here as well, so it is a shared bug rather than a Rust regression:

```bash
docker run -d --platform linux/amd64 --name fdbc -p 6510:6379 \
  docker.io/falkordb/falkordb-server:edge-c
redis-cli -p 6510 GRAPH.QUERY c "RETURN CASE null WHEN null THEN 'match' ELSE 'no match' END"
redis-cli -p 6510 GRAPH.QUERY c "RETURN null = null"
```

```text
match          <- the CASE takes the WHEN branch
(nil)          <- while its own `=` says null
```

C is internally inconsistent in the same way this engine was: its `=` returns null for `null = null`, yet its `CASE` matches. I followed Neo4j, Memgraph and the engine's own `=` rather than C. Two expectations in `test68_Case` encoded the old behaviour and now expect the `ELSE` branch


<!-- This is an auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->
## Summary by CodeRabbit

- **Bug Fixes**
  - Simple `CASE` expressions now use the same equality semantics as `=`.
  - `WHEN NULL` no longer matches a `NULL` subject; evaluation proceeds to later branches or `ELSE`.
  - Comparisons involving primitive values, arrays, maps, and nested values are handled consistently.

- **Tests**
  - Expanded coverage for null handling and simple and searched `CASE` expressions, including row-based and batch evaluations.
<!-- end of auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->

pulls.title: fix(planner): cap the row count of a unit CALL subquery
pulls.body:
## TLDR

A `CALL {}` with no `RETURN` is a unit subquery: it runs for every input row and contributes no rows of its own. It was planned as `Apply(input, Optional(body))`, and `Optional` guarantees *at least* one row without capping at one, so the body's own fan-out multiplied the outer row count. Three `:S` nodes produced nine rows, and a third level of nesting twenty-seven

This gives it a dedicated operator that drains the body and then emits the input rows unchanged

Draining is the point. The writes are why the body exists, and a body that fans out internally performs them once per row it produced, so capping with a limit would have traded a wrong row count for a wrong write count

## Correcting the issue

The issue also reports the write count as wrong, expecting three `:Tmp` where nine are written. That part is not a bug. Measured against the C engine, which this repo treats as the reference:

| | rows | `:Tmp` written |
| --- | --- | --- |
| C (`falkordb-server:edge-c`) | 3 | 9 |
| Rust, before | 9 | 9 |
| Rust, after | 3 | 9 |

Only the row count ever differed. Nine writes is right: the body runs per input row, and the inner returning subquery yields three rows each time, so the `CREATE` fires nine times while the outer cardinality stays at three

## A body that collapses rows runs per row

Draining the whole input batch through one body instance is safe for the rows it produces, since they are all discarded, but not for its writes. A body that collapses rows applied once across the batch instead of once per input row, so its side effects happened the wrong number of times. Over three input rows:

| body | expected writes | batched | now |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `WITH z LIMIT 1` | 3 | 1 | 3 |
| `WITH count(y) AS c` | 3 | 1 | 3 |
| `WITH z SKIP 1` | 3 | 5 | 3 |
| `WITH DISTINCT z` | 3 | 1 | 3 |

`SKIP` shows it most plainly: batched, it dropped one row out of six rather than one per invocation

`Apply` already draws this line for its own sub-plan, so the operator reuses the same predicate. A body containing an aggregation, `LIMIT`, `SKIP`, `DISTINCT`, `SORT`, `UNION`, `MERGE`, `OPTIONAL`, a cartesian product or a nested apply runs one row at a time, with the value dedupers cleared between invocations since each execution is its own `DISTINCT` scope. Bodies with nothing to collapse still run batched, so the fan-out this branch set out to contain stays contained

## User Flow

`GRAPH.QUERY` with a `CALL {}` that has no `RETURN` and whose body produces more than one row

Closes #2310

pulls.title: fix(parser): reject a repeated bare node pattern in CREATE
pulls.body:
## TLDR

`CREATE (n),(n)` created one node and reported success. A pattern keeps one node per alias, so the second `(n)` was dropped on the way in and the redeclaration was never visible to any check

Neo4j and Memgraph reject it as a redeclaration, and FalkorDB already rejects the same mistake written other ways: `CREATE (n) CREATE (n)` and the relationship form `CREATE ()-[e:R]->()-[e:R]->()` both error with `The bound variable ... can't be redeclared in a CREATE clause`. The inconsistency was confined to this one shape

This reports it the same way, off the value `add_pattern_node` already computes about whether the alias is new to the pattern

Reusing an alias to attach a relationship is a reference rather than a declaration, so `CREATE (a),(b),(a)-[:R]->(b)` stays valid. The check therefore only fires on a path that opens on a bare repeat, decided by peeking for the relationship token the path parser is about to read anyway

Unaliased nodes need no exemption. Each is given a fresh `_anon_<n>` from a per-parse counter, so its alias is unique and it passes the "alias is new" test on its own. An earlier revision exempted the `_anon` prefix by name, which left `CREATE (_anon),(_anon)` creating one node silently, since a query may write that name itself

## User Flow

`GRAPH.QUERY` with a `CREATE` that names the same variable twice as a standalone node pattern

## Relevant issues

Closes #2274

- [x] I have added meaningful tests

## Screenshots / Proof of Fix

```bash
redis-server --port 6399 --loadmodule "$PWD/target/release/libfalkordb.dylib" &
for q in "CREATE (n),(n)" "CREATE p = (n), q = (n)" "CREATE (n)-[:R]->(m), (n)" \
         "CREATE (a),(b),(a)-[:R]->(b)" "CREATE (a)-[:R]->(b), (b)-[:S]->(c)" "CREATE (),()"; do
  redis-cli -p 6399 GRAPH.DELETE c > /dev/null 2>&1
  echo "\$ $q"; redis-cli -p 6399 GRAPH.QUERY c "$q" | head -3; echo
done
```

Before, on this branch's merge base:

```text
$ CREATE (n),(n)
Nodes created: 1

$ CREATE p = (n), q = (n)
Nodes created: 1

$ CREATE (n)-[:R]->(m), (n)
Nodes created: 2
Relationships created: 1

$ CREATE (_anon),(_anon)

```

After:

```text
$ CREATE (n),(n)
The bound variable 'n' can't be redeclared in a CREATE clause

$ CREATE p = (n), q = (n)
The bound variable 'n' can't be redeclared in a CREATE clause

$ CREATE (n)-[:R]->(m), (n)
The bound variable 'n' can't be redeclared in a CREATE clause

$ CREATE (a),(b),(a)-[:R]->(b)
Nodes created: 2
Relationships created: 1

$ CREATE (a)-[:R]->(b), (b)-[:S]->(c)
Nodes created: 3
Relationships created: 2

$ CREATE (),()
Nodes created: 2

$ CREATE (_anon),(_anon)
The bound variable '_anon' can't be redeclared in a CREATE clause

$ CREATE (),(),()
Nodes created: 3
```

🐛 Bug Fix

## Changes

`graph/src/parser/cypher.rs`, `add_pattern_node` now returns whether the alias was new, and a `reject_create_redeclaration` helper is applied at the two sites that parse the node a path opens on

`tests/flow/test_create_clause.py`, one regression test covering the rejected shapes, the alias a query could collide with, and the still-valid ones

## QA runbook

The new test fails on the merge base and passes on this branch, with the three pre-existing tests in the file unaffected either way

```text

Total Tests Run: 4, Total Tests Failed: 1, Total Tests Passed: 3
	Unhandled exception: 'CREATE (n),(n)' should have been rejected, created 1.0 nodes

# this branch
Total Tests Run: 4, Total Tests Failed: 0, Total Tests Passed: 4
```

All 23 fail inside redis-py 8.1.0 with `Redis.__init__() got an unexpected keyword argument 'himport_registry'`, a client-side version mismatch in my local venv that cannot be reached from the module

TCK passes. `tests/test_e2e.py`, `tests/test_functions.py` and `tests/test_overflow_crashes.py`: 142 passed. `cargo test -p graph`: 116 passed. `cargo fmt --all --check` clean, `CXX=clang++ cargo clippy --all-targets` exits 0 leaving only the pre-existing `too many arguments` warning in `cond_var_len_traverse.rs`

One judgement call worth a look in review. `CREATE (n)-[:R]->(m), (n)` is now rejected, since the trailing `(n)` opens a path on an alias the clause already declared. pulls.title: fix(aggregation): resolve grouping keys read outside the aggregation
pulls.body:
## TLDR

A projection item that aggregates was evaluated against the group's key row. That row carries each grouping key only under the name the clause projects it as, so a key written in any other form was simply absent and resolved to Null, which then collapsed whatever expression contained it

The same data answered two different ways depending on nothing but the projection list:

```text
RETURN paths, paths > 0 AND count(n) > 0    ->  5, true
RETURN paths > 0 AND count(n) > 0           ->  null
```

`RETURN n.a, n.a + count(*)` did not even get that far. The projected key had taken over the slot the bare variable would have used, so it failed with `Type mismatch: expected Map, Node, Edge, ... but was Integer`

This rewrites each such sub-expression to read the key by its projected name, which the key row does carry, and rejects the reads that name a key the clause never projects. openCypher [CIP2021-07-07](https://github.com/opencypher/openCypher/blob/master/cip/1.accepted/CIP2021-07-07-Grouping-keys-and-aggregation-expressions.adoc) requires exactly that: every sub-expression outside the aggregation must be a constant, a parameter, or a grouping key of the same clause. Neo4j reports the rest as "implicit grouping expressions". FalkorDB let them evaluate to Null, which is how the wrong answers got out

Recognized grouping keys are variables and property lookups, matching the CIP. Comprehensions, quantifiers and `reduce` are descended into carrying the variables they bind, so a key they capture resolves while their own variables are left alone. Pattern comprehensions are the one exception and are copied verbatim: the planner lifts them into their own sub-plan, which runs against the row feeding the aggregation rather than the group's key row, so the projected alias does not exist there

## User Flow

Any `WITH` or `RETURN` that aggregates while also reading a variable or property outside the aggregation. The reported shape was a `CASE`, but `CASE` is incidental, `RETURN paths + count(n)` is enough

## Relevant issues

Closes #2286

The issue attributes this to `CASE` and to "diagnostic projection columns". Neither is the mechanism, and no graph data is needed to see it

## Linear ticket

## Pre-Submission checklist

- [x] I have added meaningful tests
- [x] My PR passes all CI/CD checks (e.g., lint, format, unit tests)
- [x] My PR's scope is as isolated as possible; it only solves 1 specific problem

## Screenshots / Proof of Fix

Live server, release build, module loaded into a real `redis-server`

```bash
redis-server --port 6399 --loadmodule "$PWD/target/release/libfalkordb.dylib" &
redis-cli -p 6399 GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE (:P {a:10, b:20}), (:P {a:10, b:30})"

for q in "MATCH (n:P) RETURN n.a, n.a + count(*) AS r" \
         "UNWIND [1,2] AS n WITH 5 AS paths, n RETURN paths, paths > 0 AND count(n) > 0 AS both" \
         "MATCH (n:P) RETURN n.a + count(*) AS r" \
         "MATCH (n:P) RETURN n.a, n.b + count(*) AS r" \
         "UNWIND [1,2] AS n WITH 5 AS paths, n RETURN paths > 0 AND count(n) > 0 AS both" \
         "MATCH (n:P) WITH 0 AS i, n RETURN collect(n.a)[i] AS r"; do
  echo "\$ $q"; redis-cli -p 6399 GRAPH.QUERY g "$q" | head -4; echo
done
```

Before, on this branch's merge base:

```text
$ MATCH (n:P) RETURN n.a, n.a + count(*) AS r
Type mismatch: expected Map, Node, Edge, Datetime, Date, Time, Duration, Null, or Point but was Integer

$ UNWIND [1,2] AS n WITH 5 AS paths, n RETURN paths, paths > 0 AND count(n) > 0 AS both
paths / both -> 5 / true

$ MATCH (n:P) RETURN n.a + count(*) AS r
r -> (nil)

$ MATCH (n:P) RETURN n.a, n.b + count(*) AS r
Type mismatch: expected Map, Node, Edge, Datetime, Date, Time, Duration, Null, or Point but was Integer

$ UNWIND [1,2] AS n WITH 5 AS paths, n RETURN paths > 0 AND count(n) > 0 AS both
both -> (nil)

$ MATCH (n:P) WITH 0 AS i, n RETURN collect(n.a)[i] AS r
r -> (nil)
```

After:

```text
$ MATCH (n:P) RETURN n.a, n.a + count(*) AS r
n.a
r
10
12

$ UNWIND [1,2] AS n WITH 5 AS paths, n RETURN paths, paths > 0 AND count(n) > 0 AS both
paths
both
5
true

$ MATCH (n:P) RETURN n.a + count(*) AS r
'n.a' is read outside an aggregation function but is not a grouping key of this clause. Project 'n.a' alongside the aggregation, or compute it in a preceding WITH clause

$ MATCH (n:P) RETURN n.a, n.b + count(*) AS r
'n.b' is read outside an aggregation function but is not a grouping key of this clause. Project 'n.b' alongside the aggregation, or compute it in a preceding WITH clause

$ UNWIND [1,2] AS n WITH 5 AS paths, n RETURN paths > 0 AND count(n) > 0 AS both
'paths' is read outside an aggregation function but is not a grouping key of this clause. Project 'paths' alongside the aggregation, or compute it in a preceding WITH clause

$ MATCH (n:P) WITH 0 AS i, n RETURN collect(n.a)[i] AS r
'i' is read outside an aggregation function but is not a grouping key of this clause. Project 'i' alongside the aggregation, or compute it in a preceding WITH clause
```

The last one is Neo4j issue [#13200](https://github.com/neo4j/neo4j/issues/13200) verbatim, `with 0 as b return collect(1)[b]`, which Neo4j rejects for the same reason

Grouping keys captured by a construct that binds its own variables, which the second commit added:

```text
$ MATCH (n:P) RETURN n.a AS a, count(*) + reduce(s = 0, x IN [1] | s + n.a) AS r
a / r -> 10 / 12                    # was the same Type mismatch

$ MATCH (n:P) RETURN n.a AS a, count(*) + size([x IN [1] WHERE x < n.a | x]) AS r
a / r -> 10 / 3                     # was the same Type mismatch

$ MATCH (n:P) RETURN count(*) + reduce(s = 0, x IN [1,2] | s + x) AS r
r -> 5                              # s and x are local, untouched

$ MATCH (n:P) RETURN n.a AS a, count(*) + reduce(s = 0, x IN [1] | s + n.b) AS r
'n.b' is read outside an aggregation function but is not a grouping key of this clause. ...
```

And the issue's own query, which used to disagree with itself:

```text
$ ... WITH count(p) AS paths MATCH (n:N {v:1}) RETURN paths, count(n) AS updated, CASE ... END AS v
paths / updated / v -> 2 / 2 / PASS

$ ... WITH count(p) AS paths MATCH (n:N {v:1}) RETURN CASE ... END AS v
'paths' is read outside an aggregation function but is not a grouping key of this clause. ...
```

## Type

🐛 Bug Fix

## Changes

`graph/src/planner/binder.rs`, a set of free helpers plus one call in `bind_projection`

`tests/flow/test_aggregation.py`, three regression tests and a shared `assert_rejected` helper. That helper raises rather than calling `self.env.assertTrue(False)`, which does not reliably fail a test: an earlier draft of `test13` reported PASS on the merge base while its assertion was visibly firing

## QA runbook

All three new tests fail on the merge base and pass on this branch, with the ten pre-existing tests in the file unaffected either way

```text
# merge base
Total Tests Run: 13, Total Tests Failed: 3, Total Tests Passed: 10
	test_aggregation:testAggregations.test11_GroupingKeyReadOutsideAggregation
	test_aggregation:testAggregations.test12_ImplicitGroupingKeyIsRejected
	test_aggregation:testAggregations.test13_ProjectingAKeyDoesNotChangeOtherColumns

# this branch
Total Tests Run: 13, Total Tests Failed: 0, Total Tests Passed: 13
```

TCK is the load-bearing check for the accept side, since it pins the shape that must keep working:

```text
RELEASE=1 TCK_DONE=tck_done.txt pytest tests/tck/test_tck.py
56 features passed, 537 scenarios passed, 1 passed
```

An earlier revision of this change recognized only bare variables as grouping keys. TCK `Return6` scenario `[6] Handle aggregates inside non-aggregate expressions` caught it, which is what drove the property-lookup support. A second revision copied comprehensions, quantifiers and `reduce` verbatim, which left a captured key unresolved; that came out of review and is the second commit

Full flow suite: `Total Tests Run: 1411, Total Tests Failed: 23, Total Tests Passed: 1388`, identical before and after. `test_comprehension_functions` passes 25/25. All 23 fail inside redis-py 8.1.0 with `Redis.__init__() got an unexpected keyword argument 'himport_registry'`, which is a client-side version mismatch in my local venv and cannot be reached from the module

`tests/test_e2e.py`, `tests/test_functions.py` and `tests/test_overflow_crashes.py`: 142 passed. `cargo test -p graph`: 116 passed. `cargo fmt --all --check` clean, `CXX=clang++ cargo clippy --all-targets` exits 0 leaving only the pre-existing `too many arguments` warning in `cond_var_len_traverse.rs`

One deliberate narrowing worth flagging in review. The CIP also recognizes static map access as a grouping key. Dot access is covered, `WITH {k: 7} AS m, x RETURN m.k, m.k + count(x)` returns `7, 9`, but the bracket form `m['k']` is a different node and is rejected rather than grouped. It returned Null before, so nothing that worked stops working, and adding it later is a change to one helper

### Final Attestation

- [x] The tests check the right things, including the edge cases, and regressions in the respective real-world customer use-cases are not possible after this PR

pulls.title: fix(parser): chain unary signs so `- -5` parses
pulls.body:
## What

`RETURN - -5` failed with `Invalid input Dash`, and so did `--5` and `+ -5`. Valid Cypher was rejected, which bites generated or parameterised query text where the operand's sign is not known up front.

## Why it happened

The unary level consumed at most one `+` followed by at most one `-`, in that order, so a second sign fell through to the primary parser and failed there. `-` is a single-character token, so `--` is two signs rather than a comment, and the spaced form `- -5` failed the same way.

## Fix

Follow Neo4j's two rules rather than counting signs:

```
expression3   : expression2 | (PLUS | MINUS) expression2
numberLiteral : MINUS? ( DECIMAL_DOUBLE | UNSIGNED_DECIMAL_INTEGER | ... )
```

`expression3` does not recurse, so signs do not stack. What makes `- -5` legal is the second rule: the inner minus belongs to the number. So the unary level takes one sign and leaves a minus sitting directly on a number to the primary, which builds a signed literal. `- -x` and `+ +5` stay rejected, since neither operand is a signed number.

This removes the `i64::MIN` special case instead of adding to it. The literal now owns its sign, so `-9223372036854775808` is a literal rather than a negation the parser had to undo, and the out-of-range check moves to where a bare 2^63 token can only mean the literal did not fit.

Closes #2309

## Proof

```
$ redis-cli GRAPH.QUERY g "RETURN - -5"
Invalid input Dash, errCtx: RETURN - -5, pos 8      # before
5                                                    # after
```

Accepted: `-5`, `+5`, `- -5`, `--5`, `+ -5`, `-x`, `-(-5)`, `1 - -2`, `3 * -2`, `-9223372036854775808`.

Rejected, with the reason rather than a bare token name:

```
$ redis-cli GRAPH.QUERY g "RETURN - - -5"
Invalid input '-': only one sign is allowed, and only a number may carry a
second one, as in '- -1', errCtx: RETURN - - -5, pos 8
```

Same for `+ +5`, `- +5`, `- -x`. And `- -9223372036854775808` now overflows rather than returning `i64::MIN`.

## Tests

`test_unary_sign`, `test_unary_sign_beyond_the_grammar_is_rejected` and `test_unary_sign_int_min` in `tests/flow/test_parser.py` cover the accepted forms, every rejected shape, and the `i64::MIN` boundary including hex. The first fails on the merge base with `Invalid input Dash`.

Parser 8/8, function calls 93/93, null handling 8/8, list 15/15, TCK, `cargo test -p graph`, fmt and clippy all clean.

## Note on which Cypher

The three references disagree, so this follows Neo4j:

| | `- -5` | `- - -5` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| openCypher (literals unsigned) | rejected | rejected |
| Neo4j | accepted | rejected |
| FalkorDB C engine | accepted | accepted, unlimited |

openCypher would reject `- -5`, which #2309 asks for, and the C engine accepts any number of signs. Neo4j is the only one satisfying both the issue and the review. The TCK is silent here: it passes either way.


<!-- This is an auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->

## Summary by CodeRabbit

- **Bug Fixes**
  - Updated expression parsing to follow Cypher’s unary-sign rules.
  - Supports valid combinations such as `- -1`.
  - Rejects invalid stacked signs such as `- -x` and `+ +5`.

pulls.title: fix(planner): plan an inline property map once, instead of twice
pulls.body:
Closes #2389.
Closes #3173.

`MATCH (a {p: 1})` is surface syntax for a predicate. The planner lowered it to an `IR::Filter` but also left it on the `QueryNode`/`QueryRelationship` embedded in the plan, so the same predicate existed in two places. Some passes re-derived it from the copy (`select_scan_node` re-emitted the endpoint Filter, which is #2389's `And(p, p)` that no index can serve), and `CondTraverse` checked an edge predicate a second time, in the operator, against the Filter the planner had already emitted above it. Lowering is now consuming: the predicate is lowered once and stripped from the pattern.

#2389 proposed deduplicating the two copies where stacked Filters merge. This removes the second copy instead, so a planner that starts producing duplicates again cannot look healthy.

## A wrong-answer bug, first

Endpoint lowering was skipped whenever the alias was already bound. `CondTraverse` covered that at runtime by re-checking endpoints per row, but `CondVarLenTraverse` and `AllShortestPaths` only ever check the *edge*'s attrs, so for those two nothing enforced the predicate at all:

```cypher
CREATE (n1:N {x: 1}), (n2:N {x: 2}), (n3:N {x: 3}),
       (n1)-[:R]->(n2), (n2)-[:R]->(n3)

MATCH (a:N) WITH a
MATCH (a {x: 1})-[:R*1..2]->(b)
RETURN b.x ORDER BY b.x
```

returned `2, 3, 3` — the third row starts at `n2`, which does not satisfy `x = 1`. Same for the destination endpoint, and for `allShortestPaths`.

## The consumers of the second copy

Each needed re-expressing against the plan, not just deleting:

- `make_scan_subtree` re-derived the filter from the node it was rebuilding. It now salvages the `Filter`s off the pruned subtree's spine — but only where it rebuilds the *same* endpoint. On the chain-reversal paths those filters constrain the old endpoint, which the reversed traverse binds rather than scans, so they are re-attached above the traverse instead.
- Endpoint scoring needed splitting. `collect_filtered_vars` only looked above the chain, so an endpoint whose Filter sat mid-chain scored as unconstrained. Sweeping downwards as well fixes that, but made `MATCH (A:L {v:1})-->(B)-->(C), (B)-->(D:L {v:1})` tie, and the tie fell through to "nearer the leaf". `FilteredVars` keeps the two apart: a predicate that currently runs *after* the whole traversal wins the tie, because scanning from there moves it to the front.
- `utilize_index`'s inline-attr path is deleted. Filter pushdown replaces it and handles ranges and multi-attribute conjunctions, which that path never could. It also reaches through a single-child `IncludePending`, so MERGE match branches get index pushdown — keeping the Filter as a post-filter, because `IncludePending` injects rows created earlier in the same query that the index has never seen.
- `fuse_anonymous_traverse`'s vetoes were attrs probes backed by a structural accident. Now an explicit plan-wide reference check.

## Where an edge predicate lives

**Fixed-length traverses (`CondTraverse`, `ExpandInto`): only in its `Filter`.** Only `FilterOp` evaluates it. Nothing is folded into the operator and nothing is hidden: `GRAPH.EXPLAIN` and `GRAPH.PROFILE` list every plan node, `Commit` included. What the traverse still needs is whether it may collapse parallel edges to one representative per (src, dst) pair; the planner sets `emit_relationship` for an edge that carries a predicate, so the Filter sees every parallel edge.

**Var-length walks (`CondVarLenTraverse`, `AllShortestPaths`): on the walk's own pattern, as on main.** The walk checks its edge's attrs per edge as it walks. That cannot be a Filter above the walk, because there it changes the answer. With the direct a→b edge failing `{c: 1}` and a two-hop path passing it:

| query | C | Rust main | this PR |
|---|---|---|---|
| `allShortestPaths((a)-[:R* {c: 1}]->(b))` | 2 | 2 | 2 |
| `allShortestPaths((a)-[:R*]->(b)) WHERE all(e IN relationships(p) WHERE e.c = 1)` | no rows | no rows | no rows |

A Filter above the walk computes the second row. `test21` pins the first. Only the endpoints' attrs are lowered to Filters and stripped (`strip_endpoint_attrs`).

`CondVarLenTraverse` also answers a non-boolean WHERE predicate absorbed into its `edge_filter` as `FilterOp` does — a type error — instead of treating it as a rejection (#3173).

## Who reads a variable

`ir_references_variable` (now `optimizer/references.rs`) answers that for the four passes that act on a `false` — `reduce_expand_into` collapses the multi-edges, `reduce_bound_edge` stops binding the edge, `reduce_var_len_path` drops the path, `fuse_anonymous_traverse` erases the intermediate. It is now one copy instead of several, exhaustive over the IR with no `_` arm, and keyed on `(id, scope_id)` since ids are per scope. It also counts readers it used to miss: the predicates `utilize_index` and `utilize_node_by_id` relocate into a scan, the attrs a walk prunes on, the list UNWIND and FOREACH iterate, `CREATE`/`MERGE` pattern properties, and the variables an aggregating `WITH` carries.

That fixes 6 of the 16 shapes in #2896 (FOREACH, CREATE, MERGE, UNWIND, and the var-length `UNWIND p` / `CREATE {n: length(p)}`, which errored). The other ten read the variable from a sibling branch — `CALL {}`, OPTIONAL MATCH, pattern predicates and comprehensions — and need the ancestor-only walk replaced, which this PR does not do.

Note for anyone reaching for a duplicate-detector instead: on a default build a duplicate is unobservable. Emitting the endpoint filter twice produces a byte-identical plan, because `utilize_index` folds `And(p, p)` back into a single index query. It is visible only under `--features index-falkordb`, where an unserviceable `And` is a hard error — which is where #2389 found it.

## Performance

`bench measure` against main (`a9377c636`), median of three, instructions:

| row | main | this PR | ratio |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| traverse inline rel attrs | 56,449,382 | 36,204,820 | 0.64 |
| expand-into inline rel attrs | 38,641,805 | 19,731,928 | 0.51 |
| rel attr match none | 57,507,822 | 36,492,267 | 0.63 |
| rel attr match 10pct | 59,915,928 | 36,781,666 | 0.61 |
| rel attr match all | 79,504,272 | 38,609,581 | 0.49 |
| allShortestPaths edge attr | 521,683 | 524,782 | 1.01 |
| vlt edge prop filter | 425,414 | 354,694 | 0.83 |

The edge-predicate rows gain because each predicate is evaluated once instead of twice; against a local C build (wall-clock divided by `RETURN 1`) they run about twice as fast. The walks are unchanged, as intended. The `rel attr match` and `allShortestPaths edge attr` rows are new, on a `:RATED` ring added to SETUP; profiling every read row with and without it, 7 of 287 change, listed next to the ring in `queries.py`.

## Verification

Release build, every suite on its own port with the server log checked for this branch's module:

- `cargo test -p graph`: 442 pass. The one failure, `cap_at_or_above_batch_size_is_ignored`, is #2922 — macOS arm64 only, and the same on main.
- flow: 1626 of 1627. The one failure is `test02_a_drop_during_validation_is_not_resurrected`, the flake documented in that test; it passes alone.
- e2e + functions 128, mvcc + concurrency 14, TCK 2456 scenarios.
- fmt clean; clippy's three warnings are all on main too.

## Not fixed here

- #2923: an inline property map that reads a variable from another part of the same pattern (`MATCH (q:P) MATCH (m:M)-[:R {weight: q.limit}]->(x)`) silently matches nothing, on main and on this branch. The planner still places that Filter inside the Cartesian Product branch that does not bind `q`.
- #345: a var-length relationship variable is not a list of relationships, in either engine.

The branch previously held the dedup approach; its head is preserved at `78435bd669ced8b15b7d9a7c65451ababb9398fd` if the structural-equality helper is wanted for an `index-falkordb` guard later.

pulls.title: feat(index): no fallback under the flag, plus the xfail ledger and its CI gate
pulls.body:
Closes #2382
Closes #2357

**Based on #2383** — review that first; the diff here is only this layer.

Under `--features index-falkordb` the native index becomes the *only* Range index. A predicate it cannot serve raises an error instead of quietly reaching RediSearch, and the flow tests that fail because of this are recorded in a ledger that a CI job checks in both directions. With the flag off, nothing changes.

## No fallback under the flag

`NodeByIndexScan` and `EdgeByIndexScan` used to send any predicate the native index declined on to RediSearch. Under the flag they now raise:

```
native index cannot serve this predicate on node :L — equality on `x` with a non-numeric value. The `index-falkordb` build has no RediSearch fallback; this index kind or predicate shape is not implemented natively yet.
```

An error rather than an empty result, because an empty result is indistinguishable from "nothing matched" and passes any test that happens to expect few rows. A loud failure is the only way a missing index kind can be counted.

The message names the shape that was declined (`graph/src/index/falkordb/mod.rs`, `describe_predicate`), because the shapes need different work:

* equality or range with a non-numeric value or bound — says "non-numeric" only when `encode_numeric` actually rejects the value;
* a union that is not all-numeric, vs. a union that spans more than one attribute;
* a conjunction, listing each child;
* array-contains and geo predicates.

## "Still building" is not "cannot serve"

`FalkorDbIndex::query_numeric` now returns a three-way answer:

| answer | meaning | scan op does |
|---|---|---|
| `Some(NumericAnswer::Rows(..))` | served natively | iterates the rows |
| `Some(NumericAnswer::NotReady)` | the column exists, its background build has not installed the base yet | scans the label/type |
| `None` | cannot be served | raises the error above |

Without the split, every query against an index still being built would have become an error.

## Native-only writes

`FALKORDB_INDEX_ONLY` is removed. Under the flag, the per-write RediSearch commit paths (`commit_index_kind` for nodes, `commit_edge_index_locked` for relationships) no longer feed Range fields: `redisearch_fields` drops them per field, so a label that also has a Fulltext or Vector index keeps those fields. A label or relationship type whose fields are all native skips the RediSearch feed entirely — for relationships that also skips resolving each edge's endpoints. With the flag off, `redisearch_fields` returns its input unchanged.

## The xfail ledger

`tests/flow/nextgen_index_xfail.txt` lists the flow tests that fail under the flag, each placed in the group named by the `native index cannot serve ...` error it emitted:

| group | entries |
|---|---|
| array-valued properties (`ArrayContains`) | 5 |
| strings, tags, stopwords, escaping, mixed-type columns | 13 |
| conjunction the planner could not fold (same-key equality + range) | 1 |

`tests/flow/check_xfail_ledger.py` reconciles an RLTest run against it and exits non-zero on any of:

* a failing test the ledger does not list;
* a listed test that passed — its line must be deleted in the PR that fixed it;
* a listed test that never reported a result;
* a suite that exited with status > 1 (the harness died rather than reporting failures);
* a run with no parseable results at all.

It reads RLTest's per-test result lines and its "Failed Tests Summary" blocks, so it works on the combined output of several suites, and counts `[ERROR]` results as failures and `[SKIP]` results as not run.

## CI

* `build/runtime/Dockerfile` takes a `CARGO_FEATURES` build-arg, passed through by `_build-flavour.yml`. It defaults to empty, so every existing image builds as before.
* `_ci-pipeline.yml` adds `build-rc-nextgen-image` (the server image built with `index-falkordb`) and `nextgen-index-ledger`, which runs the six index flow suites (`test_index_create`, `test_index_scans`, `test_index_updates`, `test_index_delete`, `test_edge_index_scans`, `test_edge_index_updates`) against that image as a service, records each suite's exit status, and runs the reconciliation. The suites themselves do not fail the job; the reconciliation does.

  * Numeric index queries now distinguish between available results, indexes still building, and unsupported query patterns. Unsupported patterns return an error; queries against indexes still building use a scan fallback.
* **Testing**
  * Added automated checks that compare index test failures with an expected-failure list. Unexpected failures and listed tests that pass are flagged in CI.
