pulls.title: feat(index): serve `IN [...]` natively as a union of point lookups
pulls.body:
Closes #2381

**Based on #2351** — review that first; the diff here is only this layer.

## What it does

`n.a IN [...]` used to reach the index as `Or(Equal, ..)` — the scan ops expanded the list before
calling the index — and `query_numeric` declined every `Or`, so the whole query went to
RediSearch. The native numeric index now serves it.

**`IN` reaches the index as one `InList`.** The scan ops keep the same members as before
(Int/Float/String/Bool) but hand them over as `InList { key, list }` rather than an `Or` of
`Equal`s, so the index sees one attribute and a list of values. RediSearch's query builder already
turns an `InList` into the same union it built from the `Or`, and the scan op's check gives an
`InList` the rule its members got as an `Or`: non-empty, every value indexable.

**A lazy chain of point lookups.** The union walks the distinct values in turn, and only descends
the tree for a value when the previous one runs out — nothing until the first row is pulled. So
`IN $list` with many values does no work up front, and a `LIMIT` stops it early.

**Not merged into id order.** Cypher promises no order without `ORDER BY`, and nothing on the read
path relies on one: a single range lookup already yields rows in value order, not id order.

**One snapshot for the whole union.** The union keeps its own copy of the tree root (an `Arc`
clone) taken when it is created, and answers every value from it. A write that lands mid-scan is
invisible to values whose lookup had not started yet.

**Each entity once.** Values are deduplicated by encoded key. That is sufficient: an entity is
indexed under one key per column (lists are not encoded, so an array-valued property is not in the
numeric column), so two distinct keys cannot hold the same entity.

**All values, or none.** An `IN` list is served only when every value encodes to a numeric key;
otherwise the index returns `None` and the query falls back whole. Serving just the numeric values
would drop rows another kind holds — a string, say. An empty list is declined too: the scan op
empties `IN [date(..)]` by dropping the member it cannot index, and "no rows" would miss the dated
entities.

**`OR` on one attribute.** `a = 1 OR a IN [2, 3]`, and `a IN [..] OR a IN [..]`, are served as one
union. Unlike an `IN` list, an `OR` can name several attributes, so the column checks that every
member names the same one: answering a two-attribute `OR` from one column would return rows of the
wrong attribute.

**`DocIter` becomes an enum** — one cursor, or a union — rather than a boxed trait object: the scan
op already boxes the result once, and a second layer of dynamic dispatch per id would be overhead.

## Tests

- `graph/src/index/falkordb/numeric.rs`: `in_list_serves_all_numeric_and_declines_mixed_or_empty`,
  `or_serves_equalities_and_lists_on_one_attribute`,
  `or_declines_members_targeting_different_attributes`,
  `union_builds_no_cursor_before_the_first_row`,
  `union_pins_one_snapshot_across_lazily_built_cursors`.
- `graph/src/index/falkordb/falkordb_index.rs`:
  `query_numeric_serves_in_lists_and_same_attribute_unions`, through the facade.
- `graph/src/runtime/ops/node_by_index_scan.rs` and `edge_by_index_scan.rs`:
  `in_list_reaches_the_index_on_the_same_terms_as_an_or_of_its_members`.


<!-- This is an auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->
## Summary by CodeRabbit

* **New Features**
  * Numeric indexes now support nonempty `IN` lists and `OR` combinations of equality and `IN` conditions when they target the same attribute and use numeric values. Duplicate matches are returned only once.
  * Node and edge index scans can use indexes for nonempty `IN` lists containing supported, accurately represented values.
* **Behavior Changes**
  * Results from combined numeric filters are not guaranteed to be ordered. Unsupported or invalid filters use the fallback query path.

pulls.title: perf: make node deletion O(deleted) instead of O(graph)
pulls.body:
## What

`delete_nodes` cost O(graph) for a delete of *any* size. Two separate terms did it:

1. It iterated **every** entry of `node_labels_matrix` and filtered by delete-set membership, to find which labels the deleted nodes carry.
2. It built diagonal mask matrices and handed them to `remove_mask`, whose `element_wise_multiply` takes `m` as an operand — so GraphBLAS walks the base matrix's vectors.

The second was the dominant one. This PR replaces both:

- **Label lookup** uses `seek` (→ `GxB_rowIterator_seekRow`, a row jump) on a single re-seeked iterator, rather than scanning everything or constructing one iterator per node.
- **Removal** uses `VersionedMatrix::remove` per entity — `dm[i,j] = true` when `m` holds the pair, else drop it from `dp` — which is what `remove_nodes_labels` already does. Three mask matrices per delete go away with it.

Both paths are now O(|deleted|) for every input, so **there is no size threshold and no fast/slow path** — nothing about the input shape makes the old whole-matrix scan preferable.

### Why the per-entity removal is equivalent

`dp ∩ m = ∅` holds for `VersionedMatrix<bool>`: its `set` clears the `dm` tombstone when `m` already holds the pair, rather than writing a shadowing `dp` entry, and asserts as much. So `remove_mask`'s two effects — tombstone `mask ∩ m`, drop `mask ∩ dp` — can never both apply to one entry, which is exactly the per-entry choice `remove` makes. The valued matrices *do* allow `dp` to shadow `m`; `remove` is defined only on the boolean ones, and all three matrices here are boolean.

## Measured

One node created and deleted, per transaction — with the C reference for scale:

| other resident nodes | main | this PR | | C reference |
|---:|---:|---:|---|---:|
| 0 | 1,199,818 | **766,741** | −36% | 827,548 |
| 50,000 | 64,748,827 | **1,049,311** | **61.7× faster** | 588,825 |
| 200,000 | 240,431,307 | **3,128,144** | **76.9× faster** | 563,827 |

Standard bench rows (`bench measure --n 200`), main → this PR:

| row | main | after | | C reference |
|---|---:|---:|---|---:|
| write 1 | 14,187,925 | **560,464** | **−96.0%** | 427,784 |
| write 100 | 18,768,334 | 3,047,806 | −83.8% | 1,859,043 |
| delete node | 8,994,947 | 1,679,384 | −81.3% | |
| delete 100 | 44,409,701 | 9,665,562 | −78.2% | |
| delete 10k | 488,661,040 | 268,572,570 | −45.0% | |
| write 1k | 44,654,038 | 26,104,597 | −41.5% | |
| write 10k | 317,320,239 | 288,030,131 | −9.2% | 164,110,971 |
| traversal + count, label scan, create 100 / 10k | | | flat | |

`write 1` was 31.7× the C reference before this change and is 1.31× after.

**Mass deletes improve rather than regressing**, and are now flat in graph size — instructions per node deleted, deleting the same 10,000 nodes:

| other resident nodes | main | after |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 0 | 4,977 | 4,332 |
| 50,000 | 11,508 | 3,645 |
| 200,000 | 30,437 | 4,288 |

That flatness is what justifies having no threshold.

Allocated bytes fall with the instructions: `write 1` −91.7%, `write 100` −91.6%, `delete node` −77.6%, `delete 100` −65.7%, `delete 10k` −59.1%.

## Remaining

`delete_nodes` is now O(|deleted|). The one-node numbers still grow with graph size (767k → 3.1M), but that growth is no longer inside it. The obvious candidate is the MVCC copy-on-write dup of base matrices per transaction; that is **not profiled here** and is a separate change.

## Tests

- **Full flow suite: 1,385 passed / 23 failed** — and the 23 are the *identical* pre-existing set that fails on `main`, which measured 1,384 / 24 under the same conditions (concurrency, pending-query and memory-limit, slowlog and timeout tests; all load-sensitive when the suite runs at full parallelism). Failure sets diffed test-by-test: **zero regressions**.
- `cargo test -p graph` — 114 passed in both debug and release
- The delete / index / merge flow files were also run against a **debug** build, so `remove`'s `debug_assert` on the dp/m invariant was active. It did not fire.
- `test_memory_usage` 16, `test_encode_decode` 17, `test_undo_log` 22, `test_effects` 22 — all passed
- `pytest tests/test_mvcc.py tests/test_concurrency.py tests/test_e2e.py tests/test_functions.py` — 136 passed
- `cargo fmt --check`, `cargo clippy` — clean

Net diff is +42 / −40 in one file: it removes more code than it adds.

pulls.title: perf: reclaim entity ids with one ordered walk, not a rank lookup per id
pulls.body:
## What

`reserve_nodes` / `reserve_relationships` called `RoaringTreemap::select(i)` once per id being reclaimed from the deleted-id pool. `select` restarts at the first container on every call, summing cardinalities until it reaches rank `i` and then scanning words inside that container — so reclaiming N ids costs O(N × position) rather than O(pool).

This replaces the loop with a single ordered walk, `iter().skip(base).take(reclaimed)`. The ids are identical: `select(i)` is by definition the i-th smallest value, which is exactly what the skipped iterator yields.

## Why

`RoaringTreemap::select` was the hottest single leaf inside the module on a create-after-delete profile — 1,057 samples, 65% of all roaring time, ahead of GraphBLAS's `GB_quicksort_2_32_32` (738).

## Measured

Node capacity pinned at 200,000 in every graph so only the deleted-id pool varies. Query: `UNWIND range(1, 10000) AS i CREATE (:T {x: i})`. Instructions per node created, from `proc_pid_rusage` deltas:

| deleted-id pool | before | after | |
|---:|---:|---:|---|
| 0 | 7,757 | 7,823 | unchanged |
| 10,000 | 8,070 | 7,854 | −2.7% |
| 100,000 | 11,266 | **5,408** | **2.08× faster** |
| 200,000 | 10,968 | **4,974** | **2.20× faster** |

The +45% penalty for creating into a large reclaim pool is gone, and reclaiming is now *cheaper* than allocating fresh ids, since it avoids capacity growth.

Standard bench rows (`bench measure --n 200`), before → after:

| row | before | after | |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| write 10k | 317,320,239 | 294,056,053 | −7.3% |
| create 10k | 103,794,591 | 99,686,111 | −4.0% |
| write 1 / 100 / 1k | | | flat |
| delete node / 100 / 10k | | | flat |
| traversal + count, label scan, RETURN 1 | | | flat |

Nothing regressed.

## Tests

- `cargo test -p graph` — 114 passed
- `pytest tests/test_mvcc.py tests/test_concurrency.py tests/test_e2e.py` — 103 passed
- flow: `test_graph_deletion` 30, `test_access_del_entity` 18, `test_graph_create` 10, `test_index_delete` 14 — all passed
- `cargo fmt --check`, `cargo clippy` — clean

## Scope

Two call sites, both the batch reservation paths. The single-id `reserve_node` / `reserve_relationship` still use one `select` call, which is one rank lookup and not quadratic — left alone deliberately.

pulls.title: Resolve the cartesian product's column owners once, not per row
pulls.body:
Stacked on #2365 — base is `fix/cartesian-product-stream-branches`, so this diff shows only what changes on top of it. Review or merge #2365 first.

#2365 fixed the real bug (a 4-way product materialized 10⁹ rows inside one `next()` call, honoring neither the deadline nor the memory cap). It noted one cost: the multi-branch shape ended up 2.8% dearer per row than reading a pre-flattened batch. That residue is two loop-invariant computations left inside the row loop. Removing them makes multi-branch products **22–26% cheaper in instructions** than before #2365, not 2.8% dearer.

## Counter diff

`bench/` instructions, three reps a side, reproducible to 0.1%. Base is 59a278bf (#2365 tip).

```
                       rows   ────────── instructions ──────────   per row   cycles
  cartesian 1 branch     1M    312,065,818 →   314,162,700  1.01     +2.1     0.96
  cartesian 2 branches   1M    529,856,325 →   411,558,708  0.78    -118.3    0.70
  cartesian 3 branches   2M  1,384,175,860 → 1,029,818,281  0.74    -177.2    0.69
```

`bench compare` reports no regressions. Cycles are shown for direction only — instructions are the deterministic signal here; the single-branch row is +0.7% instructions against ~4% fewer cycles and flat wall-clock.

## What changed

**1. The per-column owner map (`MergePlan`).** `push_merged_many` asked, for every output row and every column, which right branch binds that column. The answer cannot differ between rows — `Batch::is_bound_at` discards its `row` argument (`batch.rs:1202` is literally `let _ = row;`) and so does the `value_only` flag it consults, because both are properties of a column. A 4-way product paid up to 12 `is_bound_at` calls per row, plus a rebuilt `Vec<(&Batch, usize)>` cursor, to recompute a constant.

`MergePlan::for_rights` resolves it once into a `Vec<MergeSource>` indexed by variable id, so `push_planned` does one indexed read per column:

```
                     column / variable id
                 ┌─────┬─────┬─────┬─────┐
                 │  0  │  1  │  2  │  3  │
  left           │ ███ │  ·  │  ·  │  ·  │
  branch 0       │  ·  │ ███ │  ·  │  ·  │
  branch 1       │  ·  │  ·  │ ███ │  ·  │
  branch 2       │  ·  │  ·  │  ·  │ ███ │
                 └─────┴─────┴─────┴─────┘
  sources    =    Left  R(0)  R(1)  R(2)      built once, read per row
```

This is a hoist, not a cache: the branches are materialized once and never replaced, so nothing can make the plan stale and there is no invalidation logic. That is also why the plan lives inside `RightSide`, beside the branches it was derived from, and why `for_rights` deliberately ignores the left batch — left batches keep arriving as the left child streams, and if `width` depended on them the plan could no longer be built once.

**2. The nested emit loop.** Resolving `self.left_batch` and reading its `origin_row` are invariant across every combination of a single left row, but the flattened loop redid both per output row. The emit loop nests again, so for a 1,000-row branch that work happens once per 1,000 rows instead of a million times.

**3. `RightSide`.** The branches and their odometer were two parallel `Vec`s whose lengths the operator maintained by hand (`vec![0; rights.len()]`, `right_pos.fill(0)`, `self.right_pos[0]`). They are now one struct where `cursor.len() == branches.len()` holds by construction and stepping the cursor is `advance`'s business alone. Branch lengths are copied into a flat `lens` vector so stepping never chases a pointer into a `Batch`, and `RightSide::new` asserts the invariant the row indexing silently relied on — branches are dense, because `Batch::concat` drops the selection vector, which is what makes `0..len()` safe instead of `active_indices()`.

**4. The single-branch fast path is deleted.** With the per-column search gone it no longer earns its keep (+0.7% instructions, −4% cycles), and one branch becomes the odometer's degenerate case. That removes the duplicated `if pos >= right_len { self.left_pos += 1; pos = 0 }` bookkeeping, which shadowed what `advance` already did.

## How (2) was found

Worth recording, because both obvious explanations for the single-branch delta are wrong and each candidate fix measured *worse*. callgrind cannot run on arm64-macOS, so attribution came from ablation, which the harness's 0.1%-reproducible counters make viable — 1-branch query, 1M rows:

```
  base (#2365, with its fast path)                          312.1M    —
  ablation: route k=1 through the old push_merged           321.9M  +3.1%
  ablation: inline the single-digit odometer, no advance()  324.8M  +4.1%
  plan + lens, flat emit loop                               318.9M  +2.2%
  plan + lens + nested emit loop  (this PR)                 314.2M  +0.7%
```

So `push_planned`'s indexed read beats `is_bound_at` plus a second `column()` lookup even with a single branch to search, and `advance()` was never the cost either. The nesting was, worth 4.6 of the 6.8 instructions per row — and being general it improved the multi-branch shapes too, rather than special-casing one. About 2.2 instructions per row remain unattributed.

## Two fixes fall out

- Materialization is recorded *before* the empty-branch bail-out, so a re-poll after `None` short-circuits instead of re-running every right sub-plan.
- A plan with no right branches passes its left rows through instead of indexing a `rights[0]` that isn't there.

## Benchmark coverage

The three `cartesian *` queries are new. **No query in the 317-row set reached this operator with more than one row a side** — every other multi-component `MATCH (a), (b)` is an id-seek pair or the `hash join` row, which is the `ValueHashJoin` rewrite of exactly this shape. A regression in the product itself was invisible to the harness, which is plausibly how the 10⁹-row materialization shipped. They are sized by row *product* rather than node count, take a different label per branch so every output column has a distinct owner, and cap `reps` for the same reason the sized writes cap theirs. `cg=False`: `CG_SETUP` has none of those labels, so under callgrind they would silently measure empty scans.

## Testing

- 6 new Rust unit tests, including a differential one: a 3-branch product with an overlapping column is built both by the odometer and by the deleted chain-`push_merged`-through-intermediate-batches algorithm, and the two must agree row-for-row on every value *and* bound bit. Precedence (later branch wins) is pinned separately.
- `cargo test -p graph --lib`: 114 pass. `bench/tests/test_queries.py`: 13 pass.
- Flow `test_multi_pattern`: 7/7. TCK: pass. MVCC + concurrency: 14 pass. e2e/functions: 121 pass, 1 unrelated failure (`test_graph_list` asserts a server with zero other graphs; passes in isolation).
- Full flow suite: 20 failures, a strict subset of the 28 the base module fails on this machine — all concurrency/stress/asyncio flakes, none new.
- `cargo fmt --all -- --check` clean; clippy adds no warnings.

## Not done

Each branch is still materialized in full before the first row leaves, so `MATCH (a), (b) ... LIMIT 1` scans all of `b` where C streams it. Lazily spooling the branches would need either O(N²) incremental `Batch::concat` or a two-level `(batch, row)` cursor per branch — reintroducing the parallel-position bookkeeping this PR removes, one level deeper — plus genuine `MergePlan` invalidation, since the plan would then be derived from batches that get replaced mid-flight. The spool is retained regardless (the left side streams, so branches must be replayed), so only true early-exit benefits. The flow test's LIMIT comment is corrected here to claim only what it checks.

pulls.title: Match GRAPH.QUERY arguments case-insensitively
pulls.body:
Closes #2368

## Problem

`GRAPH.QUERY key "<query>" TIMEOUT 1` — the documented spelling — was **silently ignored**. The handlers compared each argument with `arg == "timeout"`, so anything but lower case fell through the `if`/`else if` chain and the query ran with **no deadline at all**:

```
$ redis-cli GRAPH.QUERY g "MATCH (a),(b),(c),(d) RETURN *" TIMEOUT 1
(runs forever)
$ redis-cli GRAPH.QUERY g "MATCH (a),(b),(c),(d) RETURN *" timeout 1
(error) Query timed out
```

The C dispatcher (`cmd_dispatcher.c`) compares these with `strcasecmp`. `--compact`, `--track-memory` and `version` had the same problem.

The existing timeout tests never caught this because they all go through falkordb-py, which only ever sends `timeout` in lower case (`command.extend(["timeout", timeout])`). Any client using the documented uppercase form got no timeout enforcement.

## Fix

`eq_ignore_ascii_case` in all three handlers — `GRAPH.QUERY`, `GRAPH.RO_QUERY`, `GRAPH.PROFILE`.

## Tests

Added `test12_timeout_argument_is_case_insensitive` to `tests/flow/test_timeout.py`, issuing raw commands with `TIMEOUT` / `timeout` / `TimeOut` and asserting each both times out at 1 ms and succeeds at 5000 ms. Verified it fails without the fix on exactly the two non-lowercase spellings and passes after.

Green on this branch: flow 1407, TCK 2456 scenarios, e2e/functions/mvcc/concurrency 136, rust unit 108. `cargo fmt` clean.

pulls.title: Stream cartesian-product branches instead of materializing their product
pulls.body:
Closes #2367

## Problem

A `CartesianProduct` with more than one right child cross-multiplied every right branch into a single flat batch before joining it with the left rows. For `MATCH (a), (b), (c), (d)` over 1001 nodes that is 1001³ ≈ 10⁹ rows — built inside **one** `next()` call. The timeout and memory-capacity guards run at the top of `BatchOp::next()`, so neither could fire until that call returned.

Reproduced on 1001 nodes with `MATCH (a), (b), (c), (d) RETURN *` and a 1 ms timeout:

| | reply | elapsed | RSS |
|---|---|---|---|
| before | none (killed at 2m39s) | >159 s | 33 MB → **20.8 GB** |
| after | `Query timed out` | 25 ms | 27 MB → 28.9 MB |
| C reference | `Query timed out` | 27 ms | 23.5 MB → 25.2 MB |

## Fix

Materialize each right branch on its own (one dense batch per branch) and walk the branches as an odometer, emitting `BATCH_SIZE` rows per `next()`. Memory held is the **sum** of branch sizes instead of their product, and the deadline is checked between batches.

`BatchBuilder::push_merged_many` performs the N-way row merge directly from the N cursors, so no intermediate batch is built. `push_merged` keeps its own two-batch loop, and the operator retains the original tight scan for the single-right-branch case.

## Performance

Measured with all builds running simultaneously and measurements alternating, since sequential runs on this machine drift ~10%:

- 2-way `MATCH (a),(b)` over 1001×1001: **62.26 ms → 62.28 ms** — parity.
- 3-way: **557.5 ms → 573.1 ms (+2.8%)** — the odometer costs slightly more per row than reading a pre-flattened batch, traded for O(N) instead of O(N²) memory. C takes **45.8 s** on the same query.

## Tests

Added `test07_multi_branch_cartesian_product_is_streamed` to `tests/flow/test_multi_pattern.py`, covering both the deadline and a no-timeout `LIMIT 1`. Verified it fails on the unfixed operator (124 s / 116 s / 113 s against the 10 s bound) and passes after.

Green on this branch: flow 1407, TCK 2456 scenarios, e2e/functions/mvcc/concurrency 136, rust unit 108. `cargo fmt` clean.

  - Improved multi-branch Cartesian product queries by streaming combinations instead of materializing the entire result set.

- **Correctness**

pulls.title: docs: remove redundant community health files in favor of org-wide defaults
pulls.body:
fix #2507 

GitHub serves [default community health files](https://docs.github.com/en/communities/setting-up-your-project-for-healthy-contributions/creating-a-default-community-health-file) from the org-wide [`FalkorDB/.github`](https://github.com/FalkorDB/.github) repository to every repo that does not define its own. This repo's copies are redundant duplicates, so this PR removes them and lets the org-wide versions apply.

## Removed

- `code_of_conduct.md` — Contributor Covenant v2.0 with `info@falkordb.com` as the contact. The org default is the same Covenant text with the same contact, so this copy adds nothing. Note the filename was lowercase here, unlike every other repo in the org.
- `SECURITY.md` — a subset of the org default (same `security@falkordb.com` contact, fewer sections). It also still carries the unfilled template table whose "CVSS v3.0" column contains the literal placeholder `X.Y.Z`, which tells a reporter nothing.
- `CONTRIBUTING.md` — the org-wide default was originally copied from this very file, so the two are byte-identical. Two details in it are now stale: it points contributors at `https://github.com/FalkorDB/falkordb.github.io` (that repo has been renamed to [`FalkorDB/docs`](https://github.com/FalkorDB/docs)) and it cites a `LICENSE.txt` file, while this repo's license is actually at `LICENSE`. Its patch procedure also skips the commit step, going from `git checkout -b` straight to `git push`.

## On the licence wording

This file carried the explicit SSPL statement. The org-wide replacement instead points contributors at the `LICENSE` file of whichever repo they are contributing to, because the org spans MIT, Apache-2.0, BSD-3-Clause, AGPL-3.0 and SSPL, and the blanket SSPL claim was wrong for every repo except this one. SSPL is named in the org version's list of licences in use, and this repo's `LICENSE` remains the authoritative statement. Flagging it explicitly since it is a contributor-facing licensing change on the flagship repo — see [FalkorDB/.github#3](https://github.com/FalkorDB/.github/pull/3) for the replacement text.

## Why centralise

- One place to fix. The stale docs link and the placeholder CVSS table currently have to be corrected in every repo that copied them.
- The org-wide versions are actively maintained and are being improved in [FalkorDB/.github#3](https://github.com/FalkorDB/.github/pull/3); those improvements reach this repo automatically once the local copies are gone.

## Checked before removing

- Nothing in this repo links to any of the three files. The README's contributing section points at its own in-repo **Developer Guide** anchor for build and test instructions, so no build documentation is lost here.

## Effect

The policies still show up in this repo's Community Standards page, in the issue and PR sidebar, and at `/security/policy`; they are just served from the org repo now. Note that default files are not included in clones or release tarballs of this repository.

pulls.title: feat(index): online (background) index build
pulls.body:
Closes #2355

`CREATE INDEX` on the native numeric index now returns immediately, and the column is built in
batches while the server keeps serving, the way C populates an index (`src/index/index_construct.c`).

## Online build

`graph_writes::create_index` creates each Range column empty, in the `Building` state, and returns.
While a column is `Building`, reads on it fall back to the existing path, and writes maintain it as
usual.

The entities that already exist are indexed by `graph_writes::build_step`. Each step indexes the
next batch of the label's entities (10,000 nodes or 1,000 edges, as in C) at the values they hold
at that moment, adds them to the column, and moves the column's cursor (`BuildCursor`) past them.
The step that reaches the end flips the column `Ready`. An edge step finishes the multi-edge pair
it stops in, and the next step resumes inside the same row.

Each step is a unit of work of its own: it runs on a fresh version and is committed when it
returns, so it sees every write committed before it. Nothing written during the build has to be
remembered for later. A write to an entity no step has reached yet updates the column directly; the
step that reaches the entity reads its current value; and adding a tuple the column already holds,
or removing one it never held, changes nothing.

`DROP INDEX` mid-build removes the column and its cursor, and a re-created column starts from the
first entity. The RDB-load path (`graph_writes::populate`) still builds synchronously.

## Scheduling (`graph/src/index/falkordb/online_build.rs`)

Build steps run on a pool of their own in the graph crate: `INDEX_BUILD_THREAD_COUNT` workers (a
load-time module config, default 1), which never serve queries. The workers share one queue,
ordered by when each graph's next turn may start. After a turn a graph is queued again, not before
as long as the turn took, so its writers get the slot and the GIL between its turns while the
worker moves on to another graph. A graph is either queued or on one worker, so it never has two
turns at once.

`MvccGraph::commit` queues its own graph when the version it publishes has a `Building` column and
the graph is not queued already. That covers every way a `CREATE INDEX` can arrive (a client query,
MULTI/EXEC, a replica's effects), costs the same however many graphs exist, and queues nothing for
the builder's own commits. When a worker finds a graph done, it clears the graph's queued flag, and
puts the graph back if a commit brought in another `Building` column while it was still queued.

The builder reaches a graph through a `BuildHost`, which its host registers with the graph
(`MvccGraph::set_build_host`): `read`, the host's read access, and `publish`, what the host holds to
publish a version. Nothing else in the build depends on Redis. The Redis host (`src/graph_core.rs`)
is registered by `register_graph`; it takes the graph's read lock for `read`, and for `publish` the
GIL and then the graph's write lock, the order every Redis writer uses.
`ThreadedGraph::replace_graph` carries the registration over when a graph's coordinator is replaced
in place (the multi-key RDB load).

A turn is a writer that gives way. It takes the write slot as a build step
(`MvccGraph::write_for_build`) and does its work on its own version with no lock held, so it
neither pauses the server nor blocks a writer. A writer that wants the slot meanwhile takes it over
instead of failing: `MvccGraph::write` treats a slot held by a build step as free. That covers
client writes, `GRAPH.BULK`, and the writes that run on Redis's main thread and cannot wait for the
slot (`GRAPH.CONSTRAINT`, MULTI/EXEC and script writes, and on a replica the `GRAPH.EFFECT`
stream). Then the turn publishes: it claims the slot as a writer (`MvccGraph::claim_build`), checks
that its version is the one right after the published version, and commits; or it finds it lost
the slot and drops its batch for a later turn.

So that writers that keep taking the slot over cannot starve a build, after two lost turns in a
row the next turn holds: it publishes through the host first, takes the slot as an ordinary
writer, and keeps both for the whole step. A client write that arrives meanwhile waits on the
graph's lock rather than failing. A committed turn resets the count. A turn that finds the slot
already held by a writer does not start; its graph is retried 10 ms later.

The slot's three states (`Free`, `Writer`, `Build`) are an enum held in an `atomic_enum` wrapper,
a new dependency of the graph crate.

## Measured

On macOS arm64, with a build that logs each turn and one worker. "GIL held" is how long a turn
paused the server.

| | Turns | GIL held |
|---|---|---|
| 1M nodes, scattered values, idle master | 100 committed giving way | Median 0.002 ms, max 0.3 ms, 2.7 ms in all |
| 500k nodes on a master and its replica, 20,000 client writes on the master during the build | Master: 102 lost, 51 held. Replica: 23 committed giving way, 57 lost to the `GRAPH.EFFECT` stream, 27 held | Held turns: median 1.1 ms on the master and 1.6 ms on the replica, max 2.9 ms; 61 ms and 43 ms in all |
| 1M nodes, master under a nonstop stream of MULTI/EXEC writes | 200 lost, 100 held | Held turns: median 2.0 ms, max 4.2 ms, 195 ms in all; the build took 2.15 s |
| 10,000 graphs of 100 nodes, `CREATE INDEX` sent to each | 10,000 committed giving way | 30 ms in all; every graph built by the time the last `CREATE INDEX` returned (2.7 s) |

No write was refused in any run: 20,092 MULTI/EXEC writes and 20,000 client writes all went
through. In the master and replica run, both ended with the same data, and the replica's index
answers equaled full scans. When every turn held the GIL for its whole step, the same idle-master
build paused the server for a median 2.6 ms per turn, 278 ms in all.

The pool on its own, from a throwaway test: 200 graphs of 50,000 nodes, all queued before the pool
starts, were built in 0.261 s with 1 worker, 0.124 s with 2, and 0.059 s with 4.

## Tests

- In `graph/src/graph/graph/falkordb_index_tests.rs`:
  - A build in small steps, with writes landing behind and ahead of the cursor, ends with exactly
    the column a one-pass build of the final graph has, for nodes and for edges.
  - Any batch size gives the one-pass column.
  - A node step reads at most its batch.
  - `DROP INDEX`, re-creating the index, and indexing a second attribute, all mid-build.
  - Build turns, driven through a test host: a column built in turns that then goes idle; a turn
    that loses its batch when a writer takes the slot over; a turn that holds after two losses and
    resets the count; a refused publish that releases the slot; a turn whose version went stale
    is dropped even when its claim succeeds; a graph stays queued while it still has a `Building`
    column.
- In `graph/tests/online_build.rs`, a test binary of its own so that the pool and its queue are
  the test's alone: a commit queues its graph once however many commits follow; two workers build
  two graphs, including a write made while one was queued; a `CREATE INDEX` on an idle pool is
  queued and built.
- In `graph/src/graph/mvcc_graph.rs`, every transition of the write slot: a writer takes the slot
  over from a build step, a build step that keeps the slot commits, and a build step only ever
  takes a free slot.

* **New Features**
  * Indexes are now populated incrementally in the background after creation, rather than being fully built before the operation returns.
  * Newly created indexes become available for reads once population is complete. Graph changes made during the build are reflected in the completed index.

pulls.title: feat(index): native numeric index — CoW columns, folded-roots MVCC, read/write paths
pulls.body:
Closes #2354

Brings the native numeric index into the engine. Everything is
behind the `index-falkordb` feature, **off by default** — with the flag off the graph crate's
tests are unchanged (109 pass); with it on, 137.

## What this adds

A numeric index column per indexed `(label, attr)`, built on the CoW B-tree, with the read and
write paths wired to it.

- **Folded-roots MVCC.** The index is a `Graph` field, so `new_version()` CoW-clones it and
  publishing an index change *is* publishing a version — no separate index versioning. Cloning
  is O(1) per column (a root-`Arc` bump), so a fork shares pages with the prior version until a
  writer touches that particular column.
- **Node and edge columns are separate maps.** A node label and a relationship type can share a
  name, so one keyspace would collide. Edge columns store `edge_id`s; the read path recovers
  `(src, dst)` from the graph's own reverse index, so no endpoints are duplicated.
- **`CREATE INDEX` builds synchronously**, on the write thread, so the create returns with a
  column that already serves reads. (Making it a background build is #2351 — that is the entire
  content of the next PR.)
- **Write maintenance** removes each changed entity's old values and adds its new ones, as one
  batched merge per column per write call, removes before adds so a tuple removed and re-added
  nets to present. The delete paths run *before* the graph tears down types and attributes, so
  an edge's type is still resolvable when its removal is recorded. The replica's own write
  paths (`set_nodes_attributes_rows_of_labels`, `set_relationships_attributes_of_type`,
  `set_node_labels_product`) are maintained the same way.
- **Reads** route a numeric `Equal`/`Range` predicate to the native column and fall through to
  RediSearch for anything else — a Range index also holds strings and geo, which RediSearch
  still owns.

## Where the index code lives

`graph.rs` holds no index logic. Each graph write path makes one call, behind the feature flag:

```rust
#[cfg(feature = "index-falkordb")]
graph_writes::node_attrs_set(self, attrs);
```

`graph/src/index/falkordb/graph_writes.rs` has one function per graph event (`node_attrs_set`,
`labels_removed`, `edges_deleted`, `create_index`, …). Each takes `&mut Graph`, reads what it
needs first through `Graph`'s public API (old values, labels, types), collects the changes, then
merges them into the graph's index field, which is `pub(crate)` for this. The graph calls it
before changing anything itself, so old values are still readable. Updating the index first is
safe because the index lives in the private graph version being written: a refused write drops
that version, index included. The index never keeps a reference to the graph.

Each call merges its own changes immediately, so changes reach the index in the order the graph
makes them. Merging once per `Commit` segment instead, the way RediSearch commits its documents,
is left to #2351, which owns the merge contract its background build depends on.

## Also fixes a latent test-harness bug

`graph.rs`'s test module had its own `Once` calling `GrB_init`, alongside
`graphblas::test_init`'s `Once` calling `GxB_init`. GraphBLAS permits exactly one init per
process, so whichever lost got `GrB_INVALID_VALUE` — and because the loser's `unwrap` runs
*inside* `call_once`, it poisoned that `Once` and every later test touching GraphBLAS died.
Test names in `graph::graph::` sort before `graph::graphblas::`, so the tensor tests were the
casualties. The helper's own comment already flagged this as a TODO; it now routes through the
shared guard.

This was live on `main`'s test suite whenever ordering happened to expose it, and it is why the
suite here is verified with `--test-threads=1` rather than trusting a parallel green.

## Verification

| | flag off | flag on |
|---|---|---|
| `cargo test -p graph` | 109 pass | 137 pass |

Both single-threaded (deterministic order). `cargo fmt --all --check` clean; root crate builds
with the flag on and off.

pulls.title: Adaptive fold policy: bound MVCC delta growth on every write path
pulls.body:
Port of [falkordb-rs-next-gen#767](https://github.com/FalkorDB/falkordb-rs-next-gen/pull/767) onto this repo's `main`, plus one fix for a regression that only shows up against `main`'s newer test suite (see *What is new versus #767*).

## Summary

Outside `GRAPH.BULK`, deltas were never folded into the base matrix: `flush()` was only called from `flush_for_bulk`, so a long-lived graph accumulated unbounded `dp`/`dm` deltas and every read paid an `O(|delta|)` materialization/merge forever (measured: after the bench setup, the entire 10k-edge adjacency still lived in `dp` — `m=0, dp=10103`).

This PR makes every mutation path fold, governed by a cost model whose constants are measured rather than estimated:

- `should_fold(delta, tx_added, base_nvals)` / `should_fold_read(...)`: fold when `2·delta ≥ base_nvals`, or at the sqrt balance point `delta² ≥ K · tx_added`. `K = 2·F/w` is measured per path — read `K = 82_000` (fold at `287·sqrt(tx_added)`), write `K = 20_500_000` (fold at `4528·sqrt(tx_added)`).
- Delta sizes come from approximate atomic counters maintained by the mutation methods — `GrB_Matrix_nvals` on a delta forces its pending tuples to merge (+35% instr on single-node creates when measured).
- Decisions latch in `dup()` (version creation) and `wait()` (read path); execution happens in `flush()` before the next mutation, replacing the COW dup of both delta and base. `wait` deliberately does not schedule the fold mid-tx (a create+delete tx folding its own pending adds measured 18–63x slower small creates after `write 1m`).
- Shared-base folds build into a fresh matrix + `Cow::replace` instead of deep-copy-then-rewrite.
- Same mechanism applied to `Tensor`'s forward layers.
- `build_adjacency_matrix` gains a single-relationship-type fast path.
- `set_all_new`: an unchecked bulk delta insert for entries guaranteed absent from the committed base, plumbed as an `all_new` flag through `set_nodes_labels_bulk` (true for `GRAPH.BULK` and effect-replay creates, false for add-labels, computed from `created_nodes` in the pending commit path). `set_all` itself gains the per-entry base lookup it was missing — a fold or grow-resize can move an entry into `m` since the caller last saw it, and re-adding it to `dp` breaks the `dp ∩ m = ∅` invariant the nvals/iter arithmetic relies on.

## What is new versus #767

`main`'s `test_memory_usage:test_graph_recreate_memory_consumption` (added after #767 was branched) failed on the straight port: after `MATCH (n) DELETE n` over 250k nodes / 500k edges, deleted-state block storage was **larger** than the original state (`5 <= 2` and `14 <= 7` MB). It passes on unmodified `main`.

Cause, measured with per-layer instrumentation: the delete transaction's `dup` folds the pending creates into the base, so the deletes land as tombstones — the tensor ends up holding `m = 499_998` *and* `dm = 499_998`. The fold that would collapse them is latched, but `flush` only runs on the next mutation of that same matrix, which after a delete-everything may never come. `GRAPH.MEMORY USAGE` reported 41 MB after the delete against 25 MB before it, where `main` reports 6 MB.

Fix (third commit): `MvccGraph::commit` folds every delta that has grown comparable to its base — the `2·|delta| ≥ base_nvals` escape hatch on its own, read off the approximate counters so no delta's pending tuples get merged. Commit is the last point at which the writer still holds the write lock and the new version is not yet published, so the fold is writer-exclusive. Sub-hatch deltas stay lazy, since the sqrt balance point's whole value is landing on the `dup`.

After it, the same repro reports 6 MB deleted / 24 MB original — the same as `main` — and the flow test passes.

Cost of that extra fold, measured with it vs without on the write/delete subset (instructions):

| query | ratio | | query | ratio |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| write 1 | 1.002x | | delete node | 1.005x |
| write 10 | 1.004x | | delete edge | 0.995x |
| write 100 | 1.002x | | delete 100 | 0.96x |
| create 100 | 1.004x | | delete 10k | 1.015x |
| create 10k | 0.993x | | | |

A regression test is included: `tensor::tests::deleting_everything_folds_the_tombstones_away` (verified to fail with `flush()` in place of `fold_oversized()`).

## The fold cost model, measured

`graph/src/graph/graphblas/fold_cost_bench.rs` (`#[ignore]`d; `cargo test --release -p graph fold_cost -- --ignored --nocapture`) measures the three quantities the policy rests on. 1,048,576² capacity, entries scattered across distinct rows (one per unique `(row, col)` pair — CAP must clear the largest sample or `scatter` wraps).

**Why a sqrt and not an LSM-style ratio.** Every write transaction re-touches the *whole* delta, so with transactions of `tx_added` entries accumulating to a fold point `D`, writing `D` entries costs `Σᵏ (i·tx_added)·w + F ≈ w·D²/(2·tx_added) + F`. Per entry that is `w·D/(2·tx_added) + F/D` — a rewrite tax growing with `D` against a fold bill shrinking with it — minimized at `D* = sqrt(2·(F/w)·tx_added)`. A ratio rule (`D ≥ base/K`) is correct only when each entry is rewritten `O(1)` times between merges; it drops `tx_added` and gets both ends wrong.

**The `O(|delta|)` premise is confirmed, and the tax is the merge, not the dup.** Per-transaction cycle (dup → add `tx_added` → materialize):

| existing delta D | tx_added | dup | set | **wait** | total |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 1 | 0.2 | 0.1 | 0.7 | 1.1 µs |
| 1,024 | 1 | 0.5 | 0.1 | **50.3** | 50.8 µs |
| 4,096 | 1 | 1.1 | 0.1 | **205.3** | 206.5 µs |
| 16,384 | 1 | 3.2 | 0.2 | **838.9** | 842.3 µs |
| 65,536 | 1 | 11.6 | 0.4 | **2900.0** | 2912.0 µs |
| 1,024 | 100 | 0.4 | 2.9 | 58.3 | 61.7 µs |
| 16,384 | 100 | 4.2 | 4.0 | 965.6 | 973.8 µs |

The cost tracks `D`, not `tx_added` — adding 1 entry to a 16k delta costs the same ~900 µs as adding 100, because assembling pending tuples rebuilds the matrix.

**`w` differs 250x between the two paths, which is what the write/read split encodes.** A write nobody reads pays only the COW dup, `w_dup ≈ 0.2 ns/entry` (and duping a *pending* matrix costs the same as an assembled one, so `dup` does not assemble). A transaction whose delta is also materialized pays `w_merge ≈ 50 ns/entry`. Since `D* ∝ 1/sqrt(w)`, the write path belongs `sqrt(250) ≈ 16x` looser than the read path.

**The fold is ~82% fixed cost and independent of `nrows`:**

| base nvals | fold µs | | nrows (nvals=0) | dup µs | fold µs |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1,024 | 16.5 | | 1,024 | 0.24 | 8.09 |
| 16,384 | 707 | | 65,536 | 0.27 | 2.04 |
| 262,144 | 1,802 | | 1,048,576 | 0.27 | 2.02 |
| 1,048,576 | 2,174 | | 16,777,216 | 0.29 | 2.51 |

Flat in `nrows` across four orders of magnitude — that is what retires the `nvals + nrows` term. Against nvals it is strongly *sub*-linear: ~2 µs empty, 43 ns/entry at 16k, 2 ns/entry at 1m. Read that as two format regimes rather than one line — a delta at 1.5% density is hypersparse, one at 95% is sparse/bitmap, and eWiseAdd vectorizes only in the latter. Across 262k → 1m, `F` moves only 1.2x for 4x the entries, which is flat enough that the balance point need not track the base.

Constants are macOS measurements and `w` is cache-bound, so expect different absolute values in CI; re-measure in `ghcr.io/falkordb/falkordb-build` before re-tuning. Refitting on the corrected numbers gives `READ_FOLD_K` 86,960 and `WRITE_FOLD_K` 21,740,000 against the committed 82,000 / 20,500,000 — a 3% difference, far inside the range where being 2x off the optimum costs 25%, so the constants were left alone rather than fitted to noise.

Also unexplained: `wait` is non-monotonic above 65k (3024 µs at D=65,536, 2251 µs at D=262,144), so the linear `w·D` model should not be extrapolated past there.

## Also here: regenerated PreJIT kernels + the build fixes to get a complete set

Separable from the fold policy (happy to split), but kept together because the bench re-run this PR needs should measure the kernel set that ships — and the current one is missing 55 kernels the benchmark itself exercises.

- **`build/graphblas/PreJIT/`: 165 → 218 kernels**, harvested in `ghcr.io/falkordb/falkordb-build` per the Linux-only rule. Platform-neutrality is evidenced rather than assumed: all 151 kernels common to the old and new sets are **byte-identical**. `gen_prejit.sh` never ran `bench/`, so 55 op shapes — 27 of them carrying user-defined LAGraph operators, GraphBLAS's slowest fallback — were running as generic kernels *in the benchmark*. Adding a guarded bench step (`run_bench.py --once`) is purely additive: 55 added, 0 removed, 0 modified.
- **`graph/build.rs`: link `lagraphx → lagraph → graphblas`.** `cargo test -p graph --release` has been failing to link on Linux with 19 undefined `GrB_*` refs — GNU ld resolves archives left-to-right and graphblas came first. Silent cost: every past PreJIT harvest skipped Step 4a, losing the kernels only the unit tests exercise. macOS unaffected (ld64 ignores order).
- **`gen_prejit.sh` exports `RUSTDOCFLAGS` on Linux**, which cargo cannot supply via `[target.'cfg(…)'].rustdocflags` — without it two doctests fail to link and Step 4a reports failure despite every unit test passing.

## Correctness: COW-shared pending matrices

Any GraphBLAS call on a matrix with pending tuples finishes that work internally — a mutation. Committed bases are reachable lock-free (`m()` hands them to structural consumers, `wait` reads `m.nvals()` raw), so publishing a snapshot whose base is still pending let two concurrent readers corrupt GrB state (`GrB_INVALID_OBJECT`, heap corruption under stress).

- `Graph::wait_bases` materializes every base at MVCC commit. dp/dm stay lazy because every read of them goes through the mutex-guarded `Matrix::wait` first; waiting the deltas here too measured +35% instructions on `create 10k`.
- Targeted waits on the remaining raw accesses: `wait_all` in `flush` and before grow-resize, `m.wait()` in `remove_mask`, `dm.wait()` in `set_all`/`set_all_new`, `dp`/`dm` waits in the delta-aware `mxm`, `wait_fwd` before `set_pattern`.
- The `debug_assert`s in `set`/`remove` read the deltas raw, so they wait only *while still shared* — once dup'd the layer is writer-local, and waiting unconditionally re-merges pending tuples per element (quadratic bulk mutation in debug builds).

## Grow-resize rebuilds the base

Growing `resize` went through the Cow, so the always-shared base was deep-copied at the old dims and any lingering delta then paid another `O(|m|)` fold pass — measured 2.4–9.8 ms spikes per capacity grow on bulk creates. It now rebuilds the base at the target dims in one pass, folding both deltas in: extract the row-major tuple streams and merge `(m \ dm) ∪ dp` into a fresh matrix, with a pure-append fast path for monotonically growing ids. Shrinking keeps the old in-place path since it can drop entries. `Matrix::<bool>::build` also switches to `GxB_Matrix_build_Scalar` (no values array, iso result).

## Measured on this repo's `main`

Full 317-query suite, this branch vs `origin/main` (`e9e2b7bd`), both built and measured back to back on the same machine (macOS, arm64). Cycle and instruction ratio (branch/main), `<1.0` = faster.

Biggest improvements (instructions):

| query | instr | cycles |
|---|---|---|
| write 1 | 0.23x | 0.27x |
| write 10 | 0.25x | 0.30x |
| delete edge | 0.28x | 0.40x |
| delete node | 0.38x | 0.42x |
| write 100 | 0.41x | 0.44x |
| delete 100 | 0.65x | 0.66x |
| edge + type() | 0.86x | 0.77x |
| create edge | 0.91x | 0.83x |
| create node | 0.92x | 0.93x |
| spatial | 0.94x | 0.85x |

Rows over the 1.10x instruction threshold — the whole list, out of 317:

| query | instr | cycles |
|---|---|---|
| **create 10k** | **1.27x** | 1.51x |
| **create 100** | **1.13x** | 1.18x |

These are the *other end* of the tradeoff: the read-path balance point is a flat 287 entries, so bulk creates fold more often and pay more base rebuilds. That is the same knob that buys the 3-7x on the single-entity paths. Both sides also differ in their vendored kernel sets (165 vs 218), which is not isolated here.

The harness's `alloc_bytes` column is unusable on this machine in both directions — it reported 32 TB for `write 10k` on **both** builds (jemalloc merged-arena counter deltas), so only `instr`/`cycles` are quoted above. Residency was measured directly with `GRAPH.MEMORY USAGE` instead, in the delete/recreate repro described earlier: branch 24 MB original / 6 MB deleted / 24 MB reconstructed against main's 27 / 6 / 27.

## Testing

macOS, release build unless noted:

- `cargo fmt --all -- --check` clean; `CXX=clang++ cargo clippy --all-targets` clean apart from two `too_many_arguments` warnings that reproduce on unmodified `main`
- **114 unit tests** + 2 doctests, 0 failed (5 fold-policy tests pinning the balance points and the escape hatch, #785's `resize_leaves_base_materialized`, and the new `deleting_everything_folds_the_tombstones_away`); the 4 `fold_cost` benches are `#[ignore]`d
- e2e / functions / mvcc / concurrency: **136 passed**
- TCK: **173 features, 2456 scenarios, 10140 steps, 0 failed**
- flow: **1406/1406**

Two conflicts came out of the port, both resolved in favour of `main`: `test_slowlog`'s query size (`main` already enlarges it further than #767 did) and `bulk_insert`'s `set_nodes_labels_bulk` call (keeps `main`'s insert-wide `docs.nodes` accumulator, adds #767's `all_new = true`).

## Next step before merge

Re-measure `F`/`w` on the Linux toolchain image so the two fold constants are tuned on the platform that ships, and re-run the bench suite there — the constants above are macOS numbers.

Known and deliberately not fixed here: `graph/build.rs` symlinks `libredisearch.a` inside the toolchain image's `/data`, a side effect outside `target/` that a cached build script won't reproduce, so a warm target dir in a fresh container fails with `could not find native static library 'redisearch'`. Fix is to symlink into `OUT_DIR`; it changes linking on every platform so it wants its own PR. CI never hits it (always cold).

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

pulls.title: refactor(bench): modern Python harness, and fix the C image it measures
pulls.body:
Follow-up to #2287, applying the resolutions from its review. **Stacked on `bench-harness`**, so the diff here is this PR's delta alone; GitHub will retarget it to `main` when #2287 merges.

CI note: neither `rust-pr.yml` nor `benchmark-cov.yml` fires on a PR based on a topic branch (both filter base to `main`/`main-rs`/version branches), so **this workflow was validated by temporarily basing this PR on `main`** and labelling it. Results are summarised at the bottom. To exercise it again after the rebase, base on a trunk and re-apply the label.

## One live defect

`:edge` and `:edge-rs` now resolve to the **same digest** (`sha256:315e1ba9d1ba…`), while the C engine moved to `:edge-c` (`sha256:38fc6f834e4d…`). So `C_IMAGE: …:edge` pointed at the Rust engine: the vs-C allocated-bytes table was comparing Rust against Rust, and all 15 jobs ran inside a container chosen for being the C image. The channel promotion moved under #2287 — its posted comment's C figures (66 KB against 2.6 MB) are plainly from a real C engine, so this broke after that run.

Fixed, plus a canary in `preflight` asserting the C and base digests differ. Verified against the real thing: with `c=edge` the digests are equal and the canary fires; with `c=edge-c` they differ and it passes.

## The refactor

`bench/` is a uv project with one `bench` CLI (click): `measure | callgrind | compare | report | profile | flow`.

- **One `metrics` module behind `compare` and `report`.** They implemented comparison independently and disagreed on the same CSVs — the local gate compared raw wall-clock at 1.25x, which across two hosts is a noise detector. It now inherits the control-row normalisation and non-positive-baseline guard only the reporter had.
- **Absence has one representation.** `""` / `None` / `0.0` each meant a different kind of missing, re-derived with a `try/except` at every use. Parsed once at the CSV boundary into `float | None`.
- **`Query` is a NamedTuple**, and `cg=True` replaces the 93-name subset list that lived in the callgrind module — a second source of truth about the query set, in a different file, guarded by an assert that vanishes under `python -O`.
- **`profile.sh` folded into `bench profile`**, on samply rather than macOS `sample` (the shell version was silently macOS-only, and contradicted the profile skill).
- **75 tests** over CSV fixtures, covering guards previously described only in comments.

The 317-query set was migrated textually and **proven** equivalent: same queries, 93 cg-flagged, all 58 interleaved comments preserved, `SETUP`/`ERROR_QUERIES`/`CSV_FILES` byte-identical.

## Five bugs found while porting

1. **`redis-cli` writes error replies to stderr** and the harness read only stdout, so its setup-command error check could never fire. A `GRAPH.EXPLAIN` had been failing silently since it was added (`exists((p)-[:KNOWS]->())` is rejected by the binder), so the plan-rendering coverage it existed for never happened.
2. **The control row absorbed first-exec cost.** `RETURN 1` is measured first and paid `redis-benchmark`'s binary load: 0.3476 ms on one run vs 0.0636 ms on the next, while every other row agreed within 1%. It is the row every wall-clock ratio is divided by, so that scaled the entire column — 316 of 317 rows flagged as ">50% moved". Fixed with a warm-up exec.
3. **The local gate failed builds on wall-clock**, with ratios like `4.37x (0 -> 0)` over 0.02 ms values. `ms` is shown but never gated by default now.
4. **The measurement image inherited the base image's `ENTRYPOINT`**, so `bench measure …` became arguments to the server launcher and the harness never ran.
5. **`--bare` silently ignored `--shard`**, making the shard/matrix cross-check unreachable. It refuses now.

## CI

- **One prebaked measurement image**, built once in `preflight` and tagged by content (C image digest + `uv.lock` + `Dockerfile`), instead of 15 jobs each running `apt-get update` against Debian mirrors on the critical path. Content-addressing means a PR that changes dependencies cannot measure with a stale set, and a republished `edge-c` rebuilds automatically.
- **Composite action** for module extraction, previously duplicated verbatim.
- **Shard count single-sourced** — `preflight` emits both the matrix and the `--shard` denominator, and the harness rejects a mismatch. It was a literal `/6` beside a six-element matrix.
- **The run's verdict moved into `report`.** GitHub collapses a matrix into one `result`, so a YAML gate on `needs.measure.result` cannot tell "the C side failed" (a lost column, and `:edge-c` is a moving third-party tag) from "the base side failed" (a lost reading) — which contradicted the stated design.
- Runner sizing recorded as a comment: bigger is the wrong axis (the workload is `-c 1` sequential, and larger hosted runners still have no vPMU); bare metal would be the axis, and would retire 12 of the 18 jobs.

## Verification

**Numbers unchanged.** Old vs new over 317 queries: identical columns, identical row order, and the empty-vs-populated mask matches in every cell. `instr` median 0.9973. Four rows moved >±5%, so the old harness was run twice as a control — same character of noise, wider max spread (1.1585 vs 1.0730), and `sci notation` drifts 0.937x old-vs-old against 0.934x old-vs-new. The port adds no variance.

**The CI jobs, reproduced locally in Docker:**
- `measure` against the module extracted from `:edge-c` — `alloc_bytes` populated (jemalloc), `instr`/`cycles` empty rather than zero (no vPMU), and `UDF traverse SKIPPED (Unknown function 'bench.traverse')`, which is positive proof the module really is C. That last one is the regression test for the defect above.
- `report` with the real artifact layout, run inside the image exactly as the workflow does — quoted globs expand in-container.
- The strict gate all three ways: all sides → 0; **C deleted → 0** (the fix); base deleted → 1 with `::error::no base measurement CSV`.
- `preflight`'s tag computation (stable, changes with the Dockerfile) and the digest canary.
- `callgrind --bare`, which validates the differencing arithmetic where valgrind cannot load this module (arm64).

**Not reproduced:** the `coverage` job (needs a full instrumented build), and `callgrind` against a real module — impossible on arm64, which is why `--bare` exists.

## Deliberately not included

`p50_ms`/`p99_ms` columns. `ms` is a mean while the stated bar in CLAUDE.md is p99, and `redis-benchmark` already computes a distribution the harness discards — but adding columns is the one change that is not behaviour-preserving, so it is documented as a known gap rather than smuggled into a refactor.


---

## CI validation (run while temporarily based on `main`)

Two labelled runs on this branch, plus one round of review fixes between them.

**Run 1** (`4e88e5bd6`) — 16/18 green. Confirmed live: the digest canary against the real registry, the content-addressed bake and push of a new GHCR package, `fromJSON` matrix expansion into 12 shards, all 3 `measure` legs, all 12 `callgrind` shards, and a vs-C table with C-shaped numbers (303 comparable, 42 above C — against #2287's 303/41 from when `:edge` still *was* C). Callgrind read `RETURN 1` at **0.9994x** with no row moving >0.5% across 93 — a clean null calibration, since this PR changes no Rust. Wall-clock outliers: **none**, at a 0.81x control offset.

`report` failed *correctly*: comment posted (14,604 chars), then the run failed at the final gate citing coverage. That is the distinction the old YAML gate could not express.

`coverage` failed for real — the toolchain image has no `uv`. Fixed in `bdd78a439`.

**A workflow review then found several CI-only defects**, fixed in `701e91d1e`:
- `OMP_NUM_THREADS` had moved into the image `ENV`, so `measure` inherited callgrind's thread pinning while pinning no `THREAD_COUNT` — a configuration matching neither production nor a local run, on the job carrying the vs-C table.
- `--job-total` compared a variable against itself and could never fire; the real protection is preflight's single `shard_count`, and the comments claiming otherwise were corrected.
- `render_rc` was written and never read, so a reporter crash was reported as a missing measurement.
- `redis-tools` did not no-op as assumed (the base image's redis is outside dpkg), leaving two `redis-benchmark` builds resolved only by PATH order. Now a build-time assertion.
- Plus: `PATH` no longer prepends the checkout root for `cargo`; `uv` pinned in both fetch sites; `pyproject.toml` added to the bake hash; dead `env_thread_pinning()` and a stray `cg-bare.csv` removed.

**Run 2** (`701e91d1e`) — **`coverage` green**, so the last piece without live evidence now has it, and `coverage.sh`'s validator role confirms all 317 queries plus the expected-error set still run clean against an instrumented build. `preflight` re-baked at a new key (`c919a94f…` → `9944c062…`), which incidentally proves the hash reacts to Dockerfile/pyproject changes.

## Known follow-up, deliberately not in this PR

Every measurement leg re-resolves `:edge-c` / `:edge-rs` / `:rc-pr-N` **by tag**, 10–40 minutes after `preflight` canaried them, and `edge-rs` is republished on every trunk push. If a tag moves mid-run, shards can straddle two engines while provenance reports the pre-move digests. The composite action already computes the digest and the workflow discards it. Pre-existing behaviour, but it leaves this PR's own "a tag resolving is not evidence" argument incomplete; the fix is for `preflight` to emit `image@digest` and the legs to pull those.

pulls.title: fix(bulk): index rows appended by GRAPH.BULK into an existing graph
pulls.body:
Closes #2294.

## The bug

`GRAPH.BULK` creates a graph only when the batch carries a `BEGIN` token; a batch without one appends to the existing graph. On that append path the loaded rows were never indexed.

It is not a partial miss — the index returns **zero** rows for data that is plainly there, so any index-served query on that graph silently returns nothing:

| | index count | scan count |
|---|---|---|
| before | **0** | 100 |
| after | 100 | 100 |

## Root cause

Two separate causes, one per entity type.

**Nodes — right logic, wrong order.** `set_nodes_labels_bulk` already decides which nodes need (re)indexing:

```rust
if self.node_indexer.has_index(label) && self.node_attrs.has_attributes(id) {
    index_add_docs.entry(label_id).or_default().insert(id);
}
```

but it ran *before* `import_node_attrs_resolved`, so `has_attributes(id)` was always false and it collected nothing. The map it filled was then dropped without ever being committed. Fixed by importing the attributes first, then collecting, then publishing with `commit_index`.

**Edges — no maintenance at all.** `import_relationship_attrs_resolved` did none, unlike its `import_relationship_attrs` sibling. It now tracks the imported edges, and the caller publishes them with `commit_edge_index`. Tracking runs *before* the import because `import_attrs_resolved` drains its input. `track_edge_index_updates` now takes an iterator so both the map-shaped and `Vec`-shaped callers can use it.

Nothing repaired this afterwards: `GRAPH.BULK` does not run the post-load `populate_indexes_sync` rebuild — that belongs to the RDB and replica load paths.

## Reachability

The official `falkordb-bulk-loader` **cannot** trigger this. It always sends `BEGIN` against a fresh graph, and creates its own `-i` indexes *after* the load ("Add in Graph Indices after graph creation"), so no index can pre-exist. That is presumably why this went unnoticed.

It is reachable by any client issuing `GRAPH.BULK <key> <counts> …` without `BEGIN` against a graph that already has an index — a supported, unguarded append (e.g. incremental bulk loading from a custom client).

Issue #2294's original repro used the CLI and does not reproduce; I have corrected it there.

## Test

`test13_bulk_append_into_indexed_graph` drives the append path directly, since the CLI cannot. It reuses the loader's own serialization with the `BEGIN` token suppressed (`QueryBuffer.initial_query = False`), so there is no hand-rolled wire format.

Verified **red before the fix, green after** — 0/100 nodes and 0/99 edges indexed without it, correct with it. Full `testGraphBulkInsertFlow` class: 13/13 passing.

One caveat worth flagging for review: the test couples to `falkordb-bulk-loader` internals (`QueryBuffer`, `initial_query`, `parse_schemas`). That package is already pinned in `tests/requirements.txt`, but a loader restructure would break the test.

## Summary by CodeRabbit

- **Bug Fixes**
  - Improved bulk data insertion so node labels and relationship attributes are correctly reflected in indexes.
  - Ensured index updates are committed during bulk loading, improving indexed query accuracy.
  - Fixed appending bulk data to already indexed graphs, including workflows without an explicit transaction start.
  - Prevented failed bulk insertions from publishing incomplete index updates.

- **Tests**
  - Added coverage verifying indexed counts match full graph scans after bulk insertion.

pulls.title: Remove release exposure of `GRAPH.DEBUG SEGFAULT` crash path
pulls.body:
`GRAPH.DEBUG SEGFAULT` is a deliberate crash helper that was compiled into release builds and could terminate the server from an authenticated session permitted to run `GRAPH.DEBUG`. This change removes that release-build crash surface by restricting debug-only behavior to debug/testing builds.

- **Build-time gating of crash helper**
  - `SEGFAULT` crash routine and its dispatch path in `src/commands/cmd_debug.c` are compiled only under the debug/testing build flag.
  - In non-debug builds, the subcommand is not available.

- **Build-time gating of command registration**
  - `graph.DEBUG` command registration in `src/module.c` is guarded by the same debug/testing flag so the command is not exposed in release builds.

- **Behavioral outcome**
  - Release builds no longer ship the self-inflicted process-kill helper.
  - Debug/testing builds keep existing crash-injection behavior for internal validation.

Example (illustrative gating pattern):

```c
#ifdef FALKORDB_DEBUG
if (!strcasecmp(sub_cmd, "SEGFAULT")) {
    ThreadPool_AddWork(_Debug_SegFault, NULL, true);
    RedisModule_ReplyWithCString(ctx, "OK");
}
#endif
```

- Fixes #2327

pulls.title: GRAPH.BULK: validate token counts before argv traversal to prevent OOB read
pulls.body:
`GRAPH.BULK` accepted `node_token_count` / `relation_token_count` and used them as direct bounds over `argv[]` before confirming enough arguments were present. That allowed malformed counts (including negative/oversized values) to drive out-of-bounds reads in token validation.

- **Early count validation in `BulkInsert()`**
  - Reject negative `node_token_count` and `relation_token_count`.
  - Validate counts before any `_BulkInsert_ValidateTokens(...)` call.
  - Enforce that requested token span fits in remaining `argc`.

- **Overflow-safe bound check**
  - Guard `node_token_count + relation_token_count` against integer overflow.
  - Fail fast with client error when combined counts are invalid.

- **Runtime error path instead of assertion reliance**
  - Replace late `ASSERT`-only protection with explicit runtime checks that execute in release builds.
  - Return a proper client-facing error for malformed `GRAPH.BULK` payloads.

- **Focused regression coverage**
  - Add targeted tests for malformed token-count cases (negative and over-large totals) to ensure command rejection occurs before argv token dereference.

Example of the new guard pattern:

```c
if(node_token_count < 0 || relation_token_count < 0 ||
   node_token_count > argc || relation_token_count > argc - node_token_count) {
    return RedisModule_ReplyWithError(ctx, "ERR invalid token counts");
}
```

<!-- START COPILOT CODING AGENT SUFFIX -->

- Fixes #2328

pulls.title: Eliminate unbounded stack allocation in UNION RETURN validation
pulls.body:
`_ValidateUnion_Clauses` allocated a stack VLA sized directly by user-controlled `RETURN` projection count, allowing large queries to exhaust thread stack and crash the process. This change removes that unbounded stack-risk path in UNION validation.

- **Validation hardening**
  - Replaced projection-name storage in `_ValidateUnion_Clauses` from unbounded stack VLA to bounded-safe allocation strategy (heap-backed), so projection count no longer maps directly to stack growth.
  - Preserved existing UNION projection compatibility checks and error behavior for mismatched aliases/counts.

- **Resource-safety behavior**
  - Added explicit handling for large projection lists through safe allocation path and cleanup on all exits in validation flow.

- **Regression coverage**
  - Added focused test coverage for large `RETURN` projection lists in UNION validation to ensure the path returns query errors/validation results without stack exhaustion behavior.

```c
uint proj_count = cypher_ast_return_nprojections(return_clause);
/* before: const char *projections[proj_count];  // unbounded stack VLA */
/* after:  heap-backed projection buffer with explicit free/cleanup */
```

- Fixes #2329

pulls.title: param_parser: bound nested array/value recursion to prevent stack exhaustion
pulls.body:
The parameter parser allowed unbounded mutual recursion between `parse_array()` and `parse_value()`, so deeply nested array literals could exhaust the C stack and crash the process. This change adds an explicit nesting cap and fails parsing cleanly once the limit is exceeded.

- **Depth-bounded parsing in `src/ast/param_parser.c`**
  - Threaded a recursion-depth counter through the `parse_array`/`parse_value` call chain.
  - Added a fixed maximum nesting threshold (low-hundreds scale) appropriate for real query usage.
  - Return a parse error instead of recursing further when the threshold is reached.

- **Behavioral impact**
  - Normal parameter parsing behavior remains unchanged for valid, practical nesting.
  - Pathological deeply nested array payloads now terminate in controlled parse failure rather than stack overflow.

- **Coverage for the regression**
  - Added focused tests for nested parameter arrays:
    - parses successfully below the depth limit
    - fails deterministically at/over the limit

```c
// simplified shape of the change
static bool parse_value(const char **head, SIValue *v, uint32_t depth);

static bool parse_array(const char **head, SIValue *v, uint32_t depth) {
    if (depth >= PARAM_MAX_NESTING) return false; // parse error path
    ...
    if (!parse_value(&p, &elem, depth + 1)) return false;
}
```

<!-- START COPILOT CODING AGENT SUFFIX -->

- Fixes #2330

pulls.body:
Closes #170
Closes #2048

## Summary
Adds regression coverage for #2048, where restoring a graph `DUMP` under a
key name other than the one it was dumped from aliased the two keys.

## Changes
- Add `tests/flow/test_rdb_load.py::test_restore_under_a_different_key`:
  dump `src`, `RESTORE` it as `dst`, then assert
  - both keys appear in `GRAPH.LIST`
  - both hold the same data
  - the two graphs are independent — a write to one is not visible through
    the other, checked in **both** directions
  - both survive an RDB round trip (`DEBUG RELOAD`)
- Pass `enableDebugCommand=True` to this class's `Env` so the round trip can
  be exercised, matching `test_graph_copy` and `test_encode_decode`.

Added to `test_rdb_load.py` because that file already owns the graph
`DUMP`/`RESTORE` narrative. Its existing `test_rdb_load` only restores back
to the *same* key name, and `test_graph_copy.py` exercises the `GRAPH.COPY`
command rather than `DUMP`/`RESTORE`, so no existing test covered this.

## Testing
`TEST="tests/flow/test_rdb_load" ./flow.sh` → 2/2 pass.
Also ran `test_encode_decode`, `test_graph_copy` and `test_persistency`
alongside the touched files (88 tests) — no regressions.

Negative check — the test fails on the version the bug was reported against.
On `falkordb/falkordb:v4.20.1` the `RESTORE` decodes into the **source**
graph and then hangs the server:

```
1:M ... * <module> Graph 'src' processing virtual key: 1/1
1:M ... * <module> Graph 'src' processed 4/2 nodes
1:M ... * <module> Graph 'src' processed 2/1 edges
```

Note the graph name is `src` even though the restore target was `dst`, and
the node count has doubled (`4/2`) because the dump was decoded on top of
the existing graph. The connection never returns and a subsequent `PING`
times out.

## Memory / Performance Impact
N/A — test-only change. The added test builds a two-node graph.

## Related Issues
References #2048

## Summary
Adds regression coverage for #303, where variable length paths came back in
the wrong order from `ORDER BY length(p)` whenever `length(p)` was only a
sort key and not part of the projection.

The behaviour is correct today, but nothing pinned it down. The suite's
closest tests all miss this shape:

  with lengths 3, 3, 3, 3, 4, 4, 4 and 5.

  node names and recomputes `length(p)` from them, so it verifies the sort key
  the server actually used without depending on any tie-break order between

Closes #415

## Summary
Adds regression coverage for #415, where `CREATE` with a property that
self-references the node being created crashed the server in
`GraphEntity_Keys` instead of being rejected by the binder.

The engine now rejects every form of this query with `'<var>' not defined`,
but nothing in the suite pinned that down: `test34_self_referential_properties`
only exercised the direct form `CREATE (a:L {v: a.v})`, which took a
different path (it fails on the undefined *attribute*, not the undefined
*variable*, and never reached the crashing evaluation).

## Changes
- Extend `tests/flow/test_query_validation.py::test34_self_referential_properties`
  with the nested-comprehension variants:
  - the original report's query, in which the inner comprehension variable
    `root` shadows a node created by the same `CREATE` clause
  - minimal forms: `keys(a)`, a list comprehension over `keys(a)`, and an
    `any()` predicate reading `a.q`
- Assert the rejected `CREATE`s leave no partially applied writes behind.

Extended the existing test rather than adding a new one — the file already
owns the "self-referential properties" narrative, so a separate test would
have duplicated its setup and intent.

## Testing
`TEST="tests/flow/test_query_validation" ./flow.sh` → 44/44 pass.

Negative check — the test fails on the version the bug was reported
against. On `falkordb/falkordb:v4.14.6` the first query kills the server:

```
Error: Server closed the connection

Could not connect to Redis at 127.0.0.1:6501: Connection refused
```

pulls.title: Batch GRAPH.BULK relation topology construction
pulls.body:
The change adds a bounded relation-partitioned GRAPH.BULK transaction for declared batches from 131,072 through 1,048,576 edges, while retaining the established path outside that range. It assigns edge IDs and attributes in wire order, builds relation tensors and transposes, rebuilds all-relation adjacency, and preserves the index side effects used by bulk insertion.

Checks and public-path runs completed successfully:
- Release and debug builds passed, as did whole-diff whitespace and benchmark syntax checks.
- On the 1,000,000-edge, four-file, duplicate-size-1 shape, the change measured 5.077 s wall / 5.010 s server CPU / 441 MB peak RSS versus 5.790 s / 5.590 s / 462 MB for the comparison build.
- The 200,000-edge fresh shapes improved for one relation file and for four files with duplicate groups of eight; the 200,000-edge append shape also improved in wall time and CPU while peak RSS stayed effectively level.
- Redis-backed probes preserved counts, arrival-order IDs, indexed lookups, incoming traversal, multiedges, same-relation descriptor-file merging, overlapping relation topology, deletion-slot reuse, no-property edges, and append batches. Save/reload preserved the built topology, and the debug build passed the same multiedge and append probe.
- Boundary probes at and around the transaction threshold, just above its upper bound, and with 16 relation files showed no material regression.

The measured path is a real Redis GRAPH.BULK request and validates parser, transpose, index, append, reply, and command side effects. No material product, measurement, case-scope, or contribution defect was demonstrated.

On workload `GRAPH.BULK fresh: 1000000 edges, 4 relation files, duplicate group size 1`, median metric `wall_ns` changed from 4100849810 to 3794644954; paired median delta 322600758 (at least 19/20 confidence interval 146250097–363254571 from 10 pairs).

On workload `GRAPH.BULK fresh: 1000000 edges, 4 relation files, duplicate group size 1`, median metric `server_cpu_ns` changed from 3845000000 to 3645000000; paired median delta 225000000 (at least 19/20 confidence interval 80000000–250000000 from 10 pairs).

Full evidence: https://app.perfloop.ai/t/oss/case_fptwt283gw

```
-t ghcr.io/falkordb/${REPO}:edge          ← new
-t docker.io/falkordb/${REPO}:edge        ← new
-t ghcr.io/falkordb/${REPO}:edge-rs       ← kept (deprecated alias)
-t docker.io/falkordb/${REPO}:edge-rs     ← kept (deprecated alias)
```

Applies to both `falkordb` and `falkordb-server` via the existing matrix. It remains a **retag, never a rebuild** — the bytes PR CI validated are the bytes that ship.

Keeping `edge-rs` costs nothing: all four tags point at the same manifest, so there's no extra build. Anything already pinned to `edge-rs` keeps working; it gets dropped once consumers have moved.

## ⚠️ Ordering — #2291 must merge first

The two halves live on **different branches** and cannot be atomic. If this merges while `master` still publishes `:edge`, the tag **flip-flops per push** depending on which branch was touched last — worse than either steady state.

#2291 moves C's rolling images to the `edge-c` family. Once that's in, there is no contention on either registry:

- **Docker Hub** — C now writes `edge-c*`, this writes `edge` / `edge-rs`
- **GHCR** — C never published there at all

## Also in this PR: comment corrections

Several comments asserted the *inverse* of the new arrangement — most directly:

> `edge-rs` distinguishes the Rust port from the C port's `:edge` … so publishing to BOTH registries cannot clobber the C channel

That was true when C owned `:edge`; it now reads backwards. The trigger header, the `find-pr` notice, the `promote-edge` block header and the step name are updated to match. Stale comments that state the opposite of the code are worse than none.

## Resulting tag landscape

| tag | engine |
| --- | --- |
| `falkordb/falkordb:edge`, `-server:edge` | **Rust** (rolling, from `main`) |
| `ghcr.io/falkordb/…:edge` | **Rust** (new — C never published to GHCR) |
| `…:edge-rs` | Rust — alias, deprecated |
| `…:edge-c*` (15 tags) | C (rolling, from `master`, via #2291) |
| `…:latest` | C 4.21.x — untouched; separate 6.0 GA decision |

After this, `:edge` and `:latest` deliberately serve different engines — coherent ("edge is the future"), but it needs saying in the Docker Hub description. Tracked in #2290.

## Verification

`actionlint` reports **14 findings before and after** — none introduced. Runtime effect is observable on the first merge to `main` after this lands: `:edge` and `:edge-rs` should resolve to the same digest on both registries.


<!-- This is an auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->

## Summary by CodeRabbit

- **New Features**
  - Runtime release-candidate images are now promoted to the primary `:edge` channel.
  - The `:edge-rs` channel remains available as a deprecated alias.

- **Bug Fixes**
  - Promotion behavior now consistently uses updated `edge` terminology.
  - Toolchain and channel promotions remain limited to the appropriate main branches.
  - Promotions are safely skipped with a notice when merged pull requests are missing.
