pulls.title: ci: move C's rolling images to the edge-c channel
pulls.body:
**Step 1 of 2** for #2290. This one must merge **first** — see Ordering.

`main` (Rust engine) is now the default branch, so the plain `:edge` channel should serve the Rust image. This gives the C engine its own rolling channel rather than taking it away.

## Change

`build.yml`'s `publish-edge` job dispatches `release-image.yml` with `-f tag=edge` → **`-f tag=edge-c`**.

Because `release-image.yml` derives **every** tag it pushes from `env.TAG_NAME`, that single value renames the whole family:

```
edge-c            edge-c-x64            edge-c-arm64v8
edge-c-alpine     edge-c-alpine-x64     edge-c-alpine-arm64v8
edge-c-rhel8-x64  edge-c-rhel9-x64      edge-c-amazonlinux2023-x64
```
…plus the `falkordb-server` equivalents — 15 tags in total, all still rolling for C.

Also renames the **unreachable** `TAG_NAME="edge"` in `release-image.yml`'s `workflow_run` arm (that trigger was removed when `publish-edge` took over the hand-off). Keeping it in step means re-adding the trigger can't resurrect a C-side publisher for the plain `:edge` channel and race the Rust one.

## Why rename rather than delete

- C is maintained through 5.x and benefits from a rolling image for testing `master` before a release.
- Reverting the whole channel swap becomes a **one-line change**.
- Nothing is deleted, so no consumer loses an image outright — they just move to an explicitly-named channel.

## Ordering — this PR first

The two halves live on **different branches** and cannot be atomic. If the Rust side starts publishing `:edge` while C still does, `:edge` **flip-flops per push** depending on which branch was touched last — worse than either steady state.

Merging this first leaves `:edge` frozen-but-stable during the gap, then step 2 (on `main`) picks it up.

## Behaviour

No change beyond the tag names. The `Verify tag matches version.h` step is gated on `startsWith(env.TAG_NAME, 'v')`, which is false for `edge-c` exactly as it was for `edge`, so it still skips. `actionlint`: **28 findings before and after**.

## Resulting tag landscape (after both steps)

| tag | engine |
| --- | --- |
| `falkordb/falkordb:edge`, `-server:edge` | **Rust** (rolling, from `main`) |
| `…:edge-rs` | Rust — alias, deprecated later |
| `ghcr.io/falkordb/…:edge` | **Rust** (new; C never published to GHCR) |
| `…:edge-c*` (15 tags) | **C** (rolling, from `master`) |
| `…:latest` | C 4.21.x — untouched; that's the separate 6.0 GA decision |

## Follow-up not in this PR

Once this merges, the pre-existing `edge-alpine` / `edge-rhel8-x64` / `edge-rhel9-x64` / `edge-amazonlinux2023-x64` / `edge-x64` / `edge-arm64v8` tags (and `-server` equivalents) stop being written and sit frozen on Docker Hub — so `:edge` would be rolling Rust while `:edge-alpine` is a stale C build under the same channel name. Recommend deleting them; tracked in #2290.

pulls.title: ci: require every PR to close an issue
pulls.body:
Re-creation of #2245 against `main`. Same two commits, same single file — see the note at the bottom on why a base change wasn't possible.

Part of #2280.

## What it does

Adds `.github/workflows/pr-linked-issue.yml`, which fails a PR that doesn't close an issue — intended to become a **required status check** in branch protection.

### Detection

Queries GraphQL `closingIssuesReferences`, the only source that covers **both** a `Closes #N` keyword in the PR body **and** an issue attached through the PR's "Development" sidebar. REST exposes neither.

### Design choices worth reviewing

- **No `paths:` filter** — a required check that never reports blocks the PR indefinitely, so it must run on every PR to a covered branch.
- **`edited` in the trigger list** — re-titling or re-describing a PR re-evaluates the verdict instead of leaving a stale one.
- **Branch filter** mirrors `rust-pr.yml`: `main`, `main-rs`, `[0-9]*.[0-9]*`.
- **Read-only permissions** (`contents: read`, `pull-requests: read`).
- **No exemptions** — bot PRs must close an issue too. Deliberate policy; see the consequence below.

## How linking actually works here (verified)

**On a non-default base, the Development sidebar is the only mechanism that works.** GitHub registers a closing link from a body keyword *only* when the PR targets the repository's **default branch**.

Measured on #2245 (base `main-rs`, default `master`):

| state | `closingIssuesReferences` |
| --- | --- |
| `Closes #2243` as the first body line | **0** |
| issue attached via the Development sidebar | **1** |

Corroborated: GitHub search reported that PR as `-linked:issue`, and its timeline held no `CONNECTED_EVENT` / `CROSS_REFERENCED_EVENT`. The link genuinely doesn't exist, so no API can report it.

The failure message therefore points at the sidebar, and notes that a sidebar link emits no `pull_request` event — so the check must be **re-run** after linking. Observed live on #2245: failed at creation, passed on re-run once linked.

> **This resolves itself once `main` is the default branch.** Body keywords will register normally for PRs targeting `main`, and merging will auto-close the linked issue. Until the flip, the sidebar remains the reliable route.

## Before making it a required check

1. Let it report once so the check name exists in branch protection.
2. Be ready for it to block the next Dependabot PR and any `batch-backport` PR — there are no exemptions.

## Why this isn't just a base change on #2245

#2245's branch descends from `main-rs`. The migration commit on `main` (#2279) has a **single parent on `master`'s lineage**, so `main` and `main-rs` share **no common ancestor** — `git merge-base` returns nothing. Retargeting would have made GitHub diff the entire tree rather than this one file.

Since `main`'s tree is byte-identical to `main-rs`'s (`50390330`), the two commits cherry-picked cleanly onto a `main`-based branch. Verified afterwards: one file, 108 insertions, `actionlint` clean.

#2245 is closed in favour of this PR.


<!-- This is an auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->

## Summary by CodeRabbit

* **Chores**
  * Added automated checks to ensure pull requests targeting supported branches include at least one linked closing issue.
  * Pull requests without a linked issue now receive clear guidance and cannot pass the required check until updated.
  * Checks automatically re-run when pull request details change.

<!-- end of auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->

pulls.title: Add a per-query benchmark + coverage harness, and an on-demand CI job
pulls.body:
Closes #2288.

## Summary

Adds `bench/` — a per-query performance harness over a canonical 317-query set — and an on-demand CI workflow that measures a PR against its base and against the production C engine, plus how much of the `graph` crate the query set covers.

Trigger: add the **`benchmark-cov`** label to a PR. On-demand only, `labeled` event only, fork PRs skipped.

## What it measures, and why each metric

Nothing here compiles the engine. All three modules come from images other workflows already publish (`rc-pr-<N>`, `edge-rs`, `edge`), and all three are measured **inside the C engine's image** — verified to be redis 8.6.3 with jemalloc, the only one of the three carrying `redis-benchmark`, and able to load the C module and both Rust modules. Same redis, same allocator, no cross-environment difference to explain away.

| metric | scope | why |
|---|---|---|
| **instructions** (callgrind) | 93 queries, PR vs base | Counted in software — no PMU, and no hosted runner has one. Reproducible to **~0.2%**, so it gates. |
| **allocated bytes** (jemalloc merged-arena deltas) | all 317, PR vs base *and* vs C | Deterministic, unaffected by thread scheduling. Carries the vs-C comparison. |
| **wall-clock** | all 317, outliers only | Only after cancelling the per-runner speed offset, and only flagged past ±50%. See below. |

Wall-clock is never substituted for instructions. A time-based stand-in would turn the gate into a noise detector while still looking like a measurement.

## Measurement decisions, with the evidence

Each of these came from a run that produced a wrong answer first.

**Not macOS.** A hosted macOS runner produced *neither* metric: `proc_pid_rusage` returns 0 instructions (it is a VM) and Homebrew's redis links libc malloc, not jemalloc, so the allocation columns were empty too — 19 minutes at the 10x macOS billing rate for "No comparable rows". Linux has no PMU either, but stock redis there *is* jemalloc-built.

**Raw wall-clock is not comparable across the jobs.** On byte-identical engines the median PR/base `ms` ratio was **1.464**, with 316 of 317 rows off by more than 5% — each side runs on its own runner and runners differ in speed. Dividing by a control row (`RETURN 1`) cancels the offset: median 0.973, p99 1.110, nothing past 1.17x. Hence the ±50% threshold.

**The C engine is not measured under callgrind.** It busy-waits on a worker thread valgrind schedules arbitrarily. Measured with everything pinned (`THREAD_COUNT 1`, `OMP_NUM_THREADS=1`): **331,579,187 instructions of drift between two identical runs** of `list ops`, against ~100k for this module, and rows costing *more* on the run doing *fewer* queries. An earlier revision printed those as results — `RETURN 1` at 4.0M instructions against a true cost near 150k. vs-C lives on allocated bytes instead.

**Span selection is driven by measured drift, with a conservative floor.** Widening from a single noisy reading is self-defeating: an inflated cost asks for a *smaller* span, so the correction never fires, and the printed error bar divides by the same inflated number — the confidence looks best when the measurement is worst.

**The PR image is verified to match the head commit.** Without that, a labelled run measures whatever `rc-pr-<N>` happens to point at. Observed: a run benchmarked an image built two commits earlier because `rust-pr.yml` was still building the current head — the tag existed, so nothing complained. Preflight now waits for `build-rc-image` on this exact SHA.

## Shape of the run

`preflight` → **3 measure ∥ 12 callgrind ∥ coverage** → `report`. 18 jobs, ~10 minutes; it was 32 minutes serial. Each job uploads its own CSV, so one side failing costs that side's column and nothing else. `bench/report.py` merges them and upserts a single PR comment.

## Known limitations

- **The base side is the `edge-rs` image**, i.e. the trunk when it was last built, not the PR's merge base — so a row can move because the trunk moved. Stated in the posted comment. Building from source instead is exact and costs ~10 min of compile per side.
- **The callgrind subset is 93 of 317.** The rest either need a label/index/UDF/CSV the reduced `CG_SETUP` graph does not provide, or are hard-wired to the 10k graph (`hash join` uses `a.id = 9999 - b.id`) and would measure the empty path on the smaller one. Every one of the 93 was verified to run clean 300x on that exact graph against both engines.
- The callgrind graph is smaller than `run_bench.py`'s, so its absolute numbers are not comparable to the full-set rows — only ratios are.

## Testing

- actionlint clean; all `bench/*.py` compile; both shell scripts pass `bash -n`
- `pmc_tool.c` builds clean under `-Wall -Wextra`
- `bench/report.py` exercised over fixtures for every path: movers table, no-movers, C agreeing / disagreeing / single-pass, missing sides, sharded merge
- The workflow has run green end to end on the predecessor branch, most recently 18/18 jobs in ~10 min
- Calibration: on a null comparison (identical engine code both sides) callgrind returned **0 of 16 rows off by more than 0.5%, median 1.0001x**

## Note on `pmc_tool.c`

Fixes a CodeQL high (`cpp/uncontrolled-process-operation`). The tool is installed setuid-root and used to `execvp` a caller-supplied command — a local privilege escalation guarded only by hand-rolled uid/gid dropping. It no longer execs anything: `pmc_tool window` opens a counter window, prints `READY`, and waits on stdin while the *caller* runs the measured command unprivileged. The counters are system-wide, so bracketing in time was always sufficient. The privileged PMU sequence is byte-identical.



<!-- This is an auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->
## Summary by CodeRabbit

* **New Features**
  * Added a unified benchmark toolkit for measuring query performance, memory use, instruction counts, coverage, profiling, and flow tests.
  * Added automated benchmark coverage reporting with comparisons against the base branch and C engine.
  * Added generated reports highlighting regressions, improvements, missing measurements, and code coverage.
  * Added cross-platform performance counter support and Apple Silicon measurement capabilities.

* **Documentation**
  * Added comprehensive benchmark, profiling, workflow, setup, and results-interpretation guidance.

* **Tests**
  * Added extensive validation for metrics, reports, query definitions, coverage, and CSV output.

pulls.title: Fix negative ID range bounds
pulls.body:
## Summary

- keep evaluated node ID bounds signed until negative bounds are handled
- treat negative equality and upper bounds as empty, and negative lower bounds as unconstrained
- cover negative, contradictory, and zero-boundary predicates across labeled and unlabeled ID scans

## Root cause

`evaluate_id_filter` cast signed integer bounds to `u64` before comparison. Negative predicates therefore wrapped to very large positive IDs, producing incorrect ranges and potentially enormous allocations.

The bound now remains signed until its sign is handled. Since node IDs are non-negative, negative equality and upper-bound predicates return an empty range, while negative lower bounds impose no restriction. Only non-negative values are converted to `u64`.

## Testing

- Python flow-test syntax check
- final diff whitespace check
- full Rust and flow suites delegated to PR CI because the local Rust toolchain is unavailable and the flow launcher performs cleanup forbidden by the workspace safety policy

Supersedes #2275, which GitHub automatically closed during the unrelated-history base transition and would not allow to be reopened.

Fixes #2266

pulls.title: Migrate the default development branch to the Rust engine
pulls.body:
Fix #2280 

Replaces this branch's tree wholesale with the **Rust implementation of FalkorDB**. `main` becomes the development line for 6.0 and later; the **C engine continues on `master`** with its own CI, releases and maintenance.

## How to review this — don't read 7,000 files

The commit was built by plumbing, not by hand: its tree is **byte-identical** to `main-rs`, the branch carrying the Rust engine's full history. One command proves it:

```bash
gh api repos/FalkorDB/FalkorDB/git/commits/$(gh api repos/FalkorDB/FalkorDB/git/ref/heads/rust-migration --jq .object.sha) --jq .tree.sha
gh api repos/FalkorDB/FalkorDB/git/commits/$(gh api repos/FalkorDB/FalkorDB/git/ref/heads/main-rs        --jq .object.sha) --jq .tree.sha
# both → 50390330b99856ca2d970fd14cd3203e7abf622c
```

So the review question isn't "is every line right?" — it's **"is `main-rs` the tree we want `main` to have?"** The Rust tree has been under CI on `main-rs` throughout.

## Shape of the commit

```
main            …─ C history ─● 9d49fcd3
                               └─● cc48e5ab   ← this commit: tree = main-rs, ONE parent
main-rs   (orphan) ●─●─●─ … ─● d975d677       ← 2,873 Rust commits, NOT an ancestor
```

Single parent on `master`'s lineage, so **`git log main` stays linear** — C's history followed by one migration commit.

## ⚠️ `main-rs` must be preserved permanently

Because the Rust history is deliberately *not* an ancestor here, **`main-rs` is the only ref that reaches those 2,873 commits.** Deleting or force-pushing it makes them unreachable and eventually collectable.

- `git log` / `git blame` for Rust files resolve against **`main-rs`**, not `main`.
- Please add a deletion-protection rule on `main-rs` alongside the one for `main`.

## ⚠️ Merge method matters

The branch is a single commit whose parent is already `main`'s tip.

- ✅ **Rebase and merge** — fast-forward-equivalent, keeps the commit message
- ✅ **Squash and merge** — also linear, GitHub rewrites the message
- ❌ **Create a merge commit** — adds a second parent and defeats the linear history this design is built around

Worth setting the allowed merge methods on `main` before merging.

## Merging this is safe; the *flip* is what's gated

Merging only gives `main` the Rust tree — `main` is not the default branch, so nothing user-facing changes and no publishing behaviour moves.

**The gate is on the default-branch flip, and it is #2256.** That PR moves C's `:edge` publishing off `workflow_run` (which is default-branch-only) into `build.yml`. Flip before #2256 lands and **`:edge` silently stops publishing** — no error, no red X.

## What does *not* change

- `master` keeps building, testing and releasing exactly as today. Its `push`/`pull_request` CI is unaffected, and `release:` is ref-scoped so C's stable releases keep firing from their own version branches.
- `:edge` continues from `master`; `:edge-rs` continues from the Rust line. Docker Hub's `:latest` stays on C.
- The ~15 open PRs targeting `master` are unaffected.

## Sequence after this merges

1. Merge #2256 → `master` *(gate)*
2. Flip default `master` → `main`
3. Verify: landing page shows Rust; a `master` push still publishes `:edge`; crons now schedule from `main`
4. Branch protection on `main`; deletion protection on `main-rs`
5. Re-create #2245, #2277, #2278 against `main` — they branch off `main-rs`, which shares no ancestor with `main`, so they cannot be retargeted
6. Merge #2245 (linked-issue check) — body keywords finally register once `main` is default
7. Archive `falkordb-rs-next-gen`

> **`main-rs` is frozen as of this snapshot** (`d975d677`). Anything merged there from now on won't be in `main` and can't be retargeted — send new work to `main`.

---

pulls.title: feat(cow_btree): point lookups, memory accounting, tuple cursor + narrowable doc width
pulls.body:
Closes #2380

## What

Adds six enhancements to the always-compiled CoW B⁺-tree substrate (`graph/src/index/falkordb/data_structures/cow_btree/`), harvested from the tensor-decouple work:

1. **`first_doc(key)` / `contains_key(key)`** — allocation-free reference-descent point lookup. Unlike `point()→RangeIter` it clones no page `Arc`s and allocates no cursor stack, so it's the cheap primitive for equality filters / `EXISTS` / "one representative doc" probes. Handles the child-boundary case (a key whose entries begin at a separator) via a recorded `right_sep`.
2. **`heap_bytes()`** — approximate resident-memory accounting (leaf blob bytes + branch vec sizes), the primitive `GRAPH.MEMORY` needs. `O(pages)`; call off hot paths.
3. **`insert` / `remove` return a `#[must_use]` changed-`bool`** — lets a caller maintain an exact live cardinality in `O(1)` instead of an `O(n)` page walk, and cleanly detects idempotent-insert / absent-remove no-ops. (The change signal is distinct from `remove`'s internal underflow flag.)
4. **`DOC_BYTES` const generic** (`CowBTree<LEAF_MAX, BRANCH_MAX, const DOC_BYTES = 8>`) — narrows the fixed-stride AoS doc field (16→12 B/entry for a 4-byte doc), capturing the per-entry saving the compaction gate forfeits on high-entropy keys. **Defaults to 8** (byte-for-byte identical to today); a narrower width `assert!`s loudly on an over-width doc — no silent truncation. Nothing is instantiated below 8 in this PR.
5. **`Extract` / `TupleExtract` + `range_tuples`** — a zero-cost cursor generalization (`const NEEDS_KEY`) so a scan can also yield the encoded key for covered / index-only reads. The doc-only fast path is unchanged.
6. **`for_each_tuple`** — a bulk full-scan that matches each leaf's format once and runs a tight inner loop (for eager whole-tree consumers: memory/stats/serialize), faster than the lazy cursor.

## Why now / no call sites yet

These enhance the **substrate ahead of its consumers**: the native numeric index that uses `CowBTree` is a separate in-flight PR, and the edge-id store is its own. The methods are `pub` API of the always-compiled `cow_btree` module, so there are intentionally no in-tree callers yet. Landing them here keeps the substrate ready and lets the consumer PRs stay small.

## Compatibility & tests

- **No behavior change for existing code:** `DOC_BYTES` defaults to 8; nothing outside `cow_btree` references the tree today.

pulls.title: fix(algo): bound algo.SPpaths memory with a per-node search
pulls.body:
## What

`algo.SPpaths` / `algo.SSpaths` searched over **paths** rather than nodes. Every heap entry owned a cloned visited-set and edge-list, so the frontier held one state per partial path and grew exponentially with hop count.

Reported as an OOM in the [benchmark](https://github.com/FalkorDB/benchmark) suite against `falkordb/falkordb:edge-rs`: `ExitCode=137`, `OOM=true`, `used_memory_dataset` ≈ 100% of `used_memory`. Not a leak — memory returns to baseline after every query. It is a single unbounded query.

Reproduced on pokec-small (10k nodes / 121,716 `Friend` edges, **12 MB** in FalkorDB), one connection, running the benchmark's own `shortest_path` query:

```
[0] from=1825 to=410     877.2ms  peak=2249.0MiB  rows=1
[1] from=4507 to=4013   1550.0ms  peak=2994.7MiB  ERR Query timed out
[2] from=3658 to=2287   -> OOMKilled=true ExitCode=137
```

Pair `3658 → 2287` has no path; alone it climbed to 4.9 GiB in 21 s and killed the server. `falkordb/falkordb:edge` (C) answers `rows=0` in 4.0 ms.

The regression dates to `78f54ffae` (2026-03-29), when `algo.SPpaths` was first implemented in Rust — `algo_procedures.rs` did not exist before it, and the search has not been touched since. It sat unexposed for four months because nothing called the procedure; the benchmark switched its `shortest_path` queries from the `shortestPath()` clause to `algo.SPpaths` on 2026-07-28, two days before the report.

## How

Ports the three mechanisms `Proc_SPpathsInvoke` uses in the C engine, in place of the best-first search:

| | |
|---|---|
| `dijkstra_single_path` | Unconstrained single-shortest-path shape. One `DijkstraLabel { parent, edge, weight }` per node, 16-byte heap items, lazy deletion. Guarded on the same five conditions C uses. |
| `bfs_find_bound` | Per-node BFS. Unreachable target → return empty after one linear sweep; otherwise its weight seeds the pruning bound (for `pathCount` 0 and 1 only — the k-th path can legitimately be heavier). |
| `enumerate_paths` | DFS with backtracking for `maxLen` / `maxCost` / `pathCount`. One live path plus untried successors per depth, instead of the whole frontier. |

`check_timeout()` / `check_mem_capacity()` are now polled from inside all three loops (every 1024 iterations), so a long search returns an error rather than running until the server dies. `QUERY_MEM_CAPACITY` was previously only enforced between operators.

### Two deliberate divergences from C

Both are places where C is wrong:

1. **Weight summation order.** C sums its seed bound along the reverse parent walk and restores running totals by subtraction. Float addition is not associative, so the bound can land an ULP below the forward sum of the same edges and prune the path it came from. Here the pre-pass folds source→target and the enumeration carries per-edge prefix sums, so a given edge sequence always sums to identical bits. On a `0.1/0.2/0.3` chain C returns nothing; plain Cypher on both engines confirms the path exists.
2. **Non-finite weights.** C's gate is `weight + w <= max_weight`, which rejects NaN and infinity. The negated `> bound` form admits both, and a non-finite prefix then propagates into every path below it. Finiteness is now tested explicitly.

## Results

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| 25 random pokec pairs (benchmark query) | 877 ms / 2.2 GB, timeout / 3.0 GB, **OOM kill** | all 0.1–4.9 ms, memory flat |
| unreachable pair `3658 → 2287` | 4.9 GiB, **OOM kill** | `rows=0` in 4.9 ms |
| `maxLen` sweep, pair `1825 → 410` | +79 MiB at 4, **+2237 MiB** at 5 | +0.0 MiB at every depth |
| `pathCount` 200 / 2000 / 20000 | 38 / 92 / 477 ms | 1060 / 1047 / 1046 ms (flat in k) |

## Verification

- **Differential against the C engine**, 256 query shapes on a decimal-weighted graph — Dijkstra fast path (unweighted / weighted / +cost / incoming / both / no relTypes), every `maxLen` × `pathCount` combination, `maxCost` with and without `maxLen`, `source == target`, and all SSpaths shapes. **251/256 identical**; all 5 divergences are this branch finding paths C loses to the float bug above. One was ground-truthed with plain Cypher (w=3.81, c=4.78, 2 hops — the path exists).
- **Independent brute-force check**: ~65,500 trials against a simple-path enumerator written from the spec, over 24 random graphs with self-loops, parallel edges, disconnected nodes and unreachable targets — 0 structural failures.
- **Full flow suite**: 1328 run, 23 failed — a byte-identical failure set to the untouched baseline (all pre-existing local concurrency/timing tests). 108 Rust unit tests pass. `cargo fmt --all --check` and `CXX=clang++ cargo clippy --all-targets` clean.

## Tests

`tests/flow/test_path_algorithms.py` goes from 9 to 15 tests. The file previously had **no** coverage of the unconstrained fast path (every behavioural test pinned both `maxLen` and `maxCost`), of unbounded-depth enumeration, of `relDirection: 'both'`, or of interruptibility.

- `test09` — unreachable target across five shapes; OOM-kills the pre-fix build.
- `test10` — deep-but-reachable, asserting hop counts so the pairs cannot drift into no-ops.
- `test11` — fractional weights through the enumeration; fails with `lost the only path` if the summation fix is reverted.
- `test12` — fast-path results, including that the cheaper 2-hop route beats the direct edge.
- `test13` — `relDirection: 'both'`.
- `test14` — a search that cannot finish must surface `Query timed out`.

`test05_ss_single_path` was the only test asserting an exact path object; it now asserts membership in the set tied on (weight, cost, length), matching what `test02`–`test04` already do. Replacing best-first with DFS legitimately changes which of several equal-cost paths surfaces — measured 0/42 failures before, 3/42 after, with the returned path always tied-minimal. The full file is now 0 failures in 25 runs.

pulls.title: Fix negative ID range bounds
pulls.body:
## Summary

- keep evaluated node ID bounds signed until negative bounds are handled
- treat negative equality and upper bounds as empty, and negative lower bounds as unconstrained
- cover negative, contradictory, and zero-boundary predicates across labeled and unlabeled ID scans

## Root cause

`evaluate_id_filter` cast signed integer bounds to `u64` before comparison. Negative predicates therefore wrapped to very large positive IDs, producing incorrect ranges and potentially enormous allocations.

The bound now remains signed until its sign is handled. Since node IDs are non-negative, negative equality and upper-bound predicates return an empty range, while negative lower bounds impose no restriction. Only non-negative values are converted to `u64`.

## Testing

- Python flow-test syntax check
- final diff whitespace check
- full Rust and flow suites delegated to PR CI because the local Rust toolchain is unavailable and the flow launcher performs cleanup forbidden by the workspace safety policy

Fixes #2266

pulls.title: sync: bring main-rs up to date with falkordb-rs-next-gen/main
pulls.body:
Brings `main-rs` up to date with the **37 commits** added to `FalkorDB/falkordb-rs-next-gen`'s `main` since `main-rs` was seeded.

`main-rs` was seeded from the migration branch, and Rust development has continued in the development repo since. The two branches share ancestry (merge-base `67c71b81`), so this is an ordinary merge — not the unrelated-histories situation that applies to `master`.

## What comes across

Engine work:

- vectorize aggregates over computed expressions
- give `CASE` its own `ExprIR` variant, evaluated lazily
- dispatch fixed-arity operators directly instead of via the stack machine
- teach scan selection which variables an `Argument` binds; preserve a pruned scan subtree's `Argument` leaf when rebuilding
- replace the result cache with precomputed built-in columns; cache `dbms.functions()` keyed on the UDF version
- put `edge_endpoints` behind an `Arc` so node-only writes stop deep-cloning it
- fix a resize that left the committed base matrix pending
- report thread-pool queueing as waiting queries (stops `test_graph_info` hanging)

Plus dependency bumps: `actions/checkout` 7.0.0 → 7.0.1, `docker/login-action` 4.4.0 → 4.5.1, `thin-vec` 0.2.18 → 0.2.19, `libc` 0.2.186 → 0.2.189.

## Why a merge and not cherry-picks

Cherry-picks would land under **new SHAs**, so git would never learn those commits were already applied — every later sync would keep re-offering the same 17 non-merge commits, and the bookkeeping degrades each time. Merging records the ancestry once, so the next sync is a one-liner that brings only genuinely new work.

Conflict cost was identical either way (measured: exactly **1** of the 37 commits touches the conflicting files), and linearity is not a factor — `main-rs` is the Rust development line and is already ~39% merge commits. (The linear-history preference applies to `main`, the C-lineage branch that will take a single migration commit.)

## Conflicts: 6, all the same shape

All six are **modify/delete** — files `main-rs` deliberately removed, which `main` merely bumped pinned action SHAs in. **The deletions were kept.**

| file | removed on `main-rs` by |
| --- | --- |
| `_benchmark.yml`, `benchmark.yml`, `profile.yml`, `shellcheck.yml` | #2259 (perf-CI removal) |
| `flow-migration-rca.lock.yml`, `flow-tests-migration.lock.yml` | `603ba324` (AI flow-test workflows) |

## Verification

- **No resurrection**: `grep` across `.github/` finds no reference to any removed file, no `benchmark-edge` job back in `rust-push.yml`, and `.github/scripts/benchmark/` still absent. This was the main risk — `rust-push.yml` auto-merged, so a returning `uses: ./.github/workflows/_benchmark.yml` would have made the workflow fail to start.
- **Both sides preserved** — from `main-rs`: the product README hero, `SSPL-1.0` + `FalkorDB/FalkorDB` Cargo metadata, `release-tag.yml`, the `main-rs` trunk gates (7 in `rust-push.yml`), the `edge-rs` Docker Hub push. From `main`: the `actions/checkout` 7.0.1 and `docker/login-action` 4.5.1 bumps.
- All 15 remaining workflows parse; `actionlint` **54 findings before and after** (measured against `main-rs` via `git archive` into a temp dir) — none introduced.

Rust sources merged without conflict: `main-rs` carries no engine changes of its own, so the merged tree takes `main`'s Rust wholesale.

## Note

This does not close an issue — it's a branch sync rather than tracked work. Link one via the Development sidebar if the linked-issue check from #2245 has landed by the time this merges.

pulls.title: ci: remove the performance-CI surface (A/B benchmarks + flame-graph profiling)
pulls.body:
Closes #2258

## Why

The perf CI depends on infrastructure this repository does not have:

- it publishes dashboards and flame graphs to a **`gh-pages` branch** — this repo has only `master` and `main-rs`;
- it provisions **ephemeral GCE runners** from `vars.BENCHMARK_*` / `vars.PROFILE_*` / `GCP_ZONES_ARM`, none of which are configured here (unlike `GCP_SA_KEY` / `GCP_PROJECT_ID` / `GH_SA_TOKEN`, which C's own workflows already use);
- it is driven by PR labels and `/benchmark` slash commands that only make sense in the repo it grew up in.

Left in place it fails or silently no-ops, and it kept `contents: write` on the post-merge workflow for no reason.

## Why it all comes out together

The pieces are hard-coupled:

- `profile.yml` sparse-checkouts `.github/scripts/benchmark` and calls `profile.sh`, `view-slug.sh`, `gh-pages-push.sh`;
- `shellcheck.yml` only ever linted those scripts — its `paths:` filter is `.github/scripts/benchmark/**`, so it would never fire again once they were gone.

## Deleted

`benchmark.yml`, `_benchmark.yml`, `profile.yml`, `shellcheck.yml`, and the 16 files under `.github/scripts/benchmark/`.

## Edited

- **`rust-push.yml`** — drop the `benchmark-edge` job (the canonical-trend feed), and reduce top-level `permissions` from `deployments: write` + `contents: write` to `contents: read`. **Audited before changing:** those grants existed solely for gh-pages publishing; `find-pr`, `docker` and `promote-edge` declare their own permissions, and every remaining job needs read only. Flagging it explicitly since it's the one behavioural change beyond deletion — easy to veto if you'd rather leave permissions alone.
- **`README.md`** — remove the "A/B benchmarking vs the production (C) image" developer section (43 lines). The product link to <https://benchmark.falkordb.com/> **stays** — that's the public benchmark site, not this CI.
- **`.claude/skills/profile/SKILL.md`** — its benchmark section pointed at `_benchmark.yml` and a `gh-pages` trend URL that no longer exist. Now states plainly that there is no perf CI, and how to measure locally instead.

## Kept deliberately

- `docs/profiling.md` — purely local `samply` profiling, no CI dependency, still useful.
- The local profiling flow in the `profile` skill.
- The incidental "benchmark" mentions in `.gitignore` (local perf artifacts) and `gen_prejit.sh` (prose).

## Verification

- All **15** remaining workflows parse.
- `git grep` finds **no reference anywhere in the tree** to any deleted file.
- `actionlint` on `rust-push.yml`: **14 findings before, 14 after** — all pre-existing, none introduced.

## Follow-ups (out of scope)

- The `benchmark-*` / `profile-*` labels and the `BENCHMARK_*` / `PROFILE_*` repo variables are now unused and can be cleaned up in settings.
- If A/B benchmarking is wanted here later, reintroduce it deliberately with a `gh-pages` branch and runner variables provisioned first.

pulls.title: ci: dispatch master's crons from the default branch, and keep its Dependabot alive
pulls.body:
Closes #2255. Companion to #2256, which removes `master`'s `workflow_run` dependency and makes the CodeQL scan dispatchable. ## What actually breaks at the flip Only things GitHub reads **from the default branch** break when the default branch moves to the Rust tree: | trigger / config | default-branch-only? | handled where | | --- | --- | --- | | `schedule` (C's three crons) | **yes** | **this PR** | | `.github/dependabot.yml` | **yes** | **this PR** | | `workflow_run` (Build → `edge`) | **yes** | #2256 (dependency removed) | | `push` (build, tags) | no | nothing needed | | `release:` (stable publishing) | **no — ref-scoped** | nothing needed | ### `release:` is ref-scoped — verified GitHub reads a release-triggered workflow from the **tagged ref's own tree**, not the default branch: ``` release-event run for v4.20.1 → head_branch = v4.20.1 (not master) head_sha = efea8d99 efea8d99 vs branch 4.20 → identical efea8d99 vs master → diverged ``` GitHub's docs carry the default-branch-only note for `schedule`, `workflow_run` and `workflow_dispatch` — but **not** for `release`. **Consequence:** each engine's tags carry only that engine's workflows. A C release tag can never reach the Rust pipeline, and vice versa. There is nothing to route and nothing to version-gate, and C's stable publishing keeps working untouched. > An earlier revision of this PR added `master-release-dispatch.yml` with a major-version gate, and removed the `release:` triggers from `release-image.yml` / `release-artifacts.yml`, on the opposite assumption. All of that is **reverted** — the dispatcher is deleted and the triggers restored. Deleting it also retires the annotated-tag SHA bug Copilot flagged in it (`git/ref/tags` returns the tag object, not the commit). > > Caught by CodeRabbit on #2256. 🙏 ## What this PR adds ### `master-cron-dispatch.yml` `schedule` genuinely is default-branch-only, so C's crons must be re-fired from here. Mirrors `master`'s three cron lines **verbatim** (diffed — identical) and maps the schedule that fired back to the workflow it stands in for: | cron | dispatches on `--ref master` | | --- | --- | | `17 4 * * *` | `cleanup-rc-images.yml` | | `0 0 * * 1` | `submodule-update.yml` | | `33 5 * * 1` | `codeql-analysis.yml` | Each is dispatched independently so one missing entry point can't suppress the others. A `choice` input allows manual runs. `GITHUB_TOKEN` with `actions: write` suffices — per [GitHub's docs](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/write-workflows/choose-when-workflows-run/trigger-a-workflow), `workflow_dispatch` and `repository_dispatch` are the explicit exceptions that "always create workflow runs" even when triggered by `GITHUB_TOKEN`, so no PAT. Gated on `github.repository == 'FalkorDB/FalkorDB'` so a copy of this file elsewhere can't dispatch anything. > `codeql-analysis.yml` only becomes dispatchable once #2256 merges; until then its dispatch fails and is reported at the end of the run, while the other two still fire. ### `dependabot.yml` — one entry with `target-branch: master` Dependabot reads `.github/dependabot.yml` from the **default branch only**, so once this tree is default, `master`'s copy is never read again and C silently stops receiving dependency PRs. Fixing it on `master` would be a no-op — the entry has to live here: ```yaml - directory: / package-ecosystem: github-actions target-branch: master schedule: { interval: weekly } cooldown: { default-days: 7 } ``` Mirrors `master`'s config verbatim. That single ecosystem is C's **entire** Dependabot surface — its native dependencies are git submodules, bumped by `submodule-update.yml` (whose cron this PR dispatches), not by Dependabot. Two `updates` entries may share `package-ecosystem` + `directory` as long as `target-branch` differs — the supported way to cover several branches. All three triples in the resulting file are unique. > No `ignore` rule is needed on this entry: the `github/gh-aw-actions/**` rule on the Rust entries exists because those actions are version-locked to the gh-aw compiler **in this tree**. Checked every workflow on `master` — no gh-aw references exist there. > > Note: with the no-exemptions policy from #2243, each Dependabot PR will need an issue filed before it can merge, on both branches. ### Rust-side `browser-tests-trigger.yml` So both engines exercise the browser on a stable release. Called from `release-tag.yml` **after the `image` job**, which fixes a real ordering bug: browser tests need the **published** image, but `release:` fires the moment the release is created, racing the image push. The C side still has that race. Body is a **placeholder**, mirroring C's equivalent — the real Playwright suite in `FalkorDB/falkordb-browser` hardcodes `falkordb/falkordb:v4.18.10` in 8 places and exposes no input for the image under test, so it can't be pointed at a release until that input is added there. ## Release topology, for reference Neither `master` nor `main` cuts a stable release — they publish **rolling edge images** only. Stable releases come from **version branches**, split by engine: **C ≤ 5.x**, **Rust ≥ 6.0**. ```mermaid flowchart TD T6["tag v6.0.0
on a 6.x version branch"] --> RT["release-tag.yml
push tags v6-v9 and v10 plus
guard major must be 6 or higher"] RT --> RTC["create GitHub Release"] RTC --> RTA["release-artifacts.yml
via workflow_call"] RTC --> RTI["release-image.yml
via workflow_call - retag rc-pr-N"] RTI --> RTB["browser-tests-trigger.yml
chained AFTER image, so no race"] RTI --> OUTR["ghcr + docker.io
falkordb:6.0.0"] T5["tag v5.0.0
on version branch 5.0"] --> REL["publish GitHub Release"] REL --> EV["release: published
REF-scoped, so read from the tag's own tree"] EV --> CI["C's release-image.yml
from branch 5.0 - unaffected by the flip"] CI --> OUTC["docker.io
falkordb:5.0.0 and :latest"] ``` Rolling edge, for completeness — both engines stay entirely on their own branch, no dispatcher on either side: ```mermaid flowchart TD PM["push to master - C"] --> BM["build.yml
plain push trigger"] BM --> PE["publish-edge job in build.yml (#2256)"] PE --> IE["release-image.yml --ref master"] IE --> OE["docker.io/falkordb:edge"] PMAIN["push to main - Rust"] --> RP["rust-push.yml, promote-edge job"] RP --> OR["ghcr + docker.io
falkordb:edge-rs"] ``` ## Verification `actionlint` clean on the new files; cron lines diffed against `master`'s and identical; `dependabot.yml` parses with all three ecosystem/directory/target triples unique. Runtime behaviour is only fully exercisable after the flip — until then the dispatcher is manually dispatchable for a dry run. ⚠️ This PR and #2256 must **both** merge before the default branch is flipped.

+    def test10_unique_constraint_empty_or_whitespace_value(self):
+        # regression test (crash): a UNIQUE constraint whose constrained
+        # string value is empty or whitespace-only used to segfault the server
+        # during write-commit enforcement. RediSearch stores such a value as an
+        # empty, non-matchable TAG token, so the "find myself in the index"
+        # iterator in EnforceUniqueEntity returned NULL and the result was
+        # dereferenced (the guarding ASSERT is compiled out in release builds).
+        # see src/constraint/unique_constraint.c
+        g = self.g
+
+        # fresh label, isolated from the rest of the suite
+        create_unique_node_constraint(g, 'Blank', 'id', sync=True)
+
+        # none of these constrained values round-trip through the RediSearch
+        # TAG index (empty/all-whitespace normalize to an empty token; leading/
+        # trailing whitespace is trimmed so the raw query token no longer
+        # matches the stored, trimmed tag). before the fix any one of them
+        # crashed the server on commit
+        vals = ["''", "' '", "'  '", "'\t'", "'\n'", "' abc'", "'abc '", "'  abc  '"]
+        for val in vals:
+            g.query(f"CREATE (n:Blank) SET n.id = {val}")
+
+        # server survived and keeps serving queries
+        res = g.query("MATCH (n:Blank) RETURN count(n)")
+        self.env.assertEqual(res.result_set[0][0], len(vals))
+
+        # a normal value is still enforced: a genuine duplicate is rejected
+        g.query("CREATE (n:Blank) SET n.id = 'unique-val'")
+        try:
+            g.query("CREATE (n:Blank) SET n.id = 'unique-val'")
+            self.env.assertTrue(False) # should not reach
+        except ResponseError as e:
+            self.env.assertContains("unique constraint violation", str(e))
+
+        # async-creation path: build a constraint over a graph that ALREADY
+        # contains an empty-valued node - enforcement runs on the indexer
+        # thread and used to crash there too
+        g.query("CREATE (n:Blank2) SET n.id = ''")
+        g.query("CREATE (n:Blank2) SET n.id = 'x'")
+        create_unique_node_constraint(g, 'Blank2', 'id', sync=True)
+        res = g.query("MATCH (n:Blank2) RETURN count(n)")
+        self.env.assertEqual(res.result_set[0][0], 2)

+/*

+
+#pragma once
+
+#include <limits.h>
+#include <stdint.h>
+
+#include "entities/attribute_set.h"  // AttributeID, ATTRIBUTE_ID_ALL
+
+// central home for a graph's structural limits and the boundaries the RDB
+// decoder enforces on an untrusted payload. a count read from a payload that
+// exceeds its limit is treated as corrupt data: the decode fails cleanly
+// rather than driving a huge allocation or a long loop
+
+//------------------------------------------------------------------------------
+// attributes
+//------------------------------------------------------------------------------
+
+// AttributeID is a 16-bit type whose two top values are reserved sentinels
+// (ATTRIBUTE_ID_NONE, ATTRIBUTE_ID_ALL), so a graph holds at most
+// ATTRIBUTE_ID_ALL distinct attribute names - enforced in
+// GraphContext_FindOrAddAttribute (EMSG_MAX_ATTRIBUTES_EXCEEDED). an entity
+// can't reference more attributes than the graph defines
+#define GRAPH_MAX_ATTRIBUTES  ATTRIBUTE_ID_ALL
+
+//------------------------------------------------------------------------------
+// labels & relationship types
+//------------------------------------------------------------------------------
+
+// LabelID / RelationID are 'int' and otherwise uncapped; bound a payload-
+// supplied count well below INT_MAX so garbage fails fast instead of sizing a
+// huge allocation
+#define GRAPH_MAX_LABELS     (1 << 16)
+#define GRAPH_MAX_RELATIONS  (1 << 16)
+
+//------------------------------------------------------------------------------
+// constraints
+//------------------------------------------------------------------------------
+
+// a constraint stores its field count in a uint8 (Constraint.n_attr)
+#define GRAPH_MAX_CONSTRAINT_FIELDS  UINT8_MAX
+
+//------------------------------------------------------------------------------
+// decode payload boundaries (not graph structure, but untrusted-count bounds)
+//------------------------------------------------------------------------------
+
+// elements in a single decoded SIArray
+#define GRAPH_MAX_SIARRAY_LEN  (1 << 28)
+
+// encode-state payloads described by one (virtual) key's schema
+#define GRAPH_MAX_KEY_PAYLOADS  (1 << 16)

+/*

+
+#pragma once
+
+// internal layout of the serializer, shared between the current serializer
+// (serializer_io.c) and the previous-version buffered serializer
+// (serializer_io_prev.c)
+//
+// a serializer created by one translation unit is read and freed by functions
+// in the other, so both must agree on the exact struct layout - keeping the
+// definitions here guarantees they never drift apart
+
+#include "serializer_io.h"
+#include "../redismodule.h"
+
+#include <setjmp.h>
+#include <stdbool.h>
+#include <stdint.h>
+
+// buffered io descriptor - the backing store of a buffered serializer
+typedef struct {
+	unsigned char *buffer;  // io buffer
+	size_t cap;             // io buffer capacity
+	size_t count;           // number of bytes written to io buffer
+	RedisModuleIO *stream;  // redis module io
+	SerializerIO io;        // owning serializer; malformed framing is reported
+	                        // through it via the single SerializerIO_SetError API
+} BufferedIO;
+
+// generic serializer
+// contains a number of function pointers for data serialization
+struct SerializerIO_Opaque {
+	void (*WriteFloat)(void*, float);                 // write float
+	void (*WriteDouble)(void*, double);               // write dobule
+	void (*WriteSigned)(void*, int64_t);              // write signed int
+	void (*WriteUnsigned)(void*, uint64_t);           // write unsigned int
+	void (*WriteLongDouble)(void*, long double);      // write long double
+	void (*WriteString)(void*, RedisModuleString*);   // write RedisModuleString
+	void (*WriteBuffer)(void*, const void*, size_t);  // write bytes
+
+	float (*ReadFloat)(void*);                        // read float
+	double (*ReadDouble)(void*);                      // read dobule
+	int64_t (*ReadSigned)(void*);                     // read signed int
+	uint64_t (*ReadUnsigned)(void*);                  // read unsigned int
+	void* (*ReadBuffer)(void*, size_t*);              // read bytes
+	long double	(*ReadLongDouble)(void*);             // read long double
+	RedisModuleString* (*ReadString)(void*);          // read RedisModuleString
+
+	bool encoder;           // true is serializer is used for encoding, false decoding
+	void *stream;           // RedisModuleIO* or a Stream descriptor
+	bool free_buff;         // true if serializer has a buffer to free
+	bool error;             // decode failure flag (short read or bad data)
+	char error_reason[256];  // decoder-detected bad data, empty otherwise
+	bool (*IsError)(void*); // backend error probe, NULL for encoders
+
+	// non-local abort support (serializer_io.h). the decoder dispatcher arms one
+	// handler for the whole decode; while 'armed', a TryRead that short-reads or
+	// a SerializerIO_SetError on malformed data longjmps to 'handler' instead of
+	// returning. an unarmed reader (e.g. graph offload) latches 'error' and
+	// returns instead
+	bool armed;             // true while a handler is installed
+	jmp_buf handler;        // where to jump on a decode failure
+	void *context;          // in-flight object the landing pad tears down (gc)
+};
+
+// probe whether a buffered serializer hit a backend IO error (e.g. a short read
+// during diskless replication or a truncated RESTORE payload). malformed buffer
+// framing is reported separately, through SerializerIO_SetError on buffer->io
+static inline bool Buffered_IsError
+(
+	void *stream  // BufferedIO*
+) {
+	BufferedIO *buffer = (BufferedIO*)stream;
+	return RedisModule_IsIOError(buffer->stream);
+}

+# Locate fields inside a graph's serialized value (encoding v20), so a test can
+# corrupt exactly one field of a healthy payload and check the decoder rejects
+# it. Works on a DUMP payload and on a key's value inside an RDB file: both hold
+# the same bytes.
+#
+# A graph value is a module type id, a run of RDB strings (one per serializer
+# buffer of up to 256000 bytes) and an EOF opcode. Inside the strings every
+# value starts with a 1-byte type tag; byte buffers add an 8-byte length.
+
+import struct
+
+# serializer value tags (src/serializers/serializer_io.c)
+TAG_BYTES, TAG_FLOAT, TAG_DOUBLE, TAG_SIGNED, TAG_UNSIGNED, TAG_LONG_DOUBLE, \
+    TAG_BLOB = range(7)
+_SIZES = {TAG_FLOAT: 4, TAG_DOUBLE: 8, TAG_SIGNED: 8, TAG_UNSIGNED: 8,
+          TAG_LONG_DOUBLE: 16}
+
+# value types (src/value.h)
+T_ARRAY = 1 << 3
+T_DATETIME = 1 << 5
+T_DATE = 1 << 7
+T_TIME = 1 << 8
+T_DURATION = 1 << 10
+T_STRING = 1 << 11
+T_BOOL = 1 << 12
+T_INT64 = 1 << 13
+T_DOUBLE = 1 << 14
+T_NULL = 1 << 15
+T_POINT = 1 << 17
+T_VECTOR_F32 = 1 << 18
+T_INTERN_STRING = (1 << 19) | T_STRING
+
+# payload types (src/serializers/encode_context.h)
+NODES, DELETED_NODES, EDGES, DELETED_EDGES = 1, 2, 3, 4
+LABELS_MATRICES, RELATION_MATRICES, ADJ_MATRIX, LBLS_MATRIX, CCH_INDICES = \
+    6, 7, 8, 9, 10
+
+INDEX_FLD_VECTOR = 0x10
+
+# Redis module type ids: 9 characters of 6 bits each, then a 10-bit encver
+_MODULE_CHARSET = ("ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZabcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz"
+                   "0123456789-_")
+
+
+def rdb_len(b, p):
+    """decode an RDB length at p, returns (length, next offset)"""
+    t = b[p]
+    if t >> 6 == 0:
+        return t & 0x3F, p + 1
+    if t >> 6 == 1:
+        return ((t & 0x3F) << 8) | b[p + 1], p + 2
+    if t == 0x80:
+        return int.from_bytes(b[p + 1:p + 5], 'big'), p + 5
+    if t == 0x81:
+        return int.from_bytes(b[p + 1:p + 9], 'big'), p + 9
+    raise ValueError(f'unsupported RDB length encoding {t:#x} at {p} '
+                     '(compressed? save with rdbcompression no)')
+
+
+def rdb_len_bytes(n):
+    if n < 1 << 6:
+        return bytes([n])
+    if n < 1 << 14:
+        return bytes([0x40 | (n >> 8), n & 0xFF])
+    if n < 1 << 32:
+        return b'\x80' + n.to_bytes(4, 'big')
+    return b'\x81' + n.to_bytes(8, 'big')
+
+
+def module_type_name(module_id):
+    return ''.join(_MODULE_CHARSET[(module_id >> (64 - 6 * (i + 1))) & 63]
+                   for i in range(9))
+
+
+def module_type_id(name, encver):
+    mid = 0
+    for ch in name:
+        mid = (mid << 6) | _MODULE_CHARSET.index(ch)
+    return (mid << 10) | encver
+
+
+_CRC64_TABLE = None
+
+
+def crc64(data):
+    """CRC-64 (Jones), the checksum Redis stamps into DUMP payloads"""
+    global _CRC64_TABLE
+    POLY = 0x95ac9329ac4bc9b5
+    if _CRC64_TABLE is None:
+        table = []
+        for i in range(256):
+            crc = i
+            for _ in range(8):
+                crc = (crc >> 1) ^ POLY if (crc & 1) else (crc >> 1)
+            table.append(crc)
+        _CRC64_TABLE = table
+    crc = 0
+    for byte in data:
+        crc = _CRC64_TABLE[(crc ^ byte) & 0xFF] ^ (crc >> 8)
+    return crc & 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF
+
+
+def reframe(body, version_bytes):
+    """DUMP payload from a module body: <body><2-byte version><8-byte CRC64>"""
+    payload = bytes(body) + version_bytes
+    return payload + crc64(payload).to_bytes(8, 'little')
+
+
+def _rdb_string(b, p):
+    """read an RDB string at p, any encoding; returns (bytes, next offset)"""
+    t = b[p]
+    if t >> 6 != 3:
+        n, p = rdb_len(b, p)
+        return bytes(b[p:p + n]), p + n
+    enc = t & 0x3F
+    if enc in (0, 1, 2):                     # 8/16/32-bit integer
+        n = 1 << enc
+        return str(int.from_bytes(b[p + 1:p + 1 + n], 'little',
+                                  signed=True)).encode(), p + 1 + n
+    if enc == 3:                             # LZF, kept compressed
+        clen, q = rdb_len(b, p + 1)
+        _, q = rdb_len(b, q)
+        return bytes(b[q:q + clen]), q + clen
+    raise ValueError(f'unsupported RDB string encoding {t:#x} at {p}')
+
+
+def _module_value_end(b, p):
+    """skip a module value of any shape (p at the module id)"""
+    _, p = rdb_len(b, p)
+    while True:
+        op, p = rdb_len(b, p)
+        if op == 0:                          # EOF
+            return p
+        if op in (1, 2):                     # signed / unsigned
+            _, p = rdb_len(b, p)
+        elif op == 3:                        # float
+            p += 4
+        elif op == 4:                        # double
+            p += 8
+        elif op == 5:                        # string
+            n, p = rdb_len(b, p)
+            p += n
+        else:
+            raise ValueError(f'unexpected module opcode {op} at {p}')
+
+
+def rdb_module_values(b):
+    """(key, module type name, value start, value end) for every module key in
+    an RDB file; the value starts at the module type id. the file must hold
+    only module keys (no streams, hashes, ...)"""

+# keep only graph keys (the RDB walker parses module values only), SAVE and

+def _save_graph_rdb(conn):
+    for k in conn.keys("*"):

+    conn.config_set("rdbcompression", "no")
+    conn.save()
+    path = os.path.join(conn.config_get("dir")["dir"],
+                        conn.config_get("dbfilename")["dbfilename"])
+    with open(path, "rb") as f:
+        return f.read()

+def _set_arg(args, name, value):
+    if name in args:
+        args[args.index(name) + 1] = value
+    else:
+        args += [name, value]

+# start a server on 'rdb' and wait for it to exit; returns (exit code, log)
+def _start_on_rdb(env, rdb):
+    d = tempfile.mkdtemp()
+    try:
+        with open(os.path.join(d, "dump.rdb"), "wb") as f:
+            f.write(rdb)

+        # no TCP port (nothing to collide with), a unix socket in its place:
+        # Redis refuses to start without any listener
+        args = list(env.envRunner.masterProcess.args)
+        _set_arg(args, "--port", "0")
+        _set_arg(args, "--unixsocket", os.path.join(d, "redis.sock"))
+        _set_arg(args, "--dir", d)
+        _set_arg(args, "--dbfilename", "dump.rdb")
+        _set_arg(args, "--logfile", os.path.join(d, "redis.log"))

+        p = subprocess.Popen(args, cwd=d, stdout=subprocess.DEVNULL,
+                             stderr=subprocess.DEVNULL)
+        try:
+            exit_code = p.wait(timeout=60)
+        except subprocess.TimeoutExpired:
+            p.kill()
+            p.wait()

+
+Fix for an aggregating `WITH` dropping a grouped node before the next `MATCH` ([FalkorDB#3333](https://github.com/FalkorDB/FalkorDB/issues/3333)).

+On a path `(:V {id:1})-[:R]->(:V {id:2})-[:R]->(:V {id:3})-[:R]->(:V {id:4})`, this query returned no rows. Neo4j and Memgraph return `3, 1, 4`.

+```cypher
+MATCH (a:V {id: 1})-[:R]->(x:V)-[:R]->(m:V)

+MATCH (m)-[r:R]->(b:V {id: 4})
+RETURN m.id, c1, b.id

+
+The same pattern written as one `MATCH` was already correct. The split form lost `m`.

+**Cause.** A row slot is addressed by variable id only. `WITH` starts a new scope, so ids start again at 0 and the next clause reuses numbers from the previous scope. `Aggregate` copied the pre-projection grouping key onto the output row, leaving the old node `m` bound in a slot the next `MATCH` assigned to `b`. `CondTraverse` treated `b` as already bound to that node and rejected the real neighbor, so the query returned no rows.

+
+// central home for a graph's structural limits and the boundaries the RDB
+// decoder enforces on an untrusted payload. a count read from a payload that
+// exceeds its limit is treated as corrupt data: the decode fails cleanly
+// rather than driving a huge allocation or a long loop
+
+//------------------------------------------------------------------------------
+// attributes
+//------------------------------------------------------------------------------
+
+// AttributeID is a 16-bit type whose two top values are reserved sentinels
+// (ATTRIBUTE_ID_NONE, ATTRIBUTE_ID_ALL), so a graph holds at most
+// ATTRIBUTE_ID_ALL distinct attribute names - enforced in
+// GraphContext_FindOrAddAttribute (EMSG_MAX_ATTRIBUTES_EXCEEDED). an entity
+// can't reference more attributes than the graph defines
+#define GRAPH_MAX_ATTRIBUTES  ATTRIBUTE_ID_ALL
+
+//------------------------------------------------------------------------------
+// labels & relationship types
+//------------------------------------------------------------------------------
+
+// LabelID / RelationID are 'int' and otherwise uncapped; bound a payload-
+// supplied count well below INT_MAX so garbage fails fast instead of sizing a
+// huge allocation
+#define GRAPH_MAX_LABELS     (1 << 16)
+#define GRAPH_MAX_RELATIONS  (1 << 16)
+
+//------------------------------------------------------------------------------
+// constraints
+//------------------------------------------------------------------------------
+
+// a constraint stores its field count in a uint8 (Constraint.n_attr)
+#define GRAPH_MAX_CONSTRAINT_FIELDS  UINT8_MAX
+
+//------------------------------------------------------------------------------
+// decode payload boundaries (not graph structure, but untrusted-count bounds)
+//------------------------------------------------------------------------------
+
+// elements in a single decoded SIArray
+#define GRAPH_MAX_SIARRAY_LEN  (1 << 28)
+
+// encode-state payloads described by one (virtual) key's schema
+#define GRAPH_MAX_KEY_PAYLOADS  (1 << 16)

+import os

+
+# Module-load arguments (`--loadmodule falkordb.so NAME VALUE ...`) are parsed
+# like C's `Config_Init`: names are case-insensitive, values go through the same
+# validation as GRAPH.CONFIG SET, and an invalid value, an unknown name or an
+# odd argument count refuses the load (#3268).
+
+# (module args, config to read, expected value)
+ACCEPTED = [
+    ("CMD_INFO YES",              "CMD_INFO",           1),
+    ("cmd_info no",               "CMD_INFO",           0),
+    ("DELAY_INDEXING YES",        "DELAY_INDEXING",     1),
+    ("cache_size 10",             "CACHE_SIZE",         10),
+    ("CACHE_SIZE 5000",           "CACHE_SIZE",         5000),
+    ("ASYNC_DELETE no",           "ASYNC_DELETE",       0),
+    ("async_delete No",           "ASYNC_DELETE",       0),
+    ("timeout_max 7",             "TIMEOUT_MAX",        7),
+    ("Thread_Count 3",            "THREAD_COUNT",       3),
+    ("max_queued_queries 5",      "MAX_QUEUED_QUERIES", 5),
+    ("Vkey_Max_Entity_Count 0",   "VKEY_MAX_ENTITY_COUNT", 0),
+    ("node_creation_buffer 600",  "NODE_CREATION_BUFFER", 1024),
+    ("TIMEOUT_DEFAULT 5 TIMEOUT_MAX 10", "TIMEOUT_DEFAULT", 5),
+]
+
+# (module args, message logged before the load is refused)
+REFUSED = [
+    ("CMD_INFO garbage",          "Failed setting field 'CMD_INFO'"),
+    ("DELAY_INDEXING 1",          "Failed setting field 'DELAY_INDEXING'"),
+    ("CACHE_SIZE 0",              "Failed setting field 'CACHE_SIZE'"),
+    ("THREAD_COUNT 0",            "Failed setting field 'THREAD_COUNT'"),
+    ("OMP_THREAD_COUNT 0",        "Failed setting field 'OMP_THREAD_COUNT'"),
+    ("MAX_QUEUED_QUERIES 0",      "Failed setting field 'MAX_QUEUED_QUERIES'"),
+    ("JS_HEAP_SIZE 5",            "JS_HEAP_SIZE must be at least 1MB (1048576)"),
+    ("FOO 1",                     "Encountered unknown configuration field 'FOO'"),
+    ("CACHE_SIZE",                "FalkorDB received 1 arguments, all configurations should be key-value pairs"),
+    ("CACHE_SIZE 10 THREAD_COUNT", "FalkorDB received 3 arguments, all configurations should be key-value pairs"),
+    ("TIMEOUT 10 TIMEOUT_MAX 10", "The TIMEOUT configuration parameter should be removed"),
+    ("TIMEOUT_MAX 10 TIMEOUT 10", "The TIMEOUT configuration parameter is deprecated"),
+    ("TIMEOUT_DEFAULT 10 TIMEOUT_MAX 5", "TIMEOUT_MAX configuration parameter cannot be set to a value lower than TIMEOUT_DEFAULT"),
+]
+
+# C configs this engine accepts but does not act on
+IGNORED = ["ASYNC_DELETE", "DELAY_INDEXING", "DELTA_MAX_PENDING_CHANGES", "EFFECTS_THRESHOLD"]

+DEFAULTS = {
+    "TIMEOUT": 0,
+    "TIMEOUT_DEFAULT": 0,
+    "TIMEOUT_MAX": 0,
+    "CACHE_SIZE": 25,
+    "ASYNC_DELETE": 1,
+    "RESULTSET_SIZE": -1,
+    "VKEY_MAX_ENTITY_COUNT": 100000,
+    "QUERY_MEM_CAPACITY": 0,
+    "DELTA_MAX_PENDING_CHANGES": 10000,
+    "NODE_CREATION_BUFFER": 16384,
+    "CMD_INFO": 1,
+    "MAX_INFO_QUERIES": 1000,
+    "EFFECTS_THRESHOLD": 300,
+    "DELAY_INDEXING": 0,
+    "IMPORT_FOLDER": "/var/lib/FalkorDB/import/",
+    "TEMP_FOLDER": "/tmp",
+    "JS_HEAP_SIZE": 268435456,
+    "JS_STACK_SIZE": 1048576,
+}

+def _load_locally(module_args):
+    """Start redis-server with the module and `module_args`, without listening
+    on a port (so it exits right after loading the module), and return
+    (exit code, or None if it did not exit, and its log)."""
+    module = Defaults.module
+    if isinstance(module, (list, tuple)):
+        module = module[0]
+    log_dir = tempfile.mkdtemp()
+    log_file = os.path.join(log_dir, "redis.log")
+    cmd = [Defaults.binary, "--port", "0", "--save", "", "--dir", log_dir,
+           "--logfile", log_file, "--loadmodule", module, *module_args.split()]
+    proc = subprocess.Popen(cmd, stdout=subprocess.DEVNULL, stderr=subprocess.DEVNULL)
+    try:
+        rc = proc.wait(timeout=20)
+    except subprocess.TimeoutExpired:
+        proc.kill()
+        proc.wait()
+        rc = None
+    with open(log_file) as f:
+        log = f.read()
+    return rc, log
+
+
+class testModuleArgs():
+    def __init__(self):
+        self.env, self.db = Env()
+
+    def test01_defaults(self):
+        """No module arguments: every config keeps its default."""
+        for name, expected in DEFAULTS.items():
+            self.env.assertEqual(self.db.config_get(name), expected, message=name)
+
+    def test02_accepted(self):
+        """Valid arguments take effect, whatever the case of their name."""
+        for args, name, expected in ACCEPTED:
+            env, db = Env(moduleArgs=args)
+            env.assertEqual(db.config_get(name), expected, message=args)
+
+    def test03_refused(self):
+        """Invalid arguments refuse the load, as in C."""
+        if SANITIZER:
+            # a refused load exits with the module half-initialised
+            self.env.skip()
+
+        for args, err in REFUSED:
+            loaded = True
+            try:
+                env, _ = Env(moduleArgs=args)
+                env.getConnection().ping()
+            except Exception:
+                loaded = False
+            self.env.assertFalse(loaded, message=args)
+
+        # Locally, also check the server exits and logs why.
+        if os.getenv("FALKORDB_TEST_IMAGE"):
+            return
+        for args, err in REFUSED:
+            rc, log = _load_locally(args)
+            self.env.assertNotEqual(rc, None, message=args)
+            self.env.assertNotEqual(rc, 0, message=args)
+            self.env.assertContains(err, log, message=args)
+            self.env.assertContains("initialization failed. Module not loaded", log, message=args)
+
+    def test04_ignored_configs_logged(self):
+        """C configs this engine does not act on are accepted, stored, and
+        logged as deprecated."""
+        args = "ASYNC_DELETE no delay_indexing yes DELTA_MAX_PENDING_CHANGES 5 EFFECTS_THRESHOLD 7"
+        env, db = Env(moduleArgs=args)
+        env.assertEqual(db.config_get("ASYNC_DELETE"), 0)
+        env.assertEqual(db.config_get("DELAY_INDEXING"), 1)
+        env.assertEqual(db.config_get("DELTA_MAX_PENDING_CHANGES"), 5)
+        env.assertEqual(db.config_get("EFFECTS_THRESHOLD"), 7)
+        if env.log_path is not None:
+            with open(env.log_path) as f:
+                log = f.read()
+            for name in IGNORED:
+                env.assertContains(
+                    f"configuration field '{name}' is deprecated and has no effect", log)

+behaviour the asserts expect, so every test fails on the current Rust engine

+so each class should be run on its own (see the PR description for how).

+def _expect_error(env, graph, query, *fragments):
+    """Run `query`, expect a ResponseError whose message contains every
+    fragment, then check the server is still up."""
+    try:
+        graph.query(query)
+        env.assertTrue(False, message=f"expected an error for: {query[:80]}")
+    except ResponseError as e:
+        for f in fragments:
+            env.assertContains(f, str(e))

+
+# A genuine GRAPH.RESTORE payload for the graph
+#     CREATE (a:A)-[:R]->(b:B), (a)-[:R]->(b)
+# (two parallel A->B edges, i.e. one multi-edge pair), captured from
+# `GRAPH.COPY`'s AOF propagation on falkordb/falkordb-server:edge (Rust engine,
+# module ver 999999) on 2026-10-13, then zlib-compressed and base64-encoded so
+# the tests can reconstruct the exact bytes. It round-trips cleanly through a
+# healthy GRAPH.RESTORE and yields two edges.
+#
+# The payload is in the Rust engine's v19 BufferedWriter framing. The C engine
+# uses a different on-disk format and crashes on this payload regardless of any
+# corruption, so these tests are Rust-only; the C column is recorded n/a.
+_GOOD_PAYLOAD_ZB64 = (
+    "eNrtmsFOAjEQhmd2Da5Igj6Db4DGeCEqF2JiJCF41pt3n4AL8Ao+gwcw8WE8+DBIYneBabt0FUK"
+    "3+89lSnen2y39dv42pZh+7aVFB5EqLwukFbJLbC+QtR1Ka25NbbO8q5N3l95o33R7TYvLehVrNT"
+    "Wt5lALT7SaI/sIkMMlKjKAz2nVzbpPY+fKsrHckf27/e7153y+8BPlx8qPlJ8qH6ix7x1MZEfTW"
+    "d597Tx1er17AxKxFp21UF+JvnsYnLeKhR+vhD+q+Mgtnoo/nkzvvAi7MlAbb0STBJreT62pQHEs"
+    "UO2GjWZ5TEcyZ3q6MEEFkDIh6cJU3mMJKCJLAsWAUFyK+mCUa8XTY0WUK+9XuTKUK9Il0iWUKxa"
+    "RMP9Q5Aoo141Mlk652tLhTPkPMOmFclXzbajhcXnhLD7/IB6hXfcJ50RAOBOQjgCnH2aC0iFl9q"
+    "FeywPjpgw5AYyA0XP9qh/VIFlD38Lz6eIl399SUJssgOJ1hZL9Tix/z4kG5LBd/zprN9XYsfook"
+    "PAsfGJtb9mX9X7qy5lwz07YJEOghrMTUPG+b3vZBAO2vcq87eWUv6HhkSVhu0aRK4hiJBRvimKE"
+    "rAjB6rdgzRGcDREe2bDMzus3tt2F7eKJTAmDaPUiU2L9CPMMRQ4bxR+srYMm"
+)
+
+# Offsets into the decompressed payload, from a TLV walk of these exact bytes.
+# The tensor section for the one multi-edge pair is:
+#   8667 UNSIGNED 2   total edge_count
+#   8676 UNSIGNED 1   base group count (number of multi-edge pairs)
+#   8685 UNSIGNED 0   src node id
+#   8694 UNSIGNED 1   dst node id
+#   8703 BYTES  219   GxB-serialized bool id-vector for this pair
+#   8931 UNSIGNED 0   delta-plus group count
+# TYPE tags: UNSIGNED=4, BYTES=0. Every method asserts the tags it edits so a
+# format drift fails loudly rather than silently editing the wrong byte.
+_OFF_GROUP_COUNT = 8676   # tag at 8676, u64 value at 8677..8685
+_OFF_ENTRY = 8685         # first tensor entry: src(9)+dst(9)+blob(9+219)
+_OFF_BLOB = 8703          # BYTES tag; u64 length at 8704..8712; 219 data bytes
+_OFF_AFTER_ENTRY = 8931   # delta-plus group count onward
+
+
+def _good_payload():
+    return zlib.decompress(base64.b64decode(_GOOD_PAYLOAD_ZB64))
+
+
+def _assert_server_alive(env):
+    # A fresh connection: if the module panicked the process is gone and this
+    # raises, which is the failure these tests guard against.
+    env.assertTrue(env.getConnection().ping())
+

+    """https://github.com/FalkorDB/FalkorDB/issues/3031
+
+       GRAPH.RESTORE accepts a tensor section with more multi-edge id rows than
+       there are MULTI_EDGE markers (an orphan 'me' row for a pair that is not
+       multi-edge). That breaks the invariant edge_count relies on: edge_count
+       panics ('multi exceeds the effective pattern'), crashing the server on
+       the restore / next save. Expected: the load is refused and the server
+       stays up."""
+
+    def __init__(self):
+        self.env, self.db = Env()
+        self.con = self.env.getConnection()
+
+    def test01_orphan_me_row_is_rejected_not_fatal(self):
+        b = _good_payload()
+        # Bump the base group count 1 -> 2 and append a second tensor entry for a
+        # pair (7, 9) that has no MULTI_EDGE marker in the forward matrix, reusing
+        # the captured id blob. The decoder then builds an 'me' row with no
+        # backing marker.
+        self.env.assertEqual(b[_OFF_GROUP_COUNT], 4)  # UNSIGNED tag
+        self.env.assertEqual(
+            int.from_bytes(b[_OFF_GROUP_COUNT + 1:_OFF_GROUP_COUNT + 9], "little"), 1)
+        entry1 = b[_OFF_ENTRY:_OFF_AFTER_ENTRY]        # src(9)+dst(9)+blob(9+219)
+        self.env.assertEqual(entry1[0], 4)             # src UNSIGNED tag
+        self.env.assertEqual(entry1[9], 4)             # dst UNSIGNED tag
+        self.env.assertEqual(entry1[18], 0)            # blob BYTES tag
+        entry2 = (entry1[0:1] + (7).to_bytes(8, "little")
+                  + entry1[9:10] + (9).to_bytes(8, "little")
+                  + entry1[18:])
+        corrupt = (b[:_OFF_GROUP_COUNT + 1] + (2).to_bytes(8, "little")
+                   + entry1 + entry2 + b[_OFF_AFTER_ENTRY:])

+            # If the restore succeeded, a save must not panic either.
+            self.con.execute_command("GRAPH.QUERY", "orphan_me",
+                                     "MATCH ()-[e]->() RETURN count(e)")
+            raised = False
+        except (ResponseError, redis.ConnectionError) as e:
+            raised = True

+                message=f"orphan-row RESTORE must be a clean error, got {e!r}")
+        self.env.assertTrue(raised,
+            message="RESTORE of an orphan multi-edge row must be refused")
+        _assert_server_alive(self.env)

+class testIssue3266():
+    """https://github.com/FalkorDB/FalkorDB/issues/3266
+
+    A nested-list SIValue in a client GRAPH.EFFECT payload makes the v3 decoder
+    reserve memory quadratic in the payload size before it rejects it. Expected:
+    the malformed payload is refused immediately with a bounded amount of memory
+    and the server stays alive. Scaled down to a 128 KB payload: on the unfixed
+    decoder that already drives `used_memory_peak` to ~4.4 GB; the test asserts
+    the peak barely moves. Reserved address space only, so safe on the laptop.
+    """
+
+    def __init__(self):
+        self.env, self.db = Env()
+        self.conn = self.env.getConnection()
+
+    @staticmethod
+    def _payload(levels):
+        # One CREATE_NODE record with one attribute whose value is `levels`
+        # nested T_ARRAY headers; level k claims the most children the trailing
+        # bytes could hold, so every level passes the per-level width check.
+        T_ARRAY = 1 << 3
+        value = b''.join(
+            struct.pack('<II', T_ARRAY, 2 * (levels - k - 1))
+            for k in range(levels))
+        rec = struct.pack('<IIHHHI', 3, 1, 0, 1, 0, 1) + bytes([0, 0, 1])
+        return bytes([3, 0]) + rec + value
+
+    def test01_nested_list_effect_payload_is_bounded(self):
+        # 128 KB payload (16000 nested levels). On the unfixed Rust decoder this
+        # alone pushes `used_memory_peak` to ~4.4 GB before the buffer is
+        # rejected; the correct decoder — and C, which has no v3 decoder and
+        # refuses the version byte outright — reserves only a few MB.
+        levels = 16000
+        payload = self._payload(levels)
+
+        peak_before = self.conn.info("memory")["used_memory_peak"]
+
+        rejected = True
+        try:
+            self.conn.execute_command("GRAPH.EFFECT", "effbomb", payload)
+            rejected = False  # a malformed buffer must never be accepted
+        except redis.exceptions.ResponseError:
+            rejected = True
+
+        peak_after = self.conn.info("memory")["used_memory_peak"]
+        growth = peak_after - peak_before
+
+        # The server must still be answering after the payload.
+        self.env.assertTrue(self.conn.ping())
+
+        # The payload must have been refused, not accepted.
+        self.env.assertTrue(
+            rejected, message="malformed GRAPH.EFFECT payload was not refused")
+
+        # Decoding a 128 KB buffer must not spike peak memory into the GBs. A
+        # linear decoder stays well under 256 MB here; the quadratic one blows
+        # past 4 GB.
+        self.env.assertLess(
+            growth, 256 * 1024 * 1024,
+            message=f"GRAPH.EFFECT decode reserved {growth / 2**30:.2f} GB of "
+                    f"peak memory for a 128 KB payload (quadratic reservation)")
+

+class testIssue2946():
+    """https://github.com/FalkorDB/FalkorDB/issues/2946
+
+    A write whose entities are all created and cancelled in one query (e.g.
+    `CREATE (a:A {p:1}) DELETE a`) still grows the primary's schema/id space but
+    puts nothing on the replication stream. The next normal write's ADD_SCHEMA
+    is then refused on the replica and forces a full resync. Expected: the
+    replica converges with the primary and no forced resync happens. Run with
+    REPLICA=1.
+    """
+
+    def __init__(self):
+        if SANITIZER:
+            Environment.skip(None)
+        self.env, self.db = Env(env='oss', useSlaves=True)
+        self.master = self.env.getConnection()
+        self.replica = self.env.getSlaveConnection()
+        self.graph_id = "cancel_repl"
+
+    def _wait_offset(self, timeout=60):
+        target = self.master.info("replication")["master_repl_offset"]
+        deadline = time.time() + timeout
+        while time.time() < deadline:
+            if self.replica.info("replication").get("slave_repl_offset", -1) >= target:
+                return
+            time.sleep(0.01)
+        raise AssertionError("replica did not catch up to primary offset")
+
+    def test01_cancelled_write_then_next_write_does_not_diverge(self):
+        m = self.db.select_graph(self.graph_id)
+
+        full_before = self.master.info("stats")["sync_full"]
+
+        # A write whose every entity is cancelled in the same query: it still
+        # registers label A and attribute p on the primary, but replicates
+        # nothing on the unfixed build.
+        m.query("CREATE (a:A {p:1}) DELETE a")
+        # (The issue's `OPTIONAL MATCH (n:Nope) SET n:L6` schema-only variant is
+        # omitted: it crashes the C engine on a separate, unrelated C-side bug
+        # — blocked.c — which would mask the replication comparison here.)
+        # The next ordinary write carries ADD_SCHEMA for label B; on the unfixed
+        # build the replica assigns a different id and is forced to resync.
+        m.query("CREATE (:B {q:2})")
+
+        self._wait_offset()
+
+        # The replica must agree with the primary. Compare the node count only
+        # (the real divergence signal); numeric scalars come back typed
+        # differently across the two engines' raw replies.
+        res_m = m.ro_query("MATCH (n:B) RETURN count(n)").result_set
+        res_r = self.replica.execute_command(
+            "GRAPH.RO_QUERY", self.graph_id, "MATCH (n:B) RETURN count(n)")
+        # res_r is the raw reply; the rows live in res_r[1].
+        self.env.assertEqual(res_m, [[1]])
+        self.env.assertEqual(
+            res_r[1], [[1]],
+            message="replica does not have the B node the primary created "
+                    "(replication divergence)")
+
+        # No forced resync: the cancelled/schema-only writes must have been
+        # replicated, so the ADD_SCHEMA that followed lined up on the replica.
+        full_after = self.master.info("stats")["sync_full"]
+        self.env.assertEqual(
+            full_after, full_before,
+            message="a cancelled / schema-only write forced a full resync "
+                    "(replication divergence)")
+

+class testIssue3013():
+    """https://github.com/FalkorDB/FalkorDB/issues/3013
+
+    Flooding the server with more queued queries than a fixed 1024-slot channel
+    holds deadlocks it permanently: PING never answers and only a restart
+    recovers. Expected: the server completes the load (or caps it with
+    MAX_QUEUED_QUERIES) and stays responsive, matching C. Bound the hang with
+    TEST_TIMEOUT; the flood is spread over 16 graphs (<1024 writes each), the
+    variant C completes.
+    """
+
+    def __init__(self):
+        self.env, self.db = Env()
+        self.conn = self.env.getConnection()
+
+    @staticmethod
+    def _resp(*args):
+        out = f"*{len(args)}\r\n".encode()
+        for a in args:
+            a = a if isinstance(a, bytes) else a.encode()
+            out += f"${len(a)}\r\n".encode() + a + b"\r\n"
+        return out
+
+    def test01_flood_does_not_hang_the_server(self):
+        host = self.env.host or "127.0.0.1"
+        port = int(self.env.port)
+        n_queries = 1200   # > the 1024-slot pool queue
+        n_graphs = 16      # < 1024 writes per graph: the variant C completes
+        # A long-running write per query keeps every pool worker busy, so the
+        # bounded queue fills while the main thread is still dispatching — the
+        # condition the deadlock needs. Fire all of them from raw sockets
+        # without reading replies, so >1024 queries are in flight at once.
+        query = "UNWIND range(1,5000) AS x CREATE (:N)"
+
+        # The flood holds one socket per query open at once. Many shells and CI
+        # runners default to a soft limit of 1024 descriptors, which would make
+        # the client fail with EMFILE before the flood is ever sent.
+        soft, hard = resource.getrlimit(resource.RLIMIT_NOFILE)
+        need = n_queries + 256
+        if soft != resource.RLIM_INFINITY and soft < need:
+            if hard != resource.RLIM_INFINITY and hard < need:
+                self.env.skip()
+            resource.setrlimit(resource.RLIMIT_NOFILE, (need, hard))
+
+        socks = []
+        try:
+            for _ in range(n_queries):
+                s = socket.socket()
+                s.settimeout(30)
+                s.connect((host, port))
+                socks.append(s)
+            for i, s in enumerate(socks):
+                s.sendall(self._resp("GRAPH.QUERY", f"flood_{i % n_graphs}", query))
+
+            # The deadlock shows up as the Redis main thread never answering
+            # again: a fresh PING on its own connection times out. Poll for a

+        .iter()
+        .map(|&r| i32::try_from(r).ok())
